text.en: The Rav reads the Rambam's limit as a matter of choice: a bad sign is only where a person had no choice, and only the first night of Sukkos obliges him to eat in the sukkah.
Leaving the sukkah for rain does not end one's dwelling there, just as a man's home address does not change when he steps out; therefore the exemption of one who suffers fits the mitzvah of dwelling.
An eruv is fixed for one day by placing a meal, but the sukkah must be fixed as a home for seven days, which needs an actual eating on the first night; this is why the kezayis is learned from matzah.

Tishrei is the yearly rebuilding of Chava for Adam: Rosh Hashanah as back to back, the shofar breaking through judgment, Yom Kippur as the separation, the sukkah as chuppah, and Shemini Atzeres as 'He brought her to the man'.
The Rav applies the Ramban's rule, that what comes from love carries a lighter punishment, to explain why a nesuah is punished by strangling while an arusah is stoned.
The missing heh in the Torah's word for a young woman points to what she lacks until nisuin, when she receives the heh and is raised to be one with her husband.
The breaking of the luchos at the end of the Torah is joined to its first word, Bereishis, which holds everything like a seed; so a broken Sukkos becomes a new beginning.

Cheshvan's combination of Hashem's Name is the only one drawn across two pesukim, from 'u'dvash' that ends a passage into 'hayom hazeh' that opens a new one, teaching that the honey of Tishrei must be carried over into the month of decay.
'Av HaRachaman', the merciful Father, has the gematria of 'dvash', honey, 306: in Tishrei Hashem appears to us as sweetness.

Every person governs his own portion of creation; Noach's portion was the animals that came into the Teivah, which stayed pure amid a corrupt world, and geographically Eretz Yisrael, where no Mabul fell.
The Teivah, built with halachos to exact dimensions like the Mishkan, was not a ship but a place of kedushah, an embassy of heaven on earth, and so the Mabul's law of destruction did not apply to it.

Life in food is the word of Hashem; the purer a creature, the more it extracts from less, so the tzaddik eats little and the sheep lives on grass, while the cruel lion must eat concentrated food, meat.
The lion's attack on Noach was a result of Cham's sin, which repeated Adam's sin inside the Teivah, brought back the curse and made the lion need meat again.
Hashem makes three tries: the worlds of Adam and of Noach were spoiled, and the third world, like the third Beis HaMikdash, will be perfect.

The Rav explains that the emunah of Yidden is not a sign of weak intellect, as with the fool who believes everything, but of its height: some matters are above the mind, and wise believers accept them, so that this emunah draws down wisdom.
Because time was created from the Torah and the Torah is above time, the parsha that speaks of the beginning of time is a higher court where the decrees of Rosh Hashanah can be appealed.
The Torah ends with 'Yisrael' and begins with 'Bereishis', which the Rav connects to the letters of the Torah and the souls of Yisrael being one.
The greatest treasury above, of matnas chinam, is open only to one who truly feels he deserves nothing; this is how the Rav reads Noach finding chen when he too was meant to be erased.
The Rav explains that Avner was hinted only in the middle letters of the passuk because the erasure of a Jew can only be temporary; at his root he remains connected.
The first parsha cannot end with destruction, so it ends with 'v'Noach matza chen', a tikkun; and Noach's chen, unlike the generation of the flood's, was found in Shabbos, Torah and tefillah.

Following the Yismach Moshe, a promise made with the Name Havaya cannot be held back by sin, so the redemption must come with open miracles like Yetzias Mitzrayim, and this is the point of joining the Torah's end to Bereishis.

Since the Torah is the blueprint of the world, the first time a thing appears in it defines it; the first 'ezer', Chava, was given to Adam only after all his efforts failed and he slept, so help by its nature comes without human action, an exercise in bitul.

The Gemara's laws of sukkah focus on sleeping rather than eating, because sleep is the essence of the sukkah: only one who feels secure can sleep, and the sukkah is a flimsy hut under Hashem's protection.
Nature is itself a Torah: a bird flying fulfills a command of the Torah just as a Jew putting on tefillin does, the only difference being that man has free choice.

Because nature is written in the Torah, a miracle that changes nature changes the Torah, which is why the Gemara criticizes the man for whom nature was changed and why tzaddikim avoided making miracles.

Creation keeps its Torah only when man keeps his: in the generation of the flood even the animals strayed from their kinds, while in the generation of the desert nature flourished so that one cluster of grapes needed eight men.

Bereishis is a history of three strikes against mankind, Adam, the flood and the dispersion, after which the keys of creation passed to Avraham, and even then the nations were given a last chance at Sinai.

The nations' claim to Eretz Yisrael, unlike any other land taken by conquest, comes from its being the center and root of creation, which even its name, the Mediterranean, 'middle of the land', reflects.

The flood and Matan Torah were the same downpour: the nations rightly sensed the signs of the flood at Sinai, but what came in Noach's time as the outer shell, destruction, came at Sinai as its inner content, Torah.
Moshe's 'erase me' on behalf of his generation repaired Noach's failure to daven for his; the flood is called 'the waters of Noach' because of that failure.
The shin on the head tefillin, three-headed and four-headed and numbering 300, expresses the threefold quality of Torah that makes it lasting, the opposite of the flood.
The sukkah is an embassy of heaven on earth: one who sits in it is legally 'not in this world', so judgment against the world cannot reach him, just as tumah cannot remain in a mikveh.
The mazalos stopped during the flood because a single bright day whose mazal brings kindness could have broken a decree of destruction for a fixed time.

Moshe's teiva and Noach's teiva are one theme: the first gilgul was saved from the flood by a teiva, the second by a teiva and the daughter of Pharaoh, who corresponds to the 'bas malka' present in every word of Torah and tefillah.

The 'ach' of 'only Noach remained' carries a double message: Rashi reads it as Noach's injury from the lion, and the Rav adds that the verse no longer calls him tzaddik, because Cham's sin had affected him.
The animals that came to the Teva were the 'tzaddikim' of the animal world: they belonged to Noach's portion of creation, which his righteousness kept from corruption.

The Rav reconciles the Ibn Ezra and Chazal on the lion's food: in the Teva's pure society the lion could live on straw, as before Adam's sin and in the days of Moshiach, and only after Cham's sin did it need meat.
The more physical a being is, the more concentrated food it needs; a lion's one meal of meat equals a week of a cow's grazing, so a world fallen from its purity needs meat.
Noach's drinking is read as a mistake about the times: he thought the era of Moshiach had come, when one can drink a great cup of wine without becoming drunk, like the cup of Eliyahu at the Seder.
The parsha is built like a headline: its opening verses already say that Noach was saved only by grace, and it moves from Noach to Avraham Avinu, in whose merit the world survived.

Hashem's praise of Noach was not a compliment but chizuk: Hashem judges a person against what he could have been without his generation's obstacles, so Noach, who felt small beside earlier generations, was told he is a tzaddik in this generation.
The two readings of "in his generations", for praise and for discredit, say the same thing; the discredit is not Noach's but his generation's, which kept him from reaching Avraham's level.
The form of the word "Nefilim", like "mazik" or "chasid", describes one who not only falls but makes others fall, which is how the angels who fell polluted the atmosphere of the flood generation.
The lulav's na'anuim draw down Hashem's Name and bring it back to the chest, teaching that the knowledge of Hashem's presence must move from the mind into the heart so it remains after Sukkos.
One attached to Torah carries the sukkah within himself all year, as the Yismach Moshe was told that Gan Eden is in the Tanna; this is the inner meaning of Marcheshvan.

The raven's refusal was a lesson to Noach: it was reserved for Eliyahu, the herald of redemption, so one must wait for Hashem to send the salvation, just as the Jews did not flee Egypt during the darkness.
Unlike Avraham, who needed no support and was praised for humility, today's generation needs chizuk, so each Jew must hear "ki oscha ra'isi tzaddik" as said to him.
The Rav reads 'mecheini' as containing 'mei Noach': Moshe's readiness to be erased for Klal Yisrael was the tikkun of the waters named for Noach.
Mesiras nefesh for a generation means including oneself in it, saying 'I am one of them'; this is why Moshe broke the luchos, to declare that he too had sinned.
Avraham was not permitted mesiras nefesh in Canaan because Hashem's promise of a great nation depended on him, so Hashem revealed Sodom's fate to him in order that he pray instead.
Kayin's 'Am I my brother's keeper?' is read as true words of teshuvah: Hashem, who created the yetzer hara, is the only true guard against it.
The Gemara learns 'adam hamazik' from a verse about asking and repenting, because man's defining trait as a damager is his ability to make a tikkun.
An owner's liability for his ox reflects that his property extends his soul: the goring comes from his own middos, not from heaven.
The same 'inclination of man's heart is evil' that justified the flood became, after Noach's admission of helplessness, the ground for Hashem's promise never to flood the world again.

The Rav locates the Flood generation's worst sin not in committing evil but in legalizing it: when sin becomes written law and culture, people no longer feel shame, which is far worse than a private yetzer hara.

The animals that entered the ark and Eretz Yisrael were spared because they were Noach's portion of creation, which did not sin since he did not; Noach is Shabbos, and Eretz Yisrael is the 'Shabbos' of the lands.

The forty days and nights of the Flood's rain were the outer form of the Torah that was due to descend in Noach's time; at Matan Torah, under the same heavenly configuration, the same forty days brought down its inner treasure instead.

Moshe Rabbeinu was a reincarnation of Noach: Noach's failure to pray for his generation, for which the Flood is called 'mei Noach', was repaired when Moshe said 'erase me from Your book' for his people.

The teivah is the sukkah of Parshas Noach: just as a sukkah protects not by its wood but by the halachos that are names of Hashem, the ark's measurements are themselves Hashem's name, so learning the parsha extends Tishrei's protection.

Shimon HaTzaddik, as the last of the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, told a frightened generation that the world does not stand on the Knesses HaGedolah but on Torah, avodah and gemilus chasadim; the Rav applies this to a generation left without its great tzaddikim.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov as explained by Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, 'tzohar ta'aseh lateivah' means: make each word of Torah and tefillah luminous, for today's world is a flood and only a lit-up 'teivah' saves.
The Rav compares the Jew's belief in Hashem to the inherited knowledge of the beaver and the spider: it is not learned but part of his organism, and with Avraham a species carrying this trait began.

Since Avraham was not a continuation of mankind from Adam and Noach, he and Sarah needed a newly created power to have children, and he was told he need not honor his father, as he was not truly his father.
The man of Bereishis belongs in the land of Bereishis: Eretz Yisrael, the place from which the globe developed, is the natural home of the first Jew.
Hashem's first words to Avraham, the attribute of chesed, were a positive command to go to the land, while His first words to Yitzchak, the attribute of din, were a prohibition against leaving it.
Applying the Maharal on Moshe's parents, the Rav explains that the Torah omits Avraham's merits because the Jewish nation's existence is a necessity, not a reward.

The Rav reads the Ramban's harsh judgment of Avraham as deliberate: by showing at the outset that Avraham could sin and still be chosen, it teaches that the Jewish nation does not rest on anyone's righteousness.
Avraham's descent to Mitzrayim and Sarah's steadfastness in Pharaoh's house prepared the purity that kept the Jewish women holy in Mitzrayim.

The difference in the Torah's wording of the two missions follows the birds' natures: the raven, a taker, would come back to Noach until the land was fully dry, so its return could only signal dryness; the dove, a giver, would stop returning as soon as it found any food, even bitter, so its mission could only test whether the water had lessened.

The same verse, 'for the inclination of man's heart is evil', appears as the reason for the flood and for never bringing another flood, because Noach's korban reached the root where a reason for judgment becomes a reason for mercy, just as a deeper look in a sugya can turn the same sevara from chayav to patur.

A unanimous conviction acquits because the sages, who usually see Torah colored by their own soul's channel, all agreeing shows they reached the colorless root of Torah, where even a reason to convict can be turned to acquittal.

Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that chametz is removed only by burning reflects his root as a gilgul of Yehuda, the yud of Shem Havaya and the element of fire: he wants evil uprooted from its root, and that is why he gives simanim for the makos, to reach the root and draw down healing for Israel.

The mikveh's forty se'ah are Shem Havaya: four letters in plain spelling and ten in full spelling, like the reshus hayachid of Shabbos that is four wide and ten high, so whoever immerses enters the Name itself.

Breathing stops underwater, which the Rav connects to the verse about all that has the breath of life perishing in the flood: in the mikveh a person's earthly life is suspended and he comes out like one revived, a new person.

Noach's teivah, the sukkah and the mikveh are all built from halachos, and halachos are holy names; that is why the teivah's dimensions follow Shem Havaya, and why Haman's beam taken from the teivah fulfilled 'Hashem's war with Amalek'.

The Rav explains that decay entered the world through the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, a breach of bris, so wherever bris is kept nothing spoils: the ark's food, Yosef's grain, the bodies of tzaddikim.
According to the Rav, every person owns a portion of creation that his sins spoil; Noach's animals and his land, Eretz Yisrael, had not sinned, which is why the flood did not fall there.
The Rav holds that the lion in the ark ate straw as in the world of tikkun, so Noach brought no meat at all, and the Ibn Ezra's question about carnivores never arises.
The Rav explains the lion's blow: after Cham's sin the lion suddenly needed meat, Noach had none, the straw came too late, and Hashem no longer made miracles for creatures that had sinned.

He reads the two descriptions of Noach as two moments: 'tzaddik in this generation' is Hashem's word before the flood, when the world was to restart from Noach, while 'tzaddik tamim in his generations', written later by Moshe, points to Avraham.
The Rav sees Tishrei as a Jew's personal world of tikkun and Cheshvan as its flood, and following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the ark he must enter is the words of Torah and tefillah.
He points out that the same evil inclination that brought the flood became the reason for the promise of no more flood, showing a Jew's power to turn things around.
The 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu, read before Rosh Hashanah, match the 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah, and each parsha's count matches one stage of teshuvah.

The Mabul was the 'envelope' of Torah without its contents; Matan Torah was the same flood returning with its inner Torah, which is why the nations feared a Mabul, and 'oz' is linked to 'mabul' by gematria.
Noach was 'mi'ketanei amanah' because at first the rain was gishmei brachah with Torah inside it, and he saw that Torah; only later did it become an empty mabul.
Building the teivah for 120 years was itself the way Noach drew teshuvah into the world, since the teivah, like a sukkah and a mikveh, is built of holy names and comes from Binah.
Those in the teivah did not want to leave because they felt its holiness, like the 'people of the sukkah', which is why Hashem had to tell Noach 'go out of the teivah'.
The world's autumn, the month called 'Bul' from 'mabul', when everything withers, is the spring of Klal Yisroel, since Parshas Noach ends with the birth of Avraham Avinu.
Rebbi's refusal to curse a king dead for centuries shows that learning a passage is not reading history: the learner is lifted into that era, where Nebuchadnezzar is still a living king.
Like the Aron that took no space, Torah came from heaven where measurement does not apply, and so it carries the learner beyond space and time.

Lechem is three times the simple Shem Havayah while matzah is three times its milui, the same value as adam, so the passuk that man lives not by bread alone points to a higher level reached through matzah.
Sefer Bereishis is Torah too sublime to be reduced to halachos about physical objects; its 'objects' are the Avos themselves, which is why it is learned by accompanying them.
The Torah leaves out Moshe's parents at his birth and Avraham's righteousness at his calling to teach that the Jewish people did not come by merit or chance but because creation itself required them.
The Ramban, who knew the Zohar's answers, deliberately opens Avraham's story with his faults so no one would think he was chosen for his tzidkus.

The lion's attack on Noach was not a lapse in Hashem's help but the result of Cham's sin: once the ark's world was damaged, Hashem no longer gave special help to its sinful inhabitants, and the flaw reached Noach himself.
Noach's drinking was a mistake about the time: he thought the world of the ark was already the renewed world, when wine may be drunk freely, as it will be when Eliyahu comes.

Bilaam's answer at Matan Torah means that the Torah was the inner content of the flood: the same flood that came down as empty water in Noach's time came down at Sinai as Torah, a 'mabul' with a shin, hinted in 'bashalom'.
The halachic measurements of the ark, like those of the sukkah, are what make it a vessel for the holy names that place it outside this world, so that judgment cannot reach whoever is inside.
Bar Daroma could have been Moshiach, and his failure came from the generation's reliance on his strength; the snake that killed him is the power that makes Jews forget that Hashem runs the world.
Noach was reborn as Moshe: having failed to daven for his generation, as Moshe he gave himself for Klal Yisrael and gave the Torah that the generation of the flood was meant to receive.
Noach planted his vineyard to make kiddush and drink Eliyahu's cup of the rectified world; instead he became drunk, and 'vayishkar' equals 'kos shel Eliyahu Hanavi' in gematria.
Noach chose the raven on purpose: as one of the sinners in the ark, sending it on a mitzvah mission on Shabbos might repair it and with it the whole sin, but its repair had to wait for Eliyahu.
The lion bit Noach because the ark had been a rectified world where a lion lives on straw; once the sin ruined it, the lion could no longer be satisfied by straw and Noach lost his heavenly help.
Moshe Rabbeinu was a gilgul of Noach, and his 'mecheini na' contains 'mei Noach': by giving himself up in prayer for Klal Yisrael he repaired Noach's failure to pray for his generation.
In a dark generation of hester panim, a Jew who still turns to Hashem in prayer makes his emunah shine more than that of earlier, greater generations.
Birds sing in the morning ('tzafra') and insects at night ('ramsha'), each at its time, but a Jew sings 'tzafra veramsha', with no limit on when he may turn to Hashem.
Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz explained the Ba'al Shem Tov: today's world is a flood, and just as the teivah saved Noach, the 'teivah', the word of prayer, shelters a Jew from drowning.
The Rav reads the debate between Yitzchak and Yishmael over Milah as the first seed of the war being fought between Yishmael and the Jews today.
'Pere adam' puts the wildness as the noun and 'adam' as the description: Yishmael is wild in essence and only looks like a man, so his education or profession does not change him.
Loving chicken is really loving oneself; true essential love, like a father's for his son, does not rest on any benefit.
Avraham's first test, the fire, was self-sacrifice for his life's ideal; the Akedah demanded sacrificing that very ideal, which is why without it the other tests would lack their value.
Milah at eight days and the Akedah are one idea: a Jew's bond to Hashem does not need understanding, so an infant's Milah is equal to an adult's.
Recalling the Bris and the Akedah when asking for mercy asks Hashem to respond from a bond beyond reason, even when Jews do not deserve it.
The melave malka belongs to David HaMelech because it alone nourishes the luz bone, untouched by Adam's sin, and David, the tikkun of Adam, is 'chai vekayam'; hence its link to techiyas hameisim.
Sefer Bereishis tells of the creation of the point of Klal Yisrael in the Avos, and Sefer Shemos of its spreading out into the twelve tribes, each with his own strength.

Since the Torah gives no reason for Avraham's choosing, his point comes from the Divine will alone, and therefore it cannot be lost through a person's choices; milah at eight days, done without the child's consent, expresses this.
Shabbos, fixed by Hashem's will and not dependent on beis din, is a day of will like the point of Avraham, which does not depend on anything a person does.
The maftir, an eighth aliyah that rereads what was already read, reflects techiyas hameisim and the eighth level of Moshiach, which is why it is followed by the berachah of 'Magen David'.
The vav before 'Tidal' hints that joining is the essence of Edom, the present exile, whose kiss is worse than a bite.
The Haggadah proves Yaakov came only to sojourn from his sons' words to Pharaoh, because Yaakov's way to avoid sinking in Egypt was to have them declare openly that they did not belong there.

Learning Torah about Eretz Yisrael is not like reading a description of a food one has never tasted: because the Torah is Toras chaim and comes from the same root as the land, the learning itself gives the taste and the bond.
Eretz Yisrael is small only to one who measures it as real estate; like a diamond, whose value is not in its size, it is the land for whose sake the world and the Torah were made.

The true 'tziyunim' of the pasuk 'set up signposts' are not those who live in the land without the Torah, but the Jews who keep the Torah in chutz laaretz; calling others by that name is a misuse of the word.

The Mishnah of the shomrim may say 'hen' (they are), but the avos nezikin cannot carry a word of being, because they stand against Hashem's Name and have no permanence; that is also why a Mishnah about them can be 'not upheld'.

The quarrel between the shepherds of Avraham and of Lot was not a by-product of the surrounding strife but a protective hatred Hashem placed between the followers of a tzaddik and a rasha, so the tzaddik would not be harmed by bad company.

Tidal 'king of nations' is Edom, which unlike the other kingdoms is a mixture of all nations; Edom's last tactic, like Esav's kiss, is to harm through friendship and joining rather than through the bite.

Each episode of the parsha, from Lot through the money of Sedom and Yishmael to milah, is one more stage of the single program of 'Lech lecha': cutting away what is not oneself to reach the pure root.
Greater praise of Hashem than the creation of heaven and earth is that men like Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov came into His world; this is why the first bracha calls Him the G-d of the Avos.
Terach could hand Avraham over to be killed because, as the Maharal explains, Avraham was a new creation with no true bond to his father; a father's instinctive mercy did not apply.
The Jewish body itself is different from the gentile body, like Shabbos, which outwardly looks like any weekday yet is another world.
Noach's covenant is a sign in the heavens, asking mankind to look up and forget the body; Avraham's is in the flesh, because the Jewish task is to make holiness shine in the body.
Avraham feared because the first promise of 'seed' could mean disciples, children of the soul, which Eliezer already fulfilled; so Hashem specified children 'from your innards'.
The Asher Yatzar bracha shows that the functioning of the lowest organs is spoken of before the Kisei HaKavod, so high is the Jewish body.
The Sanhedrin needs dayanim of yichus and fathers of children because mercy in judgment is a bodily middah passed down from the Avos.

Avraham's mention of Eliezer, who drew from his Torah and gave it to others, is part of his complaint: he already had a spiritual child to spread Hashem's name, but what he lacked was a biological child, since good midos pass only through the body.

Following the Derashos HaRan, the word 'na' made the Akeidah a request Avraham could have declined; since a tzaddik prays when a decree falls on others, he could have prayed for the sake of Klal Yisrael's midos.

Avraham's loss of his madreigos and his seeing the place 'from afar' at the Akeidah is the pattern of the hester panim of the last generation before Moshiach, so his conduct then would be duplicated in his children's last test.

The Akeidah stood at the three beginnings: Avraham the beginning of the souls of Yisrael, Har HaMoriah the beginning of place, and Yom Kippur, which Yechezkel calls Rosh Hashanah, the beginning of time; from there it reaches the furthest place, the last time and the last souls.
The words 'asher ahavta' did not just describe Avraham's love; they created in him a love for Yitzchak above natural parental love, and that created love is what he had to set aside.
Avraham chose emunah over midos, and when Yitzchak was spared he was granted both, which is why Jews today are both merciful, modest and kind and believers the children of believers.
Hashem's affectionate 'Avraham, Avraham' is heard today by every Jew with mesiras nefesh for Torah, emunah and chinuch, as heirs of Avraham's test.
The Rav reads lech lecha as 'go to yourself': to one's own soul and root, since everything around a person is only a garment of this world; the same words open and close Avraham's trials.
Lot, who tagged along with Avraham, represents Avraham's bad side: even when a servant of Hashem leaves the wicked, a part of the bad drags along with him.
Avraham was not made the first Jew because he was a tzaddik; rather, the world needed a first Jew, and he is a tzaddik because he is the root of all the tzaddikim of Klal Yisrael.

Canaan was given Eretz Yisrael precisely because he was cursed to be a servant: a servant can hold his master's land until the master comes, and the Rav applies the same reasoning to Yishmael, son of Hagar, Sarah's maidservant.
Og was named after the matzos because his report, though meant for evil, saved the sparks of Moshiach in Lot's family, and matzah carries the power of every redemption.

Og's height of nine amos and width of four amos correspond, according to the Rav, to the letters of Hashem's Name, showing how high he reached and therefore how great a kiddush Hashem his downfall was.
The lowest generation is like the heels: the lowest part of the body, yet the whole body stands on them, so all the generations stand on ours and Moshiach comes specifically to it.
The generation that is the foundation of all generations is tested in emunah, the foundation of all mitzvos.
The Satan obstructs exactly the mitzvah a generation was created to fulfil: tzitzis in the Divrei Chaim's time, emunah in ours.
Fighting doubts is like a fly in a spider's web: the more it struggles to tear itself free, the more it is stuck, so doubts must be dismissed rather than debated.
Just as the geulah of Klal Yisroel has a fixed time but can be hastened by merit, each Jew has a private geulah from his trials that prayer and mesiras nefesh can bring sooner.
Amalek is numerically equal to 'safek' (doubt), so struggling against doubts in emunah is itself the mitzvah of the war against Amalek.
Torah is the mind and tefillah the heart, the two chief organs; one without the other is not enough.

The feminine 'merivah' in Avraham's words, against the masculine 'riv' of the narrative, shows that between Avraham and Lot there was only a weak, small dispute, while among the shepherds it became a forceful quarrel.
The Rav reads the dispute between Avraham and Lot as a halachic question: whether Hashem's promise of the land to Avraham had already taken effect or would only take effect later.
Rabbi Zechariah and the Chachamim did not disagree in halachah but in assessing the situation: whether offering a blemished animal would lead people to a false halachah.
Avraham's change from zealotry in Ur Kasdim to peace in Eretz Yisrael followed from his mission: once promised a following, he was no longer allowed to risk his life, because his students needed him.
The vav that the Midrash says belongs to Tidal's name is a 'vav of joining': the fourth kingdom torments the Jews by joining with them, as Esav bit Yaakov with a kiss.
Unlike the earlier kingdoms, each of which was one nation, the fourth kingdom, 'Tidal king of nations', is many peoples united under one church with one policy toward the Jews.
Because both Rosh Hashanah Torah readings fall in Parshas Vayera, the Rav calls this Shabbos a rerun of Rosh Hashanah and a renewed time of pekidas akaros.
A man with twelve children can still be called barren if his Torah produces no chiddushim, for Torah is in a sense his wife.
The Rav suggests a new reading of 'asher asah': the calf was made with Sefer Yetzirah, so it was not meat and serving it with milk posed no problem.
A calf made with Sefer Yetzirah is not halachically meat, since it does not descend from the first animals Hashem created, unlike a clone, which comes from an animal.
The angel revealed the Me'aras HaMachpelah at the very moment of Avraham's self-sacrifice for his guests, to show that Chava's future claim of discomfort was already answered measure for measure.
Chazal knew that the service of the heart is tefillah because man is a small world: his heart corresponds to Yerushalayim, and Yerushalayim is the house of prayer.
As Yerushalayim is the heart of the world, the blessing of the avos is the heart of tefillah and of the Jewish people, which is why it alone requires kavanah.
The Torah hides Avraham's righteousness, as it first leaves Moshe's parents unnamed, to show that the Jewish people's existence did not depend on any individual's merit.
The Ramban's charge that Avraham sinned is itself praise: he was chosen despite a sin at the very start of his story, since a Jew's sin is only incidental.
Korbanos and teshuvah help a Jew because his sin is like dirt that washes off, while in a non-Jew a sin is part of his essence; this is how the korbanos answer Avraham's question 'how will I know'.
Rebbi did not curse Nebuchadnezzar when learning Yirmiyahu because Torah study carries the learner into the time of the text, when Nebuchadnezzar was still a reigning king.

The animals saved in the ark were those under Noach's share of creation: since each person's part of the world follows his deeds, Noach's righteousness kept his part pure, and Eretz Yisrael, also his share, was not flooded.
The Torah differs from other history books in that it tells not what happened but what is going to happen, so the fulfillment of its prophecies proves the coming of the end as well.

The Torah deliberately hides the merits behind the great turning points, Moshe's parents and Avraham's self-sacrifice in Ur Kasdim, so that no one should think the Jewish people came about by chance merit; it had to come from somewhere regardless.
The Ramban opens Avraham's story with his sin precisely to stress that Avraham's coming did not depend on his merits; the purpose of creation required him.

The war of the four kings was a war against Moshiach: they captured Lot because Moshiach was to descend from him, and Avraham's victory over them foreshadows the Jews passing successfully through the four exiles.
Esav's kiss was another form of his bite, and the exile of Edom, after failing to destroy the Jews by force, succeeds more by embracing them.

The Rav reads Adam and Chava's objection as a real claim of fairness: as the first owners of the cave they were entitled to privacy, like the halacha that a neighbor may demand a fence against being looked at.
Measure for measure in the law of fairness itself: one who sets aside his own comfort for guests loses the protection of others' comfort, so Avraham's hospitality is what opened the cave to him.
Taking Adam 'by the hand' means overcoming him with chesed, since in Chazal's language 'hand' stands for the attribute of chesed.
'Avraham will become a great nation' is the reason for revealing Sedom: a person who will leave behind a people serving Hashem has the status of the many, and his prayer works even after the decree.
In the name of the Yitav Lev: no prayer is lost. Avraham's unanswered prayer for Sedom was kept in reserve for his children, for in an emergency there is no time to start davening.
'We have a little sister and she has no breasts' describes a generation without mashpi'im, which must live on the remnants the great ones of the past left behind.
The Rav links the 600,000 Shabbosos of the world's history to the 600,000 souls of Israel and the 600,000 letters of the Torah: just as every soul is unique, no Shabbos ever repeats.
What the sedra describes happens again spiritually that week: on Shabbos Vayera Hashem visits a sick generation as He visited Avraham on the third day after his milah.
Because both Rosh Hashanah readings are in Vayera, this Shabbos carries something of Rosh Hashanah, and one who feels his Rosh Hashanah was lacking can complete it then.
The proof of Avraham's simcha is that he walked at the same pace as Yitzchak, who did not know, and that he returned 'together' as if he had done nothing special.
Yitzchak's milah at eight days was not a loss of a chance for devotion: it shows that a Jew is a Jew by birth, beyond choice, while Yishmael's devotion is only a matter of the mind, like tefillin.
The Rambam's explanation of coerced consent shows that a Jew's true will is always to do Hashem's will; the flogging only subdues the body from which the yetzer hara comes.
Mesiras nefesh of whole communities without exception is explained by intrinsic love, which needs no reason, as opposed to devotion that must be trained and indoctrinated.

The Rav links three generations as one group of souls: the builders of the Tower who wanted 'a name' became Sedom, and the survivors of Tzoar became Korach's 'anshei shem', each return carrying the unpaid account of the last.
Through the Chasam Sofer, 'G-d of all flesh' is read as G-d of the body and not only of the soul: a reincarnated soul's sin is not a reason to make the new, innocent body suffer.

The Rav distinguishes repairing a blemish from being punished for it: a tzaddik or baal teshuvah may still need to mend an old pegam, yet he is a new person before Hashem and his body does not suffer for the old sin.

'Elokei Avraham' is itself the malchus of the first bracha of Shemoneh Esrei, which does not say 'Melech ha'olam', because Hashem's kingship is shown by His having a tzaddik like Avraham in the world.

Avraham's chesed was mesirus nefesh precisely because it went to those he had most reason to reject: he, who understood better than anyone how to despise idolatry, served idolaters, and he prayed for Sedom, who would have lynched him.
Following the Lubliner Rav, Onkelos's rendering of Avraham's words to Sarah came from his own life: as a convert he felt, as Avraham did, the chesed of being taken out of idolatry.

The Akeidah and Yishmael's expulsion are one test: Avraham, the embodiment of chesed, had to act with gevurah against his own nature, and according to the Ran he did so when it was only a request, not a command.

Rebbi cursed Nevuchadnetzar only when reading the Megillah and not while learning a passage where he was alive, showing that learning Torah places a person in the very time of the events, not in a history book.
Each year's shofar thins the partition holding back Moshiach, so even after thousands of years the Satan is more frightened than before (in the name of the Satmar Rav).
Moshiach's root is hidden in the most shameful origin, Moav, born of Lot's daughters, so that the forces of impurity should never think to look for it there.

The successive sealings, Yom Kippur, Hoshana Rabbah and Chanukah, were revealed one after another as the generations weakened: fasting for the great, joy for the weaker, and simple routine for the generation of ikvesa d'meshicha.
The first quarter of the year, from 25 Elul to 25 Kislev, is like infancy that does not yet count, and likewise a person's first twenty years are his time before the seal.
'He saw the place from afar' means Avraham went to the Akeidah without feeling, and this last test of Avraham corresponds to the last generation before Moshiach, which serves without emotion.
The missing vav in Eliezer's retelling marks the moment his hidden interest surfaced: only once Rivka was certain to marry Yitzchak could he see that 'perhaps' had meant 'to me'.
Theories about how the world works are like guessing at a watch's mechanism while the watchmaker's own book lies in the library: the Creator wrote the Chumash.
In Lashon HaKodesh a verb ending in nun loses it as a noun, so aman, to believe, becomes em, mother, showing that emunah comes from the mother.
Trying to grasp G-d with the mind is like trying to hear a painting: the failure is not weakness of the organ but using the wrong sense altogether.
Sins act like insulation on a live wire, cutting the mind off from the neshamah's contact with G-d; a tzaddik still feels some of the current, to the degree of his righteousness.
Ein Keloheinu is said before Mi Keloheinu so that the answer comes before the question, since even a moment of entertaining the question without the answer is a departure from emunah.
Chanamel's sale was a plan to keep the fruits of his field by trusting in Yirmiyahu's righteousness, but Yirmiyahu, knowing he was Shlomo's gilgul who caused the churban, took it as mockery.
'I am the G-d of all flesh' teaches that a reincarnated soul pays its old debt, but the new body is judged on its own and can be a tzaddik.
Korach's threat 'will you gouge out the eyes of these men' reveals that his men had once been the people of Sodom, who were struck with blindness.

Since only two cities may be burned as an ir hanidachas, Admah and Tzevoim were only overturned, and their remaining judgment of burning was carried out in Korach's eidah, which was both swallowed and burned.
Lot's living in a cave was a way of fulfilling the decree of Sodom in a mild form, the way going into the sukkah can stand in for a decree of galus.
Avraham had the water brought by a messenger because washing off the guests' idolatrous dust himself would have shamed them; his hatred of avodah zarah yielded to his chesed.
The same 'vayashkem Avraham baboker' appears when he sent away Yishmael and when he went to the akeidah, showing that his chesed was avodas Hashem and he could act against it when Hashem wished.

The Rav reads the Ba'al Shem Tov as saying that immorality is the finest middah, chesed, the very middah with which Hashem created the world, spent on base things; this is why the Torah calls it 'chesed'.

The right tefillin strap is longer than the left because din must be shorter and chesed dominant, and even a sofer writing right to left draws the base of a letter from left to right, mixing in some din.

The Jewish leap year, which aligns the lunar year with the solar seasons, expresses the blend of chesed (the white moon) with din (the red sun), while the Arabs' purely lunar calendar reflects unblended chesed.
Yitzchak, pure din, never has a sidra alone, while Bereishis opens with Avraham alone and ends with Yaakov alone, since pure din is not allowed to stand by itself.

Sodom's condemnation lay in combining opposite extremes: cruelty alone could be excused as a nature of din and immorality alone as an excess of love, but both together reveal a deliberate rebellion against Hashem.

Since Eretz Yisrael is tied to the 'bris esh' of milah and esh is the first of the four elements, giving the land to Yishmael also gave his descendants the element of fire, energy, which the Rav sees in their control of the world's oil.
Yishmael's expulsion comes immediately after Yitzchak's milah: once a true milah appears, the imitation is darkened, a sign for the future of Yishmael's hold on the land.
The word nisayon is read as raising up: a test is like a child's exam for promotion, and the tenth test was Avraham's 'graduation'.
For a prophet who sees Hashem, obeying is easy; the real test was a command that seemed to contradict Hashem's own promise.
The answer to Avraham's question was so simple a child could give it; the point of a test is that the answer is hidden, and when Moshiach comes history's questions will have equally simple answers.
The last generation corresponds to the heels of Adam's body: just as a prick in the heel is hardly felt, these souls barely feel Hashem, and that is why emunah is their test.
Avraham's mesirus nefesh at the Akeidah went against his own life's ideal, and so proved retroactively that his nine earlier sacrifices were not for an ideal or for honor.
Small acts of going beyond one's habit each count as a little mesirus nefesh, and they add up to a great sum, the Jewish answer to Yishmael's boasting of self-sacrifice.
Shidduchim are where Hashem briefly shows Himself as the One who runs the world, and from that open case one may make a hekesh, an inference, to all the hidden ones.

Cleopatra's question 'what does Hashem do since creation' reflects the view that He made the world like a tape recorder that runs without its maker; the answer 'He makes matches' points to the area where that view visibly fails.
Since Hashem makes the shidduch but will not say a lie, the shadchan's fee is payment for the lie he tells, which explains Rabbi Yaakov Emden's seemingly jesting words.
The lie in a shidduch is the Satan's portion, like the se'ir la'azazel and the goat hairs left sticking out of the tefillin: with the greatest mitzvos he is given something so he will not spoil them.
Eliezer's name is absent from the whole parsha of the shidduch because that shidduch needed no lie and no shadchan; Hashem made it, and Eliezer was only Avraham's messenger.
Eliezer withheld gifts from Besuel because he knew by ruach hakodesh that Besuel would die that night, and did not want to be blamed for poisoning him.

The Rav reasons that just as Kiryas Sefer held the three thousand forgotten halachos, so Chevron and the Machpela correspond to the parsha and halachos of milah, and this is why Mamre, the owner of Chevron, was the one who advised Avraham on milah.

According to the Rav, 'kings shall come from you' ends the parsha of milah and was said in Chevron, David became king in Chevron, and the Torah first calls Avraham a king when he acquires Efron's field: all because the place of milah is the place of kingship.
The Rav reads Efron as the orlah of the place of milah, whose narrow eye opposed holiness of the bris, so that buying the field from him was itself a kind of milah that revealed kingship there.
He explains that Avraham discovered the Machpela on the third day after his milah, the day of the festive meal, because the cave was the gift for the mitzvah of milah.

The Rav explains that Lavan, seeing the bracelets on beautiful Rivka, assumed Eliezer had stumbled with his eyes and so fallen into his power, and ran 'to the ayin', to the eye he thought was blemished.
He compares matching couples to a man's own business: anyone may eat or write beside him, but opening the same business intrudes; so too zivugim are Hashem's business, and no one can interfere.

The Rav explains that the Torah, like water poured into colored glass, takes on the color of the soul receiving it; the disputes of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel reflect their roots in din and chesed, and Avraham and Yitzchak differ in the same way.

Beis Shammai require two males because the world was first conceived with din, in which the male would be din, while Beis Hillel follow the present order in which the male represents chesed; in the future, when the world can stand with din, the halacha will follow Beis Shammai.

Bnei Yishmael remain the greatest ba'alei taavah despite their milah, against the Rambam's reason that milah weakens desire; the Rav concludes that a gentile is entirely orlah, so their milah removes nothing, and the holiness of Jews comes from a holy soul and body, not from a medical effect.
Because Eretz Yisrael, the foundation of creation, corresponds to fire, the root element, the Arabs who lost it were given oil, the world's fire and energy, as a cheap substitute.

Canaan, the kelipah opposite chesed, is named from 'submitting': in kelipah the female, din, is stronger, so Canaan subordinates chesed to din, and this is why Avraham would not take a wife for Yitzchak from them.

The angel sent to overturn Sedom needed Avraham's psak whether 'Moavi velo Moavis' holds, since Dovid HaMelech must descend from Lot; the angels' question 'where is Sarah' and the answer 'in the tent' gave him the psak, so he could not destroy Sedom until Lot was saved.

Yehoshua's spies disguised themselves as sellers of clay pots because a kli cheres has no worth in its material, only in its use, and so becomes tamei only from inside; the spies carried them as a reminder that they mattered only as Hashem's messengers.
The Rav reads Shlomo's words 'Hashem said He would dwell in the thick cloud' as Shlomo's foresight of galus: the same Shechinah that filled the Mikdash would remain among Jews in hiding.
The Machpelah is an extension of the Mikdash; they had to be in two places because if the avos lay in Yerushalayim, the churban would have touched the place of their hidden presence.
Chevron is the opposite of churban: churban means cut off, Chevron means joined, so even when Yerushalayim lies in ruins, one remains connected to the avos through the Machpelah.
The Machpelah is the 'hester within hester' that the Ba'al Shem Tov feared, yet even there the avos are alive and pray for the Jews.
Ornan, the other name of Aravna, equals 'aish' (fire) in gematria, while Efron recalls 'afar' (earth): the Mikdash is fire that can be extinguished, the Machpelah earth that never passes.
Had Rachel, who embodies revelation, been buried in the Machpelah, she would have brought light into the place of concealment and galus could not have existed.
Parshas Vayeira ends with revelation at the Akeidah and Chayei Sarah follows at once with the Machpelah, where Hashem and the avos are not seen.
Eliezer's name is withheld precisely in the parsha where he makes the shidduch, because he is the father of all shadchanim and the Torah wants to show that the shadchan does not make the match.
Kiddushin learned from a burial cave is not a bad omen but the best one: the couples of the Me'aras HaMachpela show that the bond of the souls outlives the bodily kiddushin that ends at death.
A shidduch is like Malchus Beis David, which comes from so high a place that even Shmuel HaNavi did not recognize the king; so too the malach does not know the shidduch and must guess.

The tenth maamar opens with 'it is not good' and ends with 'a helper opposite him', mirroring how shidduchim begin with options that are not good before the right one; and it corresponds to 'do not covet', taking one's own and not another's.

The shadchan is paid not for arranging the match, which Hashem does, but for saying the lie that the Satan must be thrown, which explains Rabbi Yaakov Emden's saying that the shadchan takes money for his words.
The seventh day is really the tenth, since three 'days' preceded creation, so Shabbos is Malchus, the tenth; the kallah is Shabbos, which is why the tenth maamar about Chava belonged to Shabbos.

The Torah dwells on Eliezer's words more than on the deeds of the Avos because the Avos' greatness is beyond our understanding, while Eliezer, a smaller man, can be understood, so his awareness of hashgacha is something we can learn from.
Rivka and Lavan heard the same account of Eliezer; what each took from it reveals who they were: she was drawn to the tzaddik, he saw an easy mark for his greed.

Rivka did not take off her new bracelets to show her mother, defying the very nature on which the halachos of jewelry on Shabbos in perek Bameh Ishah are built, because she was absorbed in the tzaddik she had seen.

'Tzemidim' is written in full when Rivka receives the bracelets and without the letter yud when Lavan sees them, showing that she sensed the holiness of the bracelets that corresponded to the Luchos and he did not.
Keeping holy bracelets on is like a Jew who davened well and does not want to take off his tallis and tefillin afterwards.
The Rav reads Eliezer 'standing over the camels, over the spring' as standing over his eye: his eye does not dictate to him, he decides when it may look.
Moshiach will not conquer the world with weapons but with the power of his word, the same power Avraham showed when his hesped moved the people of Ches to give him the grave.
Eliezer's negiah went unnoticed even by him until he retold the events and reflected on them; only on review did he realize he had a personal interest.
Eliezer chose kindness as the sign rather than piety or long davening, because middos pass down by inheritance while other virtues he himself also had.
The greatest success is when the force of evil itself consents to the blessing, so that it can no longer accuse; this happened when Lavan-Bilam said 'blessed of Hashem'.

Rivkah's leaving Lavan's house was a model of the Exodus: a sorcery held that none could leave, and when the moment came that she could no longer remain in impurity, she left in haste with self-sacrifice.

The Ramban's plain reading that Yitzchak went to chat with friends hints at the Kedushas Levi's idea: in a time of great accusation, a tzaddik's prayer is hidden in ordinary speech so the accusing angels let it through.
Avraham was granted Me'aras HaMachpelah measure for measure: because he ignored his own comfort for his guests, Adam and Chava had to give up their comfort for him.

The root of bracha spells doubling in three orders of magnitude: beis is two, chaf twenty, reish two hundred, as alef is one; this is why Yosef, the sixth of the ushpizin, had his blessing doubled into two shevatim.

Time is a creation: each day comes down, is inscribed with what a person does, and ascends; therefore teshuvah is easier before the day goes up, at night before sleep, on Erev Shabbos and on Erev Rosh Hashanah.
Rashi's 'thirteen' is not a misprint: the boys became bar mitzvah-grown not by age but by what they absorbed on the day of Avraham's passing, Yaakov from Avraham's days and Esav from Nimrod's tumah.
Yaakov's words 'sell me as this day' mean that the very nature of that day, which made Esav a denier of the World to Come, showed that he had no use for the bechorah.
Onkelos and Rashi do not disagree: Yitzchak loved Esav for the food he ate from his hunting, and that was Esav's deception, since the food with its kedushah was really Yaakov's.
Yitzchak concluded from the kedushah in the food that Esav was a concealed tzaddik, one of the thirty-six, who is greater than a revealed one; this is why he favored him.

A bas Levi who remarried on one witness loses maaser because, by not sensing that her husband was alive, she showed she lacks the sensitivity to a bond that defines Shevet Levi, the tribe that sensed Hashem's bond with Klal Yisrael at the eigel.
The mizbe'ach weeps over a divorce because every husband and wife were once together in the earth taken from beneath it, so it testifies that they belong together.

The mizbe'ach measures of the three Batei Mikdash correspond to the relation of Klal Yisrael to its land: twenty-eight for the 'koach' of the first passuk, thirty-two for the 'lev' of a people abroad with their hearts in Eretz Yisrael, and sixty for the shalom of Birkas Kohanim.

Miriam bas Bilgah kicked specifically the mizbe'ach, not the menorah or the Kodesh HaKodashim, because the mizbe'ach testified to the zivug she had betrayed, and a guilty conscience cannot bear its accuser.

Rivkah's birth coinciding with the akeidah is explained by place: the akeidah was on the mekom hamizbe'ach, the source of all zivugim, and as with a zaken mamrei the place itself has power, so there the accusations against Yitzchak's having children were overcome.
Avraham trusted Eliezer with all his wealth without checking him, yet made him swear about Yitzchak's shidduch, showing that a shidduch demands more care than any business.
Eliezer's name, read as 'my G-d is help', points to the 'ezer kenegdo', the helpmate he went to find for Yitzchak; it is left out precisely because this shidduch needed no human helper.
R' Yaakov Emden's reading of the word shadchan as 'speaks falsehood, takes money' is no joke: the shadchan is paid precisely because his lie is what lets something so holy come down into this world.

The Torah spells out Eliezer's prayers at length because the Avos served Hashem in a hidden way, while the avodah of a servant, on a lower level, is visible, so through him one sees what avodas Hashem looks like.

The bracelets Lavan saw still on Rivka's hands show that she never took them off to show them, so absorbed was she in Eliezer's avodah; Lavan read the same scene as a pious man 'above the camels' of treasure who could be exploited.
Following the Bnei Yissaschar, the word for bracelets is written with a yud when Eliezer gives them but without it when Lavan sees them, because Lavan did not see the Ten Commandments they stood for.
Avraham eulogized Sarah before negotiating for the grave so that his words of mussar would break the Bnei Ches' love of money, and they would not demand everything he had.

Sarah's first three years, before she served Hashem, were made up by her rising at night, as in 'she rises while it is still night' in Eishes Chayil; so all 127 years were equally good, and Esther merited all 127 provinces.

Eating is not only for strength to serve Hashem: every moment brings a new heavenly influence, and food is one of the channels through which a person takes in that new holiness; this is why the righteous will eat the Leviasan feast before a new order begins.
Yitzchak loved Esav for a real holiness he tasted, but it was Yaakov's: Yaakov secretly prepared the food Esav served, so Yitzchak concluded that Esav was a hidden tzaddik greater than Yaakov.

"Ki tzayid befiv" is the Torah's way of recording what happened without writing a falsehood: it was Esav's hunt only in his mouth, by his claim, while the extra hei in "tzeidah", written but not read, hints that Yaakov did the slaughtering.

The blessing of the dew of heaven and the fat of the land came measure for measure: because Yaakov's food was full of holiness, he was blessed with food whose inner side is holiness and which brings Torah.
Yitzchak left Rechovos precisely when he finally had peace, because comfort itself told him he was not in the place a person is sent to this world for.

Following the Yaaros Devash, the Rav explains that asking to be a seal on Hashem's heart was not proper, since a heart is sometimes open and sometimes closed; the hands, one's deeds, are always revealed, and that is where a Jew is measured.

According to the Yismach Moshe, Yaakov and Esav were born together so that each would have free choice through contact with the other, and Yaakov received the blessing in Esav's clothes to show that even then a Jew merits blessing.
The three letters of bracha each mean addition at a different level: beis is one becoming two, chaf is ten becoming twenty, reish is a hundred becoming two hundred.
Six is bracha: Yosef, whose name means adding, is the sixth of the Ushpizin, and Toldos, the sixth sedra, is the sedra filled with bracha.
'Michra kayom' means 'sell according to today': by Esav's philosophy of today the bechorah is worthless, by Yaakov's it is worth everything, so the sale fits both views.
Eliyahu could give Elisha double what he had because on his last day all his days gathered to him, making him far greater than on any single day.
A tzaddik and his opponent are a balanced match, so when the tzaddik leaves the world his opponent leaves too or loses his strength: Nimrod with Avraham, Esav with Yaakov.
Vayigdelu hane'arim refers to the fifteenth birthday, when Yaakov absorbed the kedusha at Avraham's passing and Esav the tumah at Nimrod's killing.
Yitzchak loved Esav more because the food Esav brought was secretly prepared by Rivka with kedusha, so Yitzchak felt kedusha in it and took Esav for a hidden tzaddik.

The Rav reads the name 'Toldos' as the theme of the whole sedra: the inner reality of Yaakov's children is not Esav's garments they appear to wear, and their blessing comes from being Avraham's children.
Yishmael's hold on Eretz Yisrael matches his bris: an empty milah earns an empty land, while a Jew's bris is a lifelong guarding of eyes, tongue and bris.
A time ripe for geulah that passes unused does not leave things as they were; because the Satan accuses at such a time, it brings harsher decrees.
The world-wide agreement that Eretz Yisrael belongs to Yishmael may itself be the reversal before the geulah, just as the nations will soon agree to Yaakov's blessings.
From Rashi's calculation the Rav derives that Yaakov's beginning of Torah toil at Shem and Ever is what caused Yishmael's death, so Yishmael's fall comes through Jewish Torah study.
Bachurim, who have no money for tzedakah, can still join in the two things that redeem Israel, since teaching Torah to another is itself chesed.

Rashi's ranking of a tzaddik ben tzaddik applies to an individual's tefillah, but in a tzibur everyone's merits pass through the shaliach tzibur, so a tzaddik ben rasha at the amud adds the merit of drawing near the distant.
Leitzanus is not mere lightheadedness: it is the power to deny what one's own mind recognizes, which makes it the exact counterpart of emunah, the power to believe beyond what the mind sees.
Pharaoh could withstand plague after plague, though he clearly saw the hand of Hashem, only because a good joke gave him and his people relief and courage to deny what they saw.

The Rambam's ruling that Moshiach need not show signs elevates him: Eliyahu needed fire from heaven, while Avraham, and Moshiach after him, draw the world by the truth of their word alone; needing a sign would be a disgrace for Moshiach.

Esav was not an unbeliever: he grew up seeing angels and ruach hakodesh in Yitzchak's home, and his weeping over the brachos shows he believed; his kefirah was the kefirah of leitzanus, mocking away what he knew.

The principle of the se'ir la'azazel, giving the sitra achra a measured portion only as the Torah directs, explains the seudah at a siyum, shadchan money, and Yaakov's 'mirmah', which he did only by Rivka's prophecy.
Since Yaakov had already received the blessing of the existing world, Esav had to be given something that did not yet exist, Italia shel Yavan, formed later in the sea.
Yitzchak's love of 'game in his mouth' was not appetite: he loved Eisav because he felt kedushah in the food he served, and the food was in truth cooked by Rivkah.
Rashi's two readings of 'game in his mouth' are both true and need each other: Eisav brought him food, and with that same food he deceived him into thinking he was a hidden tzaddik.
The spelling of 'tzayid' hides and reveals: the missing vav shows it was not Eisav's game, and the extra heh hints it was Rivkah's, kept as a secret from Yitzchak as it happened.

Yitzchak blessed Yaakov measure for measure: food that had brought him Torah became a blessing of food from Eretz Yisroel that brings Mikra, Mishnah, halachah and aggadah, which is the deep plain meaning, not a drash against it.
Yishmael, the kelipah of chesed (water), now holds the world's 'fire', which belongs to Yitzchak's attribute of gevurah; his fall means handing that fire back to Yitzchak.
The Torah records Yishmael's years only so Yaakov's hidden years in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever can be counted, hinting that Yishmael's fall comes through that hidden learning.

The Rav reads 'Vayigdelu' as the day both brothers grew at once, each at a different passing: Yaakov absorbing Avraham's kedushah, Esav absorbing Nimrod's evil, which also explains why Rashi's thirteen must be fifteen.
Just as the mitzvos of a tzaddik gather to escort him at his passing, the aveiros of a rasha gather to drag him down, and each passing creates an atmosphere that whoever is susceptible absorbs.

The Rav explains Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's answer by the rule of parallels: the great opponents of the Jews exist only as the counterpart of a tzaddik of the same level, so they leave the scene with him.
Physical pollution of air, water and forests mirrors the spiritual pollution carried by the airwaves into homes.

Purim may not pass the fifteenth because the waning half of the month is Esav's territory, yet Chanukah deliberately falls when the moon disappears, at night, in the reshus harabim, to bring kedushah into the domain of darkness.

The Greeks' decree to write on every door that Jews have no share in the G-d of Israel was the opposite of the mezuzah, and the Chanukah light answers it by carrying the Beis Hamikdash out into their territory.
The empty cups of the menorah, filled one more each night, are neshamos waiting to be lit until all are lit on the eighth day, the number of Moshiach.
The Torah hides the fact of Yaakov's fourteen years in Beis Ever inside the count of Yishmael's years to teach that Yishmael's death came about through Yaakov accepting the yoke of Torah.

The Rav reads Yishmael's control of oil and energy as holding the element of fire, which belongs to Yitzchak; this explains why the Baal HaTurim links Yishmael's fall to the sprouting of Moshiach from Yitzchak's offspring.
A machzor acrostic spells Yitzchak in one column and Rivkah opposite it in words of praise, showing that their prayer 'opposite each other' was praise sung before the salvation.
On the day of passing all of a person's days gather into one, so Eliyahu could give Elisha double what he had only at the moment he was taken.

Rashi's 'thirteen' and the fact that Avraham died when they were fifteen are reconciled: on the day of Avraham's passing Yaakov grew in holiness and Esav, killing Nimrod, grew in tumah, so 'the lads grew' happened that day.

Pharaoh's butler dreamed of working the grapes into wine, a healthy dream of toil, while the baker dreamed of bread growing on his head; the Rav reads the different outcomes as the difference between working for something and wishing for it.

The Plishtim's stopping the wells is the cooling of Avraham's living avodah into lifeless habit, a 'mitzvas anashim melumadah'; Yitzchak's re-digging is renewing the very same path with fresh vitality.
Mockery of long davening is not a sign of error: it has always been the lot of those devoted to tefillah, because tefillah stands at the height of the world and people belittle it.
Bilgah's closed window is each person's channel of blessing from his soul's root; when it is blocked, the remedy is a 'bypass': drawing from a friend's open channel until one's own reopens.
Lateness reveals that the service is not dear, and it carries over to the next world: one who comes late here may find his own tikkun arriving too late above.
A shliach tzibbur who starts Hodu softly out of humility errs: a niggun may begin quietly, but the baal tefillah must begin with boldness to lift the congregation.
A fine voice, like every talent, is given for a person's tikkun; refusing to use it for the tzibbur in the name of modesty squanders what Hashem gave for that purpose.
Learning and davening depend on each other: learning purifies the mind so one can daven, and davening purifies the heart so one can learn.

The Rav reads the Greeks' breaching of the Temple walls as an attempt to add to a domain that was not theirs, the mirror image of Chanukah's increase in kedushah that reaches even the public domain below ten tefachim.
The letter yud stretched becomes a vav and stretched further a nun, so the very name Yavan alludes to Greece's drive to expand.
Yitzchak's 'matamim as I love' were not tasty food; what he tasted and loved was the kedushah the preparer put into it.
Yitzchak tasted kedushah in the food Esav served, prepared secretly by Rivka, and concluded that Esav was a hidden tzaddik, who is greater than a revealed one.
'Ki tzayid befiv' is read as Esav's deception: he brought his father food that he had not prepared himself.
Yaakov's 'kayom' means 'by your view of today': since Esav lives for today's pleasure and expects to die, by his own logic the bechorah is worthless to him.

The twelve nesiim of Yishmael are countered by the twelve nesiim of the Mishkan's dedication, so the Chanukah reading of the nesiim makes Chanukah and Kislev a time for nullifying the klipah of Yishmael.
Yishmael's hold on Eretz Yisrael rests on a milah without content, so his claim lasts only while the land is empty of Jews.
The Rav finds 'Yishmael ben Avraham' in the gematria both of 'Hashem melech olam va'ed avdu goyim me'artzo' and of the name Arafat as spelled in Hebrew letters.
The letters of 'barach' each double a value: beis from one to two, chaf from ten to twenty, reish from a hundred to two hundred, so bracha is multiplication in every order.

Six is the number of bracha: Yosef the sixth of the ro'im, the sixth sedra Toldos, its sixth aliyah 'Veyiten lecha' opening with a vav, Yitzchak at sixty, and the lulav shaped like a vav on which the bracha is made.
Just as a talmid at his rebbe's petirah receives a double portion of kedushah, Esav, present at Nimrod's death, received a double portion of tumah; a tzaddik and his adversary die on the same day.
Vayetzei is the only sedra written as one continuous parsha with no break, because Yaakov never had a moment's interruption from the way of his father's house during twenty years in Charan.
Be'er Sheva is read as the oath (shevuah): like a man lowering himself into a deep pit tied by a strong rope to the top, Yaakov could enter Charan only because his oath bound him to Hashem.
Rachel and Leah correspond to the two aspects of the Shechinah mourned in Tikkun Rachel and Tikkun Leah, which is why Yaakov had to prepare seven years for each, like counting seven times seven.
Hashem answered every request in Yaakov's vow except bread and clothing; the silence itself is the answer: rely on Me, I have not forsaken you until now.
Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls he raised from the level of animal to the level of speech, and every Jew still carries a point from Yaakov Avinu's shepherding.
Rachel was buried on the road so she could help her children in exile who cannot drink under gentile shepherds; this is what Yaakov saw and wept over at the well.
The Arizal delighted in the Alshich's derashah not for its depth but because Lavan himself came to listen and nodded each time the Alshich exposed one of his deceptions.
Yaakov's own galus cut a road through the wilderness: what he broke through became a path and a strength for later generations to survive their galus.

The people of Charan who accused Yaakov of immodesty were Lavan's circle, and Lavan is Bilaam, whose advice later was to corrupt Klal Yisrael through immorality; the nations parade virtue exactly where they are most sunk.
Rachel's burial outside Me'aras HaMachpelah expresses the galus of the revealed Shechinah: had Rachel been there, bound forever to Yaakov, there could have been no galus.
Kiddushin is learned from a grave purchase because that is the best sign of all: the bond of two halves of one soul outlasts even death.
Parshas Vayetzei is written without any break because Yaakov never paused, even for a moment, from his attachment while in Lavan's house.
Bnei Kedem are 'the forward people', the progressive and educated; the lowest galus, the heels, is a land of progress and higher education.
Lavan's 'nakvah secharcha' was spoken to a man he thought a fool for working seven more years; Yaakov was working for the Shechinah, not for Lavan.

The Rav reads 'vayifga bamakom' and 'vayifgeu bo malachei Elokim' as a reversal: leaving, Yaakov was astonished at the angels; returning after twenty years in Haran, the angels were astonished at him.
Yaakov is the choicest of the Avos not despite his earthly affairs but because of them: he showed that Hashem can dwell on a person through family, work and wealth.

The difference between olah and shelamim mirrors the difference between the nations and Yisrael: a goy may bring only an olah, wholly given to G-d, while a Jew's shelamim, eaten at a feast, shows that his own enjoyment can be holy; Klal Yisrael became a nation through the Korban Pesach, which is eaten.
Yaakov kissed and wept at once because he kissed Rachel as one kisses tefillin, seeing in her the Shechinah, and wept out of pity for the onlookers who mocked him and could not see what he saw.

The seven years seemed like days, the reverse of ordinary longing, because for Yaakov the preparation was itself avodas Hashem, just as building a sukkah is a mitzvah to be enjoyed and not only a preparation.
Yaakov's striving for Lavan's sheep, which looks like cunning on the surface, was the redemption of Jewish neshamos held captive by Lavan, who became the 600,000 Jews in Mitzrayim.

Yaakov's fourteen years in the yeshiva of Shem and Ever correspond to the preparation of Shacharis with tallis and tefillin, which readies a Jew to hallow his workday as Yaakov hallowed his work in Haran.

The Torah hides Yaakov's fourteen years in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever the way someone hides a diamond in a garbage can: inside the count of Yishmael's years, where nobody would look, matching the way Yaakov himself was hidden.
Esav did not pursue Yaakov to Lavan because he reckoned that Lavan, who was Bilam and the essence of impurity, would do a better job of destroying Yaakov than he could.
The seventy souls were the one stage of growth that took place in Eretz Yisrael, because their number stands against the seventy nations, whose borders lie outside the land.

Yaakov's sheep, brought by angels from Lavan's flocks, were the root of the souls of the six hundred thousand who later went down to Egypt; his sticks only made the sheep look as if they came naturally.

Eretz Yisrael is the Shabbos of geography, and galus is the weekday on which one prepares for it: just as only one who toils on Erev Shabbos eats on Shabbos, the nation must be formed in galus to be worthy of the land and of Moshiach.

Vayeitzei comes just before Chanukah, the Yom Tov of weekday clothes, whose menorah is placed on the left side facing the street in the long dark nights, to teach that galus is not only a punishment but the place of Klal Yisrael's growth.

The Midrash's criticism of Yaakov and Chazal's lesson from him are not a contradiction but two layers of Torah, drash and sod, worn like garments one over another; they clash only because the world has not yet reached its tikkun since Adam's sin.

Rachel's merit before Hashem was not only that she gave Leah the signs, but that she understood exile and its contradictions are needed before the tikkun, and that the Jews' sins come from the state of the world rather than from their essence.
Esav's angel appeared to Yaakov as a talmid chacham, and so the final exile is that of the erev rav, who can bring proofs no one can refute; only Hashem Himself can unmask him.
The am ha'aretz could innovate the reading of 'minchah yashivu' because his own soul came from the souls sent to Esav in Yaakov's gift, and he was only temporarily in Esav's camp.
Havdalah, the separation between holy and mundane, requires a sense of smell; so too the tzaddikim who could tell holy from unholy were those with a 'chush rei'ach', a sign associated with Moshiach.
Reading the names of the alufim of Esav brings Esav back to his root in the Torah, where he has no existence of his own, and so nullifies his power; this is a preparation for Chanukah.

Women's not lighting Chanukah candles is itself the fulfilment of the mitzvah's purpose: the segulah of sons who are talmidei chachamim comes from tznius, so by staying home they keep what Yehudis gave her life for.

According to the Parashas Derachim's view that the brothers had the status of bnei Noach, Dina, conceived by Rachel, remained Rachel's daughter, so Shimon was permitted to marry her as a sister from the father alone.

The holiest places are first covered by their opposite, as the shell covers the fruit and the orlah the bris; so Shechem, the place of Shem Kevod Malchuso and of Yosef, was first held by the son of Chamor the Chivi.
Shimon and Levi's killing was the real 'milah' of Shechem: since the whole people was orlah, removing them left the holy place whole, just as removing the orlah leaves a Jew whole.
Worldly desires exist only as a mashal for the love of Hashem; that is why the Midrash learns Hashem's love for Israel from the parsha of the rasha Shechem.
Even a war that is justified needs the sanction of a gadol; done on one's own, the harsh deed shapes the doer, which is how Shimon and Levi came from Shechem to the plot against Yosef.
Lavan's 'the daughters are my daughters' after Yaakov's convincing argument shows that a person's reasoning is shaped by the house he learned to think in, not by the merits of the case.
The hatred of the nations is not something to be explained away; like the hatred between animals it is instinctive, and it serves as a preservative that keeps Jews from mixing with them.
The Jewish state, meant to cure antisemitism, has itself become its leading cause: the hatred simply follows the Jews whether they have a country or not.
Lavan's sheep were not ordinary property: they held the souls of the Dor HaMabul, the Dor Haflagah and Sedom, numbering 600,000, which Yaakov redeemed and which became the Jews who left Mitzrayim.
Before Matan Torah the tzaddikim could build their own 'switches' for the upper lights; Yaakov's peeled stripes on the rods were his way of fulfilling the mitzvah of tefillin, not a trick.
Esav did not chase Yaakov at Lavan's house because Lavan, the merkava of the Samech-Mem, was a greater danger than Esav himself; only Hashem's protection saved Yaakov there.
Yaakov's years with Lavan are a mirror of all of golus: Jews bring prosperity to their hosts and are accused of being parasites, as in the libels against Jewish finance ministers.
Yaakov's eight bowings to Esav are not a weakness that brought on the eight kings of Edom as a punishment; they are the path of 'diminution after diminution', which in the end leads to increase.
Lavan's flocks were Jewish souls who had lost their tzelem Elokim through earlier generations' sins, and Yaakov's years of shepherding were the work of restoring their human form.
The Midrash reads 'shifchah' as Avigail because the same force in her soul that stopped David from killing Naval, Lavan reborn, is what held Yaakov back from fighting Lavan.
The touch on Yaakov's thigh, the Jews killed for kiddush Hashem, is not Esav's victory but the opposite: these loftiest souls will bring about Esav's downfall.
Shabbos requires a person to rise to Hashem, but on Chanukah Hashem comes down, just as the Mikdash came to Yaakov because the souls he carried could not rise to it.
The eighth king, Hadar, of whom no death is written, is the tikkun, and he corresponds to the eight days of Chanukah and to the time of Moshiach.
The oil Yaakov poured on the stone at Beis El was the very cruse of oil the Chashmonaim later found, so the light of Chanukah was revealed already then.

The Rav reads the angels' error in Sodom through the Arizal on Egypt: a place of extreme impurity can damage even Gavriel and Rafael, and from this he shows the power of a bad environment and bad company.
The angels expelled after Sodom waited for a tzaddik who could enter a place of impurity unharmed; this explains why they were restored only when Yaakov came, after Shem and Ever and Lavan.
'Vayifga' is reversed: on the way to Charan Yaakov had the surprise of meeting the angels, but on the way back it was the angels' joy to meet Yaakov, who had redeemed them.
Yaakov sent to Esav precisely the angels who had once fallen in an impure place, because only they could testify from experience that he had lived with Lavan without being harmed.

The two nearly identical Kabbalas Shabbos psalms describe two kinds of redemption: one of din, in the way of Tishrei, judged 'bemeisharim', and one of chesed, in the way of Nissan, earned by a generation that keeps hoping 'ki va, ki va' with emunah.
The 'chamor' on which Moshiach rides is the physical, toiling Jew whose davening is hard; the greater his spark of Moshiach, the harder his prayer, and Moshiach comes through such groaning prayers.

Yaakov's demand that the angel of Esav concede the blessings is the same as the bad angel answering amen on Friday night: the completeness of the redemption is when even the side of evil must acknowledge the good.
The angels of Sedom were not punished only for the words 'ki mashchisim anachnu'; entering the tumah of Sedom itself blemished them, as the Arizal explains about Mitzrayim.
The Rav suggests that 'k'eretz Mitzrayim' in the passuk about Sedom is not praise of its fertility but a statement that it was as impure as Mitzrayim.
Only a tzaddik who had himself lived in a place of tumah without being blemished could repair the blemished angels, which is why they waited until Yaakov.

Yaakov went to Shem and Ever rather than staying with Yitzchak because Yitzchak learned in a sheltered holy place, while Shem and Ever, living among goyim, taught how to serve Hashem in such surroundings.
Lavan switched the sisters as a plan to kill Yaakov: a man married to someone else's zivug must eventually divorce or die, and he knew Yaakov would not divorce Leah.
Tears can change what even tefillah cannot: as Eisav's tears opened the gates of brachah, Leah's tears changed her very root from Eisav to Yaakov.
The Akeidah was the hardest test because it required each of the Avos to act against his own midah: Avraham of chesed had to slaughter, and Yitzchak of din had to give himself up out of love.
