Hashem arranged that Yitzchak bless Yaakov thinking he was Esav, to show that Jews are blessed even when they act like Esav, and that Hashem, not Yitzchak, chooses whom to bless.
Since Torah is compared to water, the Dor HaMabul, who refused the Torah meant for them, received it as the waters of the flood, over forty days like the forty days of Matan Torah.

The Gemara's derivation of Moshe from 'beshagam hu basar' is explained by the Zohar: Noach was meant to be Moshe, and Moshe's plea 'mecheini na' repaired Noach's failure to daven for his generation, which is why the flood is called 'mei Noach'.
Lavan's sheep were a stage in the cleansing of the souls of the Dor HaMabul and Dor HaHaflagah, between the Haflagah and Mitzrayim; the Yismach Moshe remembered being one of them.

Yaakov's sticks were the mitzvah of tefillin, which recall Yetzias Mitzrayim, because extricating these souls from Lavan was itself a redemption like Yetzias Mitzrayim; it was concealed as a trick so that the Satan would not interfere.
Lavan's claim that everything Yaakov had was his, though Yaakov had brought him blessing, is the pattern of all golus: the nations prosper through the Jews and then accuse them of draining them.
The Rav reads 'passim' as 'pas yam': the coat declared Yosef the tzaddik for whom the sea would split, and that, not favoritism, is what alarmed the brothers.
Rachel's silence when Leah was brought to the chupah is a form of guarding the bris, since guarding speech and guarding the bris are one, and this is why her son became the provider of the world.
The law that raising an orphan makes one a parent was hidden even from Yaakov until Yosef passed his test, and then it was learned specifically from a passuk about Yosef.
Yosef's request 'remember me' really meant 'do not remember me unless you need me': he preferred two more years in prison to a geulah owed to a human favor.
In the dream, Yaakov and Rachel bowing to the ground hint at Hakadosh Baruch Hu and the Shechinah descending to the earth, and Yaakov's outcry was a cry over the length of the galus.
The cupbearer's dream, with its fourfold 'kos', was a dream of Yosef's and Klal Yisrael's geulah, so its interpretation as release came true, while the baker's was a dream of galus.

Hashem answered Yaakov's fear of Esav's two merits with Yosef, because Yosef became the tzaddik precisely when he was cut off from both his father and Eretz Yisroel; the Yehuda and Tamar episode shows the reverse.

Because kibud av lights up the attribute of Av above, Avimi, who kept it supremely, was shown that the churban was an act of a merciful Father, and the month of the churban is named Av for that reason.
Esav's outward kibud av, though empty, gives him a hold on the month of Av, which is why the churbanos of the Jewish people came in that month.
Esav excels in kibud av the way a pig shows its split hooves: what looks like his greatest virtue is exactly where his outwardness is exposed.
Both of Chazal's stories of gentile kibud av take place in Ashkelon, a Philistine city, because the Philistines descend from mamzerus and have no root, which exposes the hollowness of such honor.
Kibud av and yishuv Eretz Yisroel are the same mitzvah, honoring one's root, which is why the Torah gives kibud av the reward of length of days on the land.
The Chanukah light placed below ten tefachim is the Father bending down to His child, reaching into the deepest exile as Yosef's father's image reached him in Egypt.

The greater the light, the more deeply it must be hidden: Hashem hid the light of Moshiach inside the most troubling stories of Vayeshev, as one hides a diamond in a garbage can where no thief would look.

The parsha moves from questions on the Shevatim to Yosef being imprisoned for his righteousness, mirroring the Rambam's point that speaking against tzaddikim leads to speaking against Hashem; this makes Vayeshev a drill in emunah.
Because the Torah is the soul of Klal Yisrael, its scattered halachos reflect the people's exile, and the many collections of seforim in our time reflect the beginning of their ingathering.
Yosef supported Yaakov for seventeen years to repay the seventeen years Yaakov supported him, because Yosef's nature is to be a giver, not a receiver.
Just as the world and the calendar have the structure of a body, Mitzrayim is the lowest land and Nittel the lowest day, and Yosef won his greatest perfection precisely in that place and on that day.

Nitzavim, Vayelech and Ha'azinu together have 122 pesukim, matching the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah, and the last passuk, about seeing the land from afar without entering, matches the Chanukah lights, which may be looked at but not used.
Chanukah's date is fixed by neither Shabbos nor Rosh Chodesh but by the number eight, which is above time, so on Chanukah a Jew can still complete what belongs to Rosh Hashanah.

The names of the chief of evil, without the divine letters that sustain him, together with his mate Lilis, equal 580, the count of Yaakov's gift; so the gift is like the Yom Kippur goat, a bone thrown to the forces of evil to leave Yaakov alone.
Unlike Eliyahu's ox, which had to be persuaded, Yaakov's animals volunteered to go to Esav, because Yaakov's level raised his animals above those of Eliyahu.

The unlearned man's chiddush concerned Esav's gift because his own letter in the Torah lay in the verses of the animals sent to Esav; that is why he was unlearned, and why this chiddush belonged to his soul.

The unlearned man's wish to be quoted was his soul's hidden plea: since repeating Torah in the speaker's name brings redemption, he sought redemption from his exile under Esav, and his public declaration that he will return itself speeds his return.
Yaakov was not faulted for failing to seek a rasha for his daughter; he owed Esav a wife because he married Leah, who was Esav's match, so Dina should have been the 581st animal of the gift.

What Esav took through Shechem he had to give back: Osnas married Yosef, who was given Shechem and buried there, and Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon came from this episode, a sign that the whole gift will return.

Yosef credits his mother's silence rather than her greater active deed because his kingship and power to sustain others came from shmiras habris, and her silence, not shaming Leah, was a guarding of the bris of the mouth.

The halacha that raising an orphan makes one a parent was withheld from Yaakov and Potiphar's wife on purpose: had it been known, Yosef would have married Osnas without the trial that raised him to the level of the Avos; it was revealed retroactively, and its root in the Torah is Yosef's own dream.

Because the Satan fears Moshiach, the line of David is hidden in unlikely places like Lot's daughters and Moav, as a diamond is hidden in a garbage can, and the halacha permitting a Moabite woman was revealed only when needed.
Yavan opposed chodesh, Shabbos and milah because each is a havdalah, and creation itself is built of havdalos; Chanukah answers measure for measure by bringing light into the darkest nights.

The letters of Yosef's name hint at his role: yud and vav are the giving letters of Hashem's name, and samech and pei hint at sixty masechtos and eighty braisos, which is why the kesones 'passim' carried the same samech and pei.
Osnas held to kedushah alone in Egypt because she saw Yosef's conduct and drew from his example; like the Chanukah light, Yosef brings light into the very place of darkness.
Yaakov's wish to 'dwell in tranquility' was a wish to live the World to Come in this world; because this world cannot hold even a trace of it, the sign turned into reality and the true exile began.
The dreidel, spun on Chanukah while Parshas Vayeshev is read, embodies Rashi's 'gilguleihem': all its turns hide that Moshiach stands at its center, since its letters equal Moshiach.

The eighth king of Edom, Hadar, of whom no death is written, alludes to the 'mehadrin' of Chanukah and to Moshiach; the dark, seemingly unimportant parsha of the kings of Edom hides the whole of Divine providence.
The Greeks broke into the Mikdash; the Chanukah miracle reversed this, sending the lights of the Mikdash out into the weekday, the exile and the public domain.

The Chanukah miracle was not in the oil at all but in time: under the light of Moshiach nature slowed, so the twenty-fifth of Kislev lasted eight days in the Mikdash and the oil burned naturally, allowing a real mitzvah.

A mitzvah works from below to above; in Rabbi Chanina's miracle the light came from above to below, so it was a sign of mercy but not a mitzvah, while Chanukah was a mitzvah and hence 'mitzvas shemonas yemei Chanukah'.
The Midrash reads 'megurei' in all three of its meanings at once, each explaining the others: Yitzchak made converts by merely dwelling in the land, and did it that way because his midah was fear.
Because Yitzchak's kiruv was hidden, the Torah tells it in a hidden way, by an innocent word, since the Torah is the blueprint of what happens in the world.
The three parts of a candle, ner, pesilah and shemen, spell nefesh, the bodily soul that holds the heavenly flame down on earth.

The halachos of the Chanukah light, in the public domain, at the left of the door, below ten tefachim, in the long nights of Teves, all place it in Esav's territory, showing that on Chanukah the Shechinah goes down to the distant.
Yosef's dream of the sun, moon and stars bowing to him is the picture of a Jew stooping to light the Chanukah candle, and Yaakov's 'shall we come down?' was an exclamation, not a question.
The letters of 'choshech', the darkness that stands for Yavan, rearranged spell 'shikchah', forgetting, since Yavan's aim was to make Jews forget the Torah.

The Rav reads Yaakov's ignorance of a simple Gemara as deliberate concealment from Above: the law had to stay hidden so that Yosef would face his trials and earn kingship, and it was revealed only once he became king.
Potiphar's wife was right in her astrology, since Asenath, whom she raised, truly counts as her daughter; her error came only from not knowing that chiddush.

The brothers' retort 'will you reign over us' meant that one who speaks lashon hara has broken the bris of the tongue and cannot be king; Yosef answered that he would reign in the merit of his mother's silence.

Yosef as the hidden light was placed specifically in Egypt, the reshus harabim and place of the other side, just as the Chanukah light is placed facing the public domain, low, on the left and in the darkest nights.

Asenath's name comes from the thornbush (sneh): like Hashem in the thornbush and like Yosef, she remained noble and holy in Egypt, which matched her to Yosef, blessed by 'the One who dwells in the thornbush'.
The Chanukah lights can kindle souls that even Shabbos cannot, the 'inferior oils', because the Chanukah light was made to shine into places that are otherwise unfit.

Even the greatest soul cannot attain on its own a portion of Torah that belongs to another living tzaddik; such a level passes on only when its holder leaves the world, as the Ba'al Shem Tov received a level when the Or HaChaim passed away.
Yaakov's Torah from Shem and Ever and Yosef's own Taharos are two kinds of Torah: what is received through the chain of tradition, and the portion that is the root of one's own soul.
Seder Taharos, the sixth order and the order learned on the sixth day, belongs to Yosef, whose trials of holiness earned him that level from heaven.
One does not say Avraham the tzaddik or Yitzchak the tzaddik, only Yosef the tzaddik: this title is Yosef's new contribution, not inherited from Yaakov.
The Chanukah flame is the level of Yosef, as the passuk calls the house of Yosef a flame, which ties Yosef's holiness to the lights of Chanukah.

The wicks and oils that may not be lit on Shabbos but may be lit on Chanukah stand for souls that Shabbos cannot kindle, while the light of Chanukah, drawn down by the Chashmonaim's mesirus nefesh, can.
Although the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim, the Chanukah lamp is placed below ten, because on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down to those lying low who have no strength to rise.
Both parshiyos open with a descent, Yehuda's going down and Yosef's being brought down, hinting that the light of both Mashiachs comes down to the heel, the lowest generation.
Potiphar's wife's intention for Heaven was flawed: Tamar was ready to be burned rather than shame Yehuda, but Potiphar's wife, whose intention was mixed with desire, had Yosef thrown into prison.
Rashi notes that the day was the Egyptians' festival because on that day, the tekufah, Torah is not learned, so Yosef lacked the protection from impure thoughts that, per the Rambam, Torah gives.

The sitra achra always imitates kedushah: as the Jews light up the darkest nights on the 25th of Kislev, the nations darken the 25th of their month with their lights, the opposite of the light revealed on Chanukah.

The halacha that a raiser counts as a parent was hidden even from Yaakov by design: had it been known, Eshes Potiphar would have sent Asnas to Yosef, and Yosef would never have had the tests that made him a tzaddik.
A title like tzaddik is earned only through tests; Yosef's brothers were also holy, but without tests they did not earn the name.
Eshes Potiphar sought Moshiach ben Yosef just as Tamar sought Moshiach ben David, which is a further reason the two parshiyos stand side by side.

Yishmael's milah, being surgery rather than a bris, is empty, so they were given Eretz Yisrael only while it is empty; as the land fills with Jews they sense their end and resist like a candle flaring before it dies.
The Avos could read the Torah from the world, as an architect can read the blueprint from a finished building.
Melech Yavan equals Yosef in gematria (156), showing that the war of Chanukah was a battle of the holiness of Yosef.

History is a train running between two terminals, creation and the perfected world, on two tracks that seem to lead opposite ways, knowledge and free choice; the question stays unanswered, yet the train keeps running toward its goal.

The ninth of Teves is a fast for a reason not understood, because it continues the darkness that came when the Torah was translated and Jews began to mix culturally with the nations, a darkness in which even Ezra's passing and the loss of true leadership could go unnoticed.

The pairing of Tamar with Potiphar's wife shows two Moshiachs: Moshiach ben Dovid came about through Yehuda's deed, while Potiphar's wife sought Moshiach ben Yosef and Yosef refused, holding that he was obligated only to keep the Torah.
Because the Satan blocks Moshiach, Hashem hides him in the least expected places, like a diamond in garbage, which is why Moshiach's roots pass through Lot, Yehuda and Tamar, and Dovid and Bas Sheva.

Idolatry is rationalization: a person will not admit his weakness and finds an outside justification, and Baal Peor was the idol that made a disgusting act into service of Hashem by its good intention, fitting a sin that began with the intention to bring Moshiach; its gematria equals 'the king Moshiach'.

The pesukim shift from Bnos Moav to Bnos Midian because Bilaam, who knew that Moshiach could come from a union with Moav, sent Midianite women disguised as Moavites, so the tribes' intention could never succeed.
Read as 'vey geshrien', the word Vayigash itself is the cry of woe of the Midrash, the fear of the day of judgment and rebuke.

The brothers' terror was not fear of punishment but the shock of seeing Yosef's concealed holiness, the inner point of the bris hidden under the orlah of Egyptian garments; the shame of the future will be the same discovery about the whole world.
The same wagons that carried Yaakov into galus hint to the 'tzabim' in which the nations will bring the Jews back, for the geulah is hinted in the very place of the galus.
Yaakov's refusal to be consoled proves he knew Yosef was alive, since one is consoled only over the dead; his grief was fear for Yosef's spiritual life.
A wheel, which turns around one point that itself does not turn, was Yosef's message that everything revolves around the inner point of Yesod, and that this point in him had held firm.
Since people avoid the number connected with their failing, Yosef's choosing to send six wagons, the number of his middah, was proof that he had not fallen in it.
The departure of Shabbos Vayigash, leading into Asarah b'Teves, is itself a levayah, as Yaakov escorted Yosef and as Hashem promised to go down with Yaakov.
The Rav locates the turning point of Yosef's rise in his love for others: he noticed the sad faces of Pharaoh's two servants and cared enough to ask.
Yosef's concealment is read as a hidden yichud: like the silent Shemoneh Esrei that must precede the loud repetition, the gathering of the shevatim in Egypt had to stay secret until it was complete.
Through the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'there is none as wise as you', the Rav teaches that one can only understand someone from above him, so we cannot judge tzaddikim.
A tzaddik's persecution of another can be a hidden kindness: by an explanation the Rav cites, the Ropshitzer's harsh opposition spared the Lentshner from heavier judgment in heaven.
The Rav treats yiras shamayim as a faculty of perception: the Mechaber demands it of a shochet not as piety alone but as what lets his fingers feel a fine nick.

On the ninth of Teves, the Rav explains that Ezra 'died a second time' when Klal Yisrael lost the sensitivity behind his takanah, as Rav Ada bar Ahava tore kriah again for Rav when his teaching was found missing.
An owner pays for his animal's damage because, as the Ba'al Shem Tov teaches, his property is an extension of his soul; the damage reveals a flaw in himself.

The Rav reads the moment before 'Ani Yosef' as the loss of both Meshichim: Yosef, root of Moshiach ben Yosef, was gone, and Yehuda, seed of Moshiach ben David, was about to become a slave, so the revelation restored both at once.

Galus Mitzrayim, the root of all galuyos, begins with 'Vey, Yidden shreit gevalt', and the final galus under Yishmael ends the same way; the name Yishmael itself guarantees that the cry will be heard.

Serach is counted twice because her good news to Yaakov, who embodied all Klal Yisrael, was a collective besorah like Eliyahu's announcement of Moshiach, so Eliyahu dwelt in her permanently rather than for a moment.
Whichever answer is taken for the seventieth soul, Eliyahu, Yocheved the mother of the redeemer, or Hashem, the one who completes the count of those entering galus is a bearer of geulah.
Asara b'Teves is in one respect graver than Tisha B'Av, since the beginning of the churban contains everything that follows, and Vayigash is read on the Shabbos before it.

The 'pearl' in Yocheved's birth between the walls is that the root of a thing holds all its strength: the redeemer's mother was born at the very first step of galus, so the redemption is built into the exile itself.
The same Pesach night that fixes the day of yetzias Mitzrayim fixes the day of Tisha b'Av, because Tisha b'Av too must end in geulah.

Serach's news to Yaakov, who embodied all of Klal Yisroel, that Yosef lives was the pattern of Eliyahu announcing Moshiach; therefore Eliyahu joined her, she could not taste death, and she counts as two.
Eliyahu is mentioned on Motzaei Shabbos because the passage from Shabbos, which is like Eretz Yisroel, into the weekdays is a small going-into-galus, and no galus begins without Eliyahu coming along.
Galus is not a bitter fate but the purpose of creation: had redemption been the goal, the souls could have stayed singing by the Kisei HaKavod; they came down to grow in the places of darkness.
A shtiebel is named after the small upper room the Shunamite built for Elisha: small on purpose, so it is roomy for those who seek Hashem and too narrow for a Gechazi who comes for his own gain.

The Rav reads the absence of a break before Vayechi as a hint to Rebbi: the white space of the Torah is the Oral Torah, which should not be written, and Rebbi, a gilgul of Yaakov, filled it only because of the troubles of exile.
The Rav turns the Midrash's 'all troubles were closed from him' into a stance: through bitachon a Jew in exile knows Hashem is with him, so the troubles are closed off from him even while they exist.

Shabbos, in the Lechovitcher's parable, is the inn where the frozen traveler warms up to continue; Hashem did not send the soul down for Shabbos, which it already had beneath the Throne of Glory, but for the weekdays.

From Rashi's 'the hearts of Yisrael were closed, so the parsha is closed' the Rav learns that a Jew does not only relate to the Torah but affects it: when his heart is closed, the Torah itself becomes closed.
Yaakov, a man of truth, did reveal the end: the very closing of the hearts is the sign, since Moshiach will come in the darkest time, when even many Jews forget him.

The Rav sees hashgachah in the yeshivos learning Yevamos during Shovavim: a masechta about yibum, bringing back a soul that did not complete its task, is itself a tikkun hanefesh, and that is why it is hard.

Praise of Hashem requires kedushah: the ofanim rise to the level of the seraphim by saying 'kadosh', and so the order of praise in Shemoneh Esrei ends with HaKel HaKadosh, the bracha set against Yaakov.

The white parchment around the letters of a Sefer Torah is the Oral Torah; the missing space before Vayechi, a closed parsha, is where Rebbe 'wrote what should not be written', and that is his hint in the Torah.
Rebbe opened the Mishnah with Shema at night, the words the Shevatim said to Yaakov, continuing Yaakov's acceptance of Heaven's yoke in the night of exile.

The day of Yosef's climactic test was the Egyptians' festival, identified in a sefer as Nittel; on the most impure day he became the holiest Jew, showing that growth comes davka where the air is impure.

Since a person's bones come from his father, Yosef's bones are Yaakov's continuation, so bringing them up completes Yaakov's burial; this explains why he told his brothers rather than his sons, and why all the tribes' bones were taken.
Kiryas Sefer is both a real city and the three thousand halachos, because each part of Eretz Yisrael has Torah written upon it; whoever restored those halachos held the key to that territory.
Yosef's 'I too will be carried up' was not selfishness at his father's deathbed: since a son's bones come from his father, carrying Yosef's bones was a hiddur in Yaakov's own burial.
Yosef said 'my bones' rather than 'me' precisely to show that he meant his father's part in him and the mitzvah, not his own person.
Yosef commanded his brothers and not his sons because the completion of Yaakov's burial belongs to Yaakov's sons before his grandsons.
'Yaakov Avinu did not die' belongs to the drush of Torah, which is read not in the Sefer Torah but in Jewish hearts, where Yaakov lives on.
The parsha in which Yaakov passes away is called Vayechi, 'and he lived', because Yaakov still lives in every Jew.
Melave Malka reaches higher than the Shabbos meals because after Shabbos the Jew lifts himself toward the Shabbos of the days of Moshiach, the future of David HaMelech.
'Too late' is said only of someone who died; since Yaakov did not die and no part of a Jew dies, no Jew is ever too late for teshuvah.
Because the Jews are the Torah itself, their spiritual state is mirrored in the very layout of the Torah: the closing of their hearts in Egypt shows up as a closed parsha.
Yaakov read in the absence of ches and tes from the tribes' names that knowing the end is not part of a Jew's mission, since each name hints at its bearer's mission.
Covering the shofar until it is blown, the matzah at the Seder and the challos, and the hidden lineage of Moshiach, all follow one rule: the greatest good is hidden so the Satan should not accuse.

The two opinions on the pilegesh of Givah are both true: the husband did not mind the fly, but the hair revealed that she lacked the traits of Jewish daughters, turning the fly in hindsight into negligence.
The punishment for not protesting Michah's idol waited until Givah, because only when the Jews fought for a person's honor did it become clear that they could have fought for Hashem's.
The widow's laxness about uncovered water is a hint to Knesses Yisrael in galus: without 'the fear of the husband' she is exposed to the snake's poison.
The missing space of nine letters before Vayechi is filled by the words 'Vayechi Yaakov': where the closing is, there one finds that Yaakov lives.
The darkness at the end of an exile is itself a sign that the salvation is near, because the forces that the tikkun will nullify fight hardest at that moment.
The Rav reads 'bechomer' as kal vachomer and 'bilveinim' as clarifying halacha: the toil that once had to be paid in bricks and mortar can be paid today through toil in learning.
The first and second Batei Mikdash were not eternal because human hands were involved in them, and the same reasoning led the gedolim to reject a redemption brought by nations and armies.
Each churban prepared a later flowering: the bondage of Mitzrayim enabled the Exodus, and the troubles of the second churban prepared Rabbi Akiva's generation, which set down the Oral Torah.

When Yaakov spoke of the end of days, he was looking at the small, leaderless Jews of our generation, wondering how they would hold on, and his advice for them was to gather and speak of the redemption.
The opening of the 'gates of wisdom' expected in 5600 did take place, but the nations seized it, and it became the scientific revolution.
Yosef said 'my bones' not because he feared decay but to point to the part of him that came from his father, so the request was about Yaakov, not himself.
A son's inheritance is not ordinary inheritance by a relative: he inherits because he is the father's own continuation, and that continuation lies in the bones he received from him.
The bones endure because they are white and carry the quality of chesed from the father, while the red flesh and blood carry din from the mother and decompose.

Closeness to Yaakov comes in levels: Yaakov could not bear even temporary burial in Mitzrayim, Yosef, one level removed, could wait for the geulah, and later generations will be brought up only when Moshiach comes.
Rebbi did not curse Nebuchadnezzar while teaching Yirmiyah because in learning Torah one is present at the moment described, when he was still a living king.

Since time, place and soul mirror one another, just as there is a place where Torah may not be learned there is a corresponding time, which is the night of Nittel; yet time is holier than place, so the impurity has less grip on it.

Sefer Shemos is read precisely in the dark weeks of Teves because it belongs to a level above time and above the rule of the forces of darkness; a Jew whose mind is in the parshiyos of geulah is lifted out of the darkness, since a person is where his thoughts are.

Read as a preview of history, Bereishis reaches the days of Moshiach right where Yaakov seeks to live in peace, and the sale of Yosef breaks off the picture: this world is not equipped to display the joy of the days of Moshiach.

'Shamos' in 'asher sam shamos ba'aretz' is not plain destruction but a destruction that arouses wonder, related to shamayim, what is beyond our senses; and 'al tikri shamos ela shemos' teaches that each such wonder is a mission.
Pharaoh first gave the midwives Egyptian names, Shifrah and Puah, so that the power of evil in those names would draw them into his trap before he ordered them to kill.

Rashi identifies Dasan and Aviram by the small sin of leaving over the manna because it reveals the root of all their later rebellion: a lack of bitachon, which led them to worry about a livelihood, seek careers among the Egyptians and learn chutzpah.

The Torah inserts 'veYosef haya veMitzrayim' into the book of geulah to distinguish Yosef, who was forced into the high places of Egypt and therefore protected, from Dasan and Aviram, who chose to go there.
A name is like a battery: it does not only describe a person's mission but supplies the strength to carry it out, which is why a sick person may be given an added name with a new mission.

Pharaoh's two separate commands to the midwives were a strategy: Egyptian names would draw tumah onto them, after which they would obey an order to kill; their refusal to take the names was what saved the children.

The Gemara's 'do not read shamos but shemos' answers the question of bewildering destruction: such a generation is not mere ruin but a gathering of souls with a shared mission to repair a flaw in creation.
Even the English word 'calling' reflects that a mission and a name are one: what a person is called is what he is called to do.
'Shem' (name) shares a root with 'sham' (there) and 'shamayim': a name belongs to the remote, heavenly realm, which is why the reasons behind names and missions are beyond human grasp.
Chazal read Hagar's 'vateta' as a return to idolatry because a believer cannot be physically lost; the only real straying is from Hashem.
The obstacles that keep blocking a person's strong desire are a sign that this is his mission, since that is where the Satan fights hardest.

Moshe not entering Eretz Yisrael was itself the reward for his mesiras nefesh: because he would not lead the war, the generation of the desert and later Klal Yisrael were saved, since Hashem poured His wrath on wood and stones.

Avraham gave water through a messenger out of chesed: hating avodah zarah intensely, he let someone else wash the guests' feet so they would not feel his irritation, and measure for measure Klal Yisrael received water in the desert through Moshe, which spared them.
Pharaoh's 'I made myself' and the claim that the world made itself are one position: the source of creation lies within the creature itself, so that the creation and the creator are the same.
The greatest wonder of the Exodus was that the Egyptians, after all the wonders, still denied; the Torah records this because the same Pharaoh lives in every person.

Following the Satmar Rav, the limbs of a holy person become a vessel for their counterparts above, so an eye or heart without fear of Hashem is only an organ, not truly an eye or a heart; this is the meaning of the Midrash that Pharaoh had no heart.

The souls of the generation of Mitzrayim, to whom 'veheveisi' was promised but not fulfilled, return in the generation before Moshiach: they did not believe when they saw, and now they believe without seeing.
Rashi's two readings of 'shever', food and hope, are one: the food itself carried the taste and fragrance that only Yosef, the embodiment of Seder Taharos, could give it, so the grain was the hope.
The Baal HaTurim's acronym for 'zekunim' leaves out Taharos because Yosef did not need to be taught it: having been raised to a shepherd, he grasped his own seder by himself.
The six days of creation are six midos, each a channel from which both one of the shepherds' souls and one seder of Mishnah flow, so each shepherd knew his own seder without a teacher.
Avraham, as the first midah, is like the first letter of a word that contains the whole word, so he knew all the sedarim by himself while even Yaakov knew only Nashim.
The Yishmaelim, steeped in immorality and carrying foul smells, wrap themselves in an outward show of tznius, as a klipah appears pure in exactly the area where it is most spoiled.
The end is a replay of the beginning: the last generation must pass nisyonos like those of Avraham Avinu at the start of Klal Yisrael.

Torah is not a record of the past: Rebbi refrained from cursing Nevuchadnetzar in ordinary speech yet cursed him while reading Yirmiyahu, because whoever learns a sefer stands in its time, when the wicked king is alive.
The Seder itself shows the makkos are healing for Israel: the very cup from which drops are spilled for the ten makkos is the cup over which Hallel and the geulah are said.
'Bni bechori Yisrael' is Hashem's protest in the sense of chazakah law: as long as the true owner protests, the nations who hold the Jews in galus gain no ownership over them.

Tzidkiyahu imprisoned Yirmiyahu in the hall where Shlomo planned the Beis HaMikdash so that the prophet of calamity, Shlomo's own reincarnation, would receive a prophecy of consolation in Shlomo's merit.

The same place could bring consolation but not annulment: the room where the Beis HaMikdash was planned, on the day Hashem's anger began, is itself the accuser, and an accuser cannot become a defender.

Rashi's first and last Torah frame one message: his first answers the nations who call the Jews thieves of the land, and his last, on chezkas habatim, teaches that the land and the Beis HaMikdash remain the Jews' by Hashem's chazakah.

The Rav reads Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's 'go to Negaim and Ohalos' as a hint: those tractates of the gravest tumah open with 'shnayim', showing that tumah cannot start from 'one', and so the frog plague could not have grown from a single mother frog.

Since the frog is a partnership of pure and impure, neither one root frog nor two frogs fits; Rabbi Elazar's whistle, one calling and many coming, expresses the yachid and the rabim together, the mixture itself.
The frog's song is the only one in Perek Shirah that is not a passuk, because it is the song sung from the beis hakisei, where a passuk may not be said, and it must be said quietly.

Each impure species has a pure counterpart on land or in the sea that serves as its shliach tzibbur for song, but the dog, impure in both, has none, which is why its song needed a special merit: its tongue.
The dog's lowliness is its total nullification to a human master; its song 'come let us bow before Hashem' is the future tikun of that trait, bowing to Hashem instead.
Hotza'ah on Shabbos is a mixing of the reshus of the One with the reshus of the many, which is why Maseches Shabbos opens with 'yetzios haShabbos shtayim'.

Beis Shammai's Rosh Hashanah for trees on Rosh Chodesh Shevat is not a disagreement with Beis Hillel but a finer perception: the renewal of the Jewish soul, Hashem's tree, begins then, and only the sharper great ones feel it already on Rosh Chodesh.
Shevat is related to 'judging', since beis and pei interchange: in Shevat each person is judged on how he can adapt to the new Torah and the new conduct that come down.

The title 'one who feared the word of Hashem' belongs to someone who breaks his klipah to follow the tzaddik, not to someone who protected his animals because experience at the pestilence taught him Moshe was right.
The hail, the seventh plague, corresponds to the seventh commandment from the top, Shabbos, and to malchus; therefore it came in Shevat, which the Chasam Sofer reads as Shabbos.

Moshe's prayer to stop the hail was really a prayer for the Jews of the last generation: that the unfallen hail stay suspended as a reserve of yiras shamayim for the war against emunah before Moshiach.
Moshe had to leave the city and spread his hands only at the hail because a prayer for Jews' emunah draws many accusers, while a salvation for a goy, as at the frogs, is easy.

The Jews said 'Hashem will reign' and not 'Hashem reigns' because Pharaoh's horses survived the hail through God-fearing Egyptians: the hail had not come down in full, so the redemption was not yet complete.

Pharaoh knew the righteous midwives would never kill, so he first stripped them of their Jewish names: the name itself is a dike of kedushah, and once it is breached by a name of tumah the rest can follow.
The 'al tikri' of shamos as shemos is not a change of reading: the devastations that astound people can only be understood through the names, the missions, of those who suffer them.
The Gemara's question where Moshe is hinted in the Torah asks who Moshe was before he was born; the answer is Noach, and the teivah and rescue from water repeat in Moshe's life.
Moshe's 'mecheini' is a rearrangement of 'mei Noach': by risking himself for his generation he repaired Noach's failure to daven for his.
Bereishis teaches visible reward and punishment, while Shemos opens with unexplained suffering and immediately lists names, telling that the sufferers had missions.

Just as the same letters of Hashem's name give Nissan or Teves depending on their order, two people with the same name may have different inner arrangements; free choice decides tzaddik or rasha, not one's traits.
The final letters of 'Bnei Yisrael haba'im Mitzraymah' spell milah: the names in Shemos are given like names at a bris, on the day of geulah.
The tree and the moon are the 'two witnesses' that the Jewish people, which seems dead to the nations, will revive, which is why the new year of the trees falls in the week of Parshas HaChodesh.
Beis Shammai, belonging to the world of Moshiach, sense renewal already at its point of origin, so their new year for trees is Rosh Chodesh Shevat, when the renewal is still only a point.
The Mishnah states Beis Shammai's view as the main one because, unlike other halachos, here a Jew awaiting Moshiach already needs to know their ruling, since it may apply retroactively.
Nature keeps the Torah of creation as a mitzvah: grass grows by the same kind of command by which a Jew wears tzitzis, so a miracle is a change in the Torah and must follow the Torah's own rules.
The world, like the human body, has a built-in control system: just as a fever fights germs, history and the Flood show that no creature can ruin nature beyond a set limit.
The nations' demand to internationalize Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim comes from sensing that it is the root of the world, so being driven from it feels like being driven off the planet.

The whole Torah from Bereishis to 'HaChodesh hazeh lachem' is an introduction to the first mitzvah and an answer to the nations why only the nation that is 'reishis' may hold the land that is 'reishis'.
The Rav reads 'and they did not rebel against His word' as praise of the Jews: during choshech they could have walked out of a paralyzed Egypt, but they stayed because Moshe told them to wait.

Those who died during the darkness were the wealthy and the 'intelligentsia' close to the government, who did not want to leave; the bnei Efrayim who left early failed for lack of emunas chachamim, not even asking Amram.
Rebuke suits a strong generation, as in Yeshayahu's time; Malachi, the last prophet, speaks to the broken generation before Moshiach, so he opens with 'I have loved you'.
Hashem calling Klal Yisrael 'mother' is like a grandmother who calls the baby 'mamele' out of love, and the mitzvos even of the simplest Jews become pearls in Hashem's crown.
Hashem says 'Bo', come, rather than 'go', because He goes along with Moshe: like a mother who goes with her child into a dark room, Hashem is with a Jew even in a place of impurity.
Yehudah married right after the sale of Yosef because, having lost all his worlds, he chose to begin from the beginning; this is the lesson of the first mitzvos of the Torah.

Every creature is a 'recipe' of one or more of the ten utterances, hidden behind its material form; the makkos made those hidden utterances visible, and the Zohar matches them in reverse, so Makas Bechoros reveals 'Bereishis' and Choshech undoes 'let there be light'.
Pharaoh's 'kaved' heart is a liver, which hardens the more it is cooked; this heartlessness, like the donkey that defied the king, was the vessel through which all the makkos came.

The Torah calls Egyptians 'those who feared the word of Hashem' only by Barad because Barad, the seventh makkah corresponding to Malchus, rained down real yiras Shamayim; when Pharaoh's plea cut it short, their fear left them, which is how they could chase the Jews with those same horses.

Moshe Rabbeinu's tefillah with spread hands outside the city was not for Mitzrayim but that the unfinished Barad remain suspended, so the Jews before Moshiach could draw yiras Shamayim from it, for example at shalosh seudos.
Every song is emunah, because song is harmony and conflicting thoughts are its opposite.

Barad fell on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, and Shevat and Shabbos are phonetically one; Shevat brings the new crop of Torah and Shabbos is the day of Torah, so Shevat, Torah, Shabbos and Barad are 'all cousins'.
The Barad that broke the trees of Mitzrayim was, for the Jews, the first stage of the blossoming of their own tree, the tree of Torah.
The Rav reads the Midrash that even a poor man may not eat on Pesach night until he reclines as teaching the essence of the Exodus: a Jew must have Someone to lean on, the Ribono shel Olam.
Playing on the custom of eating kasha on Shabbos Shirah, the Rav says the parsha of shirah and emunah teaches a Jew to swallow a kushya and remain a Jew.
The word mazal means a flow or channel: each person has a particular channel through which his flow of blessing comes down.
Before birth every soul agrees to the mazal it is given, since it knows that this is what its tikkun requires; only once clothed in the body does it no longer see what is good for it.
The drive, energy and aggressiveness of successful businessmen are not the cause of their wealth but part of the mazal of wealth they were created with, so dishonesty adds nothing.
The career choices of a yeshiva bachur carry a 'casualty rate' for the soul just as a war carries one for the body, and people fear the second far more only for lack of emunah.
The Jewish tree, like a citrus tree, cannot grow in foreign soil; the Rav sees 'tevi'emo vetita'emo' in this parsha as a prayer that Hashem transplant the Jews to where they truly belong.
The sea refused to split because its condition from creation was tied to the complete geulah; it split only when shown that the redemption had been divided in two.
The Midrash says the sea returned 'to its first condition' only when it closed, because by splitting at the Exodus it had not yet fulfilled its condition; it still awaits a second splitting.
'The sea saw and fled' mirrors Yosef who 'fled and went outside': Yosef escaped the moment he would lose his free choice, and Hashem, measure for measure, rescued Israel at that same point.

Yosef promised more than Yaakov asked: since a son's bones are his father's, not burying himself in Egypt completed Yaakov's own burial, and calling himself 'bones' stressed that it was all for his father's honor.
Beis Shammai, being sharper, sensed the new year of trees already on the first of Shevat, while Beis Hillel sensed it only on the fifteenth.
The sea saw in Yosef's bones the life of Yaakov carried on in his son, the proof that Klal Yisrael never dies; the same life underlies the Tu BiShvat tree.

The Rav reads the Midrash that even a poor man must recline, learned from 'vayasev', as saying that the forty years in the desert were a forty-year haseivah: the manna taught the Jews to lean on Hashem, and in that leaning rich and poor are equal.
Since every mitzvah contains Hashem's Name, the Arizal's practice of keeping the afikoman under the haseivah cushion means one is literally leaning on the Ribono shel Olam.
Amalek equals 'safek' (doubt) in gematria, so Moshe's hands that were 'emunah' were the direct answer to Amalek.

The desert generation is the youth of Klal Yisrael, and as a young man's years of learning set a habit for life, the forty years of learning set the habit of Torah for all later generations; this is the lesson of the long way around.

Serach bas Asher, who brought Yaakov the good news that Yosef lives, was clothed with the full aspect of Eliyahu; therefore she lives forever, counts as two in the seventy souls, and knew the secret of the redemption.

Because the redemption from Egypt was incomplete, the ox of the Merkavah, which is Yosef, had not yet been changed to a keruv; so Moshe called 'come up, ox' and the women sang their own feminine song, the song Perek Shirah gives the ox.

Beshalach's haftarah is Devorah's song, ending in forty years of quiet, while Shvi'i shel Pesach reads Dovid's song, ending in everlasting salvation, because Beshalach is only the reading of the Exodus while Shvi'i shel Pesach is its time.

Because the makkos replay the maamaros in reverse, makkas bechoros matches 'Bereishis', both meaning the beginning, and darkness matches 'yehi or', when the Yidden had light; the makkos made visible the ten powers of creation that no one saw.
The Rav reads 'vatashchisem' in Tehillim as the frog making the Egyptians barren, the opposite of yesod, which is the source of reproduction.

The machlokes between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya turns on numbers: a frog, being a mixture with kedushah in it, cannot start from two alone nor from one alone, so Rabbi Elazar describes one frog whistling to the many, one and many together.
Two belongs to the sitra achra, which is why the two masechtos of the most severe tumah, Ohalos and Negaim, both open with the word 'shnayim'.

The frog's croak, now the least beautiful song, is really 'Baruch shem', Yaakov Avinu's yichud, which in the future will surpass even Shema and the Tehillim of David HaMelech, since it reveals that Hashem reigned even where tumah seemed to be.

The Rav suggests that Moshe stopping the frogs at Pharaoh's request may mean that the time of the geulah had not yet come: had the makkah run its full course, the Yidden would have reached a loud 'Baruch shem', and they were not yet ready.
The prohibition of returning to Egypt explains why the miracle had to happen at the sea: a brachah on a miracle is made at its place, and only a place outside Egypt could be visited to make it.
The Shabbos cholent, though by nature an unhealthy dish, carries a trace of the mann, since Shabbos food prepared on Erev Shabbos draws the blessing that rested on the mann.
Laws, decrees and takanos come from the Sages, but minhagim rise from the people, even the simple folk, out of the ruach hakodesh hidden in the collective of Klal Yisroel.
The names of border cities are expounded because each border hints that every tribe and every person has his own boundary of parnassa that no one else can cross.

Shira is said only for what is above nature; since nature exists to protect the tzaddik, the righteous women's rescue was natural, and only the Egyptians' downfall was a miracle for them, which is why Miriam sang just that one passuk.

The Rambam and Raavad do not argue in principle: the Rambam cites Yeshayahu, which sets no condition of righteousness, while the Raavad cites Bechukosai, which promises the end of wild beasts only if the Torah is kept, as the Ramban explains.
By not requiring wonders, the Rambam demands more of Moshiach: Eliyahu's fire from heaven did not change the people for long, while Moshiach will move every Jew to leave everything by his word alone.
Healing comes from tiferes and hod, the middos of harmony and balance, which is why a mi sheberach for the sick is said after the fifth aliyah, and illness is an imbalance in the body.
Musical harmony is three notes apart because the third middah is tiferes, and the chord adds the fifth, hod: the laws of music follow the middos.
The half-tones are the middah of din, since halving is division; a tune only on the black keys comes out sad, yet broken notes like shevarim and teruah also blend into the great song.
The blank spaces in Shiras HaYam are as much part of the song as the letters, just as the empty periods of a person's life belong to his song to Hashem.
Singing a niggun an octave lower when one cannot reach the high notes keeps the same tune, and this is the way of teshuvah: going down to rise to the eighth.
The rasha also has a shirah, his own downfall, which is why Esav's angel fought Yaakov exactly when his time to sing arrived.
The Kinneres is the seventh sea and the harp of the world, and every Jew, a small world, has his own Kinneres; a Jew who does not sing on Shabbos is as if his seas dried up.
Humor eases suffering precisely because it denies reality, carrying a person into a world of fantasy where the trouble does not exist; the same power is what makes it destructive.
Hashem's 'mockery' of Egypt was measure for measure: Pharaoh had resisted the plagues by joking about them, so Hashem turned Egypt into a joke.
Amalek's jump into the boiling bath was itself a joke: everyone laughed, the awe of Israel became humor, and so other nations lost their fear of attacking them.
Because Adar's organ is the spleen, the organ of laughter, the month of Amalek's defeat is when laughter is turned back against avodah zarah and the wicked.
A joke about the rebbe needs no argument at all, yet it cuts the rope of mesorah that stretches from rebbe to talmid back to Moshe at Sinai.
Against emes no logic can prevail; only the falsehood and fantasy of a joke can push it away, which is why the final war against Hashem is fought with jokes and Hashem answers with laughter.
The makkos in Mitzrayim were a rerun of creation, replaying the ten maamaros in reverse, so that whoever did not witness the creation could see it in Mitzrayim.

The seven makkos of Va'eira match the seven midos and the three of Bo match chochmah, binah and da'as, like the six simanim with the ke'arah beneath them and the three matzos above on the seder plate.
The 'fear of Hashem's word' of some Egyptians at barad was not their own achievement but a flow of yiras Shamayim brought down by the plague of malchus, and it ended when the hail was stopped.
Moshe's unusual tefillah with outspread hands outside the city was not really for Pharaoh but for the Jews of the last generation, that the suspended hail should bring them yiras Shamayim.
Barad fell in Shevat, a month of yiras Shamayim that the Rav links phonetically to Shabbos, and so Shevat already begins to usher in Moshiach.
The Mishnah's insistence on the date of the new year for trees prepares a farmer for the days of Moshiach, when the halacha will follow Beis Shammai retroactively.
The Rav calls the parsha itself a mikveh: just as one immerses in water, one must immerse oneself in the sea of emunah that the parsha holds.
The sunrise is no less a miracle than the mann; people only take it for granted because they are used to it, while the mann had no habit behind it, so trusting it was pure emunah.
Since the last line of a letter sums it up, the last passuk of Tehillim, read with Chazal as thanks for every breath, is the summary of the whole sefer.
Amalek, the doubt at Masa and the serpent's seduction of Chava are one force: doubt that enters a Jew's mind and makes him question whether Hashem is among us.
Not being ashamed while davening is not brazenness; it means being so absorbed that one does not know where one is or that people are watching.
A segulah is like a free remedy whose workings no one can explain, yet it can achieve what costly medicines do; the Sefer Charedim's segulos atone for sin without the cost of fasts and afflictions.
Amalek attacked right after the Jews asked whether Hashem is among them: a lapse in emunah is what opened the door to Amalek, whose essence is casting doubt.
Even a prayer for something trivial, like winning color war, is an act of emunah, because it shows the belief that Hashem can help.
Avraham's trial at the Akeidah was not the willingness to give his son, which he already had, but going on with joy in the face of an apparent contradiction to Hashem's promise.
Closing the eyes at Shema expresses accepting Hashem's kingship blindly, without seeing or understanding, with readiness for mesirus nefesh.
History has months like the year: Nisan is the time of open miracles, while our era is history's Adar, the hidden last month before the end.
The 'sefer' in Daniel in which those to be saved are written is the 'sefer zikaron' of Malachi, which records those who hold on to emunah.
'Shema Yisrael' is addressed not to Yaakov Avinu in heaven but to the bit of Yaakov's life within each Jew, who is a branch of his tree.
'Elokei avi' is measured concretely: if what was treif for one's great-grandfather is kosher for oneself, it is no longer the G-d of one's father.
Even a small change is a deviation, and the further the line runs the further it veers from the straight center.
Following the Chozeh of Lublin, the waters of Marah were bitter because the people were bitter; a talmid chacham is the 'etz' that sweetens them, since one takes 'etzah' from him with submission.
A Pesachdik dish is useless in a chometzdik vessel: the rebbe's word helps only one who makes himself a vessel to receive it.
A broken vessel is a whole vessel: the Karliner way of brokenness is what makes a person fit to receive.
The first stirring of redemption in Egypt was not wasted even when bondage grew worse; it was a seed, and the remembrance came after it.
The spilled wine at the Seder is the makkah of Mitzrayim and the refilled cup over which the Haggadah is said is the Jews' healing, so the very same act of the makkos is reenacted in two directions.
The fourth expression of redemption is set in a separate passuk for the same reason the chazir is: Edom, the fourth exile, outweighs all the others, and so does its redemption.
The ten makkos run backwards against the ten utterances: the last makkah, bechoros, undoes 'Bereishis', and the ninth, choshech, undoes 'yehi or'.

Barad is the Shabbos among the makkos, and since Shabbos is yiras Shamayim, the hail literally rained yiras Shamayim; the Egyptians' fear came from the hail and vanished when it stopped, which is why they later pursued the Jews.
Had Moshe Rabbeinu not been obliged to stop the barad at Pharaoh's plea, the yiras Shamayim it brought down would have restored the world to its state before Adam's sin and brought Moshiach.
The hail still suspended from Mitzrayim is what will fall in the war of Gog uMagog, a war against emunah, and shalosh seudos in the dark, emunah without seeing, protects from it.

The Rav explains that Moshiach is one comprehensive soul joining Moshe and David, and that until the generation merits its full revelation it can appear in parts, as Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben David.
The upheavals before Moshiach are like the cleaning and cooking in a kitchen on erev Shabbos: the noise of preparation for the great Shabbos.
A person looking at a tragedy is like a fly on a great painting that sees only the black spot beneath it; only the great tzaddikim see the whole picture and the old accounts being settled.

Even when a decree is sealed and the tzaddik's counsel seems to fail, a churban that comes while Jews follow the tzaddik is far better, and more are saved, than one that comes through those who rejected him.
The sale of Yosef did not cause the exile, which was already decreed; it only made Yaakov go down to Mitzrayim with honor instead of in chains.
Yisro's question teaches that even the greatest open miracle does not protect from Amalek's coldness; therefore he left Midian to live near Moshe and among the Jews.
Leitzanus is the strongest weapon against truth, because by making something absurd it can dismiss anything without answering it.

The Ten Commandments are counted by the Masorah as ten parshiyos rather than thirteen pesukim, which is why it gives 72 pesukim for Yisro; the Rav calls this a strained answer that is nevertheless true.
The 'mistake' in the count of Parshas Yisro is itself the lesson: the place of the luchos, like the Aron that occupied no space, is not subject to arithmetic.
The fiftieth day of sefirah is not counted because it is a heavenly day beyond the fifty gates, on which Hashem brought heaven down to Har Sinai.

The levels of talmidei chachamim parallel the holy days: one who does nothing but learn is like Shabbos, one who works only for food is like Yom Tov, and lesser levels are like Chol HaMoed and Rosh Chodesh.
The Masorah's sign for the 72 pesukim of Yisro, 'v'Nadav', hints at the Rambam's words about one whose spirit moves him to give himself to Hashem.
Yisro was moved specifically by the war with Amalek because Amalek attacked the latecomers, and Hashem's anger at that showed Yisro that a latecomer is still precious to Hashem.
Hachodesh hazeh lachem is the first mitzvah only retroactively: once Hashem at Har Sinai commanded belief in all that Moshe says, it became the first mitzvah received through Moshe.
Even the mitzvos of the Avos and the stories of Bereishis are not believed on the authority of the Avos or of historical records, but only because Moshe, appointed at Sinai, wrote them.

The Rav compares the obligation to heed a navi to the obligation to accept two witnesses: in both, belief rests on Hashem's command, not on the person's feats, while belief in Sinai itself rests on fact.
The other religions' acceptance of Matan Torah, and their fight over Yerushalayim, are themselves evidence that the Jewish mesorah cannot be refuted.
Something first carries the quality of reishis, like the head from which every action of the body comes; that is why Rashi expects the Torah's opening to be the first mitzvah.
Kiddush HaChodesh belongs to Eretz Yisrael because it was the first land created, yet a greater chacham abroad may declare the month, since the neshamah outweighs geography.
Jews count every day as part of the new month, even the thirtieth, when the moon is dark: a Jew is always within renewal.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah's case shows that 'beyond the letter of the law' is relative: for a person of his stature, that very standard was the law.
'Vachai bahem' is read by level: for a tzaddik whose life is bound up with Torah, being drawn away from a mitzvah is itself a loss of life.
Yovel, as the eighth after seven times seven, belongs to the same level as milah on the eighth day: something above the natural order of the seven days of creation.
The Rashbam's 'all his days' and Chazal's 'until Yovel' meet: since Yovel is above the world, 'le'olam' in its deepest sense means the world of Yovel.
The acceleration of inventions and communication in our time is like the rush of erev Shabbos before Shabbos arrives.

The Rav reads 'from My mizbeach you shall take him to die' not as a time condition but as the source of power: the beis din draws its authority over life and death from the mizbeach itself, the opposite of what Rashi's reasoning about iron would suggest.

Death by beis din comes 'from the mizbeach', the place from which Adam's body was formed, so it brings a quick tikkun and a fast return into a Jewish body; what seems the harshest din is the greatest chesed.

Following the Alexander Rebbe, being prevented from learning Torah does not remove free choice; since Torah is a person's best friend and source of help, being cut off from it is itself part of the decree.
Heaven follows the Jewish beis din: a halacha as Jews learn and rule it below is how it is decided above, so Torah study and Jewish courts actually move the tikkun of souls forward.

The Rav explains that before Moshiach Hashem settles the accounts of thousands of years at once, so the six million were given a fast tikkun and will soon return as new souls who merit to greet Moshiach.
Dovid HaMelech insisted on ruling himself, checking with Mefiboshes only for accuracy, because the psak of the king of all Israel, a soul from Atzilus, affects all worlds and all of Klal Yisroel.

Had the Maggid's students declared him the tzaddik of the generation, that ruling of a beis din below would have been accepted above; the same was true of Moshe Rabbeinu, whom the Jews should have wanted as their sole judge.

The Rav reads 'do not go up by steps on My altar' as addressed to one who has already risen: for him pride is like arayos, since both are called to'evah, and its placement before 'v'eileh hamishpatim' shows that this is strict din, not piety.

The six weeks of Shovavim stand against the six weekdays and the melachos of Egypt, and Mishpatim is their Shabbos; like the Hebrew servant who works six years and goes free in the seventh, a Jew goes free after the tikkun.

The flood generation, whose punishment was not yet complete, came back as the children thrown into the river, and the generation of the dispersion, who said 'let us make bricks', came back to labor with mortar and bricks in Egypt.
The rush of modern inventions is the hurry of Erev Shabbos before Moshiach: every person is sent to repair things in distant places, and the tikkunim must now be done fast.

The proof in the Haggadah is from the end of the passuk: before Pharaoh the brothers did not praise Egypt, or even say they were hungry, but said they came for their flocks; that is what it means to stay a stranger.
Mordechai was blamed for Haman's decree as the tzaddikim of Europe were blamed for the churban, though Mordechai refused to bow in order to be a kaparah for Klal Yisrael's sin with the image.
The pauses in music and the blank spaces of the shira in the Sefer Torah show that a person's empty periods are themselves part of his song, not interruptions of it.
Every creature sings by being what it is, but man alone chooses whether to sing along; the tzaddik, the neshama of the last verse of Tehillim, conducts the whole orchestra of creation.
Preparing on Friday for Shabbos while gathering no man for tomorrow mirrors life: one should worry about the 'tomorrow' of Olam Haba and store up mitzvos, not about tomorrow in this world.

The Israelites' doubt at Masa uMeriva is the snake's original venom: following the Megaleh Amukos, the letters of 'hayesh' and 'ayin' make up 'hishiani', the word Chava used for the snake's enticement.
The kasha eaten on Shabbos Shira is a lesson in emunah: learn to 'swallow a kasha', even a black one, and remain a believing Jew.
If the Jewish tree yields sour fruit, perhaps the fault is in the soil and not the tree; replanted in the Beis HaMikdash, as the shira ends, it will yield golden fruit.
The donkey, the most physical of creatures, is far from holiness, yet Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's holiness reached even it; this is the measure of repair demanded at the end of Shovavim.
'Adam hamazik' is a contradiction in terms, since a true person does not damage; the term can only mean the man who repairs his damage, which is why the Gemara's proof for it is a passuk of teshuvah.
Kayin's 'am I my brother's keeper' is read as a complaint that Hashem is the guardian of the world; his failing was that he did not appoint Hashem as his own guardian.
The 'shomer' of the passuk from which the Gemara learns that mav'eh is adam is Hashem, the guardian of one who does teshuvah.
The Mishnah's unusual first-person 'hichsharti' hints that when a person's ox damages, his own anger, appetite and bad habits are responsible.
Statements of extreme severity in the Zohar or the Rambam, absent from the Gemara, are addressed to people of a high level, for whom a small flaw is like an ink spot on a silk shirt.
The last passuk of Yisro is derush, but by Mishpatim, after Shovavim, its demand against arrogance becomes din, as hinted in 'these are the laws'.
A ruling that seems false is not a failure of the Shechinah's presence in the beis din: it is how an account from an earlier gilgul is repaid.
The Rav reads 'tzadku yachdav' as 'just when taken together': across many lifetimes, as a gabbai balances aliyos over many Shabbosim.
The severe 'as if' and 'liable to death' of Chazal and the Zohar are the din for a higher soul, while the Shulchan Aruch speaks to every Jew.
When Rav told Rabbah bar bar Chanah 'this is the din', he meant that for him, beyond the letter of the law is the law itself.
The juxtaposition of the end of Yisro with 've'eleh hamishpatim' teaches that what is a level of chassidus for others becomes din for one who has reached it.

Terumah and Tetzaveh are the seventh and eighth parshiyos of Shemos: Terumah, the sanctuary of wood and stone, is a lower teshuvah of 'seven', while Tetzaveh, where the kohen himself is the sanctuary, is the higher teshuvah of 'eight'.
Oil rises above every other liquid and can be lit, and fire reaches upward against the pull of the world; this is why oil receives the light of the eighth, and why its name, shemen, echoes shemini.

Pinchas became Eliyahu, the angel of the covenant, through mesiras nefesh that went against every creature's drive to preserve itself, and so Eliyahu, who is beyond nature, comes to each bris, which also goes against nature.

The Chanukah oil had to be found under the seal of the kohen gadol because the hidden light belonged to Moshe Rabbeinu, and it burned eight days because the light has no connection to the seven of creation.
Moshe was hidden at every stage, in his first months, in Pharaoh's house and in Midyan, because his whole essence is milah, the breaking of the boundaries nature creates.

Moshe as Noach and Shes: they were tzaddikim of the 'outer courtyard' of nature who survived when others were wiped out, while Moshe refused to remain alone and so rose to the inner, hidden light of the eighth.
Since nature was made to serve the tzaddikim, a miracle for a tzaddik is barely a miracle; the true miracle is when Hashem breaks nature for someone who does not keep the Torah's own laws.
The same Torah that set how water behaves sets how a Jew should behave, so nature has a claim to keep its laws for someone who does not keep his.

The punishment of the wicked is a separate part of a miracle, not needed for the tzaddikim's survival, so even tzaddikim must sing over it; this is why the women sang only the verse about the horse and rider.

The Chasam Sofer's reading resolves Tosafos' question on the Rashbam: the women were the cause of the miracle precisely because they were tzaddikos, and for that reason they were only secondary in it.
The jar of man was kept in the Kodesh HaKodashim beside the Torah because emunah that Hashem provides is what allows a person to learn Torah instead of worrying about a livelihood.
The nachash's word 'hishiani' contains 'yesh ayin', the same doubt as 'hayesh Hashem b'kirbeinu im ayin' that brought Amalek.
Tu B'Shvat is a judgment for people too, since a person is compared to a tree: everyone is rooted in Hashem, but not everyone yields the fruit of mitzvos and good deeds.

The two menorah parshiyos reflect two aspects of the menorah: as one vessel of the Mishkan it belongs to the whole building, but as Torah it is a mitzvah of its own that functions even where the building is not complete or no longer stands.
'Outside the paroches' is not a negative instruction where not to place the menorah, but a statement that the menorah belongs even outside, even when the Mikdash is destroyed.
The ner maaravi parallels the Kosel Maaravi: precisely in the west, where the sun of Israel sets, there remains a light that is never extinguished, the essence of Torah.
Moshe's name being hidden in Tetzaveh is his reward, not his punishment: one hides what one wants to preserve, so the man who offered to be lost for Israel is preserved as the hidden light.
Moshe's 'erase me' stands against Amalek's erasure: because he was ready to be erased so that Israel would exist, he is present in every war against Amalek until Moshiach.

Moshe's plea to enter Eretz Yisrael was, in one explanation, a wish to intercalate the year, which means making the lunar year equal to the solar year, so that Knesses Yisrael, the moon, would be equal to the sun.

The Jews declined to make Purim a yom tov because a yom tov, like Shabbos, has no poor and lacks nothing, while they wanted a day of matanos l'evyonim, which draws Hashem's blessing to Knesses Yisrael even in galus.

Aharon's garments and Achashverosh's display share the same word, 'tiferes', but the Kohen Gadol wore that beauty for Hashem's honor, while Achashverosh used it 'to show', and that difference separates holy beauty from luxury.

Achashverosh was not punished for wearing the priestly garments, which are royal garments worn by a king, but at once for giving the holy vessels to common guests, because that debased malchus itself.
Achashverosh made the hidden frames of his beds silver and the visible legs gold, the opposite of the Ruzhiner tzaddik's rule that what one lacks inside one does not show outside.
Shmuel HaRamasi took his vessels with him because 'his home was in Ramah': his home was on high, so here, on his journey, he needed nothing, just as the Chofetz Chaim answered his visitor.
The Samael flees to Botzrah because 'botzrah' means strength: he flees to his strength, the female side, which is why the end of galus brings a rise of the feminine side of the sitra achra.
The verse says Vashti made a 'women's feast', not a feast 'for women', because it was a feast with a cause: a convention to raise the standing of women, like the movements of the Rav's day.
Both readings of Memuchan, Haman and Daniel, are true: Haman was Daniel's bad side, and Daniel's prayers for the rebuilding were carried out through Haman's advice to remove Vashti.

The Rav joins Rashi's point that the future Mikdash will come down built by Hashem with the idea that all melacha stems from sin, so that the Mishkan's construction is itself a product of sin and cannot override Shabbos.
The word 'kallah' is read as 'kolel', all-inclusive, and the bond of each kallah to Knesses Yisrael is modeled on Chavah, built from Adam's own body: the partner is a piece of the person himself.
The Mikdash is the Shabbos of place and Shabbos the Mikdash of time; since time stands above place, the 'ach' limiting Shabbos refers to the smaller Shabbos, the Mishkan, yielding to the greater one.

Dovid HaMelech did not build the Mikdash because he himself was the seventh, the embodiment of Shabbos; building a Mikdash of place would have been a lessening for one who already carried the Mikdash of Shabbos in his heart.
'Ledorosam' read as 'ledirosam' means both that each Jew becomes a dwelling for Shabbos and that a home steeped in Shabbos is a guarantee that the coming generations will remain Jews.
The rising kedushah of Shabbos explains the shrinking kiddush: Friday night needs the full blessing, the morning only wine, and at Shalosh Seudos the eating itself sanctifies Shabbos.

The Rav links 'kashin l'zavgan k'krias Yam Suf' to the hidden world: a shidduch is hard like Krias Yam Suf because both reveal the alma d'iskasya, which is why even the bas kol does not know the right match at first.
The bas kol could not identify who revealed the secrets of the Targum because Yonasan ben Uziel came from a world higher than the bas kol, and this is why his place is the place of shidduchim.
Targum, equal to tardeimah, goes down into the language of the nations to draw close hidden Jewish souls, and so the first Targum came from Onkelos the convert.
Yaakov took Leah, Esav's intended, from him, so he owed Esav a match, which explains why he was punished for hiding Dina.
Purim is a 'grabbed-away' Yom Tov, taken from Esav's months with tears, corresponding to Leah who took herself away from Esav with her tears.
Tehillim's 'He rebuked the Yam Suf' refers to the sea splitting a second time for Dasan and Aviram, who lacked Yosef's merit, so it had to be compelled.
Since 'ki va sus Paroh' is a forecast of the future Shirah at the second Krias Yam Suf, it is not part of the Shirah, as the Ramban says, yet it is written in the Shirah's layout.

The physical spring and the days getting longer reflect a spiritual spring: Nissan is when the Jewish soul blossoms, and the Sefirah count, each day adding to the one before, mirrors daily growth toward Shavuos.

The Rav shows that the content of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah is read in the Sefirah weeks, so the parshiyos themselves teach the 'purify us and sanctify us' of preparing for the Torah.
A bochur's yeshiva years are his private Sefirah, and the day he becomes a talmid chacham is his private Shavuos.
The requirement that the garment fit is written specifically by the lowliest avodah, because that is where a person is likely to feel the task is beneath him.
Greatness is measured by the ability to value small avodah; the bigger a person is, the more he understands the importance of a lesser task.
Bringing even fruitless trees into shul on Shavuos shows that one who did not reach the highest level but is content with his portion also has a share in the giving of the Torah.

The Rav reads the halacha that tefillin must be from an animal permitted to be eaten through the lens of emunah: tefillin carry yetzias Mitzrayim, the foundation of emunah, and forbidden food damages emunah, so they cannot be written on something forbidden.

The two laws of kedushah missing from the Sefirah sedros, basar bechalav and tumas meis, are higher matters that belong to the fiftieth day, Shavuos, when the Torah came through the angels who ate meat and milk and the giving of the Torah removed death.

Eating from someone makes a person subservient to him; therefore eating the four impure animals, which carry the roots of the four kingdoms, draws a Jew back into the subjugation that yetzias Mitzrayim ended.

Following the Kli Yakar, an impure animal that shows one sign of purity is worse than one that shows none, like a hypocrite; the Rav applies this to food carrying a doubtful hechsher, which can mislead a Jew who would never eat plainly unkosher food.

A Jew is like a vessel that absorbed forbidden food: as long as its essence is not ruined it can be kashered, and the Rav says a person can likewise purge the effects through crying out to Hashem with tears.
The Rav explains that the short after-blessing asks for the mizbeach while full bentching does not, because a meal with bread, salt and all its mitzvos is itself a mizbeach.

The sea's refusal to split was not defiance of its condition: it sensed that this was not yet the time of universal joy, and Yosef's coffin, recalling 'Yosif Hashem shenis', told it that this splitting was only the first of two.

The twelve paths of the sea match the twelve notes of the octave, seven white and five black, because the splitting held both song for leaving Mitzrayim and weeping for the golus still ahead; the future seven paths match the seven pure notes.
Piano keys are called 'keys' because, as the Tikkunei Zohar teaches, niggun is what opens certain heavenly chambers.
Musical harmony is a shidduch made in Heaven: notes that belong together give pleasure as a good match does, and today's noisy music is the opposite of a shidduch, an expression of promiscuity.
The white keys are chesed and the black keys are din; the black notes are broken like the shevarim of the shofar, and only they can produce a sad niggun.
An eighth string on the future harp is not a small addition: as adding a digit multiplies the possible numbers, one more note will multiply music many times over into a song never yet heard.
The Rav reads the order of the parshiyos as a lesson: Shemini, right after Pesach, guards what enters the mouth, and Tazria-Metzora then guards what leaves it.
Since today the tefillos stand in place of the korbanos, the mouth is the mizbeach, and food that is not truly kosher defiles the altar on which the tefillah is offered.

The great tzaddikim of earlier generations already built the large parts of the heavenly Beis HaMikdash; the generation's task is only the finishing touches, and the King of Glory will not enter until they are done.

A test is measured by the person: refusing a doubtful candy or holding back a joke would be laughable as a test for the Chofetz Chaim, yet for a child it is a real nisayon, and so it counts in building the Beis HaMikdash.
The metzora's covered mouth is the fitting response to a mouth that was not bound when he was healthy; a Jew's mouth is not hefker.
Restraint known to no one but Hashem is exactly what goes up to heaven and polishes the Beis HaMikdash.

Eliyahu's offering 'outside' on Carmel had to take that form: Jews pushed outside the camp by idol worship could only be raised by an offering that was itself outside, and its acceptance showed the door was open to them.

Eliyahu never sinned and needed no atonement; since he lives in the rectified world where Jerusalem reaches Damascus and includes Carmel, his offering and his 'exile' to Damascus only looked like chutz and galus to ordinary eyes.
Mikdash and Damesek are made of the same letters: the two opposites will become one, and out of Damascus, root of tzaraas, Mikdash will come.

Damascus is spelled with a reish only in Divrei Hayamim, the book of completed malchus; reish stands for shalom, the cure for tzaraas, and Damascus with that reish equals 'machaneh Yisroel' in gematria.
A 'teiku' in the Gemara is rooted in a questioned Jew whose letter in the Torah carries a kushya; Eliyahu answers the Gemara's questions by answering the questions on those Jews.
'Mevaser tov' equals Eliyahu, Elisha and Gechazi in gematria: the true good tidings are when Eliyahu comes together with Elisha and the rectified Gechazi.

The rule of making the brachah over the more important food is not about valuing quality for its own sake, but because the more important food awakens a stronger feeling of thanks, which is the point of a brachah.

The advantage of a whole loaf is of a different kind: not gratitude but shleimus, on which Hashem's Name rests, as learned from the kohen and korban with a blemish; this is why Rabbi Yochanan uses a different wording from Rav Huna.

Jews do not gain their bond to Olam Haba, Torah and Eretz Yisrael through mitzvos; the reverse is true: because they are bound to them, they were given mitzvos. This is why the Torah opens with Bereishis rather than the first mitzvah.

Just as a Jew and a non-Jew, and Shabbos and the weekdays, are different in kind, Eretz Yisrael is the 'Jewish land' whose inner essence is Torah and Shabbos; therefore it too keeps Shabbos, and its Yovel parallels Yom Kippur, the Shabbos of Shabbos.

The seven nations of Canaan are the seven middos; conquering the land means refining one's own middos during the seven weeks of Sefirah, until even the weekdays become 'Jewish' and everything is drawn into Shabbos.
The shedim were left without bodies not for lack of time but because they were created lacking shleimus, so that they could have no connection to Shabbos, which is wholeness.

The Rav reconciles the Targum's 'latecomers' with Rashi's 'expelled by the cloud': both are true, since Hashem rejects no Jew, but their own tardiness at the call to travel left them outside the camp's protection.

Rashi chose Kriyas Yam Suf and the war of Amalek because each showed Hashem's love for latecomers: a private splitting of the sea for Dasan and Aviram, and eternal anger at Amalek for attacking the stragglers. This is what gave Yisro the courage to come late.
Parshas Zachor is the one portion Hashem Himself requires to be read from the Torah, not Shema and not the Ten Commandments, and its message is how much Hashem cares for Jews who seem rejected.
Parshas Yisro is a second Matan Torah for latecomers: it is read long after Shavuos, opens with the story of a convert who came late, and the sefarim say the light of Shavuos comes down on it.

The two Haftaros mirror the two paths: Yechezkel, on Shavuos, reaches the vision through four barriers and in a place of purity by a river; Yeshaya, on Yisro, sees Hashem in the first passuk, in a year of impurity when King Uziyahu was a metzora.
The vav added to Yeser's name, which forms Yisro, is the vav of attachment: a vav is a nail, shaped like one, and like the hooks of the Mishkan's pillars it joins two things into one.

According to the Midrash the Rav brings, Amalek's 'karcha' means he cooled them off: he got into the stragglers' hearts and told them they did not deserve to be Jews, killing their fervor before killing them.
