The Rav reads the parallel of time, place and soul so literally that he can say Shabbos, Eretz Yisrael and every Jew are each 'a Yid', while Sunday and America are 'a goy'.
Because the inner side of Eretz Yisrael is the Jewish soul, the land is not an object used for a mitzvah like tzitzis; the land itself is the one that keeps the mitzvah, and its mitzvah is Shabbos.
Not only do Jews need Eretz Yisrael; the land needs Jews, just as Shabbos needs Jews, and this is why the tochachah ends with the remembrance of the land.

Forcing the Torah at Sinai was a greater honor than accepting it by choice: what comes by choice is a level that can be lost, while what is necessary, like life itself, is eternal, as with a woman taken by force who may never be sent away.

Korbanos can atone only because sin is incidental to a Jew: ink poured into water becomes one with it, but dirt on a person or a diamond comes off, and Avraham's question at the bris bein habesarim was answered with exactly this.
Yirmiyahu's question about buying a field on the eve of the churban is the same as Avraham's 'bameh eida', and both are answered by the same principle that sin is only incidental to Jews.
The Torah was given in the desert and not in Eretz Yisrael as a comfort for all generations: when Jews cannot come to their root, the root comes to them, just as Har Moriah came to Har Sinai.
The sea fled and the mountains danced away at Matan Torah not out of awe but because their gashmiyus blocked their natural pull to Hashem, the way clay between a magnet and iron stops the attraction.
The word Shabbos carries two meanings, stopping and returning, and they are one: by stopping work a person returns to his root.

Osniel ben Kenaz could restore the 3,000 forgotten halachos because the land he conquered corresponded to them; owning the land made him master of the halachos rooted in it, showing that derash is the depth of pshat.

The mizbeach weeps specifically over divorcing a first wife because husband and wife were one soul at the place of the mizbeach, from where Adam was formed, so it alone feels the pain of their separation.
Yom Kippur and Shavuos are both the fiftieth: on Yom Kippur a Jew rises to heaven and lives like an angel, while on Shavuos heaven comes down and even chametz becomes an offering.
The women were told first at Sinai to show that the Torah was given as a complete union between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, which follows no order of rank and no reckoning, and which no sin can break.
The Rav identifies the four laws Moshe had to ask about as all belonging to Yovel, the fiftieth gate, so that they were given at Sinai yet hidden from Moshe because they stand above all grasp.

Wine stands for the heart's intuition and bread for intellect; matters of Yovel are reached by feeling, which is why women, the daughters of Tzelofchad and the wise woman of Dovid's time, revealed that no Jew is cast off.
The wood-gatherer was liable by the law a beis din must follow, yet in the depth known only to Hashem he was not, since he acted for the sake of Heaven; such judgment belongs to the level of Yovel.

Hashem commanded that the showbread be eaten after nine days, though it looked stale, to teach against the blasphemer's claim that the Jewish camp is 'stale' and mixed, and that every Jew is holy and must be loved.

The Rav reads 'Shulamis' as a passive form: Knesses Yisrael receives the nations' greeting but does not return it or mingle with them, the opposite of Shlomis bas Divri who greeted everyone and lost her son his place in the camp.
Like the four letters of Hashem's Name, the hidden and revealed parts of the Torah are bound together, so whoever learns the revealed Torah receives the hidden within it, even without grasping it.

On Shavuos the Aseres HaDibros are read because it is the fiftieth day of Sefirah, but on Shabbos Yisro they are read because of the Shabbos, so that Shabbos Yisro may be an even more powerful acceptance of the Torah than Shavuos.

Rashi's question of what Yisro heard is answered by two stories of latecomers, Dasan and Aviram at the sea and the Bnei Dan outside the clouds, from which Yisro learned that he too, though late, would be welcomed.
Hashem had to rebuke the sea because its original condition from creation had already been fulfilled; splitting a second time for Dasan and Aviram was outside that condition.
Hashem's war against Amalek in every generation stems from Amalek's attack on His children who were late and outside the clouds; nearly four thousand years later His anger still burns over it.

The Masorah's sign for the count of Yisro, Yanadav, alludes to the Rambam's one whose spirit volunteers, and the discrepancy between 72 and 75 itself shows that Torah, like the Kodesh HaKodashim, stands above arithmetic.
Just as the Torah given on the fifty-first day is still counted as the fiftieth, a person who takes on the yoke of Torah is not subject to the calculations of income and expenses.

The Rav treats the Jew, Shabbos and Eretz Yisrael as one distinction in three dimensions: Eretz Yisrael is the 'Jew' of geography and Shabbos the Jewish day, a different reality altogether, not a better version of the same thing.
Shemitah comes every seventh year rather than every seventh day because the land lives on a slower clock than a person.
The Chasam Sofer's no-eating in yovel follows from yovel being the land's Yom Kippur and Shavuos; Moshe went without food on Sinai because he was in the world of yovel.
Osniel ben Kenaz could restore forgotten halachos by winning Kiryas Sefer, because every spot in Eretz Yisrael is bound to a particular halachah; the land is a Sefer Torah.
Boaz's renewal of the halachah permitting a Moabite woman, together with the field he acquired with Rus, parallels Osniel: a halachah renewed together with a field that belongs to it.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is a soul of yovel, which is why the halachah follows him in the laws of Shabbos, and why his view that one should only learn will become halachah in the time of yovel.
A thief's punishment of being sold fits his sin: lacking bitachon he took what was not his and cut himself off from his own root in the Torah, so he is made to eat from a root that is not his.
Shemitah and yovel are not merely one example of Torah from Sinai: their structure of seven sevens and the fiftieth is the very structure of Sefirah and Shavuos, so they embody what Sinai is.
Yerushalayim is to place what Shabbos is to time: Hashem's private domain inside the world, which is why its houses were not rented and nothing was planted there, making it an endless shemitah.

The twelve tribes, the twelve months and the twelve middle blessings of Shemoneh Esrei are all 'weekday' concepts, while Yaakov Avinu, the trunk from which the twelve branches grow, is the Shabbos above them.

There are three levels: weekday (the tribes, Eretz Yisrael), Shabbos (shemitah, Yerushalayim, the kohen), and yovel (the Beis HaMikdash, the Kohen Gadol, Yom Kippur, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai), the last being above time and place.

The holiness of Eretz Yisrael came through human conquest and could be undone, like Rosh Chodesh which needs a beis din; the holiness of Yerushalayim, like Shabbos, comes from the Shechinah and is never annulled.
The Aron taking no space is not counted among the ten miracles of the Mikdash because in the Kodesh HaKodashim, which is above place, this is simply its nature.

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who held that one should learn constantly, is 'Shabbos' for whom every weekday is Shabbos, and indeed 'Shabbos of Shabbosos', the fiftieth, which is why his day carries the light of Shavuos.
The Rav calls the count to yovel 'a Xerox copy' of Sefiras HaOmer: seven sabbaths of years then the fiftieth year, as seven weeks then the fiftieth day, so Shavuos is a yovel.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is like Hashem, who is G-d for everyone: as Rebbe he demands no shtreimel, kapote or beard, because he sees the secret in every Jew.
The Torah says 'eiker' because avodah zarah itself will be uprooted, yet the Jew sold to it will be rescued: the uprooting is for the idol, the redemption for the Jew.
The 'ends of the heavens' teaches that even the most distant Jew is still bound to the last step of heaven, which goes with him wherever he is cast.
Shifchah and mishpachah share a root meaning attachment: the shifchah is attached where there is no Torah, and yovel returns each Jew to his true mishpachah, rooted in Eretz Yisrael and Matan Torah.

In the holiest places the klipah is strongest: Beis Lechem, place of Moshiach, became the cradle of Christianity, as the site of the Beis HaMikdash and the peak of Har HaCarmel are covered by foreign worship.
A Yom Tov is drawn not only from its date but from the parsha that describes it: since the world was made from the Torah, reading a parsha reaches the source from which the calendar itself flows.
Yisro is greater than Rus because Shavuos belongs to the calendar, which Klal Yisrael sets, while Shabbos Yisro belongs to the Torah and to Shabbos, which Hashem gives without our effort.
The haftarah of Yisro opens with Uziyahu's tzara'as, the greatest tumah of a living person, to show that on this Shabbos the Torah is given even against a background of tumah and without preparation.
Parshas Yisro is to the Torah what the Aron was to the Kodesh HaKodashim: as the place of the Aron was not measured, the parsha that holds the Aseres HaDibros is not bound by its count of pesukim.
A dedicated talmid chacham is a third form of the Aseres HaDibros, after the Luchos in the Kodesh HaKodashim and the pesukim in Parshas Yisro, so his parnassah, like the manna, is beyond the numbers.
According to the Ba'al Shem Tov as the Rav brings him, those who followed Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and failed had imitated the style without the dveikus and love of Torah that bring the guarantee.
From 'Moshe yedaber' in the future tense the Rav learns that Moshe speaks with each Jew every Shavuos, not only at the original Matan Torah.
Mesiras nefesh means giving over one's will, since 'nefesh' means will, as in 'im yesh es nafshechem'.
Shavuos is a greater day of judgment than Rosh Hashanah, because Rosh Hashanah judges material matters while Shavuos decides the spiritual life of the coming year.
Calling a person to the Torah by his name and his father's name mirrors Moshe's counting 'by their families and fathers' houses', binding him to his root letter.
The fiftieth day is not counted and Shavuos has no fixed calendar date because it is the root, above time and number, just as the Levi'im, the camp of the Shechinah, are not counted.
The four camps correspond to four books of the Chumash, with Vayikra, the book of the Kohanim and Levi'im, in the middle like the camp of the Shechinah.
The days of sefirah prepare the body as parchment, rubbing and smoothing it so that Hashem's Sefer Torah can be written on each Jew.

Yissachar's two hundred heads of Sanhedrin outweigh Reuven's two hundred and fifty, because Reuven's were in the desert where everyone learned, while Yissachar's arose centuries later when Jews worked the land; the effect of living beside Moshe lasted that long.

Through Sefer Yetzirah's time, place and soul, the Rav maps talmidei chachamim onto Shabbos and the festivals: the supporters of a talmid chacham are like weekdays that think they provide for Shabbos, when in truth the blessing of the week comes from Shabbos.
A mo'ed is where the Shechinah meets Israel, so Shabbos and the festivals, the Mishkan and the talmid chacham all share the name, and Moshe, a living mo'ed, camped by the Ohel Mo'ed.

Just as each Jew's letter lies in the parsha of the mitzvah he is bound to, such as a great giver of tzedakah, Moshe's own parsha is the moadim, which is why the Torah says specifically that he spoke the moadim to Israel.
Moshe's added day before Matan Torah was meant to lift all Israel, at least at the original giving of the Torah, to his own level where the Torah alone is the eishes chayil.
The seven weeks of Sefirah are like seven clean days counted toward purity, and the night of Shavuos is the immersion; its purpose is the avodah of the day.

According to the Chasam Sofer, the ox that killed is a soul that came down to be repaired and failed; the ban on eating its flesh is the second part of its punishment, for it loses the tikkun of a Jew making a brachah over it.

The Chiddushei HaRim explains that every sin is also theft from Hashem, since one uses the life and strengths given to serve Him for himself; this is why the Torah places teshuvah and vidui by the thief.

The Rav explains that the thief sold as a servant returns to the state of Klal Yisrael before the Exodus, so his release in the seventh year matches the pasuk that Shabbos is a remembrance of leaving Mitzrayim.
Shabbos is the dimensionless point, like the yud of a Yid, that sits inside the six sides of every object; it can be covered but never extinguished, like a pilot light, and it brings a Jew back.
The word 'chinam' means amnesty: the servant who has not repaid his theft is pardoned like a debtor whose IOU is torn, just as the Baal Shem Tov tore the document.
The Rav suggests that the six million correspond to the 600,000 letters of the Torah multiplied by ten, the number of completeness in kedushah, so that they represented the whole of Klal Yisrael.

The psak of the Torah governs nature itself: Reb Chaim Ozer told a man whose lung condition is treif according to the Rema but kosher according to the Beis Yosef to move to Eretz Yisrael, where the Beis Yosef is followed, and he lived.

The spies' failure lay in whose agents they were: as agents of the people and their poor intent, they lacked Moshe's protecting power, and 'send for yourself' was Moshe's attempt to let them become his agents instead.

Following the Arizal, Yosef's 'you are spies' was a foretelling: the souls of the shevatim entered Moshe's spies to help them, and Yosef's own soul entered Menashe's spy, which is why 'the tribe of Yosef' is written there and not by Efraim.

The world is one body, and Mitzrayim is its 'ervah'; Yishmael, the waste of Avraham's chesed turned to lust, fits that land, which is why his sar took over Mitzrayim and why Yosef had to earn the title tzaddik precisely there.

Rashi's second explanation of Avraham's 'now I know' explains the first: that Avraham, who never looked, suddenly noticed Sarah's beauty was itself the sign that he had entered Mitzrayim's domain and needed a stronger guard.
The Canaanites 'buried treasures' in the land with their sins: the greater the holiness hidden in a place, the thicker the klipah over it, and only one who digs finds it.

Tamuz and Av correspond to the two eyes; the spies' sin was a sin of the eyes in those days, so Kalev and Yehoshua, who did not fail, are the roots of Moshiach ben David and Moshiach ben Yosef who rebuild what the eyes destroyed.

'Bereishis' hints at 'He created the sixth', the midda of Yosef, which is why the sixth (hakafah, aliyah, ushpizin) carries special weight, and why 'Tziyon', equal to Yosef in gematria, is where Hashem is great.

The contradiction between Devarim and Shelach is resolved by both being true: Hashem commanded Moshe to send the meraglim precisely so that they could go as His shluchim rather than as shluchim of a people with impure intentions, and their failure lay in not staying bound to that sending.

Yosef's brothers were the first meraglim: by going down to Mitzrayim unknowingly and withstanding its tests, they, like Yosef and Sarah before them, left an imprint of kedushah that later let all of Israel keep their purity there.

The 'treasures hidden by the Canaanim' are the kedushah of Eretz Yisrael covered over by kelipah; the command 'dig out the land' meant uncovering it through Torah, avodah and mesiras nefesh, which the Rav likens to a bris milah of the land.

The permutation of Hashem's Name for Tammuz is the only one drawn from Megillas Esther, from Haman's words, and since the whole theme of the Megillah is 'venahafoch hu', the reversed permutation itself hints that it can be turned around to good.

Kalev of Yehudah and Yehoshua of Yosef, the two who did not fail among the meraglim, are the tribes of Moshiach ben Dovid and Moshiach ben Yosef; whoever does not fail in the 'territory' of Tammuz and Av likewise brings Moshiach.
Tzitzis equals all the mitzvos because each mitzvah forms only a piece of the soul's future garment, while tzitzis is itself a complete garment and so includes the whole.

The summer travel season falls exactly on the spies' forty days, from erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha b'Av; Hashem sends Jews travelling then so that by travelling as true shluchim they rectify the spies' journey.
The spies' sin was that while touring the land they forgot they were shluchim and saw only what they wanted; this is the danger of every trip.
A tree in the Catskills has waited thousands of years for a particular boy to make a bracha with kavanah on its apple; only then is it raised up and fulfils the purpose for which it was created.
When a Jew davens in the morning he calls on all creation, the mountains, trees, animals and birds, to praise Hashem with him, and the mitzvos he does in a place are their mitzvos too.
In the parable's lesson, worldly treats are the tallow candles: prized down here, but spoiled and thrown away at the gate of the next world, where only Torah and mitzvos, the diamonds, are let in.

In the city Hashem's creation is hidden behind buildings, so one sees only what people made; the country reveals His heavens, fields and creatures, and this is a chance to reach love and fear of Hashem.
The four avos nezikin are the four forces of tumah standing opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name, which the four parshiyos represent; tumah destroys where kedushah builds.
'Adam hamazik' is a contradiction in terms: a damager is not an adam, and Rav proves that maveh is a person from a teshuvah passuk because a damager earns the name adam only when he repents.
A person's possessions belong to his soul the way Chava belonged to Adam; that is why the same heavenly voice that assigns a wife also assigns a house and a field.
Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey was not a special animal; his own righteousness extended into it.
Each damager reflects a fault of the owner: keren his anger, shen his pursuit of pleasure, and regel, from 'ragil', his habits.
Kayin's complaint was that Hashem, the Shomer of the world, did not guard him; the Rav turns this into the prayer that Hashem be one's guardian.

The parah adumah is a chok because it rests on Hashem's will, and Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael is likewise a will without reason, flowing from the souls being part of Him, as a mother's love flows from the child coming from her.
Shlomo HaMelech's 'and it is far from me' means that he wanted to become wisdom itself, as Moshe had become Torah itself, and this remained apart from him.
Moshe's humility was itself a chok: he did not try to understand why Hashem made him great, and so his root lay in the mitzvah of the parah adumah.
The staff with which Moshe performed his miracles hints that he saw himself as nothing more than a staff in Hashem's hand.

Hitting the rock is leadership as the king's messenger, in another's merit; speaking to it is malchus, ruling through speech in one's own merit, like Moshiach who will act through the breath of his lips.
Three consecutive parshiyos teach three levels of emunah: Shlach in Hashem, Korach in the tzaddik, and Chukas in oneself.
The parsha moves from the chok of the parah to the shirah because the lessons of emunah lead to shirah, preparing for the geulah as at the Yam Suf.

The Rav reads 'zos chukas haTorah' to mean that parah adumah is the chok within the whole Torah: every mitzvah, even one we understand, has a dimension above understanding that draws from parah adumah.
The custom of traveling in Tammuz and Av is a rectification of the spies' forty-day journey, which spoiled emunah.
Rashi says Hagar 'strayed' back to idolatry rather than simply got lost, because for a believer there is no getting lost; only leaving emunah is called wandering.
Moshe struck the rock like a policeman with a stick instead of speaking like a king, because his humility would not let him act by his own merit once Miriam's merit was gone.
Building on Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch's pairing of Shelach and Korach, the Rav adds that Chukas teaches a third emunah, belief in oneself.
The spies sent to Yazer succeeded where those of Shelach failed because they went with emunah and knew who sent them.

The message that the Jews' good is essential was given through Bilam precisely because a concession from the adversary, like the yetzer hara forced to answer amen at the Shabbos table, is the greatest praise.
The chachamim's reduction of forty lashes to thirty-nine expresses the Oral Torah's knowledge that the first of a Jew's forty days of formation never sinned.
The Written Torah records the curses of Ki Savo and the Oral Torah the blessings, because blessing belongs to the Oral Torah, the kallah that is the source of blessing.
Parah adumah is called a chok, though it atones for the egel, so that accusers who ask its reason in order to recall the sin are answered that it is beyond understanding.
In the Holy of Holies, full of gold, there is no reminder of the egel, because at the innermost place the love for Yisrael shows that there was never a sin.
Shiva Asar B'Tammuz, the fortieth day on which the Oral Torah came down, is the 'fortieth lash' that the Oral Torah does not give, and so it is truly a consolation.
Moshe forgot what he did with the surplus silver because its donors were 'forgotten' souls outside the Mishkan, and a person's money, an extension of his soul, shares his fate.
The word nisayon means both a test and raising up, like a banner; a test exists to promote, and after ten tests Avraham 'graduated'.
The akeida was harder than the furnace of Ur Kasdim because there Avraham felt Hashem near, while at the akeida Hashem seemed far and Avraham had to act against his own understanding.
Eikev, the heel, is the least sensitive part of the body; the generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha is in the dark and insensitive, and that is its test.
The rejected Jews are like the crowns on the letters: outside the letter itself, yet expounded by Rabbi Akiva, and they can express nuances of holiness that the letters alone do not.
The hooks are called vavim because a vav connects: the surplus Jews may be outside, but they are connected, and their hooks were crowned.
Unlike Yom Kippur, where one must go up, Purim comes down to the Jew; if it made non-Jews into Jews it can make a Jew a better Jew.

The drash is the depth of the pshat: the Torah tells of Bilam foolishly cursing Moav for money, which only cleared the way for Israel, to show the lowliness of one ruled by desire; the drash draws the opposite, that those who rule their yetzer make a cheshbon of what will come later.

Since Bilam was Lavan, he knew that Lavan's blessing to Rivka had caused Hashem to delay her children so that Israel's blessing would not be credited to him; Bilam wished to bless Israel so that their blessing would likewise be held back.

The land Sichon took from Moav belongs to Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni, corresponding to Binah, the place where judgments are sweetened, which is why Bilam's curse of Moav turned into a blessing for Israel.

Og, descended from the Nefilim, survived the Flood by clinging to the outside of the teiva, while Noach was inside it; seeing the Anakim in Chevron taught Kalev that in a generation of Nefilim one survives only by grasping the inner teiva, the words of tefillah.
The Rav reads the command to make a light for the teiva in two ways: to make the word shine and to set a gem in it, since every word of tefillah both gives light and is a diamond.
One cries out in tefillah not so that Hashem will hear but so that we will hear; in a time when everyone is spiritually asleep, the shouting is what wakes a person.

The two hundred heads of Sanhedrin from Yissachar date from the time of the second Beis Hamikdash, after Torah had been forgotten in Bavel, so they show the effect of having camped next to Moshe a thousand years earlier.

The Rav reads Zimri's act through the Arizal on Shlomo HaMelech: taking a king's daughter was an attempt to draw her whole nation under the Shechinah, which is why the angels, awaiting the end of days, sided with Zimri.

Zimri's error is repaired in reverse in Rabbi Akiva: Zimri risked turning Jewish seed into gentile seed, and Rabbi Akiva came into the world from converts, gentile seed that became Jewish, and married the wife of Turnus Rufus after a proper conversion.

Pinchas's reward fits his act exactly: because he guarded the Jewish body from mixing with the seed of the serpent, his own body was purified as at Sinai, so he lives on in the body and may enter the Holy of Holies.
The small yud in Pinchas's name stands for the smallest point of Jewishness, which even the lowest Jew carries and which will one day flare into a great flame.

The Kosel Maaravi corresponds to the point of Avraham Avinu in every Jew: the Even Shesiyah extends to it, so in a time of destruction it is the place one can still reach, as the point in the heart is.

Nadav and Avihu's strange fire was an attempt to hasten what must come as fire from heaven; their souls entered Pinchas so that he would repair it, and like Eliyahu he must wait for the Beis HaMikdash to descend in fire.

A person's nefesh extends into his property, which is why chametz, the yetzer hara, must not even be in one's possession on Pesach; Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey would not eat untithed grain because it was part of its owner's nefesh.
Emunah is instinctive in every Jew; the mitzvah is not to acquire it but to keep it from being damaged, just as a healthy heart must be protected from clogged arteries.
The four kingdoms are like a cloud that keeps changing shape: in Avraham's day they were the four kings, in Shemini they are the four impure animals, and in Tazria they are the four kinds of nega'im.
The Masorah's sign for the 91 pesukim of Shemini, the name Ovadiah, is itself a hint that the chazir will return to kashrus, since Ovadiah was the first of Esav to become a ger and a navi.

The middle of the Torah falls at the burnt se'ir of Rosh Chodesh Nissan because the Torah is the blueprint of creation, and its center must correspond to Yerushalayim, the center of the world, and to that day, the center of time.

Shemini, which holds the middle of the Torah according to Rabbi Yehoshua, is read on the first Shabbos after Pesach, while Bereishis, the center according to Rabbi Eliezer, is read on the first Shabbos after Sukkos.
The large vav of 'gachon', the middle letter of the Torah, hints that the nachash, who now crawls on its belly, will stand upright again when Moshiach comes.
Pinchas merited precisely because he was small: Hashem chose a moment when even the Sanhedrin, the nesi'im and Moshe Rabbeinu stood by, to show that greatness is not the monopoly of the great.

Klal Yisrael is like a rope: the higher the elevated Jew climbs, the more he pulls the simple Jew up, and when he lowers himself, the end of the rope falls even lower; so 'Yisrael', the elevated, sitting in idleness led 'ha'am' to the worst sins.

On 'ki gamar chasid, ki pasu emunim' the Rav brings both readings, that the chassid's fall caused the people's emunah to fail and that the people's fall dragged down the chassid, and says both are true.
A mashpia comes from 'shipua', a slope: influence flows downward from the higher one, but one must be careful not to slide down oneself.
One who does not hear the song of creation is like a deaf man at a wedding who thinks the dancers mad; to him those who sway in davening look crazy.
Melamdim are compared to stars because a star looks like a tiny dot yet is far larger than the earth; so a melamed seems small in people's eyes but is truly great.
The Rav reads the placement of the goral verse between the two commands to drive out the nations as a statement that a land held by Hashem's lot cannot be shared with the nations.
He shows from the dual meaning of the root (yerushah, to inherit; horashah, to drive out), like 'saklu me'even', that the inheritance bond is one that cannot be cut off.
A fashion designer creates a new style because his nation's angel above dresses that way, which is why the laws of dress are part of the laws of avodah zarah.
Moshe recognized from the very sound of the shouting at the egel that it was avodah zarah, not war; the Rav applies this to the frenzied shouting of ball games.
The Arizal, the soul of sod, passed away in the Nine Days, because these days, like his teaching, hold a hidden good whose time to be revealed has not yet come.
Dovid HaMelech swam alone in deep waters, and a tzaddik passes trials so that his followers need not; in our generation one must have a 'buddy'.
Citing the Eretz Tzvi, he explains that Jerusalem fell over Kamtza because a son reveals his father's inner self: Kamtza's son's hatred showed Kamtza was a friend only outwardly.
The mann's whiteness is the point of the rebuke: white is pure chesed, and the mann fed Israel as milk feeds a baby, so complaining about it was complaining against open chesed.
The custom of eating milk in the Nine Days is not merely avoiding meat: white foods draw down the chesed that is hidden in these days, while red meat belongs to sorrow and din.
From every Yom Tov one takes something for the whole year, and from Tisha B'Av, also a moed, one takes the comfort that Hashem is with the Jews in their exile and suffering.
History has its own calendar: the generation of the desert was its Pesach, and ikvesa d'Meshicha is its Tisha B'Av, when every accepted sanctuary is destroyed to make room for the new building.
Avraham's first test had no contradiction to his understanding, but the Akeidah set Hashem's command against Hashem's own promise; its greatness is serving Hashem while the questions remain open.
Tanach places Rus right after Malachi because the building of David's kingdom, like the coming of Moshiach, begins with signs of destruction and chutzpah.

The Rav reads Rabbi Yochanan's 'Eliyahu will expound this passage' not as a lack of an answer, since he surely knew Ravina's answer, but as a hint that neveilah and treifah allude to the Erev Rav, whom only Eliyahu will bring to teshuvah.
A bris mila is a small-scale geulah: cutting away the four layers of the orlah parallels subduing the four kingdoms, which is why Eliyahu, the herald of the geulah, is present.
A kashya on a passage of Torah is at the same time a kashya on the Jew whose soul is rooted in that passage, so explaining a difficult text is a way of bringing that Jew to teshuvah.
Eliyahu's role of answering the unresolved questions (Teiku) and his role of bringing Jews to teshuvah are one role, because answering a kashya and repairing a soul are the same act.

Behind every midrash peliah stands a neshama peliah, a concealed soul; one who explains such a midrash reaches a level of gilui Eliyahu, since every good Torah thought is Eliyahu working through one's own body.
The advice to grieve over Yerushalayim when stuck on a kashya is explained by the fact that all Jews together are called Yerushalayim: their teshuvah is its rebuilding, and then the Torah opens.

The Rav explains that the pleasure of a song or niggun is not in any word or note but in the connection between them, and this is what David meant by calling the Torah zemiros: its smuchim are its music.
The seven days of creation are seven notes of an octave; only with the seventh note, Shabbos, can music be played, which is why Shabbos alone has a 'mizmor shir' and why the Torah has seven books.

The four blank lines between the books, from which a get's twelve lines are learned, mirror the exile as a divorce; in the future they will be revealed as the white of the Torah sheb'al peh, showing there never was a get.

David, the soul of Moshiach, lived in the future state in which the whole Torah is song; he was right, but was punished for saying it before its time, and so the Rambam rules according to the present.
Sefer Devarim, whose four lines are not counted for the get, is the seventh book, the book of song and of Moshiach, and it begins on Shabbos Chazon, the day before Tisha b'Av, when Moshiach is born.
The Kinneres, named for the kinor, is the shaliach tzibbur of the seas, completing the seven like Shabbos among days and Eretz Yisrael among lands.
Pesukei dezimra 'cut through' (zemer meaning to cut) the forces that block prayer; it is the war of David, the warrior king, waged with his songs.
The less obligatory a thing is, the dearer it is to Hashem; doing what one need not do shows greater devotion.
In Hallel Hagadol each angel can say only one praise, while a Jew who says them all includes the whole row of angels.
On weekdays the alphabetic blessing has a word per letter, on Shabbos a whole phrase per letter, because Shabbos's added holiness spreads into whole phrases of song.
A person's soul is scattered in many places, and he is led to a place to gather its parts and redeem the souls found there.
When a person is attacked by doubts about a good deed, it is a sign he carries something precious, as robbers ambush only the truck with money.
The first thought on waking to get up and serve Hashem comes from the soul; the second, which talks one out of it, is only a reaction of imagination.

Malki-Tzedek's blessing of Avraham before Hashem, for which he lost the kehunah, is read by the Rav as also an acknowledgment that Avraham was greater, through whom he could reach a higher bittul to Hashem.
Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of the world: like Shabbos, it produces nothing of its own, and for that very reason it is the source of blessing.
The miracle that the people stood crowded yet bowed with room is explained by bittul: one who is batel to Hashem takes up no space.

A king of Dovid's house may sit in the Azarah because his complete bittul makes him part of the building itself, like its stones and wood; this also explains why Dovid is mentioned right before the closing of Boneh Yerushalayim.
In Avraham's war with the kings, throwing dust was not a lack of trust but an expression of bittul: before Hashem the kings were nothing, like dust.
The law that the avodah is done standing appears among the people's duties to the kohen because the kohen's standing bittul is the very reason one is batel to him.
The Rav sees the calendar placement of Shemini next to Pesach as a lesson: one tells what not to eat and the other what to eat, and together they show how central food is to Yiddishkeit.
He reads the Torah's word for becoming impure through forbidden food as hinting at being stuffed up, so that holiness cannot enter.
He describes forbidden food as strengthening the yetzer hara and thereby leading to other aveiros, so it harms every area of Yiddishkeit, not only the act of eating.
He explains the Seder custom that the children should not fall asleep as the children's words to Hashem, asking Him to wake His children from the sleep of golus through the geulah.

The kohen's duty to stand during the avodah is not a law of the avodah but of mora Mikdash and bittul, which is why the Torah places it among the 'rights of the kohanim' in Shoftim rather than in Vayikra.

Malki Tzedek's loss of the kehunah was not a punishment but a revelation of the truth: ordinary people must begin by accepting a rebbe, while the king of Yerushalayim, the highest, had to begin with praise of Hashem Himself.

There is no aliyah l'regel on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur because then the King comes to every Jew; on the festivals the Jew goes to the King, but on the Yamim Noraim His kingship spreads over the whole world.

Kings of the house of David may sit in the Azarah because David's bittul made him like the dust of the Azarah, part of the building of the Mikdash, just as earth placed in a sukkah becomes part of it only when wholly batel.

The 'giving' of the weekdays to Shabbos, of the world to Yerushalayim and of the unlearned to the talmid chacham is like the people giving to their king: in truth it is the receiver who sustains the giver.
Eretz Yisroel is Rosh Hashanah in place, Rosh Hashanah is Eretz Yisroel in time, and the tzaddikim are it in soul; this is why chassidim traveled to their rebbe for Rosh Hashanah.

The Rav pairs 'l'shichno sidreshu' with the king 'asher yivchar Hashem': neither the chosen place nor the chosen king is named in the Torah, and only the chosen soul of Dovid could find the chosen place, which is what Doeg recognized and envied.
Yaakov's 'shifchah' is Avigail: since Naval was Lavan reincarnated, Yaakov's restraint toward Lavan was itself the power of Avigail, who taught Dovid to wait until Hashem acted.

Moshiach's soul comes through unlikely and even disreputable channels so the Satan will not notice, and for the same reason the false rumor about Dovid and Bas Sheva was allowed to spread until the Beis HaMikdash was built.

Dovid considered Naval a rebel even before he reigned, because malchus beis Dovid, anointed with Moshe's oil, is a kingship of the Shechinah; Avigail's two arguments answered the ordinary kingship and the heavenly one separately.
'Avigail eishes Naval' equals 'Dovid melech Yisrael chai v'kayam' in gematria: Avigail is the guarantee of Dovid's eternity, the 'Magen Dovid' that protects the point of Dovid.

Sefer Devarim is the last hei of Hashem's name and the esrog among the four species: it stands apart like teshuvah, and the faults at its beginning are the esrog's delicate tip, cleaned in Elul until all sins become merits.
Following Sefer Yetzirah, Elul is Yerushalayim in time: in Elul one enters Yerushalayim, on Rosh Hashanah the Beis HaMikdash, and on Yom Kippur the Kodesh.

The Torah opens with Bereishis, creation in thought (Tishrei), rather than with the month of action (Nissan), to show that what is first in thought is primary; so Israel, though created later, is 'reishis' and has the true claim to the land.
Hashem deliberately gave the Torah's measures through fruits whose size cannot be fixed, so that no Jew could manage without a talmid chacham.

Bikkurim served a halachic purpose: the kohen in Yerushalayim who saw the seven species from all over the land each year could rule on that year's shiurim, which explains 'the kohen of those days', the yearly blessing, and the restriction to the seven species.

One can stand on the soil of Eretz Yisrael, even on Har HaBayis, and not be in Eretz Yisrael, just as one can be in the day of Shabbos without being in Shabbos; the bikkurim declaration, recalling the Exodus, proclaims that the bringer has left the land of the nations.
Eretz Yisrael is to space what Rosh Hashanah is to the year, and the forty days from Elul to Yom Kippur are Eretz Yisrael in time, which is why Ki Savo is read then.
The statement that a ben sorer umoreh never was and never will be teaches that no Jew can be given up on as lost; whoever looks like the worst can become the best.
Ki Savo's curses end without consolation because they themselves are concealed blessings, and the work of Elul is to uncover them.

The Rav applies the Or HaChaim's explanation of tumas ohel to childbirth: the mother's tumah is not a sign of anything wrong but the trace left by the great holiness of the child who learned Torah inside her.

The shorter tumah after a boy is not because there was less holiness but because the bris, with Eliyahu HaNavi's presence, interrupts it; the Torah places the bris right after the seven days to show this.
Just as kinship obligates a mother in mourning, it also gives her a share in the joy of her son's bris, which is why she too may eat on a postponed Tisha B'Av.
The natural law that everything returns to its source is what loshon hakodesh calls yovel, and it underlies teshuvah, the shofar and the fiftieth level reached on Pesach night.
Esav's nations write from the left because they are the impurity of Yitzchak's Din, and Yishmael's from the right because they are the impurity of Avraham's Chesed.

Aviv is read as the aleph-beis from the right, Chesed, while Tishrei's letters run the aleph-beis backwards, Din; the yud-beis in Aviv adds up to gimel and also hints at the twelve opening days of Nisan.

The Rav reads the bringing of bikkurim as a po'el dimyoni: the seven species stand for seven kinds of Jews, and carrying them to Yerushalayim with song is a symbolic act that assures the exiles will be brought back the same way.
Chazal chose Arami oved avi for the telling of the Exodus because it contains the fiftieth mention of the Exodus in the Torah, which carries the power of the final redemption from the fiftieth gate.

Rosh Hashana is the Beis Hamikdash in time: as the world spread out from the place of the Mikdash, the whole year spreads out from Rosh Hashana, and on it the Mikdash comes to the Jew rather than the Jew going to the Mikdash.
Since time is higher than place, the destroyers of the Mikdash ruled only over its place; the sanctity of Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur and Shabbos, the Mikdash in time, remained beyond their reach.
There is no aliya l'regel on Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur because the Mikdash then comes to every Jew, which is why one bows fully on Yom Kippur even today, 'before Hashem'.
Death entered the world as aging, the loss of freshness; chaim means freshness, and the Mikdash, the place of reishis, is where aging and sleep had no hold.
A fruit that ripens before all others holds a precious soul with zerizus, so it belongs in the place of reishis, and the owner gives it to the Kohen as his messenger to elevate it.

The leaves grow first but the tree was planted for the fruit; so too the world was created in thought in Tishrei but in deed in Nisan, and the Torah opens with Bereishis to show that what is first in thought, Israel and the talmid chacham, is the primary thing.
The Torah deliberately left its shiurim unclear so that a Jew would never be able to manage alone and would always need to ask a talmid chacham.
The purpose of bringing bikkurim to the kohen was to learn halachah: from the seven species brought from every region, the kohen could fix that year's shiurim, which changed with Israel's merits.
A gentile in Eretz Yisrael walks on a strip of foreign land; likewise a Jew can live in the Land, or stand in Shabbos or in Elul, without being in it, unless he connects to it.
Since the purpose is learning, the kohen of one's own days is essential; today the 'kohen' to whom one brings bikkurim can be a rebbe, a friend, or the author of a sefer.
The ben sorer umoreh teaches that no Jew is ever lost: the one that Tanna saw later became such a tzaddik that people sat at his grave.

The proof that the four lepers were Gehazi and his sons is that they were not cured: in a time when Elisha healed even a non-Jew like Naaman, only those under his own eternal curse would remain lepers.

The lepers' words 'this is a day of good tidings and we are silent' express their hope to be cured: since all healing comes from the aspect of Eliyahu, and the bearer of good news receives that aspect, gladdening a whole city could lift the tzaraas.

The Navi records the lepers' full reasoning to show how compelling it was, so that the king's refusal stands out as irrational; his later acceptance of a two-horse search proves the refusal came only so that Gehazi would not become the bearer of good tidings.

The first report reached only 'the house of the king', as if spoken to the walls, because the good tidings of Gehazi were not accepted; the second report, from the searchers, was told to the king himself.
Gehazi, who kept talmidim from Elisha, became measure for measure the teacher of all Klal Yisrael, since the halacha of risking chayei sha'ah for a cure is learned from his words.

The same halacha that Gehazi taught argues for his own return: if a Jewish body is so precious that its healing overrides chayei sha'ah, which itself overrides Shabbos, how much more must one go out of the way to heal a Jewish soul.

The elder trampled on Erev Pesach, a gilgul of the mocking officer, died just before the night of freedom; had he reached Pesach, which like Yovel returns everyone who was pushed away, he would have had his tikkun.

The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the 'formation' of the new year, like the forty days of an embryo's formation, during which prayer can still decide whether the year is a 'male' of blessing or a 'female' of curse.

Under the orlah of the heart, as under the orlah of a bris, lies the Divine Name; 'mi ya'aleh lanu hashamayma' begins with the letters of milah and ends with the letters of the Name, teaching that one ascends to heaven through milah, and in Elul Hashem Himself is the mohel.

The twenty-sixth day counted from Rosh Chodesh Elul matches the numerical value of the Divine Name, and 'umal Hashem' is the twenty-sixth verse of the sedra, while its fortieth and last verse, 'ki hu chayecha', corresponds to Yom Kippur, the fortieth day.

The mazal of Elul, the maiden, is the one who escaped a force far stronger than herself by taking the angel's own wings; likewise the yetzer hara is an angel, and a Jew escapes him by using his own fire and wings to fly to Hashem.

Shevet Dan, cast out of the Clouds of Glory measure for measure, were given the task of returning lost objects, because lost souls are the ones whose mission is to bring back what was lost; Elul, in the cycle of camps and books, is Dan's time.
The verse says the dispersed will be gathered 'from the end of the heavens', not of the earth: however far a Jew falls, a thread of heaven still goes with him, by which he can pull himself up.

Chana mentioned nursing rather than her other organs as a way of praying through gates that were still open, just as the Gemara prefers praying about hunger over plague, since granting sustenance includes granting life.
The Rav reads the place of the Mikdash, Rosh Hashana and the king's soul as three parallel 'heads' of place, time and soul, each tied to the first letter of Bereishis that contains the whole Torah.
Only the king could reveal the place of the Mikdash, because its laws are his own portion in the Torah; scholarship alone could not find it from the same verses.
'From the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water' describes not the lowest class of one generation but the last generations, whose avodah in darkness feels like the hardest physical labor.
The later custom that everyone, even children, fasts on erev Rosh Hashana, where the Midrash spoke only of tzaddikim, shows that today's simple Jews are counted as the great ones of the past.
The shofar returns to Hashem the very breath of life He blew into man on Rosh Hashana, so blowing it is crowning Him with one's own soul.
If, as Reb Pinchas says, there is a new Satan every year, then by the principle that good outweighs bad there is also a new yetzer tov every year, so past failures need not decide the coming year.

The Rav reads 'Rosh' Hashanah like the first letter of a word, which already holds the whole word in potential: the whole year is contained in Rosh Hashanah, and in the same way Haazinu contains the whole Torah.
Haazinu itself answers the question of why the Jews of Europe did not resist: one could chase a thousand only because Hashem had handed them over, and Haazinu foretold it.
Jews rejoice in the Day of Judgment because they want to be judged by Hashem Himself, like a child who runs to his mother even knowing she may slap him.
What comes from Hashem can be bitter but never bad, like a bitter wine that is in fact excellent, as only a connoisseur knows.
The hundred sounds of the shofar correspond to the ten utterances of creation, each including ten, so that hearing the shofar is like standing at the root of the year's whole course.

Malchiyos opens with Aleinu because Yehoshua said it when he broke through the walls of Yericho: accepting Hashem's kingship means breaking the wall around one's own heart to reach the point of yechidah.
Rebbi's suffering for the calf was not a punishment that Yom Kippur could atone for, but a reality: Hashem's mercy toward a person follows that person's own mercy.
Shabbos holds the kedushah of acharis and Rosh Chodesh the kedushah of reishis, so a Shabbos Rosh Chodesh joins both, which Klal Yisrael has and Amalek, with a beginning but no end, lacks.

Avner was hinted in the middle letters because the first and last letters contain the whole word: a Jew who strays loses only his middle, while his beginning and end, his connection to the Avos, remain.
A mother carrying a child is like a walking beis medrash, since the child learns Torah from a malach in the womb; her tumah after birth is the emptying of that kedushah.

Eliyahu HaNavi, whose neshamah did not eat from the Eitz HaDaas, is connected to the eighth, the level of Moshiach, and wherever he comes tumah is pushed away; this is why the passuk of the yoledes mentions milah.

Like the father, mohel and sandek, the mother may eat at a bris on a postponed Tisha B'Av because her shaychus neshamah with the child shares in his simchah, and the same closeness lets Eliyahu's purity reach her.
Because of lashon hara Klal Yisrael became like a metzora sent out of Yerushalayim, and Moshiach himself sits as a metzora who cannot bring them back until the sin is repaired.
The Ramban's reading of Haazinu as a testimony makes the parsha itself a proof of emunah: what has already come true guarantees what has not yet, which is why it is a segulah for emunah.
Because writing Haazinu means writing the whole Torah, and each Jew is one of the Torah's letters, Haazinu, a miniature of the Torah, contains every Jewish soul.
The place of the hint is itself the message: first letters are a Jew's root and last letters his end, which can never be erased; only the middle letters, a passing state, could carry Avner's erasure.
The Shabbos that contains the whole year reads the parsha that contains the whole Torah and every soul, so that all souls and all of the year can be repaired on it.

Like the Megillah, whose miracle is understood to begin from its first verse only once the king's sleepless night revealed it, the redemption the Arizal saw for 5736 may already have begun without being seen.
A person is like a switch: accepting Hashem's kingship on oneself is what turns on His kingship over the whole world.
In tefillah we speak to Hashem and in Torah He speaks to us; that is why only the middle brachah of Yom Kippur contains pesukim, for on Yom Kippur Hashem speaks to the Jew as a Father.
The Rav reads 'shmitah to Hashem' as a mirror: by letting go of the debts others owe us, we cause Hashem to let go of the debt our sins have created.
Because the shmitah of years is counted from Tishrei, Rosh Hashanah is itself a time of release, and every Shabbos, the seventh day, is a small Rosh Hashanah with the same power.
Letzanus is the exact opposite of emunah: emunah is the gate into serving Hashem, and letzanus is the gate out of it.

Following Rabbi Tzadok, the Gemara's statement that scoffers do not receive the Shechinah means that the scoffer is kept out of the palaces of tefillah, so that even while davening his mind wanders elsewhere.
Pharaoh's superhuman stubbornness through the plagues came from his humor: a joke lets a person escape reality, so he never has to face it.
Pharaoh's punishment, 'that I made sport of Egypt', was measure for measure: Hashem let him make good jokes and then made a joke of him.
Just as the Torah was not satisfied with building cities of refuge but demanded signs at every crossroads, Elul does not help on its own: it must be announced and pointed out, or people pass it by.
Elul's verse, 'a road in the sea', describes a path that does not hold still: without constant signposts one drifts, and the forty days are gone before one notices.
One who truly relies only on Hashem is judged by Hashem alone and not by the lower courts, which explains the Arizal's promise that the sayer of L'Dovid emerges meritorious.
Following Rashi, the heart's stirring in Elul is itself Hashem's message, delivered through the heart as His messenger, telling a Jew to seek Him.

Every hour of the forty days is one lug of a mikveh; wasted hours are like drawn water poured in, and the remedy is to join oneself to Hashem, the true tzaddik, as a mikveh is repaired through contact with a kosher one.
Elul's own verse speaks of a killer, hinting that the teshuvah of Elul is for the 'bloodshed' of shaming and hurting another.
The word 'this' in 'this Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah expounded' is the finger of a generation that saw the Churban, pointing at sins between man and his fellow as its cause.
The camp of Israel in the desert, seen from above with ruach hakodesh, was itself a Sefer Torah, with Levi in the middle like Vayikra among the five Chumashim.
The megadef's two complaints, about the camp and about the lechem hapanim, are one: if the loaves are cold, Hashem's love for Dan has cooled and Dan can take in an outsider.
The claim that Hashem's love for the Jews has cooled and passed to others is, according to the Rav, the whole teaching of Yeshu, the later incarnation of the megadef according to the Arizal.
The twelve loaves match the twelve distinct arrangements of Hashem's four-letter Name, since its two identical letters reduce twenty-four to twelve, so each tribe has its own unique holiness.
The Arizal could not fathom the secret of the lechem hapanim because it is the depth of the Jewish soul, which is deeper than any mitzvah.
Revealing the secrets of the Torah is revealing the hidden secret of every Jew, so Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai after the second Churban did what Yechezkel's Merkavah did after the first.
Lag BaOmer and Purim fall on the same weekday because both are for those who stumbled, the tribe of Dan whom the clouds did not protect and Amalek attacked.

The Rav reads 'the place causes' of the rebellious elder as the meeting of the central soul with the central place: even the greatest sage of the Sanhedrin decides for all of Israel only when he sits where creation, and Torah, go out to the world.
The structure of the Torah mirrors creation: according to the Masorah, the middle pasuk of Sefer Devarim is the very pasuk of 'min hamakom hahu', from which 'the place causes' is learned.
Just as Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, only the highest laws, those carrying kares, belong to the Great Sanhedrin in the highest place, while local matters stay with local courts.
The halachah books record the rashei teivos of Elul, something not done for other halachos, because a 'rosh' contains the whole word just as Rosh Hashanah contains the year.
The Avos are called mountains and were born in Tishrei because they are the small kernels from which the whole Jewish people grew, a point in time and in soul that holds much.

The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur parallel the forty days in which a child is formed: during them it is easy to pray that the year be blessed, while afterwards change is still possible but only with great effort.

The Rav reads bikkurim as a poel dimyoni: each of the seven species stands for a kind of Jew, so carrying them with music to the Mikdash enacts in advance the return of all Jews to Tziyon after the churban.

He counts back from the end of the Torah to show that the fiftieth praiseworthy mention of yetzias Mitzrayim is the bikkurim declaration, so the future geulah is tied to bikkurim and to the reading before Rosh Hashanah.
Since time is higher than place, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the Mikdash of time, rise above the regalim of place, and no enemy, Bavel or Rome, could ever destroy them.
He explains the custom that the chazzan begins Hamelech from his place before reaching the amud: on Rosh Hashanah the King comes to each Jew, and he need not walk to the mizbeach.

Moshe instituted a prayer before prayer only on entering Eretz Yisroel, because only there did he feel a holiness greater than the heaven over chutz la'aretz; 'the heaven of heavens' in his praise is Eretz Yisroel.
The Rav defines life as freshness and death as aging; Adam's sin on Rosh Hashanah brought aging, and the Mikdash, where bread stayed warm and no one slept, is the place where that sin has no rule.
The fig that ripened before all others holds a soul of zrizus, so it belongs to the Mikdash, the place of reishis; this is why bikkurim, the first-ripened fruit, are brought there.

The Rav reads the Satan's flight to Botzrah as instinct, not reasoning: in sudden panic a being runs to its root, as the sea dog runs to dry land, so the flight itself reveals that Botzrah, the heart of Edom's harsh judgment, is his root.

Using the Yismach Moshe's rule that a gentile's unintentional act is at root deliberate, the Rav shows that the Satan's three 'errors' are not errors at all: fleeing to Botzrah reveals him as deliberate and therefore no angel protected by a refuge city.
The Rav connects the Kodesh HaKodashim, where no blemish enters, with the inner point of every Jew's heart where even the worst sinner never sinned, so Yerushalayim includes all the cities of refuge.

Since the mitzvah of three additional cities of refuge is the one mitzvah never fulfilled, the Rav sees it as Moshiach's own mitzvah, the one the Satan holds back, and which a Jew awakens when he runs to Hashem through Torah.
A murderer loses his place because he emptied the place of a person sent with a mission; by the same rule a Jew in galus has lost his place, and Yerushalayim, above place, gives it back.
The Rav links the Satan, whose name he connects with the number one hundred and with forgetting, to the hundred daily brachos, which are meant to keep a person remembering Hashem.
The Rav reads 'asher tikre'u osam' not only as Jews fixing the moadim but as Jews being the moadim themselves, each in his place in the calendar.
Because melacha comes from the 39 curses after the sin, Shabbos, which is blessing, has no place for it; a talmid chacham who is Shabbos is likewise freed from labor by those who are 'weekdays'.
Tisha B'Av is the one moed absent from Emor, because it is a moed that turned sour, like a gifted boy who strayed, waiting to be restored when Moshiach comes.
Rashi's two explanations of the ben ish Mitzri are one: refused a place in Dan's camp, he denied that the lowly tribe's challah, Hashem's love for it, stays fresh.
Each challah being baked separately shows that even Dan has its own individual importance before Hashem.
The Gemara's reading of 'yeshno' as 'grown old' makes Haman's claim the same as the ben ish Mitzri's, which is why this parsha belongs with Purim.

The souls of the very end, the forgotten and neglected ones, are bound to the very beginning, just as the last words of the Torah, 'le'einei kol Yisrael', are joined to Bereishis; in them lies the spark of Moshiach.

Moshe forgot the 1,775 shekels not as a lapse but because those Jews' very existence was shikchah: their half-shekel hung outside the Mishkan's curtain, so by Torah law they were 'to be forgotten', and Hashem, who never forgets, reminded him.
Haman's ten thousand talents redeemed only the half-shekels that became sockets; he thought he need pay nothing for the forgotten Jews, and that was his error.
Elul, like Adar, ends a half-year, and both are the time of hashavas aveidah: Dan the 'me'asef' and Esther, the lost one who is sought, are its souls, in contrast to Amalek who makes Jews lost.
The full spelling of the letters of kesef equals esh, the Rav says; so 'kesef malei' given by Avraham and Dovid was money with fire, while Haman's silver lacked it.
The numerical value of Yisrael minus that of Amalek is the value of esh: the whole difference between them is that Yisrael gives with fire and Amalek without it.

The Rav reads 'ki yipalei' as a matter belonging to the fiftieth gate, beyond the grasp of each tribe's judges, which is why it must go up to Yerushalayim, where 'the tribes went up' above their division.
Yaakov did not need to teach Yosef Taharos because Yosef, corresponding to Friday and Taharos, mastered it on his own, and this is the 'ben zekunim' for which Yaakov loved him more than his brothers.

Since tahara gives fruit its taste and smell, Yaakov sensed in the grain from Egypt the fragrance only Yosef, the order of Taharos, could put into it, and so 'saw that there was shever in Egypt', hope that Yosef lived.
Elul is not Yosef's month by the tribal banners, but it is by the seven shepherds; as the sixth, like Friday, it is Moshiach ben Yosef preparing for Tishrei, Moshiach ben David.
Elul has an advantage over Tishrei: like Shiloh, where kodashim were eaten wherever it was seen, it has no wall, and Yosef merited this open sanctity because he guarded his eyes.
Tzedakah, the midah of Yosef and yesod, draws down chesed that no other good deed can bring, because chesed is a free gift beyond what one deserves.

Following Rav Tzadok, the Rav contrasts the mikveh, where a person exerts himself and goes down, with water sprinkled from above while he does nothing; Sefirah is the second kind, since the Yidden only count and the purity comes down from Hashem.
When Klal Yisrael reaches Hod shebeHod, Hashem is already at Tiferes shebeTiferes coming toward them, as a chassan goes out of the chuppah to meet his kallah; this is the special love of Lag Baomer.

The poor man receives grain that falls to the ground and grain that is forgotten because he himself is down on the ground and forgotten; in the same way, every kind of grain, and even the bread a Jew buys, has a connection to a particular soul.
The Rav reads 'vehenif es ha'Omer' as Hashem's command to the kohen, the tzaddik, to pick up the fallen Yidden, and ties it by gematria to 'Sukkas David hanofeles'.
The two loaves of Shavuos are chametz, unlike every other mincha, because by then the chametz itself has gone through the lifting of the Omer and all the Yidden are holy.
Tisha B'Av is a moed because it belongs to those who had the ability to be great but ruined themselves; they will be rebuilt, and it will become the greatest simcha.
The double measure of flour with the Omer, though a sheep normally takes one, reflects a double purification: the Yidden count, and Hashem counts.
The place of the Mikdash is not stated in the Torah because it is not a place of nature: as the root point of creation it is hidden and can only be reached by seeking it.
Yerushalayim is the highest place not in elevation but because on a globe the 'top' is the point where its formation began.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur parallel the forty days in which a child is formed, so the year's formation is given into a person's hands through tefillah during them.
The middle verse of Sefer Devarim, about the Sanhedrin's ruling 'from that place', corresponds to the middle of the world, because the root of the Torah must sit in the root of creation.
Doeg's envy was not over a mere chiddush: by finding the place of the Mikdash, which is his own root, Dovid showed that he was the true king and not Shaul.
The Yamim Nora'im are named for the Beis HaMikdash, 'how awesome is this place', because they are the Mikdash in time.

The Rav reads the Chasam Sofer's explanation of hakhel as the way of Avraham rather than Chanoch: Chanoch withdrew and became like an angel, while Avraham gave up some of his own ascent to teach others, which is why Hashem praised Avraham, and why Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who expounded the reward of bringing the children, is called Avraham's descendant.

The Rav draws a parallel between the king and Rosh Hashanah: as the king heads and includes the nation in the dimension of soul, Rosh Hashanah heads and includes the year in the dimension of time, so the head of the nation decides when the head of the year falls.

He answers his opening question by reading the order of the Mishnah as a statement: the chapter on a Rosh Hashanah 'sanctified by Heaven' precedes the shofar, because with the shofar one asks for a Rosh Hashanah and a king of revealed kingship, he'aras panim, not one of hidden face.

The Rav compares the infants at hakhel to every Jew at the shofar: the shofar speaks in thoughts too high for words that the mind does not grasp but the soul hears, just as the children absorb the king's words without understanding, and they may even receive what their grown parents no longer can.

He explains that the fear asked for on Rosh Hashanah is a fear of Hashem's goodness and majesty, 'mehadar geono', which for a Jew is the sweetest pleasure, the more fear the more delight, whereas a gentile only fears when something threatens him.

Through Hoshea the Rav shows why the Rosh Hashanah tears are tears of joy: Hashem told the prophet who suggested exchanging Israel that one cannot exchange a child, so the sinner who returns weeps as a child returning to his Father, with shame mixed with happiness.
Rosh Hashanah is like the factory where an item can be made exactly to order; during the year one is only at the store, where what was made can merely be redirected.
Daily tefillah can change the channel through which the blessing allotted on Rosh Hashanah flows, from wealth to children, but cannot add to its total.

Just as Yerushalayim is the place from which the world began, Rosh Hashanah is the Yerushalayim of the calendar; on the regalim Jews go up to the King, but on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the King comes to every Jew.
Yerushalayim is a barren mother whose remembrance, like that of Sarah, Rachel and Chana, must come on Rosh Hashanah itself, and every Jew can be the one who brings it.
The commotion people make on earth is like a radio picking up waves from heaven, yet the nations' uproar over Eretz Yisrael is empty rebellion, and its only effect above is Hashem's laughter.
Because Rosh Hashanah is creation from nothing, only one who makes himself nothing can be created anew on it, which is why the more bent the shofar, the better.
'Teruah' means friendship: by joining with all of Klal Yisrael, as a fingernail shares in the body's good year, a person draws the judgment away from himself.

The fact that the same Chumash and Gemara serve a child, a lifelong scholar and every generation back to Moshe Rabbeinu, unlike any secular textbook, is itself a visible miracle showing that Torah comes from heaven.
The Torah calls idolatry by the unusual name 'eiker' only where a Jew is sold to it, because there it voices Hashem's protest: the idolatry will be uprooted so that the Jew is not.
The slave's descending levels mirror Mitzrayim: Hashem lets a person sink by his own choice, but cuts the time short before the point of no return, as He took the Jews out at the forty-ninth gate.
The redemptions of the sold Jew follow the order of Shemoneh Esrei: first the uprooting of heresy, then redemption through attaching to a tzaddik, then Moshiach ben David hinted in 'dodo'.
Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is a Yovel of return: the word contains Shabbos, which means return, and on it heaven comes down to a person instead of his having to rise to it.
Rus returned from the field of Moav to Beis Lechem Yehudah, whose initial letters spell Yovel, which is why her story belongs to Shavuos.
Yovel means both a shofar and a stream, and the two meanings meet: with the shofar of redemption a Jew's roots are replanted by the stream of Torah.

In the mashal the shofar is the merchant's advocate and Shabbos his relative: on a Shabbos Rosh Hashanah Shabbos defends the Jew, but only if he has not slighted it, so the Torah's 'no melachah' is advice to make peace with Shabbos.

The Torah, foreseeing the Rabbinic decree, gave 'zichron teruah' as a second path: since the shofar is withheld only for the sake of Shabbos, the withholding itself is a merit of Shabbos, and in the Mikdash, where there was no decree and so no such merit, the shofar had to be blown.

Shemittah frees a person from debts, and his greatest debts are sins; yovel, called by the shofar's own name, is a Shabbos of Shabbosos with the power of Yom Kippur, which is why one may confess between the tekios though sin is otherwise not mentioned on Rosh Hashanah.
Like the Gemara's teaching that refraining from praying for the sick on Shabbos itself brings healing, refraining from the shofar on Shabbos lets Shabbos itself have mercy and plead for the Jew.

Since Hashem created the world through ten utterances and ceased from them on Shabbos, the core of Shabbos observance for a refined Jew is ceasing from weekday speech, and even weekday thought, since the world was first conceived in thought.

The Rosh Hashanah readings speak only of Sarah and Chana being remembered and say nothing of judgment or creation, because the great barren one still awaiting remembrance is Yerushalayim; one should put her name in his prayers just as one asks a friend to pray for him.

The Rav, following the Arvei Nachal, reads 'all labor you shall not do' on Rosh Hashana that falls on Shabbos as Hashem's advice to appease Shabbos, which then pleads for Israel even more powerfully than the shofar.
Shabbos, as the day of the additional soul, is cast as a relative close to the Jewish soul who holds the highest office in the King's court, and before whom even the Satan trembles.
The Rav argues that because Hashem created the world with speech and thought, not with the hand, a ben Torah's rest on Shabbos must reach his speech and his thought.
Citing the Shelah, the Rav reads 'you shall call Shabbos a delight' as an obligation that Shabbos itself have pleasure from the person, not only that the person enjoy Shabbos.
The Rav explains that each verse of malchiyos, zichronos and shofaros is like one of the ten utterances, so the person saying it is creating the coming year's world, and himself along with it.
Since the final sealing extends to the last day of Chanukah, which this year falls on Shabbos, a person who has befriended Shabbos has an advocate even then.

The Mishnah places the story of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua just before the shofar chapter because it teaches that the nasi, the 'Rosh Hashanah of souls', fixes the Rosh Hashanah of time; the shofar chapter is then the acceptance of that King.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, a nasi appointed by Heaven through a miracle, darshened that children come to hakhel because his own root was a Father turning His face to His children; 'the generation is not orphaned' in which he lives.
Hakhel and Rosh Hashanah are parallel gatherings: hakhel gathers all souls, each a letter of the Torah, to the king who reads them; Rosh Hashanah gathers all days to their king.
A gentile who lacks something is afraid, but for a Jew it is the reverse: 'there is no lack for those who fear Him', for the one who lacks is the one without fear of Heaven.
Fear can be fear of goodness itself, as in 'they will fear Hashem and His goodness': one can be afraid of a gun or a wicked man, but the fear of Hashem's goodness is a sweet fear.

The tekios follow the Avos and David: tekiah, shevarim and teruah draw down Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov with David between them, and the tekiah gedolah is the shofar of Moshiach, the great hakhel of all souls.
Shavuos is one day but really a whole week, the eighth week above nature, which is why its offerings may still be brought all seven days.
One who violated Shemitah loses his bond to Shabbos, so Shabbos feels to him like a prison; that is why Shemitah cannot free him and only Yovel can.
The Torah was given in forty days, the mem of 'mishpacha'; a Jew who loses it is left with 'shifcha', and Yovel restores him to the mishpacha.

Counting the nineteen 'geulos' of Behar against Shemoneh Esrei, the redemption of the man sold to the idol falls on the twelfth, the bracha against heretics, and the one who redeems him on the thirteenth, the bracha of the tzaddikim.
The soul of Malchus Beis David was hidden among Moav like a diamond in a garbage can, where the Satan would never think to look.
The Rav suggests, saying he has not seen it in a sefer, that the parsha of Yovel is written in Beis Lechem Yehudah, which explains why Rus returned there and why Rachel is buried there.
The Rashbam's 'forever' does not argue with the halachah; it describes what a servant who refused Shemitah deserves, and Yovel rescues him anyway.

The three places the Torah speaks of Moshiach correspond to the three signs of Moshiach in the Rambam, and the cities of refuge in Shoftim are the one mitzvah of the Torah never yet fulfilled, which Moshiach will complete.

The greatness of the Akeidah over the first trial is not the self-sacrifice itself, but that Avraham fell from his clear closeness to Hashem, saw Him only from afar, and faced questions that had no answer.
That the simple answer, that Hashem never commanded the slaughter, did not occur to a sage like Avraham is itself the definition of a trial: the answer is hidden while the test lasts.
At the Akeidah Avraham was lowered into the spiritual state of the last generation, so his victory there planted the strength of emunah specifically into the generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha.

Shema is the head and 'emes', the hidden word not written in the Torah that the shliach tzibbur supplies, is the heel: in the last generation truth is hidden, and the leader's cry of 'emes' brings it in for the whole congregation.
Esther's self-sacrifice was greater than a martyr's, since she gave up even her good name, letting people think she had ties to Haman; this is the same quality as Avraham's at the Akeidah.
The 'mishpat' of the G-d of Yaakov is read as the kal vachomer Yaakov can claim from Eisav: if Eisav's three tears won blessings, the tears of Yaakov's children must surely be answered.
The ram is not a substitute that lessens the akeidah but its completion: Avraham's longing to sacrifice joined to the deed of offering the ram, so the two are really one act.
The word 'itto' in 'nimolu itto' teaches that Avraham's longing to do the mitzvah again was joined to the circumcision of his household, so it counted as his own mitzvah more than once.
Moshe Rabbeinu cited the ram of the akeidah to ask that his longing not remain thought alone, and 'rav lach' answered that his longing was so great that no deed was needed.
'Kol hame'aneg es haShabbos' is read as one who gives delight to Shabbos, not one who takes pleasure on Shabbos.
Rosh Hashanah needs no aliyah l'regel because on it the quality of Yerushalayim, Hashem's kingship, comes out into the whole world, reaching even the Jews of chutz la'aretz.

When Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos and the shofar is silent, the Shabbos itself takes the shofar's place as the Jews' advocate, so making peace with the Shabbos becomes the urgent avodah of Shabbos Shuva.
Since the esrog is like the heart, Hashem is the heart of Yisroel and Shabbos is His name, on a Shabbos when no lulav is taken the Shabbos itself serves as the Jews' esrog.
Shabbos is one sixtieth of Olam Haba, yet unlike a forbidden taste that is nullified in sixty, its taste of Olam Haba can still be felt if one prepares for it.
Hashem gave Moshe a third sign so as not to rule between Rebbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on chazakah, because the Written Torah does not decide disputes of the Oral Torah.
In Haazinu one ushpiz of a disputed day is named explicitly and the other only hinted, so that the Torah does not decide between the Arizal's order and the other order of the ushpizin.
The last pasuk of Haazinu, the 122nd from Rosh Chodesh Elul, corresponds to Zos Chanukah: one may look at the hidden light but not yet use it, as Moshe could see the land but not enter.

The Ramak teaches that the fiftieth mention of Yetzias Mitzrayim in the Torah, which stands for the coming of Moshiach, is not the fiftieth in order but the one right after the tochachah in Bechukosai.
The 49 curses of the tochachah can be seen as the 49 gates of galus, with the fiftieth gate, the end of galus, following immediately after.

Jews keep even mitzvos given to the Avos, like milah and gid hanasheh, only because Moshe Rabbeinu commanded them, since belief in Moshe rests on Hashem appointing him before the whole nation at Sinai.
The laws of nature are themselves a Torah: a bird flies and a tree grows because Hashem commanded it, and He breaks nature only rarely, as one would set aside a mitzvah only when truly needed.
Shemitah is a Har Sinai that never ended: Matan Torah was a one-time open miracle, while Shemitah defies nature in Eretz Yisrael in every cycle for all to see.
The Torah's willingness to promise things that every Jew could test, like the safety of the land during the pilgrimages, is itself a proof that it comes from Hashem.

The knocking of the Avos in these days is explained as a meeting of two roots: the Avos are the root of every Jewish soul, and the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, corresponding to the ten utterances of creation, are the root of the year, so when the root of time arrives the root of the soul stirs.

Yom Kippur is the one day of 'echad' because yechidah is the level where all Jewish souls fuse, as in Yaakov Avinu before the tribes divided; therefore hatred toward another Jew is a barrier to the day itself, not only a separate sin.

The precious stone the tailor found in his fish is read as the seven blessings of the Yom Kippur Shemoneh Esrei: the fish, a creature that stayed pure before the Mabul, gave him sparks of righteousness that let him daven a true Yom Kippur prayer.
The word for tailor is taken as an image of Yom Kippur: a tailor takes separate cut pieces and joins them into one garment, and a Jew's success on Yom Kippur is fitting himself into that unity.

The sealing at Ne'ilah is the engraving of the second luchos on each Jewish heart, cut as deep as the heart was softened through teshuvah, so the real 'good sealing' is a heart for avodas Hashem all year.

On Yom Kippur Jews do eat: they eat the mann in its original angelic form, the food Moshe ate on the mountain, so the fast is itself the oneg Shabbos and the greater the affliction, the greater the delight.
Kol Nidrei opens Yom Kippur because, as Rabbah bar bar Chana's story hints, the vow to annul is Hashem's own oath to keep Israel in galus.

The Rav reads the Hebrew servant's release at yovel as a picture of teshuvah: even one who has fallen so far that the seventh year cannot move him goes free when he hears the yovel shofar, as even the lost will come running at Moshiach's shofar.
Yovel is not just a law of land and servants but a law of creation: everything that wandered from its root must return, and teshuvah is that law applied to the soul hewn from the Kisei HaKavod.

The requirement that yovel apply only when all inhabitants are in the land is not a technical detail: yovel is the return to the root of Kol Yisrael where all souls are one, so without all Jews together there is no yovel, and likewise one who is not at peace with other Jews is not in the world of Yom Kippur.
The Rav explains why the tekiah blown after Yom Kippur has no teruah: it is already an awakening of the shofar gadol of Moshiach, the climax of return.

Melaveh malkah belongs to David HaMelech, the greatest, precisely because it comes after Shabbos: at the end of each seven there is a chance that instead of a new week the eighth day of Moshiach, a day that is all Shabbos, will begin.
