The Rav calls the Tishrei after shemittah the 'shalosh seudos' of shemittah: just as the end of Shabbos is a time of eis ratzon, the end of the shemittah year is a great eis ratzon when prayers are accepted.
The three longest units in Torah, Naso, Tehillim 119 and Bava Basra, share 176 because 176 is eight times the twenty-two letters, the number of Torah raised to the number above nature.
Wine, yayin, equals seventy and sanctifies Shabbos, the seventh day; oil, shemen, is related to shemonah and sanctifies Chanukah, whose eight days are borrowed from the days of Moshiach.
Bava Basra counts 176 daf only together with the missing first daf, because at the very source of Torah one does not try to understand and begins with faith.
Shavuos and Chanukah are 'cousins' through the number eight: both are free of a fixed date, both fall in the third month of their half-year, and both are read in Naso.
Cut-off Jews are like hair, which grows even on the dead; the Nazir, who may not cut his hair, holds them, and Moshiach will replant them as the crown on the head of Adam HaRishon.
Yaakov Avinu was not mistaken in seeing Moshiach in Shimshon; Shimshon truly could have been Moshiach, but the generation did not merit it.
The lion Shimshon tore apart alludes to the lion that destroyed the Beis HaMikdash, the mazal of Av, showing that Shimshon had the makings of Moshiach.
Just as the Beis HaMikdash is a mountain in place rising to the holy of holies, the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul are a mountain in time, and Yom Kippur at Ne'ilah is its holy of holies.

The pesukim of the season's parshiyos match the levels of teshuvah: Vayeilech's thirty for those who walk ahead, Nitzavim's forty for those who stand still, Ha'azinu's fifty-two for those who need until Shemini Atzeres, and together 122, the days to Zos Chanukah.
When Yom Kippur falls on Shabbos, the Shabbos is strengthened by Yom Kippur and the day is compounded, so its kapparah is greater than that of an ordinary Yom Kippur.
Dividing the sixth millennium into twenty-four 'hours' of about 250 years, the Rav shows that 5751 enters the midday of the world's Erev Shabbos, when one may already begin to prepare for Shabbos.

Rabbi Yaakov Kamenetsky's remark that Shabbos was brought back in America but Erev Shabbos was not becomes, for the Rav, the key to the world's Erev Shabbos: as a Jew honors Erev Shabbos below, Heaven begins the Shabbos of the world.

Through the Tiferes Shlomo, the Rav reads 'the last generation will say' as a description of whoever cries out: the generation that demands of Hashem why strangers hold Eretz Yisroel becomes the last generation of the galus.
The crown that Jews' tefillos make for the King of Glory is the very crown that will rest on Moshiach's head, so it is up to Jews now to 'hammer out' that crown.

The Rav concedes that the Tzedukim's reasoning about honoring a king seems correct, and locates their error not in the halachah but in their view of the relationship: before a King one prepares outside, but a wife cooks freely in her husband's presence.

He ties the Tzedukim's denial of the Oral Torah to the ketores: the Chachamim are the akeres habayis who run the house of Torah, and whoever denies them also denies that Klal Yisroel is Hashem's wife and sees Him only as a King.

In the Rosh Hashanah Shemoneh Esrei Klal Yisroel speaks to Hashem, as subjects to a king; the novelty of the Yom Kippur Shemoneh Esrei is that Hashem speaks to Klal Yisroel with affection, as a husband to his wife.
Because smell alone was not damaged in the sin of the Etz HaDaas, the ketores expresses a love untouched by any sin; fittingly, the Tzeduki who denied that love was punished in his nose.
Shir HaShirim, a short megillah said before Mincha on Erev Shabbos, is full of fragrances from its first verses to its last, which shows that it is the same matter as the ketores.
In kedushah, unlike tumah which is separation, love and fear can exist together; the fear of Rosh Hashanah is a fear born of love.

Sitting in real huts at war would have been no reminder of war at all, since a soldier's way is to hide in trenches; the huts show instead that the protection of the Clouds of Glory went out with the Jews.
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva do not disagree about the miracle at all; according to both the Clouds of Glory protected the Jews, which removes the difficulty with the Shulchan Aruch and the Bach.
If the protection could leave the camp and go with the soldiers from place to place, it can also go from time to time; this is how 'so that your generations will know' reaches every generation.
The second half of the passuk, 'all the citizens in Israel shall dwell in sukkos', refers to the whole year: a Jew living in his apartment is still dwelling in the sukkah that went along with him.
When Moshe wrote 'vayamos sham Moshe' while still alive, he gave his soul into the Torah, so that his passing lies in those words; in the same way a passuk can carry the life of a day.
The Rav reads the business reason for a trip as mere bait: the true reason a person is brought to a place is a brachah or mitzvah that only he can do there, which he himself does not know.
The rush of summer travel that begins with Tammuz is not by chance: golus is a journey to mend the world, and these months of churban are when the traveling must accomplish the most.

Dan, traveling at the rear and returning lost objects, is a model for the end of every cycle: the end of the year and the end of Jewish history are times of hashavas aveidah, bringing back lost days, mitzvos and souls.
Vayehi binsoa is short because it is unfinished: in the future it will be filled in with every Jew's travels and the mitzvos he did on them, and take its place among the books of the Torah.
Sukkos as the Chag HaAsif is the festival of the lost being gathered back: even Dan, expelled from the clouds of glory, returns under the sukkah of Hashem.
Eretz Yisrael magnifies the neshama: a tzaddik there becomes greater and a rasha more destructive, which the Rav says explains why irreligious people there are more hostile than those abroad.
Some tzaddikim were kept out of Eretz Yisrael not for lack of merit but because their arrival would have brought the Geulah before its time.

Comfort as a condition of a mitzvah appears only where the mitzvah is itself a physical act made holy, like eating, dwelling in Eretz Yisrael or dwelling in the sukkah; there suffering means the mitzvah is not being done at all.
The tzaddikim who stayed in the sukkah in the rain did not override the exemption of one who suffers; leaving would have made them suffer more, so for them the halachah itself required staying.
Rashi's 'so as not to trouble him with guests' is turned around: Hashem saw that the heat did not trouble Avraham at all, but the lack of guests did, so He sent guests.

Rabbi Zeira reads 'a shelter from storm and rain' as the sukkah's own nature: a sukkah kept in perfection, like the Clouds of Glory, keeps out the rain, so the Ba'al Shem Tov's dry sukkah was the mitzvah in its completeness, not a miracle.
Under every forced reading of Tosafos lies something hidden, like a bulge under a fine tablecloth that hides an ornament rather than a craftsman's mistake.

The angels were damaged by Sodom's impurity just as an angel would have been by Egypt's; their repair had to come through Yaakov, who did the opposite and grew greater in the place of greatest impurity.
The angels were the fitting messengers to Esav because they were the living witnesses that Yaakov had not been damaged at Lavan's, since their own repair depended on it.
The Torah's repetition of 'in the seventh month' is a demand to go against nature: exactly when everything withers, a Jew is to take living species and stay fresh.
The esrog is taken first because it is the one exception in nature that does not dry out in winter; it can pass through all the seasons and remain alive.

The dispute between the Mechaber and the Rema over a split middle leaf rests on whether the top leaf is a separate leaf or a seamless continuation of the spine; if it is the spine, even a fully split leaf is still only a minority of the spine, so 'most of it is like all of it' does not apply.
The leaves of the lulav are the parts of the year, and its head is the head of the year, the period from Rosh Hashanah to Shemini Atzeres; if the head is dried out, the whole year suffers.
The special joy of Sukkos is freshness itself, the opposite of drowsiness, as shown by those who did not sleep at Simchas Beis Hashoeva.
The sukkah is a measure of Yerushalayim confined within its walls, while Shemini Atzeres is higher: its Yerushalayim breaks through the walls and spreads to the whole world.
The sukkah is the 'Hashem around His people' of Tehillim: a Yerushalayim whose surrounding wall is Hashem Himself, which no enemy can breach, unlike the physical mountains around the city.

Shem's reward for covering his father with zeal was living mekifim like the sukkah, the mitzvah of life, while Yefes, who only followed along, received 'dead' mekifim, the burial of Gog read about in the Sukkos haftarah.
The many requests of Shemoneh Esrei do not contradict the rule to pray for one thing, since every lack, of mind, health or peace, is a lack in the one request to serve Hashem with a settled mind.
The water of the simchas beis hashoevah is only a physical envelope for ruach hakodesh; the celebration is named after the drawing because simcha is the bucket that draws it.

Only Sukkos is called 'seven days in the year', because what is drawn in these seven days enters the whole year; sleeping through them would mean sleeping away a whole year, as Moshe could not sleep on the mountain knowing what each minute held.

The ruach hakodesh of Sukkos is the 'speaking spirit' of Onkelos: after Yom Kippur a Jew is like a newborn, and just as a father teaches Torah to a child who begins to talk, Hashem teaches him to speak, culminating in Simchas Torah.
Ruach hakodesh does not mean knowing which number will win a sweepstakes; it means speaking true words of Torah and tefillah, a level open to every Jew according to his level.

The melodious pazer note means scattering: its sweet tune carries the bitter message of the golus, and its seven occurrences in Behaaloscha mirror the seven nations from which the seventy nations of the dispersion branch out.
Seventy is seven multiplied by ten, ten being the number of completeness, so the seventy nations are the seven nations brought to completion.
The seven weeks of nechamah after Tisha b'Av are the counterweight to the seven pazers, and the comfort is that the golus was good all along, as will become clear when Moshiach comes.
Adding a name to a gravely sick person works when his illness comes because he has finished his shlichus: the new name is a new shlichus and an addition to his neshamah.
The summer vacation season falls in Tammuz, when the spies set out, so that the travels of Jews today can repair the spies' failed shlichus and bring the geulah.
The Nefilim whom the spies saw were angels who fell from their level, and their name was a hint to the spies not to fall; the spies missed it.
The Rav reads the joy of Simchas Beis Hashoevah as the joy of the water itself, returning to its root, with the Jews rejoicing together with the water.
He parallels the Foundation Stone, the root of place from which the world was founded, with Tishrei, the root of time, hinted in the letters of Bereishis.
Since the libation is halachah given to Moshe at Sinai and Torah cannot be destroyed, the libation continues in a hidden way even after the destruction, and the waters still have their ascent.
The place from which the waters return to Hashem, the shafts beneath the altar, is the same place from which Jewish souls come, since Adam was created from the earth of the altar.
Dancing is a leap toward heaven: one cannot touch the sky, but the jump shows the will to be there, which is why the Mishnah mentions dancing only at Simchas Beis Hashoevah.
Science can explain how the waves rise but not why nature was made so; the sefarim say the waves rise out of longing to be near the King, knowing they will not reach Him.

The Rav reasons that Sukkos, coming after Pesach and Shavuos, cannot share Pesach's level of emunah; the 'shade of emunah' must be higher than the 'food of emunah', and he identifies it as bitachon, which alone brings simcha.
Commemorating the clouds of glory rather than the well or the manna is explained by the clouds containing every need, so the sukkah itself carries the blessing of parnassah.

A gift is a sign of mission: Navos's sweet voice showed his task was song, and the vineyard, whose wine is the vehicle of song, was given him for that task, so when he stopped singing both the vineyard and his life were taken.

Achav's desire for the vineyard was a true pull toward sparks of his own soul; by law the vineyard would have reached him anyway, and his sin was in not waiting, yet the vineyard still brought him to teshuvah.

The closing words of Melachim, 'from the king' without 'of Bavel', reflect revealed providence: Yehoyachin, a tzaddik, knew his bread came from Hashem, while Yirmiyahu, the book of the churban, records how it looked under hidden providence.
The 'flood' the nations feared at Matan Torah was a flood of Torah; likewise the danger feared in the coming year can be turned into blessing by Jews who accept the Torah.
The cantillation note 'pazer' (scatter) appears seven times in Beha'aloscha, read just after Chof Sivan, mirroring in reverse the seven weeks of Sefirah that gathered Klal Yisrael to Shavuos.
A traveler's own reason for a trip is not Hashem's reason: the businessman goes to Chicago for a meeting, but Heaven sends him for one glass of water that needs his brachah.
Even the work of a gentile is for a Jew: the miner who produces steel is related in some way to the Jew who stirs his coffee with a spoon made from it.
Changing a sick person's name works because a name is a shlichus: if he is departing because his mission is done, a new name gives him a new mission to live for.
The summer 'travel fever' of Tammuz and Av is a soul's urge to repair the meraglim's failed journey in the same season.
Tammuz and Av belong to Reuven and Shimon, the shevatim whose nesi'im failed, which is why these two months fell, though by right Reuven and Shimon should have been first.
Yehoshua and Kalev, who did not join the meraglim, came from Ephraim and Yehuda, the shevatim of Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben David, so the faithful shluchim are tied to the geulah.

The Rav explains Samael's 'mistake' as flight, not ignorance: he knows Betzer is the city of refuge, but Betzer, Moshe's city and the place of Moshiach's mitzvah, smells of Moshiach, so he cannot bear to stay there.
According to the Rav, Moshiach is called chasan Torah because he completes the keeping of the Torah through the three added cities of refuge, the only mitzvah still missing.

He shows that 'ויספת לך עוד שלש' equals in gematria the mitzvah of appointing a king, and that 'אז יבדיל משה שלש ערים' likewise matches it, so the cities of refuge are the king's mitzvah, begun by Moshe and finished by Moshiach.

The Rav explains that kingship is not native to Israel and had to be imported from Moav, which is gematria 49, malchus shebemalchus; David is the holy spark freed from Moav's klipah, and 'ומחץ פאתי מואב' is his breaking it.
He reads Yishmael's name as a promise: because his exile is the bitterest, Hashem will hear the prayers of Jews in it, and a prayer that reaches the Thirteen Attributes is accepted.
The Rav explains that the final seal can come after Yom Kippur because the sukkah has the quality of Eretz Yisrael, where a fugitive's sentence is reopened for the land's merit.
From the Mishnah of the sea creature that flees to land, the Rav learns that where a creature runs in danger shows its root, and a Jew in distress runs to Hashem, the sukkah and the Torah.

The Torah commands a remembrance of the Clouds of Glory and not of the mann, because bread and water are necessities, while the clouds were a gift of comfort that shows Hashem wants His people to be at ease.

The halachic requirement that rain can enter concerns the building of the sukkah; when rain did not enter the Ba'al Shem Tov's sukkah, the sechach still let it in and the Ba'al Shem Tov kept it out, so the two do not conflict.

The word simcha is bound up with leaning on Hashem: the one who relies on Him is calm and lacks nothing, while the passuk's 'ne'ezav', forsaken, is read as sad, since being alone with no one to lean on is the opposite of simcha.

The Ba'al Shem Tov did not intend a miracle when rain stayed out of his sukkah; he sat with the feeling of truly being under the wings of the Shechinah, as the Jews were in the desert, and that is the true mitzvah of sukkah.
Rabbi Zeira's derivation from a passuk about the days of Moshiach still stands, because a glimmer of that future shelter exists today in the sukkah of individual tzaddikim.

There is no contradiction between the Zohar, which reads 'betzilo chimadti' on the sukkah, and the Midrash, which reads it on the Beis HaMikdash, because the sukkah itself carries the holiness of the Beis HaMikdash.
Yaakov's kfitzas haderech meant that the Beis HaMikdash came to him in chutz la'aretz; in the same way the sukkah, which Yaakov founded, brings the Mikdash to every Jew wherever he is.

Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer agree that the miracle was the clouds of glory; Rabbi Akiva's 'actual sukkos' add that their protection left the camp with the soldiers, which is why they sat in flimsy huts at war instead of digging trenches.

The Rambam limits the bad sign of rain to the first night because the first meal is what establishes the sukkah as one's dwelling; once established, later rain is like a leak that does not change one's address.

Measurement belongs to the lowest level, malchus; the Torah measures the teivah, the Mishkan and the sukkah precisely because a light far above this world can only be drawn into it through a cheshbon.
Simcha is related to 'somech', having something firm to lean on, while atzvus comes from 'azuv', being forsaken; so joy grows from bitachon.

Since entering the sukkah is entering Eretz Yisrael and the Mikdash, the Gemara's rule that one who flees to Eretz Yisrael has his judgment reopened explains why the sealing of judgment extends beyond Yom Kippur.

The Satmar Rav: every journey in the desert had its function, and because they waited seven days for Miriam the forty days of the meraglim ended exactly on Tisha B'Av, an ill-fated day; otherwise the whole episode might not have happened.

Since the churban began with Miriam's lashon hara, the great movement in recent decades to learn the laws of lashon hara is Hashem sending agents to repair this flaw as the time of the Geulah approaches.
A sefer the Rav brings sees the same pattern at Sinai: Moshe added a day for more preparation and purity, so the forty days ended on Shiva Asar B'Tammuz and the luchos were broken.
The Rav compares Tisha B'Av to a gifted bochur who could have become a great talmid chacham but went sour: he too is a 'mo'ed', can be brought back, and will become one of the greatest.
Days are like people: there are tzaddik days and rasha days, each person is rooted in his day, and when a rasha does teshuvah not only his soul but his day is transformed.
Building on Tosafos' 'hidden' gematria, the Rav computes the hidden letters of the words Tisha B'Av and finds in them the third Beis HaMikdash.

The meraglim had a hidden root of good, and because their sin fell on Tisha B'Av, which also has a hidden root, the two combined to give them hope of a tikkun; this is why waiting for Miriam was a reward.

The Rav pairs the two Gemara statements with the two days: Yom Kippur, the atonement of the golden calf, teaches teshuvah for the many, while Hoshana Rabbah, Dovid's day, teaches teshuvah for the individual.
The 'individual' is the Jew who cannot be included in the klal because of a barrier; this is why the Hoshana Rabbah aravah is taken apart from the lulav bundle that binds all Jews together.
The hoshana beaten on the ground, lowered to the dust, is then raised to become a crown on the aron kodesh, an image of 'mekimi me'afar dal' and of Dovid HaMelech.
The seventy nations fought on Sukkos are in truth the spiritual forces of the yetzer hara that can enter a Jewish heart.

Just as Hashem guards the hidden point of emunah inherited from Avraham (Magen Avraham), He guards the point of tefillah each Jew has from Dovid (Magen Dovid), so that even in his lowest state a Jew can pour out his heart.
'Every man in debt' among Dovid's men includes the Jew who does not even know he owes a debt to Hashem; such people too enlist with Dovid.
Moshiach is called poor not because he lacks anything of his own but because he lacks us: his poverty is his longing for Klal Yisrael.
Since the great kehillos of earlier generations did not bring Moshiach with their teshuvah, the promise of 'one kehillah' must be fulfilled by a humble kehillah of our own time.
In the deep hester panim of today, every small movement of a kehillah toward Hashem is worth as much as the great avodos of earlier generations.

'Lo se'ametz es levavcha' is read as a call not to harden one's heart to the longing of Moshiach and the Shechinah, since through people fulfilling Hashem's will Moshiach is given the strength to bring the tikkun.
Saying Dovid's songs in Pesukei Dezimra and Hallel makes Jews, as it were, Dovid HaMelech's minyan: he says them and we say them together with him.

The Rav reads the report that the moon helped the attackers on Hoshana Rabbah night together with the shadow seen by moonlight that night and the Ramban on 'sar tzilam', concluding that the moon itself has a share in this war.
The battlefield abroad is only a 'hookup'; the real front of the war is in the batei midrash, where the Jews circle Yericho with the four minim on Hoshana Rabbah and its walls fall.
The three books opened on the Day of Judgment are not lists already written; they are blank, and each Jew registers himself in the book where he chooses to belong.
Writing oneself into the book of tzaddikim without real commitment is like writing a check and not signing it; Hoshana Rabbah and Shemini Atzeres are the signature, the taking of responsibility.

On Shemini Atzeres the Torah does not count the day as it counts the days of Sukkos; the single bull, against the seventy brought for the nations, shows a day when only Hashem and the Jew who is batel to Him exist.
Torah and tefillah strengthen each other: Torah is the mind and tefillah the heart, and both are needed.
Adam is the 'challah of the world': Hashem plucked his earth out of the place of the Mizbeach as a woman plucks challah from her dough, and Chava in turn is the challah plucked out of Adam.
The shisin, the cavity under the Mizbeach into which the wine of nesachim flows, is the very hole left where Hashem took out Adam's earth.
Newton described gravity but not its reason; the reason is that everything came from the earth and is drawn back to its source, the same law that makes a marriage a reunion rather than a union.
The sotah is tested with dust from the Mikdash, and the Mizbeach weeps at a divorce, because husband and wife were once together in the dust beneath the Mizbeach.

Gittin opens with a get sent from overseas to Eretz Yisrael because a man's land and his wife are one source; being cut off from one is being cut off from the other, which is also why the Gemara of the Churban is in Gittin.
Wine, which brings simcha, is poured into the very place from which Adam was taken, to bring joy back to the source that the spies saddened by their unfaithfulness.
The aravah, which has neither taste nor smell, is the present generation, and Tehillim's 'He turned to the prayer of the destitute' was written for that last generation.
Dovid is the esrog, the most beautiful of the species, yet on Hoshana Rabbah he lowers himself to the aravah, the lowest, to accept the prayer of the destitute.
The events reported in the news from the war are only a reflection of the battle fought in the shul.
Pesukei dezimra are a weapon because they cut down the klipos, and the seven hakafos on the seventh day bring down the walls as at Yericho.
When Jews say Dovid's songs with intent and outpouring of the soul, they arouse Dovid himself to daven together with them.
The aravah's lack of taste and smell, its emptiness, is exactly what makes it the mitzvah of the day of Dovid, whose malchus is to have nothing of his own.
The largest treasury, that of free gifts, is not reached by everyone because it only opens for one who truly feels he deserves nothing and has no claim on Hashem.
Dovid said not 'I pray' but 'I am tefillah': like a poor man in rags whose appearance needs no explanation, his very state was his request.
The lowly state of today's generation, compared with the tearful avodah of earlier simple Jews, can itself become its tefillah, as in 'va'ani tefillah'.
All the Yamim Tovim circle around Shemini Atzeres, which is not itself a 'chag' but the center point where Hashem stands, and Hoshana Rabbah's higher teshuvah is the preparation to enter it.

The Rav distinguishes two wars of Gog and Magog: a physical one with the nations that will come with Moshiach, and a spiritual one against the ministers of the nations, against emunah and the handing down of Torah, which is already burning now.

He links the seven Canaanite nations to the seven middos and, in general, to the seventy nations, and the seven days of circling the bimah to the seven days around Yericho, whose fallen wall is the yetzer hara that separates a Jew from Hashem.

The three kinds of men in Dovid's army, the pressed, the debtor and the bitter of soul, describe every Jew today, who is in debt to Hashem through his sins; precisely this qualifies him for Dovid's army.

Following the Chiddushei HaRim, the Rav reads 've'ein moshia lah' as pointing to the level of 'ayin', a level above measure where the accusers have no entry, so crying out reaches a place they cannot block.

The aravah, which has neither taste nor smell, is held after setting aside the other species, and beating it on the ground expresses that a Jew comes before Hashem with nothing but his lowliness, which is what brings the chasimah.
Hoshana Rabbah is the day of tefillah, while Shemini Atzeres and Simchas Torah are already Torah, so the day's success is taking tefillah on oneself for the whole year.
Hoping for Moshiach is a test of belief: since Moshiach brings even material good that everyone wants, one who is not eager for him shows that he does not really believe he is coming.

Korach's and Dasan and Aviram's quarrel was a premature attempt to bring the order of the world of tikkun, in which the Leviim and the firstborn would serve as Kohanim, as they were originally meant to.

The two orders of the shevatim reflect two worlds: Yehudah first in the present flawed world, Reuven first in the world of tikkun; so Tammuz, Reuven's month, is now fourth and bitter but will become the highest.
Because Dasan and Aviram represent the month of Tammuz, the Rema MiPano's view that they have a tikkun is also the promise that Tammuz will be transformed from grief to joy.
Balak, who sought to curse Klal Yisrael, carried within himself the seed of Moshiach through Ruth, so the parsha read in Tammuz holds blessings born out of curses.
Yiftach's demand to be leader was not ambition: as a 'Tammuz soul' he knew that Tammuz and the rejected souls like him belong on top, and that they hold the keys to the Geulah.
The aravah, which has neither taste nor smell, is the tefillah of Dovid HaMelech: prayer is open to the lowliest Jew, and on Hoshana Rabbah the aravah takes the most important place after Hallel.
Moshe's tefillos were in fact accepted: they completed the roof of the heavenly Mikdash, so the lesson to daven in a time of trouble is learned from an answered prayer, not an unanswered one.

Shiloh's roof was of curtains, and the roofs of the first two Batei Mikdash were unsanctified, because the roof corresponds to keser, which can rest only in Yerushalayim and only once Amalek, gematria ram, is gone.
Before every Mikdash there was a war with Amalek, by Yehoshua, Shaul and Mordechai, but none was a full victory, which is why each Mikdash fell short of the Mikdash above.

Rabban Gamliel's beracha against the heretics is the only one whose Name is pointed with a kamatz, corresponding to keser; it was needed only after the Churban, and this may be the hidden meaning of the child's translation in Lublin.
Moshe built the fifth camp with 515 tefillos, five times machaneh; Moshiach with his camp will be the sixth, which brings the Mikdash with its holy roof down to this world.

The 515 hours from Rosh Hashanah until the last hour of Shemini Atzeres morning match Moshe's 515 tefillos, so his prayer was a Hoshana Rabbah prayer, and the missing last hour is left for later generations to daven.
Shemini Atzeres is not called 'chag' because 'chag' means going around in a circle, while Shemini Atzeres is the point in the middle, where one can point and say 'this is our G-d'.
Just as the aravah, last mitzvah of Sukkos, stands for the lips, casting it away marks the move to a day that can no longer be put into words.

Torah is always tied to the eighth: it was given at the start of the eighth week of the Sefirah, and in Tehillim 19 seven verses speak of nature while the eighth, 'Toras Hashem temimah', is above nature.
Shlomo sending the people away on the eighth day hints that the King of kings sends the nations home with their gifts, while His children run after Him into the palace.
Tefillas geshem is said in the blessing of techiyas hameisim to teach that one must not be lifeless: learning, davening and mitzvos must all be done with vitality.

The Sefer Torah is read from the beginning again because all Jews, each a letter in it, form a circle around Hashem in the middle, as the Gemara at the end of Taanis describes the circle of tzaddikim.

Because the generations keep shrinking, the Zohar's promise of a kenishta chada that brings the geulah must be fulfilled by a later generation, whose small turning to Hashem is worth more than much of the earlier generations' service.

Following the Imrei Emes, the falls in the house of Yehuda were not from wickedness but by Heaven's design: the king, who includes all his subjects across the generations, had to descend to the lowest depths the nation would ever reach so he could pick them up from there.

The Rav reads the low state of the generation as its strength: just as only earth, the lowest element, creates growth from nothing, the lowest generation is the soil from which the Tzemach David sprouts.

Moav equals forty-nine in gematria and Arvos Moav was the forty-ninth stop in the Midbar, parallel to Malchus shebeMalchus on the last day of Sefirah, so reaching Moav means reaching rock bottom, the point right before the fiftieth, the shofar of Moshiach.

Using the three dimensions of Sefer Yetzirah, the Rav shows Moshiach imprisoned in Moav in place, in soul and in time; the place and soul were already freed when Rus emerged, but the time, Tammuz and Av, still holds him, which is why Bein HaMetzarim equals 'Bas Lot' in gematria.

Ploni Almoni is called a widower of Torah because the chiddush of 'Moavi and not Moavis' was hidden in Rus, and a man's chiddushei Torah are hidden in his zivug; only Boaz, whose zivug she was, could bring it out.
The yud in 'Sdei Moav' stands for Atika, the hidden level beyond understanding, matching why Moshiach must come from so low an origin; once Rus is released the word is written with a heh.
Balak asked to keep Shiva Asar B'Tammuz as his day, supplying korbanos himself so the tamid would cease, yet the Gemara teaches that his very korbanos brought about Moshiach's lineage.
Mourning for Yerushalayim is not only a sign of loss but the first step of its rebuilding, which is why the building of the kallah begins on Tisha B'Av.
The reading cycle of Devarim, from Shabbos Chazon to Simchas Torah, matches the building of the kallah from Tisha B'Av to Shemini Atzeres, since Devarim is the seventh book and the kallah.
The esrog is held apart from the bound lulav, and Devarim alone does not begin with a vav, because the kallah must first be separate, like Chavah from Adam, so that their reunion brings joy.
Shir Hashirim praises the kallah from the feet up because the lowest generations are the most precious to Hashem, and the last generation is the true beauty of Knesses Yisroel.
Shimshon's strength lay in his hair because hair is the last thing formed in a person, the aspect of Dan and of acharis, and the last generation must likewise not let itself be shorn.

On Simchas Torah one rejoices at the end of the Torah, the place of forgotten halachos and of the forgotten Jews of the last generations, because it is joined at once to Bereishis, so every Jew will have a tikkun.

Following the Tzemach Tzedek, the Rav reads 'Hashem Elokeichem malkechem' not as a rejection of kingship but as its purpose: the people needed a king who would show them that Hashem is their King, a bridge through whose bittul they too become batel.
The Rav explains that prostration on stone was allowed only in the Beis HaMikdash because full prostration expresses the greatest bittul, and that is possible only in the place of malchus.

Netilas yadayim, the Rav explains, means lifting the hands: the ten fingers stand for all of a person's powers, and like Rebbi raising his ten fingers, one declares that nothing is for oneself, only for Hashem.

Shlomo's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter on the eve of the Mikdash's dedication was, for him, part of building it: he hoped to subdue the greatest kelipah and so spread malchus shamayim over the world, but that attempt failed and brought the decree of destruction.
The Rav explains that the line of Moshiach always emerged through episodes that looked unseemly, so that the Satan would not suspect it, and only after Hashem's oath to David could it be revealed.
Since Shlomo was reincarnated in Yirmiyahu, the Rav sees the season from Tisha b'Av to Shemini Atzeres as turning Yirmiyahu back into Shlomo, Eichah into Shir HaShirim, and churban into binyan.
Shemini Atzeres is not called 'chag', which means a circle, because it is the point in the center: Hashem Himself, without garments.

The Chashmonaim's cry 'Mi laHashem elai' was a repetition of Moshe's cry at the Golden Calf, when Shevet Levi set aside their own interests; the Chashmonaim, as Levi'im, renewed that mesiras nefesh, and the cry repeats every Chanukah.

Since nefesh means will, a person who bends his will for Hashem throughout the day performs mesiras nefesh in small pieces, which can outweigh a one-time giving of one's life, as in the mashal of the stone broken into pebbles.

Shevet Levi's lack of land is not a lack but a gift open to everyone: whoever looks to the Ribono shel Olam instead of a field as his inheritance joins Levi, and on Chanukah, the Yom Tov of the Chashmonaim who were Levi'im, every Jew can become part of that tribe.

In earlier times the Chanukah light was lit outside because the Jewish home was full of light and could shine into the street; today the street has entered the home, so the light must first be lit within.

Avraham's first test was mesiras nefesh for a G-d he had found by himself, before Hashem ever spoke to him; his last, the Akeidah, was a test of emunah against Hashem's own promise, and that last test is the pattern of the final test before Moshiach.

'Erev' means mixture, when things cannot be distinguished, while 'boker' comes from examining; the period before Moshiach is such an 'erev', and Chanukah's small light in the darkest season belongs to it.
Zimri's three names are three stages of one neshama, greatness, fall and rise, and the month of Av, Shimon's month, passes through the same three stages.
When Shelumiel fell, Pinchas took over the 'shalom' and the name of Shakai from his name, and so became Eliyahu, the angel of the bris.
The fox Rabbi Akiva saw, shual, is Shaul ben haKenaanis, since ayin and aleph interchange; it was part of his own neshama, admitted into the Kodesh HaKodashim because its tikkun was coming.
The Tannaim's words 'Akiva nichamtanu' are the gematria of Kozbi bas Tzur, the other half of Rabbi Akiva's neshama, which is why the Gemara stresses that wording and says it twice.
Galus always carries an ayin, seventy, as the Chasam Sofer reads in the agalos Yosef sent; the redemption is the ayin turning into an aleph, as in Rabbi Meir's 'kasnos or' with an aleph.
Zimri is called Shaul because he only lent himself to sin; unlike one who sells himself, he remained his own master and can reclaim his neshama.
Adam's garment of light, 'kasnos or' with an aleph, is the gematria of Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai, Shimon in his splendor.

Aharon's bashfulness kept him from the nesi'im's bold voluntary offering, and his consolation was precisely that his descendants would one day need holy boldness, to defeat Yavan, the kingdom of brazenness.
The 'ox' on whose horn the Greeks demanded the Jews write was the golden calf: their claim was that a nation capable of serving it has lost its bond with Hashem.
A bas Levi who remarried on a false report loses maaser because she lacked the trait of Levi, the inner sense of an essential bond that would have told her that her husband was alive.
Chanukah has no festive meal because it celebrates the hidden essential bond, which cannot be displayed, unlike the festivals whose greatness was shown in the Beis HaMikdash service.
Chanukah's light is revealed more as history approaches Moshiach: barely mentioned in the Mishnah, it expanded greatly from the Arizal and the Ba'al Shem Tov onward.

Following Rebbe Tzadok HaKohen, the extra verse of redemption added beyond the alphabetical order of a chapter of Tehillim shows a conduct above the natural order, by which Hashem does not let any Jew be lost.

Dovid HaMelech ruled on questions of purity himself because, as king of all Israel with a soul from Atzilus, his ruling to permit a wife to her husband acted in all the worlds on the bond of Israel with Hashem.

Just as oils that will not burn well enough for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah, there are Jews whom Shabbos cannot kindle but Chanukah can, because on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down to them rather than asking them to rise.
The slave who chose to stay is freed only by yovel, the 'eighth'; so too Chanukah, which is of yovel, can free a Jew whom the 'seven' of Shabbos cannot.
Shabbos is sanctified with wine, of the world of seven, while Chanukah is sanctified with oil; shemen shares its root with shemoneh, eight.
Oil rises above every other liquid, like fire that always rises, because it belongs to the higher world of the eighth and strives back to its source.

Yevamos, Eruvin and Nidah are the hardest masechtos because all three deal with the coming of Moshiach: the tikkun of souls, turning the world into a reshus hayachid, and ending the exile likened to nidah.
The Chanukah light set at the door, in the public domain, brings the light of Moshiach into the reshus harabim and so makes it a reshus hayachid.

The pesukim of the parshiyos read around Rosh Hashanah map the stages of teshuvah: Vayelech's 30 pesukim are the 30 days of the tzaddikim, and Haazinu's 52 are the 52 days until the final sealing on Shemini Atzeres.
The 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah equal the 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu together, so that Chanukah contains the whole of the days of teshuvah.
Ki Savo, read to end the year with its curses, also has 122 pesukim, hinting that the curses of the passing year come from its 122 days of teshuvah left unused.

The 24 days from Rosh Chodesh Kislev to Chanukah correspond to the 24 letters of Baruch Shem, a lesser acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, and Chanukah to the 25 letters of Shema Yisrael, a greater one, just as Shema is printed in large letters and Baruch Shem in small ones.

Rosh Chodesh Kislev is the letter beis of Baruch, the true beginning of Chanukah, just as the Torah begins with the beis of Bereishis; as a first day that includes everything after it, this may be why it is called a day of teshuvah like Yom Kippur.
Zos Chanukah is hinted in the pasuk 'b'zos yechupar avon Yaakov', that through 'zos' the sin of Yaakov is atoned.
The Rav reads the rule that the first day of Pesach falls on the weekday of Tisha B'Av as proof that a Jewish churban is never without geulah: it is planted by the geulah and exists to produce it.

He applies the halachic idea of ben yomo to the calendar: Nissan, every day of which is Rosh Chodesh according to the Shelah, is a 'yerach ben yomo', a month whose freshness never goes stale, mirroring Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael.
The shofar, the symbol of ingathering, equals with its milui the two notes karnei parah and yerach ben yomo together, showing that it unites the month of division with the month of geulah.

He explains that the Torah required kashering the vessels of Midian even when not ben yomo measure for measure: Bilam tried to make Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael lose its freshness, so Midian's forbidden taste never loses its own.
Reading nasheh as forgetting, the Rav makes the gid hanasheh the forgotten neshamos that Yaakov lost to Esav, and Tisha B'Av, the gid hanasheh among the days of the year, the day of those souls.

Dina was destined from birth to bear Osnas, the wife of Yosef and mother of Moshiach ben Yosef, so that Shechem, which looks like Yaakov's loss, held a hidden spark of Moshiach; Shechem ben Chamor equals 'haMelech haMashiach ben Yosef' in gematria.
When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos and is pushed off, eating on that day is like eating the gid hanasheh in holiness, a sign of the time when Yaakov will no longer limp and the lost neshamos return.

Chanukah is the one time the Shechinah breaks its own rule of not descending below ten tefachim, because it comes for Jews who are themselves 'below ten', in the public domain rather than the domain of the One of the world.
Following the Tur Bareket, the Chanukah light precedes the Shabbos light because it is elevated and enters into the Shabbos light, so a low, weekday light rises into Shabbos.

The Chanukah miracle fell at tekufas Teves, the longest night, in a month left to the sitra achra and at the end of the lunar month: the darkest point from every side is exactly where the Shechinah came down.
Ner, pesilah and shemen form the initials of neshamah, so the oils and wicks unfit for Shabbos but fit for Chanukah stand for souls that Shabbos cannot kindle but Chanukah can.
Yosef's test on the idolaters' festival day was so great because on that night one does not learn, so he lacked the Gemara's advice of Torah learning as protection.
Even a wicked informer who lit Chanukah lights shone in all the worlds; had he grasped that light and repented, it would have accompanied him into the morning Hallel and protected him.
Unlike the Hallel of the Yamim Tovim, Chanukah's Hallel is an obligation on weekdays, which is why the Rambam places all the laws of Hallel in Hilchos Chanukah, the end of Sefer Zmanim.

Following the Chasam Sofer, Yaakov's wish to dwell in tranquility was not a desire for ease: having lived out every sign of galus through Gog uMagog, he sought to be the sign of the days of Moshiach, but this world has no vessel for such a sign, so instead galus began anew with Yosef.

Emunah in what is beyond the intellect is real because every Jew has some measure of ruach hakodesh, and that is why the Greeks, who wanted to uproot it, attacked through tumah, which cuts a Jew off from his pure neshamah.
Though impure oil could have been used, the beauty of the miracle was that the oil was pure, symbolizing the victory of 'tamei'im b'yad tehorim'.

The jar of oil was most likely hidden under the loose stone from which the sotah's dust was taken, so it was guarded in the very place that guards the purity of Jewish daughters, which was what the Greeks sought to destroy.
Esav, unable to bite Yaakov, kissed him; the Rav sees this as the tactic of the nations before Moshiach, who seek to destroy Jews through embrace and togetherness rather than persecution.
Chanukah, read as chaf-heh, alludes to the 25 letters of Shema Yisrael, because emunah includes not only that Hashem is One but also that one is Yisrael, the very point the Greeks attacked.

Yaakov's insistence on the angel's concession at once, rather than at Beis El, is explained by the coming encounter with Shechem: the name Yisrael was the weapon against Yavan, which is why the angel fought so hard against conceding it.
Since every mitzvah in the Torah has a continuation, the Rav reads Chanukah, the last mitzvah from the last miracle, as pointing directly to the next miracle, the coming of Moshiach.

The Chanukah lamp below ten tefachim shows Hashem bending down to His children in galus, like a king who bends only for his own son; Chanukah is a weekday festival on which Hashem visits His sick people.

Tamar's delay was deliberate: because she carried Moshiach, she knew the Satan would block him, and only Yehuda's acceptance of public shame, a form of mesiras nefesh, could leave the Satan powerless.
Er and Onan fell not despite their lineage but because of it: the Satan concentrates all his force on the one from whom Moshiach is to come, as he would on the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur.
The unprecedented trials of this generation are themselves a sign of its role: the Satan knows this generation must bring Moshiach, so he throws at it tests no generation has had.
The Chanukah lamp stands opposite the mezuzah, which holds the Shema with its acceptance of mesiras nefesh, showing that the light of Moshiach is reached by giving up one's will for Hashem's.

The Rav reads 'Bereishis is also a maamar' as showing that the first maamar is so lofty it never descended into the words 'vayomer', and he parallels the hidden first three maamaros with the three hidden nations promised to Avraham.

He makes the ten weeks from Shiva Asar B'Tammuz to Rosh Hashanah parallel the ten nations, so that the Three Weeks are the 'Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni' of the year, destined to become its most joyful days.

The Rav proposes that Rashi's 'koach maasav higid l'amo' answers the nations by revealing that Klal Yisrael is destined for the Kadmoni, Esav's realm and the whole world, so complaining over the seven nations is beside the point.
Gimmel-Reish, used in the sefarim for the first three, is read by the Rav as Gad and Reuven, the two tribes bound to 'reishis' and to the geulah.

Following Rav Shimshon of Ostropoli, the forty days of the spies, which are Tammuz and the nine days, are the domain of the Samech Mem, hinted in the letters preceding 'anavim'; when Har Esav is judged, 'anavim' will be complete with its yud.
Like belief in techiyas hameisim, which the Rav calls a sign rather than a punishment, the tribes' instinctive desire for this land was a sign that their souls belonged to the days of Moshiach.
The washing out of every blemish in the time of tikun may be why one does not wash during the nine days, since they are not yet that time.
Matisyahu, the 'soul' of Chanukah, is in gematria 'Beis Hamikdash': in the days of Matisyahu every Jew merits a Beis Hamikdash in his own home.
Lighting the menorah needs no kohen while preparing it does, because the lighting already belongs to the light of the future, when every Jew will be a kohen.

The letters of Chashmon hint at chodesh, Shabbos, milah and ner: the three mitzvos the Greeks tried to abolish and the mitzvah of ner Chanukah that was added in response, as Purim was added when Haman resented the Jewish festivals.

One may enjoy the Shabbos light but not the Chanukah light, though both are the hidden light, because on Shabbos a Jew is raised to a higher world, whereas on Chanukah that world comes down into weekday exile, where it is not yet the time to use it.
The order of lighting inside the home reflects the approach of Moshiach's days, when the public domain pushes into the Jewish home, as it does today through television, radio and the internet.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the sign that a chiddush comes from kedushah is that another Jew builds a further chiddush on it; this is 'banim l'vanecha', grandchildren in Torah.
The Rambam places the laws of hallel in hilchos Chanukah, which shows that the root of hallel is Chanukah.
The Rav reads the Rambam's choice of words as a sign of something particular to Chanukah: the Rambam singles out this mitzvah alone as cherished.
He presents mosif v'holech, the nightly increase of the lights, as describing Chanukah itself: a time of adding in kedushah.
He speaks of engaging in holy matters not for oneself but for the sake of Hashem.
The Rav reads the law of gravity as the Torah's principle that everything returns to its origin: earth falls to the earth, fire rises to its source, and the neshamah rises to where it came from.

A shidduch has two origins: the isha's origin in the ish, and the origin of that origin, Adam's in the earth of the mizbeach. Therefore one cut off from his wife is cut off from Eretz Yisrael, which the Rav sees in the first Mishnah of Gittin speaking of a get from outside the land.

The difference between the daughters of Tzelafchad and Nadav and Avihu: the daughters were tzidkaniyos whose heart was a true magnet; it drew them to no one because their match was tied to a nachalah not yet given, and the moment it was given they married their nearby cousins without being choosy.
Land in Eretz Yisrael returns at Yovel because a field is bound to its owner's neshamah and his portion of Torah; what was bought belongs to someone else's neshamah and must go back to its origin.

Gilad is the land of return: Eliyahu, herald of the final Yovel, chose to live there, and like Amalek it could be conquered only by Rachel's children, the neshamah of return, which is why Moshe left it for Machir.
Moshe's explaining the Torah in seventy languages prepared the people for the seventy levels of galus, so that the Torah would reach down with them into the lowest one.
Milah expresses the eighth: nature makes a person with an orlah like the nations, and the Jew cuts it off and binds himself to Hashem above nature.
The oil miracle broke the bounds of arithmetic itself: the oil was no longer limited by how much a measure of oil can burn, so it burned exactly eight times as long.
Torah was given on the fiftieth day, the first day of the eighth week after seven times seven, so Torah too belongs to the eighth, and Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Torah's victory.
Zos Chanukah breaks the one-nasi-per-day pattern: one day reads several nesi'im, and on it all the leftover wicks of Chanukah burn together, a little day that holds a lot.

The Chozeh's reply shows that the Chanukah lights of even an informer revealed a light that shone in all worlds, more than his other mitzvos, because they uncover the hidden light of Moshiach in a Jew.
The Rav ties the thirty-six candles of Chanukah to the thirty-six hours the hidden light served, so that the Chanukah lights are where that light still shines.
He reads the name Chashmonai as the letters of shemen and ches, oil and eight, the eight days of the miracle of the oil.
The letters of Yavan show its nature: a yud stretched into a vav and then into a nun, an expansion that pushes into the place of kedushah.
Korach was swallowed into the earth because, by denying havdalah, a foundation of creation, he undid what made him a created man from the earth.
Every Jew is a whole world with his own Beis HaMikdash; even if the Greeks break into it, the sealed jug of oil, the Ohr HaGanuz within him, remains.
The 'oils' that were defiled are a person's thoughts: the yetzer hara convinces him that all of them are impure, yet one sealed jug remains from which Chanukah's light can be kindled.

The dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan is not over the relative worth of Torah and tefillah, but over which a place enhances more: a shul's power to make tefillah accepted, or a beis medrash's power to magnify Torah.

Torah's inability to make miracles beyond nature comes from its greatness, not its weakness: nature is the Torah's own law, and a tzaddik who changes the order of Creation is in effect changing the Torah.

The Mikdash is where heaven ends and earth begins, so the heavenly order, beyond place, time and reckoning, applies there; miracles there are not a change of nature but nature of heaven dictated by the Torah.
The oil that held for eight days was the same kind of miracle as the few defeating the many, so the lights served as a mirror in which the hidden miracle of the war could be seen.
'Zeidim b'yad oskei sorasecha' in Al HaNissim names the source of the victory: the wicked fell into the hands of those who toil in Torah, because the miracle was made through Torah.

The Rav reverses the Chasam Sofer's order: the people asked first, and Hashem added Himself as a sender so His intention would also count, giving the meraglim a choice; that is why Kalev and Yehoshua were saved.
The angel's 'why do you ask my name' was not evasion but his real name: the mission of the yetzer hara is to make a person refuse to ask about his own name and mission.

In 'yemei bikurei anavim', 'bikurei' hints to the letters that come before those of 'anavim', which spell the names of the Satan, and the full spelling of 'Amalek' equals the gematria of 'yemei bikurei anavim'.
By reason the meraglim were right that Klal Yisrael could not conquer the land; their sin was relying on their understanding where Hashem had said they could, instead of going with emunah.

Tzitzis hang at the bottom edge of the garment just as this generation stands at the end of history; Klal Yisrael has been weaving one garment since Matan Torah, and the last thread, where tzitzis go, is where Moshiach is found.
Krias Shema's last word, 'emes', is not written in the parsha and must be added and called out, a sign that in the end of days the truth is hidden and has to be dug out.
Shlichus requires a neshama that is a part of G-d; a non-Jew cannot be a shaliach, and the concept was first given with the korban Pesach when the Jews became a people.
In Yosef's first dream he only watches from outside; in the second the whole holy structure, Yaakov and the Shechinah, must come down to him in his exile, so that he not sink there.

Placing the Chanukah light below ten tefachim, where the Shechinah never went, is a bikur cholim: in a festival of exile the great come down to the sick, as Hashem made Chizkiyahu ill so that Yeshayahu would come to him.

The blue of a flame, which consumes the wick, is Beis Shammai's midas hadin; the white, which gives light to others, is Beis Hillel's rachamim; and the 'borei' and 'me'orei' of their dispute follow from this.

Beis Shammai decrease the lights because they put sur mera first; Beis Hillel increase because aseh tov comes first and draws the sur mera after it, so a Jew should not wait to clean himself of sins before beginning.
The years of yeshiva are the 'chinuch' of a life: the oil poured in then must be enough to burn 'until the foot leaves the market', through the long years of parnassah outside the beis medrash.
The Torah is like the wife of whom it says 'beiso zo ishto': even when a Jew is away from the Gemara, his home and life must be run by it, so that his halichos become halachos.

The heavenly voice about Chanina ben Dosa still speaks in every generation, because each generation has a 'Chanina', one who knows that all he has is a free gift; the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh came from that same awareness.
What makes the Chanukah lights 'especially dear', unlike other mitzvos, is that Chanukah is the only festival created by human mesiras nefesh.
Since nefesh means will, mesiras nefesh is within everyone's reach daily: each time a Jew gives up his will, he gives over his nefesh.
Holding back a witty but hurtful remark, or not looking at what one should not see, is itself mesiras nefesh, the same quality that created Chanukah.
The answer to the Greek decree of 'no part in the G-d of Israel' is for each Jew to inscribe, as it were, on all his mitzvos that he has a part.
True self-sacrifice bends one's own comfort only; it never makes others pay for one's devotion, as Avraham Avinu showed.

The Rav reads the extension of teshuvah until Zos Chanukah as a gift for weaker generations: the great generations were expected to finish by Yom Kippur, and the later, smaller ones were given more time.

The four stages of the season of teshuvah correspond to the number of pesukim in the parshiyos of that season, with Ki Savo's 122 pesukim equal to the 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to the end of Chanukah.

Since Ki Savo belongs to the ending year with its curses, its 122 pesukim ask a person what he did with last year's 122 days, and the new 122 days call for a fresh start rather than the routine of past years.
Today the private domain of the Jewish home has become a public domain, connected through the media to every opinion in the world, and Chanukah's lights of Torah are the answer to this.
The nesiim read on Chanukah are, according to the Targum Yonasan as the Rav brings it, a counter-weapon against the twelve princes of Yishmael, and the avodah of Chanukah can nullify their power.
The sparks in an object are matched to one person's nefesh so precisely that a lost pen is found only by the person whose sparks are left in it, after the owner has finished raising his own.

Leket, shikchah and pe'ah belong to the poor because they share his condition: fallen to the ground, forgotten, and at the edge, as the poor man is trodden on, seems forgotten, and lives at the fringe of society.
Bikurim is a matching of beginnings: the fig that rises before the other trees goes to the Beis HaMikdash, the 'early riser' of creation, and to the kohanim, whose nature is zerizus.
As the first forty days after conception decide whether a child is male, the forty days of Elul and the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah decide the 'gender', the character, of the coming year.

The pesukim of the parshiyos read in the teshuvah season match the four periods: thirty of Vayelech, forty of Nitzavim as the Rav counts them, and fifty-two of Haazinu, together the 122 days that end with Chanukah.
Ki Savo's 122 pesukim do not speak of the coming year but rebuke the past one: they remind that its 122 days of teshuvah were wasted, and the year turned out accordingly.

The Mishnah's only law touching Chanukah, the lamp placed below ten tefachim that sets a passing camel's flax on fire, is not incidental: it holds the whole essence of Chanukah, a light that goes down into the public domain.

Chanukah was barely discussed by earlier generations because its light is the hidden light of Moshiach; only generations close to Moshiach, from the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov on, speak of it at length.

Moshiach's ancestry came through hidden, lowly-seeming events so that the Satan, who knows Moshiach will end him, would not notice, like money hidden in the thief's own sack where he will never search.

Tamar waited until she was already burning before sending to Yehudah because the Satan had defeated two earlier chances for Moshiach through Er and Onan, and mesirus nefesh is the one thing he cannot oppose.
Er and Onan, through whom the Satan had blocked Moshiach, came back as Peretz and Zerach, so Tamar's mesirus nefesh repaired the earlier failure.
The Alter Rebbe's arrest was the earthly echo of a heavenly accusation against revealing pnimiyus haTorah, the Torah of Moshiach, which brings Moshiach closer.
Ner Chanukah, the last mitzvah, corresponds to the lowest Jew of the last generation, as the final letter of the Aseres Hadibros, the long final kaf of 'lerei'echa', reaches below the line.
Yaakov did not receive the name Yisrael when he defeated the angel, but only after the mesiras nefesh of Shechem, since the name means oneness with Hashem, and that is earned through mesiras nefesh.
When the sons of Yaakov said 'we will become one people', which Shechem had not even asked for, they were not speaking to Shechem but praying to Hashem for a wall between Israel and the nations.
Assimilation is like carrying out of the private domain into the public domain on Shabbos, and the Chanukah lamp at the doorway marks the techum of the Jewish domain.
The twenty-four days of Kislev before Chanukah correspond to the twenty-four letters of 'Baruch shem kevod', and the twenty-fifth to the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael.
The chassidim of Chabad who served Hashem with mesiras nefesh in Russia are today's Chashmonaim, and their merit brought about the fall of Soviet Russia.
Anger at another person is really anger at Hashem, since nothing good or bad can come through a person without Hashem's will; one who habitually thinks this way will never become angry.
From the Midrash's parable the Rav learns that relying on Hashem is itself the merit that saves: the king freed the man only because he had relied on him.
Chananiah, Mishael and Azariah were saved specifically in the merit of Yaakov, the one whose mention the wicked mocked, and the mockers were the ones burned.
Not fearing scoffers is the precondition for the whole Shulchan Aruch: one who fears mockery gains nothing from learning halachos he will not fulfill.
'Yoshev b'seser', which the Chashmonaim said going into battle, mentions no mitzvos, tefillos or merits at all, only bitachon itself.
Unlike Kiddush, where others fulfill their obligation through one person, on Chanukah the family itself lights, so when one member lights it is as though each has lit.
Because Chanukah is a mitzvah of the family, it increases each day, like a family that must grow.

The Baal HaTurim's 'zekunim' leaves out Taharos not because Yaakov withheld it but because Yosef, the ro'eh corresponding to Seder Taharos, already knew it by himself; and that is why Yaakov loved him more, since he had less to teach him.
Yosef was not one of the twelve shevatim but one of the seven ro'im, which is why his sons took his place among the shevatim and why the brothers misread his elevated conduct as arrogance.

The future split of the sea into seven streams instead of twelve paths marks the elevation of the shevatim from separate branches to the level of the seven ro'im, a level touched already on Shabbos, when the twelve weekday requests give way to one brachah.

Because the first contains everything, Avraham, 'ba bayamim', comes with all seven days and knew the whole Torah by instinct, while each later av knew by himself only the order of Mishnah of his own day.

Taharah gives taste and fragrance: Yaakov recognized from the holy fragrance of the produce that came from impure Mitzrayim that Yosef, the embodiment of Seder Taharos, was handling it, which joins Rashi's and Targum Yonasan's readings into one.

Mishkan Shiloh, Yosef's sanctuary, had a quality Yerushalayim lacked: its holiness reached as far as it could be seen, a merit of Yosef's holy eyes; so Elul is Shiloh and the Ten Days are Yerushalayim.
Elul relates to Rosh Hashanah as Friday to Shabbos and as taharah to kedusha: without the purity of Elul one cannot reach 'HaMelech HaKadosh' of Rosh Hashanah.
The Chanukah light's place at the door marks the point where a Jew leaves Hashem's private domain for the public domain of the kelipos; the hidden light is sent precisely there.
No one recognized Yosef because he was the hidden light; the brothers saw only a ruler, and even Yosef's greatness as a tzaddik stayed concealed.
Unlike Yom Kippur, when teshuvah rises up to the Kisei HaKavod, on Zos Chanukah the Kisei HaKavod comes down to the Jew in the lowest place, as it came down to Yosef.
The day of Yosef's test, the idolaters' festival, fell at the winter tekufah, around the time of Chanukah, so the light that saved him was a Chanukah light.
'Hashem Elokai yagiah choshki' means that Hashem writes a commentary on the darkness, as a later scholar adds glosses to a Rishon no one understood; Chanukah is that commentary.

The eight nights of Chanukah correspond to the attributes of mercy from 'notzer' to 'venakeh', which are 'mazal', above any reckoning of merits; that is why Chanukah is for those whose merits cannot be counted and who live by emunah alone.
On the eighth day the nations' festival brings thick darkness, while for Jews the eighth light brings the hidden light in full.
The Gemara's answer to 'Mai Chanukah' is not an explanation but the eight days themselves: since Chanukah is above reason, the full answer cannot be given, and that is itself the answer.
The name Chashmonaim holds the letters of shemen and ches (eight), with the remaining letters spelling 'mai', the Gemara's question.

The only Chanukah law hinted in the Mishnah, placing the light below ten handbreadths, comes through Rebbi of the house of Dovid, because the aspect of Moshiach is to bring the highest light down to the lowest place.
The Ramban's reading, that Aharon's eternal share is Chanukah, and the Chiddushei HaRim's, that his menorah was hidden still burning, are one: both mean the hidden light of Chanukah.
Like the blessing of Shemini Atzeres, which does not leave when the day leaves because death was decreed only on this-worldly things, Chanukah's eighth day is never nullified.
Rashi's kal vachomer in the middle of the Yosef story teaches that the Torah's 'Hashem found the sin' about the pure shevatim exists so one can reason that He searches even more for merit.
The 'lo chen' of the wicked is their denial of the hidden, and for that reason they have no standing in the judgment completed on Zos Chanukah.

Nitzavim with its 40 pesukim comes before Vayeilech with 30, although Rosh Hashanah precedes Yom Kippur, because the Torah follows the majority, who are not tzaddikim gemurim and need the full 40 days.
The 122 pesukim of Ki Savo look back: they reproach the 122 days of teshuvah that were given last year and not used, which is why the year ended with curses.

The Torah states 30, 40 and 52 days openly, but the full 122 only through a combination of three sedros, because it is shameful to need until Chanukah, just as Moshe's rebuke was given by hint out of respect for Klal Yisrael.

The 48th and 50th pesukim of Haazinu, matching the fourth and sixth days of Sukkos, name Moshe and Aharon openly and hint at Yosef in both, so that the Chassidic and Ashkenazic orders of the ushpizin each have a source and neither is slighted.
Even a first thought of the Gemara that it later abandons is Torah: deriving the sukkah's height from the kapores reveals a real bond between the sukkah and the Kodesh HaKodashim.

Sukkah and Chanukah are opposites: the sukkah stays above ten tefachim like the Shechinah, while the Chanukah light is placed below ten, on the left side, in the public domain and the long nights of Teves, bringing holiness into the realm of darkness.
Years of pekidah have often been tragic precisely because they are fitting for Moshiach: the Satan, knowing Moshiach means his end, brings up the sins of Klal Yisrael to accuse them.
Eliyahu is called a kohen not by lineage but because, as the herald of the redemption, he always lives in the state of the days of Moshiach, when every Jew will be a kohen.
Eliyahu's answer that the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon was not a mere deflection for him: in the future the halacha will follow Rabbi Shimon, and Eliyahu already lives in that time.
Rabbi Shimon is not followed now because he is on the level of Shabbos, the whole year Shabbos for him, a level the world has not yet reached.
Since lighting Chanukah candles reveals the light of Moshiach as a returning light, not only does the home become a Beis HaMikdash but the Jew himself becomes a kohen.
The Rav reads the Tzvi LaTzaddik's caution, that he would not have said an answer unknown to the Rishonim were it not the truth, as a sign that a new answer on Chanukah is itself a new revelation.

Because reality in this world follows the psak, as with the Rambam on the Mishnah in Niddah, each chacham's answer about the first night does not merely explain the past but brings a new kind of miracle into his own generation.
The answer of an empty flask with only a trace of oil was revealed specifically to our generation, because only such a miracle fits a generation that is itself an empty vessel.
The seal of the Kohen Gadol on the flask is the point of emunah inherited from Avraham Avinu, called a Kohen Gadol in the Midrash, which no Greek influence can defile even when the flask is empty.
The Rav reads 'dor ledor yeshabach' with the Beis Aharon: precisely because generations grow worse, their small avodah is more precious, so the world grows better.
The eighth light, which stood empty all of Chanukah, is a picture of the empty souls of the end of days, and its lighting on Zos Chanukah shows that they too are lit.

Beha'aloscha repeats that the menorah is mikshah down to its base because it speaks of the Chanukah menorah, teaching that the lowest souls are not attached pieces but one piece with the lights above.
The Rav reads the twelve days of the nesi'im as their Yom Tov and Chanukah as the Yom Tov of Aharon and his tribe, so that the Ramban's Chanukah lights are Aharon's own festival.
In Parshas Masei Aharon's age and his passing on Rosh Chodesh Av are given because there he stands for the Beis Hamikdash, the parshah of the journeys speaking of the exiles.
The menorah of the future Beis Hamikdash is being built in Heaven by the Chanukah lights of all generations, each adding its part.
The verse says 'beha'aloscha', raising the lights, and not kindling, because it speaks of the Chanukah menorah, where a new light is added each day.
'Mikshah hi ad yerechah ad pirchah' teaches that the lowest generations, who make the base, are one piece with the great ones who made the flowers.
The chasimah of Zos Chanukah is made by each Jew with his own hands, through his avodah with the Chanukah lights, Hallel and Al Hanisim.

The number of pesukim in Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu mirrors the stages of judgment: 40 for those who need Elul and the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, 30 for tzaddikim, 52 until Shemini Atzeres, and 122 together until Zos Chanukah.
Ki Savo's own 122 pesukim belong to the outgoing year: they point an accusing finger at the 122 days of teshuvah that were granted last year and not used.
Zos Chanukah is a concentrate of all 122 days, so on it a person can run through the whole period again and do teshuvah.

The Ba'al HaTurim's link between Yishmael's falling at the end of Chayei Sarah and 'Yitzchak ben Avraham' right after teaches that Moshiach, from Yitzchak, comes when Yishmael falls suddenly at his height.
Among the seven barren mothers, the seventh is Tziyon; so the Rosh Hashanah kriah of Sarah's remembrance is really a tefillah for Yerushalayim's children to return.
The second part of the Rosh Hashanah kriah, Sarah's demand to send away Yishmael because the land belongs to Yitzchak, is the tefillah to be saved from the fear of Yishmael.

The Rav reads 'ken asah es hamenorah' in Beha'aloscha as speaking of the Chanukah menorah: Aharon's lighting prepared the Chashmonaim's menorah and every Jew's menorah, which is why the only detail repeated there is mikshah.
The menorah's unlit lamps are not idle: they stand for the nations and the 'decreasing' side of the miracle, so lighting with empty lamps is as much a mitzvah and pirsumei nisa as the full ones.
The Rav explains the oil miracle as the 'long days' of Moshiach shining then: one day stretched to eight, like the long days that will follow the exile of Edom.
The seven dark lamps left on the first night correspond to the seven kings of Edom of whom the Torah says 'and he died'; of the eighth it does not say so.
The halachic requirement that a brachah not be made over empty vessels explains why the menorah must be one piece: joined to a lit lamp, the empty lamps are not an empty vessel.
Following the Sfas Emes that Chanukah continues Sukkos, Zos Chanukah is its Shemini Atzeres: the nations, who shared in the seven days, have no part, and all eight lamps are full and holy.
'Chanina' is not only a person of the past but a type of soul present in every generation, the one who knows nothing is due to him, and for whose sake the world is still sustained.
The father's name 'Yochanan' is added to Matisyahu because, like Mordechai's lineage in the Gemara, it describes the same person's soul: a gift from Hashem, received as grace.

Rabbi Chanina could ask for vinegar to burn, although tzaddikim do not ask for miracles, because for him there was no difference between oil and vinegar; only one who thinks oil burns by itself sees a miracle in vinegar.
Bread growing from the earth is no less a wonder than manna falling from heaven; the generation of the desert was amazed by it only because they were used to the opposite.
Emunah is called 'Zeraim' because a Jew plants knowing the growth is a miracle; a gentile also plants and expects growth, but out of habit.
Zos Chanukah is the day the oil burned naturally, and that is its lesson: after seven days of miracles one recognizes that natural burning is also a miracle.
The order of the mitzvos parallels the order of the generations: they begin with Anochi and end with Chanukah, so the last generation is given the mitzvah of emunah.

The Rav explains Aharon's eternal lighting through the Arizal's teaching on the soul of a tzaddik joining one who does his favorite mitzvah: Aharon, who never changed in his lighting, is drawn into every Jew who lights Chanukah candles, and this is why every Jew becomes a kohen on Chanukah.
Hoda'ah, the heart of Chanukah, is Aharon's middah of hod, and hod is the Bais HaMikdash; the Rav adds that hoda'ah equals 'Aharon HaKohen' in gematria.

The Rav explains why an informer was protected while lighting: the Chanukah light is the hidden light of Moshiach, and lighting kindles the hidden light in a person's own soul, so at that moment no harm could touch him.

On Zos Chanukah judgment is according to how a Jew will look in the days of Moshiach, by his hidden good; therefore even a small teshuvah, according to one's strength, is accepted then, which explains the Ruzhiner's saying that what tzaddikim achieve on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur a simple Jew can achieve on Zos Chanukah.

Following the Meiri, the Rav reads the precedence of shalom bayis as avoiding a quarrel between husband and wife over whose mitzvah to do, and explains that Chazal revealed the greatness of peace specifically through the Chanukah light because Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Aharon, lover of peace.

The Rav reads 'a man according to his praise' in Mishlei as: just as the crucible purifies silver and the furnace gold, praising Hashem purifies a person, and after such davening the light hidden in the Torah is revealed to him.

The three places in the Torah that promise Moshiach correspond to the Rambam's three simanim: the war in Balak, the ingathering in Nitzavim, and strengthening the whole Torah in the mitzvah of the additional cities of refuge.

Since every Jew is rooted in one mitzvah, the Rav proposes that Moshiach's mitzvah is ir miklat: it is the one mitzvah all generations together have not yet fulfilled, so by adding the three cities he becomes the one who completes the Torah.

Kriyas Shema is the ir miklat within the Torah: its six opening words and the 42 words of 'V'ahavta' match the six cities and the 42 Levite cities, 48 in all, because acceptance of Malchus Shamayim is the refuge from the yetzer hara.
By gematria, 'v'yasafta lecha od shalosh' and 'az yavdil Moshe shalosh arim' both equal 'som tasim alecha melech', tying the cities of refuge to the mitzvah of appointing a king, Moshe and Moshiach.

The Satan does go first to Betzer, but senses Moshiach there, since Betzer in ribua gematria equals David ben Yishai, so he reasons that Bozrah is Betzer's feminine counterpart, because in tumah the feminine dominates.
Malchus is not native to Yisrael but imported from Moav, through Rus to Yisrael and through Bozrah to Edom, so the Satan flees from the malchus of kedushah to its counterpart in tumah.

The pesukim of the sedras read in this season match the stages of teshuvah: Vayelech 30, Nitzavim 40, Haazinu 52, together 122, the days to the end of Chanukah, while Ki Savo's 122 refer to last year.
The Rav reads 'kol kesef hakelim' at the end of the Nesi'im as the moment the tribes stop being counted one by one and are counted as one, and this is what Zos Chanukah means.
The custom of burning the leftover wicks together on Zos Chanukah shows that the thirty-six masechtos, each with its own halachos, merge into one flame.
Burial of Avraham proves Yishmael's teshuvah not by learning, davening or fasting, but because he let his younger brother Yitzchak go first.
Only Chanukah and a few others are introduced with 'What is...?' because, like the Exodus, it comes from the fiftieth gate, and that level is awakened through questions.
'Mikshah te'aseh hamenorah' equals in gematria 'the third Beis HaMikdash'; the menorah alone was already part of the third Beis HaMikdash.
The empty cups on the one-piece menorah are not empty: they stand for Jews whose hidden light will shine when Moshiach comes, and Hashem judges by that.
The name 'seudas reshus' is read as an incomplete phrase: 'reshus' alone lacks a word, and the singing at the meal supplies 'hayachid', turning the public domain into Hashem's private domain.
The lean cows 'stood' because they were stunned, like a person who stops mid-step on seeing Jerusalem: the sitra achra is awed by the power of holiness it swallows.
Like a person who overeats and then vomits not only the excess but everything, the sitra achra will have to spit out all it holds, so that holiness gains from the exile.
The answer to why a calculated ketz passed lies in the passuk of 'Mikeitz' itself, which speaks of Yosef's set time being extended by two years.
Each night's new Chanukah candle is lit in a place in the menorah that was dark the night before, bringing a private domain of holiness into the public domain.
A nisayon is also a raising up: like a child promoted after each exam, each test lifted Avraham higher, and the Akeidah was his final graduation.
The Akeidah was harder than Ur Kasdim not because of the sacrifice but because Avraham had to obey while Hashem seemed far away and contradictory, without the clarity he had always had.
The questions people have on Hashem have no substance; during a test the answers are hidden by Heavenly decree, and they become simple only afterward, as the Rashi on the Akeidah shows.

At the Akeidah Avraham was transported into the condition of ikvesa d'Meshicha, and 'eikev asher shamata' means he obeyed in the condition of the heel; that is why his emunah reaching the heel sustains the last generation.
Emes, the last word of Shema, corresponds to the heel; it is not written in the Sefer Torah but added by us, just as in the last generation the truth is not seen and must be believed in the dark.
Shema Yisrael, the last verse of Malchiyos, equals 'shofar shel ayil' in gematria: the shofar of the Akeidah's ram is how Klal Yisrael accepts Hashem's kingship.
