The calendar year mirrors world history: as the shofar disperses the year-end clouds, the great shofar will disperse the clouds of the end of days and the world will start anew, with the strength of the ram hinted at in 'Bereishis'.
The Rav reads 'pach shel shemen' as a jar that had held oil and was almost empty: all eight nights burned from its leftover drops, a light that belongs to the level of eight, beyond counting.
Rosh Hashanah, before letters existed, is served with the shofar's breath alone; Chanukah brings that same breath of life down into speech, as hallel and thanks.
The Gemara asks where the blessing over mitzvos comes from specifically in the laws of Chanukah because the first night's light matches Berachos, the first masechta.
The Torah totals the nesi'im's offerings on Zos Chanukah, though anyone could add them up, to show that on that day everything joins into one.

Applying Rav Chaim Vital's teaching that a soul who excelled in a mitzvah joins whoever does it, the Rav suggests that Aharon HaKohen joins every Jew who lights; this is how 'yours is greater than theirs' applies to all.
It works in both directions: since the hidden Menorah still burns, every Jew's Chanukah lighting also kindles Aharon's Menorah.
Precisely because Shemini Atzeres has no reason of its own, it shows Hashem's love: a distant relative needs a reason to attend a simcha, a father does not.
Chanukah is greater than Shemini Atzeres in closeness: there the Jews come up to Hashem, here Hashem comes down to the souls scattered in the street.
On Zos Chanukah Hashem does not ask the Jews to stay with Him above, as on Shemini Atzeres; He says that He will stay below with them.
Twelve nesiim of Israel stand against twelve princes of Yishmael and of Esav who lead the sitra achra, and the korbanos of the nesiim read on Zos Chanukah nullify them.
Yehuda's long retelling of what everyone already knew is read as an act of emunah: going over every detail so as to agree to and accept Hashem's guidance in each one.
The Rav applies the same idea to the end of Chanukah: one reviews what was said during the days only to settle them within oneself and pack them up to take along.
Bris milah on the eighth day is the Jew's answer to nature: nature says he was born with an orlah, and the Jew, coming from the eighth world, laughs at nature.

The final sealing of Zos Chanukah works by the Chanukah miracle's rule of 'the few in the hands of the many': a small point of mitzvos prevails over many sins, which is why it is for those who could not be acquitted on Rosh Hashanah.
The 'western wall' in a shul, where the plain Jews sit, is linked to the ner maaravi and to the Kosel Hamaaravi: what seems lowest holds the point that is never extinguished or destroyed.
The verse 'selach na' contains the initials of Chanukah only from 'hazeh' on, because on Chanukah sin is not mentioned at all.

Because shanah means repetition, the year is like a turning rotary file of days: when Rosh Hashanah comes around, what happened on that day, the creation of Adam with the breath of life, actually happens again.
The shofar answers the 'vayipach': Hashem blew His breath into us, and on the day that breath is renewed we blow it back to Him in His service.

The word 'Bereishis', the hidden tenth utterance that does not say 'vayomer', corresponds to the innermost point of the Jew, above speech and intellect, where no Jew wants to sin; this is the root of Yom Kippur's atonement, the tenth day.
The makri does not call out the first tekiah because at that level words have not yet been created; only after it does speech begin.
The ten pesukim each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofaros are the ten utterances by which man re-creates the world, and the hundred sounds are ten times ten.
From the burning of the Beis HaMikdash on the tenth of Av until Rosh Hashanah is fifty days, so Rosh Hashanah is a fiftieth day of return like Shavuos and the Yovel, marked by the shofar.
Aharon's consolation was not only the lighting in his own day: his ner hama'aravi never went out, and the Chanukah lights of every generation draw from it.
'Zos Chanukah' refers to Aharon's own dedication, which had no day of its own among the princes and continues to this day.
Because the Chanukah miracle came from mesirus nefesh above nature, its mitzvah too asks for more than a person's means, and through that effort one comes to feel the light of the mitzvah.
The Yom Tov of Chanukah is placed inside the Hallel itself: it is the praise that makes the day a Yom Tov, which is why songs of praise turn the meal into a seudas mitzvah.
As Hashem sent Lot the angels so he would have the merit of hospitality, the new chance for kiruv is a mitzvah sent from Heaven to give Klal Yisrael merit before the ingathering of the exiles.
The mezuzah and the ner Chanukah face opposite directions: the mezuzah, on the right of one entering, guards the inside; the ner Chanukah, on the right of one leaving, sends the kedushah outward.
The same pairing runs through milah and priah, and through lo sa'aseh and mitzvas aseh: one keeps the outside forces away, the other reveals the glory of Hashem.
The cold of a mitzvah done without feeling is purified by snow, and the eight lights of Zos Chanukah are the fire that stands against that snow.
Because the eighth day is above time, it is not confined to its days and can stretch the light of Chanukah over the whole year.
The Beraisa fixes Chanukah through Hallel and hoda'ah rather than the lights because these are what remain after the lighting ends.
Since Hallel on Chanukah is a full obligation, it gives its kedushah to the whole of Shacharis, as a day with Mussaf gives Shacharis the kedushah of Mussaf.
Zos Chanukah relates to the whole of Chanukah as the mitzvah tantz relates to a wedding: the final moment that leaves its impression on the whole life that follows.
Although each nasi had his own day, on Zos Chanukah all of them are read and 'enter' that day, which makes it the gathering of all of Chanukah.
Calculation suits an individual's life, but the hanhagah of Klal Yisrael as a whole is above calculation, so its outcomes come as surprises no one can foresee.
Before Hashem a single Jew is a 'rov', a majority, unlike the world's view in which one Jew counts for nothing.
The Chashmonaim went to war for Hashem's sake, yet Hashem made the miracles not for Himself but for the Jews, to show His love for them.
Judgment is not the essence of Rosh Hashanah but a byproduct of the coronation: because Hashem is re-creating His world, He decides who belongs in it.
The word shanah, year, means repetition: each year the creation is repeated, with each of the ten days of teshuvah creating another part of the world, parallel to the ten utterances.
Since every new year is a higher world, a person who stays as he was last year fails, even if he got a good mark then; he must be promoted with the world.
Although earlier generations had greater souls, the innermost chamber of the heart, which longs for Hashem, grows better in each generation.
As there is a Kodesh HaKodashim in space, there is one in time, Yom Kippur, and one in every Jew's heart, the point that wants only Hashem's will.
Keeping Shabbos Shuvah, as testimony to creation, makes a Jew a partner in Hashem's creation of the new year.
Teves is to time what Mitzrayim is to place: both are the domain of darkness and hester panim, so Yaakov's descent to Mitzrayim in Parshas Vayigash is the model for entering Teves.
Chanukah falls at the head of Teves so that its light crushes the 'head' of the month, and its power extends through the whole month, as Rosh Chodesh includes the whole month.
The 'visions of the night' in which Hashem spoke to Yaakov correspond to the long nights of Teves, and the doubled 'Yaakov, Yaakov' is a language of love spoken precisely on the threshold of exile.
Chanukah is called a beloved mitzvah because it exists to show Jews that Hashem loves them, just as they are about to enter the darkness of Teves.
Hallel means to illuminate, so the last Hallel of Chanukah is meant to light up the whole of nature in hard times.
Ordinary singing does not make a meal a seudas mitzvah, but at the Chanukah meal it does, because praise and thanksgiving are the very mitzvah for which Chanukah was established.

The division of roles, that a kohen may not be king and the king must come from Yehudah, belongs to this measured world; in the eighth world above measure one person can hold them all, which is why the first Chashmonaim were permitted both.
The Masorah counts words, not verses, only in Mikeitz, the Chanukah parsha, because a word joins letters, which stand above speech and comprehension.

The two orders of the tribes match the two views: for Beis Shammai the last is Binyamin, the last stone of the choshen and the place of the Beis Hamikdash; for Beis Hillel it is Dan, the gatherer who brings back what the others lost.
As the generations descend, they need more time for teshuvah, so a later sealing on Zos Chanukah was revealed only in later generations.
On the eighth day several nesi'im are included in one day, because above measure the little holds the much, like the small cruse of oil.

Yaakov loved Yosef for 'ben zekunim' not simply because he learned with him, but because Yosef needed only five of the six sedarim: grasping Taharos on his own showed he was a shepherd above the Shevatim.
Avraham needed no teacher because, as the first, he includes all seven shepherds, just as the first letter of a word includes the whole word and Rosh Hashanah includes the year.
Yosef personally sold the grain so that his taharah would enter it; the good taste and smell of that grain is how Yaakov knew Yosef was alive, uniting Rashi's two readings of 'yesh shever'.
The spices the Yishmaelim carried were in Yosef's honor: his taharah, which also took the taste and smell from fruit when it ceased, brings a good fragrance even into the goods of his captors.
Following Rav Tzadok, the nations clothe a bad trait in a kosher-looking exterior, like the pig showing its split hooves, whereas with Yosef the purity is real and is sensed as fragrance.
The shofar is the regular advocate on Rosh Hashanah, and when it is silent on Shabbos, Shabbos replaces it as an even better advocate, since she is the King's own daughter.
Shabbos is called the Jew's cousin, since both come from the same heavenly source and on Shabbos it becomes part of the Jewish soul as the neshamah yeseirah.
Chillul Shabbos is pictured as the servant abusing the princess: the very one who must plead for the Jews could instead bring out their guilt unless they first make peace with her.
Because Hashem created the world through speech in the six days and rested on Shabbos, a Jew's resting on Shabbos must include speech that is unlike weekday speech.
The measure of keeping Shabbos is whether Shabbos itself derives pleasure from the way it is kept; Shabbos then reciprocates with a pleasure no worldly delight can match.
The halachic order of blessings on the seven species, by closeness to the word Eretz, is read as a ranking of closeness to Olam Haba and yiras shamayim.

Of all the measures learned from the seven species, only the pomegranate's is negative: it defines when a vessel stops being a vessel, so it speaks of what is outside the Torah's measures, as the farthest Jews are.

The dispute of Rav Hamnuna and Rav Chisda over dates and pomegranates turns on whether 'Eretz chitah' is like 'a cup of wine', a place holding the fruit, or like 'a cup of gold', the fruit's very essence being bound to Eretz.

Heaven rejected the date parable for Acher but accepted the pomegranate parable because, by Rabbah bar Shila's reckoning, the last fruit is the pomegranate, which is still bound to Eretz and so to Olam Haba.
The Torah writes Eretz twice, though listing the fruits in order would have sufficed, to show that every fruit, and so every Jew, has a bond to Olam Haba, even the Torah of Acher.
The spies' fall is tied to the season: they went in Tammuz and Av, the pomegranate of the year, and Moshe's 'take of the fruit' was strength for a low time.
Amalek's ability to stay unmoved by the splitting of the sea came from his view of everything as chance; this is the root of the war against him.
Calling the splitting of the sea a natural wind does not escape the miracle: that it came exactly when the Jews fled and the Egyptians pursued is itself a greater miracle.
Amalek's attack before Matan Torah brought a coolness into the Jews' acceptance of the Torah, which was completed only when Amalek was destroyed in the days of Purim.
Unlike religions built on one individual, the Torah rests on testimony that millions passed on to their children; a fabricated mass event would have been questioned by the very next generation.

Rates measured in a laboratory cannot be extrapolated back over eons, as water shows by expanding again near freezing; the Mabul's boiling waters could do in a short time what they reckon as a billion years.
Like electricity in a wire, which is unseen but known from what it does, Hashem's presence in the world is known from life and from the harmony of creation.
The Ba'alei Mussar read Hashem's availability in the ten days through Rav standing at the butcher's door: the same nearness that is a gift becomes grounds for a greater punishment when it is ignored.
Carrying the Sefer Torah around the shul on Yom Kippur night enacts the same idea: the Torah comes to us, so that each Jew can kiss it and ask its forgiveness.
Yom Kippur is itself the 'Shabbos of Shabbosos', into which all the Shabbosos of the year flow; when it falls on Shabbos, each day fortifies the other.
In the Arvei Nachal's mashal, Shabbos and the Torah are the king's daughter and son who defend Klal Yisrael, and the advice is to fall at their feet and ask their forgiveness.
Since Hashem created the world with speech and rested on the seventh day, the rest of Shabbos includes rest from ordinary speech.

The Rav parallels soul and time: just as the souls before Moshiach are the 'heels' of the generations, Adar, the month furthest from Nisan, is the 'heels' of the year, with the same inner G-dliness under more garments.
Adar Sheini is read as hester upon hester: just when it seems Adar is over and Nisan has come, another Adar begins.
The custom of dressing up on Purim teaches that garments mean nothing: a Jew is not fooled by someone dressed as Haman or Achashverosh, for behind everything stands Hashem.

David's sparing of Shimi, which seemed to cause the decree, was really the root of the rescue: because David saw Hashem's name even in Shimi's curse, measure for measure Mordechai descended from Shimi and revealed that Haman is nothing.
The very existence of the Jewish people proclaims morality, and this, the Rav says, is what arouses the nations' hatred.
Yaakov blessed Naftali not with a virtue but with swiftness; Adar is Naftali's month, so in Adar things change quickly, and speed itself is a sign of Hashem's hand.

The Rav reads the Rema's switch from 'mishteh v'simcha' to 'add a little to the meal' as deliberate: the seudah is not Mordechai's enactment, which the custom rejects, but a thanksgiving meal on the model of a private miracle day, so it fulfils the stringent view without uprooting the minhag.
The leap month is the moon, Knesses Yisroel, catching up with the sun, Hashem, and Purim Katan belongs to the 'small luminary' that rules the night.
Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim opens with 'shivisi Hashem l'negdi tamid' and its last halachos, those of Purim Katan, close with 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid': the two 'tamid's frame a Jew's whole day.
Because no one commands it, Purim Katan can accomplish more than Purim itself: an uncommanded thanks offered in the darkness of hester panim gives Hashem special nachas.

The Midrash's 'we will rejoice in Him' teaches that rejoicing with Hashem does not depend on a day set aside with halachos, so even a day the calendar does not demand can be filled with joy in Hashem.
The final, added month can repair what was lacking in all the months before it, making the end of the year a renewal like a new creation.
The Megillah has two faces: all year it is on the level of Kesuvim, and on Purim it receives a new light; this is why a Megillah written among the Kesuvim is invalid.
For the Megillah to be written above the level of Kesuvim, Esther had to be one of the seven prophetesses.
The Rav reads 'lechalosam' in the days of Haman as 'to His kallah': like a king who goes to his bride in a disgraceful place, Hashem comes to Klal Yisroel even in its lowest state.
The bracha 'al mikra megillah' equals 'chosson v'kallah' in gematria, because the Megillah reveals Klal Yisroel as Hashem's kallah.
On Purim Katan the Megillah is read in the heavenly yeshiva that follows Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Yosi, and on Purim a Jew can enter the heichal of whichever tanna he wishes.
A small avodah of a Jew today, such as washing negel vasser, may bring Hashem more nachas than the great mesiras nefesh of earlier generations.
A mikveh can take different forms: forty se'ah of water, a day in time, and on Yom Kippur Hashem Himself is the mikveh.

Through the Chiddushei HaRim, the Rav reads 'Magen Avraham' as Hashem shielding the hidden point of Avraham Avinu in every Jew, like a pilot light that can set the whole person aflame with love and fear of Hashem.

The forty lashes of the Torah correspond to the forty days of forming a person, and only thirty-nine are given because the fortieth point never sinned; the same count explains Adam's thirty-nine curses and the thirty-nine melachos of Shabbos.
Yom Kippur is the fortieth day of teshuvah, corresponding to that fortieth point, and so on it a Jew reaches the Holy of Holies in his own heart where no Satan or angel enters.
On Yom Kippur, unlike any other tefillah, even Rosh Hashanah, Hashem speaks back to the Jew in the tefillos, saying He erases his sins and calls him to return.

The Rav reads the dispute about feasting on Adar I in light of the Magen Avraham: even if Mordechai and Esther instituted nothing for Adar I, the general duty to commemorate a miracle remains, and so cannot simply be pushed off to Adar II.

He suggests that the dispute over Adar I may parallel the dispute between Rav Nachman and Rava on whether Hallel is required on Purim: if no Hallel is required, as Rava holds, there may also be no duty to commemorate.
He explains Pharaoh's doubled dream as the model for Purim: a second time does not add a new thing but fixes and strengthens the first.
Like fire, which rises because it does not belong to this world, Purim's lights belong to a place above this world and tend to go back up, so they must be held with 'iron grips' through repetition.
Esther's delay to a second feast is explained as her understanding that the Purim she was creating needed a repetition to take hold.
Because the thirteenth month is a deeper darkness than the twelfth, a leap year's Purim must lift Jews from a greater lowliness, which is why it needs two Purims together.

The Rav reads 'one who reads the Megillah backwards has not fulfilled his obligation' as aimed at one who sees Purim only as a past event and does not know that its miracles come down today, and that the main Purim is just before Moshiach.

Since Esther is hinted in 'haster astir', which the Torah says of the end of days, the deeper the hiddenness near the end, the stronger the Purim; this is why the present generation has a greater Purim than earlier ones.

The first petichta of the Midrash on the Megillah, about cutting off Babylon, seems unrelated to the Purim story; the Rav explains that it speaks of the last and greatest Purim, when Babylon is clothed in Amalek and is finally destroyed.

Achashverosh is called a king who ruled 'by himself' to show that a ruler through whom salvation comes to the Jews is appointed by Hashem and not chosen by the people, just as the Torah had to be given by compulsion and not only because the Jews wanted it.
Haman's whole power was fear, and 'v'nahafoch' means turning that fear back onto the enemy, as in 'tipol aleihem eimasa vafachad'.
The Rav notes that the Gemara speaks of sleep, not eating, in connection with bitachon: Chizkiyahu's sleep on the night Sancheriv surrounded Yerushalayim showed his emunah.
Following a rule that whatever the Gemara brings in, even incidentally, belongs to its sugya, the Rav reads the long Avigail story as part of the meaning of Purim.

The yom tov was not accepted because the Megillah, written with ruach hakodesh, speaks of the King, Hashem, and of the final war with Amalek; the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah understood that its full yom tov belongs to the final redemption.

Because the Satan fears the kingdom of David, it always emerges through roots that invite talk, like Rus the Moabite and Bas Sheva, so that he will not suspect it; David himself caused the talk on purpose.
Avigail's 'lo sihyeh zos lecha lefukah' was her answer to David's thought that Moshiach would come from her: the kingdom would come through Bas Sheva, not through her.

Avigail the wife of David equals Esther Hamalkah in gematria, and the missing yud in her name shows the missing malchus: she is the aspect of Purim, the beginning of the kingdom that is completed at Pesach.
The Rav reads the Ba'al HaTanya's statement that we cannot bow today as meaning that real bowing, surrender of one's existence, can only be done in the place of Malchus; elsewhere it would be false.

Following the Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of place, time and soul, the Kodesh HaKodashim in place corresponds to Yom Kippur in time and to the Kohen Gadol in soul, and the ten days of teshuvah are the Beis HaMikdash in time.
There is no mitzvah to go to Yerushalayim on Yom Kippur, the holiest day, because on these days one need not come to the place of Malchus: Malchus comes to us.
The custom that the chazzan of Shacharis calls out HaMelech from his place before walking to the amud shows that the King comes to us wherever we are.
The dog is despised because it is dependent on a substitute master and happy with him; true freedom is to be a servant of Hashem alone.

The Rav compares remembering a miracle to reading Parshas Zachor each year: the remembrance must come within a span in which it would otherwise be forgotten, so a year with two Adars seemingly needs the celebration already in the first Adar.
He separates the general duty to celebrate a miracle from the specific Purim law of drinking wine, instituted because the miracle came through wine; Purim Katan has the first but not the second.
By this distinction the Rav reads the Rema's wording precisely: on Purim Katan he does not speak of a 'mishteh v'simcha' but of adding somewhat to the meal as a remembrance of the miracle.
The deeper joy of Purim Katan is the acceptance of the Torah with love on Purim, a joy so great that a Jew cannot wait with it until Purim Gadol.
He reads Boaz's 'vayitav libo' as joy in Torah study, linking the 'good heart' of Boaz to the Rema's 'a good heart is a constant feast' on Purim Katan.

The Rav reads the Chasam Sofer's account as proof that joining redemption to redemption is not a law at all: Haman, who knew the calendar, was not concerned with a Torah or rabbinic law, only with keeping salvation away, so it must be a segulah.

Because the second Adar was chosen only for the salvation Jews need in galus, the Rav suggests that in the days of Moshiach, when Purim is only a remembrance, the reason of not passing over mitzvos will prevail and Purim of a leap year will be in Adar Rishon.
The day is called Purim Katan, not Purim Rishon like Pesach Rishon, because Adar Rishon belongs to the small luminary, the moon, and is the month that fills in its diminution.

The Rav traces a chain of jealousy from the moon's diminution: the brothers against Yosef, the spies, and the rivalry of the kingdom of the House of David with that of Yosef, all of which Moshiach will heal.
Esther is the moon, and since the whole Purim story grows out of the moon's diminution, her counsel to gather all the Jews was the way to fill it in.
Shaul's merit of hiding his kingship, out of lowliness, is what brought forth Mordechai, who had the same lowliness; to such a person Hashem stands at his right hand.
The Rav reads matanos la'evyonim in light of 'there is no poverty except in da'as': the main poor one Hashem gives to is the one poor in understanding.
The very absence of da'as at a bris is its beauty: the infant who understands nothing is bound to the hidden root of Avraham Avinu, something a later, conscious act could not achieve in the same way.
The joy of Purim is the joy of a Jew at the point he does not feel: like an eight-day-old at his bris, one rejoices with the hidden love present in every Jew.

Milah, given without da'as at eight days, and tefillin, given with da'as at thirteen, are two sides of one bond, and Purim, whose 'sasson' is milah and 'yekar' is tefillin, joins them up to the peak of 'ad d'lo yada'.
Since 'the king' in the Megillah means the Ribono shel Olam, the decree to bow to Haman came from Hashem, and its whole purpose was to bring out Mordechai's mesiras nefesh from the hidden root.

The Rav reads the thirty-nine lashes through the Rambam's rule of compelled consent: the beatings only suppress the body, and the Rabbanan, who see into the depth of a Jew, know that his innermost fortieth level never consented to the sin.
He maps the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul onto the forty days of a child's formation, so that the year is formed in these days and Yom Kippur is its fortieth stage.
The thirty-nine lashes on Erev Yom Kippur match the thirty-nine days before it; the fortieth day, Yom Kippur itself, needs no lash because then the true will comes out.
Each of the forty days adds a se'ah, so Yom Kippur completes the mikveh of Klal Yisrael; an unresolved quarrel is then a chatzitzah that keeps the mikveh from working.
The 'proof' the tailor brought was the price itself: no one pays far beyond worth unless out of love, and since Hashem returns the love shown to Him, the overpayment proves forgiveness.
The Rav reads the Rema's switch from 'mishteh vesimcha' to 'yarbeh ketzas biseudah' as deliberate: the Rema is not adopting the Ran's obligation but the feast every view agrees to.

The Rav distinguishes two dinim of joy: the Magen Avraham's general yom tov for a miracle, which can be kept in any way, and Purim's own mishteh, a remembrance of a miracle that came through wine, which requires wine.
Chanukah has no din of mishteh vesimcha despite the kal vachomer of Hallel, which shows that Purim's feasting is not derived from that kal vachomer.
The Rema's rule not to go against a minhag applies where one visibly opposes it; since Jews always drink l'chaim, a little wine at the meal does not visibly break the custom.
The joy of Adar was taught by the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas because his family, descended from Haman, became Jews only through the Purim miracle.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Rav separates the joy of Purim, which is the core obligation of remembering the miracle, from the seudah and gifts, which the Sages only added as its form.
The Rav reads the Yerushalmi's moving of a Shabbos Purim seudah to Sunday as proof that the joy of Purim is a distinct joy that may not be mixed with another.
Joining Rashi's comparison of the twenty-four books to a kallah's adornments with the Megillah, the Rav says Megillas Esther itself became a kallah, so the joy of the Megillah is a kallah's joy.

With the mashal of a king whose kallah is found in a disgraceful place, the Rav explains that it is no disgrace for the king to go to her, since she is his kallah; so the joy of Purim is Hashem's closeness to the Jewish people even in their lowest state.

The Rav reads the Rambam's coerced consent as the body being pushed aside so that the soul, which always wants Hashem's will, can speak, and identifies this inner will with the Yechida that Yom Kippur reveals.

From the Ohr HaChaim on Korach the Rav derives that a sinner's blemish climbs up through his ancestry but stops before Yaakov Avinu, the trunk of the tree, so no Jew can fall low enough to damage that point in himself.

The Rav links the missing fortieth lash to the first day of a person's formation, when he was in direct contact with his Creator, and finds the same thirty-nine-not-forty pattern in Adam's curses and the melachos of Shabbos.
He suggests that the image of his father that Yosef saw was the point of Yaakov Avinu within himself, the same point a Jew is meant to meet on Yom Kippur.

The Rav explains that lashes are received on Erev Yom Kippur, the thirty-ninth day of the forty from Rosh Chodesh Elul, and that this is why the Torah's lashes stop at thirty-nine: the fortieth day is Yom Kippur, where no sin reaches.
He describes the forty days of Elul as pouring one se'ah of teshuvah a day into the mikveh of Yom Kippur, so that on Yom Kippur the mikveh is complete.

Every substance carries a fixed measure of spiritual 'units' set at creation, so a half-shekel of silver holds exactly enough love to arouse Hashem's love in return, like the five sela'im of pidyon haben.

The letters of 'barech' show doubling in the ones, tens and hundreds, and blessing reaches its full measure at a hundredfold; this is why the hundred kikar of shekalim, given in Adar, became ten thousand.
Haman gave a hundred times what the Jews gave in order to capture the power of the number one hundred, but the Jews had already preceded him with a hundred kikar given generously.
Yehoash's soul is rooted in Parshas Shekalim, so his life, saved by the Kodesh HaKodashim despite his later sin there, is itself the explanation of what Shekalim is: a place no sin can blemish.
Haman took a beam from the Kodesh HaKodashim for the gallows because his war was against the innermost point of the Jews, and that very beam took revenge on him.
Haman's slander that the Jews were 'asleep from mitzvos' could reach the lower letters of the Name in a Jew's soul, but not the yud and its tip, which precede them.
The name Yehoash contains the letters yud-hei-vav of the Name together with 'esh', fire, the element of the yud and of the coin of fire shown to Moshe.
The Rav reads Moshe's forgetting of the extra shekels as a sign of where they came from: they were given by the 'forgotten' souls outside the camp, so the forgetting itself belongs to them.
The hooks made from the outsiders' silver hung partly outside the holy courtyard yet held the curtains to the pillars, just as those Jews stand outside yet remain bound to the camp.
Haman priced the Jews by the shekalim of the 600,000 alone, repeating Amalek's error of thinking the sinning Jews outside the camp no longer count before Hashem.

Adar Sheni, the thirteenth month that has no permutation of Hashem's name, corresponds to the Jews expelled beyond the twelve tribes' camps, which is why Adar is the 'forgotten' month that Haman's lottery found.

Rabbi Akiva, who expounded the crowns of the letters that are shaped like hooks, is the one who reminded Moshe of the hooks of the pillars, and his name hints at 'ikvesa d'Meshicha', the last generations.
Parshas Zachor must be read from the scroll precisely because its message, that no Jew is cut off, has to be fully understood with all its derashos by every Jew.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Megillah opens with Achashverosh's feast to show that Hashem began the salvation in the very midst of the Jews' sin.

Unlike every other nation, which falls when Hashem topples its heavenly prince, Amalek's prince is the yetzer hara in the Jewish heart; Hashem leaves this war to the Jews, and only when they win it does physical Amalek fall, the reverse of the usual order.

The two faces of Amalek, attacking milah and casting doubt in emunah, are one thing: the clear emunah of the Jews is Avraham's inheritance through the bris, so a blemish of the bris clouds the emunah.

Heresy comes from the heart, not the head: a person who will not admit a weakness invents a philosophy that justifies it, so the demand for logical proof is really a cover for a lack of shmiras habris.

Tefillin are the keser, worn on the body but not part of it, because Elokus lies beyond even the mind; they are black because emunah in galus has no grasp, and this is the 'yikar' written in the Targum-language of galus.
The orlah, an extra part on the body that belongs to no other creature, answers the heretic: if the body can hold something that does not belong to it, it can also carry tefillin, something above it.

Just as Mitzrayim is the 'ervas ha'aretz' of place, the era before Moshiach is the 'ervas hazman' of time, when heresy and immorality spread together; Purim, the last month of the year, is given as strength for it.

The emunah of today's Jews in the deepest darkness of galus gives Hashem a nachas ruach He did not have even in the time of the Beis HaMikdash, and in this the present generations are greater than earlier ones.

The Rav explains that the Tzedukim's logic, that a king's meal is prepared outside, is correct for a king, but on Yom Kippur Hashem relates to Yisrael as husband to wife, and alone together the wife may prepare the food in his presence.

He ties the dispute to Torah sheba'al peh: the Chachmei Yisrael are the mistress of the house who run its affairs, and the Tzedukim, who denied this, rejected the whole concept of Yisrael as Hashem's beloved.
He explains that the Chachamim gave no reply in the Yerushalmi because this is not a single point that one argument can settle; it is an entire outlook, and one who rejects it cannot be answered.
Only in the Shemoneh Esrei of Yom Kippur does Hashem speak to us, in the words 'shuvah eilai ki ge'alticha', showing that the relationship of chassan and kallah belongs to Yom Kippur.
Since smell was the one sense not damaged by the sin of the Eitz HaDa'as, the ketores and Shir HaShirim, both built on fragrance, express a love that never suffers any blemish.
The Tzeduki Kohen Gadol was punished with worms coming out of his nose, the organ of smell, because he denied the sense of smell and the level of Shir HaShirim.
Hereditary office is not a social arrangement: because kingship is Hashem's alone and His kingship is 'in every generation', a king who is a vessel for it must pass it on to his son.

The Rav distinguishes kingship from service: the bigger Eisav's nation, the more its ruler is their servant, and likewise a chazan appointed only temporarily is a servant, so the Rema's condition does not contradict the Torah's promise of inheritance.

Before David received the promise, Moshiach could come from any tribe; Shaul reigned exactly when Edom's eight kings had passed, so he could have been the one, which the Rav sees hinted in a gematria linking Shiloh and Shaul.

From the Targum that Shaul counted the people by their Pesach lambs, the Rav concludes that his war on Amalek fell on the eve of Pesach, the destined time, so delaying by even a day meant the chance was gone.

Shaul did not dispute Shmuel's prophecy, only his halachic ruling, and was entitled to his own reasoning; his failure was that the war against Amalek, the opposite of self-nullification, required him to yield to the elder of the generation.
Esther is the counterpart of Shaul: as queen she still obeyed Mordechai as she had as a girl, and that self-nullification is what let her prevail over Haman.
Purim's meal falls on a weekday because its task is to elevate kelipas nogah, which cannot be done on Shabbos and which only a Jew, not a gentile, can raise to holiness.

Just as a dead animal has every limb of a living one and lacks only its life, every thing, Amalek included, has an inner life-force, and Parshas Zachor targets that life-force rather than Amalek's body.
The Rav notes that Amalek has the numerical value of 'safek', doubt, which is how Amalek's power cools a Jew's emunah.
The two verses about erasing Amalek, 'timcheh' in Ki Seitzei and 'emcheh' in Beshalach, show that our part is to weaken him while the full erasure belongs to Hashem in the days of Moshiach.
Holy things are kept covered so the forces of harm do not envy them, yet the whole Megillah is opened, because Purim's holiness spreads out over the whole world.

The absence of Hashem's Name from the Megillah reflects that Purim, like Yom Kippur, reaches a level above the Name Havaya, so the Name appears only hidden in initial and final letters, and in 'zeh einenu shoveh li' even backwards.
Just as on Purim one gives to whoever stretches out a hand without checking the order of priority, Hashem on Purim grants every request, even more than on Shabbos.
The garments Hashem made for Adam were a measure-for-measure reward: because Adam covered Chava's shame with praise rather than blaming her, Heaven covered them with garments of honor.
Rabbi Meir's 'kosnos or' with an aleph is read as the inner insight of a person who sees through the Torah's narratives: clothing itself carries a light.
The hiddenness of the Purim miracle is not a sign of its smallness but of its greatness: its source was too high to be revealed to physical eyes.
Achashverosh's months of feasting were the gift of oneg Shabbos, taken from the Jews when they did not honor Shabbos and handed to him.
Purim comes in a masquerade because its light is too great to face directly, and drinking is like the anesthetic given before surgery so that one does not feel what is being done.
The holier a part of a person is, the more it must be covered, so the dignity of a human being is precisely in his being covered.
Vashti's fashions drew the Jewish women to the party, ending the Shabbos zemiros at home; the Rav reads the Megillah's opening as a loss of tznius that cost the Jews their Shabbos song.
The Gemara's leniency to use inferior wicks and oils on Chanukah becomes a statement about souls: Chanukah reaches Jews whom even Shabbos cannot set alight.
The halachah that the Chanukah lamp belongs below ten tefachim, the one place the Shechinah never goes, shows that on Chanukah Hashem descends to those who cannot ascend.
The hidden light conceals itself by nature, which is why Yosef's brothers and Yehuda failed to see the light of Moshiach in Yosef and in Tamar until it was revealed.
The name Chashmonaim spells Chodesh, Shabbos, Milah and Ner: Hashem answered the Greeks' attempt to uproot three mitzvos by adding a fourth.
The single sealed flask of oil that the Greeks could not defile is the hidden point of faith in every Jew, which no impurity can reach.
The Rav explains that Canaan corresponds to chesed precisely because in the sitra achra the male side is subdued ('nichna'), the reverse of holiness, where gevurah yields to chesed.
The kri/ksiv of 'iro' shows the hidden tziruf of Adar: only because the word ends with heh is the Name complete, hinting that in Adar the male yields to the female.

The Gemara's 'Memuchan is Haman' and the Midrash's 'Memuchan is Daniel' do not conflict: Daniel, the soul of redemption, ruled for the heavenly court that the right side prevail, and Haman ruled the same thing below.

Rabbi Yehuda's simanim for the plagues follow his view that chametz must be burned: as the soul of Yehuda, corresponding to fire, the root of all elements, he insists on reaching the root, the initials.

Har HaBayis, bought from Aravnah, whose name begins with the letters of 'or' (the element of fire), and Me'aras HaMachpelah, bought from Efron, whose name spells 'afar' (earth), are Israel's 'reishis' and 'acharis', and both hold the same Adam and Avos.
Moshe's name is missing from Tetzaveh, read in the week of his yahrzeit, because Moshe takes a different name in each generation; in Haman's time he was Mordechai.
Mishloach manos makes all Jewish families one, like an eruv chatzeiros, where a shared meal unites separate households, and Amalek's power of mockery cannot bear such unity.
The Purim miracles are not lesser for being hidden; they are greater, and precisely because they are so great they had to be concealed so that no harm could take hold of them.

Jewish dress works opposite to the nations' custom: they honor by uncovering, while Jews honor and guard holiness by adding layers, a yarmulke and over it a hat, because the Shechinah rests on the head of one who serves Hashem.
Achashverosh's 127 provinces express a lowered image of the heavenly order: seven for the lower world, twenty for the middle world and one hundred for the upper world, each placed in a lower 'digit'.

The sin at Achashverosh's feast was not the food but its spirit: attending a celebration that kingship remains with the nations is rejoicing in the exile of the Shechinah, even when everything served is kosher.
The dispute whether Achashverosh was wise or foolish is really a dispute about what reveals true kingship: the far who accept it, or the near who stand around the king.
In Heaven the feast that opens the Megillah is read as a feast for the distant: Hashem showed the Jews of the exile that the small service of a Jew in Adar outweighs the great avodah of Temple times.
The Rav reads 'Zachor es yom haShabbos l'kadsho' as an instruction to make a Shabbos worth remembering: a Shabbos of such davening, learning and singing that one remembers it long afterwards.
The lechem hapanim is not a korban placed on a vessel but part of the Table itself, which explains both why its 'tamid' is written in Parshas Terumah and why its baking does not override Shabbos.
The kohanim eating the lechem hapanim on Shabbos expresses that on Shabbos a Jew himself becomes the Mishkan, taking a piece of the Mishkan into himself.
Achashverosh's 'k'tov lev hamelech bayayin' on the seventh day shows a Shabbos without preparation: since by mazal Shabbos is a heavy day for him, he needed wine to cheer himself up.
The seventh officer, Memuchan, whose name the Gemara reads as 'heichinu', corresponds to Shabbos, because the whole character of Shabbos is that it cannot be had without preparation.
Purim is like an anesthetic before surgery: its revelation is too great for a person to bear consciously, so one drinks until 'lo yada'.
Sin is a 'passing of Moshe' within a person, but teshuvah turns it into a 'birth of Moshe' on a higher level, as Moshe Rabbeinu passed away and was born in Adar.
The Rav reads the Gemara's 100 versus 101 times as a definition: being an oved Hashem is measured by going beyond one's own accepted standard, not by the level one has reached.
A masmid who fought his way to eight hours of learning a day was an oved Hashem while he struggled, but once that is his routine and he stops striving he is 'lo avado' again.

The Rav links Beis Hillel's adding a candle to 'do good' and Beis Shammai's decreasing to 'turn from evil', and shows that the mehadrin's growth applies to holding back from sin as well, such as taking on stringencies in kashrus.

Building on the Chasam Sofer's reading of Chashmonaim as 'oil' and 'eight', the Rav reads the letters of Chanukah as 'kohen' and eight: for eight days every Jew is a kohen preparing the lights in his home, which becomes like a Mikdash.
The Rav explains the Rambam's calling Chanukah especially cherished through Rashi's reason that milah was dear to Avraham Avinu: what comes through pain and mesiras nefesh becomes beloved.

The unprecedented temptations of modern times, from new inventions to the state of the streets, are the Satan's 'last meal' before he is slaughtered, granted so that it will be tested who serves Hashem.
Since nefesh means one's will, holding back from a desire, such as a clever joke at someone's expense or a word during seder, is real mesiras nefesh, a small fraction of the Akeidah.
Shmuel's opening 'Hashem sent me to anoint you king' is not a preface but the condition for the war: only one who includes all of Klal Yisrael can fight Amalek, who includes all impurity.

Shaul's sparing of the animals came from humility, not desire: not believing he was king, he tried to acquire the all-including power through korbanos on the mizbeach in Binyamin's portion, turning the war into a preparation for the mizbeach.
Binyamin's stone on the choshen lacks the letters of the avos precisely because Binyamin is himself the unity of Israel, the place of the mizbeach.
The donations of the nesi'im, the shoham and milu'im stones, were of the aspect of the months and shevatim rather than of Shabbos, unlike every other gift to the Mishkan.

Haman's lottery read Adar as weak, Binyamin's month without the names of the avos and the month of Moshe's death, but in Adar Sheni the all-including power was present through Mordechai, a spark of Moshe, and through Binyamin's mizbeach.
Reading the Megillah 'backwards' means reading it as past history; one who does so does not fulfill the mitzvah, because its salvations happen again each year at the reading.
The Purim seudah is like taking a medicine or vitamin: each bite brings in the strength of the renewed acceptance of Torah, since Mordechai instituted it.

The Rav reads the Megillah's double name as a key: a sefer is written for anyone who buys it, but an iggeres is addressed to one person, so every Jew should feel that the Megillah was written to him, the way a son feels news from home.

He contrasts the Megillah with lofty mitzvos that are covered, like the shofar, the matzos and the Sefer Torah, of which only the column being read is opened: the Megillah is spread open entirely, because it reveals what is hidden and spreads its lights through the world.
Since Purim's nature is to descend, the lowness of the generation is no obstacle but the reverse: the lower the generation, the greater its Purim, and the greater Mordechai becomes.
He explains Hashem's special love for Esther as His love for a generation that serves Him in hiddenness, without the sweetness earlier generations felt, and says such service merits keser malchus.
Citing R' Yitzchak of Vorka, he identifies the earlier days on which the Megillah may be read as the three days of preparation before Purim's kabbalas haTorah of love, as before Shavuos.
He explains the custom of disguising oneself on Purim from the fact that Purim's lights, greater in one respect than Shabbos, come down clothed and hidden.

The Rav applies the Mishnah's practice of salting a cow's womb, so that it loves the calf born in pain, to explain why the Rambam calls Chanukah, acquired with mesiras nefesh, an exceedingly dear mitzvah.

The Rav suggests that the name Chashmon is an acronym of Chodesh, Shabbos, Milah and Ner: since the Greeks sought to uproot three mitzvos, Hashem added a fourth, just as the Midrash says He answered Haman with Purim.

Because the Greeks invaded the Beis HaMikdash, a domain that was not theirs, the Rav explains that Chanukah answers measure for measure by invading the domain of tumah: night, the left side, the public domain and the longest nights of Teves.

The Rav reads 'vayehi kehayom' in Yosef's trial as the twenty-fifth day, the tekufah when the nations held their festival and no Torah was learned, and sees Chanukah on the twenty-fifth as its counterweight.

The Rav explains that the letters of Yavan, yud, vav and final nun, are one point stretched ever lower, showing the Greeks spreading in tumah, while Chanukah's lights spread more each night in kedushah.

The Rav contrasts Shabbos, when a Jew rises to the kedushah, with Chanukah, when the kedushah descends below ten tefachim; this is why even inferior oils and wicks are allowed on Chanukah, and why souls that Shabbos does not reach can be kindled.
The Megillah writes 'turning over' twice, for the day and for the month, so the whole month carries the power of reversal, including a person turning his own ways around.
The three days before Purim on which the Megillah could once be read are three days of preparation, as before Shavuos, since Purim is a receiving of the Torah with love.
'Yom Kippurim' is read as 'a day like Purim', not the reverse, showing that Purim is the greater day.
Food, unlike other mitzvos, enters the body and becomes part of the person, which is why each Yom Tov has a food that lets a Jew carry the day's holiness with him after it ends.
A Sefer Torah is kept covered because it is holy, but the Megillah, holier still, is opened entirely, since 'Megillah' comes from revealing and its holiness must spread over the world.
The great tzaddikim could not ask for the geulah on Purim because then they were shown that galus is not mere punishment but has tikkunim still to be done.
Torah learned with love and awe does what the passing of tzaddikim otherwise does: it lifts the judgments to their root in Binah and sweetens them there.

Rashi joins Mordechai and Esther in one explanation because both sought to die as an atonement, and 'what came upon them' is the next verse, 'kiymu v'kiblu': their self-sacrifice brought Torah with love, so the sacrifice itself was no longer needed.
Following the Chasam Sofer, an early improvement can be a trick of the Satan to weaken prayer while the decree still stands, which is why Mordechai returned to his sackcloth and fasting.
Amalek attacked just as the Jews were climbing toward Sinai, because their desire for Torah had weakened; Haman, his descendant, rose under the same conditions, when the Jews were lax in mitzvos.
The souls of a beis medrash's chevra are bound together from above, corresponding to a chevra on high, so the people who come together to one beis medrash are not there by chance.
Just as Ezra had to separate the people from foreign wives before the Second Temple, mass intermarriage today precedes the Third, since everything written in Tanach is eternal.
In the Satmar Rav's story, what troubled the tzaddik was not the missed custom itself but that he had become worse, and the Rav says a person must likewise ask why he has cooled off.
Haman chose Adar thinking Moshe's merit ended with his death, but for Jews 'death of Moshe' does not exist: a Yehoshua always follows to carry the Torah, so Moshe's influence never ends.

The stragglers whom Amalek struck were cast out by the cloud and called 'not fearing G-d' by the passuk, yet precisely for them Hashem declares eternal war on Amalek, which shows how dear even such a Jew is.
Purim, unlike other Yamim Tovim, needs no preparation because it came by lot, and a lot reveals what is one's own without effort: the Jew's bond to Hashem, who chose him as His portion.
The Megillah is called an iggeres because it is a personal letter from the King to each Jew by name, and the further a Jew is, the more it is addressed to him.
Drinking on Purim is needed because the holiness revealed then is too great to receive in a conscious state, just as some things can only be borne under anesthesia.
The two mentions of 'once a year' at the end of Tetzaveh hint at two atonements: the avodah of Yom Kippur and Purim's 'avodah without avodah', a Yom Tov made for the stragglers.

Aharon earned the choshen, which carries the judgment of Bnei Yisrael on the heart, because he rejoiced in his younger brother's greatness; only one without personal interest can hold Klal Yisrael in his heart.
The empty receptacles of the menorah, which seem to contradict the rule that a brachah rests on fullness, are themselves the message: they are souls still waiting to be kindled.

The reshus harabim, whose very name means 'the many', stands opposite the oneness of the Yachid shel Olam, yet the Chanukah lights were meant to be lit there to bring kedushah into the territory of tumah.
The Satan targets the finer souls, which is why returnees are often more devoted than those born into observance.
Unlike the seven-branched menorah of the Beis HaMikdash, the Chanukah menorah's eight lights show what the menorah will be like when Moshiach comes.
Each night's added light is another soul retrieved from the Satan's captivity, and the eighth night corresponds to Moshiach, when no receptacle will remain empty.
Purim did not only add another holy day to the calendar like Shabbos and the Yamim Tovim; it brought into being a new world above that had never existed, the root of Mordechai's soul.

Yom Kippur and Purim reach the same world of yechidah from opposite directions: on Yom Kippur Jews leave the world and rise like angels, while on Purim the light descends into eating and drinking and sanctifies the body.

The Yom Kippur requirement to make peace with others before the day is not only a separate obligation: without becoming one soul with all Jews one simply has no Yom Kippur, and the same holds for Purim.
The word 'mikra' in the blessing on the Megillah is read as 'calling': the blessing is a summons to the hidden light of the Megillah to come down.
The halachah that the Megillah is spread out fully and folded rather than rolled reflects its essence: it is the revelation of what was hidden, the light concealed above becoming revealed.
Purim wine and Purim tzedakah are a different kind of wine and tzedakah, just as an esrog that costs little before Sukkos becomes a precious mitzvah object when Sukkos arrives.
A miracle cloaked in nature is not smaller than the splitting of the sea but greater, since Hashem achieved the salvation without needing to change nature at all.
The months descend from Nissan to Adar just as the generations descend toward the end of days; our era is the Adar of history, in which the miracles are as real as ever but hidden.
The word 'happened' does not belong in a Jew's dictionary: calling events chance is itself the 'karcha' of Amalek, which cooled the warmth of Jewish faith.
Hamelech, kes and Haman share the gematria 95: Haman's presence is what forces the Megillah to say 'the King' instead of Hashem's name.
The pshat and the derash of 'the King' do not conflict: the verse means Achashverosh, but Achashverosh acted as he did because the King above pulled the strings.
Yom Kippur and Purim are opposites in direction: on Yom Kippur we rise to Hashem, while on Purim Hashem descends to the lowest levels and holiness enters nature itself.
Reading the Megillah backwards, as an old story from long ago, is not fulfilling the mitzvah, because the Megillah happens anew every year when Adar and Purim come.

The direction of the hidden Name follows the story: in order when Esther invites the king and Haman, a sign of kindness; reversed in the final letters when Haman says 'all this is worth nothing to me', a sign of judgment beginning against him.

At the climax of the Megillah both judgment and kindness were needed, one for Haman's downfall and one for the salvation of the Jews, which is why the Gemara concludes to say both blessings after the reading.
A month's weather reflects its permutation of the Name: Nissan, its Name in order in the initial letters, is pleasant and kind, while Tammuz, its Name reversed, is the harshest month.
The world's leaders are like Purim players in costume: an honest Jew sees that even a world leader has no free choice to move a finger except for the sake of the Jewish people.
Haman's own advice as Memuchan, to remove Vashti, prepared his downfall: the Megillah's miracles are a chain of natural events that could not have lined up by chance.

The Mishnah says the Megillah 'is read' rather than 'one reads' it; when the reading falls away on Shabbos in Yerushalayim, the Rav says the Megillah reads itself, as it were by Hashem, and must be heard with spiritual ears.
The thirty-six hours of the hidden light correspond to the thirty-six tractates of Shas and to the thirty-six candles lit over the eight days of Chanukah.
Shechem, whom the Rav calls a monster, carried a spark of Moshiach ben Yosef; Hashem hid it there as one hides a diamond in a garbage can, where thieves and the Satan would never look.
The Chanukah candle is the one mitzvah that draws the Shechinah below ten tefachim, into the domain of the Satan, to bring out holiness from there, and this is the pattern of Moshiach.
Dina, who was first conceived as Yosef, provided Yosef's match through Osnas, and the letters of her name spelled out in full equal Moshiach ben Yosef in gematria.
Yaakov hiding Dina in a box was no accident: she belongs concealed, because she is the Chanukah light and the hidden light.
Ovadia, a convert from Esav, prophesies Esav's downfall, like the axe whose handle is cut from the very forest it chops down.
Purim was created in galus, so in some ways Purim is better in galus than in Eretz Yisroel; Purim of the walled cities belongs to higher levels than Purim made for those outside them.
Every Jew in galus is a shliach, and his home on 16th Avenue or 42nd Street is like a Chabad house; the "converts" the Jews are exiled to gather are sparks of holiness.
When prophecy ended, Purim began a new era: ruach hakodesh today means arriving at the truth in the Gemara and in halachah through clear learning.
Simcha is the test of learning: one who seeks Hashem in the Gemara feels joy, and one who feels none was not seeking Hashem's will in his learning.
Torah is of the mind and tefillah of the heart; just as a hole in the heart or the brain makes a creature treif, a person needs both Torah and tefillah to live with deveikus.
Deveikus is for everyone: learning even a piece of Chumash with Rashi with taste and vitality is deveikus at one's own level.
Purim Meshulash and Shabbos Erev Pesach always come together: when Purim falls on Friday, Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos, so Purim Meshulash carries the geulah kevius of the Imrei Noam.

The Rav reads 'velo ya'avor' through the moon: the second half of the month is Eisav's domain, so Purim, the wiping out of Amalek, cannot cross into it until Moshiach, just as Edom told Yisrael 'lo sa'avor bi'.
The Sunday seudah of Purim Meshulash, held on the sixteenth, is the one time in decades that the Jews step into Eisav's domain.
Hillel's rise to the nesius on a Shabbos Erev Pesach, a nesius of Beis Dovid, was itself a sign of Moshiach ben David on that kevius.
R' Chezkel of Kuzmir's claim that Moshiach would come in his weaker generation is no joke: less is expected of later generations, whose trials are greater.
Since Torah and tefillah must enter through the mouth, a mouth soiled by forbidden speech blocks them; the Pesach mitzvos of eating and telling purify the mouth so that 'Toras Hashem' may be in it.
The lowest generation is the 'heel' of Moshiach, and its very lowness is its task: Moshiach comes to the lowest generation.
The wicks and oils that burn poorly stand for souls that Shabbos cannot ignite; on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down to them, so they are fit for Chanukah lights.
The Beraisa says 'on the 25th of Kislev the days of Chanukah are eight' without 'begin', because in the Mikdash all eight days were literally one day, the 25th.

The Kohanim's crying was not over a lost mitzvah but over the Menorah above: as long as the Menorah below burns, the Menorah above glows and sends light and blessing; if it goes out there is galus and darkness.
The Kohanim lit naturally, not by a miracle: Hashem, who prepared at creation the nature for now and the nature for later, moved the nature of Yemos HaMashiach into the time of the Chashmonaim.
The Rambam holds back the laws of Hallel until the end of Sefer Zmanim, in the laws of Chanukah, because hallel and thanks are the particular blessing of Chanukah.
Jews who are not yet worthy can 'borrow' from their future: because they will be good, they may already call Hashem 'Father' now, and this was Esther's plea for salvation that very day.
A large alef is seen from afar, a small alef only from close up: in Adar's hiddenness the call of love seems absent, but once one is brought near through Purim one sees it was there all along.

The hooks of the pillars, made from the forgotten extra silver, stood outside the holy courtyard; they are the forgotten Jews, who are still destined to be fastened to the great pillars of Torah and chessed.
The extra Jews are linked to the forgetting of Torah, and Rabbi Akiva's soul, the root of pilpul, could account for them, because sharp Torah study can recover even what fell to the fiftieth gate.
Like a diamond given up to save a life that then lives on in every descendant, Moshe's Mishkan was not lost: its holiness took the wrath meant for Israel and keeps the people alive.
Hashem's Name is concealed in the Megillah because its light comes from a hidden world that cannot be revealed outward, and the reading of the Megillah is what calls that light down.
Esther wanted only kindness, but Hashem agreed only in part: Purim needed both chassadim for Israel and judgment on Haman, so her words carry the Name both ways.
The 300 killed in Shushan on the second day were new Amalekites: men with a finer spark of Amalek who would not count as Amalek for a simple Jew but do for the higher Jew of Shushan Purim.

Mordechai left Jerusalem for Shushan to raise Esther because his light could be revealed only in a place of hester panim, planting for all generations the power of hidden Jews to bind themselves to the light of Purim.
In Shushan the light is called Shoshanah rather than Esther: Esther is hiddenness, while Shoshanah is the rose that blooms openly in its beauty.

Mordechai's two answers in the Targum do not contradict: bowing to Haman as the controller of one's livelihood is idolatry in the higher tractate of Avodah Zarah, and Haman's image 'from behind' is even a passing thought that someone other than Hashem gives one's bread.

Mordechai turned the slave-for-bread claim around: it is not Haman who gives him bread but he who gives Haman bread, since all blessing comes down first to Israel and only through them to the nations.
The seudah of Shushan Purim is a seudas bris milah: both remove the orlah and reveal the holy point, giving a glimmer of the days of Moshiach.

Esther named Shushan only because Achashverosh would never grant a Yom Tov for Jerusalem, knowing that Shushan would vanish while Jerusalem, the one place that is certainly a walled city, would remain.

The Torah does not write 'and he died' of Hadar, the eighth king, while Ezra's pesukim do; the Rav learns from this that each tzaddik records events by his own soul's root, which explains why Ezra placed Mordechai lower.
Haman's error was that he saw Moshe had died in Adar but did not know that Moshe was born in Adar, meaning that Moshe lives on in Mordechai, the Moshe of the generation.
Mordechai is mor dror, musk, which the Rambam holds kosher and the Raavad forbids; so too some judged Mordechai unfit, and mor dror equals in gematria 'on the seventh of Adar Moshe was born'.
Yaakov's dealings with Lavan's sheep, and all his work in Lavan's house, brought out deep Torah from hiding.
The first three names in the passuk form the initials of a shin, whose three heads allude to the three Avos, hinting that the men listed before Mordechai were counted by appearance alone.
On Purim the light of Mordechai's soul-root comes down, a light so great that even at Matan Torah no such light came down.

Every feature of Chanukah breaks the Jewish preference for favorable times and places: end of the month instead of its first half, left instead of right, night in Teves, the public domain, below ten tefachim. The Rav reads this as Chanukah being the Yom Tov of the deepest galus.

Going out to the public domain is going out of Hashem's 'atmosphere', which is why carrying out on Shabbos is forbidden; lighting there means conquering territory from the Satan and bringing back neshamos that fell to the side of the yetzer hara.

The candle is the neshamah ('ner Hashem nishmas adam'), so the Chanukah lights kindled in the dark stand for blown-out neshamos given a new sparkle, and the words 'haneiros halalu kodesh hem' refer to them.
The Rav reads the Midrash on 'Vayehi ba'eis hahi' as the answer to the questions of our own dark time: each of the Avos and Shevatim was busy with his own trouble, and Hashem was preparing Moshiach.
The dark episodes of the parsha produced both Mashiachs: from Dina and Shechem came Asnas, Yosef's wife and the source of Moshiach ben Yosef, and from Yehudah and Tamar came Moshiach ben David.

A mitzvah is like a button at the bottom of the Empire State Building that turns on every light: our 248 limbs correspond to 248 mitzvos, and each movement brings light or the opposite into the world without our seeing how.
Achashverosh thought Vashti was killed on Pesach, but the wise men told him the day was Shushan Purim, so the Megillah's miracle both begins and ends on Shushan Purim.

The Chasam Sofer's reading of the decree on the day of the omer waving (the war on Amalek on erev Pesach, the Beis Hamikdash that night) explains why the kings who feared its rebuilding celebrated only after Pesach passed.
Shaul counted the people with sheep because they were the Pesach lambs to be offered right after the war on erev Pesach.
Building on the Ruzhiner, the Rav explains that Shmuel's night-long cry was a tefillah that Shaul's plan, sparing Agag so Haman and Purim would come, should succeed.
The Satan blocks with 'water' precisely what decides the eternity of Israel: he did so at the Akeidah, which answered Yishmael, and again when Mordechai went to gather the Jews.
Today's exile, with its politics, parties and elections, is itself the Satan's great 'water', and the mesiras nefesh of Mordechai's cry is what lets Jews pass through it.
The Satan of Yishmael hates wine because he knows his downfall will come when Jews drink wine on Purim.
Kaddish is said in Aramaic, the language of the 'back side' of holiness, because its whole content is that Hashem's kingship be revealed even in the place of the sitra achra.
The Megillah has a 'second Targum' because it belongs to Adar, the last month, which itself has a second Adar beyond the order of months: its light reaches even lower.
A large part of the Targum Sheni, seemingly unrelated to the Megillah, speaks about Shlomo Hamelech, because like the Megillah he went down into the lowest places to reveal Hashem's kingship.
Esther's messenger to Mordechai was a shed, which explains the plural 'vayagidu', the plural of the 'others' of the sitra achra, and why Mordechai had to go into water after speaking with it.

Yaakov left Lavan's deepest sparks because the lowest klipah holds the highest sparks; he could repair them only at Gilad, the place of Eliyahu, where 'yegar sahadusa' equals 'malchuso bakol mashalah' in gematria.
The 'yekar' of the Megillah's Targum equals 'ketzeh ha'am' and 'pisgam' equals 'chodesh Adar' in gematria: the Megillah's Targum speaks to those who have fallen to the edge of the camp.
Shushan Purim, the Purim of walled Yerushalayim, is the day of the final letter tzaddik, the future redemption, which is why Yerushalayim's 'wall of fire' is tied to it.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Megillah is the same Torah of Moshe accepted willingly rather than under compulsion, and so it reveals greater light and will be understood ever more in the future.

Ezra's writing 'and he died' of Hadar, and his listing Mordechai as having fallen, have one root: his book records things at the level of his prophecy, which does not reach the world of the eighth king to which Mordechai belonged.
Wisdom can grasp beyond prophecy, yet as long as Amalek is in the world nothing more can be grasped; Mordechai, living after Amalek's eradication, could reach further.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof from the end of the verse, 'lo yasuf', rather than its beginning, reflects the higher level of Shushan Purim, while the beginning of the verse reflects Purim as it is understood today and as Ezra understood it.
True mesiras nefesh means going without expecting a miracle: Avraham was saved in Ur Kasdim, while Haran, who went only because he expected a miracle, was burned.
Pesach was a rescue from suffering, but Chanukah was itself the product of suffering, and that is why the Rambam singles it out as beloved.
Chanukah closes the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros, making it both a Yom Tov in itself and the Yom Tov of the siyum of all the mitzvos.
The 36 hours Adam enjoyed the ohr haganuz correspond to the 36 masechtos of Gemara where the light is hidden, and to the 36 candles of Chanukah.
The Jewish people grew into a nation at every stage outside its homeland, and received the Torah in the desert, to show that its existence rests on the Torah, which is above nature.
Shemen is linked to shemini, eight, and rises above all liquids, unlike yayin, which is seventy; so the hidden light appears on Chanukah through the oil.
The Rav reads 'malkah' in 'Esther HaMalkah wrote' as ruach hakodesh, not political rank: her authority over the Chachamim came from prophecy, not from the throne.

The verse about Achashverosh's tax, which seems to interrupt Esther's dialogue with the Chachamim, is the premise of her answer: he was no king, so the 'kings of Madai and Paras' are Mordechai and Esther.
A Jewish king is a giver of kedushah and a king of the nations is a taker; Achashverosh, who levies a tax, loses the vav of giving from his name, as Efron did.
Shlomo HaMelech, who ruled the world without war, is a model of the future Yerushalayim that will need no physical wall because Hashem will be its wall of fire.
The Jews of Shushan, who had sinned more, received a greater day precisely because nothing remained in them but the indestructible inner point of Yerushalayim.
The Rav reads 'kosel' as the Name of Hashem together with 'tel', a ruin: even in destruction the Name is there, and so the Kosel Maaravi in every Jew's heart can never be destroyed.

The Midrash and the Zohar on Yaakov's bowing are both true: each speaks from its own world, and Yaakov, who knew both, chose to accept a flaw in the world of drush for a far greater tikun in the world of sod.
The Gemara's unflattering names for Devorah and Chulda do not fault them personally; they mark a time when the world was out of order, with din ruling over chesed.
The first letters, 'let every man rule in his house', were not a foolish decree but the very beginning of the miracle, reversing the order of din over chesed.

The Megillah has two statuses: all year it is one of the books of Kesuvim, but on Purim it becomes an iggeres of the world of tikun, so that being written together with the other books is a disgrace to it.
The word iggeres, spelled out in full, equals in gematria 'yom shekulo Shabbos', the day that is entirely Shabbos, for Mordechai belonged to that future world.
Because Mordechai repaired the world of drush, the Gemara expounds the Megillah verse by verse from beginning to end, and the Megillah itself ends with 'doresh tov l'amo'.

Flax, called 'bad' in the holy tongue because each stalk rises 'bad bevad', alone, embodies separation; that is why Rav objected to planting it on Purim, the day of gathering, and why flax could be used for holiness only in the Beis HaMikdash.
The descent of the Megillah into the Persian chronicles is the opposite of the Greek translation of the Torah: what there brought darkness here brought 'light and joy' to the Jews.

The Baal HaTanya's parable of the jewel poured out over the ill prince explains why the highest, previously hidden Torah was spread widely despite the risk of disgrace: some of it will reach and revive the prince.

The Rav applies the same parable to the Megillah: its light, greater than at Matan Torah, was poured into Achashverosh's feast and the Persian chronicles for the sake of the prince, the Jewish people in hiding.

Esther's fate and the Megillah's fate are one: just as Esther, the soul of the Jewish people, was lost in Achashverosh's palace, so the light of the Torah went down into a Megillah without Hashem's name.
The letters of the word bracha each show a doubling: beis is one become two, chaf is ten become twenty, and reish is a hundred become two hundred.

Yavan is the opposite of Yosef: Yosef is addition in kedushah, Yavan is addition in tumah that invades what is not its own, and the letters yud, vav, nun, each an extension of the one before, show this.
On Chanukah the Jews in turn enter the domain of tumah: the lights are lit in the darkness of night, at the left side of the door, which represents the sitra achra and the public domain.
Placing 'evening, morning and afternoon' after 'Your miracles that are with us every day' carries a second intention: that there are miracles three times every day.
The whole month of Kislev is Chanukah: the twenty-four days before it belong to the twenty-fifth, which the Rav links to Shema Yisrael and mesiras nefesh.
Reading the offerings of the twelve Nesi'im on Chanukah is a zechus against the twelve princes of Yishmael.

The Chasam Sofer models the ten sons of Haman on Moshe, Aharon and Miriam: as each of the three gifts passed to the survivor until all ended with Moshe, so each son's power passed to the next until everything collapsed with Vayzasa.
The odd wording 'v'lo ya'avor' ('it shall not pass') rather than 'it shall not be added' hints at Esav's words 'lo sa'avor bi': the sixteenth of Adar is Esav's border, which Purim cannot cross.

Esther asked for 'tomorrow' as well, yet could not ask for the sixteenth and seventeenth, because asking for that would mean asking for the waning of the moon itself to be undone, which belongs to the perfected world.

The lower seven sons of Haman stand against the seven shepherds, so Vayzasa, the last, stands against Dovid HaMelech; just as nachash has the numerical value of Moshiach, the Rav suggests Vayzasa is the counterpart of Moshiach ben Dovid.

Moshe Rabbeinu's last words, 'v'atah al bamoseimo tidroch', were what Mordechai answered Haman when he stepped on him, a hint that in the footsteps of Moshiach the Jews will tread on Haman completely.

The Rav explains why a goral reveals what reason cannot: wealth from business or an inheritance has an understandable cause, but winning by lot has none, so the lot reaches the root that only Hashem knows.

By the angels' own logic they were right to oppose Menashe's teshuvah; Hashem did not overrule them openly but made a hidden tunnel, because the inner point of a Jew cannot be explained to pure intellect.

Haman's lot, meant for destruction, registered above as a judgment 'by lot', and so it moved the case to the one court where the Jews could only be found meritorious: what Haman did below aroused its counterpart above.

The Rav notes that 'hipil pur hu hagoral' has the gematria of 'Moshiach ben David': Haman's lot aroused the world of Moshiach, when the inner purpose of creation, that Yisrael rose first in Hashem's thought, will be revealed.
'Arur Haman' and 'baruch Mordechai' share a gematria because at the inner point all Jews are equal, like the future circle dance of the tzaddikim, where no one stands nearer or farther.

Rashi's unusually sharp word 'mistake' against those who say terumah can be redeemed reflects that Jews are Hashem's terumah; a view that terumah can be exchanged echoes the claim that the Jews can be replaced by another nation.
Tarshish, the stone of Asher, has the same gematria as 'reishis goyim Amalek': Haman wanted the title 'first', which belongs to Yisrael as 'reishis tevuaso', to pass to Amalek.
The Rav argues that the Greek rule of accepting only what one understands is itself illogical, since the mind grasps only a tiny part of what exists; it is emunah that is logical.
Emunah is not only belief but faithfulness, the instinctive loyalty of a wife to her husband; the Avnei Nezer shows such an instinct is reliable enough that a woman may remarry on one witness.
Levi felt the bond with Hashem more strongly because Levi's very name came from the bond of husband and wife, which is why Levi answered 'Mi laShem elai' both with Moshe and with Matisyahu.
Klal Yisrael bears the name Yisrael as a wife bears her husband's name: 'yashar' joined with Hashem's Name.
Because tumah is a barrier in the bond with the pure G-d, a war against emunah is in essence a war of tumah; the Greeks entered the Heichal to defile rather than to destroy.

The pach shemen, the symbol of taharah's victory, was hidden under the very marble slab from which the dust for the sotah was taken, the place that testifies to the purity of a wife and of Knesses Yisrael.
Yaakov needed the name Yisrael from the angel before Beis El because he would first face Shechem, which, like Yavan, sought to rip out the name Yisrael.

The Ba'al HaTanya's mezuzos differed from another man's not in the sofer's kavanos but only in being written on the fifteenth, the full moon, which shows what Esther sought in a Purim on the fifteenth.
The fourteenth is a preparation, a 'seat', for Shushan Purim: the Purim of the weaker Jews came through the goral, but one who uses it properly is lifted from it into the fifteenth, which is earned.

The Rav suggests that the spark of holiness in Haman, which the Arizal says must be kept alive on Purim, is Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, a descendant of Zeresh, and that this is why one may 'confuse' and bless Zeresh.

The tannaim's seder in Bnei Brak, which lasted until the time of the morning kriyas shema, came to repair the blemish of Haman's descendants there, whose grandmother Zeresh had advised stopping the morning kriyas shema.
Haman was hanged on the day of the omer harvest because that day begins the count to fifty, the level he tried to seize; and kriyas shema, by gematria, is that same day.

Even the suffix of Hashem's Name may not be erased; the lowest Jews of the last generation are attached to the 'kem' of 'Elokeichem', and Amalek, who tried to erase what may not be erased, is erased measure for measure.

The Gemara's question why Purim is not extended to the sixteenth and seventeenth is a tefillah that the geulah come, when Esav's border will be crossed and those days too will hold the victory over Amalek.
The Rav reads the letters of the months: the season of Nissan, 'aviv', runs alef-beis in order, the way of chesed, while Tishrei runs the alphabet backwards (tav-shin-reish), the way of din.

'Shanah' means repetition, and is related to 'yashan', old, and 'sheinah', sleep; so the nations, who have only a year, live in dormant repetition, while the Jewish 'chodesh' is the opposite, a waking renewal.

The light of the first day lacks 'vayehi ken' because 'ken' means something that stays in place, and that light was hidden on account of the wicked; this is the meaning of 'lo ken haresha'im', and that same hidden light will one day judge them.

'Yeshuos b'mekupos' means salvation on credit: just as the redemption from Egypt was paid for by the future acceptance of the Torah, a Jew may ask Hashem in Nissan for salvation now against the good he will do later.
Kiddush hachodesh shows the Jews stand above time: they decide when the month begins, even when mistaken, rather than time dictating their duties.
The Egyptians plowing over the hidden Jewish children is a symbol of the whole exile, and when the Jews are redeemed the Torah too will be redeemed, revealing new midrashim not yet disclosed.
Nissan is the 'pesichas ha'aron' of the calendar: as the opening of the aron is an eis ratzon, so in Nissan a Jew's prayer is more readily accepted than at any other time.
The small aleph of Vayikra can only be seen from close up; one far from Hashem reads 'vayikar' and sees coincidence, while one who draws near in Nissan sees that every event is a call from Hashem.
The custom of 'stealing' the afikoman may come from Yaakov, who on Pesach night took Yitzchak's blessing of tal in a way that looked like theft, while the Shechinah smiled on it.
Nissan is called 'Aviv' because it begins with aleph-beis in order, chesed, while Tishrei follows the reversed order, tav-shin-reish, the order of din.
