The matzah's physical form is only a capsule for its spirituality, which is eternal; therefore 'ha lachma anya' is literally true, since the inner matzah is the one eaten in Egypt.
'Simcha' is linked to 'somech', leaning, since shin and samech interchange, and 'atzvus' to 'azuv', forsaken: joy is having Someone to lean on.
Leaning on the afikoman hidden under the pillow, though one may not lean on a sefer, shows that a Jew leans on Hashem Himself, since the matzah is His holy Names.
The translation of the Torah into Greek, though it raised the nations above idol worship, was the Torah itself going into galus, like a Jew leaving Eretz Yisrael for gentile territory.
Just as a pure person perceives a hidden light in the Chanukah and Shabbos candles, he should perceive a hidden darkness in the gentile decorations of the season.
Whatever exists in place corresponds to something in time: Dan's place at the end of the camp corresponds to the last period of Jewish history, our generation.
The foot of the tav, which reaches outside the camp of holiness, is Dan, and the tav itself is formed of a dalet and a nun, the letters of Dan.

Yocheved was born exactly between the walls as the family entered Mitzrayim because galus cannot begin without the redeemer already prepared, just as the first day of Pesach determines the day of Tisha B'Av.
The pearl of geulah is found in the depths of darkness, so our generation, sunk lower than any before, is the one that dives down to bring up such treasures.
The initial letters of Gadlu laShem iti uneromemah shemo, the passuk of Teves, spell Shaul, the culprit among the seventy, teaching that even the fallen will be raised to join in Hashem's praise.
Each failed Nissan creation was followed by a smaller, more concentrated one: from the whole world, to Klal Yisrael, to a corner of holiness in the Mishkan where the intended ideal world would exist.
Hashem Himself 'did not tire' of renewing the world after failures, so a Jew who falls is taught to begin anew rather than despair.
The Targum's word for matzah, 'petira', means opening, linking matzah to opening the door at the seder, the opened heavens and the call 'open to Me' in Shir haShirim.
Chametz is dough that time has ruled over, eighteen minutes being the measure of time, and so it swells and takes up space; matzah is free of both time and place, like emunah.
Lechem equals three times the name Havayah, one for each of nefesh, ruach and neshamah, while matzah equals three times the name spelled out in full (45), a higher holiness.
The many times the word 'mah' appears in the Haggadah express emunah: one can only ask 'what', never fully know.
Hashem does not want a separate 'Pesach house' that chametz never touched; He wants the chametz removed and matzah brought into the very same place, as with the yetzer hara.

Rabbi Eliezer, a disciple of Beis Shammai whose way is din, holds the world was created in Tishrei, the time of din; Rabbi Yehoshua of Beis Hillel, whose way is chesed, holds it was created in Nissan, the month of chesed. Each follows his own approach.
The month is called 'aviv' because its letters, alef and beis, run forward in order, which is chesed, while the letters of Tishrei run backwards from the end of the alef-beis, which is din.
Trees shedding the 'white shrouds' of winter and putting on green in Nissan are a picture of techiyas hameisim, and Pesach is the time of techiyas hameisim.

Bread (lechem) equals three times the simple Name of Hashem, 78, but matzah equals three times the Name spelled in full, 45, which is 'adam'; so 'not by bread alone does adam live', and matzah makes a person into an adam.
On Chol HaMoed one does not wear tefillin because the matzah stands in their place; therefore matzah deserves the same standard one expects of tefillin.

From the builders of the Tower, who kept repeating 'havah' to put more impurity into it, the Bnei Yissaschar learns that in holiness too each repetition of 'l'shem matzas mitzvah' puts new holiness into the matzah.

The frog, at home both in water and on land, is the intermediate between the tahor and tamei kinds, so it embodies a mixture of good and evil; it therefore punished the Egyptians, whose plan to intermarry was an attempt to create exactly such a mixture.
Baruch shem is whispered because it proclaims that Hashem rules even in the places of the sitra achra; this is the frog's song, which is why it alone in Perek Shirah does not sing a passuk.

Ohalos and Negaim both open with 'shnayim' because tumah is division; Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah sent Rabbi Akiva there to show that the frog is neither purely 'one' nor purely 'two' but a mixture of both.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's words 'sharak lahem', she whistled to them, hint at the shuruk, the vowel of yesod, the attribute the frog corresponds to.

The sudden wave of modern inventions is a heavenly power of renewal sent down for the Jews; because they did not seize it, the nations and the sitra achra did, and it now takes away a Jew's peace and time.

Rabbi Elazar ben Arach, a soul with a spark of Moshiach, held on to 'hachodesh hazeh lachem', the first mitzvah, which belongs to the souls of Moshiach; his reading 'hacharesh haya libam' was a lament that the people's hearts did not hear the call of renewal.

A beginning holds the strength of the whole: just as the first day of Sefirah already carries the fiftieth day, so Teves, opening the last degel, carries the full weight of the end, while Adar, at rock bottom, must rise.
Since everything foretold in Haazinu, all the troubles of galus, has already come true, the one missing part, the geulah, is certain, and it does not depend on teshuvah.
Using the Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of space, time and soul, the Rav explains that just as there are places where the Torah forbids learning, there must be a time, and that is Nittel.
The Jews of the last galus are the most precious to Hashem because their night is so dark that even a small act of avodah, like a hurried Minchah, is precious to Him.

The word 'samach' teaches that mere nearness to a rasha lets his tumah in even before any wall is breached, and the same power works for good when one is near a tzaddik, as Yehudah felt kedushah near Yosef.

The Rav reads the terumas hadeshen, a night avodah that is only bedi'eved and done in work clothes, as the avodah most dear to Hashem, and sees in it the avodah of the generation before Moshiach and the sweeping of the house before Pesach.

The history of the world is told as four Nissans, each a narrower attempt at a perfected world: all of mankind, then only Klal Yisrael, then only the small corner of the Mishkan, and finally the geulah.

Moshe Rabbeinu's sin at Mei Merivah was a lack of emunah in himself: he saw himself as a policeman who strikes in Miriam's merit rather than a king whose word acts, and so Rav Hirsch pairs Shelach, Korach and Chukas with emunah in Hashem, in the chachamim, and in oneself.
The Targum's word for matzah, 'petir', means opening: Pesach is the opening, and the seder begins with opening a child's heart and ends with opening the door.
A person's strengths that come from his mazal are no cause for pride; his real test lies in the weakness of his animal, such as the lion's urge to tear at others or the snake's poison of speech.
Prayer itself is emunah: beyond asking for one's needs, the very act of turning to Hashem is pure faith.
Because every mitzvah is a remembrance of the Exodus, Pesach is not only the first festival but the embryo that contains all the festivals within it.

Like a ball, the round world has no natural top or center; only its Maker knows the point He began from, and that point, the foundation stone, is what makes the Beis Hamikdash 'higher than all places'.
The 'place causes' rule for the rebellious elder reflects that the Sanhedrin, the central souls from whom Torah goes out, has its full power only when seated at the world's root point.
The two opinions on when the world was created yield two centers of the Torah: Bereishis for Tishrei and the Kohen Gadol, and 'darosh darash Moshe', the middle word, for Nissan and Moshe the king.
The moon's waning is the earth's physicality coming between the sun and Knesses Yisrael, and the Rosh Chodesh atonement 'for Hashem' answers the questions this concealment raises against Him.

The Rosh Chodesh Nissan goat in the middle of the Torah was burned because that day revealed a taste of the end of days, when it will be clear Hashem never needed atonement, a reward for Aharon's silent faith.
The nations count by the solar 'shanah', meaning repetition, while Jews have the 'chodesh', renewal, the root of teshuvah.

The Rav links Chizkiyahu's two puzzling acts: just as he held that a day merely fit to be Nissan is not yet Nissan, he held that being fit to be Moshiach is not yet being appointed, so he could not sing the tenth shirah.
There are souls of 'rishon' (Nissan) and souls of 'Adar', even of the second Adar pushed outside the order, and the redemption is delayed so that these too reach their tikkun.
The main victory came on the seventh of Nissan, the day of Efrayim's nasi, because Yosef, sold by the Yishmaelim, is holy bris milah, while Yishmael's milah is empty of content.
Chametz represents the nations, from whom some benefit can come, while se'or, unfit to eat, represents Yishmael, from whom no good comes at all.
A natural explanation of the splitting of the sea does not lessen the nes: the convergence of every factor at exactly that moment is an even greater, hidden nes, like Purim.
Shiloh's roof of curtains, and the lack of kedushah on the roof of the Beis HaMikdash, reflect that the roof corresponds to keser, and Amalek, 'ram' in gematria, blocks it until he is wiped out.
The present salvation is sweet and bitter: the comfort it brings in galus may mean the exile will last longer, as the Chasam Sofer's mashal of the banished prince shows.
The Rav reads the absence of Taharos from the acronym zekunim as a sign of Yosef's greatness: Yaakov did not need to teach it to him, because Yosef's own soul was Seder Taharos.
Yaakov taught all the orders to his other sons, but seeing that Yosef mastered Taharos by himself showed him how high Yosef stood, and that is why he loved him.
Avraham could master the whole Torah alone because his middah, chesed, accompanies all the other middos, while Yitzchak's gevurah does not, so he knew by himself only Moed.
A tzaddik's soul extends into his possessions, so they are free of the decay that came into the world with death; this is why Yosef's stored grain did not rot while the Egyptians' grain did.

Yaakov's 'seeing' that there was grain in Mitzrayim was a perception of its holiness: grain with such taste and smell could only come from a tzaddik in Mitzrayim, which gave him hope that Yosef was there.
Since Yosef, who guarded the bris, is Friday, the day that prepares for Shabbos, kedushas habris is what makes a person worthy of Shabbos.
In Nissan chesed pours from heaven like rain into a bucket; zerizus is the bucket that holds it, and laziness is the hole through which the blessing runs out.

There are four Nissans of Hashem's plan: creation, the Exodus and the Mishkan were each a smaller version of the original Gan Eden that was spoiled, and the fourth, the final redemption, is guaranteed to succeed.
The Mishkan was erected and dismantled seven times during the miluim and stood on the eighth, illustrating that a tzaddik falls seven times and rises.
Chametz is dough left standing out of laziness; it grows bigger only because air enters it, so its greatness is emptiness, whereas matzah is baked in haste and with kedushah.
Avraham Avinu is the spring of Yiddishkeit: as nature begins to grow in spring, Yiddishkeit began with the first Jew, whose month is Nissan.
The spring revival of nature after winter is itself tchiyas hameisim, which is why the haftarah of the dry bones is read on Pesach.
The Rav says the depth of the Maharal does not come from sharpness or constructions; the sweetness is that once explained, it is seen to be simple truth.
A 'sechel nivdal' is a mind whose only drive is to know what Hashem says in His Torah, free of the biases that every person's experiences leave on his reasoning.
Six hundred thousand reflects six in units, hundreds and thousands, and six is completeness: a body with four sides, a top and a bottom.
Galus is always to the opposite of what Yisrael are, so the depth of their fall, as with the daughter of Nakdimon ben Gurion, reveals their height; this is 'ashreichem Yisrael'.
A beginning is the 'one', not the 'five'; it must come out of nothing, so Avraham was born as the two thousand years of tohu ended, just as light comes when darkness ends.
Avraham was to the Jewish people what Adam was to mankind: a new species whose tie to Terach was cut, which is why Rashi says he was freed from honoring his father.
The order of the letters decides which middah rules: masculine first means chesed sweetens din, feminine first means din dominates, which is why Esav put his wives before his sons.
Writing right to left follows the Aleph-Beis order of chesed: Esav writes the other way, while the descendants of Avraham also write from right to left.
Tu B'Shvat falls on the fifteenth because the din of Teves overlaps into the first half of Shevat, just as the din of Tammuz lasts in Av until Chamishah Asar B'Av.
Seraf equals 580, the numerical value of the two names of tumah and of Seir, and ilan equals 91, Havaya and Adnus together; the sap rising in the tree is tumah being raised into kedushah.
The roshei teivos of the passuk for Nissan read in the Aleph-Beis order, while the arrangement of Tammuz and Teves comes from sofei teivos, the Aleph-Beis backwards.
In the borei pri ha'etz of Tu B'Shvat lies a remez to the pri etz hadar, the esrog, and the great success of Klal Yisrael comes through the four minim.

The greatness of Avraham's emunah, per the Maharal, was not believing in miracles but believing against his own reasonable fear that sin might cancel the promise, simply because he saw Hashem wanted it; the Rav calls this the meaning of emunah, believing where one does not understand.
The Written Torah deliberately hides Avraham's mesiras nefesh and gives no reason for 'Lech lecha', so that no one should think a Jew's chosenness was earned; a Jew is a Jew 'without any reason'.

The Ramban's harsh 'great sin' is itself a praise of Avraham: precisely in the first account of the first Jew the Torah shows a sin, to teach that a Jew's sin is external and never touches his inner self.
Emunah is the opposite of subjugation: one who depends on Hashem alone cannot be enslaved, which is why the Exodus came through emunah.
Following the Maharal, the dog is the universal insult because it is entirely dependent on its master, whereas a person should be independent of people and dependent only on Hashem.
According to the Maharal, Moshe's sin at Mei Merivah was the anger itself: full emunah leaves no room for anger, since no one can do a person harm or good except Hashem.

The Rav reads Hashem's answer to Avraham, 'in the merit of korbanos', as a proof about the Jewish essence: if a korban can wipe away a Jew's sin, his sin is only incidental, so his children must return to Eretz Yisrael.
A Jew who sins is like a man who fell into black mud: soap and water restore him, whereas for a man with dark skin no scrubbing helps, for the color is his essence.
Eretz Yisrael is 'a Jew in geography': everything that belongs to a Jewish soul belongs to the Jewish place, which is why it spits out sinners just as the Jewish soul spits out evil.

Yosef's goblet, 'gevia', hints at the three levels: gimmel for the three avos, beis-yud for the twelve shevatim, ayin for the seventy souls; once the seventy existed, the family could go down to Mitzrayim.
Pesach determines the weekday of Tisha b'Av because a Jewish churban is always rooted in geulah; the Rav says a time will come when Tisha b'Av will be perhaps the most beautiful Yom Tov of the year.

Serach, who brought Yaakov the news that Yosef lived, took on the quality of Eliyahu, who is appointed over good news; she is thus 'two' and completes the seventy, hinting that redemption already walks with the Jews into galus.
The Gemara (Yocheved) and the Midrash (Serach) do not argue: Yocheved is the root of the redeemer Moshe, Serach carries Eliyahu who announces the geulah, and both say that galus begins with geulah.
Edom, the hardest galus, is the least significant of the kingdoms: like the uncut bird, it need not even be cut; one can step over it.
Edom is a 'robber': its culture, art, literature and scientific progress were all taken from the Jews, and the yetzer hara's strength is likewise stolen from the good part of a person.

The Bris Bein HaBesarim was the birth of the Jewish people, and since a person's destiny depends on the moment of birth, Hashem showed Avraham then the whole future of Klal Yisroel, including the four kingdoms.
Avraham, the root and essence of Klal Yisroel, could have no servitude, since bondage cannot touch the root; a Jew can be enslaved only in his outer part, which relates to the seventy.
The levels of yachid and twelve shevatim have no relation to the nations and so no conflict with them; only at the level of seventy is there a correspondence, and with it competition and galus.

The nations need geographic borders, while the Jews, whose soul is the Torah, remain bound to the inner, heavenly Eretz Yisroel even outside it; so they became seventy souls exactly when they first stepped out of their land into Mitzrayim.

The shevatim correspond to the twelve combinations of Hashem's four-letter Name, which the nations do not relate to, and a Jew reaches this level through his own chiddushei Torah, revealed especially in the month of Shevat.

Following the Alshich, the Rav reads the apiryon passuk as saying that Hashem, who lacks no silver or gold, wanted the Beis Hamikdash only for the glowing love inside it; that love gave the building a neshama, unlike the cold marble of Rome.

Efron's name comes from afar, earth: when Avraham's shekalim reached his hands their fire had already risen, leaving him cold metal, while 'Machpelah' alludes to Avraham's gift being compounded above.
Yehoash survived six years in the Kodesh HaKadashim because his neshama came from there, from the mitzvah of shekalim, the money of atonement linked to Yom Kippur.
By killing the Kohen Gadol in the Mikdash on Yom Kippur, Yehoash defiled the Kodesh HaKadashim in all three of Sefer Yetzirah's dimensions: place, time and soul.
Because Haman's decree was total annihilation, it could not take effect: the shekel touches the nucleus in every Jew that can never be destroyed.
The equal half-shekel reflects the level where Jews are children rather than servants: a servant can be better or worse as a servant, but a son is never more or less a son.
The Jews' shekalim came before Haman's because theirs are the yud, the first letter and fire, while his are earth, the last; the yud is the tiniest letter but the greatest.

Yocheved's renewed youth was not only a miracle for her: since Moshe's soul comes from the source of all renewal, a flow of chiddush came down with his birth, and his first mitzvah to Israel was Kiddush HaChodesh.

Three times establishes a habit, so by the third Rosh Chodesh after the Exodus its newness should have faded; the Torah was given precisely then, teaching that Torah must stay as new as Rosh Chodesh itself.
Water is always a plural word because it has no defined form or single essence, while Moshe, the greatest form in the world, is unique, as 'there arose no prophet like Moshe'.

The astrologers rightly sensed that only water could oppose the coming redeemer, but they missed that form must overcome matter; throwing him into the water became a cause of the redemption, and he later split the sea.
The Flood, which wiped out all that has form through water, was delayed 120 years in the merit of Moshe, the embodiment of form, who would live 120 years.

Dasan, from 'das', stood against Moshe the giver of Torah, while Aviram, 'the father is great', stood against Aharon, whose holiness passes by inheritance; their opposition mirrors Moshe's spiritual greatness and Aharon's holiness of the body.
Because Moshe's third test concerned injustice among gentiles, the Torah he was chosen to give is a Torah of kindness for Israel and for all mankind.
Being born circumcised is not a mere wonder but a sign: the orlah expresses a share in evil and nature, and only one who came to the world solely to repair others could be born without it.

Malki-tzedek, himself born circumcised, could not prove from milah that man can improve on nature, so he made the point to Avraham with bread and wine, the two foods whose brachah rises when they are changed.
The aron is so named from 'or', light, yet Torah's light is felt only after the weeks of Shovavim have removed the orlah; then milah itself becomes a feast of joy rather than pain.
Water, which has no form of its own, is the opposite of Moshe, the pure form; the astrologers saw this but erred, since water ruled him only through the sin at Mei Merivah.
Moshe's marriage to a convert reflects his greatness: being above the six hundred thousand, his match had to be someone who also stood outside them.
Yisro's wandering through every idol was itself a sign of an all-inclusive soul, fitting him to be father-in-law to Moshe, who includes all Israel.
Yisro recognized Sarah's descendant precisely in Moshe not coming to collect thanks: modesty is the 'trademark' of Sarah's children, the source of blessing.
The Rav describes chametz as made of three ingredients, flour, water and time; matzah lacks the third, and so it suits the exodus, which happened above time.
The first of anything is not yet time, since time is only the distance from a starting point; that is why the exodus had to be in the month called 'first'.
Witnesses are tested on time and place, and chametz, which time swells to fill more place than its truth, is a false witness, while matzah is a true one.
Roasting concentrates a thing and draws it into itself while cooking breaks it apart, so the korban Pesach is roasted to express oneness.
The frog alone in Perek Shirah says 'Baruch Shem', not a passuk, and quietly, because its song rises from places of tumah where words of Tanach may not be said.
R' Elazar ben Azaryah's retort 'go to Negaim and Oholos' points to their opening word 'two': a mixture of kedushah and tumah like the frog cannot be called 'one'.

From Sefer HaKanah the Rav shows that the letters of 'Baruch Shem kevod malchuso' are the only ones that can join with Hashem's name, and from this he draws the advice to bind oneself to those who are better.

The Rav learns from Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's valley of gold that a Jew's word and desire can create real 'coins', so the heavenly shekalim of every year are made by Jews who yearn to give when they hear Parshas Shekalim.

The Rav reads the Rambam on a coerced 'I want' as a secret of the Jewish heart, not just a halachic device: the beating only subdues the body, and the inner point that always wants Hashem's will comes out.
Shekalim corresponds to the tip of the yud, above the Name itself, the same level the Rav finds in 'lifnei Hashem' of Yom Kippur, where no blemish of sin reaches.

Of all people, Yehoash, who sinned against the Holy of Holies in place, time and soul at once, is the one the haftarah credits with the shekalim, which shows that the inner point of a Jew stays untouched even after such a sin.
A lottery is a fitting vehicle for Yom Kippur and Purim because, like a lottery win, the closeness of every Jew at that root point has no reason that any angel could explain.
Rav told Rabbah bar bar Chanah that paying the workers was the din, not just middas chassidus, because for a person on a higher level a higher standard becomes his law.

By the at-bash sign, the sixth day of Pesach falls on the weekday of the Purim before it; the Rav reads this as Nissan revealing what was hidden in Adar, just as Vayikra's small aleph shows that the call was always one of love.
Since the Targum renders matzah with a word meaning opening, the Rav calls matzah the key that opens a Jew's heart to Hashem on Pesach, the festival of opening.

The world was created in Tishrei in deed but in Nissan in thought, because the Exodus, when Klal Yisrael became a nation, completed creation; this is why the first commandment speaks of the Exodus rather than of creation.

Chametz has stringencies no other prohibition has because it is the yetzer hara; Amalek, whose numerical value equals safek (doubt), is fought on Erev Pesach, and so the Beis HaMikdash, which follows the war on Amalek, is linked to Pesach.
Emunah is spiritual and does not cling to the body, so Hashem gave it in a capsule: matzah is ordinary flour and water that carries emunah inside it.
Simcha is tied to leaning (samach): joy is the feeling of having someone to lean on, while atzvus is the feeling of being abandoned, which is why idols, which cannot be leaned on, are called atzabim.
Haggadah comes from gid, a vein that carries life to the limbs, and from gad, mazal that flows down from its root: the Haggadah channels emunah and salvation from above.

Because matzah is the 'food of emunah' and emunah is the root of all the mitzvos, 'ushmartem es hamatzos' read as 'mitzvos' is not a mere wordplay: matzah truly holds all the mitzvos, and as one treats matzah so he will have mitzvos all year.
The visible matzah is like a capsule from the pharmacy: what one sees is only flour and water, the outer shell, while the real content inside is emunah.

Nissan's spring, when farmers water their fields and everything sprouts, is the time for a Jew to 'water' his emunah, and matzah and the four cups bring down halachah and yiras Shamayim for the whole year.

Just as speech aloud for avodah zarah draws a spirit of impurity into a house, speech aloud 'l'shem mitzvah' draws kedushah into the matzah, and repeating it many times adds more, as the generation of the dispersion repeated 'havah'.
The matzah absorbs the words spoken while baking it: just as it absorbs the telling of yetzias Mitzrayim, it can sadly absorb leitzanus.
With the Radbaz, the Rav says that with chametz the hint is itself the plain meaning: for other mitzvos the yetzer hara is a remez, but for chametz it is the very reason for its severity.

Following the Chiddushei HaRim, the Rav reads kares not only as a punishment but as a sign: a mitzvah whose neglect cuts a person off is one whose fulfillment binds him, so Pesach and milah are the mitzvos of attachment to Avraham and to Klal Yisrael.
The Rav contrasts the names of the months: the Torah's name for Nissan, Aviv, runs aleph-beis in order from the right, the way of chesed, while Tishrei runs the letters backward, the way of din.

Unlike a commemoration, each festival repeats its original event; so the spring awakening of nature is the renewal in heaven reaching down, and the person who sees the trees come back to life must ask why he should stay behind.

The ten plagues mirrored the ten utterances of creation in reverse: the first utterance created the 'first', and the last plague struck the firstborn; the second utterance was light, and the second-to-last plague was darkness.
'Would have' does not belong in a Jew's vocabulary: complaining about what would have happened had someone acted differently is a lack of faith in hashgacha pratis.

Chametz is made of flour, water and time, and once leavened it rises and takes up space, so it is ruled by time and place; matzah is kept from time and does not expand, and so it is the food of emunah, which is above time and place.
Bread is three times the Name Havayah in simple letters (3 × 26 = 78), while matzah is three times the Name spelled out in full (3 × 45 = 135), showing matzah's higher holiness.

The feminine 'hasheinis' refers not to the second month but to the second reading of the Megillah: in a leap year it is read first in heaven on Purim Katan, and the second reading is therefore more powerful.
The leap year is read as the moon (Klal Yisrael) falling behind the sun (Hashem); in the first Adar we are too far from Him to keep Purim properly.
The pauses in spiritual life are like the beat in music or the pause between heartbeats: they are part of life, and after the pause the fervor returns stronger.
'Hamelech', 'kes Kah' and 'Haman' all equal 95 in gematria: Haman's existence is what reduces Hashem's revealed name to the hidden 'king', and 'machi Amalek' equals 'kisei Havayah'.
A miracle that comes through perfect timing within nature is greater than one that breaks nature, and the Megillah's miracle has countless such pieces falling into place.
Purim costumes embody the lesson: just as one is not alarmed by a costumed visitor, one should see that world leaders are costumes over Hashem's hand.
Because David saw Hashem behind Shimi's curse and spared him, Mordechai, Shimi's descendant, was born to defeat Haman's philosophy of chance and to write the Megillah.

The Rav reads the 'im' of the omer and of yovel as expressing not doubt about the obligation but that their level is above this world and cannot be grasped with certainty, like the Mikdash that must be sought.
Place, time and soul each have a 'king' that is their 'pele': the Mikdash, Nissan, and the king of Israel; and only the 'pele' of the soul, David, could find the 'pele' of place.

Just as Shmuel, head of the prophets, had to search out which son of Yishai was king, David had to toil to find the Mikdash; the Rav ties 'lishichno tidreshu' and 'som tasim alecha melech' together by gematria.
A father's hidden inner self appears in his son: David is Shabbos, the seventh, but his inner depth, yovel, was revealed in Shlomo, which is why David longed to build the Mikdash and Shlomo built it.

The fiftieth mention of the Exodus in the Torah, counting only mentions in praise, is in 'Arami oved avi', which is why it is expounded on the Seder night: it draws down the fiftieth gate and the coming of Moshiach.

Heaven made Hillel forget the law of the knife so that it would be revealed that his knowing that Pesach overrides Shabbos came from his soul's root as Shlomo, not only from his teachers, as he humbly claimed.

Haman and Yishmael are 'adam velo melech': even impure kingship holds a spark of accepting Hashem's kingship, as the Girgashi and Achashverosh show, but Yishmael has no king at all, only princes, and so his galus is the hardest.
Pesach belongs to Avraham because both are firsts: the first Jew and the first Yom Tov of the year, which opens with 'this month shall be for you the first of months'.
By eating matzah, the food of emunah, a Jew in a sense takes in Avraham himself: eating matzah is eating emunah.
Pesach was the turning point of Avraham's life, and the events of Sarah in Pharaoh's house, with plagues and gifts, foreshadowed the Exodus of his children.
The 'great wealth' promised to Avraham is read as emunah, worth more than millions and billions of dollars.
Moshiach will name the children one by one as the ones who brought him, because they learned, davened and guarded themselves from sin.

The eternal war of Hashem with Amalek is a measure of His love for sinners: Amalek is punished for all generations precisely because he attacked Jews who had served idols and been spat out of the clouds.

The silver hooks of the pillars, which protrude beyond the curtains of the Mishkan, stand for the Jews at the borderline, and the word for their bands, 'chashukeihem', hints that these Jews are cherished by Hashem.

Rabbi Akiva, whose name contains 'eikev', the heel, is the soul of the lowest level of Klal Yisrael and the head of Torah she'baal peh in golus, so it was his soul that reminded Moshe of the forgotten Jews.
The lower and more distant a Jew is from Torah and mitzvos, the more reason he has to rejoice on Purim, since Purim proves that Hashem remembers him.

Since only twelve combinations of the Shem Havayah exist, matching twelve months and twelve tribes, Adar Sheni stands outside like the Jews outside the camp, and it was for such Jews that the miracle of Purim came.

The three regalim are the inheritance of the three Avos: Pesach is Avraham's chesed and emunah, Shavuos, when the Torah was heard 'from the mouth of the Gevurah', is Yitzchak's, and Sukkos is Yaakov's; each is higher than the one before, yet Pesach remains the foundation.

Hashem wanted the clarity of emunah revealed at makkas bechoros to stay with the Jews, so He invested it in the matzah, a food, so that it would become part of their flesh, blood and bones; likewise every yom tov's gift is carried in its food.

Kareis means being cut off, so its opposite is being bound; that kareis applies to chametz, to the korban Pesach and to milah, which belongs to Avraham, shows that Pesach binds a Jew to Hashem more than Shavuos and Sukkos.
A great tzaddik and a simple Jew put on tefillin in exactly the same way; what makes the tzaddik's act greater is only the clarity of his emunah, and by this a Jew is measured.

The order of the makkos climbs through creation: blood in the water, the lowest element, then frogs, lice in the earth, wild animals on it, boils of fire, hail in the air, darkness in the luminaries, and the firstborn's souls above the heavens, answering Pharaoh that Hashem rules from bottom to top.
The ten makkos reveal the ten utterances of creation in reverse: makkas bechoros corresponds to 'Bereishis', darkness to 'let there be light', and the locusts to the firmament.

Telling a miracle can make it happen again, so saying the makkos at the Seder draws blows upon the enemies of Israel and healing upon the Jews, and the Haggadah's multiplication of makkos multiplies both.
Mitzrayim is 'meitzar yam': 'yam' equals fifty in gematria, and Egypt is what blocked the Jews from the fifty gates of understanding.

The rasha who denies yetzias Mitzrayim stands in the fiftieth gate, which is heresy; yet the Haggadah's 'one the Torah speaks of' means that even he can be pulled out through the telling of the Exodus.
Following his rebbe, 'lesaper' also means 'to count': the mitzvah includes counting the fifty mentions of yetzias Mitzrayim in the Torah that are in praise of Hashem's taking us out.
The severity of kares for chametz shows the reverse: as kares cuts a person off, Pesach binds him to Hashem.
The sefer Torah is holier than the sofer who wrote it because he was only a messenger, like a mailman who brings a letter he did not write; once the work is done his agency ends.
The physical matzah is only an envelope for the holy names within it, which are the same as those in the matzah eaten in Egypt; this is why one may say 'ha lachma anya', this is the bread.
The stringencies of Pesach follow from its being a beginning: what is laid at the start must be entirely firm.
Everything spiritual is reflected in the physical: the blossoming of trees in Nissan mirrors the spiritual beginning of the nation.
Pesach, where full Hallel is said only on the first day, and a bachur are both not yet at completeness.
The unearned light a bachur feels in learning and davening is like a chassan's gifts: a sign of the start of a bond, so important that a teshuvah treats their absence as grounds to break a shidduch.
Nissan should feel to a bachur like his own friend, since both are the days of growth.
Read event by event, the Megillah contains nothing a newspaper could not report; its miracle lies only in how the natural events fit together.
Natural growth of wheat is as great a miracle as the manna; the children born in the desert, used to bread from heaven, saw bread from the ground as the wonder.
The months descend from Nisan, named for open miracles, to Adar, whose name means a cloak, so Adar's miracles are the cloaked ones.
The Rav calls the Megillah's hidden miracles 'even bigger' than the supernatural miracles of the Exodus.
Purim's costumes become a lesson: the world's kings and rulers are only dressed in the 'aderes' of Adar, while Hashem controls them from behind.

The lowness of the last generations is itself their greatness: because they have fallen so low, they reach sparks from a root so high that the Tannaim and Amoraim could not reach them, and the redemption to come will be from the fiftieth gate, beyond the forty-nine of Egypt.
The kares for chametz and for missing the korban Pesach, absent on Shavuos and Sukkos, shows that Pesach binds a Jew to the very root, to emunah, even though the later festivals are greater.
The blessing Magen David is said only after maftir, the eighth aliyah, which corresponds to Moshiach and is above the world, because the world cannot yet make that blessing in its own place.
Yetzias Mitzrayim is the visible testimony of creation: the ten plagues reveal, in reverse order, the ten sayings by which the world was made, so both reasons for Shabbos say one thing.
A Jew who calls himself a kofer is only 'coated over', as the Torah uses the word for the pitch on the teivah; at a moment of danger he cries out to Hashem.
Matzah takes the place of tefillin as the sign of Pesach, so a matzah baked carelessly is like tefillin written by someone unfit.
The gematria of d'tzach adash b'achav is 'Yishmaelim'; since the Yishmaelim began galus Mitzrayim by bringing Yosef down, the wine poured at these simanim draws judgment on them.
A nation that identifies itself with another takes on its din: as the Amalekites who dressed and spoke as Canaanites had the din of Canaan, so the Arabs of Iraq who identify with Bavel are Bavel.
Wine has two powers, drawing kindness to Jews and judgment to the wicked, which is why the Haggadah multiplies the count of the makkos: the more makkos, the more blessing for Jews.

Edom and Yishmael are two kinds of enemy: converts and tannaim came from Edom, but no one converts from Yishmael; correspondingly se'or, inedible, and chametz, edible, are the two kinds of chametz to be burned.
A minhag can be greater than a halachah, because a custom arises from all of Klal Yisrael, which as a whole still has prophecy; hence even reading the Nesiim in Nissan has great power.
The Rav calls Yishmael and Amalek the se'or and chametz of the world, so the pre-Pesach cleaning is part of removing them.

Because a pilegesh has no true bond, Timna's line ran through Amalek like an insulated wire: the spark of her desire for Avraham's family passed through the generations without mixing in, which is why Haman's descendants could convert.

Esther invited Haman to her feast so that, by enjoying it, the holy spark in him would be freed; 'yavo hamelech veHaman hayom' holds Hashem's Name and equals in gematria 'they learned Torah in Bnei Brak'.
Following the Ruzhiner, Shaul's 'I have fulfilled the word of Hashem' meant that by sparing Agag he had brought Purim into the world, which is why Shmuel never rebuked him for it.
The difficulty of the people of Bnei Brak with the morning Krias Shema was inherited from Zeresh, who wanted to hang Mordechai in the morning before his Krias Shema.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov's rule that one not obligated cannot exempt others, the Tannaim had to share the flaw of Haman's descendants; by missing the matzah, as the Jews did in Haman's time, they could repair them.
The fast that cancelled Pesach in Esther's time was the appeasement given to the Sitra Achra so that the great success of Purim could be established.
A Birkas Hachama on erev Pesach is greater than usual, because the war against Amalek, Shaul's against Agag and Moshiach ben Yosef's, falls on erev Pesach.

The 3,550 Jews beyond the 600,000 are the 'forgotten' Jews: their silver did not go into the adanim, which bear Hashem's name, but into hooks that jutted outside the holiness of the Mishkan, where a tamei person may touch them.
The word adanim contains Hashem's name of Adnus, and the hundred adanim are the root of the hundred brachos said each day.
The hooks are called vavim because a vav joins one word to the next; so the Jews outside the camp, the Jews of Adar Sheni, remain connected to it.
Because the thirteenth month has no combination of Hashem's four-letter name and the Megillah never names Him, Adar Sheni is the special Purim of Jews in whom Hashem cannot be seen.
Moshe forgot the extra silver because the souls at the end of the Torah, like its last eight pesukim, belong to forgetting; Rabbi Akiva, whose root is beyond forgetting, could remind him.
Haman paid ten thousand talents only for the 600,000, not for the extra 3,550, because he made Amalek's mistake of thinking those Jews are rejected and not part of Klal Yisrael.
The double hiding of 'haster astir' describes our generation: the son not only cannot see his father but does not even know his father is there.

The command to borrow from the Egyptians belongs inside the warning of makas bechoros because that plague broke Egypt's root of tzaras ayin; the Egyptians' willing giving with chen was itself a result of the plague.
Rashi's two reasons for the donkey's mitzvah map onto its two mitzvos: its help in carrying out the wealth earns redemption, while its likeness to Egypt calls for breaking its neck.

Breaking the neck is for the owner with a begrudging eye: his trait enters the donkey, so it has no kedushah for the Kohen, and destroying it purifies his heart as burning chametz removes the chametz of the heart.
The donkey of Avraham, Moshe and Moshiach was created at twilight on Erev Shabbos, a time of haste, so it joins the donkey's simplicity with the zrizus of matzah and lacks the donkey's laziness.
The lack of great attainments in the last generation is itself what fits it to bring Moshiach: the simpler the emunah, the more strength it gives Moshiach's simple donkey.
At the Akeidah Avraham's levels and sense of Hashem were taken from him, lowering him to the state of the generation before Moshiach, and he went forward on the donkey with simple emunah.

The twelve paths in the sea against the seven streams of the future express the difference between a redemption still divided, like the twelve tribes, and the complete redemption of the seven, Shabbos and David.

The sea returned 'to its first condition' because its original condition was for the final redemption; it split early only for Yosef, whose self-sacrifice broke nature, and so it remains bound to that condition.
Yaakov's gift of 'zimras ha'aretz' was a niggun from Eretz Yisroel sent to awaken the union of Yosef and Yehuda, yesod and malchus, which led to 'Vayigash elav Yehuda'.
The piano's seven white keys of chesed and five black half-keys of din, together twelve, mirror exile, a song mixed with weeping; the future will have only the seven white tones.
Music whose tones have no connection to each other arouses lowly desires, because it is the opposite of the heavenly match that a true niggun is.
The war against the Jews in Eretz Yisroel is a war against Hashem, and it is decided in the batei medrash through Torah, tefillah and the daily Shirah.

A shidduch comes from the hidden world and is too lofty to descend into this world on its own; the shadchan's untruth gives it the 'lowering' it needs, which is why the Divrei Chaim paid even shadchanim whose matches failed.

A bas kol, lower than prophecy, cannot grasp what belongs to the hidden world; therefore it announces wrong matches before the right one, and therefore it did not know that Yonasan ben Uziel had revealed its secrets.

Leah belonged to the hidden world like Esav, while Rachel belonged to the revealed world; her tears, which changed her mazal, were themselves a revelation of the hidden world like the splitting of the sea.

The repeated 'uvnei Yisrael halchu bayabasha' after the sea closed refers to Dasan and Aviram crossing later, which reconciles the Ibn Ezra and the Ramban: it is a Shirah, but that of Dasan and Aviram, not of all Israel.
Following the Rama MiFano, the two bulls of Eliyahu were Dasan and Aviram, and their tikkun comes at Ne'ilah of Yom Kippur, the peak of achdus, when their verse 'Hashem hu haElokim' is called out.
Acharon shel Pesach is called 'acharon', the last, because on it even the last and most lost Jew can be raised.

Just as the Satan provoked the two men's quarrel specifically on erev Shabbos to keep Shabbos, which is peace, from entering, so the machlokes of today comes because history stands at the erev Shabbos before Moshiach.
Adar, from 'aderes', a cloak, is the month furthest from Nisan: Nisan's miracles are revealed, Adar's are wrapped in nature, a nes twelve levels removed from an open nes.
For a child raised in the desert on the mann, bread rising from the ground would be the wonder; what we call nature is a miracle we are simply used to.
The news of the day is a Megillah being written now: events like Russia's collapse just before the Gulf War are pieces of one plan to protect the Jews.
Gossip from the king's court that a yeshiva boy rightly refuses to hear was, in Shushan, the very unfolding of the nes without which the Jews would not exist today.
Just as 'HaMelech' in the Megillah alludes to Hashem, a believer reading about the president in the newspaper understands that the real ruler is Hashem, and the leaders are marionettes.
Purim masks teach that the whole world is a masked world, and under the mask Hashem directs nations, families and every small happening.

Chanoch, who withdrew and became an angel but neglected his generation, embodies 'Hashem'; Avraham, who went down to the lowest people, embodies 'Elokeichem'; 'kedoshim tihyu' asks for holiness that does not contradict closeness to people.
Nissan is the birth of creation and Tishrei its bar mitzvah; Rabbi Eliezer, a man of din, holds the world was created in Tishrei, and Rabbi Yehoshua, of Beis Hillel's chesed, in Nissan.
The first se'ir of Rosh Chodesh was burned not as a failure but as the best sign: on the day of the Mishkan the moon was whole, so the atonement for its lessening was not needed.

Nadav and Avihu entered after drinking wine because they already felt the time of Eliyahu, when the Gemara says one will be able to make wine a fixed meal and wine will no longer harm; it was a sign of their greatness.

Yayin (70) is the Name of Hashem (26) plus dam (44): a little wine, used for kedushah, is the Name, while too much leaves only blood; this is why Kiddush begins 'Yom hashishi vayechulu', whose initials spell the Name.
Sefirah and Elul-Tishrei each last fifty-one days, and the thirtieth day of each, Pesach Sheni and Rosh Hashanah, is a day of tikkun.
The three teshuvah seasons follow nature: Nissan, when roots sprout, repairs the middos; Tishrei, the harvest, repairs deeds; Shovavim is a laundry season to remove the stains left after teshuvah.
Middos are missing from the Torah not because they matter less, but because they are its entrance requirement: the Torah was given to people, and a person without middos is like an animal.
The barley Omer, animal food, brought on Pesach, and the human food brought on Shavuos mark the journey of Sefirah from beast to 'adam'.
Rachel's test, which brings the geulah, was not about how she davened or kept mitzvos but about her middos: she would not let her sister be shamed.
Tamar and Potiphar's wife both acted for Heaven's sake to bring Moshiach; the difference that made one praised and the other shamed forever was whether she was willing to shame another person.
The Divrei Chaim proves that burying a rasha is no mitzvah: though Jews buried the wicked during the plague of darkness, they still had no mitzvos and needed Pesach and milah.
The poor man's bird, burned with its foul-smelling feathers, is still a pleasing aroma to Hashem; so too a weak chiddush offered by a bochur must be received warmly.

'Panim' comes from 'penimiyus': each face shows a different neshamah and middos, so differing opinions each have a root, as Hillel's chessed and Shammai's gevurah showed on their faces and in their rulings.
Haman's ten thousand kikar were charity, given to neutralize the merit of the Jews' half-shekels.
The only silver of the Mishkan that ended up outside the holy courtyard, the protruding hooks, came from the extra Jews beyond 600,000 whom the clouds had expelled.
The last eight pesukim of the Torah are pesukim of forgetting, and the souls outside the camp correspond to them; that is why Moshe Rabbeinu forgot their silver, while Hashem forgets no Jew.
The extra yud in 'Yehudim' that is written but not read, and the kashrus of a Megillah with half-erased letters, show that imperfect Jews still belong in the Megillah.
Haman rejoiced that the lot fell on Adar because he thought the Jewish year ends there, but the Jewish year is a circle and Nisan follows Adar, as Moshiach follows the last generation.
Tzedakah given on Purim is elevated above ordinary tzedakah, as an esrog on Sukkos calls for a different brachah than an esrog eaten on Purim.
The Seder night's leap out of the 49 gates was an unearned gift that faded; the counting of sefirah is the work of earning the same level oneself, one gate a day.
Every generation of galus is one of the 49 journeys of the desert, so the whole exile is one long sefirah leading to the geulah.

The omer offering is of barley, animal food, like the sotah's offering, because during sefirah the Jews stand under suspicion like a sotah; on Shavuos, cleared, they bring loaves of wheat, human food.
The daf of Sotah learned on erev Shavuos, the day of malchus shebemalchus, is exactly the mishnah of the footsteps of Moshiach, the lowest point of galus.
The high prices of the footsteps of Moshiach are notable because they defy the law of supply and demand: the vine gives its fruit, yet wine is expensive.
Minus is worse than idolatry: an idolater who believed in a false god still held himself back, but one who believes in nothing has no one to restrain him.

The Rav applies the Ohr HaChaim's parable of flies on an emptied barrel of honey to the yoledes: her tumah is not a defect but the residue of the great holiness of carrying a child who learned Torah with an angel.

Because a bris borrows a few moments of the days of Moshiach, when Eliyahu, who never ate from the Etz HaDaas, is present, the tumah that came from the sin of Adam is cut short; this is why the yoledes of a boy is tamei for less time.
The verse of milah on the eighth day interrupts the laws of the yoledes to answer the question the reader is about to ask, why a boy brings less tumah than a girl.
Shavuos is both the fiftieth day and the first day of the eighth week, like the eighth day on which a tamei person immerses; the day of Shavuos is itself the mikveh.
The days of Sefirah are a davar shebeminyan: like counted, important items that are never nullified even in a thousand, the counted days are too precious to be lost.
Rabbi Akiva's students died specifically between Pesach and Shavuos because in these weeks of preparing for Matan Torah, lacking midos is judged more strictly than during the rest of the year.
Since a person is where his thoughts are, one who speaks lashon hara is not allowed to direct his Shemoneh Esrei toward Yerushalayim, and so is exiled from Yerushalayim even today.

The custom of learning Sotah in Sefirah is more than a way to keep count: the sotah's barley offering clears suspicion from one woman, and the barley Omer, counted toward Shavuos, clears the suspicion the Egyptians and the nations cast on the purity of all Klal Yisrael.

The order of the generations runs down the body of Adam HaRishon: the generation of the desert, which learned Torah forty years, is the head; David's era of song and tefillah is the heart; and our generation is the heel, so even its leaders are only 'heads of the heel'.

The forty-nine days of Sefirah, the forty-nine levels of Klal Yisrael's descent through the generations, and the forty-nine dafim of Sotah run parallel, so the last daf, with the baraisa of the heels of Moshiach, is our own generation, just before the fiftieth level.
Like Adar, the last month, which turns into Nisan, the first, the lowest generation will be overturned to become the head of all generations together with Moshe and David.

Klal Yisrael began with emunah, with Avraham and with Anochi at Sinai, and it ends with emunah: the closing words of the baraisa, that we can rely only on our Father in Heaven, are the task of the generation before Moshiach.
Even a selfish prayer, such as a boy's request for a dog and a bicycle, is a true tefillah because it rests on believing that Hashem can give, and that belief is emunah.

The Rav reads the Mishnah 'all of Israel has a share' as naming a world called 'Kol Yisrael', the root of the souls in Yaakov Avinu, where even those the Mishnah excludes are not rejected, because the trace of holiness in a Jew can never be erased.

The Jews 'at the end of the Sefer Torah' are like the hooks of the Mishkan's pillars that Moshe Rabbeinu forgot, which protrude outside; Amalek and Haman thought such Jews were forgotten, but the Torah ends with 'before the eyes of all Israel' and swings right back into Bereishis.

'The king loved Esther more than all the women' refers to Hashem's love for the generation of concealment, which suffered from not feeling His love and still held on to Him, more than for earlier generations of great tzaddikim.

The lottery of Purim and Yom Kippur shows a choice with no reason, like a lottery win or a bride who finds favor beyond her qualities: Hashem's bond with His people comes from a will beyond reason, so even when Yaakov looks like Esav, Hashem knows he is His.
Holy objects such as matzah, the Sefer Torah and the shofar are kept covered for fear of the Satan, but the Megillah is unfolded entirely because it is an iggeres and on Purim there is no accuser.

Esther's 'gather all the Jews' was the answer to Haman's 'scattered and divided', and Shushan keeps Purim with Yerushalayim because its unity made it like Yerushalayim, the city that joins all Jews together.
The students of Rabbi Akiva lacked respect all year, but were punished in Sefirah because these are the days designated for refining middos before receiving the Torah.
The Torah does not reveal which tree was the Etz HaDa'as so that the tree should not be shamed, showing Hashem's care for the honor even of a plant.

The juxtaposed parshiyos of Tamar and Potiphar's wife describe the origins of the two Moshiachs, and both women acted for Heaven; only good middos separated them, so one merited and the other did not.
One who takes his own life has no atonement because death, which normally atones, is itself the sin; yet Tamar chose death over shaming Yehudah, so shaming is graver than suicide.
The word panim reflects that the face is a window to the inside: each face differs because each character differs, so one may no more resent another's opinions than his face.
A Kohen does not bless 'who did not make me a Yisrael', since that would be gaining honor through the disgrace of other Jews whose ancestors sinned at the Golden Calf.
The Torah lists the pig's kosher sign before its disqualifying one, opening even with a compliment to an impure animal.
The Rav reads the Maharal on Kamtza as a lesson that one who stands beside a baal machlokes as his friend and ally shares in the churban, even if he did nothing himself.

He explains R' Sholom of Belz's acrostic on the word 'frummer', and contrasts the 'frummer' who brushes off a broken-hearted person before Ne'ilah with the erlicher Yid who listens, since that is a chessed.

He sees the practices of the baal korei reading for everyone and of singing at a hakafah of yichus as built on the same principle as the borrowed clothes of Tu B'Av: one who can do more must still follow the custom, so as not to expose those who cannot.
From R' Yisrael Salanter's last night the Rav learns that a person's final moment reflects his whole life: the tzaddik spent it sparing another Jew from fear, which shows what his life was.

On the Mishnah 'the brazen go to Gehinnom', the Rav explains that every sinner can do teshuvah, but the brazen never does, so he has a one-way road; this is why the Chofetz Chaim would not keep the insolent bochur.
R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld weighed comforting a widow by letting her son lead Mussaf as a greater honor for the congregation than the rule about who should lead.
The Rav reads ordinary courtesies, such as a visible house number or a phone number said slowly, as continuing Hashem's own middas hachesed, which can sweeten a decree on the one who does them.
Singing in the middle of a chasan's drasha, which a capable bochur may resent, is presented as a deliberate chesed for the chasan who cannot speak.

Through the mashal of an ink stain, the Rav explains that a blemish ignored on a sack is a real flaw on a silk shirt; so a tzaddik is held to account for indirectly causing shame even when his psak was correct.
R' Akiva Eiger preferred to step down from the bimah seemingly without an answer rather than show the rav of the city that his kushya was no kushya.

On 'az panim l'Gehinom', the Rav explains that teshuvah helps for every sin, but the Mishnah knows a brazen person will not do teshuvah, which is why the insolent bochur was sent away while the one who sinned was kept.
Giving slightly less than requested, or bargaining over a price, can itself be a chesed, so that the other person does not regret having asked too little.
The haste throughout the Megillah is not incidental: a miracle from a place beyond time cannot fit into the measured pace of time, so it pushes time out of its way.
At Matan Torah earth is raised to heaven, but on Purim heaven comes down to earth; this is why Purim cannot be grasped with an earthly mind and is 'ad d'lo yada'.
In the Megillah's hidden names, the direction and placement of the letters decide whether din or chesed is drawn down, and Esther's reversal of them is the 'v'nahafoch hu' of Purim.
A giver of tzedakah himself forms Hashem's name: the coin is the yud, the five fingers the hei, the arm the vav, and the receiver's hand the last hei.
The halachah that Purim tzedakah is given to anyone who asks mirrors how Hashem gives on Purim: whoever stretches out his hand to Him in true emunah receives.
A seudah eaten 'at night' means one eaten sleepily and without excitement; the Purim seudah must have the character of day, bright and alert.
The Rav identifies the ten utterances of creation with the ten sefiros and calls understanding this a key to much of what is written in Chassidic seforim.
Since time itself is a creation, the Torah's preceding the world by 'two thousand years' cannot mean years; it means the Torah is two levels above chesed, where creation begins.
Tiferes means beauty because beauty is harmony: a picture painted in one color is not beautiful, while a blend of many colors is, just as Yaakov blends Avraham's chesed with Yitzchak's gevurah.
Netzach and hod are two opposite ways of holding one's ground: one by overcoming, as a man with a stick defeats a dog, and one by bowing and yielding.
Every midah contains all the others, so the work of sefirah is not only on the main midah of each week but on each combination, such as chesed shebechesed and gevurah shebechesed.
Binah is understood as building: taking what was learned and building one thing upon another until a new chiddush emerges.
Iyar's combination keeps the first half of the Name in the order of chesed but reverses the second half, hei before vav, so the month carries some din alongside the straight combination of Nisan.
Because Torah is G-dliness itself, one who understands a piece of Gemara understands Hashem; this is the inner meaning of 'haskel veyado'a osi', which makes Iyar's combination a call to Torah.
Rav Chaim Vital merited to grasp the Arizal's deep Torah after the Arizal had him drink from Miriam's well in the Kinneret, which shows that the well, given in Iyar, brings Torah.
The days of Sefirah leave a greater mark than Tishrei; Tishrei is judgment with the attribute of din, so one fasts and says selichos, while Nisan through Sivan are judgment with chesed.
The three Shabbos meals match the three tefillos of the Avos, and melaveh malkah, the meal of Dovid, matches a fourth tefillah of tzaddikim, tikkun chatzos.
Yeshayahu, speaking of the future, mentions Rosh Chodesh even before Shabbos, because when Moshiach comes Rosh Chodesh will be like Shabbos and even more.
The Rambam's explanation of 'until he says I want' is read as a statement about the root of every Jewish soul: the coercion only weakens the body's interference so that his true will emerges.
Yom Kippur reaches the level of 'I want' only after climbing through ten days, while Purim reveals it even in Jews who had sinned, which is why Yom Kippur is only 'a day like Purim'.

The order of the Torah, of the tribes and of the months runs from top to bottom: the last letters, Shevet Dan and the month of Adar all correspond to the lowest Jews of the generations before Moshiach.
Keeping Purim in the second Adar, next to Nisan, teaches that even the low Jews of Adar cannot be cut off from their root in Nisan and Bereishis.

The mekalel's mockery of 'stale' bread was a claim that Hashem no longer cares for the lowest Jews; the miracle of the bread staying fresh is the answer, and Haman made the same claim about the Jews in exile.
The less observant a Jew is, the happier he tends to be on Purim, because Purim is the day Hashem turns to the lowest and shows him love.

Netzach and hod are the two legs on which a person stands: netzach survives by resisting, hod survives like grass that bends before the storm while cedars break; for a Jew, the ability to submit is itself beauty.

The Holy of Holies, Yom Kippur and the Kohen Gadol are one point in place, time and soul; so Aharon is the 'soul-Beis Hamikdash', and his death in Av, the month of hod, foreshadowed the churban in the same month.

The minyan is learned specifically from the meraglim to show that ten Jews, even reshaim, reveal the inner point where none is wicked, which nine tzaddikim cannot do; there is no need to emend the Gemara.

Since Hashem makes no duplicates, each Jew has a purpose no one else can fulfill, and in that point the worst Jew is greater than the greatest tzaddik; this is what Rabbi Akiva's students failed to see.

Chazal derive mourning from a festival because its root is joy: mourning belongs only to the body, and Tisha B'Av always falls on the weekday of Pesach, showing that Jewish mourning is rooted in redemption.

After the churban Hashem sent Rashbi's soul to fill the place of the Beis Hamikdash; the inner Torah was revealed to him precisely while he was hidden in the cave, as the inner place is never revealed.
'Ohr' equals 'raz': the inner point is a secret even from oneself, yet it gives light, and this is why Lag BaOmer is marked with so much fire and light.
The Aron that Shlomo hid beneath the Kodesh HaKodashim corresponds to the ahavah mesuteres, the concealed love of Hashem hidden in every Jew's heart, which churban never reaches.
The vavim, the only part of the Mishkan outside the camp, were made from the extra half-shekels, which presumably came from the Jews who had fallen outside the camp; that is why Moshe forgot them.
Rabbi Akiva's name contains the word akev, the heel: his soul reaches down to the lowest Jews, and so it was he who reminded Moshe of the forgotten ones.
The Torah shares the fate of the Jews: just as they are scattered in galus, its halachos are scattered, with laws of Shabbos found in Menachos and the reverse.
Yishmael's strength is the bow, the middah of yesod he holds through milah; Lag Ba'omer, completing hod shebehod, is when Klal Yisrael seizes that bow from him.

The 70 tikkunim of the Tikkunei Zohar, each an explanation of the word Bereishis, repair the seventy faces of Klal Yisrael, connecting the end to the beginning; "vayehi roveh kashes" equals "shivim tikkunim" in gematria.
Eliyahu's promise that the Jews will leave exile through the Zohar applies to all the sefarim built on it, especially chassidus, because the Ba'al Shem Tov was the soul of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

Following the Ramchal, the 'shevi', the captive that Moshe brought down from on high with great difficulty, is the soul of Rabbi Shimon, and the same letters recur in the names of the Arizal and the Ba'al Shem Tov, souls that reveal the secrets of the Torah.
'Rotzeh ani', the inner will of a Jew that the Rambam says is real even when it comes out under compulsion, equals Yom Kippur in gematria, and Yom Kippur reveals it in every Jew.

Purim reveals the inner core of a Jew, which is why the simplest Jews rejoice on Purim more than elevated ones, and Rabbi Shimon himself revealed this when he taught that the Jews in Haman's time sinned only outwardly.

Counting the omer and every other remembrance of the Beis Hamikdash is a way of seeking Zion that arouses a seeking of Zion above, and Lag Ba'omer, which comes from the Holy of Holies, the summit of Zion, is a whole day of it.
Like Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, the Jews in Eretz Yisrael have become so accustomed to miracles that they no longer notice them.
The Rav compares Purim's clowning and wine to an anesthetic: the remedy Hashem gives on Purim is so strong for the soul that it must be taken without seeing it, and it works regardless.
Rashi's unusual, almost poetic term 'the letter of Purim' signals that the Megillah is a personally addressed letter: each reader must study it as if written to him alone.
The last generation is like the fingernail: formed last and least sensitive, yet once contained in the embryo together with the head, so the end remains bound to the beginning.
Nisan comes from 'nes', a flag on a high pole where Hashem shows Himself, while Adar comes from 'aderes', a cloak; Adar holds as many miracles as Nisan, only concealed.

Adar corresponds to Dan, the tribe at the rear that Amalek attacked because it seemed rejected by Hashem; Amalek is the voice telling a Jew he is lost, and the Megillah and Zachor answer that Hashem forsakes no Jewish soul.
Since the Divine Name has only twelve permutations, Adar Sheni has none and is counted as the 'kolel'; the One who is added is Hashem Himself, who joins Klal Yisrael and makes up whatever is lacking.
Shabbos is felt most by tzaddikim, but Purim is the opposite: it is made for the lowest and most distant, and the lower a person is, the more Purim he has.

The lowest point of the sefirah tikkun, hod sheb'hod, is exactly where the highest light, that of Moshe, Moshiach and Rashbi, shines, just as the Torah's last parsha, tied to the lowest souls, is joined to Bereishis.
Because the fiftieth day is above time, Moshe's added day before Matan Torah is not really another day: one cannot count it on a calendar of torn-off pages.
Aharon is himself 'kodesh kodashim': as hod and the Beis Hamikdash is hod, he is the Beis Hamikdash in the soul, which is why he alone may enter the Holy of Holies.
Aveilus is only relative to this world; the Kodesh haKodashim is the 'embassy' of the World to Come, so the Kohen Gadol, and Rashbi's place in Meron, stand outside mourning.

In pshat the large beis of Bereishis outranks the lamed of 'l'einei kol Yisrael', but in sod the last is bound to the first and the lamed has a virtue even the beis lacks; so every Jew, however small, is indispensable.
The 'pnei Elokim' Jews long to see is the innermost part of the name Elokim, which is pure mercy; only its outer side is judgment.
Lag Baomer always falls on the weekday of Purim, and both are days for the lowly whose hidden worth an outsider like Amalek cannot see.
Gevurah, though itself judgment, is close to binah, with only chesed between them; hod is far removed, the lowest of the middos of judgment, and so the hardest to sweeten.
The letters of hod reversed spell the impurity of blood that Eichah ascribes to Yerushalayim: the overturned hod is the red of judgment.
Lag Ba'Omer is the start of the last third of sefirah, like the dawn watch of the night, and from it the count already connects to the fiftieth day.
The custom of dairy on Shavuos expresses the completion of sefirah's work: the blood of din has been whitened into milk, the chesed that began flowing on Lag Ba'Omer.

Av, the fifth month, mirrors the fifth middah: the Beis Hamikdash fell then, and the fifth of Av, hod shebehod of Av, is the passing of the Arizal, a gilgul of Rabbi Shimon, just as Lag Ba'Omer is hod shebehod of sefirah.
The Arizal's Torah stayed in the hidden realm, with no halachos from him, while Rabbi Shimon's teachings came down also into the Mishnah and braisos, the world of pshat.
Rabbi Shimon is the soul of 'al tishkechi kol gemulav', the passuk from which the Gemara learns that milk was placed at the seat of binah, so he is the one who sweetens.
The Rema is the revealed side of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, which is why the Rema's yahrzeit falls on Rabbi Shimon's day.
Rabbi Shimon's way was the dove, which finds the hidden good even in the tochacha; the Rema's way, as the revealed Torah, was the raven, which exposes what is not in order.
Because Rabbi Shimon expounded the secret of each letter, and each letter is a Jew, he expounded the hidden tzaddik in every Jew, even in the lowliest.

The 'lightest of the light', the souls found in the tochacha, also carry a hidden secret; the passuk there that is the fiftieth mention of the Exodus holds the fiftieth gate and the secret of the geulah.
The Rav reads 'mipi zaro' in Rabbi Shimon's proof as a hint to his own name, Bar Yochai, through whom the Torah will not be forgotten.
History moves not in a straight line but in a circle, so the lowest generation, the heel, is the one that will become the head of all generations.
The name Adar is read as aderes, a cloak: the month in which Hashem is present but wrapped up and unseen, in contrast to Nisan, the month of nissim.

Adar Sheni is an appendage to the calendar just as the last eight pesukim, written by Moshe in tears, are an appendage to the Sefer Torah; both carry the mark of death and forgetting, which is why Haman rejoiced at them.
The greatest nissim are the ones within nature, where each event alone is insignificant and only the timing of all of them together reveals Hashem's hand.

A story like Vashti's refusal, which a yeshiva would dismiss as idle news, turned out to be part of the nes we read every year; so too today's events, even elections, may be part of a future Megillah.
The higher a light is, the lower it reaches; therefore Rabbi Shimon's joy grows as the generations go down, and later generations feel more light on Lag BaOmer than earlier ones did.
The breaking of the vessels came from the receivers' refusal to submit to the giver, the claim "I will rule", like a cup that wants to stand higher than the pitcher and so receives nothing.

The eighth king of Edom, who has no "and he died" and whose wife is named, stands for a receiver that receives from the giver without breaking; the Rav brings that "in this year of Yovel" equals the wife's name in gematria.
A table is called shulchan because the food on it was sent (shalach) by Hashem to the person, as a mission to repair the sparks in it.
Unlike other Yamim Tovim, Lag BaOmer grows greater as night falls, because this Yom Tov comes down to the person rather than requiring him to rise to it.
The companions held hands in a closed circle like an electric circuit; talking or letting go in the middle of a dance breaks that circuit.
Rabbi Shimon is the soul that is Shabbos, and his view that all Jews are princes, all equal, will become the halacha when Moshiach comes.
Yovel is the fiftieth gate, where all Jewish souls merge into one soul, and this is the inner meaning of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, whose day gathers all Jews together.

The Gemara says Osniel ben Kenaz restored forgotten halachos because he conquered the matching part of the land; the Ba'al Shem Tov reads it the other way: learning the halachos is what conquers the land.
The hair of the first three years parallels the three years of orlah, and the fourth year's 'kodesh hilulim' is the gematria of Har Esav, so the upsherin stands against Esav.
The sons of Keturah have milah but no priah because their bodies come from the three impure kelipos and not from kelipas nogah, which priah addresses.
Lag BaOmer is the great fall of Esav, the 'head' struck in the passuk, and from it the attribute of chessed begins to lead toward the fiftieth day.

Yaakov could complete only the 24 letters of Baruch Shem because the Shechinah had no Mishkan yet; the 25 letters of the verse calling Moshe from the Ohel Moed show that the 25-letter unity became possible only once the Mishkan stood.

The order of saying Baruch Shem after Shema follows importance, but the order of tikkun was Yaakov's 24 first; counted that way, the 33rd letter falls on the first yud of Hashem's name, which is why Lag Baomer reveals the point of every Jew.

The four parts of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, correspond to ascending worlds: Yaakov died only in the world of pshat, while in drush and above he lives, and so Rabbi Shimon, who revealed sod, did not die in that realm.
Both Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon passed away with the word 'chaim': Yaakov's last words ended with 'bnei Ches', and Rabbi Shimon died in the middle of saying 'chaim'.

Rabbi Akiva's students were surely respectful of a greater man; their failing was that the greater one did not honor the lesser, not recognizing the hidden sod in the other that makes him irreplaceable, like a letter without which a Sefer Torah is invalid.

Achashverosh's feast celebrated his calculation that the seventy years were over with no Beis Hamikdash, so taking part in it was a denial of the coming of Moshiach and the geulah, one of the thirteen principles.

The Megillah's light exceeds that of the Torah of Moshe precisely because it was given to a generation that had fallen lowest, with intermarriage like today; one who goes down into a deep pit needs a stronger light.
The Megillah stays even in the days of Moshiach because its real story has not yet been told: it will be the story of the last Purim of galus, which ushers in the geulah.
Adar Sheni is like those who trailed behind the camp outside the clouds of glory; on such a Purim the Shechinah comes down even to those cast out, which makes it a more powerful Purim.
Even if the splitting of the sea had a natural cause, as Graetz claimed, its happening at exactly that moment would be a greater miracle, the kind of hidden miracle the Megillah is made of.
Amalek dared attack right after the splitting of the sea because to him everything is 'mikreh', chance, and Haman, as Mordechai told Esther, carried on that same 'korcha' view.
The seven ministers of Achashverosh had names that alluded to korbanos, so that their heavenly counterparts, the seven angels with the same names, could plead for the Jews in Vashti's judgment.
The angels' concern with the leap year was, at root, the moon's repair: Esther is the moon, and her kingship restores the moon's rule.
The moon's jealousy of the sun is the root of the narrow eye in the world, which leads through the sin of the Tree of Knowledge and Kayin to the sale of Yosef and the exile.
The number thirteen ties the repairs together: the thirteenth month, the thirteenth middah of seeing another's good, and the thirteenth year of Yosef in prison and of Rabbi Shimon in the cave.
Lag BaOmer and Purim are a pair: 'sheves achim gam yachad' of Rabbi Shimon and the gathering of all the Jews on Purim are one repair of the sale of Yosef.
The Rav reads 'all Jews are sons of kings' through the hidden virtue: since each Jew has something no other Jew has, in that respect he is a king over all of them.

Just as each Jew corresponds to a letter of the Torah and the Torah has pshat, remez, drush and sod, each Jew has a sod part, the hidden virtue, which is why Rabbi Shimon, the revealer of the Torah's secrets, is the one who reveals it.
The sin of Rabbi Akiva's students is understood as failing to honor the other's hidden virtue, even when one is truly greater in learning and yiras Shamayim; Rabbi Shimon's revelation undid that.

The Rav links Lag Ba'omer to parshas Behar, read around that time: the shemitah of the land shows that the Shabbos reaches the earth, the lowest element, just as Rabbi Shimon reaches the lowliest Jews.
In the Zohar's words at Rabbi Shimon's passing, the earth may not be proud that all return to it, since Rabbi Shimon is not consumed by it; his aspect rules over the earth.

The angel opposite Memuchan, who is Haman, pleads with the lechem hapanim because Haman's error was the opposite of its lesson: he held that Hashem's love for the rejected had gone cold, while the bread that stayed warm shows that it never does.
The surplus silver used for the protruding hooks, outside the kedushah of the Mishkan, came from the cast-outs of Dan, and Moshe Rabbeinu forgot it because they were forgotten Jews.
The ben ish Mitzri's mockery of the stale lechem hapanim and his claim that Dan's camp was open to him were one position, the same as Amalek's: that the rejected are outside Hashem's love.
The two goats of Yom Kippur must be identical because Yaakov and Esav can look the same, yet Hashem loves Yaakov for the hidden point within him.
Haman matched the main half-shekels but ignored the surplus of the rejected; that overlooked silver, given first, is what nullified his decree.
The Rav suggests that today's Jews are gilgulim of Shevet Dan, so Purim, the Yom Tov of the rejected, is their Yom Tov and grows greater the lower they fall.

The Magen Avraham's question how the sixth of Sivan can be called 'the day of the giving of our Torah' is answered simply: the Torah is given anew each Shavuos, so this year's Shavuos is truly that day.
The Jews reached Sinai on Rosh Chodesh because the moon's renewal renews the 'crops' of every Jew's soul, which grow from the moon, making it the time for new kabbalos.
Through Rabbi Gedalia Chayun, a convert's every later mitzvah is 'compounded' with the mitzvah of her conversion, because without that acceptance she would never have done it.
The world did not wait for the giving of the Torah but for the Jews' acceptance of it, as the Gemara's 'one of your eyes' refers to the moment of acceptance before fulfillment.

Rashi's 'wherever it says neged, it means facing east' becomes a call to keep all of life turned toward one point, the glorification of Hashem, rising like the dawn, without being scattered by obstacles or by looking back.
The world's apathy in the face of danger is described as a disease, a failure to notice what is happening.
Refidim is read as 'perud', separation: Amalek's power came from the lack of unity, so the teshuvah that Rashi says they did on leaving Refidim was their becoming one before Sinai.
Citing tzaddikim, the Rav says that when two Jews come together they form Hashem's Name, written with two yuds.
Nearing Sinai without the Torah was already a gift: the unity of Rosh Chodesh was the klal of the Torah, and the giving of the Torah on Shavuos brought only its particulars.
Because the darkness of the later generations is greater, Hashem lights greater lamps, as seen in the growing revelations from Rashbi to the Arizal to the Ba'al Shem Tov.
At the level of the fiftieth day, 'one' is not the smallest number but the only one; that is why the fiftieth day, like the Levi'im, is not counted.
