The Aron taking no space, bowing with room in the Azarah, and finding lodging in Yerushalayim are one miracle at three levels: the closer to the Kodesh HaKodashim, the less it is even a miracle, since there heaven's nature rules.
Moshe Rabbeinu, called the shofar of Klal Yisrael, was above time and could move the day of Matan Torah; 'Vayedaber Moshe es mo'adei Hashem' means he carries the festivals to the Jews each year.

The Rav reads Targum Yonasan's night journey to Yerushalayim and back as Hashem first showing the Jews where they truly belong, then sending them back to reach it through their own work, like a king's son who must still go through his training.
He compares the Korban Pesach's leap over levels to dancing: in a dance one jumps higher than one really is.

The second of Sivan is not a commemoration: since the Torah is eternal, every year each Jewish soul again declares 'na'aseh', even if the body does not hear it, just as the Arizal describes souls acting at night without the person knowing.

Since each Jewish soul belongs to a letter of Hashem's Sefer Torah, a missing soul would make the whole Torah invalid; this is why every Jew must come to his tikkun, and he links it to the Shavuos custom of bringing all the Sifrei Torah.

Boaz's mention of 'vinegar' was not discouraging talk to a convert but comfort: even the 'vinegar' from her line, Menashe, would become the teacher of all Israel, since every hamotzi follows his halachah.

The place 'baked first' is chosen for the brachah not because it is the best piece but because it shows Hashem's plan that this part reach its tikkun first; so the halachah of a soul whose own way was through tikkun came through Menashe.
He reads the melachos of bread in Hilchos Shabbos as the stages of tikkun after Adam's sin, with baking as the final stage after which the bread is ready for a brachah.

The 960 hours of forty full days correspond to the 960 lugin of a mikveh, the measure in which even a whole creature is nullified, so Matan Torah, a rebirth like a mikveh, could not use 'part of the day counts as a whole'.
Adam's sin, the error before the Golden Calf and the error at Achashverosh's feast share one root, not waiting, and Mordechai, who urged the Jews to wait, was a repair of Adam's sin.
The five final letters are letters of din, yet the Midrash calls them letters of redemption; the purpose of din is to be transformed into geulah.

Haman's ten thousand kikar offset only the shekalim of the 600,000; the extra 1775 shekalim, linked to the rejected Jews of Dan, had nothing against them, and so it was they who brought the salvation.
The sum of the whole aleph-beis together with the five final letters is 1775, the number of forgotten shekalim, showing that those outside are still included in Klal Yisrael.
Beyond the Tanya's answer, the Rav adds that the red heifer is prepared outside the camp, unlike a chatas, and so it brings salvation to those who are outside, like the rejected of Dan.
Naomi is the Shechinah going down into Moav, the territory of the sitra achra, to rescue the spark from which David and Moshiach will come; the famine and Elimelech's departure served this purpose.

The disorder before Moshiach is like a bone thrown to a dog: just as the Satan was sent to Iyov so he would not obstruct the splitting of the sea, the lower forces of evil are given something to occupy them so they will not disturb the preparation of Moshiach.
The Rav reads 'Your right hand, Hashem, shatters the enemy' as alluding to Iyov, since oyev and Iyov share the same letters.

Chazal read immodesty into the verses of Rus but not into the maidens of Shaul's time, because the signs of ikvesa d'Meshicha belonged to the time when the spark of Moshiach was being born, not to David's settled generation.
Chutzpah serves as the camouflage of Moshiach's coming: the line of Moshiach began with the brazen naming of Moav, and 'chutzpah will increase' is the first sign listed in the Baraisa.
Rus is placed right after Malachi because Malachi's closing describes the torn generations before Eliyahu comes, and that is exactly the state of 'the days when the judges were judged'.
Rus's complete reward was to live to see Shlomo's kingship, a time when converts are not accepted, because she converted when being a Jew was hard and could then see how good it is to be a Jew.
The world is called olam because it hides its Creator; on Shavuos, the fiftieth day that is beyond counting, the hidden things begin to be revealed.
The angels' taking permission from one another teaches that no one should push himself forward; each one's song only counts as part of the whole choir.
The truest song is what remains unsaid: each Jew's private grasp of Hashem, which he cannot explain even to others, is the 'secret of the Torah'.
Even the simplest Jew has a point in his soul through which he knows Hashem more deeply than the greatest tzaddik.
The angels long all their existence for one chance to sing, while a Jew has that chance every minute of his life.
Each accepted prayer of a Jew becomes a precious stone in Hashem's crown, set opposite His tefillin, and on Shavuos this crown is revealed.
The holier a thing is, the more easily it is affected; therefore Olam Haba was hidden even from the prophets.
The Midrash says 'zman' for the earlier turning points but 'eis' for Matan Torah, because 'eis' (related to 'atah', now) is a dimensionless point between past and future, and the Torah is above time.
Although the Torah says to count fifty days, the count ends at forty-nine: the fiftieth day, like Yovel and Yom Kippur, belongs to a level above time that a person cannot count.
The chametz of the two loaves is the refined 'chametz of the future', a yetzer hara made holy, so on the day of the Torah one brings a new kind of service to Hashem from chametz.

The counting runs from chesed down to malchus because the Avos and Moshe brought the Shechinah down from the seventh heaven step by step, and every person is meant to become a Har Sinai on which Heaven descends.
For a tzaddik, what is beyond the letter of the law for others becomes his law, and 'kedoshim tihyu' means that yesterday's extra becomes today's baseline.

The son's question 'tomorrow' is the question of the morning after the Seder, when the elevation is gone; the strong hand of Pesach is not the purpose, since man was created to sanctify himself by his own work.
An 'ohr chadash' differs from a new object: new shoes are new for a week, but the light of Purim is new by its essence and remains a surprise every year.
The word 'Megillah' itself means revealing, while Esther points to hiding: on Purim what was hidden becomes revealed.
Haman's war on Mordechai was a contest of reishis: Amalek, the reishis of tumah, tried to reach the fiftieth level of tumah to overpower Mordechai, whose strength also came from reishis.
The miracles of the Megillah were deliberately natural, events the nations could read in the newspapers, because on Purim the heavenly comes down into nature rather than nature rising above itself.
The Megillah must be read from a parchment scroll written in ink because the reading purifies the very materials of nature, animal hide and earthly chemicals, together with the reader's gashmiyus.
Because the world has sunk lower this year, the light of the Megillah must reach deeper than ever, so no one is too low to receive it.

Each Jew's portion of Eretz Yisrael is his letter in the Torah and the source of his chiddushim; so Boaz, whose land it was, revealed the heter of a Moabite woman, while the other relative, with no tie to that place, had no tie to the halacha either.
The cut branches brought in for Shavuos wilt because they are cut from their root; they stand for Jewish souls in galus, and one davens that they return to their root.
Menashe, the wicked king, became the rav of all Israel for hamotzi; this was Boaz's comfort to Rus, that even the 'vinegar' from her would teach every Jew how to break bread.

The part of the loaf baked first is the part Hashem wants fixed first; malchus Beis Dovid is that part, which is why Hashem accepted Menashe's teshuvah before its time, through a tunnel past the middas hadin.
The berachah hamotzi literally 'takes out' the spark of a soul hidden in the bread, as Hashem took Israel out from under the burdens of Mitzrayim.
Of the three melachos of sorting, only winnowing is done by the wind and not by the person; Boaz winnowing on the night Rus came shows Hashem Himself refining the soul of malchus Beis Dovid.
The eleven melachos of bread correspond to eleven levels of klipah that a soul's spark must break through; only grain of Eretz Yisrael, plowed over its whole surface, goes through all eleven.

The hagbalah at Sinai, being told to stay below, is not the opposite of preparing for Torah but the preparation itself: knowing one is limited and unworthy readies a person to receive the Torah as a gift.

The verse of the last week of sefirah is "afsei aretz", the ends of the earth: one who began sefirah with great hopes ends at the lowest point, and from there, with the cry "shavaseinu kabel", he comes to receive the Torah.

Megillas Ruth is read on Shavuos because Torah and tefillah go together: Ruth is the root of Dovid, the pillar of tefillah, and the megillah's opening about ten famines points to the last famine, for the word of Hashem, which only prayer can break.

The Targum repeats at the end of Ruth what it said at the start, that Boaz ended the famine through prayer, because the megillah is a psak written by Shmuel on Dovid's lineage, and a psak restates its reason at the end.
Ruth and Orpah both accepted the yoke of Heaven; the only difference was that Ruth's acceptance stayed fresh, and that small difference produced Dovid on one side and Golias on the other.
Following Tosafos, what disqualified a ba'al keri before Matan Torah was not tumah, which did not yet exist, but kalus rosh, the opposite of the awe with which Torah must be received.
Staying up on Shavuos night with toil in Torah repairs the acceptance of the Oral Torah, which according to Midrash Tanchuma was not accepted willingly at Sinai.

The Rav reads the word 'shanah' (year) as coming from 'shinui', repetition: the year is like a rotating card file, and when a day's card comes down to the lower world, what happened on that date happens again.

Like a patient under anesthetic at the dentist, a coarse person may feel nothing at Matan Torah, yet the procedure is real: his soul receives the lights of Matan Torah and carries them through the year.
Unlike every other Yom Tov, named for what happens on it, Shavuos is named for the counting of the weeks before it, showing how essential the preparation is.
A mikveh, like a sukkah, is not its water or its boards and straw but the holy names that its halachos draw into it; the mikveh of Shavuos carries different holy names than during the year.

Staying up all night and sleeping through Krias HaTorah is like a chassan who paid for the caterer, photographers and flowers but came to the chuppah without the ring, since Israel is the chassan and the Torah the kallah.
Rosh Chodesh Sivan, the head of the month, already contains all of Shavuos, as Rosh Hashanah contains the whole year.
Adar, the last month, mirrors Nisan in reverse: Nisan is named for its open miracles, while Adar means a cloak, the covering of miracles, and its Megillah has none.
The Megillah names Memuchan, Chazal's Haman, only at its start, to signal the reader to watch Haman, because Haman is the one who made the whole Megillah.

Mordechai's greatness had to be designed by Haman: a tzaddik full of rachmanus would have made a painless death for his enemy and asked for little honor or house, while only cruel, honor-seeking Haman knew how to make a fifty-amah gallows, a royal parade and a palace.

The lowest tribe, Dan, produced Chushim, who could not hear or speak, yet he is the one who killed Esav; the Rav links this to the generation before Moshiach, a generation of Chushim and hester panim.

Adar Sheini stands outside the order of the twelve months, like the last eight pesukim of the Torah, which have a separate status; Haman thought the Jews there were outside the camp, but they too belong to it.

Number and counting are a limitation of this world; the fiftieth day belongs to Heaven, so by Heaven's reckoning the day Moshe chose is the fiftieth even though the calendar calls it the fifty-first, and both days of Shavuos can be 'the time of the giving of our Torah'.

The place of the aron that took up no space, the pesukim of the Ten Commandments whose count does not fit, and the fiftieth day that is not counted all express one idea: where the Torah is, it is above time, place and number.
Emunah was received on the fiftieth day precisely because 'Anochi' was given above intellect; something understood is knowledge, and only something above understanding is believed.

The fiftieth gate of impurity is the mirror of the fiftieth gate of holiness: as holiness peaks in emunah, impurity peaks in apikorsus, and Amalek, whose gematria equals 'safek', puts doubt into Jewish hearts.
The suffering a bachur feels over his doubts is itself proof of his faith: someone who did not believe would be glad of the doubts.
A thought of doubt is sent from Heaven as an opportunity: the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru' is not that the thought never comes, but that one drives it out when it does.

The Chasam Sofer's parable: the yetzer hara is a firm that, once people learn to beware of it, reopens under a new name, and its latest name is 'today's world', so the argument 'in today's world one does not do that' is the yetzer hara speaking.
Shlomis's 'shalom' is outward, reaching every passer-by, while Shulamis's 'shalom' is inner wholeness inside her own walls; Knesses Yisrael rejects the first and lives by the second.

The 'dance of the camps' that Knesses Yisrael asks of the nations is the separate camps of the desert, set against the camps of angels around the Kisei HaKavod, a society with no link to today's world.

The chutzpah and immorality of the Shoftim period in Megillas Ruth are the cover under which the root of Moshiach sprouted, hidden from the Satan, just as the signs of ikvesa d'meshicha at the end of Sotah open with chutzpah.
Yissachar's two hundred heads of Sanhedrin in the days of the return from Bavel, almost a thousand years later, show how long the influence of living next to Moshe and Aharon lasted.
Today's world is itself extreme, unashamed and breaking a tradition of generations, so the one who wants to stay normal must be what it calls 'extreme'.
Parah and Pur are equal in gematria with the kolel, and Parshas Parah is a step beyond Purim: Purim comforts those left outside the camp, while Parah purifies them and brings them inside.

Parah is read just before Parshas HaChodesh so that when the Satan claims there is no reason to redeem the Jews, Hashem can answer that as they keep a chok without a reason, He can redeem them without one.
Nachash and Satan share a gematria; the ches of the Nachash, open below, inverts into the tes of the Satan, open above, and the two letters together spell chet, sin.
The Nachash could not tempt Adam and Chava with bodily desire, only with a higher intellect, and so the cure for the death he brought is a mitzvah kept without understanding.
How Parah Adumah works and when Moshiach will come are the two related matters where the mind meets a red light, since both concern the end of death in the world.

The Eitz HaDaas was a vine whose grapes Adam was meant to keep for Kiddush on Shabbos; the golden calf and Shaul's offering repeated that failure to wait, while Dovid, who waited, is the root of Moshiach.

A tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah can rule over heavenly ministers without knowing it himself, as the Mishneh LaMelech's shake of the head cast down the minister of Russia while only the Ba'al Shem Tov knew.

The rule that the lower prevails explains both the order of meat and milk and the dispute at Sinai: the angels held the upper prevails, so the Torah should stay in heaven, and by their own rule their meal at Avraham's table was meat with milk.
Milk on Shavuos reflects the transformation of din into chesed: as blood becomes milk, the red days of sefirah become white.
A Sefer Torah is written on an animal's hide to show that the Torah's letters must rest on the person's refined animal side, made clean and white.

The camp of Israel in the wilderness was a living Sefer Torah, so a person who did not belong in a camp was like an extra letter that invalidates the scroll; this, not exclusion, is why the blasphemer was kept out.
The Levi'im were counted from thirty days old, the start of a person's root, because they are the roots of the letters, matching the 22 letters as 22,000.
The commandments were said in the singular so that even in a guilty generation the Torah endures through individuals, whose worth then is like that of Adam, created alone.
Unlike the nations, who merely commemorate a past event on its date, for Jews the same lights of the original day actually return each year, which is why a year is called shanah, repetition.
Every soul relives matan Torah each Shavuos; a sin is like the insulation on an electric wire, which keeps the body from feeling the current the soul experiences.
On Rosh Hashanah one is judged for parnassah, but on Shavuos one is judged for one's share in Torah and closeness to Hashem, so Shavuos calls for even more fear.
The one who stays awake all night and then sleeps at the Aseres Hadibros is like a chasan who paid for the hall, music and flowers but will not buy the ring, without which there is no kiddushin.

Just as physical air and rivers are polluted today, so is the spiritual atmosphere, following the principle that one can recognize the state of ruchniyus from gashmiyus; for that reason a struggling Jew's avodah is worth more now.

The left horn of Yitzchak's ram was already sounded at Sinai, and the right horn remains for Moshiach; the Torah comes from Hashem's right hand, so Kabbalas HaTorah is a time to arouse that right side in mercy.
The Rav connects the summer travel season with the meraglim's forty days: the world travels in exactly these weeks because their failed journey must be repaired by journeys done right.
A seemingly trivial act, a brachah on a glass of water in a distant city, can be the very repair for which a person was sent there, and no one else can do it.
Noach did not spoil his portion of the world, so his animals remained righteous and his portion, Eretz Yisrael, was not flooded.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, Rashi and Onkelos do not argue about Bilaam: his blind eye, never defiled by looking at impurity, was the one that saw prophecy well.

The difference between the failed and successful spies was tefillah, and the two who had it are the ancestors of Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben Dovid, bringing redemption where the others brought exile.
Tzitzis means looking, and the mitzvah brings holiness into the eyes, the very organ with which the meraglim sinned.
All of creation sings to Hashem by doing His will, and a Jew's song is learning, davening and avoiding aveiros; one who does not is the lone exception in the choir.
Haman took Adar, the last month, as the end of the Jews, but for Jews time is a circle: the end touches the beginning and everything starts over.

The Egel was the same sin as the Eitz HaDaas, acting on one's own understanding, and therefore it brought back the death that Matan Torah had abolished; Parah only partly atones, removing tumas meis but not death itself.
The Satan's argument against the Geulah is that there is no reason for it, and Parah, a mitzvah with no reason that Jews keep anyway, answers him in kind.
Parah is read before both seasons of potential Geulah: before Nisan, when chesed is aroused, and as Parshas Chukas before the three weeks, when rachamim is aroused through the Churban.
In the Beis HaMikdash there was no hester panim, so even the aged Chafetz Chaim would have reached the Mizbeach first if he had the merit; the race measured merit, not strength.
Since no two Jews stand on the same level, a tie in the race was a sign that on that day merits did not count and Hashem was leading as with children, so the whole group entered the goral.
Mikveh requires one's own act of immersion and cannot remove tumas meis, while the water of Parah is sprinkled on a person by someone else, from above, and purifies even tumas meis.
Balak's parsha is named not for the evil in him but for the hidden thing inside him, the root of Moshiach through Ruth.
Chevron and Shechem, the places of Avraham's milah and of Yosef, are exactly where the enemies fight, because great tumah sits where great holiness lies hidden.
As there is orlah in the body, there is orlah in time: the three weeks are the orlah of the year, and beneath them lies a special brightness.
The two midrashim on Pinchas's covenant fit together: Eliyahu attends the milah of each child and will perform the great milah of the whole world at the geulah.
Tammuz and Av are the months of Reuven and Shimon, fourth and fifth in the degalim; their fall made these months fall, and in the order of tikkun they will be first.
Balak's words 'yoshev mimuli' express his fear that Israel would cut him off as one removes an orlah.
Tammuz and Av correspond to the two eyes, which is why these are the months that call for special guarding of the eyes.
The two nesi'im who stumbled, one at Korach's congregation and the nasi of Shimon at Zimri's deed, correspond to the two months of Tammuz and Av, which were stricken by the sin of the meraglim.
The same pattern of Moshiach hidden under an orlah appears in soul (Balak), in place (Amon and Moav) and in time (Tammuz and Av), following the Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of world, year and soul.
Balak's inner self was good, since Moshiach was within him; it was his body, a great kelipah, that refused to let it out.
'V'hu yoshev mimuli' hints that Balak wanted to sit as the sandek and cut off the orlah of Amon and Moav, Tammuz and Av, beneath which Moshiach lies.
A bochur's especially strong yetzer hara is a sign that a great soul lies under his orlah, waiting to be revealed.
Each part of Eretz Yisrael holds a part of the Torah, so Osniel ben Kenaz's restoration of the forgotten halachos and his conquest of Kiryas Sefer were one and the same.
The souls of the last generations, 'bnei shomemah', are Tammuz-and-Av souls who struggle more and face greater trials, and so can achieve more than earlier tzaddikim.

Aharon's life was the Beis Hamikdash: his 123 years correspond to the Mishkan's thirty, twenty and ten amos, from the outer view to the Kodesh Hakodashim, so his passing on Rosh Chodesh Av is the root of Tisha B'Av.
Joining two parshiyos on one Shabbos is itself a tikkun for baseless hatred, which is why it happens only at the times of geulah or of repairing the churban.
Since all souls form one rope from top to bottom, a weakening of simple Jews' emunah can pull down the chassid's chassidus, and the reverse is equally true.
Kamtza and Bar Kamtza could have saved Yerushalayim with a handshake and a l'chaim, because two individuals making peace can tip a whole city.
The kingship of Yehuda and Moshiach came through Yehuda's refinement in not reclaiming his pledge from Tamar, not through his piety alone.
Av corresponds to Shimon, the tribe of 'hearing'; when Aharon passed, the 'hearing', the bond of togetherness, went into galus to the Kenaani.
Every Nisan since Creation is not the original but an offshoot of the Rosh Chodesh Nisan on which Adam was created, the Nisan meant to bring the world into an everlasting Shabbos.
Just as a soul can return as a gilgul or enter another as an ibbur, a time can be 'reincarnated': the original Nisan was brought down again into the Nisan of Yetzias Mitzrayim and of the Mishkan.
An unexpectedly elevated Shabbos, felt after the mikveh, can be an ibbur: the soul of a tzaddik connected to a mitzvah one did has entered him for a while to help.
Kareis applies to only two positive mitzvos, milah and korban Pesach, because both belong to Avraham Avinu and both are the covenant binding a Jew to Hashem.

Lechem equals three times the Name Havaya (78), and matzah is that lechem with the Name spelled out in full (three times 45, the value of Adam), so eating matzah makes a person the 'Adam' of 'na'aseh adam'.
Since Nisan is the new year for kings, when Hashem appoints new heavenly ministers and kings, the time calls for Klal Yisrael to proclaim Hashem alone as King.
The Rav reads the doctors' white coats and the kohanim's white garments as unwitting and commanded ways of drawing down chessed, the same chessed that made the manna and an infant's milk white.

Esav's territory has a counterpart in time: the Three Weeks are Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni, the highest Shabbosos of the year, hidden because they are still Esav's province; that is why simcha may not be brought into them.
Because blessing means increase and Shabbos carries tosefes beyond its borders, Shabbos alone can cross Esav's boundary; this is why Shabbos Chazon already shows the coming consolation.

Moshe's private part of the Torah, Sefer Devarim, corresponds to his conquest of Sichon and Og: as Osniel ben Kenaz recovered halachos by conquering Kiryas Sefer, each conquest of land reveals hidden Torah.

Yerushalayim is a permanent shemittah: no one owns it, it was never divided among the tribes, and in the seventh year it extends over the whole land, a model of the future when all Eretz Yisroel becomes Yerushalayim.

Eliyahu answered Rabbah bar Avuha with Rabbi Shimon's view rather than saying he was not a kohen, because he already lives in the days of Moshiach, when all Jews are kohanim and the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon.
The three who said 'eicha', read together on Shabbos Chazon, are the shoshvinin of a wedding, making Shabbos Chazon an aufruf before the great wedding in Yerushalayim.
The Rav reads the destruction as only apparent: the kedushah of the Mikdash never left, and Tisha B'Av itself was meant to be a great Yom Tov.
Davening together with the chazzan is not a private act but the tefillah of the many as one, and this is the tefillah the Arizal spoke of for the last generation.
The quiet davening of Tisha B'Av may serve to show heaven what Tisha B'Av looks like when Jews do not daven aloud, so that it should no longer be a Tisha B'Av the next year.
What should be stressed as 'the main thing' depends on what has weakened: learning when learning is weak, davening when davening is weak.

The Rav reads the difference between the two verses as two scenarios of the geulah: an early coming judged by the measure of Torah, and a delayed coming, after 'he comes, he comes' with nothing happening, judged by emunah alone.

Chavakuk's essence lies in his name, given with the words 'you will embrace a son': his message is embracing and holding on, and the emunah of 'a tzaddik lives by his emunah' is what the Jews hold on to through disappointments.

Darkness is not essentially dark: it is light too great to be received, as one is blinded by looking at the sun; this is why 'creating' is said of darkness, a higher level than 'forming' said of light.

The joy of Rabbi Shimon's day of passing comes from his power to reveal the hidden through the revealed; the Arizal taught no revealed Torah, so the joy hidden in the Nine Days of his passing is not yet fit to be revealed.
When learning has taste, that is the revelation of Rabbi Shimon; when it has none, one is like learning the Arizal's words, and one must still know that it is good.
The Rav reads 'I believe with complete faith' as also believing that one's own emunah is whole, even when questions trouble a person.
The Rav turns the war in Iraq into a scale for mitzvos: a blatt Gemara is a 'MOAB' bomb, a blatt Gemara with Tosafos is a missile that does not miss, and Amen yehei shmei rabba is a Patriot missile.
Since prophecy ended for individuals but not for Klal Yisrael as a whole, a minhag that all Jews take on is a prophecy from Hashem, fitted to the tikkunim that particular time needs.
The reading of the Nesi'im in Nissan is a weapon against Yishmael, whose twelve Nesi'im are subdued by the Nesi'im of Yisrael; without them Yishmael would have destroyed the Jews.

Through Reb Levi Yitzchak, the Rav shows that women scrubbing and kashering for Pesach are, without knowing it, destroying the yetzer hara, and every piece of chametz scrubbed off may be a whole enemy division.

Rashi's explanation that Og came while Avraham was baking matzos shows that the war against the four kings was on Pesach, linking the four kingdoms of galus to the four elements through which chametz is destroyed.
The worst chametz is atzvus; the Rav ties being an 'adam' on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, when Adam was created, to overcoming Yishmael, the 'pere adam'.
The holy words Bilaam spoke did not truly come out of his own mouth: Hashem set a foreign thing in it as a barrier, and the words came out from that.
Rashi and the Targum read 'shesum ha'ayin' at opposite extremes, one as a blinded eye and one as sharp sight, and the Ba'al Shem Tov shows how both are true of Bilaam.
According to the Ba'al Shem Tov, Bilaam's blind eye was Hashem's doing, so that he could not cause harm with it.
The Rav presents the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Ohr HaChaim as holding two parts of Moshiach's soul, the nefesh and the ruach, so that their meeting would have revealed Moshiach.
Because in the world of tikkun everything that lost its virtue regains it, the Seventeenth of Tammuz, the day of the first luchos, carries a hidden power for the sprouting of the redemption.
Reading 'evyon' as one who longs for what he lacks turns the passuk about the poor into a description of Moshiach longing for Klal Yisrael.
The Rav explains that Chazal's promise that one congregation's teshuvah would bring Moshiach has not yet come true because each generation is asked for a different level of teshuvah.
The 'hard heart' the passuk warns against is read as indifference to Moshiach's pain; a soft heart joins in his longing to come.

The Rav reads the history of Nisan as successive, ever more localized attempts at the perfect world of creation: the whole world with Adam, one nation at Yetzias Mitzrayim, one place in the Mishkan, until the fourth Nisan restores it on the large scale.

The seven days in which the Mishkan was built and taken apart mirror Hashem's own repeated attempts in Nisan, teaching that a disappointment in one's relationship with Hashem is a reason to get up and try again.

Chesed must be harnessed: the Jewish lunar calendar of chesed is aligned with the solar year of din, while the Arabs' purely lunar year lets their festival drift through the seasons, and the gentiles use the sun alone.

Matzah equals three times Mah (45) while bread equals three times Havaya (26), showing that matzah belongs to the world of Mah, a world one can only ask about; this is why the Seder opens with Mah Nishtanah.

Bread needs time to rise and so takes up space, while matzah is allowed no time and does not rise, so it stands above the two dimensions that define this world, the same 'when and where' on which witnesses are examined.
Kares for chametz is the opposite of the kesher, the bond with Hashem, that Pesach creates as the beginning of the year's festivals, which is why only one with a bris may eat the korban Pesach.

The 'deception' of the prophets was deliberate kindness: by instituting terumah and maaser outside Eretz Yisrael they made Jews feel Moshiach was near, keeping alive a hope that a revealed long exile would have crushed.
The very fact that Jews still sing Ani Maamin and await Moshiach after two thousand years shows their bond with Hashem, and is itself the sign that they must be redeemed.
Yerushalayim is read as 'yirah' and 'shalom' together, paralleling Shabbos: Friday night is the sweetness of fear of Heaven, Shabbos day is love and unity.
In these days the only valid 'passport' into Heaven is weeping and mourning, because Heaven itself is now in mourning; joy, normally the key, does not admit one now.

Because Hashem creates the world anew each moment, the burning of the Beis HaMikdash was a new fire every moment; so R' Yochanan can hold 'isho mishum chitzav' and still date the main burning to the tenth of Av.
The fire with which Hashem will rebuild Zion is the warmth of Jewish tefillos and tears, and it extinguishes the fire of sin that burned it.
Moshe's 515 prayers were in truth accepted, lacking only one more prayer, which Klal Yisrael must complete over the generations so that Moshe can enter the land with Moshiach.
What looked like rejection, the shrinking and then empty envelope, was in fact the Rebbe's way of bringing the disciple to the place where he had a task.
A single shehakol and borei nefashos said with kavanah at the edge of life brought a tikkun to souls that had waited for hundreds of years.
The mark of a talmid of Rebbe Reb Elimelech is that even when thirst makes a man like an animal, he stops to make a bracha with deveikus.
The particular tree, the particular water and the particular bread a person meets are each part of his shlichus, even when he thinks he is simply going his own way.
Shlomo conquered the world's hearts through wisdom and fear of Heaven alone; even the sword for the judgment of the two women had to be fetched, because none was at hand.
The haftorah's claim that Shlomo completed all he desired is possible only because his reign was a taste of the days of Moshiach, raised above the limits of time.
Since time and soul correspond, Yirmiyahu being a gilgul of Shlomo means Tisha B'Av is a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres.
In an ordinary year the one who reads the maftir of Pinchas reads about Shemini Atzeres and then at once says Divrei Yirmiyahu, so that Yirmiyahu himself studies Shemini Atzeres again.
The 'Shlomo' of Moshiach's day is the seudah hamafsekes of a Shabbos erev Tisha B'Av, eaten like Shlomo's feast 'in his time', when he was still king.
The laughter of Moshiach's time is that the great tzaddikim could not bring him, while the small, lowly last generations will.
Tisha B'Av is the one moed not listed among the yomim tovim, like a bochur who could have been a yom tov but fell, and can still return.
Rosh Chodesh Nissan recurs in history as a series of new beginnings: the creation of man, the Exodus and the setting up of the Mishkan, with a fourth still awaited.
Hashem's repeated 'attempts' at creation, like the Rosh Chodesh offering for diminishing the moon, are meant as a model for a Jew who fails and must begin again.
Na'aseh adam is renewed each Nissan: when all creation rejuvenates, a person who does not renew himself has excluded himself from creation.
Being an Adam does not mean erasing the animal traits of one's mazal, but ruling over them and raising them for avodas Hashem, like rising like a lion in the morning.
The kares for chametz, unlike the lesser punishments on Shavuos and Sukkos, shows that Pesach is the bond itself between Hashem and Klal Yisroel, so its opposite is being cut off.
The first failure, the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, is undone on Pesach: chametz is the Tree of Knowledge, and matzah, the food of emunah, is the Tree of Life that Hashem intended from the start.
The Rav notes the Rambam's precise wording: attributing troubles to chance is not called wickedness but cruelty, because it brings further troubles on the people.
This week's passuk 'a people heard the voice of G-d speaking from the fire' is read as Hashem speaking to the camp now through its fire, since every passuk applies to every person at every time.

Fire is the one damager that makes no distinction, consuming everything; therefore one who makes havdalah again and again is protected from fire measure for measure, which explains the segulah of relighting the havdalah candle.

The torch for havdalah distinguishes between Jews: the plain Jew sees only gross differences, like kosher shechitah, by a small candle, while the refined Jew needs a torch to see the fine print of the siddur.
Jerusalem was destroyed for keeping to the letter of the law because Jerusalem demands going beyond it; a fire, which does not distinguish, came on those who did not distinguish.
Yerushalayim is yirah and shalem: wherever there is yiras shamayim there is Jerusalem, so each Jewish heart holds a piece of the Mikdash to rebuild.
On the day the enemies ran to defile the sifrei Torah, the bochurim in the camp ran to save the sifrei Torah and tefillin, and the Rav hopes this is remembered favorably in Heaven.
The 'yerach ben yomo' of Masei, a trop found nowhere else, serves the 'karnei parah' of the first Shabbos of Av: the freshness of Nissan serves and repairs the division of Av.
A cow's horn is unfit for a shofar because its layers make it 'many shofars'; the shofar stands for unity and ingathering, while the layered horn mirrors the baseless hatred that caused the exile.

Because Bilaam, Moav and Midian tried to spoil Hashem's ever-fresh love for Israel, measure for measure their impurity is always 'ben yomo', which is why Midian's vessels needed kashering even when not used that day.

Yaakov's gid hanasheh, injured on Tisha B'Av according to sforim, stands for forgotten souls; Shabbos heals it, as Yaakov came 'shalem' to Shechem on Shabbos, which is why Tisha B'Av falling on Shabbos is a sign of healing.
Dinah's captivity in Shechem was not merely a punishment but Hashem's plan: she was born to redeem the spark of Moshiach ben Yosef hidden there, which came out through Osnas.
When Moshiach comes, Jews will long for the exile and even the nations will understand the greatness Israel had in exile.

The season itself has a bris: the Three Weeks cut off like milah, and the week from Tisha b'Av to the fifteenth of Av is its periah, so the joy of the fifteenth of Av is like the celebration when the mohel finishes.
The descendants of Keturah have milah but not periah because their bodies come from the three impure kelipos and have no part in nogah; periah, which elevates, belongs only to Yisrael.

The olah, burnt entirely, is the service of the nations, which can only renounce; the shelamim, whose meat is eaten as if on the altar, is the service of Yisrael, who can turn eating itself into avodah.

Orlah and neta revai follow the same pattern as milah and periah: three years of fruit are cut off entirely, and the fourth year's fruit is elevated in Yerushalayim, which is also where the Gemara learns brachos on food.

Metzitzah draws blood from the distant places of the body; so too after the fifteenth of Av even the bodily powers, far from Hashem, are drawn close to Him, as a preparation for crowning Him on Rosh Hashanah.
Tov v'hameitiv may only be said when another shares the good; this is why the reason of tov v'hameitiv belongs to the fifteenth of Av, the day that repairs sinas chinam.
A bachur who comes late to davening affects the angels above, since their kedushah in unison depends on Jews below saying it together.
Matzah equals three times the filled-out Name of Hashem (45), and geulah also equals 45, so matzah is three times geulah and carries the very Names with which Hashem redeemed the Jews from Mitzrayim.

Since it was the holy Names and not the flour and water that took the Jews out of Mitzrayim, the matzah eaten today is the identical matzah, worth more than an ancient piece an archaeologist might dig up.
Yaakov taking the blessings on the night of Pesach, when the treasuries of dew open, may be a hint to the custom of 'stealing' the afikoman at the Seder.
The Haggadah keeps multiplying the count of the plagues because saying them activates them: the more plagues counted, the more blows to the enemy and the more healing for the Jews.
Tashbisu equals the gematria of Shema Yisrael, and Vaizasa, the tenth son of Haman, equals Moshiach ben David, so destroying all ten parts of the chametz prepares the way for Moshiach.
Tu b'Av has no place in the atbash calendar sign because a sign can only be made for something that has already happened, while Tu b'Av is a festival of what will be.
Like a child who gives six excuses, the Gemara's very listing of six reasons, none sufficient alone, reveals that the true reason for Tu b'Av is still unknown.
The slain of Beitar who did not decay show that the hope for Moshiach, even when attached to a false Moshiach, is a living force, and a living thing does not decay.
The borrowed white garments of Tu b'Av hint that a Jew may borrow now from the good person he will become.
The pointing finger of the future dance of the tzaddikim conveys what words cannot: the depth of a Jewish heart that keeps hoping after so many disappointments.
The Shulchan Aruch's calendar sign leaves out the seventh day of Pesach because the festival it fixes, the Fifteenth of Av, celebrates an event that has not yet happened.
A holy event shines before it happens: as Avraham ate matzos before the Exodus, the six joys of the Fifteenth of Av were glimmers of the future redemption.
Bnos Tzelofchad grasped what Moshe Rabbeinu did not, because the share in the land means a share in Olam Haba, which is grasped with the heart rather than the intellect.
Yirmiyahu's curse on his birthday was a statement of fact, since he was born on Tisha B'Av; yet that same day is the birthday of Moshiach, so Yirmiyahu will one day bless it.
Yirmiyahu writing Eichah is Shlomo, the author of Shir HaShirim, in black garments, and 'renew our days as of old' is his plea to become Shlomo again.
When Shlomo judged the two women no sword was found among his soldiers, a sign that he ruled the world through Torah and peace, not weapons.

Jews themselves are festivals: a talmid chacham is Shabbos, who gives to the weekday Jews rather than receiving from them, and a gifted person who wastes his life is 'Reb Tisha B'Av', a mo'ed lying in the grave.
Emunah is a hereditary instinct in a Jew, just as a beaver isolated from birth still builds a dam and a spider spins its mother's web; Avraham Avinu introduced a new species into creation.
A Jew who denies Hashem is not lacking emunah but has a sick emunah, like a man who ate sawdust and lost his hunger; aveiros and forbidden food clog the heart.
Unlike faiths founded on one charismatic individual, the Torah rests on an event experienced by millions at once, which can no more be faked than the existence of George Washington or Julius Caesar.
Rashi's question is answered by the Rambam's principle: milah is kept only because Moshe Rabbeinu told it, so the first mitzvah received through Moshe, HaChodesh hazeh lachem, is truly the first.
The nation's first mitzvah is by its very character renewal: a new moon out of a dark sky, a new nation out of dark Mitzrayim, and so the nation carries the message that one can always renew oneself.
Pesach is the only moed with kares because its essence is kesher, a new bond with Hashem; the one who misses it is cut off.
The renewal of nature in Nisan is an impact of the nation's renewal in that month, which enters even into physical nature.

The 'shidduch' of Chamishah Asar b'Av is between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and the tenaim one must look over before the match are the passuk of parshas Eikev: to fear Hashem, walk in His ways and love Him.
Since teshuvah begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av and ends on Yom Kippur, and the end is embedded in the beginning, the good choice a Jew has on Yom Kippur is already present on Chamishah Asar b'Av.
Yerushalayim is 'yirah shleimah': holy fear of Hashem flows from wholeness, unlike ordinary fear, which comes from a person's lack, as one fears a lion because he lacks its strength.

Tisha b'Av contains two opposites, the churban and the gain that our avodah became more precious; the gain cannot be celebrated on Tisha b'Av itself, so Chamishah Asar b'Av, when the mourning ends, was set as its yom tov.

Because 'every generation in whose days the Beis Hamikdash is not rebuilt' suffers a new churban, each year's avodah is more precious than the last, which is why the Gemara says to add in learning from Chamishah Asar b'Av.
The Rav reads the moon's name yareach as coming from rei'ach, smell: the moon is malchus and yiras shamayim, and yiras shamayim is perceived through smell, as said of Moshiach.

He explains the Sfas Emes's 'I do not smell techeiles' through this: one might prove scientifically that a dye is techeiles, but it lacks the root of yiras shamayim from the upper moon, and that is why there will be no techeiles until Moshiach.

The dor hamidbar could see a nearly full physical moon on the fourteenth and still doubt, because since the meraglim the moon one 'smells', middas malchus, was hidden from them; on Tu b'Av they sensed it again.

The upper sun and lower sun resolve both the Ramchal's question on the daily 'opening of the gates of the east' and, in the Divrei Yoel, the objection that the senses contradict Rabbeinu Tam's 72 minutes.

The moon is hidden on Rosh Hashanah because malchus must be aroused from below, through the shofar and the acceptance of malchus shamayim; Tu b'Av, as the start of that awakening, is when the moon was revealed to the dor hamidbar.
Since a name expresses the soul, and the soul of one who learns lishmah becomes one with the Torah, the very names of the chachamim in the baraisa are Torah.
Like meat placed in the middle of a fire that itself becomes fire, a talmid chacham's soul becomes Torah itself.
The announcement of dawn in the Beis Hamikdash mentioned Chevron in order to recall the Avos, showing that merely mentioning a holy name draws down salvation.
'Mishnah' means doubling: a tzaddik's words to a person carry a second address to Hashem, which is why David's blessings to Naval were not flattery.
The same Torah takes on the color of each receiver's middah, like water poured into glasses of different colors.
Refinement brings sensitivity: wine, used for Kiddush and likened to Olam Haba, is affected even by a goy's touch, and Olam Haba is so delicate that even a glance affects it.
Sukkos is the climax of the Yomim Tovim, yet Pesach, like an embryo, is the beginning, and the beginning is the main thing.
The kareis attached only to Pesach shows that Pesach is the bond with Hashem; its opposite, the kesher, is like a ring of kiddushin between a Jew and the Ribono shel Olam.
Matzah is not a mitzvah one does but one ingests, so its emunah becomes part of one's bones; for a Jew emunah is not information but part of him, in his genes.
Every animal eats food that matches its middah, a lion red meat for gevurah and a sheep white kernels for chesed, while man, who includes everything, eats bread, which includes all ten.
Lechem, 78, is three times Hashem's Name; matzah, 135, is three times its filled-out form of 45, so the bread is only a capsule while matzah holds the Name in its fullness.
Because the holy names of Yetzias Mitzrayim are in our matzah just as in theirs, one can say 'Ha lachma anya', this is the bread they ate, with a clear conscience.

The Oral Torah is 'written' on the heart and mouth of the Jew who learns properly, a private code between Hashem and His people; therefore even when its words are available in translation, it is not truly Oral Torah for the nations.
'From Sinai' means 'because of Sinai': as Hashem chose the lowest mountain, Moshe reasoned that he, who saw himself as the lowest man, was the one obligated to receive the Torah.

The prophets speak for Hashem, the chassan, so they could not praise Him with what was not seen; the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah speak for Knesses Yisroel, the kallah, who sees the survival of the lamb among the wolves as His might, and so they restored the praise.
The Mishnah says Moshe 'received' rather than that Hashem 'gave over', because no human can take over the infinite Torah entirely; but Moshe did give all of it over to Yehoshua.
The last words of the Torah allude to the broken luchos, and the last generations before Moshiach are those broken luchos; yet broken luchos were also kept in the aron.
Today's 'might and awe' of Hashem is the Jew who still manages to say words of tefillah and Torah while the wolves of the yetzer hara tear at his mouth.

The three directives of the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah answer three ways the Torah weakens over the generations: deliberation in judgment for lost knowledge and siyata diShmaya, many students for fewer learners, and a fence for weakened yiras Shamayim.
The meraglim lacked Moshe Rabbeinu's power because, as Devarim shows, the people asked for the mission, so the spies were really the agents of a people that included men with flawed intentions.

The travel that begins in Tammuz and Av, the months of the meraglim's journey, is arranged by Hashem as a repair of their failed mission, and had Jews traveled with this awareness Moshiach might already have come.
The angel's seemingly disrespectful 'why do you ask my name' was not sarcasm but his mission speaking: the yetzer hara's task is to make people stop asking what their mission is.

The word emes, which closes Shema but is not written in the Torah's parsha, reflects the generation of the heels before Moshiach, when truth is absent; precisely because it is hidden it must be cried out.
The sin of the meraglim was politics: as nesiim they knew that entering Eretz Yisroel would bring new leaders, and the generation before Moshiach faces the same test of partisan disputes.
A tzaddik read 'yoshvei kranos' as those who sit in the beis medrash with horns, learning but goring others so they feel unwelcome.
The two parshiyos written out of place, Pesach Sheni and Vayehi binsoa, are themselves the 'letters' of souls in exile, and their displacement in the Torah is their tikkun.
Clothing is a garment of malchus shamayim, so stripping down in the country is the very symbol of throwing off the yoke of Heaven.

The order of the camps' travel maps onto the months: Gershon and Merari are the exiled souls, Reuven and Shimon, unblessed by Yaakov, are Tamuz and Av, and Gad, Eliyahu's tribe, brings the consolation.
Inserting a yud into the spies' 'anavim' removes the Satan's name hidden in it, which is the work of a Jew who brings holiness into Tamuz and Av.
The spies' grapes, the instrument of their sin, became wine for the nesachim, showing that the days of their failure are meant to become the tikkun.
Tefillah was the one thing that separated Kalev and Yehoshua from the other spies, so the defense in these days is to pray not to stumble.
The days of preparation before Pesach are themselves days of joy, like the kohanim's seven days of miluim before they began the avodah in the Mishkan.
Maariv was only a reshus not because it is lesser, but because, as the tefillah of Yaakov, it belongs to a higher world that not everyone is ready for.
Tikkun Chatzos is the tefillah of Dovid HaMelech, and Melaveh Malkah, the fourth seudah, corresponds to it as the seudah of Dovid.
Morning is called tzafra after the birds and night ramsha after the creeping creatures that sing then, while a Jew sings both by day and by night.
Matzah equals three times 45, the filled-out Name of Hashem that equals adam, so it holds a deeper holiness than ordinary bread, which is three times 26.
'Ha lachma anya' is literally true: the geulah inside the matzah is identical to what our forefathers ate, and only the outer envelope of flour and water is different.
The Rav reads Chazal's parting wish that no talmid 'spoil his dish in public' as a call to every ben Torah to guard against chillul Hashem when he goes out among strangers.
He explains Devorah's name as a bee, which goes around buzzing 'bin, bin' ('I am, I am'), a picture of one who thinks himself great.
Group pride, whether nation, team, chassidus or beis medrash, is one kelipah with many names, and a bachur should not display it among others.
Since the Beis Hamikdash is almost complete, what is missing today is like a thumbtack, and holding back a cutting joke or a look in the street supplies it.
Chizuk is like vitamin C, which the body does not store, so yesterday's chizuk is gone and must be taken again today.
A bachur who has no money to give maaser can give maaser of his time to help another.
The summer camp season, which falls in the days the meraglim went out, is a chance to repair their failed mission by being faithful shluchim.
Korach's dispute was split within itself because each side sought itself; only when all seek Hashem's honor are they bound together, even in disagreement.
The Mishnah ends one perek with 'all needs of milah are done on Shabbos' and opens the next by continuing it, to teach that hilchos milah are themselves hilchos Shabbos.
Avraham delayed his milah so it could fall on Yom Kippur, the root of Shabbos, because milah must be bound up with Shabbos.
A loud voice in tefillah is not for Hashem to hear but to awaken the one davening; this answers the Pri Megadim's question.
Iyov was punished for his silence even though shouting would not have helped, because one who truly feels the pain cries out regardless.

Quoting Rabbi Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, the Rav says the Ba'al Shem Tov did not hang his teaching about davening on the teivah pasuk at random: the world is a flood of desires, and tefilah is the ark that saves from it.

Amalek attaches itself to the weak souls of Dan at the edge of the camp, which hint at the lowest souls of the last generations; the defense against him is 'bo atah el hateivah', entering into tefilah.
Learning has many motives, recognition among them, while long davening only brings ridicule; this is exactly what the Gemara means when it applies 'kerum zulus' to tefilah.
Those who mock loud davening shout at Ne'ilah because they know it is a serious moment; the Rav wants every tefilah to be a Ne'ilah.
The sealed ring of Bilgah is like a heart bypass: their avodah shebalev was blocked, so they had to receive from other kohanim.
Leaving right after Shemoneh Esrei is like paying for a watch and walking out without it: the shefa comes down after Shemoneh Esrei, and one must stay to take it home.
Ahavas chaverim, 'shevet achim gam yachad', is the cure for the forces of Shiva Asar b'Tammuz and the breaking of the luchos.

The four ways of destroying chametz mirror the four elements that come from the four letters of Hashem's Name: scattering to the wind, throwing into the sea, burning, and bitul, which makes it like the dust of the earth.
Avraham Avinu's dust that became weapons against the four kings was itself bitul chametz, nullifying the four kingdoms, and he did it on Pesach.

The authority of the nations is captured malchus of the Jewish people, passed from Bavel to Madai, Yavan and Rome, and it must be returned to Moshiach; Yishmael is not counted because his rule is his own.
The same four klipos appear as the four layers at a bris, the four marks of tzara'as and the four years of orlah; the fourth, Edom, is raised rather than cut off, since it holds kedushah.
Chametz, fit to eat, is Edom, from whom converts came, while se'or, unfit to eat, is Yishmael, from whom no good came.
Each of the four cups has two sides: the wine spilled at the makkos is a cup of poison for Mitzrayim, and the refilled cups are the Jews' cups of geulah.
Pinchas, who is Eliyahu, avenged the sale of Yosef only on Midian; the main sellers, the Yishmaelim, remain for him, which links the cup of Eliyahu to the reckoning with Yishmael.
Following Rashi, the Rav explains that in Modim d'Rabbanan we thank Hashem for the very ability to thank, and that thanking arouses heaven and opens the gates of more thanks.
Thanking Hashem for every detail is not only thanks; it is an exercise in emunah, training a person to see that nothing happens by chance.
The second rabbi at a seudas hodaah is required to show that hodaah has no end: after one chacham has finished listing reasons to thank, another still finds more.
Modim d'Rabbanan is assembled from the versions of many rabbanan, because with hodaah one person's words, even the chazzan's, can never suffice.
The korban todah's short eating time was meant to force its owner to invite more people, so that more would hear of the kindness.

The Rav resolves Tosafos' question on the Rashbam by distinguishing the open leaders of a miracle from its hidden cause: Moshe and Aharon led, but the righteous women's mesirus nefesh was the hidden heart of the redemption.
Leah's thanks was new in the world because it was a mother's thanks for a child, born of her devotion to building Klal Yisroel.
Emes, the last of Krias Shema's 248 words, matches the heel, so the generation of the heel before Moshiach is the one charged with emes.
The word emes is not written in the Torah's parsha of Shema; we add it ourselves, hinting that the last generation must itself supply the truth.
Without emes, divine service loses its life: remove the aleph of emes and only 'mes', death, remains.
Truth is by nature one, like the single correct time on a clock; a multitude of competing 'truths' is itself the sign of falsehood foretold for the end of days.
Treating one's chassidus like a sports team, to feel great through the group, is the pride the Steipler describes, and the very opposite of chassidus.
Different chassidic paths are like the twelve tribes with their twelve gates: legitimate differences of root, which must not become hatred.
A bad thought about a fellow Jew is worse than bad speech, because thought reaches higher worlds; by the same measure a good thought about him does more good than good speech.
The Rav reads kares and kashrus as opposites: just as eating chametz on Pesach cuts the bond with Hashem, eating matzah ties it, a level of connection no other Yom Tov's mitzvah reaches.

The spring that reawakens nature in Nisan is the earthly reflection of the joy in Heaven over the new bond with Klal Yisrael, the song of the Chassan and Kallah that Shlomo HaMelech put into Shir Hashirim.

Bread equals three times the Name of Hashem (78), while matzah equals three times its full spelling, 'Mah' (135): matzah draws from a holiness so high it can only be asked about, which is why the Seder begins with questions.
The matzah is the key of birth that Hashem keeps for Himself, and the Targum calls matzah 'patira', an opening, like 'peter rechem'.

Following the Ba'al HaTanya, the matzah's flour and water are only a capsule; inside is the same light of Yetzias Mitzrayim that the Jews ate in Mitzrayim, so the matzah is the original and not a copy.
The tal of 'my head is filled with dew' is the first three letters of the Name in full spelling (39), which descends to the final hei, Klal Yisrael, and that is the matzah.
Pharaoh's real target in 'tichbad ha'avodah' was not the bricks but the Shabbos gatherings where the Jews read their scrolls of redemption; heavy work was meant to cut off their hope.
'Beis avadim' means a house with a way of life: Egypt's culture itself was slavery, work without thinking, and the Exodus freed the Jewish mind from that way of thinking.
Pharaoh feared even the half-conscious sigh of an exhausted Jew at Minchah, since such a sigh pierces the heavens.
The same hard labor that made a European Jew's sigh precious makes an American Jew a sinner, because there it was forced and here it is chosen.
Labor-saving inventions do not bring rest, because the time they free is filled by new forms of the same klipah.
'Melech l'sadeh ne'evad': the person who thinks he rules his affairs is really their slave.
The Rosh Chodesh meal is the Jews' share in the korban Hashem asked for the diminished moon: like kohanim eating a korban, their seudah is a pleasing offering before Hashem.
Shaul's fury at Dovid's family feast came because the seudah of Rosh Chodesh belongs to the king; a Rosh Chodesh feast of Dovid looked to him like rebellion, a seudah of Moshiach.

The Yismach Moshe, who could eat soap water without noticing, does not refute the rule that man needs pleasure; he proves it, since no one enjoyed the world more than he did through Gemara and tefillah.
Hashem can forgive a person for the taavos he was created with, but one who brings in new ones has gone far beyond them, to the other side of the sea.
Even overindulging in a Jewish piece of kugel is kelipas nogah that can be elevated, but goyish pleasures cannot be, and that is the meaning of 'do not rejoice like the nations'.
Gan Eden and Gehinnom are one place: the same long davening is Gan Eden for one who is connected to it and Gehinnom for one who is not.
The seudah of Rosh Chodesh is itself a miracle like the survival of avodas Hashem: the moon that died rises again, like techiyas hameisim, and it is the meal of Dovid, king of Israel, who lives on.

Torah is a 'small that holds the many' even in a physical sense: the same printed Chumash or Gemara serves a five-year-old and the greatest gedolim, who need no other book because they see more in the same words.

Rabbi Akiva's teachings were beyond Moshe Rabbeinu not from Moshe's lack but because the tagim, the crowns attached to the letters, come from a higher world, as converts attached to Klal Yisroel can reach higher things.

Learning the parsha of the korbanos earns the reward of the large korban: 'zos toras hayoledes' is written by the rich woman's korban, not the poor one's, because through Torah anyone can reach the greatest level.

In the future, the nations' claim that they built roads for Yisroel will be shown false and true at once: they built for themselves, yet in truth everything they made existed only so that Jews could serve Hashem.

Normally aleph signals curse and beis blessing, but where Torah begins, with the aleph of 'Anochi', the aleph is even higher than the beis, as pepper's sharpness gives food more taste than sweetness alone.
The Mishnah lists 'rei'a' and 'ohev' without saying to whom, because Torah unites Hashem and the Jewish soul so fully that there is no separate address to name.
Loving a Jew does not divide one's love of Hashem, since one loves the Jew for his G-dly portion; therefore love of Hashem can be measured by love of Yisroel.

The Rav reads the halachic status of a pilegesh spiritually: unlike a wife, who merges with her husband, a pilegesh keeps her own identity, so Timna's holy longing passed through Amalek's line without ever becoming part of it.
Esther's seudah destroyed Haman by drawing him out of tumah to the edge of kedusha, which he could not enter, so that he was left with no source of life at all.
Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, a descendant of Haman, is the one who taught that when Adar enters one increases simcha, because his root lay in the simcha Haman drew from Esther's Pesach seudah.

The Rav connects the Haggadah's Bnei Brak to Haman's descendants: the talmidim who could not reach Krias Shema of Shacharis carried Zeresh's attempt to stop Mordechai's morning Shema, and the Tannaim chose Pesach to free them.
The Rambam's pairing of Shema Yisrael with 'va'achos Lotan Timna' becomes the story of Bnei Brak: the Tannaim lifted the children of the passuk Menashe mocked to the level of Shema.
The Rav reads 'malbishto anavah' precisely: true humility is too lofty for a physical person to own in essence, so Torah gives it to him as a garment he wears.
A person's possessions are an extension of his soul, so the holiness of one who learns lishmah spreads even to his animal, which is why Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey refused untithed food.

Torah is the eighth verse of Tehillim 19 after seven verses on nature, and the eighth corresponds to a world above the seven days of creation; Tehillim 119 goes through the alef-beis eight times for the same reason.
Through Sha'arei Orah the Rav links yovel, Binah, geulah, Yom Kippur, the shofar, milah and neder as names of one level above nature, so each of them can free a person from the 'nets' of this world.

The Ramban's distinction between 'by Hashem' and 'to Hashem' becomes a key: a shevuah binds a person through the G-dliness present in this world, while a neder ties him to Binah above it, which is why a neder helps where tefillah, which comes from malchus, cannot.

The custom of checking tzitzis each morning is explained not as a technical precaution but as preparation for the battle of tefillah: through their eight threads one connects to the eighth world before davening.

Through the Chasam Sofer, the Rav reads 'be warm at my hesped, for I will be standing there' to mean that the departed tzaddik puts the words into the speaker's mouth, so speaking about him is in a sense hearing him.

Every curse in Ki Savo can be turned to blessing by the Oral Torah, but the death of tzaddikim is not written at all; it exists only through the Oral Torah, so no further layer of Oral Torah can reverse it. The only remedy is that the tzaddik not truly be gone.

The difference between the bnei haneviim, who lost their prophecy when Eliyahu departed, and Elisha, who grew twice as great, is whether one carries on the tzaddik's Torah; the Rav brings this from the Satmar Rav's own sefer.
Because every night of Chanukah was fresh for the Satmar Rav like the first, the Rav sees meaning in his answering every night the Beis Yosef's question about the miracle of the first night.

Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai's last words about clearing the vessels were a deliberate ruling that tzaddikim impart tumah, and he knew no error was involved because Chizkiyahu, the greatest master of tumah and taharah, came to greet him.
The Rav presents the Satmar Rav, like Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai, as the true 'doresh l'Tzion': precisely because he loved Zion he could tolerate no stain on its redemption.

Like Rav Ketina mocking the necromancer, the Kosel ruling was meant so that people not be drawn after the Zionists; its greater benefit was to the many who still go but, remembering it, are not drawn.
Yerushalayim is in a constant state of shemitah, and the seventh year is not a new holiness but Yerushalayim overflowing onto all of Eretz Yisrael.
Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, is Shabbos and the tribes are the weekday Roshei Chodesh; so Eretz Yisrael was divided among the tribes, while Yerushalayim, belonging to the trunk, was not.
In shemitah every Jew becomes like a Levi or kohen without a field, a foretaste of the World to Come when all Jews will be kohanim.
Since shemitah itself is a tosefes on Yerushalayim, every tosefes in the Torah, even tosefes Shabbos, is learned from shemitah.
Rabbi Akiva, a descendant of converts who are an addition to Klal Yisrael, is the one who expounded the crowns added to the letters and who taught tosefes from shemitah.
A Jew who enters the sukkah after Yom Kippur is like a convicted man who flees to Eretz Yisrael, where the verdict is reopened and Hashem Himself judges with mercy.
Ki Savo, read before Rosh Hashanah, is a mussar on the 122 days of the past year that were not used, while Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu hint at the 122 days now beginning.
The Rav compares the descent of Hashem's attributes into human middos to water passing from invisible vapor to steam, water and ice: the same substance, more physical the further it comes down.
A mother clutching her baby on the stairs shows gevurah within chesed: her fear is aroused by her love.
According to the Rav, Yishmael's milah without a bris is an empty milah, which is why it earned him Eretz Yisroel only while the land was empty of Jews.
The sa'ir to Azazel carries Israel's sins to Esav because a Jew's inner will is always to do Hashem's will; the sin belongs to the yetzer hara, Esav's angel.
Yishmael, the klipah of yesod, always pursues Yosef, the tzaddik of yesod; it was Yishmaelim who brought Yosef down to Mitzrayim, the ervas ha'aretz.
The Rav reads the world's attention on Eretz Yisroel as a screen of a heavenly din Torah, whose real front is a bochur in the street who turns his eyes away.

The Rav reads the whole layout of parshas Re'eh as a map of a Jew's path: holy eating that binds to Hashem, the fall through forbidden food that leaves one open to the meisis, and the closing aser te'aser as the teshuvah of one who breaks back through, which is greater than the tzaddik who never fell.

He explains the halacha of a bas Levi who remarried on one witness through feeling: a wife whose husband lives would sense it, so her mistake shows she lacks the sense of connection a daughter of Levi must have, the tribe that felt its bond with Hashem at the egel.
He notes that 'hapa'am yilaveh ishi elai', the verse of Levi's naming, equals in gematria 've'atem hadveikim', the verse about those who did not fall to Baal Peor.
He explains that Shemini Atzeres is not called a chag because chag comes from machog, a circle, and Shemini Atzeres stands above the cycle of the festivals.

He answers the Tzlach's question on Rosh Chodesh by explaining that melacha is a curse from Adam's eating, so a day of brachah is not harmed by the time taken for a fourth aliyah; the women's brachah from not giving to the egel spreads to their husbands.

He connects women's merit of Rosh Chodesh to their sensitivity: Rosh Chodesh, which is not yet a full Yom Tov in this time, can only be felt with a heightened feeling, the same feeling with which they sensed at the egel that one cannot be cut off from the living G-d.

Shemitah is not a new state that appears every seven years; it is the permanent shemitah of Yerushalayim overflowing its banks for one year over all of Eretz Yisrael, so that the whole land becomes Yerushalayim and every Jew a kohen.

Because shemitah as a whole is tosefes, the law of adding to holy times is learned specifically from it, and by Rabbi Akiva, a descendant of converts who were themselves an 'addition' to Israel and who expounded the crowns added to the letters.

The aron taking no space was not counted as a miracle because in the Kodesh HaKodashim, where heaven meets earth, being above measure is simply heaven's nature; the same idea explains why the fiftieth year can count for two cycles.

At the end of every Shabbos and every shemitah there is a 'doubt in heaven' whether what follows will be a new first or the eighth, which is why Moshiach is expected then, why melave malka belongs to David, and why chassidic rebbes extended shalosh seudos past Shabbos.
'Magen David' is said only in the haftarah blessings after maftir, the eighth aliyah, because David's true greatness, beyond the Avos, belongs to the eighth world and cannot yet be grasped.

The king, Yerushalayim and Yom Kippur are the heart of soul, place and time; at Hakhel in the eighth year the king stands in Yerushalayim at the turn of the year, and this is why the Rambam describes Hakhel as hearing the Torah as at Sinai.
The Rav reads 'Let there be light' as the creation of liberty, so that each twenty-fifth of Elul is a renewal of the gift of freedom to the world.
He describes the whole world as a big prison: people think they are free, but whoever must obey his yetzer hara has no free choice.

Serving Hashem from the darkness of galus and chutz la'aretz, especially in the low generations before Moshiach, is an avodah that even the generation of Moshe Rabbeinu did not have, and even great tzaddikim in Eretz Yisrael cannot achieve such a cry from the depths.

Because malchus is the lowest level, Rosh Hashana, the day of malchus, is about bringing the kingship of Heaven down to the lowest place a Jew is in; this may be why Rosh Hashana has no aliyah l'regel to Yerushalayim.
Yosef left prison on Rosh Hashana to become ruler: whoever accepts the kingship of Heaven even in prison is himself the king and the free man.
The fourfold Torah of pshat, remez, drush and sod is mirrored in every Jew: what people see is only his pshat, while his sod, the trait that makes him dear to Hashem, stays hidden.
The Gemara counts the talmidim as 12,000 pairs to show where the flaw lay: in each pair the lesser chavrusa honored the greater, but the greater did not honor the lesser.
The dying stopped in the week of Hod because Hod, yielding, is exactly the middah that teaches a greater person to respect a lesser one.
The date of Pesach Sheini, which commemorates nothing from Yetzias Mitzrayim, has no explanation on purpose: it is a sod, like the hidden worth of the temei'im it was given to.
The calendar sign 'peleg', that Lag BaOmer falls on Purim's weekday, reveals that both days celebrate the hidden worth of the lowest Jews.
Unlike the Torah of other Tannaim and poskim, which speaks to those who can learn it, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's revelation of sod speaks to the simplest Jew, telling him he too carries a secret.
The final date of the Geulah is the greatest sod, since it comes even for complete reshaim by virtue of the sod each of them carries.
Ten Jews joined as a tzibbur are not ten individuals but a new entity with a collective soul, which is why a tzibbur can say Kedushah and read the Torah, something no single tzaddik can do.
The bond that makes a zimun is created by eating together: three who ate separately and then meet cannot bench with a zimun.
'Yachdav' means bound, not merely together: as with shaatnez, wool and linen lying loosely one on the other are not 'yachdav'.

Not believing in techiyas hameisim is not punished by losing it but is a symptom of having no share in it; likewise Ammon and Moav's not bringing bread and water was a sign that they have no connection to Klal Yisrael.
Each exile struck in another dimension: Bavel in breadth, Yavan in height against the Shechinah (the fifteen amos), and Edom also in time, an exile without an end (the hundred and fifty days).

The thirty letters of a line in a Sefer Torah are learned from the korban Pesach and not from Noach's families leaving the teivah, because there the group was breaking up while at the Pesach it was gathering into one chaburah.
The Rav explains the pull of texting psychologically: a person's built-in shame and self-restraint work face to face, and the screen removes them, so jokes flow that he would never say aloud.
Reading the opening of Tehillim, the Rav says 'moshav leitzim' and 'Toras Hashem cheftzo' are two sides of a divide: a person must stand on one side, he cannot have both.

From the Rashbam on one who shuts his eyes while passing women at the river, the Rav derives that need is what turns a dangerous road into a legitimate test: with no other way, a person becomes a ba'al bechirah; without need, closing his eyes does not save him from being a rasha.

The Rav asks why the yud of 'yarbeh', and not another letter, complained about Shlomo HaMelech, and answers that the small yud is the letter of bitul: even if Shlomo was right, one must submit to the Torah.

A heter given for business, the Rav says, is like chametz, kosher all year and forbidden at its time: the phone is permitted only during the hours it is needed, and the rule that what was permitted for a need is permitted without need does not apply.
The Rav sees the new tests of this generation as a sign that it is being prepared for Moshiach and for the greatest greatness.
The Sefirah mourning ends on Lag BaOmer because hod shebehod is the Kodesh HaKodashim and Rashbi is its Kohen Gadol after the churban, and a Kohen Gadol is untouched by mourning.

Rashbi's revealing of the hidden Torah is the revealing of the hidden point in every Jew, since each soul corresponds to a letter of the Sefer Torah; this is the cure for the sin of Rabbi Akiva's students.
The students' failure was not a lack of false modesty, since one may truly know more than his chavrusa; what they missed is the unseen point in which the other is superior.

The makom ha'aron was not counted among the miracles of the Beis HaMikdash because it was permanent; like the different laws of the sea or of Heaven, the Kodesh HaKodashim simply has laws above time and space.
The four seasons in which sedras are combined are exactly the times connected to redemption and to the breach of achdus, including Sefirah, when Rabbi Akiva's students fell.
Lag BaOmer falls on Purim's day of the week because both are hod, days that bring out the hidden worth of every Jew even when he is accused.
Counting the 24 letters of Baruch Shem and then the letters of Shema, the 33rd letter is the first yud of Hashem's name, the point that contains the other letters: Lag BaOmer is that point.
Following the catalog, the Rav frames bringing a lost soul back to Hashem as a form of returning a lost object to its Owner.
He applies the rebuke over the one who strayed and was not brought back to those responsible for guiding Jewish souls.
The Rav presents the refusal to say 'it cannot be' as something particular to Jews.

Amalek's war 'from generation to generation' means his tactics change with each generation; before Moshiach, like a losing army sensing the sword at its neck, he fights harder than ever to delay the end.
The Rav reads 'vehayah eikev tishma'un', as the seforim of the Besht's talmidim do, as joy for Hashem in ikvesa d'Meshicha: the emunah of Jews in the heel of the exile is itself a great simcha above.
Just as the Megillah was unnecessary before Purim but indispensable after it, because a new era of hester panim began, so Chassidus is the new necessity of the era that began with the Besht.

The seforim of the Besht's talmidim are like the sample chapters an author releases before his book: a preview of the Torah that will be learned when Moshiach comes, the hidden Torah Rashi describes on 'yishakeini'.
Malachi, the prophet who speaks to the last generation, opens not with rebuke like Yeshayahu but with 'I have loved you', showing how the generation before Moshiach must be addressed.
Where Chassidus took hold, in Poland, Galicia and Russia, haskalah had no success until Chassidus weakened; where it did not, haskalah caused great destruction.
The Torah opens with Bereishis rather than the mitzvah of the new moon because Bereishis alludes to the sun and to nature, and the world of nature was itself created for Yisroel.
Birchas HaChamah declares that the sun, the source of giving in nature, truly belongs to Yisroel, even while in exile Yisroel receives only the leftovers from the nations.
Rashi's reading of 'me'oros' as a curse means that luminaries serving to give light is itself a lack; their true role is for seasons, days and years, while the light should come from Hashem Himself.
Because a mitzvah done with a thing puts strength into it, Jews blessing the sun on the day that stands for Tammuz infuses the sun with Yisroel's power and is a sign that Esav's dominion will end.
The twenty-eight-year return of the sun to its starting point is also a call for a person to return to his own starting point, the upright state in which Hashem created him.

The hierarchy of the Sefer Torah, from letter to word to column to parshah, mirrors Klal Yisrael from individual to family to shevet to the Avos, and Eretz Yisrael is divided the same way, with Yerushalayim as the shared root above the shevatim.
Tiferes is like a niggun: not every combination of notes is music, as a cat walking on a piano shows; the harmony that blends opposites creates something new.

Sefirah is counted from both sides: Klal Yisrael, the kallah, counts from Chesed down, while Hashem, the chassan going out toward her, counts from Malchus up, and on that count Lag BaOmer is Tiferes sheb'Tiferes.

The combined sedras at the edges of Nisan and Tishrei, in Sefirah and in the Three Weeks are a repair for sinas chinam, breaking the barriers between groups of Jews whose Shabbosos are otherwise separate.
