The dispute over the most honored aliyah, shlishi or shishi, is an echo of the old strife between Yehuda and Yosef, and the Midrash of the Yam Suf, created on the third day, yielding to man, created on the sixth, shows that when Jews are in trouble seniority quarrels must give way.

A leap year needs no combined sedras because the extra month lets the lunar year catch up with the solar year, undoing the diminishing of the moon; the word 'haSheni' in Adar Sheni has the numerical value 365, matching the sun's days.

The Rav reads the naming of a parsha after Balak as a sign that his curse held the root of Moshiach, and the reading of Balak in the Three Weeks as showing that these days hide redemption within their curse.
The letters preceding those of 'anavim' hint at the power of evil, so 'the days of the first grapes' are days under its rule, yet the same words describe days in which fruit ripens.
Moshiach does not wait for all Jews to learn; he waits for the bnei Torah, the bearers of the mesorah, not to be idle.
The meraglim's sin and the jealousy over aliyos and honors in a group are one root, so overcoming that jealousy is the repair of the meraglim in these days.
Just as the top of a lulav is disqualified by a smaller flaw than the bottom, a person in a high position is more easily ruined, so not having to face such tests is itself a success.
The proof that a loud voice arouses kavanah is Ne'ilah, when in every beis medrash everyone davens aloud; the Kotzker's 'every Maariv is Kol Nidrei' teaches that this need not wait for Ne'ilah.

Eliyahu's forbidden offering outside on Har HaCarmel was itself the descent of the tzaddik: like a korban slaughtered outside, he reached the souls outside the camp of Israel, and that is why he then needed atonement and exile.

From Eliyahu's own standpoint the offering was not outside at all: Har HaCarmel will be inside the future Yerushalayim and the Beis HaMikdash will stand there, so he already stood in the Yerushalayim of the world of tikkun.

The dispute over Gechazi resolves in the future: a metzora cannot enter Yerushalayim, but when Yerushalayim spreads to Damascus, the seat of tzaraas, the outcasts there will find themselves inside the camp of Israel.

Divrei HaYamim, the last book of Tanach which completes malchus and leans toward the world of tikkun, spells Damascus 'Darmesek', with a reish that equals machaneh Yisrael, and spells David with a yud as it will be in the redemption.

Because every Jew is a letter in the Torah, a kushya in the Torah is a kushya on some Jew; one who toils to answer a hard Gemara or Tosafos brings teshuvah to that Jew, and this is the deeper meaning of 'Tishbi will answer the kushyos'.
Following the Chiddushei HaRim, the highest gilui Eliyahu is when Eliyahu comes with Elisha and Gechazi runs after them; in the end Gechazi will catch up, so that all Jews reach their tikkun.
The small avodah of the lowest generation is like the cheap pearl brought from the depths of the sea: it proves the King's reign reaches even there, and so it is set at the head of the crown.

The Rav reads the two titles of Moshe as two vantage points: Yehoshua could only write 'eved Hashem' because he could describe Moshe only from his own level, and so the Rav, like a blade of grass that also benefits from the sun, describes Reb Shraga Feivel as an eved Hashem.

Shabbos is shleimus and shirah is harmony: just as a melody needs all seven notes, the seventh day completes creation, and a person who has all the parts in harmony has a neshamah of Shabbos and of song.
Eretz Yisrael, the seventh land, is a land of song, and the seventh sea, the Kinneret, carries the name of the kinor, the harp.
Since every leaf sings shirah to Hashem, tearing a leaf for no purpose interrupts its song, and a lone moving leaf among still ones is the chazan with the others answering.
The Rav presents Reb Shraga Feivel's harmony between Hungarian Jews, Litvish roshei yeshiva and chassidus as an expression of his neshamah of shirah.
A niggun can outlast its singer: the Rav says Reb Shraga Feivel's niggun is still sung in the yeshiva and in America, and his leaf will not be torn off.
The eved nirtza has fallen so low that when Shemitah throws him a rope he does not grab it; only Yovel, the great return, takes him out, and Rashbi's mitzvah is this Yovel.
Bringing Jews back to Yerushalayim, in the Rambam's sign of Moshiach, is not a geographical matter but bringing them back to their roots and to serving Hashem.

The jealousy that killed Rabbi Akiva's students, began with the moon, and runs through Kayin, Yosef's brothers and the kings, is the same baseless hatred that destroyed the Beis HaMikdash, the place of unity; Moshiach and Rashbi repair it.

The Gemara tells of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza to teach that the last small act completes what generations accumulated: just as they gave the last tug to destruction, the last generation, like a child, will give the last tug to the building.

Through the At-Bash rule, Pesach does not tell us when Purim was; rather Purim looks forward to the coming Pesach, the Pesach of the future redemption, and Lag Ba'omer, which falls on Purim's weekday, likewise heralds Moshiach.

Yovel's two promises, return to one's holding and return to one's family, match nefesh and the higher levels: Pesach Sheni restores only property, while Lag Ba'omer restores the higher level of family.

Following Rabbi Dovid of Lelov, the place of hachnasas kallah in the list of birchos hashachar, right after visiting the sick and before what follows, shows that it rescues from what would otherwise come next.

The Rav finds it significant that the Haiti earthquake came in the week of Parshas Va'eira, where Rashi teaches that Hashem's punishment of the nations is a lesson aimed at the Jews; so the disaster should be the headline of the Jewish papers.

Just as the Jews in Mitzrayim saw Hashem punish the Egyptians, took the lesson, did teshuvah and merited the geulah, so too now great plans for geulah are prepared in Heaven and all that is missing is that Jews take mussar.

Hachnasas kallah was chosen as the interruption because 'leshem yichud' shows that every mitzvah is meant to bring the Chassan, Hashem, together with the Kallah, Klal Yisrael; the purpose of all the mitzvos is itself a hachnasas kallah.

A collector who interrupts davening calling 'hachnasas kallah' should be thanked, because, as the Ba'al Shem Tov teaches that Hashem speaks to a person through everything he sees, he is reminding him that his davening itself must be a hachnasas kallah.
Following the Kedushas Levi, even a rasha has a 'song' to Hashem: his downfall, which brings out Hashem's honor; the tzaddik, by contrast, praises Hashem while alive, through his life.
The Rav reads 'with my extra being' in the passuk as 'with the gifted, extra years': these too must be used to sing to Hashem.
The Gerrer Rebbe, for whom even two lost minutes still counted half a year later, considered himself defeated by people whose need or longing outweighed his reckoning of time.
Through the korbanos of the twelve nesiim, the twelve princes of Yishmael fall, and the Rav says this generation in particular must work hard in these days to push away that klipah.
Each tribe's own color on the choshen and the degel stands for a distinct middah, a distinct tafkid, and with these the nesiim of Yishmael are nullified.
Chanukas hamizbe'ach means inaugurating the avodah of the Mikdash, and since a Jew is himself a mikdash, these are days to inaugurate oneself anew.
The reversal of purity between land and sea exists so that every species can sing: the pure member in one realm serves as shliach tzibbur for its impure counterpart in the other.
The frog, at home both in the sea and on land, is a mixture of tamei and tahor, so it was the fitting plague for Egyptians who sought to mix good and evil.
The frog's 'Baruch shem' is the song of the sitra achra itself: Hashem wants even the impure realm to praise Him, quietly, through the lower unity.
Tumah is rooted in twoness, which is why Ohalos and Negaim open with 'two'; the frog, being a mixture, needed both one and many, which reconciles Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah.

The frog of Perek Shirah that tells King David its song is finer stands for the Jew of the heel of Moshiach speaking to the generation of the Beis HaMikdash: his weaker song is harder and therefore finer.
The princess who craves the scrapings of the pot is an image for Hashem's preference for the lowly service of the last generation over the finer service of earlier ones.

The fifth week of consolation corresponds to hod, the lowest level, and its haftarah 'for more are the children of the desolate' is the gematria of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the source of strength for the lowest.

The Rav reads the two parts of a fingernail as two kinds of distant Jews: the part still attached, painful to remove, is the sinner who still believes and comes to shul on Yom Kippur; the protruding part, cut off painlessly, is the heretic.
Cutting the nails before Shabbos stands for the Jew who refuses Shabbos's rescue, like one who does not catch the rope thrown to him; Shabbos can do nothing for him, but Yovel still brings him back.
Rus is said to have 'returned' to a land she had never been in, which shows that she was a Jewish soul snatched away by the Sitra Achra and born in the palace of the king of Moav.

The week of Hod is bracketed by two days of second chances: Pesach Sheni for those excluded from the Exodus, and Lag Ba'omer, Hod sheb'Hod, the lowest level, where holiness is strong enough to reach the very bottom.
There is no mourning by Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai for the same reason the Kohen Gadol does not mourn: one connected to the Holy of Holies, the place of complete unity, lacks nothing.
The Kosel and Meron are the two places where the entire spectrum of Jews, from the greatest tzaddik to the greatest sinner, still comes together, because Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is like the Mikdash.
Just as Shabbos kept Adam HaRishon in Gan Eden, Shabbos keeps Lag Ba'omer, which falls on Friday this year, from leaving, giving two days of Lag Ba'omer.
Amalek, the klipah of 'reishis', concentrates on beginnings, so a new beis medrash and a new effort in tefillah meet the strongest opposition.
Like a patient for whom orange juice is at the moment more important than bread, in the days before Moshiach tefillah takes first place without lessening the greatness of Torah study.
Many small daily sacrifices of one's wishes add up to a mesiras nefesh greater even than the one great act of giving up life.
Eating and farbrenging together in the shtibel after davening is no interruption of tefillah but can itself lead to accepting the yoke of Heaven.
The differences of nusach and custom between Jewish groups reflect the twelve gates in heaven, one for each shevet, which is why the Torah says to appoint judges 'for your tribes'.
When Providence draws certain people together as friends, it shows they share a root of the soul, and the love between them must be stronger.
The Rav reads the threats and hardships of his own day, Iran and the economic crisis, as the same kind of 'history-making' darkness that came just before the Exodus and the Purim miracle.
Since Iran is the ancient Paras where Haman fell, and a place where Jews had a miracle, the Rav hopes for a repeat of that same miracle there in his day.
The lack of money to give is compared to Pharaoh's decree of bricks without straw: Hashem deliberately leaves the givers with only a little, so that giving becomes mesiras nefesh.

Tamar's indirect hint to Yehuda, rather than open disclosure, was a plan so that both of them would act with mesiras nefesh, the only thing that could defeat the Satan's efforts against the birth of Moshiach's line.
Hashem's 'gift' to Lot, by which he was saved, was guests whom he had to take in with mesiras nefesh; in the same way the needy kallahs of today are Hashem's present to those who can help.
From 'im yesh es nafshechem' the Rav learns that nefesh means will, so mesiras nefesh is acting against one's own will for Hashem, not only giving up one's life.
The 101st review is what makes an oved Hashem because it goes past the routine of a hundred and takes mesiras nefesh.
Families, neighborhoods and communities correspond to the Torah's words, columns and sedras: people live together because their letters stood together in the Sefer Torah.
The custom of combined sedras is a calendar-wide demonstration of ahavas chinam, falling at the seasons connected to the churban, the hoped-for redemption and the students of Rabbi Akiva.

The Rav maps the dispute over giving a Rav shlishi or shishi onto the Midrash in which the sea, created on the third day, refused to yield to man, created on the sixth, until it saw Yosef, who is shishi.
Even tzaddikim are not fully free of kinah, which is why one tzaddik traveled specially to Rav Yisrael of Vizhnitz, who was free of it.
Yehuda and David are the moon and Ephraim stands opposite them, so the strife between Yehuda and Ephraim flows from the moon's diminution, and Yehonasan's love for David is a symbol of its repair.
A leap year itself carries the lesson of unity, because the extra month brings the moon and sun together, so in that year the Sefirah sedras need not be joined.
A Jew is like a switchboard: his mitzvos and aveiros register in all of creation, so removing kinah from his own heart removes it from the world.
The Rav reads Daniel's three verbs as three stages of refining the souls: sifting out, washing white like laundering, and smelting like silver, where the waste falls away and the pure metal remains.
He sees the modern movements as a single process of borer, Hashem separating the waste from the food: each movement swept away multitudes and left behind the souls that hold onto Yiddishkeit.
Communism was the first true 'kingdom of heresy' in history: earlier kingdoms served idols and believed in something, while minus means believing in nothing.
The Rav identifies electronics as the real spiritual chametz of today, so that biur chametz means removing it from the home, the heart, the head and the soul.
When all of nature is renewed in Nissan, a Jew should not be the exception; the trees reviving and the haftarah of the dry bones show that the renewal of Nissan reaches down into the physical world.
Part of today's test is hester panim: in earlier generations people saw wonders from the gedolim, while today everything is hidden and rests on emunah alone.
Pinchas knew his act might cost him the kehunah, yet he went ahead only to make a kiddush Hashem; his reward of kehunah came from the act itself, not from being Aharon's grandson.
The point of 'in their midst' is that the zealotry belonged to Klal Yisrael as a whole: Pinchas acted as a simple Jew among them, so that through him the people itself was zealous.
The Rav reads Zimri's name as the one small part of the soul that sinned out of a personal calculation, a foreign growth on a Jew, while the people as a whole stay separate from it.
Eliyahu is gematria 'ben' (son), and the word Eliyahu appears nine times in the haftarah; through Eliyahu it will be clarified that Jews are Hashem's children.
The child did not suffer on account of others, nor did the family suffer on his account: he came into the world for this, as part of his own tikkun.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the revealer of secrets, is the patron of the lowest souls, because he sees the secret hidden even in the lowest Jew.
Kingship, the most dangerous position for pride, is entrusted only to Yehudah, whose very name comes from thanks for receiving more than one's share.
The Korban Pesach has no chametz loaves although it is a thanks offering, because it thanks for kindness that came regardless of deeds.
Saying Modeh Ani with impure hands is itself the defeat of the kelipah: declaring that it is nothing before Hashem makes it nothing, as Avraham's dust did to the kings.
The 'king's daughter' of the kelipah is a counterfeit royalty that holds itself great, while the Jew is the true king's son whose greatness is in his smallness.
Pesach Sheini falls in the week of hod to show that even the lowest souls bring the Korban Pesach, their Modeh Ani.

Counting 'by the number of names' is a count that keeps both sides: a name is individuality and a number is the collective, and Moshe's count joined each Jew's individual self to his being part of the whole.

The sages were called soferim not because they could count letters, which anyone can do, but because each letter was for them a davar shebeminyan, a counted thing that is never nullified, since they knew what each letter stands for.
The five camps correspond to the five Chumashim, with the Kohanim and Levi'im in the center just as Vayikra, Toras Kohanim, stands in the middle of the Torah.
The 22,000 Levi'im correspond to the 22 letters of the aleph-beis, the roots of the 600,000 letters, multiplied by a thousand, 'elef', which goes back to the aleph.
The megadef had to be evicted from the camp of Dan because the camp was a Sefer Torah, and adding a letter that does not belong renders a Sefer Torah pasul.
A line of a Sefer Torah, whose width the Gemara sets at three times the word for 'families', is a neighborhood of three Jewish families, and each word is a family.
Moshe's blessing that Levi will teach Torah is still visible: Kohanim and Levi'im are about a tenth of a congregation, yet well over half of the teachers of Torah.

The Rav applies the Rambam's warning against calling troubles chance directly to the present: ignoring the Iranian threat and staying busy with trivialities is exactly the 'cruel' response the Rambam describes.
He identifies Paras of the Gemara and the Pesikta with today's Iran, the land of Achashverosh where Haman sought to kill all the Jews, and, through the Maharal, with Yishmael and Islam.

From Manoach's wife the Rav derives a principle: had Hashem wanted to harm the Jews, He would not have shown them such open miracles, so the wonders in Eretz Yisrael are themselves a sign of coming salvation.
He says the miracles are not made for the Israeli government but for Klal Yisrael: those who learn Torah, keep mitzvos and will yet return.

Since sefarim say that learning Torah is Shabbos, a rest from all work, the Rav argues that answering a cellphone in the middle of learning in a beis medrash brings the marketplace and the office into Shabbos and desecrates it.

Through the half shekel, where each Jew is a half and two together make one, and Korach's men whose share was not accepted because of their dispute, the Rav shows that unity was the answer to Haman then and is the needed merit now.
From the Ba'al HaTanya's arrangement the Rav learns that the aim is not only for each person to finish his own masechta: in a group completing Shas, each one is linked to the entire Shas.
Completing the whole Shas is beyond anyone's grasp, as is even one halachah; yet through the bond of souls in the group, a person who learned a small part is counted as having finished it all.
The Rav reads the Midrash's 'sixty are the queens' as teaching that learning a masechta is a form of malchus, and that even one who learns halachah after halachah is connected to this malchus.
Malchus here means that a Jew has a say in Heaven, and this is what Jews need at a time like this.
When Jews in Eretz Yisroel and abroad each learn and daven for the other, their tefillos join, since all tefillah goes up through Eretz Yisroel and Yerushalayim.
The Rav reads the seven haftaros of consolation as a dialogue: for six weeks the navi consoles and Klal Yisrael is silent, and only in the seventh does she answer Hashem herself, as a bride.
Following the Maharal, the two middle handbreadths of the luchos, held by neither Hashem nor Moshe, were the partnership itself between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, like two who hold a garment together.

A wife's bond can be ended by divorce, a daughter's cannot be cut but her father can be angry, while a mother's love for her infant cannot be weakened at all; Hashem calls Klal Yisrael 'my mother', the love of the mother to her child.

Like a hospital with its own generator, when the calf severed the bond of groom and bride, the higher bond of 'my daughter' and 'my mother' remained as a backup, so the calf could be forgotten while Sinai was not.

The Amora's unusual sharpness against anyone who says terumah can be redeemed is explained because Klal Yisrael is Hashem's terumah: the claim that Hashem exchanged the Jews for another nation is Bilaam's view.
Yom Kippur equals 'rotzeh ani' in gematria: it is the day when each Jew's inner will to do Hashem's will comes out.

Ending the Torah on Simchas Torah with 'l'einei kol Yisrael', the breaking of the luchos that brought forgetting, and beginning Bereishis at once shows that the forgetting does not reach Klal Yisrael, for whom the world was created.

The Rav reads the count of Bamidbar, on the Shabbos before Shavuos, as the aufruf of the kallah: counting the Jews is counting the letters of the Torah, and that is adorning the kallah before the wedding.
Amen joins the written Name, Havaya (26), with the spoken Name, Adnus (65), making 91, because we perceive Hashem only through His Shechinah dwelling on Klal Yisrael, the kallah.
A Jew's face carries the aleph: the two eyes are its two yuds and the nose its vav, together the Shem Havaya, and the mouth below is the patach of chochmah.
Numbers erase individuality: the Nazis tattooed numbers on Jews to make them like branded animals, while Hashem counts 'by names', each Jew a distinct shlichus with no duplicates.
Shevet Levi is the root of the 600,000 letters, the 22 letters of the alef-beis, which is why the Levi'im numbered 22,000, and this resolves 600,000 versus 22,000 malachim at Sinai.
Staying up Shavuos night and sleeping through the davening is like a chassan who pays for everything but skips the ring: without it there is no wedding.
Shevuah comes from sheva, seven: an oath reaches the root of a person's seven middos and binds them all to Hashem's Name, beyond any weakness in a particular middah.
Mashbia, to make swear, shares a root with mashpia, to bestow, since beis and pei interchange: making someone swear infuses him with strength from Heaven to do Hashem's will.
The Vizhnitzer Rebbe read 'lo nishba l'mirmah' as the soul's oath before birth to be a tzaddik: the one who ascends Hashem's mountain is the one who did not betray that oath.

Avraham's oath was not distrust of Eliezer: in Lavan's house, where the yetzer hara was overwhelming and Eliezer had a personal interest, only the kedushah drawn through the oath could keep him faithful.
Following the Divrei Yechezkel, the clothes Eliezer gave Rivka were a sample of the dress of Avraham's household: a message that joining that family means dressing that way.
Adam and Chava knew how to make clothes, yet Hashem made garments for them, to show that the clothing He is pleased with is not what people themselves consider sufficient.
Chanukah's 'mosif v'holech' is the model for a Jewish couple: as the Chasam Sofer ruled, a wife cannot object that her husband grew in yiras Shamayim, since a Jew must always become better.
Because emunah belongs to the heart, and the heart and mind are life itself, a person who lacks emunah does not merely lack one limb at techiyas hameisim but cannot rise at all.
Yaakov, fleeing danger, asked only for bread and a garment because he meant the soul's needs in the next world: Torah as its food and mitzvos as its garments.
Just as clothing costs more than food, mitzvos cost more than Torah: anyone can learn, but a mezuzah or tefillin costs money.
Chavakuk basing all the mitzvos on emunah does not free anyone from the others; it means concentrating on one mitzvah through which all the others are kept.
Emunah is like a building's basement: no one counts it as a room, yet it holds the furnace and boiler that make the whole building livable.
Love of Hashem can be commanded, unlike loving a food, because every Jew already loves Hashem inwardly; the mitzvah is to bring it out into the open.
The Rav reads shifcha as mishpacha missing its mem: the Eved Ivri who becomes permitted to a shifcha has lost the mem, the forty days of Matan Torah that made Klal Yisrael a family.
Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is a miniature Yovel, the fiftieth year: the great shofar at Sinai parallels the shofar of Yovel that frees the slave and returns each man to his portion.

The camps in the wilderness mirror the Chumash: four camps around the center for five Chumashim, with Vayikra, about the Mishkan, Kohanim and Levi'im, in the middle; so each Jew stood in the camp exactly where his letter is.
The Rav explains the extraordinary heresy of our time by the generation's mitzvah being emunah: what a person or generation is rooted in is exactly where he must struggle.
The last seven letters of the Aseres Hadibros, 'asher lerei'echa', correspond to the seven rabbinic mitzvos, since the true friends who seek our welfare are the Chachamim.
Rus and Yisro, both read on Shavuos, are built of the same letters, Yisro being Rus with an extra yud, because both embody the soul's return to its source.
A year is called shanah because it means repetition: whatever happened on a Yom Tov repeats itself each year, so Matan Torah truly recurs every Shavuos.
The Rav uses the inborn knowledge of animals, such as a spider that never saw its mother yet weaves her exact web, as a model for how emunah can be inherited by a Jew.
The mitzvah of 'Anochi Hashem' is phrased as a fact because the Jew already believes; the command within it is not to spoil what he was born with.
Weak emunah is not an absence but an illness: like a man who ruined his appetite with a bad breakfast, the desire is there and only needs treatment.
Forbidden food and arayos are the spiritual cholesterol of the soul, clogging the heart of emunah as cholesterol blocks the arteries.
As the first tree contained every tree that would grow from its seeds, every Jew was once actually part of Avraham, and Yaakov held within him Avraham and Yitzchak.
Although a trait usually thins out over generations, it grows stronger when both partners carry it; since Klal Yisrael all descends from Avraham, Jews are almost entirely Avraham.
Chazal locate heresy in the heart rather than the mind: the verse warns against straying 'after your hearts', and the heart is the seat of desires, so kefirah is born of wanting, not of thinking.
Chiel of Beis El, burying son after son as Yehoshua's curse came true and still building, is the Navi's picture of denial: a person can watch the truth happen before his eyes and refuse to admit it.

The evolving, constantly revised theories of creation are themselves a sign of rationalization: having rejected the Chumash's account for reasons of the heart, the apikores must keep rewriting his own.
The Rav compares rejecting the Torah to the nations who refused it at Sinai: they too rejected it because a particular commandment opposed their nature, not because it made no sense.

The two driving forces of the soul, taivah and gaavah, explain who returns at the end of life: when desire fades the excuse is gone and people do teshuvah, but gaavah does not leave with age, and admitting a life lived in error would wound the ego.
The barrenness of Avraham and Sarah was needed to break the natural continuity from father to son, so that what was born to them would be a new creation rather than an extension of Terach.
Avraham's exemption from honoring his father follows from his being a new species: kibbud av expresses a son's bond with his father, and that bond was cut.
The kofer is named for the pitch, 'kofer', that covered Noach's ark: his denial is only a coating over a belief that remains underneath.
The three matzos correspond to the Avos because grain gives intellect, which comes from the father, and the four cups to the Imahos because wine gives feeling, which comes from the mother.
Although lineage and inheritance follow the father, Jewishness follows the mother because it rests on emunah, which is transmitted through the mother.
Just as the noun drops the final nun of its root (shen, gan), 'emunah' is linked to 'em', mother, showing that emunah comes from the mother.
The Rav reads the Gemara's 'until anger' as a sign of success: like a reaction to an inoculation, the anger shows the rebuke has stirred up an inner struggle with the yetzer hara.
Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand parables are explained as three thousand descending levels, each parable explaining the one above it, until his thought reached people's understanding.
The ten levels of holiness parallel the ten utterances of creation, so the Kodesh HaKodashim, the tenth, corresponds to the union of chassan and kallah, which explains the keruvim there.
Matan Torah was the moment the holiness of Shir HaShirim, otherwise confined to the Kodesh HaKodashim, came down into the physical world.
Yishmael and Esav are the refuse of Avraham's chesed and Yitzchak's gevurah, cast off like side effects of a medicine so that Yitzchak and Yaakov could come out pure.
Netzach and hod are the two legs that let a person stand: one by fighting, the other by yielding, like grass that bends in a storm while a stiff tree cracks.
All the laws of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah fall in the sedros read during Sefirah, because these are the kallah's days of holiness and purity.

Philosophy is not a Jewish article: no Gemara or Midrash anywhere tries to establish the foundations of emunah through logical arguments, and the Rav takes this absence itself as a sign that it is a foreign import.
Trying to grasp Hashem with the intellect is like trying to hear a picture: even hearing a million times sharper would not help, because it is the wrong faculty altogether, not a weak one.
The sudden flash that makes a whole sugya clear to a simple, upright Jew is a small appearance of the ruach hakodesh that every Jew has through his neshamah.
Aveiros act like the insulation on an electric wire: the current of the neshamah is still there, but the person has no contact with it.

One need not survey the whole creation to see the Creator; a person's own body, with its self-adjusting and self-repairing systems, is enough, which is the meaning the Rav gives to 'from my flesh I see G-d'.
The Rav compares the world to the body: just as no system of the body can exist without the others, no part of nature, from plants to planets, can exist without the rest.
Denying a Creator is not an intellectual conclusion but a rationalization: people make themselves blind because recognizing the Ribono shel Olam would put the brakes on their desires.
The brain cells that never get replaced are what make memory possible, so that a person still remembers the aleph-beis he learned as a small child.
Water behaves like every other substance until it nears freezing, and only then reverses, precisely so that ice floats and life in rivers survives the winter.

The Rav traces the Maharsham's well-known leniency in psak to the instruction he received from Reb Ayzikl of Zidichov after being saved, that making things hard for Jews is no skill and one must make things easy.

In the story, the defense that saves the Maharsham is that in a bitter exile with so much hiding of Hashem's face, a young man sitting and learning Torah is very precious above, even if not purely for Heaven's sake.
The Rav reads the Kotzker Rebbe's reply as a deep point: though he is sure the Kotzker also saw the ushpizin, he chose to say that he believes, because believing is greater than seeing.

The Rav presents the concentration of Kohanim and Levi'im among halachic authorities, from the Shulchan Aruch's commentators to the roshei yeshiva of his own beis medrash, as a visible, present-day proof of the truth of Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing.
The Rav contrasts the Chassidic Rebbes, among whom one does not find this pattern of Kohanim and Levi'im, but rather descent from the royal house of David.
The Rav describes Shabbos as a rope thrown to the eved to return, and Yovel as the lifeguard who pulls him out by the hair when he will not grab it; the shofar of Moshiach will do the same.
The Rav says he is convinced, though he has not seen it in a sefer, that the place of Yovel is Beis Lechem Yehudah, the home of David HaMelech, whose malchus gathers Jews back.
Boaz's 'dip your bread in vinegar' becomes a blessing: her bread will be dipped in the halacha that Menashe taught about how to make hamotzi.
The Mishnah and the Gemara on Menashe's share are both true at different levels, just as a deeper level of judgment in Eretz Yisrael can reopen a case closed abroad.
Yibum itself is Hashem's tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod: hard work digging to bring a lost soul to its tikkun, which is why it belongs to Moshiach.

Baking is the last stage in the tikkun of a soul in bread, so the part baked first shows that Hashem is hurrying its tikkun; that is why the bracha is made there, and why Menashe of malchus Beis David taught it.

The Rav presents the absence of open revelations in this generation as its particular test: believing without seeing is a great tikun, and through it this generation can accomplish more than earlier ones and bring the days of Moshiach.

The proof is in what the books do not need: a textbook is discarded once outgrown, but a Chumash is never obsolete, and the very same Gemara is learned by a nine-year-old and by the greatest roshei yeshiva.
The Rav argues that no human being could compose a wisdom that is plain to a child and endlessly deep to a genius, so the Torah's endless depth is itself a wonder testifying to its divine origin.
A Torah sefer from the Infinite has no bottom, while digging into a secular book only makes a hole in the page: its wisdom goes no deeper than the paper.
The Rav reads the Greeks' failure to defile the one sealed jar as a matter of sight: they looked at it again and again and did not see it, because they were not given permission to see it.

Avraham Avinu's discovery of Hashem through the order of the world is presented as a path for everyone: whoever strengthens his emunah will reach a point where Hashem shows him 'I am here' through wonders in his Torah and his daily life.
The Rav calls emunah a created instinct, parallel to the appetite for food: Hashem builds a desire into whatever a person needs, and a person needs emunah to reach the purpose of his creation.
He explains Greek rationalism as a means rather than an honest search: by declaring that only proven things are believed, the Greeks freed themselves from the yoke.

Because an instinct must be gratified, the Greeks who denied G-d did not stop believing; they redirected the instinct of emunah onto physical strength and beauty, which the Rav sees as the root of sport and of fashion worship.
Like Moshiach, whose gematria equals nachash because he repairs what the snake spoiled, Chanukah has the gematria of guf, because it stands against the worship of the body.
The order Ein k'Elokeinu before Mi k'Elokeinu teaches that one may not ask the question about Hashem before first stating the answer.
Emunah, being a mitzvah, has halachos like a sukkah: the instinctive, natural and philosophical paths to faith are not its halachic definition.
The Rambam in the Yad speaks of emunah as halacha, differently from his philosophical approach in the Moreh Nevuchim.
Even other religions accept the Torah because a public revelation cannot be denied; they can only claim it was later replaced.
Moshe's wonders, such as the splitting of the sea and the mann, were done because they were needed, not as proofs that he was right.
Belief in a navi works like belief in witnesses: not certainty about the person, but trust in Hashem's command, for Hashem stands among the judges.
The Rav presents Yovel as a law of nature like gravity: just as an apple must fall back to the ground it came from, every Yid must eventually return to his source in Eretz Yisrael and in Hashem.

The difference between the seventh year and Yovel is that in the seventh year Hashem throws the drowning slave a rope that he can refuse, while at Yovel He dives in like a lifeguard and pulls him out by the hair.
The fifty days from Mitzrayim to Matan Torah parallel the fifty years of Yovel, so that the shofar at Sinai is the shofar of freedom calling the Yidden back to their roots.
Since the chance of Moshiach coming is even every day, like a spinning penny that does not remember its past throws, two thousand years of waiting do not lessen the chance that he comes this Shavuos.
The teshuvah the Yidden did on arriving at Sinai returns every Rosh Chodesh Sivan, and the Torah demands preparation only for Shavuos, not for Pesach or Sukkos.
Belief in any prophet but Moshe is only a decree, like trusting two witnesses who could be lying; true knowledge of Hashem belongs to Klal Yisroel alone through what they saw at Sinai.
The verse 'Hashem is not a man that He should lie or change His mind' was said by Bilaam, a gentile, so the nations' own prophet testifies against the idea of a new testament.
Rashi's statement that HaChodesh is the first mitzvah Yisroel were commanded is simple according to the Rambam: it is the first mitzvah received from Moshe, the only prophet believed with certainty.
The Rambam's words that Moshe is 'father to the prophets before him' mean that even the Avos and Adam are believed only because Moshe recorded their mitzvos.
A Jew who kept the Torah all his life never recants at death, while sinners often repent then, because at death rationalization falls away and only the truth remains.

The Rav reads the Yaavetz as showing empirically that philosophical proofs of faith fail under trial: those who had proven Hashem's truth by logic converted, while those without such proofs went into exile for their faith.
Because the whole of Jewish faith rests on Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah as transmitted to one's children, the Rav says it is especially important to learn the sedros now being read.

Even differences of girsa that remain between Rashi and Tosafos are, in the Rav's view, both true, like a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, since Hashem allowed both readings to stand among the gedolim who learned them.
The Rav points out that Shaarei Teshuvah, one of the most important mussar works, came about as a direct result of Rabbeinu Yonah's teshuvah over his part in the burning of the Rambam's works.

The Rav explains Chavakuk's founding all mitzvos on emunah not as a release from the other mitzvos but as a response to shrinking generations, who can no longer concentrate on everything and must make one mitzvah the foundation.
Shabbos is a return one may decline, like the eved who chooses to stay at Shemitah, but Yom Kippur and Yovel pull a person out by force, so Yovel is the return that is for everyone.
In the Ramak's fiftieth mention of yetzias Mitzrayim the Torah says 'I took them out' in the third person, because the fiftieth level is hidden and beyond us.
After the forty-nine klalos in groups of seven, the fiftieth mention comes, showing that the sitra achra has a grip on forty-nine levels but not on the fiftieth.
The kedushah of Yosef and Serach protected every Jew in Mitzrayim up to, but not including, the fiftieth level, and Shlomis's son needed exactly that level, so she stumbled.
Rus is said to 'return' from Moav though she had never been in Eretz Yisrael, because her neshamah belonged there; Beis Lechem, where Rachel is, corresponds to the mitzvah of Yovel.
The fifty thousand Yovlos the Rav heard are not a measure of time but of levels: the tikkun of the lowest requires a level made of fifty thousand Yovlos.
The Rav reads hafrashas challah on erev Shabbos as a reenactment of creation: Hashem kneaded the world and took Adam HaRishon out of it as its challah on the first erev Shabbos.

A person's root in Adam HaRishon fixes what he excels at, not whether he is good: one from the head who does not choose to be a tzaddik becomes a philosopher or scientist, one from the heart a poet or novelist.
Like a fern whose every leaf is a small fern, each generation is a full body of Adam, and the whole chain of generations is again one body from head to heel.
The insensitivity of the heel is by design, so a person can walk on stones; the Rav applies this to our generation's dulled feeling for Yiddishkeit.

Yerushalayim is both the head and the heart of the world: it holds the Lishkas HaGazis and the house of prayer, and the world's constant preoccupation with Eretz Yisroel shows it is the world's heartbeat.
The Purim story, at the end of the Babylonian exile, was itself an ikvesa dimeshicha after the first Churban, parallel to our time after the second.
Adar is read as 'cloak': its miracles are the same as Nissan's, only wrapped in nature, as the fish of the mazal of Adar live hidden under the water.
Achashverosh's swings from one extreme to the other, in his marriages and in his taxes, prove he had no character of his own and was only moved from above.
The absence of Hashem's name from the Megillah reflects the incompleteness of the name while Amalek, whose gematria equals safek, spreads doubt in the world.
Reading the world is like reading an x-ray: to the layman it is meaningless splashes, while the specialist, like the man of emunah, sees exactly what is there.
Learning the Megillah is an exercise: once one can find Hashem's name between its lines, one can do the same with the New York Times.
Once Hashem is found, as in the Ba'al Shem Tov's hide-and-seek, He no longer needs to hide, and the finding itself is the joy of Purim.
The Rav reads the Chofetz Chaim's statement as a deliberate withdrawal of the supernatural: dibbukim stopped because open sights would leave no room for the test of emunah.
Tzaddikim today are no smaller; only the permission to show wonders openly was taken from them, so wonders appear rarely, like lightning in the middle of the night.
The Rav applies the sign of a personal test, what is hard yet desired, to a whole generation: collectively, emunah is our test.
Each era has its own target for the Satan: in the Divrei Chaim's time it flooded the market with invalid machine tzitzis, and today it works against emunah itself.
The pollution of air, water and land today is a mirror of the spiritual world, where everything is contaminated as well.
The Rav reads the eved Ivri who refuses to leave as a picture of a person who prefers his chains, and the Yovel shofar as a holiness of freedom that descends and makes even him want to go free.
Sefiras ha'omer mirrors Shemitah and Yovel: seven times seven, with the fiftieth day corresponding to the fiftieth year, so the shofar at Har Sinai is the Yovel shofar of the Jewish people.

The smoker who says one cigarette cannot shorten his life is refuted by simple arithmetic: ten thousand cigarettes are ten thousand times one cigarette, so each one shortens it, and his laughter shows he is kidding himself.
Akdamus, said with the Sefer Torah already on the bimah, is understood as a last stage of preparation, a lesson in emunah before hearing the Aseres Hadibros.
Shavuos differs from the Fourth of July: nothing happens on Independence Day besides remembering, while on Shavuos the Torah is actually given again, a whole year's supply.
The Sanzer Rav's answer shows that being shown a spiritual vision is little; the goal is to grow until one can see it with his own strength.
Earlier dates for Moshiach given by gedolim were not mistakes: each was a pekidah, a time especially suited for the geulah had the generation merited it.

An eis ratzon for the geulah that is not merited does not simply pass: the Satan argues that the Jews are unworthy, and the resulting kitrug brings harsh judgment, as the Rav sees in the war that broke out in 1914.

The Rav reads Nitzavim-Vayeilech, one parsha of the Gaon's count, as the current century: Vayeilech's double hester panim is its first half, the Holocaust, and Nitzavim's teshuvah and ingathering is its second half.
Nitzavim, the refuah, precedes Vayeilech, the makah, because Hashem prepares the cure before striking Yisrael, like a surgeon whose prepared bandages show he is a healer and not a murderer.
They are two separate sidros although one parsha because the geulah will be an entirely different order of life, in which the suffering will be remembered like a dream that was not real.
Since the suffering began in the first year of the century, 5700, the Rav hopes this is a sign that the geulah will begin in the first year of its second half, 5750.
The Tree of Knowledge was good: it was a vine whose grapes Adam was meant to press for Kiddush on Friday night, which would have begun an eternal Shabbos; his sin was only that he did not wait.
The Malbim's remark that the maskilim 'know better' than him means only that they may eat on waking, while a Jew must wait: wash, daven and make a brachah first.
Since in loshon hakodesh one root carries both meanings, 'nisayon' as test and 'nes' as raising up reveal each other: the purpose of every test is to lift a person higher.
Avraham's difficulty at the Akeidah was not the deed itself but that he was in katnus: when a person must do something hard, a defense mechanism makes him ask questions.
Not knowing a simple answer is itself part of the test: Avraham, the great sage, did not think of what a child learning Chumash sees, until after the test.
By the Ramban's rule, Avraham's ten tests foreshadow ten tests for the Jewish people, so the last test before Moshiach is the Akeidah's: Hashem seems remote and there are questions without answers.

Dovid HaMelech's recognition, at the moment of Shimi's curse, that Hashem was behind it is what made him the fourth leg of the Divine chariot, and it also brought about that Mordechai, who stood against Haman, would descend from Shimi.
Emunah is the one mitzvah that can stand in for all 613 for souls who have failed again and again, but only if it is complete enough to exclude every 'volt'.
The ecological contamination of recent decades, air, rain, water and food, is a mirror of a spiritual contamination that makes even a blatt Gemara or a kapitel Tehillim harder today than years ago.
The machlokes of great tzaddikim may be l'sheim Shamayim, but when the masses take sides it becomes rechilus and bizayon haTorah, and that is what held back Moshiach then and holds him back now.
In a time of great trials, Torah learned even not for its own sake is precious in Heaven and can tip the scale; the Rav sees in this the different standard by which our generation is judged.

The Rav reads the modern idea of freedom, doing whatever one wants, as the very slavery the Torah frees a Jew from: the smoker who claims freedom is enslaved to his yetzer hara, while the free man is one who chooses to serve Hashem.
He links the fiftieth year of Yovel with the fiftieth day of Sefirah: both are freedom and return, going out from being a slave to the yetzer hara to being a servant of Hashem.
The year is like a rotating card file: each day carries what happened on it, so a Yom Tov is a real return of the original event and not a commemoration like the Fourth of July.
He explains why the parsha of the Yamim Tovim in Emor begins with Shabbos, which is not one of them: each Yom Tov draws its blessing from the Shabbos before it.

The twenty-four books of Tanach said on Shavuos night are the twenty-four ornaments of the kallah, paralleled by the twenty-four permutations of the four letters of the Name of Adnus, which represents the kallah.
He offers a simple reading of a Midrash Peliah: Shavuos is a time to become a Jew anew, as Yisro and Rus did, and as the Yid HaKadosh did every day.

The Jews' loss of faith right before Yetzias Mitzrayim was not a decline in them but the Satan's last, strongest assault on emunah before a geulah, and the same pattern repeats before the final geulah.
The difficulty of being a Jew today is itself a sign that the Satan senses his end, like a candle that flares brightest as it is about to go out.
Esav's dotted kiss is the model for modern exile: where open hatred failed, friendship and brotherhood draw far more Jews away from Yiddishkeit.
A joke cannot be answered by argument because it is by nature the opposite of logic; one can debate a philosopher, but not a leitz.
People pity someone with a broken leg or a sick heart but laugh at a madman, because laughter is aroused by whatever does not work with sense, and this is the power that leitzanus uses.
Faith in the sages is presented as a parallel to faith in Hashem: the chachamim and tzaddikim of each generation are His messengers to lead the people.
The seven species are the praise of Eretz Yisrael precisely because they are the Torah's shiurim, and the shiurim are what bind a Jew to the chacham.
The vagueness of the measures is deliberate: a people that built precise structures in Egypt was given measures by hand and finger, so that it would need the rav constantly.
Frequent questions to the rav build a closeness through which the chacham comes to guide a person in kashrus, tznius and Shabbos as well.
The world's name 'tevel', read as confusion, describes hester panim: a night in which one sees only shadows until a flash of lightning shows everything for a moment.
The Rav reads 'prices will soar' as a rise that defies supply and demand: goods are plentiful, the vine gives its fruit, and still the wine is expensive.
Never since the beginning of history was there a government founded on denial of the Creator until the Russian state, which the Rav sees as the fulfillment of 'the kingdom will turn to heresy'.

A dog walks ahead of its master, yet at every corner it turns its head to see which way the master is going; so the leaders of the generation stand in front but take their direction from the crowd behind them.
The shepherd feeds and cares for his flock while the dog only keeps it together; in the heels of Moshiach the leaders will lack the shepherd's role and keep only the dog's.
Like wheat sold in a famine, which no hungry buyer inspects, the mitzvos of the generation before Moshiach are not examined in Heaven, so the time of darkness is a time of great gain.

Tamuz's letter combination is the only one fully reversed and taken from final letters, and the fact that it comes from the Megillah of 'v'nahapoch hu' shows that the month's purpose is to be transformed.

The Rav adds that 'v'chol zeh einenu shoveh li', the source of the Tamuz combination, equals 'yemei bikurei anavim' in gematria, so the meraglim faced a judgment so strong they could hardly withstand it.

Like Shaul's 'hakimosi es dvar Hashem', which proved true through Purim, the delay for Miriam proved good: leaving seven days earlier would have put the meraglim's departure on Chof-Gimmel Sivan and spoiled that day of joy forever.

Every building of the Mikdash is preceded by wiping out Amalek: the Mishkan after the war with Amalek, Shaul's war on Erev Pesach that could have brought the eternal Mikdash, and Mordechai before the second Beis HaMikdash.

The two nesi'im who sinned, Elitzur ben Shdeiur and Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai, correspond to Tamuz and Av, read in the Shabbosos of those months, and 'otzem einav me're'os bera' equals their names in gematria.
The angel of Esav's refusal to tell Yaakov his name reveals the yetzer hara's method: a name is a person's shlichus, and the yetzer hara makes people forget who sent them.

The Chasam Sofer reconciles who sent the meraglim: in that season Hashem wanted them sent with a good report, while the Satan stirred the wicked to want them too; the Rav ties this to the travel of these months.
Loss of desire for Torah and tefillah is like loss of appetite: the soul's natural hunger for good spiritual food is spoiled by what it has taken in.
The pain and tears of a bochur over his doubts are themselves proof that he believes; a real non-believer would be glad of them, since they would free him to do as he pleases.
Doubts in emunah are Amalek, equal to safek in gematria; just as the Torah juxtaposes 'Is Hashem among us' with 'Amalek came', the doubts will vanish when Amalek is erased.
Thoughts of heresy cannot be defeated with logic because they are not logical; they are leitzanus, the shell of Amalek the scoffer, and leitzanus does not respond to reasoning.

'Velo sasuru' means not to go exploring, like the meraglim who scouted the land: welcoming a thought and discussing it is the sin, while pushing it out is the mitzvah, hinted at by the gerish note on those words.
Just as Klal Yisrael awaits the geulah, each Jew in a period of trial awaits his private geulah, and one who conducts himself properly emerges with clearer emunah than before.
The Rambam's words 'I await him every day' mean that no day is excluded: one may not make calculations that he will come at one time and not at another.
Adam's sin, the Golden Calf and Shaul's error are one failure, not waiting; David's waiting for the sign began the tikkun, and the avodah of galus is waiting.
Every person is a fragment of Adam haRishon, so each one shares in his sin and must repair his own portion of it.
The disappointments of the era are like birth pangs that end in a stillborn child, a pain Yeshaya already lamented.
Since the first part of the prophecies has been fulfilled exactly, as the Ramban argues about Haazinu, the second part, the geulah, is certain.
The hope for Moshiach is the 'wellspring of yeshuah': by attaching oneself to it, one draws personal yeshuos from it even in galus.
Answering amen is faith in what one has not yet seen, and Hashem keeps every such amen in His treasury.
From Parshas Shlach on, read as Tammuz is blessed, the Torah introduces a new kind of figure, tzaddikim who fell: the meraglim, Korach, Moshe at Mei Merivah, Zimri.
Following Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of place, time and soul, the Rav argues that just as there are fallen souls, the Nephilim, there are fallen times, and the Three Weeks are such days.

Moshe told the meraglim to 'dig' because, per the Rama MiPano, the letters before those of 'anavim' spell the name of the Satan: these are the Satan's days, but good is hidden in them for one who digs.
The Three Weeks begin and end with Moshiach: on Shiva Asar B'Tammuz Rus conceived Oved, ancestor of Dovid, and Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av.
'Somech Hashem lechol hanoflim' equals Tammuz in gematria, since Tammuz has fallen to the ground, while Av is only bent over and matches 'zokef lechol hakefufim'.
Parshas Pinchas lists the korbanos of all the Yamim Tovim, read in the Three Weeks, because these days are destined to become holidays.
Lavan's soul was quickly rectified into Barzilai because of his righteous children and son-in-law, whose initials, Bilhah, Rachel, Zilpah, Leah and Yaakov, spell Barzilai.
The Rav rests the truth of the Torah not on miracles a person must take on trust but on a public event: millions heard Hashem speak at once, and an event seen by so many cannot be denied.
He reads the mitzvah that every Jew write a sefer Torah as a test of truth: the identical Torah given to everyone described events the whole generation had seen itself, so it could be checked by all.
He points out that those who received the sefer Torah had been children under twenty in the wilderness and were now grown men who remembered everything that had happened.
He argues that a teaching that lets people eat whatever they want would be easily accepted, so the acceptance of a Torah full of hard obligations itself shows its truth.
The Megillah is read a second time because only after reaching its end does one understand how each detail at its beginning was part of the miracle; the second reading is read with that knowledge.
The Rav applies the Megillah model to all of Jewish history from Yetzias Mitzrayim until today: every part of it is a part of the miracle.
The hatred of the nations toward the Jews comes from envy, because they see that the Jew is better, as with Yosef's brothers; and despite that hatred they cannot swallow the Jews up.

Yitzchak and Yishmael were brothers, yet Yishmael's descendants number over three hundred million while the Jews number about fifteen million; this smallness was itself foretold, and the small people is the one that endures.
The Septuagint, translated by the elders long before the churban, preserves the Torah's text from that time, so the claim that passages were written in later cannot stand.
Other peoples' claims to be the best are simply laughed at; only the Jews' claim to be chosen provokes the nations, because they know in their hearts that it is true.

Since the nations cannot themselves become Jews and accept the Torah, their recognition turns into jealousy, and jealousy into hatred, as with Yosef's brothers; this is the root of the persecutions of the exile.

The admissions of Mark Twain, Tolstoy and President Adams are themselves a fulfillment of the pesukim that the nations will call Israel wise and will walk by its light; those gentiles with a point of truth concede it.
Spain, once the mightiest nation, sank into insignificance after it expelled its Jews, showing that the nations' greatness came from Jewish minds.
The Torah's warning that the land would be desolate is also a guarantee: for two thousand years no other people could settle it, and it flourishes only when the Jews return.
The Rav sees the change in Eretz Yisroel within a few decades, from desolation to fruitfulness and wealth, as the Gemara's revealed sign of the end, a wonder seen with one's own eyes.
Asaf calls the psalm of the Churban a song because the destruction of the building was itself a Father's mercy: had the anger not fallen on wood and stone, the whole nation would have been wiped out.
Avimi, whose name spells 'days of Av', was the one to grasp this, and his father's name Avuha, with hey before vav, hints that the vav-to-hey order of the curses is temporary.
Esav's kibud av is greater than Yaakov's precisely because it is external: Yaakov speaks to his father in the second person and needs no special clothes, because real closeness needs no veneer.

The Gemara learns from goyim of Ashkelon because the Pelishtim there did not know their true fathers; lacking the natural bond, they honored their fathers as kings, which a loving Jewish home would not do.

The question 'how far does kibud av reach' asks about the mitzvah's greatness, and the answer is that the Satan himself pushes the goyim to excel in it, which shows how much depends on it, including the rebuilding of the Beis HaMikdash.

Kibud av and the longing for Eretz Yisrael are one thing, since both are bonds to one's origin, and this is why Yaakov feared Esav for exactly these two mitzvos and why the reward of kibud av is long life in the land.

The idolatry in Tanach is no more a rejection of the Torah than the trials of the internet are for observant Jews today: both are a powerful yetzer hara in which people stumble while still keeping the Torah.
The present wave of baalei teshuvah is the drizzle that, as the Gemara describes, signals the coming downpour: the storm of teshuvah when Moshiach comes.
The proof lies not in any single prophecy but in their combination: each wonder contradicts the others and reason, like fact A contradicting fact B, so no historian could have extrapolated them.
Hatred of the Jews follows the natural dislike of the unlike: the greater the difference, the greater the hatred, and the separation between Israel and the nations is the greatest of all.
The German Jews' mistake was to think assimilation would end the hatred; instead it grew, and Hitler counted as Jews even those whose families had converted three generations earlier.
Unlike individual suicide bombers, whole Jewish communities chose death rather than conversion, a mesiras nefesh no other nation has shown.
Tanya's distinction is its form: the same foundations found scattered in the sefarim of the Maggid's other disciples are laid out in it as one continuous sequence, like a textbook.
The Rav reads 'ki karov' against its plain sense: yiras Shamayim is very hard, and it becomes near only for one who takes the long road, as in the Gemara's 'long-and-short' way.
The four letters of 'Tanya' are exactly the letters that form the future tense in loshon hakodesh, so the word itself speaks of 'I will be', the stance of one doing teshuvah.
Avraham's oath was not a sign of distrust in Eliezer but a provision for an emergency: an oath unlocks reserves a person cannot reach on his own.
Shevuah is tied to sheva (seven), sova (satiation) and shefa (flow), since beis and peh interchange; the Rav notes that the peh in a sefer Torah holds a white beis within it.
The oath given to the soul before birth works like Shabbos for the weekday traveler: a recharge of strength drawn from a higher place for a hard journey.
The Ra'aya Mehemna reads tzaddik v'ra lo not as a tzaddik who suffers but as a tzaddik whose evil belongs to him: it is inside him, yet he is its master, like a man leading a dog on a leash.
The angel cannot announce tzaddik or rasha because, unlike Hashem's knowledge, a decree spoken through an angel or written in the Torah would compel the outcome and take away free choice.
'Mazal' comes from flowing down, like 'nozlim': it is the channel through which a person's physical bounty descends from above, and 'gad', said at Gad's birth, means mazal for the same reason.
Rabbah, a man of truth who never interrupted his learning, could not have called himself a beinoni if a beinoni sometimes sins; this forces the definition that a beinoni never sins at all.
'Chalal' in Dovid's verse carries both meanings, empty and slain: he slew his yetzer hara through fasting, and so his heart was left empty of it.
Great tzaddikim can remember their earlier gilgulim because they have no free choice to lose; ordinary people do not remember, because such memory would make it impossible for them to sin.
Just as Hashem creates some tzaddikim complete, He also has reshaim born to be wicked, because He needs them to carry out His plan for creation.

The Rav reads the at-bash rule, that the first day of Pesach falls on the weekday of Tisha B'Av, as showing that Tisha B'Av is planted in the night of geulah, with the beitzah on the Seder plate as its sign.
Since Pesach assigns every festival its day, and Tisha B'Av takes its day from the first day of Pesach, Tisha B'Av is given the first seat among the Yamim Tovim, as Pesach's partner.
The months are fixed by the Sanhedrin, but the week is Hashem's own calendar; therefore the aveilus that begins with a week must first be allowed by Shabbos, the day of joy.
Tefillin are not worn on Tisha B'Av morning because one still hopes the day will become a Yom Tov, on which tefillin are not worn; only when most of the day has passed are they put on.
Since Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo, Tisha B'Av is a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres, and the meal before it on Shabbos is like Shlomo in his time, not like Yirmiyahu.

Just as Shemini Atzeres is the ninth day of the festival in the Diaspora, Tisha B'Av is the ninth day that will become a day of simcha; the Rav ties this to the Chasam Sofer's statement that a second Yom Tov will be kept after Moshiach comes.
Tu B'Av, seven days after Tisha B'Av like the end of shivah, is Tisha B'Av in a different garment: the Yom Tov of the ba'al teshuvah, and therefore greater than Pesach, the Yom Tov of the tzaddik.

Beyond guarding the fruit, the klipah is called a shell because it is a barrier that must be cracked to reach the fruit, and breaking it, like getting past the keruvim guarding Gan Eden, is the purpose of a person's life.

The Kotzker read 'eishes chayil' as either the Torah, to which a talmid chacham is wedded, or a physical wife: a person cannot dance at both weddings, just as one cannot stand on both sides of the fence of the sitra achra.
In the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable the walls were never real; so too, the tzaddik who breaks through finds at the end that the klipah that looked like a mountain was no more than a hair.

Eating meat makes it part of a person, but blood is the vessel of the animal's own animal soul, so eating it would strengthen his own animal soul; this, the Rav says, is why Hashem does not want it eaten.

Even the klipos come from Hashem's four-letter Name, so there are four of them, parallel to the four elements; the four coverings of a walnut picture them, with the thin skin eaten together with the nut standing for klipas nogah, which can become part of holiness.
Klipas nogah is like a translucent curtain on a window: one does not see the sun clearly, but its light comes through, unlike the other klipos, which make only darkness.

The four verbs of the Nusach Ari brachah against the wicked match the four kelipos: three call for uprooting and breaking, the impure kelipos, while the last, subduing, fits nogah, which is not destroyed but turned to the good.
Milah and periah mirror the kelipos: the layers cut away entirely are the three impure kelipos, while periah, which is not cut off but drawn back upward, is kelipas nogah turned toward the holy.

A goy's charity differs from a Jew's tzedakah not in the act but in its root: it is the animal kindness even predators show their young, exercised to satisfy oneself, while a Jew's mercy, even without conscious intent, comes from the side of kedushah.
Fire's root is in the moon, which is why fire rises and burns better at night, under the moon's rule; the Rav gives this as the reason the poskim require bedikas chametz at night.
Mockery is rooted in emptiness: a joke amuses in proportion to how far its statement is from reality, which is why leitzanus belongs to the element of air.
Sadness is a cousin of pride: it comes from a person feeling he ought to be something and is not, while true bitterness, like bitter herbs that stimulate the appetite, drives him to learn and daven.

The difference between olah and shelamim reflects the two kinds of animal soul: a goy can sacrifice something wholly to Hashem, but only a Jew can make his eating itself part of the offering, since only his animal soul, from nogah, can be turned to kedushah.
The halachah that a forbidden mixture is nullified in sixty is itself a glimmer of the days of Moshiach, since the impure klipos otherwise have no tikkun.
The nations' mercy is the same trait every animal has, so even their charity serves their own comfort, so that they can enjoy their meal knowing the poor man was fed.

Yaakov wept because a Jewish marriage is a bond of the soul that continues even after death, as the shared graves of the Machpelah show, and he saw a break in it when Rachel would not be buried with him.
Seven years seemed like a few days because Yaakov's labor for Rachel, like building a Sukkah, was itself part of serving Hashem, not a wait for his own desire.
The word zechus comes from zach, pure: a deed is a merit only when nothing of self-interest is mixed into it, and self-interest is the root of all evil in the world.

Because the mitzvos work in harmony like the organs of a body, stopping to eat at Shalosh Seudos of a Shabbos that is Tisha B'Av is not Tisha B'Av intruding on Shabbos but Shabbos's own highest hour of union, which is why shoes may stay on.
Yirmiyahu's protest over buying Chanamel's field came from knowing he was Shlomo reborn: whoever hoped to shelter in his merit was relying on the one most responsible for the Churban.
Eichah ends with 'chadesh yameinu kekedem' because Yirmiyahu, remembering how good it was to write Shir HaShirim, longed to be Shlomo again.

'Each man under his vine and fig tree' describes Shlomo's era not as abundance of food but as nezirus and Shabbos, since the vine teaches the measure of the nazir and the fig the measure for carrying on Shabbos.
The verse 'atah hor'eisa lada'as' read on Tisha B'Av and brought out again at Shemini Atzeres shows that the season from Tisha B'Av to Shemini Atzeres is one transformation of Yirmiyahu into Shlomo.
Shlomo, the strongest king in the world, had no sword in his own court and had to send for one, because he conquered with wisdom and peace, as Moshiach ben David will.
The shofar of Rosh Hashanah returns to Hashem the very breath He breathed into man: since that breath is beyond words, it is given back with a sound that has no words.
To show that every Jew, not only Adam, has the breath of Hashem, the Ba'al HaTanya brings not a verse but the blessing every Jew says each day, 'You breathed it into me'.
The mind cannot grasp G-dliness not because it is weak but because it is the wrong sense, as no ear, however strong, can hear a painting.
A Jew perceives G-dliness through his soul, not his mind, and sin is what insulates him from that soul.
The heel feels least because it is farthest from the head, the source of all feeling; so the last generation before Moshiach, the heel, hardly feels anything in Yiddishkeit.
The last word of Krias Shema corresponds to the lowest limb, and there the word emes is not written in the passage: at the bottom of the heel, truth is not seen.
The Rav reads Hashem's question to Iyov, 'where were you when I founded the earth', as asking in which part of Adam haRishon's body the person was, since all souls were in him.

Baking challah for Shabbos on Erev Shabbos repairs, on the very day of the sin, Chavah's spoiling of Adam who was the challah of the world, and through the secrets of Shabbos it puts blessing into the whole week.

The custom of cutting nails and hair on Erev Shabbos mirrors the souls of Adam's nails and hair: on the 'Erev Shabbos' of history, before Moshiach, such souls are cut off, as the Ba'al Shem Tov was told about the Frankists.
The halachic sign that hair and nails show a full nine months reveals the process of hishtalshelus: the same drop that first became the brain needs the longest change to become nails.
Yisrael are compared to the children of Kush because, as with black and white skin, the difference between souls lies only on the surface, the 'skin', while underneath they are all equal.

The Tanya, written in loshon hakodesh and careful with every word, switches to an Aramaic word for 'the end of all levels', because Targum, which equals tardemah (deep sleep) in gematria, is itself a low level.

The future tense of 'Yismach Hashem b'ma'asav' shows that even Hashem's joy in His creation is completed only with Moshiach; Shlomo, who attained all he wished, lived ahead of his time in that future.
Since Yirmiyahu is a gilgul of Shlomo, the day of Yirmiyahu is a hidden form of the day of Shlomo: Tisha B'Av would have been the completion of Shemini Atzeres.
The Rav reads 'tzom hachamishi' with rearranged letters as 'tzom hamashiach', tying the fast of Av to Moshiach's day.
The seudah before Tisha B'Av on Shabbos is like the meal of Shlomo in his time, meaning Shlomo as he was Shlomo, not as he became Yirmiyahu.
The Rav reads the Mishnah's 'go out and see King Shlomo' as a call to behold Yirmiyahu transformed back into Shlomo, wearing garments of salvation and kingship.
Reading the Shemini Atzeres maftir immediately before Yirmiyahu's first haftarah of the Three Weeks is itself a message that Tisha B'Av must be turned into Shemini Atzeres.
Din is not the opposite of chesed's purpose but its condition: without limitation the recipient cannot take in the giving at all.
The names Yisrael and Yaakov mark the two ends of one rope: 'li rosh', the head, and 'ekev', the heel; and the yud of Yaakov is the point from which every letter begins.
A Jew who sins in a way that is an aveirah for his level, even without the literal act, is counted by Chazal as that sin; this is how the Rav reads 'as if he worshipped idols'.
The am ha'aretz who supports the talmid chacham is like the weekdays that provide for Shabbos: it looks as if he gives, but the blessing actually flows from the talmid chacham to him.
Even one who quarrels with a talmid chacham still draws from him, but from behind, in a hidden way mixed with the sitra achra.
In sleep the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's soul rose to receive secrets of Torah, and to keep 'shivisi Hashem lenegdi tamid' with the part left in the body he slept facing the Name on the mezuzah.
The order of the generation mirrors the banners in the desert: each Jew draws through his officer of ten, fifty and a hundred, up to the tzaddik hador, whether or not people know who he is.

Pharaoh's complaint 'until when do you refuse to be humbled' means, with the Sfas Emes, that failing to be humble is one thing, but not even wanting to be humble cuts the last thread; a desire to have a desire still binds a Jew to Hashem.

The resentment of the wicked toward an ehrlicher Jew is envy, born of knowing deep down that he is better; that very pain is a hidden form of hachnaah, which is how they still draw from him 'from behind'.
Dovid was not punished for sins for which Shaul was, because Dovid's body came from a coarse root through Lot's daughter, and Heaven measures a person against what can be expected of him.
When a Hungarian Jew hates a Polish Jew, it is the bit of 'goy' each absorbed from his country's mazal that hates, not the Jew himself.

Later generations have more refined bodies, purified by generations of mesiras nefesh in galus, though earlier generations had greater souls; this is why sins recorded in Tanach seem incomprehensible to us.

The four letters of Hashem's Name, spelled out in full, become ten letters, so the Name is four in general and ten in detail; the Rav links this to a reshus hayachid, the domain of the One of the world, defined by four and ten.
Chochmah is the bricks and binah the building made of them, which is why binah is named for binyan; a sudden original insight is chochmah, and working it out with questions and answers is binah.
The letters of aryeh, lion, the king of fearsome creatures, equal gevurah in gematria, since gevurah is the recoil of fear.
A great scholar who can master whole masechtos and say a pilpul may still not be a ba'al daas, because daas means the responsibility to let the mind govern one's impulses.
Tiferes is not chesed and not gevurah but a new third thing born of their blend, like the effect when two people play the same niggun a few notes apart in harmony.
Hod gives existence through yielding: in a hurricane the strong tree breaks while the blade of grass survives because it bends.
Each of the ten makkos revealed one sefirah of creation, and makkas bechoros, striking the firstborn, revealed keser, the very beginning.

The Rav reads the trop pair over 'alpayim ba'amah' as the two months: kanei parah, sounding like a pazer (scattering), is Av, and yerach ben yomo, its servant note, is Nisan, which supplies Av what it lacks.
He links the cow's horn being 'gildei gildei' to the kanei parah note: a segmented horn is pizur, the opposite of the shofar's achdus, and so it belongs to Av, the month of galus.

Using the kashrus concept of ben yomo, he explains the Shelah's statement that every day of Nisan is like Rosh Chodesh: Nisan is literally a 'yerach ben yomo', a month whose freshness never fades, mirroring Hashem's love that never grows stale.

He offers a reason of pshat for kashering Midian's vessels even when they are not ben yomo: Midian tried to make Hashem's ever-fresh love stale, so Hashem's hatred of Midian stays ever-fresh, and their vessels are always treated as ben yomo.
He says that shofar, spelled with the full names of its letters, equals in gematria 'kanei parah yerach ben yomo': the shofar unites the two and lets Av enjoy the blessings of Nisan.
The same soul, Betzalel then Shlomo then Yirmiyahu, built the Mishkan and the Beis HaMikdash, wrote Shir HaShirim and then Eicha, and the Rav says it will again become Shlomo and sing Shir HaShirim.

'Alpayim ba'amah' is the techum Shabbos, a measure of distance; in the three weeks the pazer of scattering becomes distance from Hashem, yet under the kanei parah lies the yerach ben yomo of nearness.
Even daas has a kelipah side (Amalek is called the daas of kelipah), but its root is good; only the middos are truly 'double', which is why the mochin alone are called mothers.

The forty lashes correspond to the forty levels of Hashem's Name a sinner blemished; he receives only thirty-nine because the tenth level of the yud, the innermost point that never consented to the sin, was not blemished.

The thirty-nine melachos grew out of the thirty-nine curses of Adam HaRishon, who was meant to have a constant Shabbos in Gan Eden; there is no fortieth because the innermost point was not touched by the sin.
Purim is a Yom Kippur of eating and drinking: Yom Kippur fasts to repair the eating from the Eitz HaDaas, while Purim, which is even higher, reaches the point that sin never touched.
The haftorah of Yehoash, who was saved in the Kodesh HaKodashim yet later sinned against it, is read on Shekalim to show that the Kodesh HaKodashim is not reached by sin.

The yud stands for chochmah because it is a bare point and every letter begins with it; the sudden flash of a new idea, in Torah or in science, is nearly prophecy, and binah is the work of developing it.
'Koach mah' means a power of nothingness, like Moshe's 'what are we', a humility greater than Avraham's 'dust and ashes' or David's 'a worm', since dust and a worm are still something.

The Rav presents the dispute between the Ba'al HaTanya and the other students of the Maggid not as a question of truth, since both views are true, but of which path to teach the masses: the Ba'al HaTanya demanded that ordinary people learn chochmah of G-dliness, while the others may have done so themselves but worked differently with the public.
He likens this to the dispute between Yosef and his brothers: whether to work with a few strong, great people in a concentrated way or with many, where each receives only a little.

The same divide, he says, separated the Ba'al HaTanya from Rabbi Mottel of Chernobyl: whether the Rebbe lifts up the chassidim, who bind themselves to him, or whether the chassidim must lift themselves.

The Rav finds the Tanya's path in the order of the brachos of Krias Shema: Yotzer contemplates the luminaries and the angels and brings fear, Ahavah Rabbah brings love, and only then come Shema and Vehaya, accepting the yoke of Heaven and of the mitzvos.

Shechem's intense words of desire for Dinah came from a hidden spark of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon within him that longed for its own kind; from this the Rav learns that a Jew, a part of G-d above, must long for Hashem in the same way.
He adds that the love-language came specifically through Shechem because Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon was a devoted gabbai tzedakah, a spark of chesed, and chesed is love.
Fulfilling a mitzvah once in thought, speech and deed already completes that limb of the soul; the danger of gilgul is a limb never completed at all.
Klal Yisrael is itself one body with 613 parts: each Jew is a limb of it, the one who learns its head and the one who davens its heart, so a person shares in the mitzvos he himself cannot do.
Following Sefer Yetzirah's world, year and soul, the Rav finds a 'tzaddik' in each: the tzaddik of the generation in souls, Yerushalayim in place, and Yom Kippur, together with Purim, in time.
The doubled 'achas bashanah' in the passuk alludes to two days that are really one: Yom Kippur and Purim.
'Doresh tov le'amo, vedover shalom lechol zar'o' refers not only to Mordechai's own generation but to all his spiritual descendants until today: he comes into every Jew's Purim.
