Since Amalek attacked the weak ones at the rear, Purim, the victory over Amalek, belongs especially to the weak and simple; the great ones have Shavuos, Pesach and the Yamim Nora'im.
Without sod, pardes is missing a letter and becomes 'pered', a mule; a Jew must know that the Torah has an inner dimension and strive to reach it.
The Mishnah names its Tannaim not only to know who said what: a tzaddik who learns lishmah becomes so holy that his very name is Torah, so saying 'Rabbi Akiva' is like saying a word of Torah.

A name in loshon hakodesh is the creature's essence: Adam saw from each animal's nature which letters it was made of, and a sinner loses his name, which is why Zimri and Cozbi are named only after Pinchas killed them.
The holier a thing is, the more easily it is spoiled; wine, which stands for the reward of Olam Haba, is spoiled even by a gentile's look, showing how holy that reward is.
World events like Vashti's death or Nixon's resignation are reported with worldly reasons, but their true cause is the tzaddikim and Klal Yisrael, which will become clear only when Moshiach comes.
The heavenly calls to teshuvah go out every day, and the receiver that picks them up is a Jewish heart; a sudden urge to do teshuvah is the heart catching one of them.
Machlokes comes from each person's private interests; one who learns lishmah has none, which is why he can love everyone, as all will in the days of Moshiach.
Loving a fellow Jew does not divide one's love of Hashem, since every Jew's neshamah is a part of Hashem; this is why 'love your fellow as yourself' ends with 'I am Hashem'.

The Tanya calls Torah a garment, not food, because it is speaking of the mitzvah side of learning: in a mitzvah the act is the main thing and Torah accompanies it, while in learning Torah is the main thing and the mitzvah accompanies it.
The minhag that a tallis has no sleeves or shape for any limb reflects that tzitzis includes all the mitzvos, so its garment surrounds the whole body rather than a single limb.
That clothing costs more than food mirrors the spiritual order: Torah, the soul's food, is free and always available, while mitzvos, its garments, cost money and are not always at hand.
Learning Torah clothes a person twice: as a mitzvah that includes all 613, and through the mind itself, which is clothed in the Torah it grasps.
The burdens that kept the Rambam from writing more were Hashem's way of lengthening his life: had he been free, so great a masmid would have finished his measured portion of Torah while still young.
A soul's level of Torah does not alone set its greatness: a drop of wine is worth less than a barrel of orange juice, and the Beis Yosef was a giant soul of pshat, greater than a small soul of sod.

Parshas Parah falls on the last Shabbos of Adar, the lowest point of the year's order, because the parah is a tikkun for the lowest, which is why only its pshat and halachos can be learned; in this it is akin to Purim.

Intellect fails to grasp Hashem not because it is too weak but because it is the wrong sense, as ears cannot paint a picture, and a watch cannot understand the watchmaker; even a 'billion IQ' would not help.
The halachos are like a lead container around radioactive material: the garment is what lets a person hold Hashem's very presence in his mind and hands without being harmed.
Because the holiness is so great, it needs the coarsest garments, so the most worldly halachos, such as the laws of damages and of plotting witnesses, hold the highest light.
The laws of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah are all found in the sedras read during Sefirah, because purity and holiness of the middos are the foundation for receiving the Torah.
The passuk says 'pihu' rather than 'piv' because 'peh' and 'fah' join into one word, showing a union so strong that the two became one, as when a Jew learns Torah.

Hashem's 'right hand' embracing the person means the Torah, which comes from chesed and water, the right side, as the first of the seven voices of Kabbalas Shabbos is 'the voice of Hashem upon the waters'.
The Rav reads 'baruch shebachar bahem uvemishnasam' not only as praise of Hashem but as praise of the talmid who chose to devote his life to these Chachamim and their Torah.
The halachic fact that saying a Chacham's name is not a hefsek in learning Torah shows that his name itself has become Torah.
The oversized fruit of Eretz Yisrael in the meraglim's time came from the abnormal amount of Torah being learned in the Midbar, since every good word builds and blesses the world.

Unlike an English word such as 'lion', which is only an agreed label, the Hebrew name aryeh is made of the very letters that give the lion its existence and character; a Tanna's name likewise is the substance of his neshamah.
Saying 'Rabbi Meir' before his halacha is more than honor: it draws part of his neshamah into the learner, just as Moshe Rabbeinu was endowed with the power of a holy name when he said it.
The more holy something is, the more easily it is spoiled, as with levels of tumah and with wine; this is why the Olam Haba of one who learns Torah lishmah may not be seen at all.

The Rav reads the Mishnah of the four kinds of students as a warning to those who visit many rebbes and pick out precisely what is not to be imitated, such as a tzaddik's eating, sleeping or anger, whose hidden reasons they do not see.

Different customs about dress while learning come from the climate where each group's rebbes lived; each follows how his rebbe behaved in his place, while the shared principle is derech eretz for Torah.

Torah has two aspects: as a vessel it draws G-dliness only when learned properly, but in itself it always keeps some holiness, like a dead body that still bears a trace of the soul, which is why people pray at the graves of tzaddikim.

The price of an esrog shows that G-dliness is clothed in it: no thought can grasp Hashem, yet one holding the lulav and esrog holds G-dliness in his hand and spreads it to all sides of the world when he shakes them.

Although the secrets of the Torah are higher because they have fewer garments, a Gemara or halacha understood clearly gives a stronger unity, since even angels cannot fully grasp sod, while a physical halacha can be truly understood.
R' Pinchas of Koretz explains that mitzvos cost money and Torah is free because Torah is bread, a basic necessity whose price is low, while mitzvos are garments, which are expensive.
Because kedushah and impurity are evenly balanced, a person cannot tip the scale by himself; when he takes Hashem along, Hashem becomes the deciding weight.
Kelipas noga is like the thin brown skin of a walnut: removed alone it is inedible, but eaten together with the nut it becomes food.
The Masorah's siman 'noga' for the 64 pesukim of Parshas Kedoshim shows that the parsha is about raising kelipas noga to kedushah.
The halachah that the Bnei Keturah have milah but not periah has an inner reason: periah corresponds to kelipas noga, which a gentile cannot elevate.
A sefirah is named for transparency, like a window that lets light through, and so expresses bittul; impurity's powers are 'crowns' because each one claims to be king.
A child and an adult have the same middah of chesed; what differs is the intellect that gives birth to it, which directs the love to small or to large things.
The Kotzker Rebbe read the Targum's 'l'tzad' as two sides of a fence: one who wishes to stand at Sinai must be entirely on the other side from desire, and this is the meaning of sitra achra.
Ten is written as a one with a zero: below ten there is not yet full bitul, and at ten the many become 'one' again, the zero nullified to the one.
The four compartments of tefillin are learned specifically from foreign languages, because their task is to stand against the impure klipos and make the sitra achra submit.
The minyan is learned from the wicked meraglim precisely to show that only the good within each Jew joins with the others; their evil never combined.
The Aron took up no space in the Kodesh HaKodashim because something wholly nullified to Hashem does not 'occupy space', while the ba'al ga'avah, who does, leaves no room for Hashem.
The shape of the human face forms Hashem's name: the two eyes are two yuds and the nose a vav, twenty-six in all, and the mouth is a patach, the vowel of chochmah.
The sitra achra is sustained from the waste left after the good of food is separated, which is the 'behind' from which it receives, and its existence in this world is like the exile of the Shechinah.
The four layers of the walnut parallel the four klipos: three are thrown away, while the thin dark skin is eaten with the nut and nullified, like klipas nogah, which is subdued rather than destroyed.
Navos's death was not a punishment for a sin but the removal of a life that no longer served its mission, like a worker dismissed for sitting idle even though he stole nothing.
Objects have a mission too: the grape is meant to become wine for Kiddush and zemiros, so Navos's unused vineyard itself accused him and was taken from him.
Music, poetry and marriage share one root: each is a matching of parts that belong together, which is why a chasunah has song and why the vineyard, source of song, is also the place of matches.
That Achav obtained the vineyard proves it held a part of his soul; one who takes his own portion dishonestly would have received it honestly had he waited, and now he loses it.
The same vineyard of song that Achav seized became his path to teshuvah, because song stands next to teshuvah; the rebuke over the vineyard moved him where the fire on Har HaKarmel did not.
The difference between Yirmiyahu's 'from the king of Bavel' and Melachim's 'from the king' reflects hester panim versus revealed Providence: the true King of Bavel is Hashem.
A meal is a guest that traveled from the field through the mill, bakery and store to a person's table, and should be received with kavanah.
The vav that appears only before 'nogah' in Yechezkel's list shows that nogah is a separate category from the three impure klipos, like the fourth peel of a nut that is eaten together with the fruit.

Following his rebbi, Reb Feivel Mendlowitz, the Rav explains that only olos are accepted from gentiles because a gentile's eating cannot be for the sake of Heaven, while the eating of shelamim is itself part of the korban.
The Jews offered nesachim from the very fruit the meraglim brought to slander the land, showing that a Jew can turn even something used for sin to good.
Avraham threw dust at the kings on erev Pesach because dust is bitul: as one nullifies chametz by treating it as dust, one nullifies the klipos by ignoring them.

Because the world was created through the Torah, the chachamim's psak shapes reality itself: the anatomy matches the Rambam because the halachah follows him, and a chacham can change nature through a chiddush where a tzaddik cannot.
Nogah is called a scale: the same permitted act tips to holiness or to the impure klipos depending on whether it is meant for the sake of Heaven.

The Rav contrasts the Nefesh HaChaim's lishmah, learning in order to know what the Torah says, with the Tanya's lishmah, binding the soul to the G-dliness in the Torah, and says these are different levels.
Nowadays a person holds sparks of many souls, so after a few years his desire moves from one area of learning to another, as he finishes repairing one part of his soul and moves to the next.
The 'secret' of every Jew is a grace he holds before Hashem that no other Jew has and that he himself cannot name; if he thinks he has found it, that is a sign he has not.
The passuk calls Pinchas 'son of Elazar son of Aharon HaKohen' a second time because once the souls of Nadav and Avihu entered him, he became also a son of Aharon himself.

The people who were tamei were people who had dealt with Nadav and Avihu and received a spark of their souls; that spark of the inner Torah made them feel that tumah could not separate them from all other Jews.
Learning not lishmah leads to lishmah because the angels see only the outside, while Hashem sees the hidden point in the Jew that learns lishmah even then.

Speech of Torah is breath, which has almost no substance but surrounds the whole body, so learning Torah is a garment over all of a person, like tzitzis and sukkah and unlike mitzvos tied to one limb.

The Rav explains the Satmar Rav's answer, that korbanos could be taken from Egyptian animals because on the night of Yetzias Mitzrayim all the idolatry was utterly destroyed, as a sample of the end of days, when evil will be nullified at its root.

A person who cannot yet long for Hashem should at least long to long, a will to have a will; when it comes from the depth of the heart, it draws a light of the future and can uproot even the three impure kelipos already in galus.
The present wave of teshuvah is like the drizzle that comes before a long, heavy rain: a sign that the great teshuvah of the days of Moshiach is near.

The Gemara's 'one of us is like two of them' is seen plainly in that nearly all the leading rabbanim and roshei yeshivah of Eretz Yisrael came from abroad, because one who tears himself out of galus arrives with a greater thirst.

Since the sin is what made him a ba'al teshuvah, it becomes part of his greatness; for the same reason, one who sins planning to repent cannot elevate the sin, because there the teshuvah caused the sin.

The Torah writes wasted seed only by hint and not as an explicit prohibition precisely because it is easier to repair: since the Torah is truth, an explicit lav would leave no room for the tzaddikim's advice for its tikkun.
The Rav holds that a wish is only the reason a person turns to Hashem; once he turns, the purpose of the tefillah is the closeness itself, so it succeeds even if the wish is not granted.
Asking Hashem for something insignificant, like a maid not quitting, is not a lowering of one's avodah but the peak of emunah, a declaration that Hashem controls every detail.

Unlike the angels and the creatures of Perek Shirah, who sing at fixed times, a Jew needs no appointment: he may sing to Hashem whenever he calls to Him, which is why the words 'tzafra' and 'ramsha' are named for the singing of the birds and creeping things.
The Rav's Rebbe read the Ba'al Shem Tov's 'teivah' as the ark of Noach: the world is a flood of turmoil, and the word of davening is the refuge in which a person is saved.
A sudden good davening may be the reward of a nisayon a person withstood a day or a week before; it is a gift, a free taste, but lasting good davening must be earned.

The Rav reads the Gemara's twelve thousand pairs of talmidim as chavrusas in which the stronger partner looked down on the weaker; the cure is knowing that every Jew carries a hidden secret no other Jew can accomplish.
The view that nothing is truly 'reshus' and everything is either a mitzvah or a sin fits the Tanya: the thing itself stands on the scale, and only what one does with it decides.
The Creator made a composition and wrote a commentary on it: the world is the composition and the Torah is its commentary, so only one who learns Torah understands what the world is.
The wells Avraham and Yitzchak dug are the search for the 'well of living water', the point of G-dliness inside earthly things, and Yitzchak dug them as a path for all of Klal Yisroel in exile.
The Torah can tell at length of Yaakov tending Lavan's sheep, which no biographer would write of a great man, because one who learns with emunah knows these were not plain dealings.
Yitzchak blessed Yaakov with material bounty rather than Torah because the strength of the Avos was to enter material things and raise the holy sparks hidden in them.
The Torah cannot set how much a person should eat, because what is for Heaven's sake for one is too much for another; it can only forbid treif.
Even when the food itself rises through later Torah and tefillah, the imprint of the pleasure taken not for Heaven remains, and this is what chibut hakever removes.

Teshuvah out of love is a private arrival of Moshiach: just as in the days of Moshiach the sitra achra will be nullified, so in the small world of the one who returns out of love it is already nullified, which is why he can repair what for the world at large waits for Moshiach.
Since Hashem is reshus hayachid and the klipah is reshus harabim, hotza'ah is the heart of Shabbos, and Gehinnom and machlokes were created on the second day, when plurality began.
Kislev opens with Yaakov leaving Eretz Yisrael for reshus harabim, and the avodah of Chanukah is to light a candle in reshus harabim, making Har Eisav into Har Tziyon.
Chanukah's eight days come from Binah, eight levels above Malchus, and teshuvah out of love is Binah; so teshuvah out of love lifts a Jew to the very place Chanukah comes from.
A mamzer cannot be repaired in a moment because the klipah has dug itself into time through a nine-month process, so only sustained teshuvah can spread into the mamzer's body and cut off its life.

Halachic rulings follow Providence: the Mishnah Berurah's ruling that food eaten unknowingly or under coercion can be elevated was placed in his heart so that the cantonist children would not be left with a sealed heart unable to return.
The Tzemach Tzedek reads the Tanya through the laws of bracha acharonah: a bracha elevates the sparks in the food, so where no bracha may be said, the food has no elevation.
The imprint of permitted pleasure is like a stain that remains after washing: even teshuvah removes the kelipas noga, but the trace needs a stronger 'detergent', chibut hakever.
The two Gehinoms match two failures: fire for one who warmed himself to an active sin, snow for the coldness and laziness of neglecting a positive mitzvah.
Idle chatter is a drive of the middos that even animals share, barking and singing; secular wisdom is worse precisely because its impurity reaches the higher level of chabad.
Torah and secular wisdom are opposites: Torah must be learned lishmah and not as a spade, while secular wisdom may be learned only as a spade and never for its own sake.
The wisdom of the nations rises and falls opposite the sages of Torah, as zeh l'umas zeh; when the Torah's sages are gone, the nations' wise men also decline.
An aveirah cannot be done lishmah, so a good intention cannot permit studies that require learning heresy, which comes from the three impure kelipos rather than kelipas noga.

The Rav reads the heel as both the generation's weakness and its greatness: it feels nothing and stands in the dark, but the whole body rests on it, so the last generation carries all the generations before it.

Since a test is a promotion, the tenth test should be the hardest; the Rav sharpens this into a question, because the fire of Ur Kasdim, faced for a G-d Avraham had never seen, seems far harder than obeying a G-d who spoke to him.

The difficulty of the Akeidah was not the act but the distance: at Ur Kasdim Avraham jumped into the fire with fervor, while at the Akeidah he went with a heavy heart, holding to emunah when Hashem seemed far.
Avraham could not see an answer that a child learning Rashi knows, because in the time of a nisayon the answer is hidden; the Rav applies this to the questions of his own generation.

Through the Ramban's rule, the Rav makes the Akeidah the pattern of the last exile: just as it was Avraham's last and hardest test, the final generation's test is to hold on to emunah when Hashem seems distant.
The Rav says each generation has its own mitzvah, and the mitzvah of this generation is emunah.
The verse about Pharaoh says his heart was 'turned over', not merely bent: in the rasha gamur the good itself has become evil, the mirror image of the tzaddik gamur.
Tzaddikim gemurim could remember their earlier gilgulim because they have no bechirah left to lose; others are not given that memory, since remembering would take away their bechirah.
Love of Hashem and hatred of evil are measured against each other: whoever does not hate evil completely cannot love Hashem completely, except in elevated moments of davening.
Like the fragrance of a korban that rises up, the bnei aliyah take the evil itself and raise it to such a level that it ascends to Heaven, where no evil can exist.
The greatest tzaddikim serve Hashem not even to quench their own thirst for Him, but to do kindness with the Shechinah in exile, like a son toiling to redeem his parents.
The brain, though the seat of the Godly soul, is driven by the heart: the blood the heart sends up activates the brain to devise ways of fulfilling the heart's wishes.
Following the Midrash, Pharaoh's 'heavy heart' means his heart was a liver, all blood: he could admit his sin but had no heart to fear Hashem and send the people out.

The order of the morning blessings embodies the Tanya's teaching: Birchas Yotzer's contemplation of the luminaries and the angels gives birth to the love of Ahavah Rabbah, as intellect gives birth to emotion.

Eating matzah with appetite is 'stealing' the yetzer hara's drive for the mitzvah; without it the mitzvah would lack its fire and completeness, which is the meaning of serving 'with both your inclinations'.
Beyond 'avodas avodah', service by toil, there is 'avodas matanah', a gifted delight in serving Hashem that even a simple person can be granted at high moments.
Subduing the yetzer hara is like a conquering king who has not made the defeated king his friend but holds him as a prisoner, and this every Jew can achieve.
The yetzer hara's own joy, like the harlot in the Zohar's parable, is that the person not be seduced, so that even the yetzer hara is subservient to Hashem.
The shortening of the 400 years of Mitzrayim to 210 shows that even a decree written explicitly in the Torah need not be fulfilled in full, so the birth pains of Moshiach too can be reduced to fear.
In single hiding the child still knows his father is nearby and cries out to him; in hiding within hiding he does not even know there is anyone to call, which is the state before Moshiach.
The year is a miniature of all time: Nisan, from 'nes', a raised flag, is revealed miracle, while Adar, the end of the year, is like Esav born cloaked, with its miracles wrapped in nature.
The gossip about Vashti that a yeshiva boy rightly refused to hear became part of the Megillah, read with a brachah and indispensable to it; in the same way today's news is part of Hashem's plan.
Bitachon itself pierces the concealment: one who tells Hashem he relies on Him comes to see Hashem's care, breaking the hester panim.
The lack of great leaders whose word can be relied upon as the word of Hashem is itself foretold for the time before Moshiach, leaving the Jews to rely on Hashem alone.

The Rav explains that a sinful thought is 'light' only in how easily one falls into it; in its damage it is graver than a deed, because a deed blemishes Asiyah while a thought reaches Beriah, up to the Throne of Glory.

He maps the three garments onto the worlds: a good deed illuminates the world of Asiyah, a good word the higher world of Yetzirah, corresponding to ruach, and a good thought the world of Beriah; their opposites blemish those same worlds.

Even the rasha v'ra lo is not cut off: the good he drove out stays around him as a makif, as if standing at the door asking to be let back in, which is why he would still give his life rather than serve idols.
When ten Jews gather, their souls merge into one and draw down a holiness that nine tzaddikim cannot, which is why the surrounding kedushah of even a rasha v'ra lo allows him to complete the ten.

The Ba'al HaTanya called his work a book for beinonim because becoming a tzaddik cannot be taught; one must be born for it. But refusing ever to obey the yetzer hara is in every Jew's hands, so every Jew can be a beinoni.

'Never sinned and never will' does not mean literally never; it is like a report card on his present state: one who sinned and did complete teshuvah can be a beinoni, and even great people who later fell were judged by the level they stood on.

The beinoni is like a court where two judges sit: the evil judge may voice his opinion, but the beinoni listens only to the judge seated in the right chamber of the heart; during proper davening the evil one may not even speak.

The Rav distinguishes between being judged a tzaddik and being a tzaddik as a title: on the day of judgment the beinoni will be called a tzaddik because he never sinned, but by definition he is not one, since the desire for evil remains.

Foreign thoughts during davening are explained as the keruvim and the flaming sword at the gates of the heavenly chambers pushing out one who is not worthy to enter; the soul feels being thrown out, and the body feels it as stray thoughts.
The Gemara's three names of the yetzer, passer-by, guest and master, describe the stages of letting it in; the beinoni keeps it a passer-by at the door and never lets it sit down in his house.

Against those who say darkness is only an absence, the Rav holds that spiritually darkness is a creation; that a little light nevertheless drives away much darkness shows the inherent dominion of light, and likewise of holy thought over the folly of the kelipah.
When the yetzer sees it cannot get a servant of Hashem to sin, it tries to make him feel important after a good davening, and that thought alone can cause the davening to be rejected.

The Rav reads Yosef's kindness to his brothers as emunah: since the suffering had to come from somewhere, Yosef preferred that it come through holy tzaddikim, and he even owed them thanks for the atonement it brought.
Among created forces good and evil are always in balance, but the Creator of both light and darkness stands above that balance and joins the side of good, so the one on the side of good must win.
Spiritual darkness is a real entity, not merely the absence of light, yet it flees completely from light because light is Hashem's life-giving power, which nothing can neutralize.
Following the Maggid Meisharim, the tzaddik receives full credit at the judgment even though Hashem helped him, because he had the choice to be bad and chose good.

One who learns Torah lishmah all day is in a constant state like Krias Shema and tefillah, so he may never feel a desire for sin, yet his yetzer is only asleep; this is how Rabbah could think he was a beinoni.

The Chasam Sofer reads 'and this shira shall answer before it' as the remedy for troubles that contradict each other: when any prayer for one trouble worsens the other, Torah protects without taking a side.
Praying for peace is itself a problem in wartime, since the war may be the beginning of the geulah; this is what makes war a bee-and-scorpion trouble.
Achashverosh rising to power outside the normal rules shows Hashem's hand in appointing him, and the Rav sees the same in Bush becoming president with fewer popular votes.
The forcing of the Torah at Sinai is like the involuntary muscles of the heart and lungs: what life depends on is not left to a person's will.
Chizkiyahu's calm sleep on the night Sancheirev was destroyed is read into the passuk of singing on their beds: the Jews fight with their mouth, not with missiles.
The Rav defines truth by permanence: worldly pleasure is like a 'chalal', one slain, empty of content, and leaves a void, while joy in a Yom Tov, a mitzvah or a blatt Gemara remains even afterward.

Yisrael begins with the letters that make it 'li rosh', a head, and Yaakov is 'akev', the heel, with the small yud as its point; so Yaakov binds all Jews from the highest to the lowest, who has nothing but the point of a Jew.
Because each board of the Mishkan is a level of Jews and Yaakov's attribute of truth passes through all of them, the same service can be falsehood for a higher person and truth for a lower one.
Following the Yismach Moshe, for a great servant of Hashem 'vachai bahem' means the life of the soul in Torah, so for him losing a mitzvah is death, and he may give his life for it.
For the beinoni, 'sfas emes tikon la'ad' means a truth that is packed away and waits for the next prayer, when with true preparation he can again keep the yetzer hara from disturbing him.

Without a bad thought the beinoni could not fulfil 'lo sasuru', so its coming is a chance for one of the Torah's greatest mitzvos, and pushing out a thought of idolatry breaks the root of the sitra achra.
The beinoni has 'ahavah betaanugim' only at moments, so when it is absent the desire for this world fills the place, since there is no vacuum.
The Rav reads 'oved' as present tense: the beinoni is called an oved because his service is an unfinished, ongoing war, whereas for the tzaddik 'oved Hashem' is a name, like the title 'chacham'.
Like a swimmer on vacation whose exertion is pleasure, one who feels the sweetness of avodah experiences long nights of learning as recreation, not toil; but not everyone merits this at all times.
Avraham Avinu's work on himself changed his very creation into a new kind of being, one who believes in Hashem; creation was completed only with him, and from him comes every Jew's hidden love.
One who made himself a masmid through effort was an oved during the struggle, but once it became second nature he is 'lo avado', living off the dividends of his earlier toil.

Forgetting comes from the sitra achra, whose root Samech-Mem equals 100; reviewing 100 times breaks its power, and the 101st time, beyond habit, brings one into the realm of Michael, whose name equals 101.
The donkey drivers charge double for going just past their limit because it is beyond their regular routine; so too, going even slightly beyond one's habit is the hardest and most valuable step.
The oath's two halves are not of equal weight: 'do not be a rasha' is fully in a person's hands, while 'be a tzaddik' is a charge to strive, since being a tzaddik is not given to free choice.

Truth is measured by the person's level: a passing feeling of loathing for worldly pleasure is not truth for a complete tzaddik, but for the beinoni it is his truth, since he can renew it tomorrow at davening or next Shabbos.

Dovid's harp played at midnight like a piano string vibrating in response to a tuning fork: Dovid's heart was tuned to the song of the tzaddikim in Gan Eden, so it awoke by itself, with no alarm clock.
An ibbur benefits both souls: the Jew can serve with a love and joy beyond his own level, and the departed tzaddik gets to do once more the mitzvah he longed for or was missing.
Haman's ten thousand talents of charity lost to the barley omer because a non-Jew's deed stays below, while a Jew's cheapest offering is lifted (tenufah) and multiplied in the upper worlds.
'Aseres' denotes a collective and multiplication while 'isaron' denotes division, as 'ishon' (the pupil) means a small person reflected in the eye.
The Rav explains the Rebbe's extreme opposition not as harshness but as fear that a false geulah would take the place of the true one in people's minds.
He measures the Rebbe's battle against the Rambam's definition of Moshiach: only a king of the house of David who brings Israel back to Torah and the whole world to serve Hashem fits that picture.
The Rav argues that the Rebbe's opposition protected even his opponents, who by their own admission planned with his reaction in mind.
He returns to his opening image: the sun is dim and the birds muffled now, until the day the sun shines bright with the announcement of Moshiach's coming.

The Rav reads King David's request to 'visit in His palace' as the plea of one who cannot always feel Hashem's sweetness to be at least an occasional guest, which Hashem grants every Jew at times of favor such as Shabbos and Yom Tov.
The Rav applies 'a daughter of so-and-so to so-and-so' to every giver and receiver, so that Hashem matches each talmid to the rebbe with whom his soul stood at Sinai.

Counting by 'names' rather than numbers shows that each Jew is an individual letter with its own place in the Torah, which is why Moshe and the Nesi'im, who knew what lies in each Jew, had to do the counting.

Gerim are the crowns on the Torah's letters: not letters themselves but attached to them, which is why Rabbi Akiva, from a family of gerim, expounded the crowns, while Moshe Rabbeinu, the root of the letters themselves, did not grasp his teaching.

The Gemara's rule that each line of a Sefer Torah holds thirty letters so 'lemishpechoseichem' fits three times hints that the Torah's letters are arranged in families, as Jewish souls are born into the family where their letter belongs.

The Rav maps the dispute onto the sefiros: Chabad spoke of the higher faculties, chochmah, binah and da'as, while the other chassidim emphasized the middos, love, fear and tiferes, and each follows his root.

Following the Yismach Moshe, the Rav explains that 'vachai bahem' means biological life for a simple person but spiritual life for a great one, so the same Torah demands different things according to each person's level, just as 'very near' does.

Spiritual life, like the heart's beat, is a pulse rather than a steady flow: every person must go up and fall back, and this explains how the Yismach Moshe could taste the Rambam's fear from a moment of katnus.
The tzaddikim felt intense love and fear because their pure souls had no 'insulation': like an electric current, it passes through only where nothing blocks it.
According to the Ba'al Shem Tov, the mountain held over Klal Yisrael at Sinai was not for that fiery generation but for later generations, who would have to force themselves to learn and serve.

Chazal chose the word 'metzarfah', joins, rather than 'it is as if he did it' as a second intention: it hints that Hashem joins the intellectual love of the mind to the physical deed, which by nature cannot be joined.

The order of davening follows Tanya's path: korbanos and ketores clear away the kelipos, birchos krias shema contemplate the greatness of creation and the angels, and only then can one say ahavah rabbah and accept the yoke of Heaven in Shema.
Reb Zusha took the peasant's words about the hay, 'you can but you do not want to', as a rebuke to himself, since raising the fallen hei is the avodah of Jews in exile.

On the level of remez, 'galu le'Edom' means Jews fell to the conduct of Edom, and the inner exile draws the outer one; the Shechinah in exile is the spark of G-dliness in a Jew held captive by his kelipah.

Avraham's tenth trial was not the self-sacrifice of the akeidah, since he had already let himself be thrown into the furnace on the strength of his mind alone, but the closing of his heart, seeing Hashem 'from afar'.
The meraglim's trial was the same as Avraham's tenth: their lack of feeling in Eretz Yisrael was a shell to be broken like a nut, not a sign against the land.
Tamuz and Av correspond to the two eyes, and as months given over to the sitra achra they are the time to break it with a broken spirit.
The Chazon Ish's parable: what matters is not holding one's old post but standing where the battle is now, so if children understand Ivrit they must be taught in it.
The small kaf in Avraham's weeping means that Sarah did not truly die for him: separated in body, they remain united in soul.
Sarah's levayah, the first in the Torah, is placed before the first shidduch in the Torah to teach what a Jewish marriage is: kedushah and eternity.
Avraham buying the Me'aras HaMachpelah was preparing a home for his continuing marriage, a passageway to Gan Eden where each couple lies side by side.
Rivka's jewelry, like a Jewish home, has a soul: the bracelets radiated Torah and the Luchos.
A person has a fixed allotment of toil and pleasure; he can choose to spend the toil on chesed and be spared it elsewhere.
Atzvus and atzlus (sadness and laziness) are the same thing at root: both come from the element of earth, the heaviest element, which is why a sad person has no drive to fight the yetzer hara.
The Tanya's 'at set times' is like a doctor's sign 'by appointment only': sadness over sins may come in only at its appointed time, never as a guest with its own key.
Following the method of related sounds, simcha is linked to leaning on someone and atzvus to being forsaken; idols are called atzabim because one who relies on them has nothing to lean on.
Mourning the Beis HaMikdash at Tikkun Chatzos means, inwardly, mourning the mikdash in each Jew's heart that was ruined by his sins, which is regret over them.
Suffering is like a costly wine such as port: it comes from a very high world, but it tastes bitter to one who is not a connoisseur, as the finest brandy tastes bitter to a child.

Atzvus pushes a person into taavos, because he cannot bear being dissatisfied and looks for some satisfaction, such as a piece of cake; this is why the yetzer hara brings on sadness in the middle of one's work.

The hidden love is not a feeling a Jew develops, but part of his very being, like the inherited instincts of animals: an ox craves grass and a lion meat because its parents did, not because it cultivated the desire.

Yaakov's shepherding of Lavan's flocks was the freeing of Jewish souls from the sitra achra; the Midrash's 600,000 sheep are the 600,000 souls, and the opinion of 600,000 flocks reflects that a whole group of Jews belongs to each letter of the Torah.
Every tzaddik has a counterpart in kelipah of matching strength, and when the tzaddik leaves the world his counterpart falls too; therefore Nimrod was killed the very day Avraham died.

Leah is the hidden aspect of the Shechinah and Rachel the revealed one; the hidden love in every Jew is the aspect of Leah, buried deep like Leah in the Me'aras HaMachpelah, and the avodah is to bring it to the revealed aspect of Rachel.

As blond hair hidden in a dark-haired father can appear again in his son, so the great soul-powers hidden in a simple Jew can be revealed in his child; this is how a simple Jew can father a great tzaddik.
Hashem sometimes has a very lofty soul born to an unlikely parent, as Avraham to Terach and David in a hidden way, so that the Satan will not foresee it and interfere until it is too late.
A Jew who guards his eyes makes them a merkavah: two times 'ayin' equals 260, ten times the Name of Hashem, which the Rav connects to 'ki sar liros' said of Moshe.

The Rav links the calendar to the Torah reading: the meraglim set out the week after Parshas Shlach, and that is exactly the week the summer travel season begins, so the parsha is a message to the traveler.
Every place a person reaches offers him a choice between mitzvos and aveiros, and his neshamah hears Hashem sending him there even when his physical ears do not.
A tree, a brook or a faucet may have waited hundreds of years for a Jew to come and make a bracha there; through the bracha the tree itself finds life and becomes a happy tree.
The Rav reads the word meraglim as coming from 'feet': all who use their feet to go places are meraglim and shluchim of Hashem.

Through the Avnei Nezer, the Rav reads the penalty of a bas Levi who remarried on false testimony as a demand of sensitivity: her tribe stayed bound to Hashem at the Egel, so she should have felt that her husband was alive.

From the Lechovitcher the Rav shows that a talmid truly bound to his rebbe feels the bond, and his distress comes from not knowing why it is gone; once the reason is known, the feeling is natural and there is nothing to lament.
Following the Kotzker, the Targum's 'to the side of' a woman shows that love of this world and love of Torah are two sides of one fence: a person can stand on either, never on both.

Losing one's bechirah is itself a punishment for not using it earlier, which the Rav applies to Pharaoh: his hardened heart at the plagues was the penalty for oppressing the Jews while he still had choice.

The Rav connects teshuvah tata'ah with the four species as the letters of Hashem's Name: the esrog is the last heh, and holding it apart from the lulav, as in the Rokeach's dream, is a separated heh that teshuvah reunites.
As long as the heh is apart from the Name, the forces of the sitra achra stay joined, like Rome that is full while Yerushalayim is ruined; teshuvah reverses it, so the sitra achra splits apart.

Chochmah is not cleverness but the 'koach mah', the unexplained first flash that a person receives as if from heaven and then builds out with binah, which is why the Chovos HaLevavos calls it close to prophecy.
Not grasping Hashem is not a weakness of the mind: the mind is simply not the organ for it, just as no improvement of eyesight would let a person see music.

'Pesi ya'amin lechol davar' is a quality, not a lack: before Hashem everyone is a 'pesi', and Dovid HaMelech's admission that he was like a beast before Hashem is itself what keeps him always with Him.

The proof that Jewish mesirus nefesh comes from the soul's root is that those who gave their lives were never indoctrinated and often did not even understand the Shema they cried out, unlike soldiers who are trained to die.
In loshon hakodesh, 'emunah' joins belief and faithfulness in one word, and so it works both ways: Hashem believes in and is faithful to the Jews just as they believe in Him.
'Mah titzak elai' hints that the rescue of Klal Yisrael as a whole does not depend on tefillah, since the nation is bound to Hashem at its root in atika.
Tu Bishvat is the yom tov of emunah: like a tree whose sap begins to rise in its roots while it still looks dead under the snow, emunah lives at the root, and so Parshas Beshalach is read around it.

The difference between Jewish and gentile self-sacrifice: gentiles die for falsehood only after being brainwashed, while Jews who were never trained give their lives because the soul's root in chochmah acts like an instinct.
A Jew sways in davening and learning because his soul, like a flame, pulls upward; the Rav ties this to the story of identifying a Jewish child by who sways over the Gemara.
Teva is a 'borrowed name' for the point where explanation ends; calling the soul's longing teva means it is rooted above reason.
Purim belongs to the lowest Jews: Adar is the lowest of the months and Adar Sheni lower still, and the drinking of 'ad delo yada' reveals what lies above daas even in the emptiest Jew.
The 'Canaani' is called a merchant because kelipah's kindness is circular: the merchant gives only so that it comes back to him, while holy chesed goes out to give.
In the sitra achra the order is reversed: the female is stronger than the male, and the Rav connects this to the gentile custom of 'ladies first'.

Shirah means harmony: beings who are not at peace in their feelings cannot sing together, so the malachim's love for each other is what makes their song possible, and the Yidden who sang at the sea in their place needed that same love.
Hashem creates only what He likes, so nothing in the world lacks a reason to be loved; if Hashem appreciates it, a person should too.
The king who begged two devoted friends to take him into their friendship illustrates that where friends love each other as themselves, Hashem wants to be there too.
Anavah is described as a garment: it can be put on and taken off, since a leader sometimes has to show authority, and knowing when and how much takes da'as of kedushah.
A pancake that squirted hot fat into a tzaddik's face in the middle of learning was itself the sign that it was treif: such brazenness could not come from kosher food.
The yetzer hara enters the batei midrash disguised as 'Yesh', so that learning turns into a source of ego instead of anavah.
The four animals with one kosher sign symbolize the worst exiles precisely because a good feature used for evil makes something worse, and so learning without menschlichkeit makes a person worse.
The Rav treats the sinner's readiness for martyrdom and his daily sinning as the same human folly, illustrated by the smoker who would refuse to be shot yet keeps smoking.
Only man can choose to act against his own survival; no animal ever does, which shows that sin is folly rather than strong desire.
Adar, from the word for a covering cloak, is the month of hidden miracles, just as the hidden love belongs to Jews whose faith is covered; Adar Sheni is further still from Nissan.
Purim is above all the festival of the simple and the sinful, and the drinking of Purim reveals the hidden love that lies above reason.
The merit for the Jews who bowed to the image in Haman's time is that in their hearts they never denied Hashem, which comes out on Purim.

The Rav reads a puzzling Tosafos through the Tzemach Tzedek: the tzaddik who later gave his life al kiddush Hashem was a Jew who had not transgressed in this matter, since one who had would not have had the strength for mesiras nefesh.

Gentile self-sacrifice comes from daily drilling, like soldiers trained to die for the king, while Jews, even the lowest, have given their lives in hundreds of thousands out of an inner instinct that would not let them be torn from Hashem.

The donkey knows its master only through the feeding trough, whereas the ox knows its owner directly; a Jew who does not sense Hashem has numbed this instinct through sin, like a dentist's anesthetic.
A person's soul extends into his possessions; this explains why the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair would not eat untithed food and why a Canaanite slave may eat terumah.
Among created things one is the smallest number, since anything can be halved; with Hashem 'echad' is the greatest number, a oneness without limit after which there is no other.

A person thinks in a language, usually his mother tongue, yet the first stirring, like hunger, comes from the essence of the soul before any letters; an animal has the desire but no letters of thought.
What the Ba'al haTanya explains over five chapters, the Ba'al Shem Tov said in one word: one who turns away from the Torah in anything is already, in that, serving other gods.
The Rishonim's distinction that a Sanhedrin is fixed while the ruling that goes out from it is separate cannot be used for Hashem: His word never becomes separate from Him, it remains His essence.
Just as Dovid's 'I am like a desert bird' compares him to the bird only in being alone, not in feathers or beak, 'vayedaber' compares Hashem's word to speech only in its being communication.

Even a person's thought is not the first stage: it is stirred by a desire in the heart, as hunger makes the mind plan a meal, and that root is united with the person's self; Hashem's speech is united with Him in this way.

A turtle's shell is a garment that is part of the turtle itself; so too the garments of Hashem are His own essence. The Rav shows the idea in halachah: one's own hand on his head is not a covering, since it is part of him, while another person's hand is.
There are two true perspectives: from the Creator's side only His glory fills the earth, while from the side of the recipients Hashem created for them a world of imagination in which they live.
The Rav reads 'Yehi or' as 'let there be liberty': light is happiness, and the most precious happiness is freedom.
True liberty is not freedom from others' rule but freedom to do the right thing, so a person ruled by his passions is the real prisoner even when he walks about free.
The greatest freedom is to be subservient to no will other than Hashem's.
The Rav describes the future redemption as a repetition of the first Rosh Hashanah, when Hashem's voice will again be heard by all mankind.
The Rav reads Shlomo HaMelech's 'three thousand meshalim' as a chain: a mashal on a mashal on a mashal, down three thousand levels, until a very deep matter could be understood.
According to the Rav, the good tastes of this world exist so that a person should grasp, through them, the sweetness of Torah, which is called sweeter than honey.
The Rav compares a Jew washing his hands in the morning to a power station that lights a whole city: he purifies his share of creation from the defect of the night.
The Rav uses the law that one sitting on layers above a zav's seat becomes tamei without touching it to show that a mitzvah makes a person a merkavah, not merely someone in contact with holiness.
The Rav explains that sins work like an anesthetic: they dull a person's senses so that he does not feel that learning Gemara unites him with Hashem.
Not feeling the holiness of Torah study is itself a protection, the Rav says: a person who felt the light he unites with while learning would be consumed by it.
The Arizal's emphasis on tefillah before Moshiach is like a doctor ordering orange juice for a sick man: bread and meat remain the main food, but in his condition he now needs the juice.

There are two kinds of yirah: a lower one that makes a person sit down to learn, and a higher one that comes from the learning itself; relative to that higher yirah Torah is the gate, which settles the Gemara's seemingly contradictory statements.

Not feeling yirah while learning is like surgery under anesthesia: the patient feels nothing, yet the operation is truly taking place; the soul and its root feel the bond with Hashem even when the body does not.

Rabbinic laws are Hashem's own wisdom: He left them for the sages of each generation to enact at the right time with divine inspiration, and according to the Arizal they come from a higher root, which is why the second day of Yom Tov is on a higher level.
The Satan himself, like Bilaam who could not go against Hashem's word, does whatever Hashem wants; only a sinning Jew acts against Hashem's will, which is why he is worse than the sitra achra.

The goat to Azazel, the hair showing at the tefillin, kaparos, the thirty-nine lashes and the ban on matzah on Erev Pesach all leave the sitra achra a small share, at Hashem's command, so that it is not wholly nullified before Moshiach.

The Magen Avraham's custom about kiddush is not fear of Maadim's harm, since all harsh forces flee from Shabbos; rather, making kiddush in that hour would take the red wine, Maadim's own, entirely into holiness and leave the sitra achra nothing.

Even the sitra achra and the angel at the head of the forces of impurity know that Hashem rules and submit to Him; the sinner, the only creature that rebels against His will, is therefore lower than them.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Rav explains that sinning while knowing Hashem sees, as if He would let it pass, contains a spark of kefirah, even if one forgets it at the time.
Ordinary waste mixed with food still contains a little food, but the dregs of this world, its lusts and sins, are pure waste with no good at all.
A moment of sweetness in avodah is like a free sample Hashem gives to awaken a person; afterwards he must pay the full price with toil until he earns that sweetness himself.

A father in a rage at his child still snatches him from a speeding car, because his natural love, hidden under the anger, surfaces when the child's life is at stake; so too a Jew's hidden love surfaces when faced with idolatry.
The spirit of folly covers the soul only up to chochmah; idolatry touches chochmah itself, so there the hidden love wakes, while other sins slip past it.
Wild animals rule over a man only when he appears to them like a beast, having lost his tzelem Elokim through sin; one who keeps it cannot be harmed by them.

The Rav explains that the Torah's only two cases of kfitzas haderech are journeys to find a kallah because a shidduch is heavenly, and what is heavenly is not subject to the earthly limits of time and space.
According to the Rav, the bas kol errs about matches not from weakness but because a shidduch is so sublime that even a daughter of prophecy cannot grasp it in this world.
The Rav reads the opening 'lo tov' of the tenth utterance as the voice telling the bas kol 'not this one' after each wrong announcement, until 'matza isha matza tov'.

Citing the Tzemach Tzedek, the Rav explains that the shadchan's lie gives the holy union a slight blemish so it can descend into this world, and reads 'shadchan' as initials of 'sheker dover, kesef notel'.

The Rav measures each holy time by its prohibition of work, which stems from the curse of Adam, and from this shows that women's refraining from work while the Chanukah candles burn reveals their higher kedusha on Chanukah.

The Rav answers his own question on the Chasam Sofer: the women's staying inside and not lighting, for the sake of tznius, is itself the pirsumei nisa, since the miracle of Yehudis was a miracle of tznius.
Bringing the Shinever Rav, the Rav explains that Eliezer could not have known Rivka's size, so the clothing he gave her were samples of the modest dress kept in Avraham's house.
An improper thought arriving is not the sin; the sin is letting it remain in one's head, since a person is created with a body precisely to face such trials.

Because the Torah is eternal and addresses the smallest Jew as much as Moshe Rabbeinu, 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od' must be true for the smallest person too, which is why the Tanya needs a short way.
Talmud Torah is the hardest mitzvah because it claims every free moment and the full depth of understanding one is capable of.

The Gemara's ruling that one interrupts learning for the Megillah shows that bittul Torah exists even while learning: hearing the Megillah superficially is bittul compared to learning Gemara with full depth.
A shopkeeper who opens his store but serves customers half-heartedly is also guilty of idling from work; in the same way, learning below one's capacity is a form of bittul Torah.
The hidden love is like a father's love for a son he is angry at: concealed while the son sins, but revealed the moment the son is in danger.

The Rav likens a Jew's emunah to the inherited instinct of animals: just as a young bee, beaver or spider builds what its parents built without being taught, a Jew believes in Hashem because it is in his system.

Reading 'behibaram' as 'b'Avraham', the Rav says creation was not complete after 'Vayechulu': a new creature still had to be made, one who believes in Hashem by instinct, and the added hei, the letter of birth, makes that belief pass to his children.
A Jew who says he does not believe is usually deceiving himself to excuse his desires, a pattern the Rav finds in Esav blaming his wives and in Chiel explaining away the deaths of his children.
Tevilah is a new birth through self-nullification: one bends like a curled-up fetus and comes out a new creation, which is why the Rav says a shortcut of dipping a finger misses the point.

The Rav notes that a mashal holds in only one detail, and that the Avos as merkavah were more than a chariot: a chariot is nullified to its rider but not part of him, while the Avos were permeated with G-dliness in every limb.

Love and fear of Hashem are themselves the 'offspring' of chochmah and binah, father and mother, male and female, which is why the Tanya must explain how they can be included together in an inherited love.
A dollar given with simcha counts as a thousand, more than a wealthy man's hundred dollars given with a grudge, so the same coin can be multiplied by how it is given.
The collector who interrupts davening may be the very present Hashem sends to save a person from distress he does not even know is coming.
The recession itself may be a test in tzedakah, sent to teach that when giving is harder it is even more important.
The killed shluchim have not ended their shlichus: from the heichal of Moshiach they should tell Moshiach the truth about the state of the Jews in India, as Avraham Avinu pleaded for the redemption.
Like a worm in a radish who thinks radish is the sweetest thing and cannot imagine a strawberry, people in this world cannot grasp the good of the next.
A person who never had to be rescued has a bigger miracle than one who brings a korban todah after being saved, for his miracle is that it never happened to him.
Toward a person, love and fear pull against each other; only toward Hashem do they coexist, because loving Him means union and fearing Him means nullification, and both belong together.
Calling the avos a merkavah is a mashal that holds in one point only: a chariot stays a separate thing from its rider, while the avos became one with Hashem, a level of Elokus itself.
Acquired knowledge is not inherited, but what is part of a person's essence is; the avos' bond with Hashem had become their essence, which is why Jews inherit a hidden love.
Ruach and neshamah that a person never revealed still surround him as a makif connected to his inner self, so, like a hair color that skips a generation, they can appear in his children.
Vapor and ice are the same substance with a vast difference between them; so too the worlds are one light, ever more contracted and physical.
A child may be cleverer than an adult and still lack daas, since daas is not intelligence but the power to govern the midos.
The name Atzilus comes from 'etzel', near: like the nobles who stand beside the king and receive his light, Atzilus is the world closest to the Creator.
The four worlds with their ten sefiros are Hashem's reshus hayachid, ten handbreadths high and four wide, while what passes to the sitra achra is already the reshus harabim.

Like an aspirin under a sweet coating and an enteric coating, a Jew's outer garments differ, coarse for the simple Jew and refined for the talmid chacham, but what lies beneath is the same in every Jew.
Because holiness is unity and impurity is the 'world of division', a Jew can bind himself to the Avos only through unity with other Jews and the tzaddik.
In a round dance everyone stands at the same distance from the center, where Hashem is; by lifting a person above himself, dancing reveals the inner point in which all Jews are equal.
Machol and mechilah are one word: Yom Kippur brings forgiveness because on that day the inner point of every Jew, which does not want to be cut off from Hashem, is revealed.
Hashem calls the Jews 'bnei kushiyim' because, as with skin color, the difference he rebukes them for lies only in the outer layer, while beneath it all Jews are equal.
Spiritual greatness can be inherited hidden, like a physical trait or a talent for niggun that skips a generation and reappears in the grandson.
Hashem hides great souls in unlikely homes the way an owner hides diamonds where a thief would never think to look, so that the Satan, who guards the line of Moshiach, is outwitted.
Chanukah, set in Teves, the month given to Esav and the year's longest night, parallels ikvesa dimeshicha, the 'heel' of history, where Moshiach is revealed precisely in the deepest darkness.
The lower a generation has sunk, the higher its souls fell from: like a stone dropped from a roof that sinks deeper into mud, today's souls can reach sparks earlier generations could not.
An inventor can explain every part of his machine but not why the cement falls rather than rising; that given starting point, which binah builds on but cannot explain, is what is called chochmah.

In a pilpul on the Rambam everything can be explained except its starting point, which stands like a gezeirah; so too there is a power in a Jew that exists but cannot be understood, the Jewish neshamah inherited from the Avos.
The Rav reads the doubled 'haster astir' as two layers: in plain hiding one still knows the father is near and can call him; in the hiding within the hiding one does not even know he is there.
He sees the year as a miniature of all time: Nisan, from 'nes', a banner raised high, is open miracles, while Adar at its end is the hidden miracles of the end of days.

The news story about Vashti that pious bochurim would have shut out of the beis medrash became part of the Megillah, so that one who skips it has not fulfilled the mitzvah; so too today's news is part of a Megillah being written.
The Rav explains that bitachon itself breaks through the hester panim: the one who tells Hashem he relies on Him comes to see Hashem's care.
Yishmael is harder than Rome or Bavel because, as a 'pere adam' who stays wild whatever his profession, he cannot be reasoned with or moved by mercy.

Since emunah means believing what one does not understand, it does not depend on intellect at all; it comes from chochmah, which is above intellect, so the greatest talmid chacham's emunah is no more a product of his mind than that of the simplest Jew.
The Rav reads David HaMelech's 'I was a beast before You' together with 'and I am always with You': because he knew he had no understanding before Hashem, he was always bound to Him through emunah.
A Jew's readiness to die for Hashem is like a hen's readiness to fight for her eggs: not reasoning but nature, because Hashem is the Jew's source as parents are the source of a child.

Chametz on Pesach and chalav akum are singled out because they tie a Jew to the goy; the Rav connects this to Pesach itself, whose mitzvos begin with separating from avodah zarah, and to the passuk that puts the ban on molten idols next to keeping the festival of matzos.
The goyim's hatred through the galus, beginning with Hashem turning the Egyptians' hearts, was itself a protection, because it kept Jews from mixing with them.
The Rav reads the Tosfos story in light of the Tanya: since one who drank yayin nesech would not give his life, the chassid's later mesirus nefesh proves that the wine was permitted.

Through the Bnei Yissaschar's explanation of lighting Chanukah candles inside, the Rav says the public domain has entered the Jewish home, and today the internet brings every goy in the world into the living room.
Relative to Hashem every person is a 'peti' who believes without understanding, and the verse calls this simple belief the greatest wisdom.
Self-sacrifice for emunah works like the instinct of life: just as a sane person cannot jump off a roof, a Jewish soul cannot do something, such as denying Hashem, that would kill the soul.
Giving milah to a baby without kavanah answers Yishmael's claim: precisely because milah is emunah, above daas, it is fitting for an eight-day-old who has no daas.
A goy is entirely orlah from head to foot, so cutting does not make him circumcised, while a Jew's orlah is in one place only.

Just as among souls there is a Jew, in geography Eretz Yisroel is the Jew and other lands are the goyim; within it Chevron is the place of milah and Shechem, whose name equals 'periah' in gematria, the place of periah.
The custom of adding a Shabbos candle for each child expresses 'ner Hashem nishmas adam': every child born is another soul, another light.
The soul's longing to dissolve into Hashem is not a reasoned choice but a nature like a flame's, rooted in chochmah, which is above understanding.

There are two kinds of darkness: the absence of light, and a light so intense that it blinds, like staring at the sun; the plague of darkness was the second, from chochmah, which is why the blessing calls darkness 'borei', of the higher world of beriah.
Purim's light of chochmah is so lofty that it is hidden, which is why the day is bound to Esther, from concealment, and to 'yayin hameshumar', which equals Esther in gematria.

Walking about with a lowered head and an 'inferiority complex' is not humility but pride: the person wants to be something and resents that he is not. True humility, like Moshe Rabbeinu's, can belong to a king.

A merchant is called 'socher' from going around in a circle: his giving comes back to him, so the 'chesed' of the sitra achra is really self-interest, unlike the chesed of kedushah, which gives without wanting a return.
Yerushalayim is written hundreds of times without its second yud because it cannot be complete while Rome stands; only when Moshiach comes will it be written full, with the yud.
The sun is not Esav's by right: it was created for Yisrael and is only harnessed for now to Esav's wagon of nature, while Esav himself only mimics Yaakov like a monkey and is in truth a mirage.
Chametz is one of Esav's aliases, so burning chametz on Erev Pesach is destroying Amalek, whose soul is the yetzer hara.
In the side of impurity the female force is stronger than the male, the reverse of holiness, which is why the nations let the lady go first while Jews put right over left.
The 28-year cycle of the sun is its yovel, just as the fiftieth year is the yovel of a Jew: nature has 28 levels, the 28 times of Koheles and the 28 letters of the first passuk of the Torah.
No brachah is made over the sun on its daily or yearly rounds because it is then in Esav's service; only once in 28 years, at its point of origin, does it belong to Yaakov and can be blessed.
When time returns to its origin, the first 'time to be born' of Koheles, Moshiach is born; this is why his coming is called a birth and the suffering before it 'the birth pangs of Moshiach'.

The Rav reads 'the stranger in your midst will rise above you' not only as foreign rulers in exile but as the goy inside a Jew, and connects it to a goy who keeps Shabbos, so one must remove it through teshuvah before Shabbos.
The Rav stresses that the Tanya's 'sinner of Israel' whose soul is in exile is not only a Shabbos desecrator but any upright Jew at the moment he sins.

Using the sun and its rays, the Rav resolves how a sin can both fail to reach the chochmah and drag it into exile: the essence stays whole in the brain while its spreading into the heart is blemished.
The Rav explains that some sinners are so steeped in sin that they almost lose their free choice and want to be good but must sin, yet even they are moser nefesh when emunah is at stake.
In the story of the Rayatz and the vessels, the Rav brings that he lifted each vessel a second time after doing teshuvah, reasoning that if he felt no holiness perhaps a sin had dulled his sense.

The Rav reads the difference between chametz and matzah as the difference between avodah zarah and bittul: both are the same flour and water, but chametz rises, a yesh, while matzah stays low and becomes a vehicle for holy names and lights.
The sitra achra itself cannot sin, since sin needs a physical body in this world; a Jew who sins lends it his body, and harnesses his G-dly soul like a horse to the wagon of his sin.

Even idol-worshippers call Hashem the G-d of gods and believe He delegated the world; their sin is the yesh, thinking their powers are their own, and a Jew who sins against Hashem's will is worse than them.
The gnat, the creature that only takes and gives nothing, is the extreme of the sitra achra, since holiness is defined by giving; yet the sinner is lower than it.

The difference between mesirus nefesh for avodah zarah and not for other sins lies in chochmah: only outright idol worship reaches the chochmah of the soul and rouses it, while an ordinary sin reaches close to chochmah but not into it.
A wild beast attacks a man only when it sees him as an animal; a person who keeps his tzelem Elokim is feared by the beasts.
Since Shabbos is pure neshamah, the soul of Knesses Yisrael, a human being can truly be wed to it: soul joins with soul.
The seven days of sheva brachos are the couple's private Shabbos, as the eved ivri has a private shemitah, and their seventh day is a Shabbos of Shabbosos.
Beis Hillel's perutah does not lessen the kallah's dignity: it teaches that the value lies not in what is given but in how, with full awareness of who she is.
The kallah's total passivity at kiddushin, which seems to be not giving, is in fact the highest giving: she gives her very self, not something of herself.
Shabbos, like the kallah, seems only to take, since everything must be prepared for it, yet it is the greatest giver, the source of all brachos for the week.
Being a Jew means surrendering oneself to Hashem, and that is why Jewishness is inherited from the mother, whose nature is to give herself totally.
Even a light sin is a branch of idolatry, not because of its severity but because any act against Hashem's will separates a Jew from Him just as idolatry does.
The 'folly' of sin is that a Jew who would let himself be killed rather than bow to an idol will not bear a far smaller sacrifice to avoid a sin that cuts him off just the same.
Because Hashem and the bond with Him are above time, a separation 'just for a moment' is not small: in that moment the person is fully cut off.
A mitzvah done in a moment is eternal, like matzah eaten once that remains forever, because above there is nothing that exists only now.
Selach lanu is said three times daily for bittul Torah, which the tamid once atoned for; the tefillos that replace the tamid carry that atonement.
The generation in the desert, who faced no idolatrous oppressor, still needed the mitzvah of mesirus nefesh, so that the reckoning of readiness to die could strengthen them in every mitzvah.
Sadness and laziness share one root in the heaviest element, earth, which is why a depressed person is also a slow one.
Sleeping late is a sign of sadness, a flight from life by someone who expects nothing of the new day; the same person rises early on a day he looks forward to.
The Arizal placed Tehillim 51 after Tikkun Chatzos so that the mourning over one's own inner Beis HaMikdash would lead straight into learning with the joy that follows sadness.
The four tefillos parallel the four Shabbos meals: the first two are obligations, Yaakov's third is a choice and the greatest, and Dovid HaMelech's fourth is kept only by the few.
Suffering comes from the hidden letters Yud-Heh of Hashem's name, so it is a greater kindness than revealed blessing, just as the first letters of 'mitzvah' are hidden by the at-bash exchange.
The proof that spiritual sadness during business is from the yetzer is that the yetzer otherwise wants a person to forget Hashem; it sends such sadness only to drag him into cravings.
The very fact that a bad thought comes is what gives a beinoni the chance to fulfill 'velo sasuru'; had it not come, he would not have done the mitzvah.
Being shaken by bad thoughts comes from hidden gasus haruach: the person imagines he is a tzaddik to whom such thoughts should not occur, when even the Tanya's beinoni is a lofty level.
The same mitzvah binds every Jew by its pshat, yet for a great tzaddik it reaches further: for him anger is truly like avodah zarah, and 'vachai bahem' means a spiritual life.
Korach was a very great man, and his jealousy of Moshe Rabbeinu was so subtle that for ordinary people it would be a mitzvah.
The plural 'matamim' points to two kinds of nachas: the sweet dish of tzaddikim who nullify evil, and the sharp dish, like horseradish made tasty, of beinonim who subdue it.
'Vegam rasha leyom ra'ah' is read not as the wicked being made for a day of punishment, but as a person making day out of the bad, turning darkness into light.
A person's lifelong struggle with a particular kind of thought may be the very tikkun for which his soul came down into this gilgul.
Reuven's link to din is shown in his stone: the red odem stands for pure din, and its names in other languages, ruby and rubin, echo the name Reuven.
Since each month follows a shevet in the order of the degalim and a nasi's soul carries his whole shevet and month, Elitzur's and Shlumiel's sins pulled Tammuz and Av down into churban.

Machlokes was created on Monday, the day of division between the waters, and Korach's tikkun is hidden in the fact that the Monday song, by the sons of Korach, praises Yerushalayim, the place of unity.
The lower a place or time has fallen, the holier the sparks of Moshiach captive in it, so the months of mourning are exactly where the work of bringing Moshiach is greatest.
The months of geulah belong to the faithful meraglim: Kalev of Yehuda, source of Moshiach ben Dovid, with Nissan, and Yehoshua of Ephraim, source of Moshiach ben Yosef, with Tishrei.
A shlichus has two vessels, place and time; a trip to the country is a shlichus in place, and Tammuz and Av themselves are a shlichus in time.
Tzafra, morning, is named for the birds that sing then, and ramsha, evening, for the insects that sing at night, but a Jew is not limited and sings both by day and by night.
The Rav compares the angels who keep a person out of a heichal of tefillah with foreign thoughts to the cherubim and flaming sword that guard Gan Eden.
A thought is not empty: it is a complete spiritual entity, possibly a soul that needs a tikkun, and that is why a tzaddik can raise it.
The very fact that bad thoughts come exactly when a person strengthens himself in avodah shows that a real battle is under way, not that the avodah is worthless.
If a person had only one soul, a foreign thought would show that his davening is flawed; since he has two, the thought belongs to the other soul and says nothing about his davening.
The Rav ties the dismissal of foreign thoughts to 'ein od milvado': the same awareness that nothing exists besides Hashem is what lets a person treat the thoughts as nothing.
The yetzer hara is called a fly because, like a fly, it keeps coming back no matter how often it is driven away.

Reading 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem', the Rav explains that forbidden food blocks the heart, so a person who learns Torah, and should rejoice that he becomes a chariot for the Shechinah, feels nothing.
Food cooked at home with the words 'l'kavod Shabbos' carried holiness into it, as in the Kuzmir chulent whose taste of Gan Eden came from the Rebbe's beans; a chulent bought ready-made lacks this.
The light of Shabbos is felt in a person's face and in the candles, even in electric light on Chol HaMoed; only one with a dulled heart fails to notice it.
For the beinoni, the soul is like a drink poured into a person, a guest in his body; for the tzaddik it is the reverse, and the body is the stranger to whom one 'does kindness', as Hillel did.
Dovid called himself 'a worm and not a man' because a worm fulfills the purpose it was created for, while a person who does not learn and daven as he was created to do is worse than a worm.
A feeling in davening that does not last is not false for a beinoni: truth has levels, and only for a tzaddik is what fades counted as untrue.
The ger tzedek's answer, that even the smell of a Shabbos candle going out is sweeter than all worldly pleasures, is what the Rav says one should answer the yetzer hara.
Truth for a beinoni is measured by return, not permanence: an arousal that fades but comes back each time proves it was inwardly true at his level.
Because time is a creation and does not exist above, a sin of youth stands before Heaven as if done now.
Not feeling anything on Shabbos, when weekdays are fine, is a sign of Shabbos's greater holiness: at the king's court one is not forgiven what was overlooked during the week.
The yahrzeit customs reflect that a neshamah must pass through cleansing again before each yearly ascent, and the same holds for a living person rising in avodah.
Dovid's sin was always before him because at each higher moment he saw it anew and needed a fresh teshuvah.
Darkness is a real creation and there is a holy darkness of tzimtzum, which is why the Tanya compares the sitra achra's nullification specifically to darkness before physical light.

The Rav reads the Mishnah's unusual wording, stating the first of Shevat before naming Beis Shammai, as a sign that Beis Shammai's view is relevant even now, because it will be the halacha when Moshiach comes.
According to the Rav, belief in Moshiach shows itself in practice: a farmer who truly expects him this year goes out to mark his trees on Rosh Chodesh Shevat too.
The Rav reads 'the day Pharaoh was born' as the day that caused him to be born: the day he fulfilled his mission of bringing Yosef out of prison to rule Egypt.
The Rav says that whatever came before a person fulfills his mission is as if non-existent, even if a birth date is registered at City Hall.
The Rav ties the end of the shiur back to its beginning: the coming of Moshiach will be the Rosh Hashanah for the tree of Klal Yisrael.
The heading 'a song for the Shabbos day' is read as Shabbos being the singer, not the subject: no other day of the week has its own song because only Shabbos sings.

Creation in seven days is like music built from seven notes: each note alone is mere noise, the six weekdays alone are not yet music, and Shabbos completes the harp of seven strings so that the world's harmony can be sung.

The seventh of any series is its singer: the Kinneret as the seventh sea, Eretz Yisrael as the seventh land and 'chazan' of the world, the zemer as the seventh animal, and King David as the seventh of the ushpizin and 'sweet singer of Israel'.
The border of Eretz Yisrael touching the 'shoulder' of the Kinneret is read as a pat on the shoulder, the way one is praised after davening well, because the Kinneret sings the Shabbos songs.

Shabbos is tied to teshuvah because both mean returning to the root; the yovel, the 'Shabbos of Shabbosos', draws back even those too far to return on an ordinary Shabbos, like the shofar of Moshiach.

Our Shabbos is a small Shabbos that sings to the great Shabbos of the future, and a person who sees only a piece of history is like a fly on a black spot in a masterpiece, unable to see the whole picture.
A word in the chapter's last verse is written without a vav; since vav means connection, the missing letter shows that people do not see the connection and harmony in Hashem's ways.
The words 'shir l'yom' contain the letters of Yerushalayim, because the psalm is a song both to Shabbos, the Shabbos of time, and to Yerushalayim, the Shabbos of place.
The Rav reads the name Chavakuk as embrace: in the last generations a Jew must hold onto emunah with all his strength.
An octave's eighth note is really the first again; a new eighth note in Moshiach's days would multiply the possible combinations, the way an eighth digit multiplies phone numbers.
The piano's seven white keys and five black keys, the sad half-tones between them, mirror the white and black experiences of life; one cannot play a beautiful melody with only one kind.
White is the color of chesed, which is why doctors traditionally wore white, carrying a spark of the angel Refael, and why the Kohanim wore white.
A drum alone is only noise, but within an orchestra it beautifies the music; so the sad times of history are part of its beauty.
The Rav reads the physical waves of the sea as the lower waters' yearning to rise to the King, so that a law of physics reflects a law of creation.
Nisuch hamayim gave the lower waters their way to serve Hashem, which is why they began weeping again when the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed.
Following the Yismach Moshe, the exiles by the rivers of Babylon wept 'also' because they wept together with the weeping waters; both were separated from closeness to Hashem.
The passuk that Hashem praises the rising waves teaches that effort is praised even where it cannot succeed; a Jew's effort, unlike the waves', does succeed.

The Rav reads 'ki simachtani' as the joy of Shabbos rest: only when a person is free of the week's labor can he look at the harmony of creation, and that sight lets him trust that the parts he does not understand are equally deep.
'Ish ba'ar' is not an insult: even an 'ish', a person of stature, is ignorant regarding Hashem's conduct; the difference from the fool is only that the ish knows he does not know.
'Gavoha' is high but rooted in the ground, like a tall building, while 'marom' is high and detached, like a cloud; Hashem is called marom because His ways cannot be reached at all.
The wicked cannot reach the eternal Shabbos because they belong to division, like Esav's 'nafshos' in the plural, whereas Shabbos is the secret of oneness.
