Oil rises above every liquid because it belongs above, and 'shemen' is linked to 'shemonah'; the Chanukah oil that was not consumed shows the eternal 'eighth' that is the existence of Klal Yisrael.

The strength of a minhag comes from the collective ruach hakodesh of Klal Yisrael, and this same hidden ruach hakodesh is what 'tishmanah oznai' describes: the Jew hears that he will outlive his enemies.

A fruit tree stays low because its roots' strength goes into the fruit, while the fruitless cedar grows tall; the tzaddik who pours himself into students is promised both the palm's fruit and the cedar's height.
The beauty of Klal Yisrael was not seen in galus because a tree only flourishes in its own soil; only when planted again 'in the house of Hashem' will the nations wonder at them.
Rosh Chodesh Teves falls on Chanukah, and a Jew lighting Chanukah lights in the street on the longest nights of a month of din is 'cutting off the head of the house of the wicked', Esav.
Tammuz's combination of the Name comes from Haman's words 'vechol zeh einenu shoveh li', with the letters fully backwards, which is why it is a month of harsher din even than Av.
'Hashem malach' in the past tense is said looking back from the days of Moshiach: then it will be clear that He reigned even in galus when His kingship was not seen.
'Gei'us lavesh' means Hashem's seeming aloofness is a garment, and the double 'lavesh ... levush' is a hiding within a hiding; but under all the garments is the Name Havayah, the Name of chessed.
The world is called 'tevel', related to 'tevel hu', a mixture; it is a world where one does not see clearly, and miracles are like lightning in a dark night.
The first sin in the world was a sin of eating, not one of the three cardinal sins, which shows how great the power of food is.
Pharaoh's cabinet ministers over drink, bread and meat show that he understood food as the chief channel for spreading tumah, unlike a modern president whose chef is a mere employee.
Every force of evil has its counterpart in good: if tumah has its ministers over food, kedushah has them too, and these are the kashrus supervisors.
By the principle that the power of the maker is in the thing made, a supervisor's extra care puts kedushah into the food itself, as a housewife's intention puts kedushah into her Shabbos cooking.
The angels are called 'men' when they come to Avraham but 'angels' when they leave him, because his holy food fortified them in kedushah for the mission of saving Lot and the line of Moshiach.

The akeidah was hardly a test of willingness to sacrifice, since any believing Jew would obey a direct command; the test was facing Hashem's apparent contradiction of His own promise while the simple answer was hidden from Avraham.
The proof that the test was a question and not the slaughter: the posuk says Hashem tested Avraham, not Yitzchak, who was the one to be slaughtered.

The weeping of the lower waters over their distance from the King was answered by the korbanos, through which every level of creation, animal, plant and water, is brought close, and the churban renewed their weeping.
The feminine form eidosecha, rather than eidai, hints at the weakness of Israel in galus, a sheep among seventy wolves, who nevertheless remain loyal.

Edom, today's galus, includes all the earlier kingdoms, which is why Daniel saw it in a separate vision and the Torah lists the pig in a separate posuk; in America the dominant element is the galus of Yavan, the pursuit of pleasure and beauty.

The chapter sits at the border between weekday and Shabbos because its eighteen Names correspond to the weekday Shemoneh Esrei and its seven voices to the Shabbos Amidah, so it carries the holy letters and Names needed to draw down the Shabbos soul.

Kabbalas Shabbos is done with this chapter because its theme, bitul, is malchus, and Shabbos, the day Hashem rejoices in His completed creation, is when a person proclaims he is Hashem's creature and nullifies himself to His kingship.
Shabbos is the day of bitul because on it a Jew does no work and produces nothing; he is simply nothing before Hashem.
Yosef's greatest bitul was joining his brothers' minyan for the oath, letting himself be counted in the very decision to sell him.
A tzaddik who praises himself may be fully humble, since he credits the gift to Hashem and is really praising Hashem, as David says 'baHashem tishallel nafshi'.
The voice of Hashem that one hears in the world's beauty is the same voice in its destruction and upheavals; both are part of one harmony.
The 'forests' that will be stripped bare are the nations and powers that hide Hashem's kingship, the way tall trees in a forest hide the sky and the One who sends all the blessing.

With the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains that since the Jews already worked at full capacity, the straw decree really took away their Shabbos, and so the shotrim who were beaten rather than force them to work were giving their lives for Shabbos and earned a closer place at Sinai.

Rabbi Moshe of Sambor reads the shift from 'ayal' (masculine) to 'ta'arog' (feminine) as the ayalah who, in her own birth pains, behaves as if she were a male free of them and prays for water for the whole forest.

The flood and Matan Torah are the same flow from Heaven: at the flood the Torah was meant to be given, Moshe's soul was there in Noach, but the generation's sins turned it into a physical, destructive flood.
Noach's failure to pray for his generation made the waters 'mei Noach'; Moshe, the same soul, repaired it when he offered himself with 'mecheini na', and the Zohar reads 'mecheini' as 'mei Noach'.

Bilam's answer to the nations is read as 'Hashem oz l'amo yiten, Hashem yevarech es amo vashalom': the flood this time is Torah, and 'bashalom' contains 'mabul' turned around by the shin of the threefold Torah.

The Sefer Chareidim, unlike other counts of the mitzvos, orders them by the limbs, and by opening with the heart rather than the head it signals that emunah, the first mitzvah of the heart, comes first of all.
Without emunah an act loses its identity as a mitzvah: a heretic who gives money gives charity, but not tzedakah, because tzedakah means giving because Hashem commanded it.
The 'apikorus' one must be ready to answer is not only the one standing opposite, but the one within a person's own heart.
Emunah in a Jew resembles the inborn knowledge of animals: just as a bee or beaver builds without being taught, a Jew believes by instinct, as an inheritance of the soul.
Creation was incomplete until Avraham Avinu, the first believer, came to perfect it, and the Jewish people's emunah traces back to him.
A kashya against an absolute truth is only a question, not a refutation, just as a helium balloon does not make a child doubt that things fall.
The order of davening maps onto the four worlds, which is why one sits down at Yotzer: there one enters Beriah, the world of the Kisei HaKavod.
Though the generations decline, creation itself grows more elevated and souls more refined each day, so each day needs a tikkun of its own that tomorrow cannot replace.
A foreign thought during davening is not merely lost focus: it means the angels guarding that word's heichal have thrown the person out, though Hashem may admit one who toils beyond his merits.
The Rav reads 'zimra' as cutting, as in pruning a vineyard: Pesukei d'Zimra cut a path through the destructive angels, because one who goes along with Dovid Hamelech cannot be stopped.
Since a person must be broken in life anyway, the drash 'shivro' teaches that it is better to be broken before Hashem, and what one suffers for Torah and avodah is subtracted from other suffering.

In the Zohar's mashal, the one who slays the serpent receives the king's daughter; the Rav identifies the serpent as the yetzer hara and the king's daughter as tefillah, with its sweetness of deveikus.

Pesukei d'Zimra became obligatory because our generation is weaker, just as later generations are stricter in matters the Rishonim were lenient in, and just as the ketores once purified the air so prayers could rise.

The Rav reads 'b'shem kol Yisrael' as lifting a private mitzvah into the world of Klal Yisrael, the place of Yom Kippur and of the Kodesh HaKodashim, where no accuser, angel or king can enter; strife between Jews cuts a person off from that place.

He compares l'shem yichud to the moda'ah of a coerced get: just as a prior declaration voids what follows, declaring beforehand that the mitzvah is for Hashem voids any foreign thought that later slips in, like bitul chametz.

Maaseh bereishis is 'current events': like a child who thinks the switch makes the light while the dynamos must turn every second, or a glass held in the hand that falls the moment the muscles relax, the world exists only through Hashem's constant renewal.

From 'gozer u'mekayem' the Rav argues that since Hashem knows the future, a claim that He changed His mind and gave a new law cannot hold, while the giving of the Torah itself, witnessed by the whole nation, is a historical fact others cannot deny.
Because nature follows the Torah's psak, a lung that the Mechaber rules kosher can live in Eretz Yisrael, where his rulings are followed.

The Rav links the new wonders of pilpul in the Acharonim, and the long teshuvos of today, with the industrial revolution and today's technology: as Jews add wonders in Torah, Hashem opens wonders in creation.
The farther a thing is from Hashem, the stronger its longing to return, like two people who love each other and are far apart; so the earth, the lowest form of creation, has the greatest longing.

The hundred daily brachos answer the angel of forgetfulness whose power reaches a hundred, the gematria of the name of the angel of forgetfulness, while 101 is the gematria of Michael, over whom forgetfulness has no hold.
The roads to Zion mourn not as a figure of speech: the very ground of the road longs to be trodden by Jews going up to Yerushalayim for a mitzvah.
Rewarding mitzvos is itself a kindness, since a person owes Hashem everything and Hashem owes him nothing; therefore 'meshalem sachar tov' is a praise of Hashem.
In Tehillim 34 and 25 the aleph-beis stands for a fixed order of reward and punishment, and the extra verse of pidyon that follows it teaches that Hashem's redemption stands above that order.

The angel created by a sin must fulfill its purpose, so when a person does teshuvah Hashem sends it to a rasha instead; this is the meaning of 'I have given Egypt as your ransom' and the secret of kaparos.

The Rav compares the ba'al teshuvah to the migrating bird: with no memory or instruments it returns to the very tree where it was born, and so the Jew's heart navigates him back to Hashem by an inherited sense.

Chiel of Beis El found a natural explanation for each son's death, a virus, a cold, a kidney disorder, because his ambition would not let him admit Yehoshua's curse; the Rav presents this as the model of rationalization.

Old people who return to observance once their desires are gone no longer need to rationalize, while those whose driving force is ga'avah grow even prouder in old age and cannot admit their life was folly.
Avraham Avinu had to be barren because he was a new species; had he been able to have children in the natural way, Yitzchak would simply have been a grandchild of Terach.
The Rav connects the hey added to Avraham's and Sarah's names with the power to have children, and brings that Bilhah's name has two heys, one for Rachel and one for herself.
From the kofer (tar) on Noach's ark and the kapores that covers the aron, the Rav explains that apikorsus is only a cover smeared over the emunah that remains inside.

The words of Baruch Sheamar, from 'beshevachos' and 'bizmiros' through 'chai haolamim', trace the whole order of the davening that follows: Mizmor LeSodah, Pesukei Dezimra, Az Yashir, Yishtabach, Kerias Shema, Ahavah Rabbah and Shemoneh Esrei.
Mizmor LeSodah opens Pesukei Dezimra right after the brachah, just as after a brachah one first tastes the choicest fruit, and like the custom of tasting the Shabbos food on Erev Shabbos.

With a king, being called by name is a disgrace since his title is greater than his name; with Hashem it is the reverse, and His very name is the greatest praise, which is why Baruch Sheamar climbs to 'shemo hagadol'.
Thanks offered as good manners, when one feels the good was owed to him, is not hodaah; hodaah means knowing one received more than his share, which is why one bows at Modim.
Mizmor LeSodah is the hundredth psalm, corresponding to the last of the hundred daily brachos, and, as the close of Moshe Rabbeinu's eleven psalms, it is bound up with the end of days.
The Rambam's Moshiach, who shows no signs, is the greater one: a single word of his will enter every heart, so that Jews will drop everything and follow him to Eretz Yisrael.
Simcha and safek are opposites: doubt is insecurity, simcha is security, so Amalek, whose gematria is safek, attacks joy by attacking faith.

Amalek 'karcha baderech' means he made everything into mikreh, chance; the word mikreh in this sense does not belong in a Jew's vocabulary and is the voice of the forces of impurity that hide Hashem's face.
The 'heel' generations at the end of exile parallel Adar, the last and lowest month, which is why Amalek thought he could prevail over the Jews in it.
The written 'lo' with an alef and the read 'lo' with a vav in 'v'lo anachnu' contrast how things look in the newspapers, 'we are not His people', with the truth of the Oral Torah, 'we are His'.
The Samech-Mem rules up to one hundred, so the hundred brachos with amen, like learning a hundred and one times, carry a person beyond its domain.
Thanks (todah) is the gate and tehillah is the inner courtyard: one who thanks Hashem even for the beginning of service is brought further in.
Adar corresponds to Eilam, Persia, whose name means hiddenness ('ta'alumah'); Hashem 'set His throne in Eilam', and so the Purim miracle came hidden inside a story of nature.
The seventy-year decree torn up by amen yehei shmei rabbah echoes the seventy years of galus Bavel, whose darkest last stretch under Persia is the time of Purim.

The two halves of the Name match heaven and earth (the initials of 'yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz'); in heaven Hashem is seen, but on earth Amalek can hide Him behind the cloak of nature and chance.
Torah festivals are mentioned in Retzeh, the avodah, while Chanukah and Purim belong to Modim, where one bows down, because they bring holiness to the lowest places and the lowest Jews.
Levels of Jews mirror the days: the one who only learns is like Shabbos, one who works only as needed is like Yom Tov, then Chol Hamoed, then the weekday.
'Le'olam chasdo' means His kindness is hidden ('olam' from 'ne'elam'), and 'dor vador' means tumbling down, the emunah rolling down through the generations to the very last before Moshiach.
The precise Rambam's words 'many books' teach that the prohibition is not limited to a few books of idolatry but reaches all reading that plants doubts in emunah.
The seed and the tree can be seen both ways: every Yid was once in Avraham, and Avraham is now in every Yid, a 'gene' of emunah that nurtures him.
A kofer is one who covers up, as the word kofer means pitch that coats the ark; the emunah is underneath, flickering like a spark under sand.

First and last letters hold the whole word, as Rosh Hashanah holds the year and its last day holds it for teshuvah; Avner's name in the middle letters showed that only the temporary middle of a Yid can be lost, never his beginning or end.
The three matzos stand for the emunah of the three Avos and the four cups for the four Imahos, matching the three-headed and four-headed shin of the tefillin.
Dropping the final nun of 'amen' leaves 'em', mother: emunah, being feeling and instinct, is passed through the mother, which is why Jewishness alone among all traits follows her.
The Rav argues that headlines should be reversed: the news is not that someone starved, but that every creature has food every day.
He reads the alef-beis structure of Ashrei as a sign of the ordered balance of nature, in which each creature's eating also sustains its surroundings.
The Toldos Yaakov Yosef read 'Ashrei ha'am shekachah lo' as 'happy is the people that says: so be it', accepting everything as from Heaven.
The full spelling of 'Elokai' with a vav hints that Hashem's care fills a person's life completely, leaving no empty space.
The words of the daily prayers are like one basket carrying apples one day and potatoes the next: the same words hold different tikkunim each day.
Each Jew has one Shabbos in history that is his own, just as he has his own letter in the Sefer Torah, and how he keeps it affects all of creation.
Trying to grasp Hashem with the intellect is like trying to hear a painting or see a symphony: each faculty has its own object, and the intellect is not the one for Hashem.

The neshamah is not bound by space and time; a person cannot see beyond the wall or into tomorrow only because sin insulates him from his own neshamah, while tzaddikim who purify the body 'crystal clear' have ruach hakodesh.
The minhag of Klal Yisroel serves as a proof in halachah because Klal Yisroel as a collective has ruach hakodesh even today.

Unlike other faiths built on one man's word, Jewish emunah rests on an event an entire nation witnessed; a fabricated claim of national revelation would have been exposed at once, as Holocaust denial is absurd.
Like a falling stone that gathers speed, the spiritual decline between generations accelerates, so the gap between our generation and the one before it is greater than between Yehoshua and Moshe.
'Dor l'dor yeshabach ma'asecha' means that what Hashem's middas hadin did in one generation is understood in a later one, when it is revealed retroactively as part of Klal Yisroel's tikkun.
'B'chen' in Birkas Hamazon: Hashem could have sustained man with a plain nutrient fuel, like a car, but chose to feed him with beauty, taste and variety.
The Rav reads Chazal's linking of 'after your eyes' with heresy as cause and effect: a person does not become a heretic and then sin; he wants to sin and becomes a heretic to justify it.
Esav's claim that his wives cost him the brachos is the Rav's model of rationalization: he decides he himself is worthy and looks for something else to blame.
People avoid the Torah's account of creation not because of its content but because reading on leads to 'do not murder, do not steal', and one cannot drive through life with the brakes on.
Medical science itself assumes that every detail in the body has a purpose and searches for it, which is an admission of design.
Apparent conflicts between science and Torah resemble the Yemenite woman's kasha: they come from knowing Chumash without its meforshim, and are answered by learning more Torah, not less.
The Rav reads the extra vav of 'u'gedulascha' as a connection: Dovid HaMelech sees the bond between every single thing and Hashem, and tells of it calmly, as a narrative, not as a surprise.
Buying a bottle of milk so as to have strength to daven or to learn with a bochur makes a great impression in Heaven, while a famous lecture reported in the newspapers makes none.
The Rav notes that a wind requires atmospheric changes over miles; to cool one worm, Hashem changed the whole region.
The souls of a terrible generation are like a kugel made of Shabbos leftovers: Hashem gathers damaged souls of many generations into one and mixes them into something good.

A life with a bad wife or in poverty, which Chazal count as no life, lets a soul that has used up its three chances come down again, since the accuser cannot claim it has really returned to the world.
'The nega did not turn its ayin' means the letter ayin did not move: a nega that is not turned around stays a nega instead of becoming oneg.
Causing others to act is greater than acting: tzaddikim are called Hashem's 'handiwork' because they cause Hashem to act, as a tzaddik decrees and Hashem fulfills.
The Rav reads 'vachasidecha' as Klal Yisroel as a whole: compared to the nations, the Jewish people are the 'chasidim' of the world, and only they can bless Hashem rather than merely praise Him.
A gentile's good deed makes him a better person and earns him reward, but only a Jew's mitzvah brings shefa into the whole creation, or, the opposite, causes destruction.

'Lehodia livnei ha'adam gevurosav' is a parenthesis placed exactly halfway through the alef-beis of Ashrei: having said so many praises, David HaMelech stops to say that they only reach as far as people can grasp.

The disappearance of kingship and fear in the modern world is not an accident: the world is arranged so that there is nothing left to learn fear of Heaven from, making emunah the test of the generation.
Each of the ten makos corresponded to one of the ten maamaros, in reverse order, so that through the makos the Jews saw who created the world; from the ten makos came the ten dibros.
The 'samech' of 'somech Hashem' stands before the missing 'nun' of falling: Hashem's support comes before the fall, the cure prepared before the blow.

A tzaddik's fall is arranged from Heaven so that he goes down to a low place he would never have reached on his own and raises souls from there; this is how Hashem is 'somech' the fallen, through the tzaddik.

From 'nora alila al bnei adam' the Rav shows that even the dispute between Yosef and the brothers was part of a plan leading to Egypt, the Exodus and Matan Torah, so outsiders cannot judge tzaddikim's deeds.
Tefilah is an exercise in emunah: the very act of asking awakens a person to recognize that Hashem is the provider, which is why davening for parnassa is so great.
In a time of both plague and famine, praying for food covers the plague as well, since one who is decreed sustenance must live to receive it; the Rav finds this hinted in 'umasbia lechol chai'.

The decree is fixed on Rosh Hashanah, yet how much mercy accompanies it is judged each day; thus Hashem is 'tzaddik' in His decree and 'chasid' in carrying it out, and the decree can be sweetened while it remains.
A tefilah that seems unanswered is put in reserve in the heavenly account; Avraham's tefilah for Sodom was kept for later generations who would have no tzaddik great enough to daven for them.

The Rav turns the skeptic's demand for proof around: the denier cannot be sure there is no Creator, and with real risks no one acts on a one-in-a-thousand doubt, so his position shows temptation, not logic.
The generation born in the desert, raised on bread from heaven, found wheat growing from the ground astonishing; we see the same wonder daily and are unmoved only because we are used to it.
Each organ is a wonder, yet none could exist without the others, and their interaction is itself a further wonder.
Hashem made food tasty and beautiful with many colors and distinct tastes, both so that a person will want to eat and stay healthy and as a display of chen.
If the body arose by itself, some parts should have no purpose; yet every organ once thought useless, like the appendix and tonsils, turned out to have one.
The two halves of 'righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds' describe one decree: it is just, and yet Hashem's kindness allows a person who turns to Him in prayer to have it annulled.
The treasure of free gifts is given only to one who knows he cannot expect more than a free gift, one who is broken within himself.

Just as the word 'es' in 'he shall wash es his flesh' includes the hair that is secondary to the body, 'es kol ohavav' includes those who make themselves secondary to a tzaddik: his students and supporters.

King David ruled on questions himself before consulting Mefiboshes not from pride but because a ruling of purity from the king's mouth drew purity onto all of Klal Yisrael, which Mefiboshes' word could not.

Every creature exists to bring honor to Heaven; the tzaddik does so with his life and the rasha with his downfall, and David's 'I will praise Hashem with my life' declares that he praises in the first way.
'With my being' can mean praising Hashem even with the secondary parts of life, such as eating, sleeping and business, not only with the essential ones like prayer, Torah and tzedakah.
'A person who has no salvation' is read as one for whom the matter is not a salvation: one cannot expect someone to work for a cause that he himself does not see as a rescue.

The Rav reads 'sivro' (his hope) as 'shivro' (his breaking): since a person must be broken in any case, the sign of true hope in Hashem is that he breaks himself for Hashem, in toil over Torah and avodas Hashem.
A person's lifetime is described as a process of being broken, 'teitzei rucho yashuv l'admaso', so his suffering is not wasted if he directs it into his avodah.
The Rav compares seeing Hashem behind a helper to looking through an X-ray: among all who come to help, one sees Hashem Himself coming to help.

'Tziyon' is not only a place: when there is no Beis HaMikdash, the source of bitachon is found in Tziyon of the soul, the tzaddik and talmid chacham, and in Tziyon of time, Shabbos and other holy times; this is 'Elokayich Tziyon l'dor vador'.
Bringing a hidden spark of holiness out before its time is like taking the geulah by force: Hashem brings it out through means such as bitul b'rov, but a person may not do it himself.

The Rav explains that Dovid HaMelech, having finished Tehillim with Ashrei, could not hold back his appetite for praise and added 'Hallelukah, hal'li nafshi', for praising Hashem is 'na'im', pleasant.

If in the Sanzer Rav's time only the paroches was missing from the heavenly Beis Hamikdash, then today only small finishing touches remain, and a small generation completes the building with small deeds.
A sofer may not sit on a bench with the sefer Torah he himself wrote, which shows that the holiness came from Hashem through him as a messenger, not from him.
The angel who fought Yaakov withheld his name because an angel's name is his mission, and the yetzer hara's whole aim is that people should not know what they were sent for.
People travel precisely during the forty days of the meraglim because their travels are meant to repair the meraglim's flawed journey and turn Tisha B'Av into a festival.
A tree in the country may have waited more than five thousand years for a Jew to sit under it and learn Gemara, and fruits and streams wait for a particular soul to make a bracha on them.
Since Tammuz and Av are the two eyes, damaged by the meraglim's seeing, they bring the hardest tests of the eyes, and guarding the eyes then repairs that damage.

The Torah singles out the failings of only two nesi'im, Elitzur ben Shedeur in Korach's dispute and Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai in the episode of Zimri, because their tribes correspond to Tammuz and Av.
Denial of G-d is not a failure of belief but a deliberate covering up of belief, because a person who sees G-d cannot freely follow his desires; the boy compared it to driving with the brakes on.
Modern fears that progress and pollution will destroy the world are the same mistake as the Dor Haflagah, who built a tower to hold up the sky; Hashem who made the world maintains it.
Clotting that happens only on contact with air is itself the wonder: if blood clotted inside the veins it would cause thrombosis, strokes and heart attacks.
Water's exception to the rule of contraction in cold is a purposeful deviation: Hashem needs it for His world so that rivers freeze from the top and life survives below.
Just as ice has a pattern of behavior unique to it among the elements, Jews have a pattern of behavior different from the nations.
The Rav explains the Berditchever's saying through the octave: song reaches the 'eighth' note, which returns to the first, the root, and that is the gate of teshuvah right beside it.
The Rav reads the two halves of 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes' as the two signs by which the Rambam says Moshiach is known, and calls both a return like yovel and teshuvah.
The Torah read as a circle, as at the hakafos of Simchas Torah, joins the broken lamed of the last generations to the beis of Moshe; this union is Moshiach and the healing of broken hearts.
A Jew who looks like nothing is like a distant star that looks like a speck yet is far larger than the earth; Hashem knows each one by name.
Hashem's view of a Jew is above number, just as Tzion stands above the laws of mathematics: the Aron took up no space and the crowded Azarah had room for everyone.
A person may fall ill because he has finished his mission; changing his name gives him a new mission, and so a reason to go on living.
Adam, instead of blaming Chava for bringing death, called her 'mother of all life', looking at the good side; measure for measure Hashem then covered their shame with garments.
The world is like one huge computer: removing a single tiny screw ruins it, so even the smallest creature is indispensable.
The raven, which showed no mercy in the ark, abandons its own young, yet it fed Eliyahu, because Eliyahu is a soul of the days of Moshiach, when the raven will become merciful again.
The Megillah is a preview of the final redemption: when its time came everything happened in haste, because salvation comes from a place above time.
Hashem gives the cold according to the wool: the harshness of exile is measured to the warmth a person has to withstand it.

The Rav reads the order of letters in the months' names: 'aviv' runs straight forward like the chesed of Nissan, while Tishrei runs backward, as din; likewise Jews write from right to left, the side of chesed.
Whiteness is the sign of food given freely: milk for infants, who are exempt from the curse of toiling for bread, and the white manna, 'bread for nothing' from the side of chesed.
Since Noach's soul returned as Moshe, the Gemara's hint to Moshe in the word 'beshagam', said about the generation of the flood, becomes simple: Moshe was there in Noach.

Matan Torah repeated the flood, forty days against forty days, but its waters came down as Torah; the letter shin of the 'threefold Torah' added to 'mabul' makes 'b'shalom', which is why the nations were told 'Hashem will bless His people with peace'.
'Maggid' shares a root with gidim, the vessels that carry life-blood to the limbs: speech draws one's thoughts to another, and through the rain Hashem draws His word down to Yaakov.

Yitzchak could not have children until the Akeidah, where he received a new soul, and immediately afterward Rivkah's birth was announced: the Akeidah itself fulfilled the promise it seemed to contradict.
'Shamayim' comes from 'sham', 'there', the opposite of 'karov', 'here': it means the remote places, so that even the earth, seen from the heavens, is a 'there'.

The Rav reverses the usual mark of a great work: a man-made masterpiece is finished once grasped, while the Torah, like a schoolbook that is never outgrown, is used by the child of nine and the gedolim alike, and this very inexhaustibility is a proof of its Divine origin.
The endlessness of the Torah and the endlessness of nature have the same cause: both are made by Hashem, so neither can be sealed off as finished.

The Torah proves itself through predictions that could have failed: it promised that Yehoshua would cross the Jordan and conquer, though he could have fallen sick or died in battle, and it told the tribes their portions in advance, yet required a lottery that came out exactly so.
The Rav calls the existence of the Jewish people in exile a greater wonder than the Exodus, the splitting of the sea and the miracles in the wilderness, only one that people take for granted.

The cultures of Egypt, Rome and Greece are studied today by a handful of professors, while the Torah is alive among hundreds of thousands who learn it daily, not as an academic course; this contrast fulfills the promise that the Torah will not be forgotten.
The Rav reads David's commanding of the heavens as more than poetry: the tzaddik, as the soul of Adam, is the key of creation, and without his song the creations cannot sing theirs.
He explains the word 'shamayim' as 'the far places', from 'sham', there: places removed from us, and 'shmei hashamayim' as what is far even from the heavens' point of view.
The harmful forces exist only on earth, since in heaven 'evil does not dwell with You', which is why the verse lists the storm wind only among the praises from the earth.
Of the four klipos in Yechezkel's vision, the 'ruach se'arah' is the worst and 'nogah' the lightest, which can be turned to holiness, like the wisdom of Yavan that can be used for kedushah.
'Hodo al eretz veshamayim' puts earth first because the praise of beings with free choice, who could refuse, is what truly shows that Hashem's name alone is exalted.
In the days of Moshiach the angels will say kadosh before the tzaddikim, so Hashem will need a new praise: this is the 'shir chadash'.
The new song of the future is like an eighth note added to the seven: as a zero added to a number multiplies it, the melodies will be enriched beyond anything possible in exile.

The Rav reads the prohibition of eating new grain until Pesach as reflecting that each year's crop carries a greater light of Hashem's Name, which one is fit to receive only once the festival of redemption has come.

From the Midrash that Scripture says 'yismach' and not 'samach', the Rav learns that Hashem Himself has not yet had complete joy in His world, and therefore no person can attain complete fulfillment before Moshiach either.

Shlomo HaMelech, the fifteenth generation from Avraham like the moon on the fifteenth day, was the one person who fulfilled all his desires, because at the dedication of the Beis HaMikdash he was a sample of Moshiach and the third Beis HaMikdash.
The 'circle dance' of the future means that no one will stand above another and there will be no jealousy; all the tzaddikim will be equal, each pointing to Hashem in the center.
The drum, mere banging on its own, adds life to the other instruments when played with them; so the blows of galus, together with the good times, will be sung to Hashem as kindness.
Pharaoh's calm sleep on the night of the plague of the firstborn was itself arranged by Hashem, so that the plagues of Egypt would become a remedy for the Jews, feeding them with bitachon.
Yeshivos build their learning on resolving contradictions in the Rambam's halachos, yet leave his philosophy unlearned, and the Rav says there must be a reason for it.
Philosophy is like chess: a proof by a mind of IQ 200 falls before one of 300, so it can never establish a truth.
Understanding Hashem with the mind is not a matter of being smart enough; it is the wrong organ, like seeing a symphony with the eyes.
Weakness in emunah comes from aveiros, which insulate the neshamah from Hashem like the sheath on an electric wire.
The title Moreh Nevuchim shows the sefer was written for the lost, who are like a wet match that Torah cannot ignite until they first do teshuvah.
In Ein K'Elokeinu we say the answer, 'there is none like our G-d', before the question, 'who is like our G-d', because we do not trust ourselves with a kasha before the teretz.
Singing praise for a salvation that has not yet come, out of certainty that it will, is itself the 'sword in the hand' that defeats the obstacles.

Yehuda's long retelling of what Yosef already knew was a hint to him; the descent to Egypt behind the mask of the harsh ruler is a model of the whole exile, behind which Hashem waits to reveal Himself once Israel does teshuvah.

Everything connected with 'eight' is connected with hod and hadar: on Shemini Atzeres one no longer takes the esrog because the day itself is the hadar, and the eighth day of Chanukah hints to the splendor of Moshiach.
Chesed is called gedulah because it is expansion, going out beyond the borders of oneself to another, while gevurah is contraction into oneself.
The drum has no melody and only makes noise, yet it keeps the rhythm of the whole music; so even what seems like harsh knocking in the world is a measured part of the symphony of Hashem's guidance.
Psalm 148 is praise in quantity, all creation joining; Psalm 149's 'new song' asks for quality, each creature adding something new to the praise.
Galus is not a place where Jews are stuck but a journey on the way up to Yerushalayim, so the troubles David HaMelech speaks of are stepping stones toward the Beis HaMikdash.
'Sfas sheker' is read as the edge of falsehood, like the bank of a river: one must be saved even from something on the border of a lie, in line with 'midvar sheker tirchak'.
'Lashon remiya' is what the Rav calls 'politics': deceit arranged to look kosher, as one soaks and salts meat to make it kosher.
On 'mah yosif l'ba'al halashon': since speech is man's whole advantage over animals, and every animal does exactly what Hashem made it for, one who misuses speech is worse than an animal.
Tehillim 121 is the only one of the fifteen that says 'lamaalos' rather than 'hamaalos': it is a song to Hashem, who goes along with a Jew and lifts him up the steps.

Help comes 'from ayin', from nothing: when a person reaches rock bottom and can fall no lower, that itself is the sign that his salvation is coming, as the Ruzhiner's wheel parable and the Chesed L'Avraham show.

Reading 'harim' as 'horim', the Avos: Yaakov looked to his parents, who had traveled with wealth, and when he saw he had nothing, he held on to Hashem alone; the Avos' levels were taken from them so that they could set an example for their children in a fallen state.

The Beis Hamikdash is called 'heaven and earth' because it stood on earth yet, like heaven, was above place, time and number; so the help 'from Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth' can be the same kind of miracle for Jews now.
The miracle of space in Yerushalayim was not something one saw; it showed only when someone took a count of the people and the beds, while each person simply found a place to sleep.

A teacher who makes a pasuk or Midrash shine in his students' hearts has it quoted in his name, which is why the Ba'al haTanya brings a known Midrash in the Ba'al Shem Tov's name and why a pasuk in Mishlei appears in Avos in a Tanna's name.
The sign of the redeemer was not the words 'pakod pakadti', which everyone knew, but that when the true redeemer said them they would light up in the listeners' hearts.
Adar, the last month, is the darkest, yet because it is the end things suddenly turn over; for the same reason the Megillah shows no open miracles and no name of Hashem, since He is hidden.
'The sun will not strike you' means even success can harm, through envy and through a fall that comes from too much success; Hashem guards one who lives with hashgacha pratis from that.

Pharaoh's 'words of falsehood' were the Midrashim of redemption that the Jews read when they gathered on the Shabbos Moshe had won for them; by demanding the same output without straw he meant to make them work on Shabbos.
The Rav reads the name 'teivel' for the earth as 'confusion', as in the eye blemish tevallul, so that the pasuk of the lightnings describes Hashem lighting up a world of confusion.
A flash of lightning lasts only a moment, yet it is enough to show a traveler which way the road goes; so too a brief revelation in the darkness gives direction.
According to the Rav, the absence of open wonders today is not because there are no tzaddikim, but because in hester panim they are not given permission to show them.
Through the Kotzker Rebbe's reply to the Apta Rav, the Rav teaches that believing is a higher level than seeing, so the generation of hiding has its own greatness.
The Rav describes our souls as sent down into this period of darkness on a mission, so that believing despite Hashem's disguise is the calling of this world.

The Rav sees the rebuilding of the Old City's twisting streets exactly as before, done by an engineer for historical reasons, as Hashem steering him so that Yerushalayim below would match Yerushalayim above.
The Gemara's reason for the name Teveria shows, according to the Rav, that Chazal knew a holy city's name is never random, even when a wicked ruler gave it.
He reads the name Yerushalayim as a joining of Yir'eh and Shalem, which in turn is the joining of service of G-d with peace between people that no other place achieves.
The pilgrimage, in the Rav's reading, raised each tribe from its own portion to the level of Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, which is why Yerushalayim was never divided among the tribes.
The Rav links the 'shivtei Kah' to the miracles of Yerushalayim: carrying the Name Kah, the tribes are raised above place, time and calculation.

He answers the Brisker Rav's question on the closing of the brachah for Yerushalayim by saying that David is Yerushalayim, since the Davidic kings are so nullified to it that they are the city itself.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Rav distinguishes the one who trusts, the mivtach on whom he relies, and the thing he hopes for: the business is only a garment of hishtadlus, while Hashem must be the mivtach.
The extra yud of 'hayoshvi' is read as 'my' One who sits in heaven: each Jew has his own personal G-d who deals with him with individual attention.

Through the Radak, the Rav shows that a servant being struck looks to the very hand that strikes him, since no one else can save him from his master; so a Jew in suffering turns to the One who sends it.

The raised ayin of 'chazir miya'ar' is read as a hope that the ayin will become an aleph, turning the destructive forest boar of Rome into a harmless creature of the river, like the 'kosnos or' with an aleph that rectifies Adam's sin.
A repeated word in tefillah, which the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah would not add, is not part of the text but a reflexive cry from within, like a child's second 'quick!' or Eliyahu's second 'aneini'.
Turning the cheek to the striker is read as a way to end the blows: the striker is satisfied with the disgrace, and Klal Yisrael pleads that it has already had its fill of shame.

Since Jews did not merit that the nations come to them as in Shlomo's time, they must go out to the nations in galus, and the Chasam Sofer reads the plea to be gathered from the nations in this light.

A man with free choice is a greater danger than a king, whose heart is in Hashem's hand; this is why the Gemara stresses that Haman was 'a man and not a king', and the Rav illustrates it with saving someone from a man versus from a pit.

The 'waters' in the kapitel are forces of judgment, and the power of the splitting of the Yam Suf, when all the world's waters split, is eternal: every flood that threatens the Jews still splits before them.
Pre-war America was like Pisom and Raamses: whatever was built sank into the ground and had to be built again, and so the immigrants' Yiddishkeit sank into the 'clay' of America.
A bird caught in a trap escapes only by breaking a leg or a wing, but here 'the trap broke and we escaped': the Jews came out whole, as seen in the rebirth after the war.
'Maker of heaven and earth' in the present tense means Hashem constantly creates new heavens and earth, and in the new heavens a decree that was written may no longer be written.
Har Tziyon was a marker that left the imprint of G-dliness on the world; after its destruction, the Jews who trust in Hashem take over its function among the nations.
Just as, according to the Rambam, Yerushalayim's holiness from the Shechinah outlasts every conquest, the holiness of a Jew from the Shechinah cannot be taken away by the nations or by sin.

Emunas tzaddikim is part of emunah itself: the Torah describes the height of emunah at the sea as belief in Hashem and in Moshe His servant, and the Rav adds that one must also believe in oneself, since all Jews are tzaddikim.

Because Hashem looked into the Torah to create the world, anything that exists in the world must be found in the Torah; a tzaddik's knowledge of medicine or of the future is drawn from the Torah, not from outside study.

The Torah's daring promise that no one will covet a Jew's land while he goes up to Yerushalayim with his whole family is something no human author could have written; it shows the Torah's divine source.
Details reported by a single historian may be doubted, but the bare existence of a figure witnessed by multitudes cannot; this is the type of certainty on which Matan Torah rests.

The worldwide identity of the Sefer Torah is itself a proof: Jews separated for centuries by geography, with no means of contact, are found to hold the same text letter for letter, preserved by the halachah that one missing letter disqualifies a Sefer Torah.
The Rav reads the second half of the verse as a consequence of the first: because the rod of the wicked cannot stay on the tzaddikim, the tzaddikim need not stretch out their hands to fight it.
The Ruzhiner held back his power against Russia as gratitude, since Russia had once let in Jews fleeing persecution, like a man who spares the robber who once gave him refuge.
The four levels of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, correspond to the four levels of the soul, so a stringency in one sefer and a leniency in a posek can both be right.
A spot on a potato sack is nothing, while the same spot on silk demands a refund; so the same act that does not stain a simpler soul does stain a finer one.
The Rav reads 'asher tasim lifneihem' as 'lifnim': lifnim mishuras hadin is itself a mishpat, a real law, for the one at that level.
Rav Kahana's students followed even his leniency, using hadassim that were not meshulash, to show their bond with him: hiskashrus means following the Rebbe in kulos as well as chumros.

In galus Jews do not know what they accomplish: through the Torah they gave the world, the nations slowly learned some honesty, humanity and justice, and when Moshiach comes this will be revealed and rewarded beyond what anyone dreamed.

Following Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky, the Rav reads hashpa'ah as related to a slope: influence is something that flows down on its own, so the Jews influence their surroundings even when they think they make no impression.

The laughter of 'Az yimalei s'chok pinu' will be at the nations themselves: they will finally see that the greatness was with the Jews in galus, yet their grasp will remain limited, while the Jews will understand far more.
Galus makes the thirst for Hashem greater than in Temple times, just as a person lost in a desert thirsts more than one who knows water awaits him at home.

Following Rebbe Zusha, both those who serve Hashem with tears and those who serve Him with joy will reap salvation, but the one who sows in tears carries home only the seed, while the one who serves with joy brings whole sheaves.
The faith of the nations in the Creator, crooked as it is, is the planting of the Jews in galus, which is why Israel in galus is called Yizre'el.

Like the sale of Yosef, the sin of the Eitz HaDa'as and the meraglim, the destruction only appears to have been caused by Shlomo; in truth it was all part of Hashem's plan, as will be seen when Moshiach comes.
The first Beis HaMikdash was built in order to be destroyed, so that the Kosel Maaravi would remain as the place of the Shechinah in galus.
The Rav reads 'if Hashem does not build the house' as David's prophecy about the churban of the very Beis HaMikdash his son would build, set in motion when Shlomo slept late before its inauguration.
Hiddurim belong to Torah and mitzvos; in business, which is only the fulfilment of Adam's curse, a person need not beautify his effort with extra hours.
Right after hinting at Shlomo's part in the churban, David calls him 'the heritage of Hashem', teaching that what was decreed in Hashem's plan is no blemish on Shlomo.
A newborn child is called a 'nachalah', a new territory from Hashem that opens a new channel of parnassah for the family.
Light-heartedly, the Rav reads 'ashpaso' as the household's refuse: the mud children track in is itself a blessing.

The same blessing of many children that a yerei Hashem treasures means nothing to someone of the 'mashkimei kum', so 'thus shall the man who fears Hashem be blessed' can only be said to a yerei Hashem.
The Rav explains that Moshe Rabbeinu's miracles in the midbar were not done to prove anything; each was done because it was needed, such as drowning the Mitzrim or the earth swallowing the rebels.
Since every Jew heard Hashem appoint Moshe, the nevuah of Moshe is for us as clear as daylight, so no wonder can compete with it; the question is never who shows bigger miracles.
Obeying any later navi is itself a mitzvah from Moshe Rabbeinu's Torah, like obeying witnesses, and not a matter of being convinced by his miracles.
The Rav answers Rashi's question by explaining that milah and gid hanasheh are known only because Moshe told us of them, so HaChodesh hazeh lachem is the first mitzvah heard from Moshe Rabbeinu.

He reads 'Moshe av lanevi'im' as meaning that even the nevi'im before Moshe, like Avraham and Yaakov, are known through him, and those after him are believed because he commanded us to listen to them.

The difference between the covenant of Noach and that of milah is that Noach's was in the heavens, a sign to look up at, while milah is in the body, so that a Jew's very physical functions serve Hashem.
'Holech', walking, means the one still on the way is already praised, just as a hava amina that the Gemara rejects is itself Torah learning.
A vine cannot be grafted with another species, and this is the purity and holiness of the Jewish home.
A vine planted indoors keeps its roots in the house while its fruit grows outside, like children rooted in the holiness of the Jewish home who sanctify Hashem's name outside it.
A Jew has a private home and a collective home, the beis knesses, and the collective home is the main one, the source of the private home's contentment.
The nations hate the Jews for the same reason Yosef's brothers hated him: envy, an inner sense that the Jews are nobler and have a future.
Following Rav Shmelke of Nikolsburg, the curse that passersby give no blessing means that a soul reincarnated in food does not merit the brachah of a tzaddik that brings its tikkun.
Matisyahu, the soul of Chanukah, equals 'Beis HaMikdash' in gematria, so in the days of Chanukah a Jew merits a Beis HaMikdash.
The word chashman hints at chodesh, Shabbos and milah, the three mitzvos the Greeks tried to abolish, together with ner Chanukah, the mitzvah Hashem added in response.
On Shabbos a Jew is raised to the higher world, while on Chanukah the higher light descends into the weekday of exile; this is why the Shabbos light may be used and the Chanukah light may not.
The words of the psalm's blessing, 'Hashem will bless you from Zion and you will see the good of Yerushalayim', equal 'ner Shabbos, ner Chanukah' in gematria.
The letters of 'bracha' are each the first doubling in their rank of numbers (two, twenty, two hundred), showing that blessing means increase.

Achitofel's Torah was barren: nothing grew from his two teachings, yet David called him rebbe; all the more so one whose chiddush gives rise to further chiddushim, which is the meaning of 'children of your children'.
Just as every force of holiness has its opposite, emunah above the intellect is matched by a kefirah above the intellect: refusing to believe what the intellect itself sees.
What the Jews saw at the sea was knowledge, not belief, like seeing daylight through an open window; their emunah was in what lay beyond that, what Moshe Rabbeinu told them of heaven.
Amalek is listed among the chiefs of Edom who trembled at the splitting of the sea, so his attack weeks later was a denial of what he himself had seen, the exact reverse of Jewish emunah.
The other religions are not a denial of the Torah but a rationalization: unable to keep it, they claim that Hashem changed His mind.
Hashem cannot be said to change His mind, since He already knows what will be later; this is why the Torah's own promise that it will never change is decisive.
The 'depths' of the kapitel are the innermost point of the Jew, the place where he is a child of Hashem and where no sin ever reached; calling from there is what makes forgiveness possible.
The thirty-nine lashes instead of forty reflect that the highest of the levels of the soul is never touched by sin, so it is not struck.
The treasure of undeserved gifts flows from the Jew being Hashem's child: a father gives to a child not because he earned it but because a father must give.
Forgiveness leads to fear of Hashem in two ways: it keeps a sinner from despairing and abandoning himself, and it removes the barrier of sin so that he can feel Hashem's presence.
At a time destined for the geulah the Satan accuses that Jews are unworthy, and this is why such dates brought great troubles rather than redemption.
Not the irreligious, who are like children captured and know nothing, but machlokes and lashon hara among frum Jews spoiled the geulah.
The Rav reads 'mishomrim laboker' with Rashi's sense of 'shamar' as waiting for fulfillment: the soul watches for each 'morning' of possible redemption, and when one passes it waits for the next.
Moshe Rabbeinu's first coming, after which the bondage grew harsher, and his second coming that brought the redemption, parallel Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben Dovid.
At times set for a ketz, troubles often come instead of redemption, because the will in heaven to redeem awakens accusation that the Jews are unworthy.
The Tree of Knowledge was meant for squeezing its grapes for Kiddush on Friday night; Adam's sin was eating before Shabbos, so the root failure of the world was not waiting.

The alphabetical verses of Tehillim 34 represent the fixed order of creation and judgment, while the extra verse 'Podeh Hashem nefesh avadav' stands 'outside the brackets' because pedus is beyond that order.
At the Akeidah Hashem wanted Avraham, the attribute of chesed, to bind Yitzchak, the attribute of din, so that din loses its power; this repeats every Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Rebbi was punished though the ox was truly created for slaughter, because one who asks asylum must be saved, and so Hashem saves whoever seeks shelter in Him even if guilty.
The tefilah Moshe Rabbeinu was not allowed to say is being supplied by Jews' davening over three thousand years; when it adds up to the power of his one tefilah, the end will come.
Hashem sometimes reveals a decree precisely so that a tzaddik will daven in vain now, and the tefilah will be credited to his descendants when they need a yeshuah they do not deserve.
Haman's decree came exactly seventy years after the bowing to Nevuchadnetzar's image because those seventy years were a time of pekidah, and an eis ratzon is also when sins are recalled.
'Pedus' appears in Tanach without a vav except in 'v'harbeh imo fedus', which alludes to the full redemption of the third Beis HaMikdash.
The two alphabetical chapters of Tehillim end with an extra 'pei' verse of pedus after the alef-beis of reward and punishment, showing a conduct above strict judgment.
Just as Purim's miracle came from Hashem's chesed and not from merit, so on Purim one gives to whoever asks, and the day is called Yom Kippurim, a day 'like Purim'.
Dovid HaMelech's 'lo gavah libi' was not a lack of greatness: he simply placed all grandeur in the Beis HaMikdash rather than in his own palace.
Reducing the Torah to one mitzvah is a matter of concentration, not exemption: great souls could put their whole being into every mitzvah, while small souls must pour themselves into one.

The sequence of generations maps onto the body of Adam HaRishon: the desert generation, who only learned, was the head; the era of the Beis HaMikdash, when tefillah as 'service of the heart' was added, was the heart.
The name 'ikvesa deMeshicha' hints that the last generation is the heel of Adam HaRishon: like the sole of the foot, it has the least feeling and is always in the dark, even under the noon sun.
The very obstacles a person meets in some area are a sign that it is his mission, since the Satan targets precisely what a person was sent to do.
The pervasive loss of faith in today's world is itself the Satan's response to emunah being this generation's mission.
The Rav reads David's statement 'my heart was not haughty' as all the more striking because it comes from a king, the one person whose position would allow great aspirations.
Moshe, Avraham and David correspond to the three sources of influence on a person, his teacher, his father and his king, and each was a model of humility.
The splendor of tzaddikim of the house of David is no contradiction to their humility: it serves to arouse Heaven to restore the kingdom of David to its honor.
Envy of another's spiritual level comes from gaavah, so contentment with one's own portion is itself part of humility.
An infant can be given neither honor nor disgrace; this is the meaning of 'like a weaned child', the equanimity David describes.
David's restraint toward Shimi, though Shimi deserved death as a rebel, is what raised him to be the fourth leg of the Divine chariot, and it is also what made Purim possible through Mordechai.
Hashem 'remembers' David's suffering because the Satan sets itself against anyone who wants to do a great good, as it did to Avraham on the way to the Akeidah.
Eretz Yisroel stands to the world as Rosh Hashana to the year and Shabbos to the week: it is the root from which everything draws, and Yerushalayim is the Shabbos within it.
In Eretz Yisroel a Jew receives a neshama from a higher Name, like the neshama yeseira of Shabbos; like a wire carrying higher voltage, it makes both his mitzvos and his sins far greater.
Because the land is surrounded by water on all four sides, entering it is like immersing in a mikveh before Shabbos.
The kedusha of Eretz Yisroel exceeds that of a beis haknesses, since even inside a shul one must turn one's heart toward the land.
In Eretz Yisroel the yetzer hara is greater too: the one abroad is only its messenger, since whoever is greater has a greater yetzer.
Moshe Rabbeinu, at home in heaven, first needed to open with praise in the land of Sichon and Og, because the kedusha of Eretz Yisroel there awed him more than heaven itself.
Measured as land, Eretz Yisroel is a small territory; measured as a diamond, it is enormous.
The Rav reads the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's words to the penitent as showing that the hardship of the road itself does much of the work of teshuvah, before one even reaches the tzaddik.
Guarding one's eyes on the plane is not only a defense; the Rav calls it a greater preparation, since one sees Tziyon according to the eyes one brings to it.

Walled-city Purim was tied to Yehoshua bin Nun precisely because Yerushalayim lay in ruins at the time of the miracle; the day was set to give it honor, so coming there for Purim reaches the day's true intent.

The geulah did not come through the great Tanna'im, Amora'im and Rishonim; for His own reasons Hashem wants it to come through small people, so perhaps the small efforts of those preparing for Yerushalayim will bring it.

The Rav compares the longing for Eretz Yisroel to a healthy appetite: the Avos' desire was healthy, so it went to the true good, and a Jew who lacks that longing has spoiled his desire, like one who ate something sour and lost his appetite.

Yerushalayim is the place of unity because it is the concentration of all Eretz Yisroel; therefore baseless hatred meant exile from it, and one without unity does not belong in Yerushalayim, just as he does not belong in Purim.
When a holy place leaves one unmoved, the Rav applies the Ba'al Shem Tov's advice for a closed heart in davening: keep working with emunah, and the feeling will come as a gift after the toil.

The Rav reads the Chafetz Chaim's prediction that dibbukim would cease as a statement about the test of the generation: a dibbuk revealing people's hidden sins and the soul's suffering would make emunah too easy, and this generation must be tested in emunah.

He reconciles later dibbukim in Eretz Yisrael with the Chafetz Chaim's words by explaining that Hashem's guidance is seen strikingly in Eretz Yisrael anyway, so there the test of emunah is already smaller.

The Rav sees the Satan's hand in the test of each age: in the tzitzis factory whose sales spread unfit tzitzis, and, following the Yaaros Devash, in the custom of black Shabbos clothes that invites brushing off dust on Shabbos.
He contrasts the Torah, where Moshe Rabbeinu boldly foretells the future of the Jewish people, with other religions' books, which do not dare to predict because they would be proven false.
The Rav compares the rare wonders of tzaddikim today to lightning that lights up a dark world for a moment before it is dark again.
Since the exile came from despising the desirable land, the inner work of the Three Weeks is to repair that sin by valuing Eretz Yisroel and rejoicing in it.
Great tzaddikim were held back from reaching Eretz Yisroel by Heaven, because their tefillos at the gate of heaven would have hastened the geulah while the exile still had to continue.
Following Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, the meraglim's report came from seeing by ruach hakodesh the generations that would fall in the land, since its yetzer hara is as great as its holiness.
The Yamim Tovim, which give a Jew his emunah and life for the whole year, depend on the months being fixed by Jews in Eretz Yisroel, so without a Jewish settlement there Klal Yisroel could not exist.
Moshe Rabbeinu could not abolish the yetzer hara for avodah zarah, while Yehoshua and the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah could, because only they had the merit of entering Eretz Yisroel.
Rashi read 'better one day in Your courts than a thousand' as a thousand years because, as a holy man, he knew what Eretz Yisroel is worth.
Moshe Rabbeinu mentions Eretz Yisroel again and again in Sefer Devarim because speaking about the land, like speaking about tzaddikim, brings yiras shamayim.
The Rav reads Rashi's 'as if given to you today' as the measure for the love of the land: it must burn with the freshness of a new gift.
From 'goy echad ba'aretz' he derives that Jews are one nation only in Eretz Yisroel; outside it a Jew is like an animal pacing in a zoo, in a place where he does not belong.
He warns that Jerusalem can become like the daily breakfast oatmeal one stops noticing; a visit there needs freshness and preparation.
He explains 'Shabbos Chazon' from the word chazah, seeing: the vision of the third Beis HaMikdash is seen with the heart, not the eyes.
He connects Beis Lechem, Rachel's place, with Yovel, the return of each man to his inheritance, so that 'veshavu vanim ligvulam' is its fulfillment.

He traces galus to jealousy rooted in the moon's diminishing, through Kayin, the brothers and Yeravam to the hatred that destroyed the Beis HaMikdash, and says Rachel, the aspect of the moon, began its repair by overcoming jealousy.
The ten sedras of Devarim map the centuries of the sixth millennium, so the Rav reads Nitzavim-Vayelech, counted as one sedra, as the Torah's account of the century that began with Tav-Shin.
The hester panim of the end of the galus is doubled: not only does Hashem hide His face, the concealment itself is concealed, so people do not even see that He is hiding.
Moshe Rabbeinu wrote down the hester panim in advance as testimony, something the founders of other religions never dared to do, since only he knew his words would come true.

Preparing the refuah before the makah is what shows a surgeon is not a murderer, so for the Jewish people even the blow is part of the healing; Haman's decree itself was a yeshua that brought them to teshuvah.
Because a sedra is a 'program' of the world, galus and the geulah, though in one century, belong to two different orders and so need two sedras.
The teshuvah movement of today is a 'drizzle' of the full teshuvah of Moshiach's time, the beginning of Nitzavim's prophecy.
Whatever exists in time exists in place: the softer judgment of the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the aspect of Rachel, has its place all year at Kever Rachel.
Leah is the aspect of harsh judgment and Rachel of soft judgment, which the Rav maps onto the first and second days of Rosh Hashanah.
Though Yirmiyahu is the prophet of lament, the Rav says no comfort in all of Yeshayahu, the prophet of comfort, is as great as the haftorah of the second day of Rosh Hashanah.
Shmuel's fifty-two years and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's eighteen add up to seventy, which is why, as his gilgul, he said he was 'like seventy years old'.
Because Shmuel never took benefit from anyone, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, his gilgul, could not be supported as nasi by others and needed his own wealth.
Every generation has its own 'counsel of the spies', changing shape like a cloud; in this generation it is kefirah, pritzus and electronic devices.
Above, Hashem Himself looks at the hidden sod of each Jew, which no one else sees, and that sod is good.
Rachel's burial on the road is read through the contrast of home and road: the home gathers, the road scatters, so the akeres habayis had to lie on the road to bring her gathering power into exile.
Had Rachel been buried in a closed cave like the other Avos and Imahos, the Jews in exile would have had no way back, since they could not reach her.
Sefer Devarim is the seventh book and the kallah, as Shabbos is the seventh day and the kallah, which is why it is begun on Shabbos Chazon.
The barrenness the kever of Shmuel and Chana can heal is also spiritual: Torah and tefilah without siyata dishmaya are 'barren' and bear no fruit.
Shmuel embodies kingship for both lines of Klal Yisrael, anointing Shaul from Rachel and David from Leah.

Eretz Yisroel is to place what Shabbos is to time: the 'eretz chemdah' parallels the 'chemdas hayamim', and just as a blatt Gemara on Shabbos is holier and a sin on Shabbos graver, in Eretz Yisroel both merit and damage are magnified.

Using the Arizal's reason for the second day of Yom Tov abroad, a smaller neshamah that cannot absorb the light in one day, the Rav explains that the light of Shabbos Purim in Yerushalayim is so great that even a Jew of Eretz Yisroel needs three days to receive it.

Moshe Rabbeinu, though far greater, could not pray away the yetzer hara of avodah zarah because he was outside the land, while Yehoshua and, a thousand years later, the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah could, through the power of tefillah in Eretz Yisroel.

Although residency in Eretz Yisroel normally requires thirty days, one day of Purim in Yerushalayim makes a person a resident of a walled city, just as seven days of Sukkos count as dwelling because the sukkah defines dwelling.

Mordechai and Esther originally instituted reading the Megillah even on Shabbos; only later was it moved, for the honor of Shabbos. Therefore the whole power of Purim in Yerushalayim rests in its Shabbos even though the Megillah is not read then.
The earth of Eretz Yisroel is holier than the heavens of chutz la'aretz; seeing it as ordinary land is like seeing a Jew and a goy as the same person because their bodies look alike.

A tefillah without feeling can be greater than one with it: R' Avraham Kalisker concluded that his first dry tefillah in the land surpassed the famous minchah under the tree, since the feeling is a gift and the labor is the avodah.

The order of the months follows the body of Adam HaRishon: Nissan is the head and Adar the heel, so Adar belongs to the souls lowest in time and in level, and Purim's miracle is the miracle of those lowest Jews.
At the very feast whose enjoyment brought Haman's decree, Hashem was already preparing the salvation by removing Vashti so that Esther could come in.
Amalek's essence is to plant doubts in emunah, and that is the cloak that hides Hashem; this is why Hashem's name and open miracles are absent from the Megillah.
HaMelech, kes Kah and Haman each equal 95 in gematria, linking the King who stands behind the Megillah to the incomplete name caused by Amalek.
Hashem's name does appear in the Megillah, but hidden at its turning points, such as the words read in one breath by a knowledgeable ba'al korei.
Shimshon's apparently improper deeds are explained as a descent to the lowest, assimilating Jews in order to pull them out, done with self-sacrifice for Klal Yisroel.
Hair, which people cut off and which is farthest from the brain, stands for the Jews cut off from Klal Yisroel; Shimshon of Dan, the last tribe, drew his strength from exactly them.
'Nezer Elokav al rosho', said of the nazir's hair, has the gematria of ikvesa d'meshicha: the last Jews are the crown.
Just as hair is the last thing to form in a fetus and shows that it is complete, so the last generation completes Klal Yisroel.
Shimshon was ready to give his life to fight those who harm Hashem's servants, while the Plishtim of today give their lives to harm Jews; the name 'Palestinians' ties them to the Plishtim.
Rochel's 'disgrace' that Hashem took away at Yosef's birth is read as the disgrace of orlah: against Esav, who was never circumcised, came Yosef, born circumcised, the foundation of the bris.

The mazal of Elul, the maiden, was created when a maiden grabbed an angel's wing to escape corruption; Elul is therefore a month of 'grabbing', a time to seize every opportunity and fly upward in prayer.
Although Yishmael is circumcised, he counts as 'arel': milah is meant to weaken desire, and he is the greatest ba'al ta'avah, so the 'arel v'tamei' that may no longer enter Yerushalayim includes him.

Kalev's lone stand against the spies, who claimed to be the majority and the heads of Bnei Yisrael, is the model for today's test: holding to true views alone against a whole world drawn after false leaders.
Because every prayer passes through the place of the Avos, Shemoneh Esrei opens by binding the tefillah to 'the G-d of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov'.
Tu B'Av, the full moon, is the root of the joy of chassan and kallah between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael that will be complete at Shemini Atzeres and with Moshiach.
The Rav reads 'matzeves kevuras Rachel ad hayom' as meaning that the very lights Yaakov and the shevatim placed in the matzeivah are still present there today.

The thirteenth of Adar is a 'zman kehilah', and gathering in unity at Rachel, the one who unites Klal Yisroel, means gathering at the very root of kehilah, whose light is to be carried into the days of Purim.
Purim, carrying the aspect of Moshiach ben Yosef and the war with Amalek, is followed by Nissan, the aspect of Moshiach ben Dovid and the Beis Hamikdash.
Rachel's two acts of mesirus nefesh map onto two redemptions: Yosef stands for Moshiach, and Binyamin, the root of Mordechai, stands for Purim.

Through bechirah and yediah the Rav reconciles the Zohar's demand that Rachel's grave be uncovered with its being built over: had it been a matter of choice it should not have been done, but since nothing happens without Hashem's will, it shows that her grave must now be covered.
That even Rachel, the revealed one, is now hidden behind walls upon walls shows the lowest level of hester, which is exactly what Purim, the megillah of hester, comes to uncover.

Ur Kasdim was self-sacrifice for a G-d Avraham had never seen; the Akeidah was harder because he had come to know Hashem as Emes over many years, and now saw Him only 'from a distance', as if the One he knew was not keeping His word.

Avraham could not see the simple answer a child learning Rashi sees, not for lack of wisdom, but because the test required that he not know: when Hashem does not want a person to know, he does not know.
The same answer resolves how Haman, brilliant enough to calculate that Moshe died on the seventh of Adar, missed that Moshe was also born then: Hashem wanted there to be Purim.

Applying the Ramban's principle to the ten tests, the Rav says each era of Jewish history could be matched to one of Avraham's tests, and the last stretch of the golus corresponds to the Akeidah, a test of hester panim and kashyos.

The word Emes, which the Torah does not write after the parshiyos of Shema but which we add ourselves, corresponds to the 'eikev', the heels of Moshiach, when the truth cannot be seen; hence Avraham was told 'eikev asher shamata bekoli'.
Avodas Hashem is not a tax paid at set times, after which the rest of the day is one's own; the claim 'I may have my own time' is a mistake.
Whether physical activity was for Hashem is revealed retroactively: if after his needs a person turns to Torah, all of it was service; if not, the whole day was empty.
Torah study, though greater, attracts incentives such as honor and recognition, whereas tefillah is purely speaking to Hashem.
Like a sick man who must live on oranges when he cannot eat bread and meat, the weak generation before Moshiach must strengthen itself through tefillah.
Gemara must be learned, not davened, and davening must be davened, not learned.
In early generations Torah alone sufficed, but now the world is old and bent over and its main avodah is tefillah.

The Rav reads the signs of Moshiach like weather: heavy clouds with thunder and lightning make rain likely but not certain, and so the world's present turmoil makes the redemption very near without promising it.
A bachur's zeal in coming on time to davening and seder is, measure for measure, an awakening above that the redemption should come early and not be postponed.
For a bachur without money, tzedakah can be giving time to a downcast friend, encouraging him and cheering him up, and this too hastens Moshiach.
The Sanzer Rav's remark on the rotten bekeshe teaches that a garment of mitzvos done with excuses looks whole but tears at every touch in the next world.
Immersing in the morning in honor of Moshiach's coming, as one immerses in honor of Shabbos to receive its light in purity, is a way of fulfilling the mitzvah of hoping for the redemption.

Because all Jews are bound together, a small act of purity such as washing negel vasser purifies not only the person but his friends, Klal Yisroel and the whole creation, the reverse of how the generation of the Flood corrupted it.

Yitzchak's wells were not plain wells but deeds through which he worked toward the 'living waters', which is Hashem Himself; learning the Torah's account of the wells teaches that one must toil and dig to reach Him.

Following the Kol Simchah, the Plishtim's stopping of the wells was their declaration that the wells were 'just wells', nothing to learn from; that dismissive mockery is itself what blocks the source.
The earth the Plishtim filled the wells with is the element of afar, the root of laziness, so letzanus leads to laziness, and Yitzchak's re-digging stands for renewing toil in Torah and tefillah.

The Vizhnitzer reads the phrases of Nishmas as levels: the higher a person stands, the less physical motion his tefillah needs, from the yesharim who sing and shout, to the tzaddikim with their lips, the chassidim with their tongue, and the kedoshim whose davening is entirely inward.
Moments of dveikus in tefillah serve as a preparation for Torah: after such a moment a person's learning is different, like one to whom the king has spoken.
A person who would refuse to daven or do mitzvos because he does not yet know the whole Torah shows that his learning is not lishmah, which is why one must interrupt Torah for mitzvos.
The Satan concentrates his attack on whatever mitzvah is a person's main mission, so the very difficulty of emunah today shows that emunah is the mission of this generation.
The intensity of today's assault on emunah is the flare of a dying candle: the Satan knows that Moshiach means his end and is gasping for life.
Following the Tosfos Yom Tov, the Rav compares this generation to the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur: when the Satan concentrates all his force on one target, surviving it is a miracle.
Esav's kiss is itself a bite: the Church's friendliness has done more damage to the Jewish people than its persecutions, and this is the 'vayishakehu with dots' of our time.
The Satan's new power to enter the Jewish home is a condemned prisoner's 'last wish', granted because his end is near.
Those who daven together are like mountain climbers roped together: when one slips he does not fall, because the others hold him.
The angels can say their praise 'together' only because 'all are beloved', each one loving the other; so too the singers at the sea are called 'yedidim', friends.

A bachur's young years parallel the young years of Klal Yisrael, and just as at the end of the galus the emphasis falls on davening, so a bachur cannot neglect davening even though learning is his main task.

The 24 windows of the mishmaros in the Beis HaMikdash correspond to 24 windows of blessing in heaven, linked to the 24 combinations of the Name Adnus; coming late closes a person's window of chochmah, health, simchah and parnassah.
Everything is measured and counted, measure for measure: a soul that came late to davening and learning in its lifetime comes too late to its own tikkun.
One who comes early to davening and learning helps build the Beis HaMikdash, the reverse of the lateness that contributed to its destruction.
A dream of a sin is not a real sin, yet it shows some connection to it; the Maggid's dream of a blessing in vain on Tisha B'Av planted a whole garden for the sitra achra.
Each book of Tehillim stripped another layer of the sitra achra's garden: fruit, leaves, branches, and finally the trunks.
When there is a decree, learning, davening or saying Tehillim creates a new heaven where the decree does not yet exist, and so it can be annulled.
On a cloudy Shabbos, one who says chiddushei Torah at the table makes a new heaven and feels the sun shine for him, even if his neighbor does not see it.
Even the learning and yiras Shamayim of those far from Chassidus comes from the holiness the Ba'al Shem Tov brought down into a sinking world.

The ten utterances of creation were hidden, but at Yetzias Mitzrayim they were turned into the ten plagues that six hundred thousand Jews saw, so the Exodus is the visible proof that Hashem created the world; this is why the first commandment mentions the Exodus and not creation.

The plagues run backwards against the utterances: Bereishis, the first and most important utterance, is the beginning, and so the last plague, the firstborn, struck the beginning of Mitzrayim and was the most important plague.
Bereishis has no 'and He said' because it came before speech existed; it created the very power of speech, so only from the second utterance on can the Torah say 'and G-d said'.
Bread is three times the Name Havaya (78), the salt it is dipped in is again 78, and matzah equals three times the Name with its filled-in letters (135), so matzah is a higher bread.
Chametz is flour plus time plus place: time makes it rise and it takes up more space, while matzah, baked fast, is not ruled by time and place and so belongs above this world.

Hebrew is written from right to left because Yidden start from the right side, chesed, while Esav's nations write from left to right, din; Nisan's letters run forward through the alef-beis and Tishrei's run backwards.
The Rav calls 'I have no time, so I daven quickly' a false calculation: since prolonging tefillah prolongs life, the one short of time is precisely the one who should daven at length.
What allowed early generations to daven briefly was not the size of their minds but their openness: a mind not clouded by sins can daven in a moment.
