The end of dybbukim in the Chofetz Chaim's time fits the generation's task: when such things are seen, believing is easy, while the mitzvah of our generation is emunah amid hiddenness.
Though outward dybbukim ceased, the Rav says many people carry inner ones: forces created by sins that block learning, davening and good middos.
Yehuda rather than Yissachar or Levi was sent to prepare Goshen because a place is inaugurated with praise of Hashem, which drives out the opposing forces, and Yehuda's name comes from hodaah.
The Melave Malka is the chanukas habayis of the week: as the seudah of Dovid HaMelech, a descendant of Yehuda, its songs of praise drive out the accusers of the weekday.
Since the coming of Moshiach will reveal lights far greater than at the Exodus, the Rav advises using each immersion in the mikveh to prepare oneself to receive the kedushah of Moshiach.
Eating without a brachah withholds blessing from the world, because the brachah is what draws shefa onto all of creation and all Jews.
A brachah by itself is only half a brachah; its completion is the amen answered to it, so one should say it aloud for others to answer.
Even for mitzvos where the Torah does not require lishmah, declaring one's intent beforehand brings kedushah into both the person and the object, as with tefillin and tzitzis.
Saying 'in the name of all Israel' is an insurance policy for a mitzvah: accusers can attack a private person's deed, but not one bound to all of Klal Yisrael, of whom it says there is no blemish.
Beginning Baruch She'amar with the congregation makes one's whole tefillah count as tefillah b'tzibbur, even if the congregation has left before one reaches Shemoneh Esrei.

The leniency of a doubtful rabbinic law does not show it is lower; the Sages themselves chose to be lenient, like a mother who lets her child try another store, and where they did not want leniency, as with Yom Tov Sheni, it has the strictness of a Torah law.
Because the world has 248 limbs like a person, a Jew's Kerias Shema in New York can be the reason a Jew in Africa suddenly feels yiras Shamayim in the middle of a test.
Rosh Hashanah is the Kerias Shema of the whole year, the day's acceptance of Hashem's kingship that one prays should spread over the whole world.
A person's limbs are like the main switch of a power plant: a small movement lights up the highest worlds through a mitzvah or sets off a bomb there through a sin.
The yetzer hara lets a person eat kugel or make kiddush, but fights learning before davening; that very resistance proves its importance.
Different kinds of tzaddikim come from different limbs of Adam Harishon: the head yearns to learn like Moshe Rabbeinu, the throat to daven like Dovid Hamelech, the feet to go collecting tzedakah.
From the miracle that the Kohen Gadol never became tamei on Yom Kippur, the Rav learns that the Satan fights hardest exactly where the most depends, so difficulty is a sign of one's shlichus.

The variety among Jews is part of Klal Yisrael's beauty: like the twelve colored stones and flags of the shevatim, or apples on one tree that are never exactly alike, small differences coexist with an essential sameness.

The passuk's word order 'bechol she'arecha... lishvatecha' hints, according to a sefer the Rav cites, that each shevet has its own gate, like the gates of the shevatim at the end of Yechezkel and the twelve paths at the Yam Suf.

The ten makkos reproduced the ten maamaros of creation, so at Yetzias Mitzrayim the Jews saw Maaseh Bereishis and Hashem's control of nature; this is why the mitzvah of emunah is phrased as 'who took you out of Mitzrayim'.
The yetzer hara fights hardest just before Moshiach, like a flickering candle flame that flares up when it is about to go out.
Even saying 'would have' after a loss is already a blemish in emunah, since everything down to which end of a fallen straw points east is directed by Hashem.
Because money buys a person's food and is therefore part of his nefesh, as seen in the halachos of one forbidden to benefit from another, giving tzedakah is a kind of mesiras nefesh.
The Rav draws a parallel: just as the tzaddik of the generation includes all its souls, 'v'ahavta l'reiacha kamocha' includes all the mitzvos, so accepting it binds a person to all of Klal Yisroel.
Though the first ten in shul do not hear the Shechinah speaking with them, their soul feels it, and its effect is felt through the whole day.
Saying the words of Torah she'b'chsav counts as learning even without understanding, but the beraisa of the ketores is Torah she'b'al peh, so one only fulfills learning it by knowing what it means.

The Egyptians who had seen nine plagues come true would still call Moshe a liar over a few minutes; a person who does not want to believe will deny even repeated miracles, because believing would demand changing his life.
With the Midrash on 'a thousand for each tribe', the Rav explains that those who sit and learn and daven are also soldiers in the war, and saying the ketores is the Jews' 'Patriot missile'.

The Rav explains Chizkiyahu's sword through the laws of war: since Torah was the actual weapon against Sancheiriv, one who left the beis medrash was a deserter, subject to the treatment of a fleeing soldier.
Learning differs from davening: in davening a person speaks to Hashem, while in learning Hashem speaks through the person's own mouth.
The Rav cites a saying that the word Gemara relates to burning coals, so it must be learned with fire.
Amalek before Purim and chametz after Purim are the same enemy under another name, the yetzer hara, which explains the extraordinary strictness of the laws of chametz.
The two commands to erase Amalek correspond to Amalek's body, which is killed physically, and its soul, the yetzer hara, which must be nullified.
Through ahavas Yisroel a person becomes a partner in every mitzvah another Jew does, so mitzvos he cannot do himself are still completed in him and his limbs can rise at techiyas hameisim.
Hashem does not carry out a judgment on a person until the person has pronounced it on himself, which is why judging others harshly is so dangerous.
The order of davening, in the morning and at night, puts Hashem's love for Yisroel before the command to love Hashem, showing that ahavas Yisroel is the introduction to ahavas Hashem.

Each kaddish in davening is a staircase between the worlds; between Beriah and Shemoneh Esrei there is none because one may not interrupt between Ga'al Yisroel and Shemoneh Esrei, and after Shemoneh Esrei there is a kaddish on the way back down.
Unlike every war since Yehoshua's conquest, in which Jews suffered first, this war is good for the Jews, because the enemy aims to destroy Eretz Yisroel, matching the Apter Rav's prediction.
The chassid's story shows that friends accomplish what neither fear of Gehinnom nor a Rebbe can: shame before his fellow chassidim kept him from sin.
The zarzir is declared like the raven because it keeps company with it: whoever associates with a kind belongs to that family.
Souls in this generation may come from earlier gilgulim, and being exposed to its temptations while remaining Jews is their tikkun.
The placement of Ikvesa d'Meshicha on the 49th and last daf of Sotah matches the 49 days of the Omer, which descend to Malchus she'b'Malchus, the lowest level, just before heaven meets earth.
Unlike past regimes, which persecuted Jews in the name of religion, today's state forbids encouraging belief; the Rav sees this atheism as the Braisa's 'government turned to minus'.
Leaders today are like a dog walking ahead of its master: they seem to be in front but keep looking back to see which way the congregation goes.

The Rav points out that the Alter Rebbe, a strict man, chose as the harshest punishment for hasty davening being kept from hearing his Torah, which to devoted chassidim was the greatest punishment there could be.
The ridicule of long davening is itself foretold: the Gemara says that before Moshiach the G-d-fearing will be considered mad, and a tzaddik would wish his chassidim to be counted among them.

Stray thoughts in davening are not a mere lapse of attention but being pushed out of Gan Eden, like Adam HaRishon after the sin; this is why a person can find he davened half the tefillah without one word to Hashem.
The tears of real davening are tears of joy, like those of a parent and child who meet after a year apart.
Disciples of one rebbe may differ like east and west, yet all are truly his: what passes from rebbe to chassid is the point of avodah, not its outward form.
Each person lives many years but comes into the world for one day; Yosef was called Yosef HaTzaddik only after he passed his trial, and until then he was simply Yosef.
The Rav compares the test of the last generation to Avraham's last test, where the Satan's argument made sense and the test was precisely not to listen to it.
The heel of the generations is itself a large area: according to the Satmar Rav it began some 400 years ago, and we stand at its very lowest point.
The talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov broke the normal decline of the generations: they were souls of prophets, sent down for about 150 years to rescue the world.
Because Malachi is the last prophet, his closing words are his message to the last generation on how to cross the sea of galus to the shore of geulah.

Maariv being 'reshus' means it is for special people, and the same ascending order holds for the Shabbos seudos, with shalosh seudos as the greatest; melave malka is a fourth, like chatzos, the tefillah of Dovid HaMelech.
Mockery is the exact opposite of emunah: emunah holds on even without understanding, while mockery throws off even what is understood, not by argument but with a laugh.
The 'klipah' of the Plishtim is mockery: they could not answer Avraham's greatness, so they stopped up his wells by laughing at it.
The hard labor of Mitzrayim was itself a stopping of the wells: it left a Jew no time to think.
Each modern plan to end antisemitism, by assimilating in Germany or by building a nation, ended by making it worse, showing that fleeing the Ribono shel Olam does not work.
Through Rebbe Reb Bunim's vort on 'like a lost sheep', the Rav explains why the nations excuse in every other people what they condemn in the Jews.
The Ba'al Shem Tov was a neshamah not in keeping with his generation, one that could have lived in the time of the nevi'im, just as the Gra, though centuries later, could stand with the Rishonim.

The Rav explains that the two sedras read right after Pesach are placed there by design: having received emunah through the matzah, a Jew is warned at once against the two things that spoil its effect.
He compares forbidden food to clogged arteries of the heart: the heart loses its chayus and feeling, which is why a person can keep Shabbos yet feel nothing in it.

The Rav likens the Satan before the geulah to a person in mortal danger whose adrenaline gives him strength he never knew he had; sensing his end, the Satan fights ferociously by flooding the market with treif.
Through the Rambam's letter the Rav shows that doubts in emunah are not purely intellectual: the questioners asked because forbidden food had made their emunah unclear.
From the story of the kernel of wheat the Rav learns that even a month of diligent effort is not enough without tefillah; a person needs both.
The Rav reads the Ba'al Shem Tov's wonders as lessons in emunah: for one to whom it is clear that Hashem makes the candle burn, it makes no difference whether it is wax or ice, a ship or a belt.

He compares the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim to the Avos: just as Yosef's and Sarah's tests put strength into every Jewish man and woman in Mitzrayim, the early chassidic generations put strength into the generations that came after them.
The Satan's task with Iyov, to break the barrel without spilling the wine, is the Rav's picture of this generation's task: to stay pure in a place where it seems impossible.
Compared with earlier generations we are like small children who are given small tests, two times two instead of calculus, but our small tests are equal to the great tests of the earlier tzaddikim.
The word 'panim' is like an x-ray: the face shows what is inside a person, so different faces mean different inner natures, and each person is entitled to his own way of conduct.

The threefold parallel of place, time and soul applies to impurity as well: the Rav sets the beis hakisei, the one punished in boiling filth, and Nittel side by side as impurity's place, person and time.
Following the Bnei Yissaschar, the punishment of boiling filth fits wisdom cut off from holiness, which is like waste separated from the body.
The pearl is set above finer and costlier stones because it was brought from the darkness of the depths, and so the simple Jew's struggle in a dark time is placed at the head of the King's crown.
Learning amid the noise of a subway, concentrating on a Gemara or a chassidish sefer, may be prized in Heaven like the pearl, because it is brought out of a place of darkness.
Sleep does tikkunim just as eating does birurim, and it is a kind of techiyas hamesim from which a person rises a new creation.
A tzaddik reads 'ad masai atzel tishkav' as faulting the lazy man not for rising late but for lying down late.
The fiftieth gate differs from the other forty-nine in kind: they are midos, while it is daas, so in tumah it is not a bad trait but apikorsus itself.
In kedushah the right side and the giver lead, while in tumah the left and the receiver dominate; this is why the chesed of tumah is Canaani, a chesed that is subdued.
Just as emunah in kedushah is beyond reason, apikorsus in the fiftieth gate of tumah is also beyond reason: it defies logic, as in the claim that the ordered universe made itself.
Being tormented by doubts is itself a sign that one's soul stood at Sinai; one of the Erev Rav is not troubled by them but welcomes them.
Arguing with doubts only entangles a person further, like a fly struggling in a spider web, because the doubts are letzanus and do not respond to logic.
Unlike earlier ages, when people believed in idols, the present age is one of believing in nothing at all, which shows that the fiftieth gate of tumah now rules the world.
Modeh Ani precedes negel vasser even though one normally may not even attend to an optional matter before washing: the urge to thank Hashem cannot be held back.
The ten fingers are the 'control knobs' of man, who was made from all ten utterances of creation; washing them purifies the whole body and, through it, one's share in the world.
A bochur's careful negel vasser may be what keeps another Jewish bochur somewhere far away, in Paris, from sin, because each person controls a share of the world and of other souls' roots.
The Be'er Mayim Chaim reads 'arisa' (dough) as a cradle or bed: on rising from bed, the first act should be a tefillah to Hashem.
One of the great benefits of learning without a break is the training of restraint, for the yetzer works through curiosity about what is happening around.
No moment in creation is a duplicate of another; even the same mitzvah each day has a different task in fixing the world, so a missed moment cannot be made up tomorrow.
The Rav reads the Sanzer Rav's words as proof that building outpaces destruction: if the Beis HaMikdash lacked only the paroches then, today it lacks only screws.

Just as a parrot's few words amaze a king more than the wisdom of his ministers, a small avodah of a weak generation is a great chiddush in heaven and is valued like the great avodos of the tzaddikim.
Because the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah composed tefillah with ruach hakodesh, the same words do a different birur every day, so a tefillah missed today cannot be made up tomorrow.
Davening fast with hishtapchus hanefesh, as the Skverer Rebbe does when davening privately, is only for one who is completely pure; ordinary people must hold on to each word.
Each word of davening is a heichal; tzaddikim can pass through quickly, but others must hold on so as not to be pushed out, and davening with a tzaddik in his minyan lets him carry them.
Raising one's voice in davening is not a show but human nature: a person shouts when he truly means something, as in an argument or at a ball game.

A lack of desire to learn is like a lack of appetite: a symptom of a deeper cause, so incentives that only push a person to learn miss the point, just as a doctor would not simply tell such a patient to eat.
The words of Torah are like the gold case of a costly watch: the case does not show the value, which lies in the inner works; so too the knowledge of a sugya is only a vessel for the light within it.
Even a Gemara about a thief's claims carries the light of Torah, so the difference between Torah and science is not the subject matter but whether the light comes down through the learner.
Reb Aharon of Karlin's saying: mikvah is not a mitzvah, yet what it brings no mitzvah can bring, because when one purifies himself holiness comes running to him, and then learning and davening go.
Speaking about negel vasser, mikvah and a clean body is not speaking about side matters but about Torah itself, since they are its preparation.

The Rav reads the strictness of chametz, nullified by declaring it nothing, as the model for handling thoughts of doubt: the best removal is to treat them as a 'minus quantity' rather than to engage them.
He explains Avraham Avinu throwing dust at the kings as a way of declaring them nothing, the same weapon one uses against doubts.
He reads 'lo sasuru' as a warning not to scout out such thoughts the way the meraglim scouted, trying to explore them and argue against them.

Like the 'be'itah' and 'achishenah' of the general geulah, an individual's trial has a fixed end, but Hashem can shorten it for one who stands firm in emunah, as the exile in Mitzrayim was shortened from 400 to 210 years.

Not waiting for Moshiach shows a lack of belief: a man who knew he would be elected president tomorrow would surely wait for it, so one who truly believed in the promised good would long for Moshiach.
Rabbi Akiva did not truly err about Ben Koziva: he saw in him the soul of Moshiach, and it was the sins of the generation that spoiled it.

The Rambam's Moshiach, who would have every Jew leave his business to follow him and would settle disputes over the place of the mizbeach so that all accept it, is a greater miracle than the wonders the Raavad expects.
The severe statements of the sefarim that go beyond the Shulchan Aruch are not exaggerations: they are the halachah of a higher soul, for whom a small flaw is a real blemish.
Gan Eden and Gehinnom can be the same place: the same fiery davening of the tzaddikim is pleasure for those who trained for it and torment for those who did not.
A spiritual appetite works like a physical one: one who spoils his appetite with the pleasures of this world cannot take in the bread of Torah and tefillah.
A gift of inspiration is like the free taste of grapes the storekeeper offers: it is given to show the quality, but afterwards one must pay with toil.

Whether someone davens is a truer measure of whether he is still bound to Hashem than the severity of the punishment for a sin, just as going bareheaded marks a person though it is hard to name the sin.
Amalek's attack is coldness: 'asher karcha' means he cooled you, and the war against Amalek today is the struggle to daven with warmth.
The Rav applies the Ohr HaChaim's principle of tumah as the residue of departed kedushah to the yoledes: her tumah is a sign of the holy soul she carried, not a flaw in her.

He reads the placement of the milah verse between the boy's and the girl's tumah as the Torah's own answer: the eighth-day light of the bris reaches the mother and cuts off the tumah that should have been longer.
The mikvah is an embassy of the World to Come, of the eighth world where death has no hold, which is why tzaddikim went to the mikvah when their tefillos could not annul a decree.
Since aveilus is separation, the joining of parshiyos in the Sefirah weeks and the Three Weeks is itself the tikkun: like the letters of the Torah, the groups of Jews must be joined.
When the first day of Rosh Chodesh Iyar falls on the thirtieth of Nissan, the Rav sees the month of Nissan going to receive from the 'Rebbe' of Iyar, a model for learning from other groups.
Aveilus is pirud and simcha is yichud: the word chedvah, joy, contains chad, one.
Kayin's sin was not lack of greatness but lack of the point of truth: even in his protest to Hashem he meant himself.
The Rav reads the Rebbe of Lublin's praise of a man who harmed his town as a glimpse of the hidden good in him, the same hidden light that the Chanukah lights reveal.
Since every power of kedusha has its counterpart in the sitra achra, the side of holiness that fights the sitra achra must itself carry the number eleven, which is why the ketores has eleven spices.
Yosef's second dream is called 'another dream' because it is not a repetition of the first but a dream of a different kind: a dream of Chanukah and the hidden light.

Chanukah's light is bound to the number nine: it appears in Kislev, the ninth month, during Vayeshev, the ninth sedra, through its ninth verse and Yosef, the ninth sefirah, all echoing the letter tes whose good is hidden inside.

Yosef, the hidden soul whose brothers did not recognize him and whose name Tzafnas means hidden, carries the power of Chanukah, and the Shelah's gematria of Yosef as 'king of Yavan' shows that he is the one who fights Yavan.
The Rav argues that the very fact that the other major religions must accept Toras Moshe, and can only claim it was altered, testifies to its truth, because of the unique event at Sinai.
Shemitah's promise of a crop for three years is a promise only Hashem can make; a human founder could not make it, and that is why such founders removed the difficult mitzvos.
A small detail, like a story about Alexander's horse missing a tooth, can be invented by one writer, but the core of an event that multitudes lived through cannot.
The halachah that one extra or missing letter makes a Sefer Torah invalid is a built-in protection against change, which is why Sifrei Torah of long-separated communities match letter for letter.
The nations' hatred of the Jews comes from jealousy: deep down they know the greatness of the Jewish people.

Giving something while knowing one will take it back is not called changing one's mind but not giving at all; since Hashem knows the future, the claim that He changed His mind about the Torah makes Him a liar.

The Rav resolves the age difficulty in 'vayigdelu' by reading the growth not as a matter of years but of an event: each brother became 'great' by witnessing a passing on the same day, Yaakov Avraham's and Esav Nimrod's.

Just as a tzaddik's lifetime of good deeds gathers on his last day, so the evil deeds of a rasha like Nimrod gathered at his death, drawing a convention of dark forces that left an atmosphere of impurity.
Eliyahu could give Elisha more than he himself had only because on the day of his passing all his days were gathered together.
Learning a parsha is presence, not history: because Rebbi was 'in' the time of Divrei Hayamim while learning it, he would not curse a living king there, though Nebuchadnezzar had long died.
Eliezer's gift of garments to Rivka was, according to the Shinever Rav, not for wearing but a sample showing the difference between modest and immodest clothing.
Yosef's word 'asher' in 'asher mechartem' is read, as with Moshe's 'asher shibarta', as a 'yasher koach': he thanked his brothers because being sold made him Yosef HaTzaddik.

The Rav reads 'har' of the Beis Hamikdash as related to conception: the Mikdash is the first point from which everything develops, like an embryo from its first point, and is therefore called the place of thought.

He maps the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur onto the forty days of a child's formation: within them one can still pray for a year of blessing, while after Yom Kippur it is like a prayer said too late.
Because Adam HaRishon was created on Rosh Hashanah from the place of the Mikdash, the roots of place, time and soul meet in him, and Rosh Hashanah is a seed whose flaw carries through the whole year.

Every root point is hidden and needs seeking: David, the soul of Adam, was overlooked among Yishai's sons; the place of the Mikdash was mistaken at first; and Rosh Hashanah is covered even from the angels.
What the Mikdash is in place, the king is in the soul: both are the heart, which is why David, the root of malchus, was the one who found the place of the Mikdash.

Since the world mirrors the Torah, Jerusalem at the center of the world must have a counterpart at the center of the Torah, and the Rav finds it in the middle verse of Sefer Devarim, which sends halachah to 'the place'.
The Rav portrays the arba minim as weapons and ammunition in the heavenly war of Gog uMagog, with which Jews try to break through to Moshiach on Hoshana Rabbah.
Since the aravah resembles lips, the war of the day is fought not only with the species but with the heart and the mouth.
The diminishing bulls of Sukkos, ending today with the last of the seventy, are themselves part of the war of Gog uMagog: the nullification of the seventy nations that oppress the Shechinah.
The Rav applies the passuk of the oppressed and the debtors who gathered around Dovid when he fled from Shaul to Hoshana Rabbah, the day of Dovid, when every Jew must gather around him.
The prosecutors in the war against Moshiach are armed with the sins of Jews, so even small matters such as talking during chazaras hashatz decide whether Moshiach comes closer.

The Megillah is read at night and again by day because the first reading only reveals at the end that every detail was part of the miracle; the second reading can then be said from the start with joy, praise and thanks.
The Megillah's episodes look like gossip columns a yeshiva bochur should not read, yet at the end they all lock together, which is the point: the miracle is hidden inside natural events.
History is to be studied with the depth one gives to a Tosafos; studied that way, it shows that the wars and fortunes of nations all revolve around the small Jewish people.
Hashem is in disguise in history; the Megillah teaches that He hides Himself and then appears through the miracle.
A forecaster only predicts what makes sense, but the Torah predicted what makes no sense, that a nation in exile would survive forever, and it came true.
Christianity took monotheism from the Jews but made religion easy by dropping Shabbos, Shemitah and the restrictions of Jewish family life, which, the Rav says, a non-Jew could not keep.
The Chachamim who fixed the calendar so that Hoshana Rabbah never falls on Shabbos had in mind the low generations before Moshiach, whose souls are repaired by the mitzvah of aravah.
The generations follow the order of the four kinds: earlier generations were esrogim, then lulavim, then hadassim, and ours is the aravah.
The aravah is specifically a weekday mitzvah: on Shabbos the forces of impurity hide, but on a weekday they come out in strength and the aravah's power is needed to strike them.
On Hoshana Rabbah, when the last of the seventy bulls has been offered, the nations are at the height of their strength and wage the war of Gog uMagog in heaven to hold back Moshiach.
The people who gathered to Dovid, in distress, in debt and bitter of soul, are the souls of the last generation: those in debt from this and earlier lives, who feel they have done nothing for Hashem.
The Rav reads 'a way in the sea' as a way through a sea of sins: sins that block a person from holiness like a sea are given a path in Elul.
The four words of 'Ani ledodi vedodi li' each end in a yud, together forty, the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, the days the second luchos were made for those who had sinned.
The mikveh of the forty days is completed only at the very end of Yom Kippur, matching the final mishnah of Yoma, 'Mikveh Yisrael Hashem'.
Each Shabbos meal belongs to one of the Avos, so one who sits at the meal with seriousness and pure thoughts has the holy Avos with him.
The bas kol calling to teshuvah sounds every day but only a pure heart hears it; in Elul the days themselves cry out, so even one whose hearing is dulled can hear.
Learning Tomer Devorah, which teaches how to practice the Thirteen Attributes between man and his fellow, is itself a way to arouse them in Elul.
The nations' hatred is itself a sign of their recognition: they ignore other peoples' boasts but hate the Jews because, deep down, they know the Jewish claim to chosenness is true.
Envy and hatred go together, as the Torah describes Yosef's brothers first envying him and then hating him.
Hitler's attack on Talmud learners shows that even the enemy understood that Torah is what keeps the Jews alive, and the greater quantity of Torah after the war shows that he failed.
The decline in the quality of Torah is not Hitler's doing but the natural result of each generation's greater distance from Sinai, the fountain, until the new fountain of the days of Moshiach.
Spain's fall into insignificance after the Jews left, compared with Eretz Yisrael appearing daily on the front page, illustrates how the Jews drive the importance of the nations they live among.
Just as the generation raised on the mann saw bread growing from the ground as a great wonder, the survival of the Jews is a wonder that goes unnoticed only because it is familiar.
The fiftieth day, being above time, can stretch to include the fifty-first, so Shavuos can be called the time of the giving of the Torah even on the view that it was given on the fifty-first day.
Like a page of Gemara learned on Sunday and reviewed on Monday, which is one page and not two, Adar Sheni is a review of Adar Rishon, so a leap year still has only thirty days of Adar.
Since zrizin makdimin is not pushed off for a hiddur, Adar Rishon must carry a Torah-level remembrance of the miracle, and the prohibition of eulogy and fasting on Purim Katan is that remembrance.
The Chachamim deliberately did not make the festive gathering of Purim a mitzvah, knowing Jews would rejoice on their own, because doing it unbidden is what acceptance with love means.
Rabbi Meir did not write the Megillah from memory in the ordinary sense: he saw the Megillah written in creation itself, so he was copying from what he saw.
The 'skin' (or) covering creation is what hides its inner Torah; Rabbi Meir saw through it, and that is why his Torah read 'or' with an aleph, light.
Ezra's writing 'and he died' by the eighth king reflects his level of prophecy, not his wisdom; in wisdom he could grasp more than he saw in prophecy, as Rabbi Akiva could expound what Moshe saw.

Rav Yosef's rule that Torah study is greater than saving lives is true, yet Mordechai did not fall: those who separated from him judged by their own level, whose portion was the plain meaning of Torah.
Having one's portion only in the plain meaning of Torah is no lack: the Lechovitcher told such a student he was greater than others, it was simply his portion.

The leap year is read as the moon's chase after the sun: each year Knesses Yisrael falls further behind in its longing to unite with Hashem, until Adar Sheni evens the two out, which makes Purim in Adar Sheni of a wholly different kind.

Every Tanna has his own heichal in Heaven where one learns as he holds; just as one who never wore Rabbeinu Tam's tefillin will not be admitted to Rabbeinu Tam's heichal, so in Rabbi Yosi's heichal the Megillah is read in Adar Rishon.
The Megillah is read in Heaven on Purim Katan even when Jews below do not read it, so the lights of Purim come down on Purim Katan as well.
Adar Rishon, the time of distance, is itself a month of hester panim, and Purim Katan is when that concealment is broken.
The Rav reads the land's desolation in golus and its blossoming on the Jews' return as one prophecy: the land refuses to produce for anyone but its own people.
The avodah zarah in Tanach is not evidence that Yidden abandoned the Torah; it was a yetzer hara as real as the pull of arayos or money today, which can trip even a scrupulously observant Jew.
The yetzer hara for avodah zarah did not disappear but changed its form, and today it is the drive for riches.
Leaving Yiddishkeit to escape persecution did not help: the destruction began in Germany where the abandonment began, and Hitler counted even converted families as Jews.
The Torah's prophecies are two contradictory predictions, a small, hated nation and an eternal one; foretelling both together is something only the Creator could do.
The Megillah is a miniature of Jewish history: its scattered details make sense only at the end, just as everything in world history serves one purpose, the Geulah of Klal Yisroel.
The moon's shorter year (about 355 days against the sun's 365) is itself a second diminution of Knesses Yisrael, besides the diminution of its light.
The leap year is the moon catching up with the sun: Adar Sheni is where they become equal, so Adar Rishon, just before, is the height of hiddenness.

Every Tanna has his own heichal in heaven where Torah is practiced by his view; just as one who never wore Rabbeinu Tam's tefillin is not admitted to Rabbeinu Tam's heichal, there is a mesivta of Rabbi Yosi where the Megillah is read in Adar Rishon.
The Mishnah's passive 'Megillah nikreis' hints that on Purim Katan the Megillah is read in heaven even when Jews below do not read it.
Adar Rishon is the month of hester panim, alluded to in the Gemara's question where Esther is hinted at in the Torah, and the Megillah read in heaven on Purim Katan breaks that hiddenness.
Purim is a new kabbalas haTorah, something the Jews did not attain even at Matan Torah.

Each word of tefillah is a heichal, a chamber of the King, and davening is passing from one heichal into the next; feeling one has said many chapters without knowing what he said is a sign of being pushed out of the heichalos.
Esther's thirty days of feeling unable to say a warm word before Hashem were the preparation for 'vatilbash Esther malchus', the moment on which the whole miracle of Purim rested.
Esther's 'I have not been called' parallels Avraham sitting at the opening of the tent: he felt he was still outside and could not enter, and precisely then Hashem appeared to him.
A Jew who feels that his words accomplish nothing is precisely the one who can merit the heichal of the Shechinah.

According to the second approach, Esther saw the king's not calling her during the thirty days before Pesach as siyata dishmaya for preparing in purity, and Mordechai's 'al tedami venafshech' meant that even holy personal preparation must give way when Klal Yisroel needs a yeshuah.
The Rav remarks that Shushan Purim, too, is a yom tov for all Jews, even where the megillah is not read, since there are two days of Purim.
The Rav reads the golden dinars of the valley as Rashbi's own Torah secrets, which lay spread over Meron and took material form only because the students showed interest in wealth.
Silver and gold are, spiritually, love and fear; only the constrictions of this world turn them into metal, so the material object is a lowered form of a spiritual level.
Today halacha follows Beis Hillel because this is a Torah of silver, of love; when Moshiach comes there will be a Torah of gold, of the attribute of judgment.

Because the gold was Torah already present in Meron rather than a gift from heaven, its vanishing needed no miracle, which answers why the Midrash speaks of a greater miracle only for Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta.
The halacha does not follow Rabbi Shimon only because he was not grasped; in the future, when the world is full of knowledge of Hashem, it will.
A Jew who does not take his heavenly bounty materially keeps it as spiritual wealth: the joy of a blatt Gemara and the warmth of shalosh seudos.

The Rav reads the Tanya's whole program as an answer to a plain question: if the Torah says keeping it is 'very close', why do most people find it hard? The sefer exists to make that closeness understood.

An oath the soul does not remember still works: it leaves an impression that subconsciously gives courage and drive, the way Avraham's oath would give Eliezer strength against second thoughts on his mission.

Through the interchange of beis and pei, shevuah is linked to shefa, so the oath itself is a flow of strength from above; he shows that a written pei holds a white beis within it, a pei being a fortified beis.
The word mashpia is tied to meshupa, slanted: just as rain flows down only from a slanted roof, as for a mikveh, influence from above reaches a person only along an incline.
Because man contains all of creation, an oath binds every part of him; this is why even one suspected about money is not suspected about an oath, since an oath leaves no hidden exit.
In lashon hakodesh the name reveals the purpose: a shulchan is so called because its bounty is 'sent' to each person individually from Hashem, as fuel for his own mission.
The Rav links the peace among animals in the days of Moshiach to friendship among Jewish children: when the children are friends, the animals too become friends of the Jews.
Lag BaOmer marks the repair of the fault for which Rabbi Akiva's students died: through Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, friendship returned among the students and to the world.
The bow and arrow the children shoot on Lag BaOmer are Torah and tefillah, the same weapons with which Yaakov Avinu overcame his enemies, since Onkelos renders his sword and bow as his prayers.
The Rav describes the enemies of the Jews as the tigers and wolves of the prophecy, who want to swallow them, and holds that they cannot harm the Jews because Jewish children learn Torah.
Citing the Lubavitcher Rebbe, the Rav notes that the fifth night, the night of hod, is the first night on which Beis Hillel's count of lights exceeds Beis Shammai's.
The two meanings of hod, admission and praise, are one: a person who feels entitled takes kindness as natural, while one who feels nothing is owed him can thank with his whole heart.
Aharon's hod, rejoicing at Moshe's appointment because he felt nothing was owed him, is why the Chanukah lights of his descendants are his lasting share.
Matisyahu, whose beis din instituted Chanukah for thanks and praise, was a spark of Yehudah, the one named for thanks and first of the degalim.
Since only thanksgiving remains in the World to Come, a person will feel there only the kind of avodah he grew used to here; Shabbos, a taste of the World to Come, is where one trains in it.
Song is a higher level than the letters themselves, since the ta'amim stand above the nekudos and the osiyos, which is why Shabbos, the day of singing, is the day of praise.

The Rav compares the Rosh Hashanah categories to the 'tzaddik' and 'rasha' of a din Torah: the one who wins a case is called the tzaddik for that case, though in other ways he may be a complete rasha, so the labels describe the judgment, not the person.
He pictures every person as standing before a court of three judges: the yetzer tov and yetzer hara each issue a ruling in the heart, and Hashem gives the verdict.
He reads 'chalal' in David HaMelech's words as 'empty': the left chamber of the heart, the seat of the yetzer hara, stood spiritually empty, just as a corpse emptied of its soul is called a chalal.
According to the Rav, people do not remember their earlier gilgulim because the memory would remove their free choice; great tzaddikim, who have no free choice anyway, do remember.

He explains the four klipos with a walnut: three shells are peeled away, but the thin skin on the kernel is eaten with it and becomes part of the nut, which is klipas nogah, the shell that can be raised to holiness.
He finds the same four layers in the milah: three layers are cut away, while the fourth, the priah, is not cut but pushed back, corresponding to nogah.
The lean cows' standing before swallowing the fat ones is read as the astonishment of the animal soul and the sitra achra before the hidden greatness of a Jewish soul.
Pharaoh's omission of the standing from his retelling reflects his shame at admitting that he himself is overawed by the strength of a Jew.
Pharaoh's words that the swallowed cows could not be recognized are called a lie: the hidden Jewish soul remains and is ultimately effective.
What a gentile cannot even recognize as a tzarah, a life without Torah and mitzvos, was for the Jews of the Chashmonaim a real tzarah, and that is why Hashem marveled and saved them.
The Rambam singles out Chanukah alone of the mitzvos as very dear because it came with mesiras nefesh, just as Avraham swore by the milah because it came to him through pain.
Giving one's own life is hard, but demanding mesiras nefesh of others is much harder, and the Rayatz demanded it of his chassidim.
The Rav reads the Midrash that Yaakov 'did not believe' as referring not to Yaakov himself, the root of bitachon, but to the faithless souls included in him.
The Me'or Einayim's lesson that disqualified oils are lit on Chanukah is applied to fallen souls: a Jew whom Shabbos cannot kindle, Chanukah can.
Yaakov is the trunk of the tree and Shabbos, the middle blessing, while the twelve tribes correspond to the twelve middle blessings of the weekday prayer.
Chanukah is the answer to Yaakov's plea: instead of the souls rising with Shabbos, the Shechinah comes down below ten to the place of darkness.
The Alter Rebbe's path is that of Shabbos, raising chassidim upward, while the later Chabad Rebbes took the path of Chanukah, going down to the lowest to bring them up to Shabbos.
Forgiving strangers who wronged him puts a man above Yosef, who forgave only his own brothers, to whom one is anyway bound to show mercy.
The total of a hundred and twenty is not twelve times ten but a new reckoning, in which the twelve tribes can no longer be told apart and only one Klal Yisroel remains.
The wagons, one for every two nesi'im, were the preparation for the mizbe'ach's inauguration: they broke down the partitions each tribe had around itself.
The verse's second 'this is the inauguration of the mizbe'ach, after it was anointed' points to a renewed inauguration still to come, which again depends on unity among Jews.
The brothers' silence toward Yosef, which Rashi credits to their honesty, finds its repair in Vayigash, where they speak with him without any gap between mouth and heart.
The Rav reads Yaakov's seven years 'like a few days' as proof of spiritual love: physical longing makes each day a year, while love for holiness, like building a sukkah, makes years fly.
Yaakov's kiss of Rachel is compared to a tzaddik kissing his tefillin and tzitzis, since she was for him the epitome of holiness.
A Hebrew servant loses the 'mem', the forty days in which the Torah was given, from 'mishpachah', and what remains is 'shifchah'.
Chanukah, the eighth after seven like Yovel after the Shemitos, can lift souls that even Shabbos cannot.
Yaakov's grief over Rachel was the loss of the geulah she embodied, and Migdal Eder, where Moshiach will appear, was Hashem's consolation.
The Tanya says 'mamash' of the soul being part of G-d, but 'by way of a parable' of Yisrael arising in Hashem's thought, because His thought is unlike ours.
Neshamah and neshimah share one word: breath is a person's inwardness, so Hashem blowing into Adam means His own life entered him.
The blessing 'she'asa nissim' is not thanks for the oil alone; it acknowledges that the source of miracles is open now, so everything happening today comes through miracles.
Chanukah's eight days reach beyond the seven days of creation that set the order of nature; they draw down the separate order of miracles into time.
Just as during Sefirah everything a person feels and says relates to that day's sefirah, on Chanukah even the kugel, the gefilte fish and the wine hold miracles.
Chanukah is hod, the aspect of miracle, and therefore a time of hoda'ah, thanksgiving.
Even on the first night, when the oil was naturally enough, the light burned from the source of miracles, which is why a blessing on miracles is said that night too.

Barrenness is not only a woman without children: one whose davening does not go and who sees no fruit in his Torah is also 'barren', and Chanukah, a time of pekidas akaros, is when he can ask for help.
Zos Chanukah is the counterpart of Shemini Atzeres, so it carries the ushpiz of Shlomo HaMelech, and his avodah defines the day.

Chanukah begins at the end of the month, when the moon cannot be seen, and runs into Teves, the month of Esav: holiness breaks into the very time that belongs to the other side, just as the light goes into the reshus harabim.
Shlomo is the moon in its fullness, fifteen generations from Avraham like the fifteen days from the molad to the full moon; the Rav links the full moon to the daughters of kings through a gematria.

Shlomo's many wives were not what a simple reading suggests: as daughters of kings, heads of their nations, they were his way of bringing the seventy nations under holiness, and through them even the chief kelipos, the two harlots, submitted to him.
Purim and Chanukah are 'stations' between Sukkos and Pesach, given because after the churban the influence of the festivals could no longer carry a Jew through the year.

In the mashal of the queen, after two exiles Knesses Yisrael will not come back on her own; the king himself must lift her from the mud, and the light of Moshiach revealed each Chanukah is that lifting.
Although Shemoneh Esrei is said in the highest world, before the King, one asks there even for simple needs, because tefillah is said according to its plain meaning and there is no one else to ask.
Leaving before the end of davening is like a shopper who fills his cart, pays, and walks out without his bag: he loses the bounty he already earned.
The Imrei Emes's call to learn Chofetz Chaim broke the divide between chassidim and Litvaks, which fits the sefer's whole purpose: that there be no division among Jews.
Every time a person holds back a word he wants to say because the Chofetz Chaim forbids it, he is practicing yiras shamayim and conquering the yetzer, all day long.
The Chanukah lights of every generation accumulate; they are the chinuch of the light of Moshiach, just as a chanukas habayis precedes the full Beis HaMikdash.

The nations' cry that the Jews are robbers in Eretz Yisroel is exactly what Rashi addresses at the start of the Torah, and the Rav sees in it a sign that the light of Moshiach is breaking through, a reason for joy.

Breathing is not a one-time endowment: each breath is a fresh act of 'He breathed', bringing a new life and a new shlichus for that moment, which is why avodas Hashem must change from moment to moment.

Even a non-Jewish king carries a spark of malchus Shamayim, which is how the Alter Rebbe sensed that the disguised visitor was the Czar, and why Moshe was commanded to show honor to Pharaoh as a king.

The knife cuts the challah, and not the reverse, because their roots differ: bread gives life and is soft, steel destroys life and is hard, reflecting the dominance of one middah over another in this world.
Trying to grasp Hashem with the intellect is like trying to see a symphony or hear a Rembrandt: the mind is the wrong sense, while emunah is a sixth sense that every Jew has in his subconscious.

Adam HaRishon is the 'challah' of the world, the separated and holy portion of the earth's dough, and the Friday challah-baking repairs Chava's sin, committed on a Friday, which brought death to that challah.

The generations, the land and the months form one structure like a fern, where each part repeats the whole: our era is both the 'heels' of history and its 'Adar', a time of hester panim, yet the heels are destined to become the head.
Zos Chanukah gives a simple Jew the power of prayer that a tzaddik has on Rosh Hashanah.
The words 'for Your salvation we hope all day', said three times daily, are themselves the answer to the question at the judgment whether one hoped for the redemption.
The Rav stresses that the Rambam requires not only believing in Moshiach but awaiting him, and that 'awaiting' is the Rambam's own word.
He identifies malchus Romi, the fourth kingdom, with the European nations and with America, whose people are immigrants from Europe.

The Gemara's 'go and make it known' is explained through a chasan's diamond: a gift whose worth the recipient cannot see must be explained, so Hashem told Klal Yisroel that Shabbos is not 'just a mitzvah' but a personal token of His bond with them.
The prohibition 'lo s'vaaru esh... b'yom haShabbos' is read as: the fire of Shabbos cannot be lit once Shabbos arrives; it must be kindled already during the week.
The six weekdays correspond to six sefiros; erev Shabbos is Yosef and middas hayesod, so 'v'hayah bayom hashishi v'heichinu' points to kedushas habris as the preparation for Shabbos.
A tzaddik explains Nishmas: until Nishmas one davens with body and soul, but from Nishmas on with the soul alone, as if the body did not exist.
Since Hashem's 'work' in creation was speech, His resting on the seventh day means that a Jew guards Shabbos above all in his speech.
The food of Shabbos is a continuation of the mann: one who eats the Shabbos cholent eats, as it were, mann, which is why tzaddikim gave Shabbos kugel as a remedy.
The three parts of Shabbos parallel the stages of a marriage: Friday night is kiddushin, Shabbos morning is nisuin, and Shabbos mincha is yichud, when one says 'Atah Echad'.
The Shabbos seudah is even greater than the Shabbos Amidah; the tefillah is the preparation for the seudah.
The mincha Amidah of Shabbos has no pesukim because it is above pesukim, like the tip of the yud, and so shalosh seudos is a short, simple meal of challah and herring.
What is beyond place is beyond time: the manna in the Kodesh Hakodashim was not 'left over till morning', and shalosh seudos has no time until bentching.
No tevilah is required before Shabbos mincha because the time itself is the mikveh, as Yom Kippur is, and Jews gathered together are a mikveh.
Moshe Rabbeinu passed away at Shabbos mincha, rising to a place beyond human measure, and therefore no one knows his burial place.
Shabbos morning is felt less than Friday night precisely because its kedushah is higher, and mincha even more so.

Rosh Chodesh Shevat is the 'Rosh Hashanah of the tree' in its deeper sense, the tree of life that is Torah, because on that day Moshe Rabbeinu began explaining the Torah, and a new flow of Torah comes down every year.

The Rav reads the Tanya's parable with modern science: the same chromosomes found in the brain are found in the hair and nails, so the remoteness of a soul is a difference of distance and garments, not of essence.
Cutting hair and nails before Shabbos means shedding the 'goy' within oneself, like a convert's immersion, because each Shabbos is a new creation and a step toward the day that is entirely Shabbos.

Following Reb Tzadok, the Gemara piles up Achan's sins to show that even so 'he is Yisrael': Yisrael, the last word of the Torah, is bound to Bereishis, the first, as the nails are bound to the brain.
The heels of Moshiach are the hair and nails of the calendar, the end of the nine months, which is why that time is called the birth pangs of Moshiach.

The Tanya's change from 'madreigos' to the Aramaic 'dargin' is deliberate: the lowest souls fall to the level of Targum, which equals tardeimah, the deep sleep of exile, and yet even they are bound to the root.
The name Yisrael holds the rosh, together with the largest letter, lamed, and the smallest, yud, while Yaakov holds the heel; so the word itself binds the lowest levels to the highest.

The Rambam is forced to read shalom bayis literally, as avoiding a quarrel over who gets the mitzvah, because he holds that oneg Shabbos is not a Torah obligation from mikra kodesh, so Rashi's reasoning is closed to him.

Since by the Rambam the enactment is for the wife's sake, she can waive it and tell her husband to light his Chanukah light; and a man with no wife would light the Chanukah light, while by Rashi he would still need light to eat by.

Shalom bayis is not a private matter: since the home is a mashal for Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, a husband who yields to his wife arouses Hashem to yield, so to speak, His own interests for the good of Knesses Yisrael.
The Hei at the end of Avraham's 'ohalo' and the reading of Shlomo as 'the King to Whom peace belongs' express the same idea: putting the other's peace before one's own.

Asked why there is no special tefillah for shalom bayis, a gadol answered that there is one, said three times a day: the request that one's soul be like dust, which is the readiness to yield and bear with others.

The Rambam omitted the husband's yielding from the laws of Ishus and placed it in the laws of Chanukah, because on Chanukah Hashem comes into the Jewish home instead of the Jew coming to the Mikdash, showing that He honors Knesses Yisrael more than Himself.
The flood came in the measure of days that matched the giving of the Torah: the same waters that were to descend as Torah descended as the flood when the generation refused it.

Noach did not pray for his generation not out of indifference but because they were not bound to him: a tzaddik can pray only for those connected to him, and those who do not accept the leader even harm him.
Cheshvan, the month in which the flood fell, is the month of Torah: after binding themselves to Torah on Shemini Atzeres, Jews begin a new season and a new masechta in it.
The nations' answer 'Hashem will bless His people with peace' is read as a flood with a shin: the word 'bashalom' signals a flood of Torah, not of destruction.
Learning a new masechta with hasmadah is a direct reversal of the flood generation's words 'we do not desire knowledge of Your ways'.
Masechta Yevamos is a tikkun connected with bringing Moshiach.

On Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol, the Kodesh HaKodashim of souls, enters the Kodesh HaKodashim of space on the Kodesh HaKodashim of time, and the atonement comes from the strength each dimension draws from contact with the others.
Our generation is the toenail of the soul of Klal Yisrael, but Jews who keep Torah and mitzvos are the living part of the nail that still hurts if cut away.
Adar is named for 'aderes', a cloak: the month of concealment, the opposite of Nisan, though Hashem is as present in it as in Nisan.
The greater the hester panim, the greater the miracle that Klal Yisrael survives at all.

HaMelech, Haman and 'kes Kah' all equal 95, so Haman's presence is what turns Hashem's revealed Name into the veiled 'HaMelech'; 'macho emcheh' equals 107, the value of the Throne and Name made whole.
The Megillah is a training in reading between the lines; once mastered, one can read the newspaper and see Hashem's name in it.
Because the world was created with loshon hakodesh, its words explain their own concepts: Atzilus from 'etzel', near Hashem, and 'olam' from 'ne'elam', concealed.
Dovid HaMelech became the fourth leg of the Divine chariot in the very moment he accepted Shimi's curse, without a night of thought, as decreed by Hashem.
Klal Yisrael across history is one body: the dor hamidbar is the head, later eras lower down, and our generation the heel, the lowest part, which is redeemed through emunah.
The new devices of our time are a new creation of the yetzer hara, who fights emunah so hard because he knows that emunah brings the redemption and his own slaughter.

'Vayar es hamakom merachok' means that at the akeidah Avraham was put into small mind and felt Hashem far away, and in that state of a simple Jew of ikvesa dimeshicha he passed the test of our generation.
Hashem's double 'Avraham, Avraham' after the akeidah expresses His love for the last generation, which passes the same test.
A nisayon comes from the word nes, a raised banner: each test lifted Avraham to a higher level.
Dveikus is explained through speech: just as two people talking together form a yichud, a union, so a Jew speaking to Hashem in tefillah is united with Him.

Tefillah's dveikus can be stronger than Torah's, because in learning one must think into the worldly matter being discussed, an ox that gored or a thief, while in davening one thinks of cleaving to Hashem.

Klal Yisroel passes through the stages of a person's life, and our generation is in its old age; like a sick man who needs orange juice rather than bread and meat, it needs the revival of tefillah more than earlier generations.
Learning to show off one's knowledge is like the young man who learned ten years for an audience that turned out to be cats.

Moshe Rabbeinu, who gave the Torah, is the head of the learners, the mind; Dovid HaMelech, who gave Tehillim, the root of all tefillos, is the head of those who daven, the heart; one who davens well binds himself to Dovid's holiness, one who learns well to Moshe's.
Whether chassidim daven quietly or loudly follows the root of the soul of their Rebbe, just as souls are sent to the Rebbe whose root they share.
The Rav reads the Gemara's case of the river path as a model for technology: whether a smartphone is permitted depends on whether there is truly no other way.
Not looking is not enough: Chazal's harsh title falls on the choice to enter the test needlessly, even if he passes it.
Following Shaarei Teshuvah, the Rav explains that the severity of disobeying a rabbinic enactment, such as eating before Maariv, lies not in the act but in the contempt for the Sages behind it.
The Rav finds a hint that obeying the Sages is the center of the Torah in the Masorah's note that the middle passuk of Sefer Devarim is 'al pi haTorah'.
The Rav ties Hashem's help against the yetzer hara to submission to the Sages: one who belittles them loses that help, and then the yetzer hara truly is stronger than him.
The word Adam equals forty-five, the value of the Name of Havayah filled out with alefs, so man is the throne and chariot for the holiness of the ten sefiros.

Tiferes is not a mixture of chesed and gevurah, like sugar and lemon in water, but a qualitatively new creation that appears when they meet, like the beauty of a painting or the harmony of two voices.
Netzach and hod are the two legs a person stands on: the right leg survives by fighting adversaries, the left by bending and bearing the pressure, both serving the one purpose of standing.
Each day of creation adds a string to the harp, and only when Shabbos adds the seventh can music be played; this is why zemiros are sung on Shabbos.
Each animal expresses one sefira, as the lion, whose name Aryeh equals gevurah, expresses fear, while man has no single defining trait because every part of creation contributed to him.

The seven lower sefiros are called double because they can be for good or for evil; Chabad can be used for evil but is not evil in essence, and the ten sons of Haman, written from top to bottom, are the ten sefiros of impurity.
The speaker reads the youth's resistance to rabbanim as the same inborn Jewish stubbornness that kept the nation through persecution, now turned inward by the yetzer hara.
A prison and an army look the same from outside, with uniforms, numbers and orders; the whole difference is whether the person inside feels arrested or honored.
He links R' Mendel of Rimanov's words that the last battle was pushed off by 150 years to the years around 1965, when the street openly broke down and personal technology began to spread.

The danger is not only in what the device can reach but in the attitude: a device used with relish as a 'friendly' family device teaches children to enjoy it, while one used with trembling as a minimal work tool does not.
Where Hashem truly requires a device for parnassah, the one who uses it carefully is a hero on the front, not a sinner; the same act done without need is the reverse.
R' Langer reads the halachic test of a bird that swims against the current as a definition of life: being alive means being able to stand against the current of the times.
Following the Avnei Nezer, he understands 'teaching a son to swim' as an education that keeps a child afloat in the waters of this world rather than a practical skill for sea travel.
He compares the generations to a grafted branch, which lives only while bound to the older branch, and applies it to staying connected to the rabbonim.
He reads the letters of 'nokef' in the saying that no one lifts a finger below unless it is proclaimed above as an acronym for notepads, iPods and videos, computers and phones.
From R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld he brings that zealotry is a double-edged sword whose handle is the rebbe; without the handle one cuts oneself and must hold back.
The Rav reads the tree of knowledge as a 'smart tree' whose fruit were smartphones, so that a smartphone in the home is a renewal of Chava's sin, while women's mitzvos are meant to repair it.
The blessings of Sarah's tent did not stay in the merit of Avraham and Yitzchak and returned only with Rivka, showing that the woman, not the men, is the spirit and kedushah of the home.

The Shabbos lamp that burned in Sarah's tent from Shabbos to Shabbos is the model for every Jewish home: the woman draws the spirit of Shabbos into the weekdays, which the Rav reads into 'her lamp does not go out at night'.
Just as the Biur kept Reb Zusha from entering a house, a smartphone brings a tumah into the home that darkens the Shabbos lights and is the opposite of Shabbos.
The makkos ran in reverse order to the maamaros, starting from the earthly and working up to the heavenly, so that Hashem's control was shown at every level of creation.
The renewal of nature in spring is the filtering down of the heavenly renewal of Nissan, and a person who stays old while everything around him is renewed falls behind his own surroundings.
Animals each embody one trait and act predictably, while man contains all ten, which is why bread, a mixture, is the food of man.
Lechem equals three times twenty-six, the plain Shem Havayah, while matzah equals three times forty-five, the Shem Havayah spelled out in full, so matzah is a far higher food.

There are two beginnings of the year, Nissan with mercy and Tishrei with judgment, and one who places himself under Nissan's reishis through good matzos is already freed from the authority of Tishrei's judgment.

Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz read the Ba'al Shem Tov's teivah as the ark against today's flood: apikorsus, desire, envy and honor drown most of the world, and the word of tefillah is where a Jew is saved.
The Rav explains that saying the words of tefillah is a rabbinic mitzvah, while davening with the heart is the mitzvah of the Torah, 'to serve Him with all your heart'.
The Rav notes that the Shulchan Aruch normally says what to do, yet here it narrates how early chassidim davened, because every person can reach hispashtus hagashmiyus in his own measure.
Pegiah means an appointment: if a non-Jew treats an appointment with a president as a great event, a Jew at the times of tefillah has an appointment with the King of kings.
In the story of the simple Jew, his prayer reached so deep that at 'Tzam'ah nafshi' he forgot to ask to be saved and longed only for Hashem, and he was saved.
A soul that came too late for its tikkun was measured middah k'neged middah: in its lifetime it used to come late to davening and learning.
Rachel and Lavan's sheep form one theme: the mother of the exiled souls and the souls themselves, so Yaakov's rolling the stone was an act of easing their exile.
The well is Knesses Yisrael, and the stone Yaakov rolled off it is a weight lifted from the Jewish heart in exile.
Yaakov's seven years of work for Rachel were the time the souls still needed in Lavan's captivity before they could pass from Rachel to Yaakov.
Rachel's death on reaching Eretz Yisrael marks the end of her task, and her burial on the road prepares her to take it up again in later exiles.
The shepherds' words that Rachel comes with the sheep were a sign that the time had come for the souls to be handed to Yaakov and turned from sheep into six hundred thousand Jewish souls.
The Rav joins the Zohar's statement that Yaakov grabbed Elul with the Midrash that Elul's mazal, Besulah, was itself a maiden who grabbed an angel's wings, so the month's very nature is grabbing.
He reverses the usual fear: rather than the sitra achra grabbing a piece of a person, the person must grab a piece from the sitra achra for himself.

Because the moment of passing holds a whole life, and Rochel's soul left with Binyamin's birth, Binyamin carries his mother's essence of giving away her own, and that is what gives him the power to grab back.
Tu B'Av, when Binyamin's men grabbed wives at Shiloh, marks the point from which the season returns to Yaakov's portion, making it a day of grabbing.
Sitting at Rochel's grave on the last day of Av, at the edge of the grabbed month, is for the Rav the moment to resolve not to be grabbed by the yetzer hara.
The Torah does not stress middos because good middos are the entrance requirement: whoever enters the school of Torah is assumed to have graduated from the school of middos.
Da'as is responsibility: a child may out-learn adults, yet he is not a bar da'as because there is no bridge yet by which his understanding governs his middos.

Love cannot be commanded into being, just as a man cannot decide to love spinach, but fear is within one's choice; therefore yirah is the 'avodas avodah' a person works on and ahavah the 'avodas matanah' Hashem grants in return.
The intensity of the words of love by Shechem shows a spark of kedushah struggling to tear itself free of the klipah, like a bird pulling with all its strength out of a trap.
The love born of Binah is the fire in the heart thirsting for water, and that water is Chochmah, the point of G-dliness in the soul: the love yearns to return to its own source.
The Tanya calls love without Da'as 'dimyonos shav', not 'sheker': shav means there is something there, only it is useless, and later chapters say it has some worth.
Since Rosh Hashanah is 'the day the world is conceived', the place where Chana conceived Shmuel, the first of the prophets, carries the quality of Rosh Hashanah.

Eli's objection shows that the merit of a long tefillah was not yet known; it was Chana who introduced it, and tefillah remains something people belittle, though honor is shown for Torah and tzedakah.
Barrenness can be spiritual: a tefillah that is not answered, or learning without success, has no fruit, and the place where Chana's barrenness ended is a segulah against it.
Shmuel's first prophecy, the punishment of Chofni and Pinchas for keeping women from returning to their families, served to remove barrenness from Klal Yisroel.
Chana used the name Tzevaos, never found in the Chumash, to ask for children, because Tzevaos means the hosts of Jewish souls; and with Shmuel began the prophets' nourishment from netzach and hod.
The word 'vehaya' in 'vehaya ki hirbisa lehispallel' hints that Chana's tefillah was on Rosh Hashanah, since vehaya is the form tied to the month of Tishrei.

Just as Hashem made six days and a seventh that is Shabbos, among the lands the seventh is Eretz Yisroel: it is the Shabbos of geography, and like Shabbos one can be inside it without any connection to it.
Rosh Hashanah judges once a year because it heads the year in time; Eretz Yisroel, created first, is the head in place, so there one is judged every day.
The Torah that Moshe wrote begins with Eretz Yisroel, per Rashi on Bereishis, and ends with Hashem showing him the land, so Eretz Yisroel encompasses the whole Torah.
Moshe asked to be able to pray only when standing at the edge of Eretz Yisroel, not during forty days in heaven, because the ground of Eretz Yisroel is holier than the heaven above chutz la'aretz.
Eretz Yisroel is called 'wide' though it is small, as a walnut-sized diamond is huge while a room-sized plot in Manhattan is tiny: its greatness is measured by its preciousness.
Water surrounds Eretz Yisroel on all four sides so that one immerses and purifies oneself before entering the land.
The Rav calls Gehinnom a laundry: it washes off the stain of a sin committed against a mitzvah once kept, but it cannot supply a mitzvah that was never done at all.
He says people avoid the depths of Torah because understanding more makes them more responsible, and that one who accepts pshat, remez and drush without sod is a 'pered', a mule.
How high a person can reach in Torah depends on how high the roots of his soul reach, as in an inverted tree whose roots are in heaven; even the Beis Yosef fell asleep at the Arizal's shiurim on sod.
A positive commandment overrides a prohibition because it is active and comes from love, while fear only holds back; love is the son, fear the servant.

A human organ is called by the name of a divine attribute because it is a receiver for it: the eye is an 'ayin' because Hashem's seeing is drawn into it, and when guarded according to the Torah it becomes a chariot for that holiness.
The Rav reads the Midrash of the heartless donkey together with 'kaved lev Paroh': a heart that does not fear Hashem is not a heart at all, only a liver.
Fear of punishment is really fear for oneself; true fear of Hashem is the natural shame one feels before greatness, as no one would act disgracefully in front of a president.
Shlomo's love for Hashem made him so united with Him that his own name was absorbed into the name of the King to whom peace belongs; the drash of 'Shlomo' is thus the inner meaning of the plain one.
Shir Hashirim and the Holy of Holies share the name kodesh kodashim because both are the place of the chosson and kallah: the keruvim there, the love song here.
Every Yom Tov is a 'chag', a circle, dancing around Shemini Atzeres, which is not called a chag because it is the point in the middle.
Shlomo is the only person who ever reached everything he desired, because his life was a sample of the days of Moshiach, when Hashem too will have full nachas from His world.

The same soul has two sides: Shlomo, who built the Beis HaMikdash and wrote Megillas Shir Hashirim, and Yirmiyahu, who saw its destruction and wrote Megillas Eichah; and 'Shlomo HaMelech' with its letters spelled out equals Tisha B'Av in gematria.
Shlomo stood in the fifteenth generation from Avraham, like the moon full on the fifteenth day, and from him the generations declined to the destruction in the thirtieth.
Shlomo is Hashem's appointed poet, and Klal Yisrael also appointed him as theirs, so the songs of Shir Hashirim run back and forth between the chosson and the kallah.

Following Reb Feivel, the Rav explains the Midrash that the nations who sacrifice in the north will be uprooted while Klal Yisrael, who sacrifice in the south, will come: olos are slaughtered in the north and a gentile can bring only an olah, while a Jew's shelamim, slaughtered anywhere in the courtyard and eaten, shows his power to sanctify the physical.

Shir Hashirim is holy of holies precisely because it takes the most physical relationship, chassan and kallah, as the mashal for Hashem and Klal Yisrael; until Shlomo it was not known that this world holds sparks of holiness that can be raised, and that is why Rabbi Akiva said the world was never as worthy as on the day it was given.

The tenth in every set of ten concerns chassan and kallah: in the ten maamaros it is 'it is not good for man to be alone', the tenth dibbur 'lo sachmod' means a person should have his own kallah and not covet another's, and Avraham's tenth trial, the Akeidah, brought about Yitzchak's zivug.

Shlomo's name reflects his place as the fifteenth generation, the full moon of Klal Yisrael; precisely because he stood at the peak and knew the waning would begin after him, he addressed Shir Hashirim to the darkness of the moon in galus.

Every neshamah owns a portion of Torah that only it can reveal; therefore Hashem could say the halachah of the parah adumah at Sinai in Rabbi Eliezer's name, Adam's 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' belongs to Dovid's soul, and Shir Hashirim belongs to Shlomo even though it was sung at the sea and at Sinai.

Yayin has the numerical value of seventy: Klal Yisrael's answer to the nations who invite them to live like gentiles and escape persecution is that Hashem's love is better than all the 'wine' of the seventy nations.
The Rav reads the 'kiss' of the pasuk as the Shechinah resting on a Jew's lips and speaking out of his mouth when he says words of Torah or tefillah.
He explains why the Oral Torah is dearer: the Written Torah comes down from Heaven to the world, while the Oral Torah is renewed by Jews below and is received above.
He uses the halachah of hashakah, where water in a vessel touching a mikveh becomes mikveh water, to explain how learning makes a Jew part of Hashem.
He reads Shlomo HaMelech's sixty warriors as the sixty masechtos, so that his army, and the Jewish people's defense ever since, is the Torah.
Shemen, oil, hints at shemoneh, eight, above the seven of nature; therefore the Chanukah miracle came through oil and lasted eight days.
In Tehillim 19 the first seven pesukim speak of nature, and the eighth, 'Toras Hashem temimah', speaks of Torah, which is above nature.
Hitler hated even assimilated Jews who lived like Germans, which the Rav says shows that the nations know Israel is the chosen people.
Ordinarily a garment is secondary to its wearer, but the garments of Torah and mitzvos are greater than the soul they clothe, because Torah is not a product of Hashem's wisdom but G-dliness itself.

The Rav reads chalitzah through the soul: the soul in the body is like a foot in a shoe, only its lowest part, while the rest stays above as an encompassing light, and the more refined a person is, the more of it he draws in.

The Tanya's claim that the garments surpass the soul refers to the soul as it is in the body; at its root, since Yisrael preceded everything in Hashem's thought, the soul is above Torah, and Torah is secondary to it.

The mind's failure to grasp G-dliness is a matter of category, not capacity: just as hearing a million times better will never let one hear a picture, a mind of any intelligence cannot reach what lies beyond this world.

Hashem's greatness and humility appear together: His greatness is that no mind can grasp Him, and His humility is that He contracted His will and wisdom into halachos of oxen and sukkos so that our minds can.

Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand meshalim were a chain, each mashal explaining the one above it, and in the same way Torah came down through the worlds, so that people on earth grasp it better than the angels, who lack this world's concepts.
Oil makes no sound when it is poured, unlike water or wine, and so Hashem's 'oil', His miracles, His tzaddikim and the good deeds of every Jew, works quietly and in hiding.
Just as a drop of water poured into a full glass of oil pushes out a drop of oil, a word of foolishness that a person says or hears pushes out a drop of Torah.

The Rambam's Moshiach, who shows no wonders but draws the whole people after him and brings them to Eretz Yisrael, is greater than a wonder-working Moshiach, since moving every heart is the greatest miracle.

Following the Yismach Moshe, the first 'ad ya'avor' in the pasuk carries Hashem's Name and so could not be lost, while the second does not, which is why sin could hold back the miracles of the Second Beis Hamikdash.
The Chanukah light is lit below ten tefachim, in the public domain, at night, in the darkest season, because Moshiach will come down to the lowest place of the Jewish people and lift them from there.
The Rav reads 'alamos' in the pasuk as coming from 'he'elem', concealment: the fragrance of the old miracles is what keeps Jews loving Hashem even when He hides His face.

The Rav reads the Chanukah war as a war of Jews against Jews, and sees the same pattern in Russia and in the fight of Reform and Conservative against Torah Jews; the Chafetz Chaim held that a fight against the Yevsektsia, like the war against the Greeks, would have succeeded.
One year in the years of youth is worth many years later on, when a person has reached a plateau and no longer grows.
A kulah is suspect not because it is false but because its motive may be hidden: a person who calls a remote danger a reason to skip davening would not say so about going to a party.
Gerim are Jewish souls born among goyim; their restless drive is what brings them back to their root, and they 'smell' the miracles that other nations ignore.

Galus is the time of the greatest revelations of Torah: Rabbi Akiva's secrets, Yechezkel's Merkavah, and the Talmud Bavli, which Eretz Yisroel's sages did not merit to develop, all came in galus out of Hashem's compassion.
The words with which Yechezkel describes seeing the heavens open spell emunah: whoever is not granted the vision must believe it.
Following the Midrash, Shlomo HaMelech's 'we will rejoice in You' settles the ambiguity of 'in it' in Hallel: the joy of the day is joy in Hashem Himself.
The 'love more than wine' of the verse is the halachos of each Yom Tov, learned in its time: they put more warmth into a Jew's blood than wine does.
Because the Jewish people cannot exist without the moadim, and the fixed calendar depends on Jews in Eretz Yisrael, Hashem saw to it that Jews never ceased to live there through all its conquerors.
Shabbos is an oasis where a weary traveler stops to rest; Chanukah and Purim, weekday festivals, are a jump-start that lets a Jew keep moving in the midst of galus.
Physical pleasure ends in satiation, but on Shabbos a Jew can be fully sated and still delight, because his soul is bound to Hashem.
The wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos but fit for Chanukah are souls too extinguished to burn on Shabbos, which can be kindled on Chanukah because then the Shechinah comes below ten tefachim.
Weekdays, 'chol', are like illness, 'choleh'; the Chanukah lights are Hashem's house call, the Shechinah coming down to visit the sick.
The Rav reverses the common view: the physical table one can touch belongs to the imaginary world, while Hashem's presence, which seems abstract, is the true reality.
Every detail of the halachos of sukkah, such as two walls and a tefach, is a detail of the Name of Hashem from which the mitzvah comes, so the halachos cannot be explained but only accepted.
The shaking of a Jew in learning and davening is itself part of the act of Torah and is clothed in it; it comes from the fire of the soul, which moves like a flame.
Every Jew has the potential of prophecy, since the soul knows and feels everything; only the body, insulated by aveiros, fails to pick up the soul's messages.
Learning Torah in this world is grasping Hashem Himself, like the sun itself, while the souls in Gan Eden grasp only the rays of the Shechinah.
Water, which is chesed, is the medium of every physical pleasure, and Hashem's embrace of a person reaches him through the Torah, the water that comes down from above.
A philosopher can see depth in the Tanya yet miss its point entirely, like someone without an ear for music who cannot tell a symphony from a cat walking on a piano.
The proof that a Jew is good in essence is that like begets like: since he comes from the Avos, he is essentially as they were, and his sins are only incidental.
