Teshuvah means returning to one's roots; a Jew has good roots to return to, while for a gentile, whose sin is essential, it does not help in the same way.
Hashem's answer to 'is not Esav a brother to Yaakov' is that even when their deeds look alike, Esav is bad in essence and Yaakov good in essence.
Shabbos is not only a taste of Olam Haba: following Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin, it is the fountain from which Olam Haba itself draws.
The word 'Shabbos' means return: on Shabbos the soul goes back to the Kisei HaKavod it was hewn from, where no sin reaches, which unites the two Midrashim on 'black but beautiful'.
Weekdays ('chol') are like sickness ('choleh'), prison, desert and sea; Shabbos is the release for which the four who must give thanks in Hodu thank Hashem.
Checking one's garments ('begadim') on Erev Shabbos is read, in the Slonimer Rebbes' Chassidic interpretation, as checking one's betrayals ('bgidos') against Hashem and doing teshuvah.

Rabbi Yehuda, who gave the plagues their simanim, is the same Tanna who holds chametz may only be destroyed by burning: as the soul of Yehuda, head of the camps and of fire, he always reaches for the root.

Following the Ba'al HaTanya, the very reason the Torah gives for the Flood becomes the reason for never bringing another, because returning to the root transforms the cause of judgment into a cause of merit.
A mikvah is an 'embassy' of the heavens: just as a country's embassy counts as its own soil, the mikvah, made of fire and water like the heavens, places the one who immerses inside the heavens.
The letters of Hashem's Name form a space four by ten, the measure of a reshus hayachid, and four times ten gives the forty se'ah of a mikvah, so immersion is immersion in the Name itself.
The Haggadah draws down the salvations of the plagues, which is why the Tanna'im compete to count more plagues: each one counted brings more salvation.
Both mikvah and 'rachitz' mean bitachon: immersing is giving oneself over to Hashem.
Shabbos could not wait the forty-nine days of the long Exodus until Matan Torah, so it was already given at Marah.
The different reasons for Shabbos in the two luchos match the people's level: prophets see the Creator in nature itself, while after the golden calf they needed the remembered miracles of Egypt.
The ten plagues repeat the ten utterances of creation in reverse: the first utterance corresponds to the last plague, the firstborn, and 'let there be light' to the ninth plague, darkness.
Denial of the Creator is not an intellectual position but a refusal: the heretic does not believe his own house built itself, yet claims the world did, because admitting the truth would bind him.
An event seen by millions cannot be invented, so the Exodus entered history and was handed down from generation to generation, a tradition no other nation has.

Idle sitting by ten Jews is not merely wasted time: since the Shechinah is there regardless, they 'squeeze' it, like people crowding someone out of a room, and this is counted among the causes of golus.
Just as Hashem concealed His holiness in physical things through the halachos, He wrapped the deepest secrets of the Torah in even more coverings, the aggados that seem like nonsense.
The Torah is Hashem encased in physical subject matter like radioactive material in lead: the casing does not interrupt the contact, just as a caress through a sleeve is still a caress.
By learning Torah a Jew rises above the angels and the souls in Gan Eden, who receive only light that radiates from the Shechinah, while he holds the Shechinah itself.

The Gemara discusses cases that may never occur, such as a person with two heads, because each halachah is Hashem's own will about what would be if it happened, so understanding it is grasping His will.
Clothing costs more than food because mitzvos, which are clothing, should be paid for, while Torah, which is food, comes free.

The sukkah is a surrounding light and the lulav draws some of it inward; when Sukkos ends, the Torah of Simchas Torah gives an inner light, which the generation of the flood, given only an ark like a sukkah, did not merit.

The thirty-nine melachos of Shabbos correspond to the curses that Adam, Chavah, the earth and the serpent received after the sin, so refraining from them on Shabbos is a return to a state of pure blessing.
The amount of melachah permitted on a day is the inverse of the blessing it holds: Shabbos none, Yom Tov somewhat more, Chol Hamoed more, Rosh Chodesh more still.
Moshe's argument to Pharaoh that rested workers produce more is what modern scientists call the law of diminishing returns, yet the Torah's Shabbos is the opposite of such a practical day off.
Moshe's joy in 'Yismach Moshe b'matnas chelko' is that the day he had chosen in Egypt turned out to be the very day Hashem gave as Shabbos.
Food prepared with words of tefillah carries them: the fish over which Nishmas was said had Nishmas in it, which is the meaning of 'echol b'simchah' after 'Nishmas kol chai' in Menuchah v'Simchah.
Some have a Shabbosdik kugel, a kugel infused with Shabbos, and others a kugeldik Shabbos, a Shabbos that amounts to another piece of kugel.

The Rav reads the two kiddush formulas as two kinds of holiness: Shabbos comes down as Hashem's own gift, while Yom Tov's holiness is drawn from below by the Jews, and grows with how well each one prepared.
Even though Shabbos is a gift that does not depend on preparation, the receiver must be a clean vessel; the gift is the same, but in a dirty cup it has no taste.
What a person has in mind during the week is what he brings into Shabbos: the storekeeper thought of kiddush while selling and his kiddush burned, while the scholar thought of the women at kiddush.
Following the Tikkunei Zohar that 'Bereishis' holds the letters of 'yarei Shabbos', the Rav says one must approach Shabbos with fear and shame, asking whether he is a clean vessel for it.
When one prepares properly, even the physical things of Shabbos carry its holiness, as the Karliner chassid asked Hashem to give Shabbos to his wine and his fish.
The Rav reads 'Lev tahor' in Tehillim as hinting at tevilah, so that immersing before Shabbos helps one attain a pure heart.
Tanya uses the word 'crowns' only for the powers of impurity, never for holiness, because the essence of impurity is that it sees itself as something and claims greatness.
Impurity is always nine or eleven, never a true ten, which is why the Torah counts eleven amos for the Teivah, eleven goat-hair curtains and eleven spices of the ketores.
In the list of the ketores spices the order by weight is broken so that kinnamon comes last, making it both the ninth and the eleventh, the two numbers of impurity.
'Re'us ruach' means a breaking of the ruach: pursuits not done for Hashem cut the soul's connection to Him, like snapping a wire that carries current.
The proof that every Jew is batel to Hashem in potential is that even sinners have willingly given their lives rather than serve avodah zarah, as with Fayvish the thief.
Actual mesiras nefesh is found only by Avraham Avinu, not by Yitzchak or Yaakov, and Jews inherit their readiness to die for Hashem from him.
A mikveh becomes kosher by touching and joining the rainwater from heaven; in the same way, before Shabbos a Jew purifies himself by connecting to tzaddikim and their sefarim.
Since Shabbos is a gift and a giver gives generously, Hashem gave not only Shabbos but also the path to it, erev Shabbos; one cannot fall into Shabbos unprepared but must walk the path.
The passuk ties 'Hashem gave you Shabbos' to the double bread of the sixth day, showing that Friday itself is part of the gift, the road by which one enters Shabbos.
Erev Shabbos is a form of Yom Kippur, as the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's answer to the Chida shows: the Yom Kippur-like asking of forgiveness on erev Shabbos is what made his name great in heaven.
A 'shomer Shabbos' is literally one who waits for Shabbos, as 'shamar' is used for Yaakov awaiting the fulfillment of Yosef's dreams.
The seven days of the week correspond to the ushpizin; Friday is Yosef HaTzaddik, who is holiness, so the preparation for Shabbos must be with holiness, while Shabbos is Dovid.

Following the Chasam Sofer, 'lo seva'aru esh... b'yom haShabbos' is read as: do not wait until Shabbos to kindle the fire; kindle it at the start of the week in learning and davening, so that on Shabbos the fire of Shabbos flares up.

Because good joins with good while evil does not join with evil ('yispardu kol po'alei aven'), a gathering of Jews combines only their good points, like many small candles that together become one great flame.

The seven notes of music correspond to the seven days and middos; only when Shabbos, the seventh, arrives is the 'piano' complete, which is why Psalm 29 with its seven 'kol Hashem' is the seventh chapter of Kabbalas Shabbos, and only after it is Lecha Dodi sung.

Unlike the weekday psalms, which the Levi'im sang, 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' means that the Shabbos day itself sings, so the Jew's singing on Shabbos is joining in harmony with the day's own song.
At shalosh seudos 'da hi seudasa' is said only after eating a little and right before singing, because the real seudah of shalosh seudos is the singing, not the herring.

The tzaddik is compared to both the date palm and the cedar: the palm puts its strength into fruit and so does not grow tall, the cedar grows tall but bears no fruit, and the tzaddik has both qualities.
The name Kinneres hints at the kinor: the seventh sea completes the set as the seventh note completes the scale, and the lake is even shaped like a violin.

The passuk's border that 'touches the shoulder of Yam Kinneres' is read as the Shechinah going around Eretz Yisrael on Shabbos and giving the singing Kinneres an approving pat on the shoulder, like the Stoliner's pat to the Blazhever Rav.
No person has the strength to sing before the Ribono shel Olam on his own; it is only because Shabbos itself sings that Jews can join in.
The secret of a niggun is the unity of its notes, each joined to the next, which is why song fits Shabbos, the day of 'echad'.
A Shabbos meal that lacks divrei Torah and holiness is like a feast prepared for a king who was never invited: Shabbos, the queen, must be called in.
The shape of the kuf mimics the hei of Hashem's Name, but its left leg drops below the line into tumah; its very name means a monkey, which imitates a man without being one.
The Rav reads the detailed description of Achashverosh's feast in the Megillah as a deliberate substitute for the Beis HaMikdash, every detail corresponding to something there.
Davar shebikdusha could be learned from the ten spies because even they had the Shechinah among them, being tzaddikim in their inwardness.
Chanukah and Purim are 'galus Yamim Tovim': days when melachah is permitted, when one does not rise to the higher worlds but kedusha descends to the lowest place.
The thirty-nine melachos ('lamed-tes') echo 'lot', curse, so melachah is a curse, and a day is exempt from melachah to the degree it is free of the curse.
The lion and eagle are holy in the Merkava but impure below, because gevurah, unlike chesed, becomes contaminated on its way down.
The Girgashi, who corresponds to malchus and to a clod of earth, left Eretz Yisrael without war; so domem, the lowest level, is batel and the Tanya lists no klipah in it.
Since Hashem created the world with speech and rested from it on Shabbos, a person who strives higher rests on Shabbos from ordinary speech as well, not only from work.
A great spiritual level cannot be made an obligation; this is why tefillas chatzos is a takanah rather than a chiyuv.
The Rav reads 'bechorish' in the passuk about resting as related to cheresh, silence: on Shabbos a person is quiet.
Shabbos is compared to the private talk of two close friends that others are not meant to hear, a bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel alone.
The afternoon, which during the week carries harsh judgment at mincha, is on Shabbos the peak of the day and a time of great ratzon.
'Bnei Heichala' are the children of the King's palace whom the King invites to come and eat together with Him.

The 'will of wills' is read on two levels: plainly, the et ratzon of mincha within the favor of all Shabbos; more deeply, the will Hashem had before creation, which a Jew can echo by willing to become a new person.
Since the world was created on Sunday, Shabbos afternoon before motzaei Shabbos is like the time before the first day, which is why shalosh seudos is above time.
Just as the aron in the Kodesh HaKodashim took up no space, shalosh seudos is not bound by time; created limits of place and time do not apply where there is a revelation of heaven.
The three Avos received the land in different ways, and only Yaakov's promise has no borders; shalosh seudos is Yaakov's portion, so the clock announcing the end of Shabbos has no hold on it.
Because kiddush is testimony and a rasha is an invalid witness, teshuvah before kiddush is what qualifies a person to testify to creation.

The first parsha says only 'remembrance' because it is about Pesach, when tefillin are not worn; just as 'zichron teruah' refers to a Rosh Hashanah on Shabbos when the shofar is not blown and only remembered.

Since 'totafos' means the four parshiyos, and in the desert the Jews had only the first two, the first parsha could only speak of a remembrance; the second parsha already looks ahead to those born in the desert who would have all four.
Tefillin are the parsha of Yetzias Mitzrayim because both mean entering a new period of attachment to Hashem, and so every bar mitzvah boy goes through his own Yetzias Mitzrayim.
Every mitzvah a Jew does adds to Hashem's tefillin, which speak of the beauty of the Jewish people.
'Or l'arba'ah asar bodkin es hachametz' hints at the boy entering his fourteenth year, when he must search himself for chametz by the light of Torah.
As Klal Yisrael are Hashem's firstborn, the first year after a bar mitzvah is the firstborn of a person's whole life and shapes all that follows.
Enjoyment itself is a human need, like air or food, so enjoying needed food is not a fall into klipah; only excess and the absence of l'shem shamayim tip it down.
Priyah is not removed but torn and pulled upward, which is exactly how klipas nogah is treated: not discarded, but elevated into kedushah.
The Shaagas Aryeh's halachic chiddush that Bnei Yishmael are not obligated in priyah is confirmed by Kabbalah: a body rooted in the three impure klipos cannot repair nogah.
Each place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a part of the Torah, so Osniel ben Kenaz, by recovering the halachos of Kiryas Sefer, became master of the place itself.
Chevron, bought by Avraham, is the place of milah, and Shechem, bought by Yaakov and given to Yosef, is the place of priyah; this is why the Yishmaelim make the most trouble in those two places.
A gentile may bring only an olah and not a shelamim because eating as avodah means elevating nogah, which only a Jew can do.
The Rav reads the tochachah's title 'the words of the covenant' as linking it to bris milah: as the bris removes the covering, so the curses are a covering over blessing.
He matches the seven weeks of consolation to the middos, so that Ki Savo, the sixth, is the week of yesod, the middah of the bris.
He sees in the haftorah's words about the nations, those cut off and those who will serve Klal Yisrael, the two stages of milah and periah.
He notes that the sixth haftorah ends with 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim', tzaddik being the term for yesod, the middah of the week.
The Rav reads the derivation of kiddushin from the burial cave not as a bad omen but as its depth: Avraham bought the grave because his bond with Sarah was meant to continue beyond life.
He explains that halachically a marriage ends with life only from the side of the body, while the souls remain united.
He links the bar mitzvah to the kicha-kicha derivation: since the Torah is given as a kallah, receiving the Torah at bar mitzvah is itself a kiddushin.

Through the Chasam Sofer, he shows that Haman could not destroy only the talmidei chachamim, because the Torah is the inheritance of every Jew and lies within him, to come out in his children if not in himself.
He contrasts silver, tied to fire that rises, with Efron's dust, which brings sadness, so that the Machpelah of Torah is acquired with silver and zrizus.

The Rav reads the halachic terms literally: 'heter' and 'mutar' mean untied and 'asur' means tied, so a permitted thing that fell into kelipah can free itself while a forbidden thing is bound to the sitra achra.

A person's possessions are extensions of his own soul; when the work of redeeming their sparks is finished, the object is lost or broken, which the Rav connects to saying 'mazel tov' when a glass breaks, and someone else finds it to redeem the remaining sparks.

The Rav explains the growing chumros of later generations: borderline items are bound to the sitra achra by thin strings that earlier great souls could cut through their avodah and brachos, but this generation cannot.
Gehinnom is in essence a laundry: a dusty mattress is cleaned by beating, like the beating of the grave for permitted indulgence, while what has been absorbed needs hot water, like Gehinnom.

Bitul b'shishim is a small instance of the future purification that Hashem brings about when a soul deserves it; a person who mixes a forbidden drop in on purpose achieves nothing, just as the geulah cannot be taken by force.
Teshuvah from love is a private geulah: an individual can experience now, for himself, what the collective redemption will bring.

Like a bird that breaks free from a grip and flies higher than one that rises normally, the baal teshuvah escapes the sitra achra with greater force; since the sin produced that surge, it is rectified at its root and becomes a merit.
Because the blessings are derived from the curses by a hekesh, and what a teacher lacks the student cannot have, the blessings must already be present inside the curses themselves.
The curses of Ki Savo are like an orlah: a covering over great good, and a bris that removes it reveals the hidden blessing.
Elul is the bris milah of the year: Tamuz and Av are the orlah, and in Elul, with the milah and priah, it is revealed that everything was good all along and judgments turn into merits.
The curses at the end of the year in Ki Savo are themselves a bris at the end of the year, matching the bris that completes a child's formation at its end.
The passuk 'umal Hashem' speaks to the generation of Moshiach yet says 'the heart of your children', because a father's teshuvah through the circumcision of the heart takes effect in his child.
A bris is the one mitzvah a father does for his child that is entirely free of ulterior motives, since every Jewish child is circumcised and there is no honor to gain from it.
The Rav reads Yaakov's 'kayom', 'as of today', as the heart of his dispute with Esav: the same word 'today' carries two opposite philosophies of life.
He links Esav's 'I am going to die, so what is the birthright to me' with the rasha's 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'.
He explains that a bar mitzvah is a wedding in which the boy is the chassan and the holy Torah is the kallah.
He ties Toldos being the sixth sedra to yesod, the foundation of bracha and of tzaddikus, so becoming bar mitzvah in it is a good sign.
The Rav links the bris to the season through the passuk of parshas Nitzavim that speaks of Hashem circumcising the heart, which is read in the days of Elul.
He presents Elul as the preparation for Rosh Hashanah, the time that determines the whole year, so that what is done in these days carries weight for the year.
He sees a bris in Elul as made at an auspicious hour, since these are the days when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused.

The gravity of a sin and the ease of its repair are separate questions: wasted seed is the worst sin, yet because its influence found no receiver, it can be gathered back more easily than forbidden relations.
Yaakov's gift to Esav totaled 580 animals, the numerical value of Esav's force in the Sitra Achra with its female counterpart, so sending it from the side of kedushah neutralized that force.
The customs of the nations, like putting the woman first, buttoning left over right and writing left to right, follow unknowingly from their angel's left-sided order, while Jews start from the right.
The Jewish calendar blends the moon of chesed with the sun of din through the leap month, unlike the Arabs' purely lunar calendar of uncontrolled chesed, so Nisan always falls in spring.
Tumas keri is linked by the Midrash to Amalek's 'chance', so its repair, as Rav Tzadok says, is faith in Hashem's oneness, that nothing simply happens.
Following the Tzemach Tzedek, the halachah that no brachah is said on forbidden food rests on the inner purpose of a brachah: to elevate the holy sparks, which forbidden food cannot release.
Following the Avnei Nezer, a gift the Ribono shel Olam gives the Jews that they do not use is seized by the sitra achra; Achashverosh's feast was the oneg of the Shabbos the Jews failed to keep.
Following the Shem MiShmuel, milah is the source of chiyus and newness, so its neglect let Pharaoh take the "chadash" for himself: "a new king arose".
The Rav reads "kadesh li kol bechor" at the opening of tefillin as the theme of tefillin: a bechor is something that never was before, and tefillin call for that newness each day.
He contrasts weekday tefillin, kabbalas ol malchus shamayim even in darkness, with Shabbos tefillin, which bring chiyus, renewal and kabbalas ol out of love.
The joy of the guests at a bar mitzvah is their own renewal, and this renewal takes back what the new king of Egypt had seized.

The Rav pairs the ten days of teshuvah with the ten maamaros of creation, so that Yom Kippur matches "lachem yihyeh l'ochlah": the day nature would make the day of eating is the day a Jew rises above it.
He reads the order of night and day in Barchi Nafshi as the order of nature, so that rising at night in these days is itself a step above nature.
Above the sun, beyond nature, is the realm of the thirteen middos of rachamim, which no sin can reach.
Since nature made a man with an orlah, a Jew who cuts it away sets nature aside; therefore milah, on the eighth day, is above nature, as the Maharal says.
The thirteen brisos of milah correspond to the thirteen middos, so a bris in these days receives the thirteen middos that rule at this time.
Citing sefarim, he says the soul of the one whose name is given comes to the naming, and within the first year it is still more connected to this world.
The Exodus at Pesach is the Jewish people's bar mitzvah: daas left its exile and the nation came to daas.
A boy does not feel the change at thirteen because the last drop of daas, like the last drop that completes a revi'is, can only be detected with precise instruments.
Shabbos HaGadol is named for the Jewish people becoming 'gedolim', adults, as they came to daas.
The two names of the nasi of Gad, ben De'uel and ben Reuel, point to daas and ratzon, the two ways of becoming bar mitzvah, which the boy should join together.
The custom of bar mitzvah gifts below awakens gifts from Heaven, where a heavenly voice tells the boy he is born today and may ask.

The Rav reads the Tanya's term 'divrei soferim' for rabbinic law as a claim about the Rabbis' vision: because single letters were 'davar shebeminyan' to them, they saw the root of things and could know that a rabbinic prohibition draws from the klipos and is not merely a fence.
Rabbi Meir's writing a Megillah by heart did not break the rule of copying from a text, because he saw the Torah's root in heaven and copied from it.

The difference between 'or' with an ayin, skin, and 'or' with an aleph, light, describes the whole avodah of a Jew: to see the aleph, the Master of the world, inside the ayin, which sweetens all impurity.

The suspended ayin of 'chazir miyaar' stands at the middle of Tehillim because the center, the point of origin, is the place where things can be changed, so even the swine, the counterpart of the serpent, can turn from ayin to aleph there.
Chalav akum can be worse than chazir: chazir is forbidden only as itself, while chalav akum carries a connection to the goy, which reaches the root of the shedim nukhraim.
Tosafos records that the old man who drank the wine was later killed in order to prove his point: had the wine truly been yayin nesech, he would not have merited to give his life al kiddush Hashem.
Food eaten for pleasure is like dust on a mattress that stays on the surface and is beaten out, while forbidden food is absorbed like a real stain that needs the hot laundering of Gehinnom.
The brachah over the four species goes on the lulav, Yosef the mashpia, rather than the esrog of Dovid and malchus, even though malchus is the theme of every brachah.
Only Yosef among the ushpizin is called 'the tzaddik', a title he earned through his test, and this is the most important of all the middos.

Following the Chasam Sofer, 'there is none greater in this house than I' can be read as Yosef saying that in the 'house' of the Divine Name he is the highest, the lulav, and refusing to lose that rank.
Both orders of the ushpizin are true and both customs exist; by one of them this day belongs to Yosef, so a bris meal in the sukkah today makes Yosef the head of the guests.
A bar mitzvah in the days before Shavuos fits the season: just as all Jews then become a 'new offering', newborn before Hashem, the boy is reborn as a son of Hashem.
The heavenly call 'You are My son' is placed in the psalm of Gog and Magog because the bar mitzvah boy of a generation that casts off the yoke of Heaven needs it most.
'I will tell of the decree' means making it a fixed law for oneself to repeat, again and again, that one is a child of Hashem.
The two readings of 'seven and eight', the festival and the bris, are one idea: in both, eight stands beyond the realm of seven.
Seven, the seventy bulls of Sukkos for the nations and the days of creation, is the share given to the world; eight is the Jews' own bond with Hashem, in which the nations have no part.
The meeting of a bris with Shemini Atzeres is not chance but hashgachah pratis, and makes the baby a 'Shemini Atzeres child'.
Yovel, the fiftieth year after seven times seven, carries the same quality of the eighth.

The Gehinnom of fire answers active sins, since every action needs energy and generates heat, while the Gehinnom of snow answers the passive failure to do a mitzvah, a coldness in which no heat was generated for a mitzvah.

Idle talk about baseball comes from a passion of the middos and defiles only them, but substantive secular wisdom defiles Chabad, the soul's intellect, which is above the middos; this is why the more serious study is the greater blemish.
Secular wisdom is a kelipah precisely because it comes from very great lights: the vessels could not receive them and broke, and the fallen fragments of Chabad became this wisdom.
The wife's name given only for Hadar, the eighth king, shows that a receiver had now come into being alongside the giver, so that world could endure, unlike the seven kings of whom it says 'he died'.

The founding principle of Greek philosophy, still held by scientists, that one does not accept what one cannot understand, is not science but fear; a real scientist who delves into creation knows better than anyone that there are things he cannot understand.
Chanukah's unique mehadrin min hamehadrin, found by no other mitzvah, is tied to Hadar, the eighth king who did not die, because the wisdom of Yavan is not a total kelipah and can return to holiness.

The Breaking of the Vessels is like a hava amina in the Gemara, which holds holiness even though it is rejected: Hashem gave existence to something without substance so that the world would be one of free choice.
The minyan for kedushah is learned specifically from the meraglim to show that even ten Jews who are not tzaddikim join into holiness through the good point in each of them.
Combining into one exists only in good; evil has no such joining, so a gathering of Jews draws out what is holy in them.
A twelve-year-old tzaddik still cannot join a minyan, while a bar mitzvah boy can: his entry into the tzibbur, not his personal level, makes the day a public simcha.
The new power of good that the tzibbur receives through the boy is shared with everyone present who rejoices with him and with all of Klal Yisroel.
Parshas Shelach shows two kinds of shluchim, the failed meraglim and the successful Kalev and Pinchas, and every Jew is sent into the world as one or the other.
Hashem withheld the promise of the land until Avraham reached Shechem because that is Yosef's place, the place of the bris, and the land is earned through the bris.
Lech Lecha is the parsha of bris milah, and whatever happens in a given week is connected to that week's parsha.
The place where the first galus began, Yosef's sale from Shechem, is exactly where Hashem promised the land, so the start of galus already holds the promise of return.

The animal soul is what keeps creatures, people included, alive: people do not live because they decide to, but because natural desires to eat and sleep drive them, and this is Hashem's device to keep the world going.

Rashi's description of Mitzrayim and of Yisrael at Sinai uses the same phrases in reverse order: for the yetzer hara the heart comes first and then the person, for the yetzer tov the mind comes first and then the heart.

The order of the blessings of Krias Shema mirrors the Tanya: contemplating creation and the angels' awe produces fear, then love, and only with both does one say Shema; at Ahavah Rabbah the angels are no longer mentioned, since Israel stands higher.
Anger at people who live differently usually reveals insecurity about one's own path, or pride in one's Rebbe and crowd, rather than true zeal for Heaven.
The Radbaz answers why chametz is treated so strictly with searching and destroying: chametz is the yetzer hara, and in the war against it one goes with full determination.

The source of pleasure is in the mind: true intellectual delight is what one feels solving a problem alone on an island, while rushing to tell a friend shows the pleasure is already mixed with something else.
The 'bride' of the bar mitzvah boy is his new soul, the neshamah yeseirah, which is why the bar mitzvah day can be called his wedding day.
The Rav compares the bar mitzvah soul to the Shabbos soul: both are received as a crown on the head, as recited in Kegavna, that all Jews are crowned with new souls.

It is no accident that the age of thirteen is learned from the passuk calling Shimon and Levi 'brothers of Dinah': at thirteen a boy shows which family he belongs to, and they showed it by defending their sister.
Just as every leaf can be recognized as coming from its tree, a bar mitzvah boy should be recognizable as coming from his family's tree.
The custom in some places to shower the bar mitzvah boy, not only the chosson and kallah, mirrors what happens above, where he is showered with gifts from Heaven.
The Rav reads 'v'charos imo habris' as Hashem holding Avraham's hand, and from this concludes that at every bris Hashem holds the mohel's hand the way a scribe holds his pen.
Since no one can sign in another's name through an agent, the words 'chasam b'os bris kodesh' show that Hashem Himself signs every bris.
Avraham merited Chevron through his bris: the place he bought in Parshas Chayei Sarah is the place of his bris, where Hashem came to him.
The Rav reads the parsha's name, Toldos, as the power and blessing that flow from parents to their children.
He points out that the verses from Yaakov's birth until Avraham's passing are the only ones in the Torah in which all three Avos are alive together.
Three generations at a bris mirror the three Avos together in Toldos, so the parsha's blessings rest on such a family.
Nullification means the limbs serve the soul the way a pen serves a writer: the pen does not argue about what to write, and a chariot has no will of its own apart from its rider.
In holiness the mind arouses the heart; in impurity the heart's desires send up their vapors and the mind becomes their servant, devising ways to satisfy them.

Ahavah rabbah is a pleasure that does not need the heart: the mind itself has a delight of understanding, like the flash of grasping a hard idea, and this is a taste of what souls enjoy in the World to Come.
Pharaoh withstood the plagues because in him the process of the tzaddik ran in reverse: the left chamber overflowed into the right, and his heart became only liver, the seat of the yetzer hara.

Man's organs are likenesses of the powers Scripture attributes to Hashem, so a rasha's heart that does not fear Hashem does not deserve to be called a heart, and his eye that does not look to Hashem is not truly an eye.

The angel of Esav picked a fight with Yaakov on the very night before his turn to sing shirah because his shirah was to be overpowered: every creature's shirah is fulfilling its function, just as the sun's shirah is its motion.
Yehuda was not born circumcised precisely because his path is teshuvah: the orlah left for a person to remove is what milah teaches, that man perfects himself.
Grapes and wheat, unlike other fruits, gain a higher blessing when crushed and worked, a sign that being broken can raise a person.
Malki-tzedek, himself born circumcised, could not use milah as proof that one can repair oneself, so he brought bread and wine to console Avraham.
Moshiach ben David embodies teaching teshuvah, and Moshiach ben Yosef the tzaddik who is the foundation of the world.
The Rav reads Chazal's teaching that the angels brought Levi to the Kisei HaKavod to be named as describing his bris, since a name is given at the bris.
Since bris is 612 and milah completes 613, the Rav says it is not only the mitzvah of milah that comes to a bris but the whole Torah.

The Rav links the custom of bentching at a bris with the permission of the kohanim and leviim to shevet Levi's keeping milah in Mitzrayim, which also explains why Levi was named at his bris by Hashem Himself.
He connects Levi, the grandfather of Moshe Rabbeinu, and the passuk 'Torah tziva lanu Moshe' to the child named Moshe at this bris.

'Chalal' means empty: a person who dies is called a chalal because he is emptied of his nefesh, and chillul Shabbos means emptying Shabbos of its kedushah; so David's 'chalal' heart was empty of the yetzer hara.
The tzaddikim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's era were sent close to Moshiach's days, outside the normal descent of the generations, to inject Klal Yisrael with 'adrenaline' so that its heart keeps beating.

Forgetting earlier gilgulim is what makes free choice possible: whoever remembered why he was sent back would not fail to be a tzaddik; perfect tzaddikim, who live only for others, have no choice to protect and so may remember.
Even a rasha's downfall is a merit, since it brings a Kiddush Hashem; Czar Nicholas was so wicked that he was denied even that and died a natural death.

The double wording about David and Avimelech, that he was driven out and that he went, describes the yetzer hara of the incomplete tzaddik: he thinks he drove it out, but it left of its own will and is ready to attack again.

The mitzvah of matzah is achila, and achila means enjoying the eating; this is why the Apter Rav, who tasted nothing all year, would not give up the matzah of the Seder, and why on Pesach the body itself is to feel the mitzvah.
Mius, revulsion, is felt toward objects and sinah toward people; David's utmost hatred of the resha'im is the soul's revulsion at their spiritual being, as the senses are revolted by spoiled food.
Osniel ben Kenaz could restore the forgotten halachos because by conquering Kiryat Sefer he became the owner of the land in which those halachos were written.
Mamre merited that Hashem revealed Himself in his portion because he owned Chevron, the place of milah, which explains Rashi's link between his counsel on the milah and the revelation.
Chevron and Shechem are both places of milah: Chevron, the place of Avraham, the general mitzvah, and Shechem, the place of Yosef, the detail of periah.

The three parts of milah, milah, periah and metzitzah, correspond to what happened in Shechem: the circumcision of its men, the conversion of its women and children, and the war with the surrounding nations drawn from afar.
The greatest kelipos of Eretz Yisroel sit in Chevron and Shechem because these are the places of the holy bris.
The places tied to milah and to the Akeidah had to be bought with money rather than received as a gift, because the bris can only be acquired through mesiras nefesh.
The Rav reads the day's news of an enemy's capture as the visible sign that a heavenly prince of Yishmael has fallen, since kings below fall only when their prince above falls.
The reading of the Nesi'im on Chanukah is explained as breaking the twelve nesi'im of Yishmael, who are twelve angels above.
Yishmael's claim to Eretz Yisroel rests on his milah, but because his milah is empty and without tikkun, his hold on the land is empty too.

Even the preparation for a bris, from the shalom zachar on, is counted as part of the bris, as the poskim show that a father preparing for a bris cannot be called to a din Torah, and so it too helped bring down Yishmael's prince.
The two Harachaman prayers at a bris, for Moshiach and for the kohen tzedek, correspond to Moshe and Eliyahu, the very names of the child.
Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz read 'Elokim yechonecha beni' as a blessing that a child born on Chanukah be a true Chanukah child.
A child born on the first day of Chanukah whose bris falls on the last day is bound to Chanukah from birth to bris, and so fits this blessing.
The Rav describes a Chanukah child as a child of dveikus and avodas Hashem.

The Rav resolves the apparent contradiction between the 18,000 tzaddikim before Hashem and Rabbi Shimon's 'bnei aliyah are few': the 18,000 still hold a tiny dormant trace of evil, while the bnei aliyah transformed it entirely.
He reads 'chassid ha'mitchased im kono' with 'kono' as 'his nest': the true chassid does kindness with Hashem's nest, the Shechinah in the lower world, giving it a proper place to rest.

Even the desire for closeness to Hashem, if served for its own sake, still points to the self; the ben aliyah has that thirst but does his mitzvos only for Hashem, since any act for himself would mean ego and a separation from Him.

The Sitra Achra can snatch a destined union only temporarily; the Rav sees this pattern in a person's match, in Eretz Yisrael first held by Canaan, and in Bathsheba first married to another before coming to David.
Because the Satan tries to block Moshiach's coming, everything leading to Moshiach comes about in a hidden, roundabout way, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can so the thief will not look there.

A thought of sin can be worse than the deed because thought reaches the higher world where speech and action cannot, like a small grease spot that is nothing on the avenue but an offense in the king's palace.
Every person has a deep chamber in his heart that is a tzaddik gamur, and when he says 'l'shem yichud' that chamber means it with all that it implies.
A bris on Chanukah doubles the revelation of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, since both the bris and Chanukah reveal them.
The child's name Elisha is itself a sign of healing: if Elisha healed even Naaman, all the more so for Jews.
The kal vachomer in the week's sedra connects to chessed, because kal vachomer, first of the thirteen rules of exegesis, parallels 'Keil', first of the thirteen attributes of mercy.
Yosef's role as sandek for Machir's children was aimed at Gilead specifically, because Gilead was a place under the mazal of bloodshed.
The same mazal of Maadim that can produce a murderer can produce a mohel; Yosef redirected Gilead's nature from killing to milah.
Eliyahu, the angel of the bris, comes from Gilead because of the holiness of the bris that Yosef planted there as sandek.

The Midrash's piece of Torah from the am ha'aretz, that Esav will return Yaakov's animals to Moshiach, was his own portion in the Torah: the souls given over to Esav, like him, will ultimately return to Yaakov and become tzaddikim.
Just as the tzaddik never even thinks of sinning, the rasha v'ra lo is his exact counterpart who never even thinks of teshuvah.

The surplus half-shekels of the Jews beyond six hundred thousand became the silver hooks that protruded outside the holiness of the Mishkan; Haman did not bother to counter them, thinking those outcast Jews mattered to no one, and that was his mistake.

The thirteenth month has no combination of the four letters of Hashem's Name, which allow only twelve, so it stands outside the camp; the Purim miracle happening in Adar Sheni shows it was made for the Jews outside the camp.
Korach's flaw of division reached Yitzhar, Kehas and Levi but could not reach Yisrael, because the Yechidah that unites all of Klal Yisrael is untouchable.

Ordinary Purim is for the rasha v'tov lo who still has regret, while Shushan Purim of Yerushalayim, the walled city surrounded like a makif, is a higher level, for those who have nothing within themselves but the makif.
'Va'eira' can be read as a statement about every generation: Hashem shows Himself to the children too, not only to the Avos, to whoever wants to feel it.
Since Hashem appeared to the Avos with the name Keil Shakai, the name given at Avraham's bris, a bris is a time when Hashem appears even today.
The Rav says the emunah in Hashem's appearing at a bris is greater than seeing it.
Nothing about the timing is chance: a bris in Vaera, where the plagues are healing for Israel, fits the link between refuah and milah on the eighth day.
A passuk whose first and last letters both spell milah is unusual, and it shows that milah carries both chessed for Klal Yisroel and din on the wicked.
In the Megillah, Esther's words that carry Hashem's name in the first letters drew chassadim on Klal Yisroel, while Haman's own words, with the name in the last letters, drew din on the nations.
Milah was given to the Jews as they went down into the exile of Mitzrayim, because exile requires both sides of milah: protection against the nations and the flow of chessed.
Since the main tikkun of Shovevim is on Friday, the sixth day, a bris that falls on a Friday of Shovevim joins the tikkun of milah with the day's own tikkun.
The Rav stresses that the Tanya's beinoni, who never sins even in thought, is what we would call a virtual tzaddik; he is called a beinoni only because the potential for sin still lives in him.
He reads the beinoni's 'never will sin' like the Rambam's testimony of the One Who knows hidden things about a baal teshuvah: it describes how resolute he is now, not a guarantee about the future.
With an analogy of antibiotics stopped too early, he explains that the beinoni's yetzer hara is knocked out like dormant microbes that can revive, whereas the tzaddik's is dead.
He explains that since Above there is no time, the eis ratzon formed at sunrise in Eretz Yisrael travels with the sunrise, so each place has the original eis ratzon in its own morning.
He describes the air up to Shamayim as full of klipos from people's sins, so Pesukei Dezimra must cut a channel through them, matching the Arizal's reading of 'zimra' as cutting.
He compares the beinoni in davening to a Chassid dancing on Shabbos: he rises above his normal height but lands again, while the tzaddik truly stands that high.
He says an intruding thought is an opportunity: a person was sent down to wage this war, and if the enemy never came he could never fight it.
Eating matzah is literally taking geulah into oneself, since what a person eats becomes part of his flesh and blood.
'Bread from heaven' is not only the manna: since the Torah is eternal, every meal a Jew eats is food from Hashem's word rather than from the earth.
The bris seudah lets the participants eat the holiness of the bris into themselves, so refusing it amounts to refusing geulah.
Eliyahu Hanavi is present at every bris, but the degree of his revelation depends on the home and the parents of the child.
The song of Shabbos Shirah, 'Hashem will reign forever', is the song of Moshiach, connecting it with Eliyahu and the bris.
The Rav counts the hardening of the heart itself as a plague on Egypt, harsher than the others.
Since the Torah is a Torah of life, the subject of a parsha is active in the week it is read, so the week of Beshalach is a time to draw strength against hardness of heart.
A bris of the flesh performed in these weeks arouses in Heaven the greater matter of the circumcision of the heart.

The same song at the Sea has a different force on its two reading days: on Shevi'i shel Pesach the time and the reading together bring the lights of redemption, while on Shabbos Shirah the reading alone brings only a semblance.

The choice of haftaros matches the feminine and masculine songs: Shabbos Shirah's haftarah ends with a salvation limited to forty years, while Shevi'i shel Pesach's ends with an eternal salvation for Dovid's offspring.
A bris on the eighth day connects to the eight-stringed harp of the days of Moshiach, so a bris in the week of Shabbos Shirah turns that Shabbos's limited salvation into true lights of redemption.

Man, like the world created with ten utterances in four letters, has forty powers; sin involves only thirty-nine, which is why the Sages read 'forty lashes' as thirty-nine: the fortieth level, the 'tip of the yud', is never touched by sin.
The atonement of Yom Kippur, 'before Hashem', comes from above the yud of Hashem's Name, the Holy of Holies within the Jew, where sin never entered.
Amalek is the 'first' of impurity, its own 'tip of the yud', set against the innermost point of holiness; Esther feared he had penetrated even there.
Mordechai is called 'ben Kish' because he knocked on the gates of mercy, opening the Holy of Holies on an ordinary day; a tzaddik's great act affects all Jewish souls.
The Tanya omits avak lashon hara from the three daily sins because a thought can be repelled before it is a sin, but words once spoken are already a sin, and a Beinoni does not speak them.
In holiness the mind gives birth to love and fear in the heart; in impurity desire rises from the heart to the mind, and if not allowed to linger it gives birth to nothing and dissipates.
The 'next day' after Yisro's seudas bris he already added a parsha to the Torah, showing that the bris itself opens a person to Torah.
Hashem takes up the cause of those who fall behind: He fought Amalek for the stragglers outside the clouds, and drew close Yisro, who came late.
Postponing a bris for the child's health reveals how precious a Jew's body is to Hashem, and that very postponement draws down healing for all Jews.
A person cannot know what one mitzvah accomplishes; thousands of Jews may have a salvation through a single mitzvah.
Haman understood that a Jew's real birth is his bris, and he miscalculated only because he did not know Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised.
The bris is called a birth because through it the child gains his bond with Torah, mitzvos and the Ribono shel Olam.
Because the days around a birthday share in it, a bris near the day of Moshe Rabbeinu's birth carries a special sign of blessing.
Eliyahu is hidden in the Megillah under the name Charvona and appears exactly at Haman's downfall, because Haman's removal was a bris for the world and Eliyahu is the angel of the bris.
A single bris is not private: it stirs all of creation and removes another piece of the world's orlah, leading toward the revelation of Moshiach.
Joy is linked to milah because milah weakens nature, and true joy comes only when a Jew rises above nature and sees worldly pleasures as fleeting.
Through the miracle of the Megillah it became clear to the Jews that the true 'sasson' is milah and the removal of impurity from the world.
The Rav cites his father-in-law: Yosef told his brothers that their enmity was arranged by Heaven to test whether he would bear a grudge, so it was through their merit that he passed the test.
Loving one Jew more than another is only from the side of the body; from the side of the soul all Jews are one soul, so love of Israel does not divide the love of Hashem.
The word titharu equals keser in gematria, and the goral, like the skull above the brain, is above understanding; both Yom Kippur and Purim come through a goral and reach keser.
Shema, with its enlarged ayin, equals keser in gematria, which is why Haman, drawing on the keser of impurity, wanted to stop Mordechai from saying Shema.
Haman is called tzorer haYehudim because tzorer means to bind: by threatening them he caused the Jews to unite against him.
Just as an eiruv makes several families one household through shared food, mishloach manos on Purim makes all of Klal Yisrael one table.

Yosef pressed his brothers so that their suffering would finish the repair of his sale; had he held back a few more moments the repair would have been complete, and the Torah's words that he could not restrain himself are a lament.
The blessing 'Magen Avraham' refers to Hashem guarding the point of Avraham Avinu inside every Jew, so that it can never be extinguished.
Doing the greatest mitzvah on an infant, without daas or speech, is not a lack but shows that the mitzvah's depth is above daas.
Milah and tefillin, sasson and yikar, stand for two sides of Yiddishkeit: the point above understanding inherited from the Avos, and service with daas.
The 'ad delo yada' of Purim expresses the same point of Avraham Avinu that lies above intellect.

The Rav reads the Chachamim's hesitation as more than a counting rule: a fourth writing of Amalek belongs to the final, complete wiping out of Amalek, and the Megillah's concealment shows that time had not come.
Megillas Esther was given as a spark of Moshiach's light so that Jews can get used to it, since the full light, if it came at once, would be too strong to bear.
Purim will remain when other yomim tovim are nullified precisely because it is not yet finished: its full expression waits for the complete wiping out of Amalek.

Shmuel's view that Esther is not among the holy writings is reconciled: it is one of the twenty-four, but its place is still hidden in heaven until Moshiach comes and the Megillah appears in a new garment.
The Shushan Purim seudah is itself a seudah of bris milah, since the Megillah means removing idolatry from the land, just as the bris removes the orlah.
The Tanya says 'like a rasha' and not 'a rasha' because the beinoni is not wicked; he only carries the full potential to become one if he is not on guard.

Sometimes it is precisely the sin and its damage that reveals Hashem's hidden love, as a child's broken leg turns the father from discipline to mercy; this is why Moshe stressed that the sin of the Calf was great.
At the very party where the Jews sinned by joining Achashverosh's celebration, Hashem was already preparing their salvation through Vashti's removal, showing a father's love even in the worst state.
The worse concealment is not when the father hides but when the child does not even know he is there; the work of Adar is to reveal the hiding.
Adar Sheni has no combination of the four-letter name of its own, since only twelve are possible, so its concealment is greater, and for that reason the Purim miracle in it was greater.
The many names of chametz all point to a single thing, the yetzer hara, so biur chametz is in essence the removal of the yetzer hara.
The Rav reads milah through Aleinu's words about removing impurity from the land and perfecting the world under the kingship of Hashem.
A bris in Nissan joins two removals, of the orlah and of chametz, and the Rav turns them into a prayer that Hashem remove evil from the whole world.
The Rav sees every bris as a small enactment of the coming of Moshiach, which is why the bris prayers mention Eliyahu and Moshiach.
A bris on the day that was the first day of creation and on a Sunday joins the renewal of the world with the entry of a child into the covenant.
A private simcha of one family is, in the Rav's words, a potential trigger for the Geulah that the whole creation awaits.
Precisely Dan, the lowly tribe that came last, receives a yom tov in which Hashem boasts of its korban, and so too Hashem boasts of the last, lowly generation of galus.
The Rav reads 'this is the korban of Achiezer ben Ammishaddai' as said of the child at the bris: on Dan's day, the child himself is the korban Hashem boasts of.
The generation leaving the final galus will be greater than the generation that left Mitzrayim.
A stronger urge to sin need not mean a fall: it may come because the beinoni was raised to a higher level and must pass a test to show he is worthy of it.

Nefesh in mesiras nefesh means one's will, so giving up a small desire each day is itself mesiras nefesh, and Hashem counts the sum total, while people judge only the single blow, like grains of a ground-up stone.
The beinoni is a tzaddik in one chamber of his heart: there, where his hidden love of Hashem lives, he truly hates evil.

A person is built of forty levels, and the sinner receives thirty-nine lashes rather than forty because his fortieth level never sinned; on Yom Kippur, the fortieth day of teshuvah, that level surfaces and every Jew is forgiven.

Wisdom, Torah and Hashem give different answers about the sinner not as contradictions but as rising levels, and at the highest Hashem judges by the inner will of a Jew, who truly wants to do His will.
A bad thought that enters the mind is not a sin but a privilege, an opportunity; the sin is only in letting it linger and exploring it.
A bris in the days between Shabbos Hagadol and the Seder joins three meetings with Eliyahu Hanavi: the haftarah that announces him, his presence at the bris, and his visit at the Seder.
A bris looks like a private family matter, yet the Rav asks that it act like a spark plug that ignites the general redemption.
Milah is not only a mitzvah that happens to fall before Pesach; it is a precondition of the Korban Pesach, so a bris now is itself a preparation for the Yom Tov.
The severity of kareis on Pesach's mitzvos is read as a sign of their power to connect: what cuts off when missing binds when kept.
Since both Pesach and milah carry kareis and both bind a Jew to Hashem, a bris that falls on Pesach is a bond upon a bond.
Eliyahu Hanavi's presence at both Pesach and the bris, and the good tidings tied to him, make such a bris a time of favor when a person can renew himself and form a new bond with Hashem.
Bris milah is the removal of chametz within a person: what Pesach does to the kelipos in the world, milah does to the orlah.
The four kings Avraham Avinu fought on Pesach are read as the four layers of the orlah, three of the orlah itself and the fourth of the peri'ah, the four kelipos.
Aleinu is said after a bris because it speaks of removing idolatry from the land, which the bris itself models.
The usual blessing that a bris be 'in its time' applies with greater force to a bris on Pesach, since both mitzvos are bonds whose absence brings kareis.
The greatest mitzvah ever done, the Akeidah, was performed by Avraham Avinu with his levels taken from him and without feeling; this is why it is the merit invoked whenever Jews need a zechus.
A special warm tefillah or elation during a mitzvah may be the reward for an earlier hard-won victory over the yetzer, even a day or a year before.

Whether a soul is drawn to Torah or to tefillah depends on whether it was rooted in the head or the heart of Adam Harishon; one who misuses that root may become a scientist or a philosopher, or a poet or songwriter.
Like a tuning fork that sets matching piano strings vibrating, the beinoni's effort to act like a tzaddik sets the corresponding heavenly chords vibrating and draws down a tzaddik's soul.
The Tanya deliberately calls the beinoni's trained joy truth according to his level rather than absolute truth, since each person has his own level of truth.
Even when an ibbur departs, it leaves a residue of kedushah in the soul and a memory that spurs the person to try to reach that level again.
Shavuos is the one festival whose day is fixed by every Jew's counting rather than by Beis Din, which shows that the giving of the Torah belongs to each Jew.
Even a Jew who seems simple holds the Torah within him, and it can come out in his child as a great talmid chacham.
Jews differ only on the surface; beneath it every Jew has the same power for Torah.
The first letters of the passuk about the festivals of Hashem spell 'my mother' and 'my father', showing that Shabbos and the festivals raise a Jew as parents raise a child.
The Rav ties the bris to the day's word in Lamenatzeach, 'yismechu', reading the count itself as a sign of joy.
The joy of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's companions at Kedoshim shows that a Jew's true joy is in what brings him closer to Hashem.

The Rav reads the difference between 'oved' and 'eved' grammatically: 'oved' is a present participle, a man still in the act of serving, while 'eved' is a title earned, as 'ganav' names one who has actually stolen and not one able to steal.

The same yetzer hara that caused the Flood became the reason not to bring another, because the generations before it were giants held fully responsible, while the world after it is like a sick child who is left alone.
A good routine can itself mean one is not serving Hashem: one who reached the level of masmid through struggle stops being an 'oved Elokim' once it becomes second nature, unless he pushes beyond it.

A hundred reviews stay within the domain of the yetzer hara, whose name has the gematria of a hundred, while the hundred and first moves into the domain of the angel Michael, whose name equals a hundred and one, where forgetting no longer rules.
Even a natural masmid with no struggle in quantity can become an 'oved Elokim' through quality, learning better, where there is no limit to growth.
Going up to Yerushalayim on the festivals lifts each Jew above his tribal root to the shared root of the Avos, since the festivals correspond to the Avos.
The revelation to Avraham after his milah was a revelation of 'seeing', linked through milah to the command that every male appear before Hashem on the festivals.
Like Yerushalayim and the festivals, milah does not belong to any one tribe but to the root above all the tribes.
Because each week of the Omer passes through the Yesod of its middah, Yesod shebeMalchus is the point where all of Yesod has been rectified.
The Rav reads the day of the bris as a siman milsa for the child: a bris in Yesod on the day Yesod is completed points to a child prepared for tzidkus.
He links twins to Matan Torah through the mazal of Sivan, which is te'omim.
The Rav explains Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Eliyahu will expound this parsha: once forbidden foods become kosher at the geulah, the prohibition will remain only for the kohanim, the higher Jews.
Each Jew's letter in the Torah is where his learning becomes bright and his chiddushim come; Emor is where Eliyahu's letter lies, and so it is the parsha he will expound.
The Rav compares the young father, who fought for Yiddishkeit in a time when many strayed, to the bnei Tzadok who kept the charge when Yisrael strayed.
Eliyahu, whom the bris benching calls the kohen tzedek, is both the malach habris and the one whose parsha is Emor, the parsha of the kohanim.
A Jew's emunah is a hereditary knowledge, like the beaver that builds a dam with an engineer's skill though separated from its mother at birth.
Avraham and Sarah were barren because Avraham was a new species cut off from the earlier generations; the hei added to his name was a new power of birth, and with him creation was completed.
The greater a tzaddik's understanding, the more he sees that Hashem is greater still; emunah begins exactly where his understanding stops.

Milah is done at eight days, before the child has understanding, because it is the sign of emunah above daas; Yishmael's milah waits for thirteen because it is like any mitzvah that needs daas, an empty milah.
Every tzaddik has his adversary: Avraham had Nimrod, Yitzchak had Yishmael and Yaakov had Esav; the end of the exile comes through the fall of Yishmael before Yitzchak.
Milah is the most striking defiance of nature: as soon as a child is born one cuts off what nature produced, declaring that this is not how a Jew is made.
The missing lamed by Naftali shows that a count can have no practical purpose at all and still be worthwhile, because simply coming before Moshe Rabbeinu to be seen and blessed is the purpose.
Eliyahu is the angel of the bris because he himself was moser nefesh, ready to shed his own blood, for the holiness of the bris; so he comes to help a father who sheds his child's blood with joy.
The Rav links the bris to the census: just as the Ramban calls being seen by Moshe a great good, being seen by Eliyahu at a bris is a great good; if one cannot see, one can at least be seen.

Naftali was the last tribe of the last camp, and the last generations before the end of days are its counterpart in time: Bnei Naftali, a 'fallen' generation, yet bound to the first generations through Hashem's help.
Avraham's receiving his name before his milah shows that the essential covenant, a bond of the soul, came first, and the milah was given afterwards as its sign.
The Mishnah in Nedarim, which calls a Jew circumcised even if he is not, proves that the covenant of Klal Yisrael lies in the soul, not the flesh.
Because the first covenant does not depend on milah, a woman shares in it fully, which explains how Rus could take the 'bris milah' upon herself.
The Rav ties the bris to emunah: the covenant means believing in Hashem, like Avraham, the first of the believers.
The name Oved does not just mean one who served Hashem wholeheartedly, since many did; it marks one who had to toil on himself because of the heritage he carried.
The repeated genealogy from Peretz shows that the history to be rectified in Oved began earlier, with Er behind Peretz, and all of it merged into one child.
Because Oved worked so wholly on himself, he could father Yishai, one of those who died without sin, only through the serpent's counsel.
The neighbors, not Rus, named the child because Rus, remembering her origins, held back, and they reassured her that a child with such a history would become an oved.

The Rav compares a soul's development to conception, pregnancy, birth and nursing: a soul sent down before its 'birth' has not yet come into the world, so it cannot give out felt love however much it contemplates.
He shows 'ratzo vashov' as the pattern of all creation: day and night, summer and winter, and the pulse that pushes blood up and lets it fall back until the next beat.

Citing a sefer, he explains that Avraham's words 'we will return' at the Akeidah kept his soul from leaving him in his great dveikus, while Sarah, hearing that her son had been ready to give his life, was so charged with love that her soul left her.
He explains that in galus the tzaddikim long for Hashem more than in the days of the Beis HaMikdash, as a man in the desert without water thirsts more than one who has water at hand.

The Rav applies the Gemara's rule that a shliach can only do what the sender can do: the heart can be the limbs' shliach because it is physical like them, while the mind, being higher, is not a fitting shliach.
He explains that since the Ba'al HaTanya holds that all Torah and mitzvos must come from contemplation of Hashem's greatness, Chabad Chassidim learn so much Chassidus that speaks of that greatness.

He links 'Hashem combines it with the deed' to the Rema on 'u'mafli la'asos': just as Hashem wondrously joins the spiritual soul to the physical body, He joins the mind's love to the physical mitzvah.
Every element of the soul has its counterpart in time: the orlah over the bris kodesh corresponds to the covering over the brightest month of the year, and the same avodah removes both.
The Rav reads 'bein hametzarim' as the place where one who seeks the Shechinah can reach it, through toil in Torah and avodah.
Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or': the month's letter ches stands for darkness, yet its very name holds the light hidden in it.
Milah is done to an infant precisely because it expresses the root of a Jew that is above daas, like 'ad delo yada' on Purim; it does not depend on his work or understanding.
Milah and tefillin are two opposite holinesses, one above daas and one the peak of daas, and a Jew's path leads from milah to tefillin, from sasson to yekar.
The Rav distinguishes between a bris attended by Eliyahu's emissaries and a special bris that Eliyahu attends in person.
A bris after a family's hard times is, in the Rav's words, all the more precious, not less.
Being present at a bris is itself a merit, a chance to attain great things.
Aharon's praise of 'not changing' is read as a choice: every day he picked the avodah of the lamps, tied to Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim, over the ketores, tied to wealth.
The Rav sharpens the praise: in forty years Aharon did not give up the lamps even one day to gain some wealth, though a father needs money to marry off his children.
At the bris the Rav sees ketores and lamps together: a home bringing a child into the covenant of Avraham Avinu is wished both Torah and greatness at once.
The Rav reads 'ki karov' as speaking to every generation and every moment, rejecting the idea that it was meant only for the great souls of Moshe Rabbeinu's generation.
The Rav rejects 'sublimating' worldly enjoyment as a way to claim complete love of Hashem: thinking of the Creator while enjoying the ice cream is good, but if one enjoys it, the love is divided.
The Rav explains that the Tanya does not demand abstaining from pleasure; it demands that when a mitzvah comes, the mind's recognition of duty carries the action.
The felt joy of a mitzvah is its reward, which tzaddikim taste even in this world; it is not what is asked of everyone here.
The Rav suggests that the rasha's punishment after losing control follows the Gemara's principle that what starts with negligence and ends with compulsion is still culpable.
The Rav links the lower teshuvah to Chanukah: the wicks and oils that cannot burn on Shabbos burn on Chanukah, since then Hashem comes down to lift even the fallen.
The strength of the kelipah over something is itself a sign of the great kedusha hidden in it: so with the seven nations in Eretz Yisrael and the din over the long summer days of Tammuz.
A parsha named for the wicked Balak is really named for the spark of Moshiach hidden in him, not for Balak the rasha.
The Rav reads Balak's words 'v'hu yoshev mimuli' as his fear that the orlah would be removed and Moshiach revealed, which is why he sent for Bilaam.
A bris held in the week of Balak, just before bein hametzarim, is a symbolic act pointing to Hashem removing the orlah from the world and from these days.
The lifting of the nine days' mourning for a bris is itself a picture of what these days are: their kedusha is covered by an orlah, and the bris removes orlah.
The Rav applies the threefold orlah to the galus: the land is covered by an orlah in place, and the days of mourning by an orlah in time.
A bris in the nine days is a symbolic act: the mitzvah of milah and Eliyahu HaNavi, who comes to every bris, will overcome the orlah of the world, the time and the place.
Like a heavy object dropped from a roof into mud, the higher a spark of kedushah, the deeper it sank; so a rasha who sank into tumah and does teshuvah raises sparks that are beyond a tzaddik's reach.
The Avos are called fathers rather than grandfathers because, unlike ordinary ancestry whose bond weakens with each generation, their bond to every Jew stays as close as a father's.

A Jew who denies Hashem resembles a man who ate something harmful and lost his appetite: the craving is not gone, the stomach is only temporarily out of order, and so too the soul poisoned by sin still holds its emunah.
The world is beriah, yesh me'ayin, but a Jewish soul is not; even though its body is created, its bond to Hashem is a direct extension, like that of a child to a father.

The Satan guards against Moshiach's birth, so the great kedushah comes hidden in places he never suspects, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can; David's ruddy appearance even made the Satan think he was his.

Habit can change a middah, as a cruel man who keeps doing chesed is changed, but the love of Hashem in a Jew is an existing entity, which is either there or not, and the Tanya teaches that it is there in everyone.
The Rav reads Rashi's covenant over the fruits in the ark as a definition of a bris: a bris is what keeps a thing from decaying and makes it last forever.
Change and eternity coexist: each generation and moment brings a new task, yet underneath runs one unchanging thread of Klal Yisroel, and the bris is that thread.
A person's name changes with his mission, but what makes him a Jew, his bond to Hashem, does not change at all.
Most mitzvos serve the one who does them, but milah is by its nature a transfer: it hands emunah from one generation to the next.
Because Amalek attacked milah, the mitzvah of continuity, Hashem's war against him is measure for measure 'from generation to generation'.
The Rav reads Moshe Rabbeinu's delay of his son's milah as solidarity with klal Yisroel, parallel to his breaking the luchos rather than remain the one tzaddik apart from the sinners.

Because milah is a sign of belonging to the community, its kareis, like that of eating on Yom Kippur, stems from separation from the klal; so when all Jews ate at the dedication of the Beis HaMikdash, there was no such separation.
The plural 'lamulos' shows that Moshe's act aroused merit above for all the Jews, and once that merit was accepted it was decreed that the redemption from Egypt would begin.
Since Moshe Rabbeinu is connected to Moshiach, the Harachaman for Moshiach mentions his 'chasan damim', and a bris in a generation where milah is weakened is a harbinger of the final geulah.
Because a Jew's thoughts are constantly in Yerushalayim, the Rav says, he is considered as being there all the time, not only on the three festivals.
The Rav applies the Rishonim's answer to the present: a father who must run between doctor and rav to make the bris on time is literally engaged in the mitzvah day and night for all eight days.

He draws a parallel: just as a Jew who longs for Yerushalayim is there all year, a father occupied with the bris for all eight days merits, measure for measure, to see the Shechinah three times a year.
Chochmah is read as 'koach mah', a power that is a question mark: we receive its flashes but cannot know where they come from, as a watch cannot understand the watchmaker.
Tefillin are the person's Keser: part of him yet above the brain, the source from which the mind receives its flashes.
In emunah the roles flip: the 'wise man' who reasons whether to believe is the greatest fool, and the one who believes with simple faith has the greatest wisdom.

Reb Chaim Brisker's remark that a Rosh ruling without proof is firmer than one with proof, since its source is the whole of Shas that shaped his mind, explains why the Chasam Sofer could rule on the father's instinct with no proof.
Because ownership (kinyan) is in the Torah, the blueprint of creation, it is built into creation itself, so an ox knows its owner.
Yishmael's claim to greatness for undergoing milah at thirteen shows the opposite: milah is above daas, so a milah done by choice as an adult misses its point.
The question why milah is not postponed until the child can understand answers itself: milah belongs to emunah above daas, so it fits precisely the age before daas.
Milah is kept even by Jews far from observance because a person may choose between tzaddik and rasha, but his very Jewishness is above choice and above daas.
Sasson and yekar stand for two poles: milah, wholly without daas, and tefillin, from which one may not divert one's mind, the peak of daas; their coming together is a great preciousness.
Moshe was born circumcised not because he lacked the mitzvah but because, as the redeemer who will remove idolatry from the world, he had to stand outside the orlah from the start, like a mohel.
Following the Maharal, even shevet Levi was never enslaved, since the redeemer came from it and had to come from outside the bondage.
The custom of an early-morning bris is itself a plea that the geulah, which milah stands for, come quickly; a bris pushed to the edge of sunset cries out that the time is already late.
The Rav links this bris to parshas Shemos, where Moshe is born circumcised, and to the start of sefer Shemos, which the Ramban calls the book of geulah.
Wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos are fit for Chanukah: there are souls that even Shabbos does not ignite, but Chanukah, a glimpse of the light of Moshiach, can.
The flame's side-to-side flicker is its effort to tear loose from the wick, like a dentist rocking a tooth before pulling it, and the same fire in a Jew makes him sway when he learns and davens.
Because fire is rooted in the sphere of the moon, a candle burns better at night when the moon itself is present, which is why bedikas chametz is done at night.
A person who feels depressed about lacking wealth, wisdom or strength compared to others shows pride, not humility, since he feels he is something that deserves more.
In English the word 'I' is capitalized even mid-sentence, reflecting ego, whereas the Torah has no such enlarged letter for 'ani'.

Kelipah's chesed is called Kna'ani, from 'hachna'ah', submission: its giver submits to the receiving side because he really gives for himself, like a donor who wants a plaque or a darshan who speaks for pay.
In the tzaddik's case the wick is the body and the flame is the soul: the body alone holds him back from flying up to Hashem until his time comes.
Dovid's being born circumcised was no chance event: the refinement of his lineage, from Yehudah through Peretz, Nachshon, Boaz and Yishai, left no waste that milah had to remove.
The Rav reads 'michtam' as 'makoso tamah', his wound was whole, and links this temimus to the name Dovid that a child brings into the bris.
A name links a child to the first one who bore it, as a child named Avraham shares in Avraham's yiras shamayim; so a child named Dovid shares in the quality of Dovid.
The Rav reads Yom Kippur itself as a day of milah: the atonement of the day is the circumcision of the heart, rooted in Avraham's bris on that day.

From the Arizal's words about Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair he derives a general rule: doing the mitzvah that defined a tzaddik draws his soul onto the doer, so the father at a bris carries Avraham's soul and its chessed.

He contrasts Amalek, whose scorn for milah earned the erasing of his remembrance, with Israel, whose milah leaves a remembrance, and on this basis explains the custom of naming the child at the milah.

The Rav applies Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen's principle, that a person does not believe in what he has no connection to, to Esav: his other sins could stem from desire, but scorning the birthright exposed that he had no connection to 'reishis'.
He ties together Hashem as the First, the sanctity of firstborns, Israel as Hashem's firstborn and the Torah called 'reishis', so that honoring the bechor is honoring all of them.
He explains that the root of a blemish of the bris is that the first does not go to Hashem, which is why a meal honoring 'reishis' is likened to the eighty-four fasts given for that blemish.
He reads the pidyon haben meal as a reversal of Esav's meal: where Esav ate and drank in scorn of the birthright, Jews eat and drink to honor it.

Every aveirah, even a small rabbinic one, is a hidden subdivision of avodah zarah, because it throws a person under the jurisdiction of the sitra achra, the same domain as idolatry, only not its 'top' form.

A Jew's readiness to die rather than serve avodah zarah is not the product of training, as with soldiers or terrorists, but a G-dly instinct, like an animal giving itself for its young without any reasoning.
Fear of Hashem is a product of love: like a mother who holds her baby tightly on the stairs because she loves it, a Jew fears that his love should not be damaged.

From the Avnei Nezer the Rav draws that the bond between a Jew and Hashem is a felt intuition: a kohenes, from Shevet Levi who feel that bond more strongly, should have sensed that her husband was alive despite one witness.
'Ein maspikin beyado' does not lock the door of teshuvah: it only means no heavenly arousal is sent, but one who pushes his way in with his elbows is still helped.

Above, there is no 'temporary': since Heaven is beyond time, an aveirah is stamped into eternity, and the teshuvah that undoes it is likewise eternal; this is why the soul refuses even a temporary separation.
Chanukah, just before Shovevim, prepares for the darkest season; today the menorah is lit inside because the darkness has already penetrated our homes through the media.

Following the Chasam Sofer, the Rav reads Haman's 'scattered among the nations' as a halachic claim: a holiness of value among seventy nations is nullified, but Israel's holiness is of the body and is never nullified.
He distinguishes two kinds of redemption: Hashem can redeem Israel's suffering by placing it on the nations, but Israel itself, as 'reishis', can never be exchanged.
He explains Rashi's harsh word for one who says terumah can be redeemed: since Israel is 'reishis', the view that reishis can be redeemed is the view of Bilaam and his students.
Citing the Arizal, he says the firstborn is the reishis through which all the blessing of later children comes, which is why he takes a double portion.
Since the Yerushalmi says Rabbi Menachem never looked at a coin's image at all, even as a child, his holiness was inborn, and so the title 'son of holy ones' credits his parents.
Because his parents were not taken up with money, as people are when making a shidduch, their son was born unable even to look at it.
The Or HaChaim's reason for tumas ohel among Jews, that impurity gathers where great holiness departed, applies in a small way every motza'ei Shabbos when the extra soul leaves.
Rabbi Menachem bar Simai said only one havdalah because, being so holy, he did not need havdalah's protection, only the mitzvah itself.
Pidyon haben is a kind of havdalah: the firstborn must be redeemed because the holiness of the bechor that should have been his has departed, leaving a place that needs protection.
'Ki karov' is explained through a reckoning: a Jew who would give his whole life against idolatry can surely give up the 'smaller nefesh' of a single desire, since nefesh also means desire.
Refraining from an aveirah for a few minutes is not a passing act; since nothing is temporary above, that moment's union with Hashem is eternal.
In holiness 'one' is the biggest number: if a person or even a table exists alongside Hashem, there are already two, so 'Echad' demands that the self be merged into Him.
The Torah never changes; where it seems to take another form for us, it is like a cloud that changes shape yet stays the same cloud.
