The difficulty in grasping the eternity of a mitzvah is not in the logic but in a mind molded by this world, which takes the 'world of imagination' for the world of truth.
Teshuvah for a prohibition may bring forgiveness yet leave damage, like a host who forgives the guest who broke his bottle of wine while the bottle still must be replaced.
'Achta v'ashuv' applies only when the expected teshuvah is what allows the sin; one who sincerely regrets but fears his weak nature will fail again is forgiven each time.
The Torah singles out Esav's despising of the bechorah over his five grave sins because it was a flaw in outlook that reveals who he is, a sign for all generations.
Following Rav Tzadok, not believing in something is a symptom that one has no connection to it, since a person by instinct believes in what he belongs to.
Using a rule of geometry, the Rav argues that whatever has a beginning has an end; Israel, the true reishis, will have a good acharis, while Amalek's lack of a good end shows its reishis is false.
Doing the pidyon haben inside the seudah reverses Esav's feast: he celebrated despising the bechorah, while Jews feast to honor it, and that honor outweighs the mitzvah itself.
Leket, shikchah and peah, the last grain left at the end of the harvest, appear among the festivals of reishis because the last generations are as precious to Hashem as the first fruits.
The aleph-beis expresses the order by which creation runs, so a verse placed after the aleph-beis is complete speaks of something beyond that order.
Both alphabetical chapters of Tehillim close with an extra verse of 'pedus', so redemption itself is the conduct above the order.
Because pidyon is above the order, a pidyon haben in days of strict judgment brings salvation even where the order would not.

The Rav argues that the fulfillment of Moshe's prophecies is a proof the nations' scriptures cannot offer, since they avoided predictions, and the one they made, that Jews would never return, has failed.
He describes the present as late afternoon of the world's Erev Shabbos: after chatzos of the sixth day, when one is already going to the mikveh and preparing the candles.
Hester within hester is a child who not only cannot see his hidden father but does not even know a father is there; this, says the Rav, is the state of those who lost their emunah in the Holocaust.

The difference between a blow followed by a cure and a cure prepared before the blow is the difference between a stabbing and surgery: a surgeon who prepared the bandages beforehand shows the cutting itself is for healing.
Nitzavim and Vayelech are one sedra in count, matching one century, yet two sedras in theme, because galus and geulah are separate; in the geulah no pain of galus will remain.

Physical strength does not decide a wrestling match, energy does: an ox is stronger than a lion yet loses, and so too a person with greater spiritual strength loses to the yetzer hara if he is heavy with sadness.
Sadness is not only a weakness but a cause of sin: deprived of happiness, a person reaches for gratification, as an unhappy person reaches for another slice of cake.
The advantage the passuk finds in sorrow is not in the sadness itself but in its product, teshuvah, and the simcha after it is like the joy of two close friends who reconcile after a quarrel.
In its deepest sense, mourning the churban at Tikkun Chatzos is mourning one's own private Beis HaMikdash, which a person ruined through his aveiros.
Suffering comes from the higher, hidden half of the Shem Havayah; it is a closer contact with Hashem that a person is not yet conditioned to receive, so it arrives as pain.
The Alter Rebbe's power, which made him a target, was that he immunized his chassidim against anything this world has to offer, and that power is contained in the words of this chapter.
Before the war, the failure to know or think seriously about what the coming year held was itself part of the decree of concealment.

At the end of the year the old year's merits are spent and the new year's have not begun, so the world stands on Hashem's kindness alone until the tefillos and shofar create it anew; this is why the night of Rosh Hashana is a time of fearsome judgment.

A thing's right to exist after Rosh Hashana depends on its being part of Hashem's kingship; even a stone has a life-force suited to it, and when the judgment withdraws that life-force the thing breaks.
Each of the 365 days corresponds to one of the 365 negative mitzvos, so that Tisha B'Av corresponds to the prohibition of gid hanasheh, the portion of Esav, and on it Jews do not eat.

Shema, the tenth pasuk of Malchuyos, lacks the word melech for the same reason that Bereishis, the first of the ten maamaros, lacks 'vayomer': it is the root from which the rest begins, the acceptance through which Hashem becomes King.
Rosh Hashana is to the year what the morning Shema is to the day, and Elul is to Rosh Hashana what the long preparation of Shacharis is to Shema.
The Rav notes that Rabbi Akiva did not call emunah, the Ten Commandments or Shabbos 'the great rule of the Torah', but only 'love your fellow as yourself'.
A whole chevra, not only an individual, must say 'the world was created for us' and feel responsible to bring Moshiach.
Rachel's single act of sparing her sister shame achieved what the Akeidah and all the nisyonos of the Avos could not: it reversed the decree of exile.
Rachel did more than refrain from shaming Leah: she would not let Leah be shamed, and to prevent it she gave up her whole future with Yaakov.
Shaul merited kingship because he said his father would worry 'for us', counting his servant as an equal, just as Moshe said to his student 'choose for us'.
Mocking an ugly creature insults its Maker, as mocking a great artist's painting insults the artist.
The rare arrangement of the year, with Parshas Balak read now, is hashgachah pratis: its message of curse turned to blessing is what Jews need at this time.
Bilaam's claims may have been justified, yet Hashem refused even to hear them; the refusal itself expresses His love.
Hashem's love is that of a father to his beloved child, an unearned love, flowing from the attribute of chesed alone.
The navi's 'remember' is a plea that a Jew not lose the feeling of closeness and think there is a separation between him and Hashem because of his hardships.
No sin offering is brought on Shabbos, unlike the festivals, because Shabbos is a day of love, in which 'love covers all sins'.
The Rav reads the opening bracha of the Avos as an act of identifying with the Avos who instituted tefillah, so that tefillah begins by joining oneself to them.
Davening with kavanah means meeting the heart that the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah put into the nusach with our own heart, to the degree of our kavanah.
The Rav points out that the Ramban's view is in practice the stricter one, since in golus, before Moshiach, the whole world is in a time of trouble.
The twelve middle brachos parallel the twelve shevatim, the branches of the tree; on Shabbos one rises above the branches to the trunk, the Avos, like Yerushalayim which belongs to all the tribes.
The word 'leyom' teaches that on Shabbos no one sings for the day; the day itself sings, unlike Sunday, for which there is no 'song of the first day'.

Every seventh sings: Eretz Yisrael, the seventh land, is called Zimras HaAretz; the Kinneres, the seventh sea, takes its name from the kinor; and David HaMelech, the seventh of the ushpizin, is the singer of Israel.

Because there is no king without a people, a person who will not accept Hashem's kingship on Rosh Hashana has, in the Rav's words, no right to exist in the King's land, like a man who refuses allegiance to the king of a country.

The joy of Rosh Hashana is not in spite of the judgment but is the defense in it: like the prisoner who forgot his own trial for the king's joy, a Jew who rejoices in Hashem's kingship is granted a good year.
Which of the shofar's two reasons applies to a person depends on his Elul: after teshuvah he hears praise of the King; without it the shofar makes him tremble.
The name Elishama, nasi of Ephraim whose month is Tishrei, has the letters of Yishmael rearranged, showing that Tishrei is the time of the battle against Yishmael.
Zion is the seventh barren one, so Rosh Hashana, the time of remembering the barren, is also a time to pray for Zion to be remembered with her children's return.
Spiritual barrenness also counts: one whose learning and tefillah bear no fruit can be remembered on Rosh Hashana.
The Rav explains why shaming is punished more harshly than murder: precisely because the shamer does not feel he did anything terrible, he never comes to a broken heart and teshuvah.

He reads Boaz's failure to invite Manoach as an act meant for the sake of Heaven, to stir Manoach to daven harder, and still Boaz lost all his children, showing that good intentions do not permit shaming.

According to Rashi as the Rav explains it, the exemptions of the newlywed and the planter of a vineyard exist mainly as cover, so that the soldier who returns because he fears his sins will not be recognized and shamed.

He explains that the chol bird's refusal to trouble Noach is the meaning of 'we will multiply like the chol' in Hamavdil: it refers to the bird, not to sand, and teaches that good middos bring eternal life.

Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin learned from the akeidah that the command to slaughter Yitzchak came from Hashem Himself while the command to stop came through an angel: to harm a Jew even an angel's word is not enough, but to save one even an angel is obeyed.

Rabbi Avraham of Slonim observed that a chain of great descendants, each great in his own right and not merely by inheritance, is the mark of the greatest leaders, and that Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin merited it for refusing to harm a Jew.
Aharon's kehunah was a gift, while Pinchas's was earned, because he atoned for Klal Yisrael, which exists for all generations; therefore his kehunah too is for all generations.

Moshe Rabbeinu could not avenge Zimri's act, because as the leader standing above the people his act would not have meant that the people itself took revenge; it needed a simple man from within the people.

Following Chassidic seforim, the Rav says Zimri largely meant it for the sake of Heaven, but one small crumb of personal reckoning spoiled him, and that sinning part of the soul is what was called Zimri.
The masses of plain Jews who searched for the lost child did what Pinchas did: they showed the holiness of Klal Yisrael and its separation from whoever has a foreign growth attached to him.
Eliyahu equals 'ben' (son) in gematria, and through him it will become clear that Jews are children of Hashem.
Each of the moadim represents one of the midos of the Avos, and these are the traits Jews showed this week: merciful, modest and doing kindness.
Bereishis counts as the first of the ten utterances because it created speech itself, before any utterance existed, and like every beginning it contains all that follows.

Menuchah is not merely the absence of creating; the fact that Hashem rested was itself a creation, the satisfaction of lacking nothing, and that is why people sing 'Shabbos' when dancing before a chassan and kallah even on a weekday.
Pesukei D'zimra comes from the word for pruning, as in cutting the branches of a vineyard: the verses cut away the accusers who block the tefillos.
Saying David's Tehillim is like carrying a letter stamped by the king's minister: the guards must let it through, and once the way is cleared, one's own tefillos rise after it.
On weekdays the Levi'im sang for the day, but on Shabbos the day itself sings, because Shabbos is the completion of the harp's seven strings.
The song of Shabbos does not mention Shabbos because it sings of history's harmony and its purpose, the day that is entirely Shabbos, of which the weekly Shabbos is a miniature.

Creation is pictured as baking challah for Shabbos: Adam was the first 'challah of the world' and failed, the world after Noach failed again, and only the third, Avraham, rose and produced a people fit for the day that is entirely Shabbos.

A sin a person stumbles into should prompt the further question 'where is my emunah?', because with clear knowledge that Hashem is watching, as one would behave before a great tzaddik, the sin could not have happened.
Emunah outranks the other mitzvos because it was received directly from Hashem at Sinai in the first two commandments, while the rest came through Moshe Rabbeinu.

Talk that treats the election of a president as deciding the world's course holds a 'piece of apikorsus', since the president cannot dip his finger in cold water without Hashem's power and permission.

The suffering in Egypt was measure for measure: the souls of the generation of the dispersion, who built with bricks and mortar, were punished with bricks and mortar, and those of the flood generation were thrown into the river.

The Akeidah's test was the kushya, not the sacrifice: idol worshippers burned their own children, but a non-Jew abandons his god when he has a question, whereas Avraham, like a Jew covering his eyes at Shema, refused to look at the kushya.

The Rav's rebbe joins the Ba'al Shem Tov's drush to the plain meaning: the flood is the world itself, whose 'arks' of pleasure and honor swallow people, and the true ark of rescue is the word of prayer.

The Rav reads the Gemara's 'things that stand at the height of the world, which people treat lightly' as the very sign of tefillah's greatness: that good davening is mocked while good learning is praised shows how high prayer reaches.
Loud davening is both a proclamation before Hashem that we are His creations, as the Ramban writes, and a weapon: shouting over the yetzer hara, who argues for a quick and easy davening.
Pushing a slow chazzan from the amud is not merely impatience: since lengthening prayer lengthens life, the hurried worshipper drives away the long life of those who want to daven at length.

The order of a person's life mirrors the order of history: just as a person begins with Torah and later turns to avodah, the early generations' main avodah was Torah, while in the time before Moshiach it is tefillah.
Menucha is not rest but gratification, like a worker whose exhausting Sunday soccer game is his menucha; Shabbos menucha is the feeling of having reached one's goal and lacking nothing.
'L'hodos' means both to thank and to agree, as in 'the Chachamim agree with Rabbi Meir': in the future we will agree that whatever Hashem did was right.
'Boker' is related to 'bikur', examining: in the light one can inspect and understand, while 'layla' is related to 'yelala', wailing, the time when only emunah helps.
'Asor' comes from 'ashirus', rich and gratifying tunes, and 'navel' means wretched tunes; 'higayon b'chinor' means to think into the tune Hashem is playing, whichever it is.
The joy of 'simachtani' does not depend on the tune: it comes from knowing that Hashem's attention is focused on me, whether He grants happiness or surgical pain.
Fruit trees do not grow tall because they put their strength into fruit, while tall trees give no fruit; the tzaddik will have both, like the palm and the cedar together.
The vav missing in the written 'avlasa' is the vav of connection: today we do not see how events connect, but in the future the vav will be read and all of history will fit together.

The Rav explains that the shevatim, each corresponding to one of the months and to one of the twelve combinations of Hashem's Name, could not have acted wantonly; they ruled in beis din that Yosef was a rodef.

Following the Midrash, the Rav explains that Adam had to eat from the Etz haDaas so that a yetzer hara and free choice would exist, and Moshe had to fail at Mei Merivah because had he entered Eretz Yisroel no galus would have been possible.
Since the brothers held Yosef liable to death, by sending everyone out and standing alone with them Yosef risked his life, choosing danger over shaming them.

Intending the sake of Heaven is not enough: Potifar's wife also meant it for Heaven's sake, yet she is a rasha because of her bad middos, while Tamar's willingness to die rather than shame Yehuda made the difference.

The Sanzer Rav's proof: when the Jews in Egypt lacked mitzvos they were given the blood of the Pesach and of the milah; had ruining an unworthy Jew been a mitzvah, they would have had plenty, burying those who died in the darkness.

Hashem's command to remember what Amalek did, rather than Israel's doubt, is like the king who blames the biting dog so as not to tell his friend he stole; Israel was meant to understand the hint by themselves.

The Rav brings a remez that 've'ahavta es Hashem' and 've'ahavta l'reiacha kamocha ani Hashem' are equal in gematria: loving a Jew is loving Hashem, and hating a Jew is a sign that one does not love Hashem.
The Rav explains that the Jews could stay pure in Egypt yet fall at Shittim because Bilaam mobilized the full power of kishuf and impurity against them, aiming at the one thing Hashem hates.
Bilaam and Balak knew that the Jews' entry into Eretz Yisrael would lead toward Hashem's kingship over the whole world, which is why they fought it with such self-sacrifice.

The Rav reads the holy vessels taken to war as Torah and tefillah: the Urim is Torah, the Tzitz and the trumpets are tefillah, and the 'thousand per tribe' twice are Torah and tefillah, the powers of Moshe and Aharon.
Because Betzalel was a gilgul of a king, the people had to be asked about him as one asks about appointing a king, and the words 'Betzalel ben Uri ben Chur' equal in gematria 'melech biYerushalayim'.

According to the Chasam Sofer, since Shlomo rose late on the day of the Beis HaMikdash's inauguration because of Pharaoh's daughter, it was decreed that he return as Yirmiyahu to see the destruction of the house he built.

The Rav argues from the form of the verse that the Ramban appears right: a mitzvah means a command, yet 'Anochi Hashem' is written as a statement, Hashem presenting Himself, not as an order to believe.
Instinctive knowledge in animals, which no one taught them and which belongs to their very being, serves as the model for the emunah a Jew is born with.
Avraham's novelty as a 'new creation' was not physical, since he and his children see like other people, but a knowledge of Hashem that the nations do not have.
The small heh of 'behibaram' is read as 'b'Avraham': the world was completed when Avraham received the heh, the letter of birth, at his bris.
Avraham was created barren so that his line from Terach would be cut, and the new power of birth given with the heh began a new people; this is why Yitzchak has no connection to Terach.
The Rav reads 'vehe'emin' as written without a yud, the letter of chochmah, to show that Avraham's emunah was natural and not built on intellect.
The Rav explains that in the future Midas haDin itself will dictate chesed: the Jewish people will be on such a level that they will be comfortable being judged strictly.
Following the Hafla'ah, the date palm stays short because it puts its strength into fruit; so a tzaddik who spends himself on talmidim is promised that he will still grow tall like the cedar.
Hashem chose Avraham Avinu over Chanoch, even though Chanoch rose to the level of a malach, because Avraham lowered himself to reach and draw close other people.
Yaakov wanted to leave the womb despite having a malach as his rebbe, because sharing a classroom with Esav was worse than losing such a rebbe; friends count for more than the rebbe.
Avraham had Yishmael and Yitzchak had Esav first, because each had to discharge the bad side of his attribute, bad chesed and bad din, before giving rise to holy offspring.
The European habit of putting the left first, buttoning left over right, 'ladies first', and writing from the left, reflects Esav's attribute of din, female before male.

In Tammuz the Shem Havaya appears backwards and at the ends of the words of 'zeh einenu shoveh li', the harshest din; 'lehagid ki yashar Hashem' teaches that even this will be revealed as the Shem straight, chesed.

The Rav reads the Ba'al HaTanya's demand that all say each word together in light of the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that each word is a heichal: saying the same word at once puts the whole tzibbur in one heichal.
Lashon hakodesh is not only the language of the Torah; according to the Rav one can speak 'in lashon hakodesh' even in Yiddish, as tzaddikim speak words that carry hidden depths.
A foreign thought in the middle of davening, such as what shoes to buy for Yom Tov, pushes a person out of the heichal of the word he is saying.
Loud communal davening works like the angels, who receive from one another: even a person who walks in without enthusiasm gets an 'injection' from the tzibbur and begins to daven well.
The Rav contrasts the crowd that shouts over a home run with those who resent shouting in davening, the privilege of standing before Ribono shel Olam.
Kinah is the first flaw in creation itself: before any human sin, the moon's envy of the sun caused it to be diminished.
The Rav stresses that Kayin's murder is no newspaper item about ordinary people: Kayin was a great man, a son of Adam, to whom Hashem spoke, and this shows how far kinah can drag even a great person.
According to the Midrash Kayin's 'Am I my brother's keeper?' is a complaint against Hashem, the Keeper of the world, for not holding him back and for giving him such jealousy.
The Berditchever turned the blood libel around: the 'blood' that must not go into matzos is the suffering of the widows rushed in the bakery.
Heaven judges the shame caused to another even when the act was permitted: Reb Mordechai Banet was right al pi halachah to end the shidduch, yet he was penalized for shaming the kallah.
The Rav notes that the young ilui is held responsible even though at seventeen he had not yet had time to work on his middos.
A person's life is itself his song to Hashem, so killing is cutting off another Jew's song in the middle.
The killer is like the sun at Givon: because he stopped another's song, his own song falls silent and his life force is diminished.
The Levi'im heal the killer the way a tuning fork sets off a matching piano string: their song is tuned to every Jewish soul and awakens it.
David's harp played by itself at midnight because his soul was tuned to the same note as the song of Gan Eden at chatzos.
Since every sin holds something of killing, Shabbos serves as a city of refuge for every Jew, and Kabbalas Shabbos completes the seven voices.
Klal Yisrael's long waiting in galus is itself a tikkun for Adam HaRishon, whose sin was that he did not wait: had he waited until Shabbos he could have made kiddush on the wine of the tree.
The past tense Hashem Malach is the song of the days of Moshiach: only in hindsight will it be clear that Hashem reigned throughout the galus, when all the questions find their answers.

Ge'us lavesh does not mean Hashem is proud; it describes how it appears to one without emunah, as though Hashem has retired from caring for the low world, and the double lavesh means even the hiding is hidden.
Hashem needed oz, courage, to hide Himself in galus, like a surgeon father operating on his own child, who feels the child's pain more than any other doctor.

The world is called Tevel because to the non-believer it is a blurred mixture, like a vision with astigmatism, seen only in brief flashes of lightning; the pasuk promises that this very Tevel will not slip.
The word me'olam relates to concealment: Hashem is present in a hidden way and governs the world peeking out from the cracks, and because He is hidden the nations rise up like rivers.

The rivers are individual kingdoms and the breakers of the sea are empires that rule many countries, and the same nations that now raise their voice against Klal Yisrael will one day raise it to lament their own downfall.
The Rav reads the Gemara's 'aliba d'Abaye', 'according to Abaye', literally as 'according to Abaye's heart': a sage holds his view because his heart, from the root of his soul, tells him so.
From the grammar rule that a verb ending in nun drops it as a noun, the Rav derives that from aman, to believe, comes em, mother: emunah comes from the mother.

The seder's three matzos, from grain that brings intellect, stand for the Avos, and its four cups of wine, which bring out feeling, stand for the Imahos, like the three-headed and four-headed shin on the two sides of the tefillin.
A father who breaks in to his son's house without knowing it is his son's still would not harm him, because his heart knows; so too a Jew's bond to Hashem works beneath conscious knowledge.
Eisav concluded that he lost the berachos because of his wives, never imagining the fault was his own, the same rationalization as the fox and the grapes.
According to the Avnei Nezer as the Rav brings it, a woman may rely on a single witness about her husband's death because she feels whether he is alive; her believing the witness is itself the sign.
Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz, the great posek of Choshen Mishpat, saw his long davening, not his learning, as his portion from all his toil, because davening is dveykus.
The closed window of Bilgah mirrors a closed heart: what exists in Heaven exists in man, so a heart closed to the avodah closes the source of blessing above.

The camp of Israel in the desert is also a camp in time: the generation of the giving of the Torah is the front and the generation of Moshiach is Dan, the rear guard, whose flaw of lateness it must repair.
The very difficulty a person meets in a mitzvah he longs for is the sign that it is the mitzvah he came into the world for, since the yetzer hara blocks it most.
Amalek 'cooled' Israel on the way; a Jew's heart must burn with warmth and zerizus, and coldness is what makes a person slow.
A soul that was zariz in Torah and mitzvos in life arrives on time for its tikkun after life, while one that was late in life comes late then too.
The Rav reads the three 'havu' and seven 'kol' of Mizmor LeDavid as the ten utterances of creation: three upper levels beyond time and seven that crystallized into the seven days.
Music, a painting and a marriage all depend on the same thing, a true match between their parts; the music at a chasunah and the badchan's rhymes express the match of the couple.
Kabbalas Shabbos opens with song because on the seventh day the harp of seven notes is complete; only then is there harmony and yichud in the world.
Not saying the weekday brachos on Shabbos loses nothing: their blessing comes through the eighteen names in Mizmor LeDavid, and through resting from one's mundane needs.
The second day of creation lacks 'ki tov' because plurality, separation and dispute entered creation then, the opposite of Shabbos, the domain of the One.
'Kol Hashem al hamayim', the first voice of the psalm, is the border officer's first question as one enters Shabbos: did you go to the mikvah?

In the Slabodka story the Rav sees the bachur's childlessness, despite his becoming a gadol, as the punishment for publicly exposing a friend, showing that being right about a stolen chiddush does not justify shaming him.
A man who did full teshuvah before his death was still kept out of Gan Eden for one forgotten act of embarrassing a chassan, which he never asked forgiveness for.
Reb Akiva Eiger preferred that his own father-in-law think he could not learn, at the risk of losing the shidduch, rather than cause another father-in-law distress over his chassan.
Reb Akiva Eiger let a strong kashya stand against his pilpul in public, revealing the answer only privately, because answering it would have lowered the local Rav in his own town.
Reb Yisrael Salanter held that the rabbanim of a generation are held responsible above for not teaching their communities good middos and not to shame others.
According to Reb Yisrael Salanter, asking forgiveness for lashon hara when it would only pain the victim is wrong; one should rather bear the punishment oneself than cause the other distress.
A hardship whose purpose a tzaddik could not see at the time was revealed years later as the means of reaching another Jew.
Even a Jew who had married out long before was still in anguish over it, and the Rebbe in jail went over to him and tried to strengthen him.
At the engagement party, the drunken guests' insults against Jews were what made the father come to his senses.
The Chasam Sofer's ruling that a son may not kill his unaware father shows that the bond of feeling works even without knowledge, and the Rav reads the Jew's bond to Hashem the same way.
Matters of fact are the same for every mind, but in matters open to opinion the heart decides according to the root of a person's soul; thus a ruling 'according to Abaye's heart' reflects his nature.

Grain builds the intellect while wine weakens it but strengthens feeling; so the Seder pairs three matzos with the Avos and four cups with the Imahos, and the tefillin carry a three-headed shin and a four-headed shin.
The word emunah itself shows that faith comes from the mother: a verb ending in nun loses that nun when it becomes a noun, so amun becomes em.
Esav married Yishmael's daughter because he concluded from the brachos he lost that his wives were at fault, the same 'sour grapes' self-justification born of gaavah.

There is no true Jewish apikorus: his denial is a rationalization to permit his desires, as shown by the woman who asked a newspaper to stop reporting miracles so she could go to the beach on Shabbos.
The Rav reads 'bnei eilim' as the strong and respected people themselves, who are called upon to give their own power and prowess back to Hashem.
The 'kol Hashem' of the psalm is the Ten Utterances of creation, which still live inside every natural force, so the destructive might of the ocean is Hashem concealing Himself in the water.
Recognizing that an enemy's power is really Hashem's is itself a sweetening of judgment (hamtakas hadinim), after which the din has no hold over the person.

The cedars of the psalm are the great powers that, like tall trees in a forest, block a person's view of heaven; the Rav applies this to communist Russia, where belief was forbidden and which collapsed overnight.
Looking up to the sky for Hashem follows a human instinct that power comes from above, though Hashem has no place; still, seeing the sky gives emunah and kavanah.
The 39 melachos forbidden on Shabbos are the 39 curses given after the sin of the Eitz HaDaas, so Shabbos, a day of blessing, has no place for them.
The Rav presents stories of tzaddikim as a remedy for the weak emunah of the generation before Moshiach, citing tzaddikim who said that simply talking about a tzaddik already brings emunah.
In Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan's story, his refusal to reveal one poor man's name is what allowed a second, hidden poor man to trust him and ask for help.
Rabbi Shmuel Salant traced the young baal tokea's failure to a single proud thought that he could blow while the old man could not.
Rabbi Yosef Yoizel was won over not by Rabbi Yisrael Salanter's mussar talk itself but by seeing him interrupt it for a wagon driver's feelings.
Rabbi Yoizel argued that a man who claims he would give up Olam Haba to shame someone, but would not give up any Olam Hazeh, shows only how little Olam Haba is worth to him.
The Chofetz Chaim read 'az panim l'Gehinom' as a statement about teshuvah: every sinner can repent, but brazenness creates a presumption that he will not.
The real novelty of 'the last forty days were in favor' is not the first forty days but that after the sin a new time of favor came into being.
Shimon HaTzaddik's resting place is a place of favor less because of the place or the time than because of the soul of the tzaddik buried there.
Until the exile of Bavel the Written Torah was taught together with the received laws from Moshe, but the pilpul, chiddushim and toil of the Oral Torah began with Shimon HaTzaddik.
Each week of the seven consolations reflects one of the seven middos; this week is tiferes, which is Torah, and the haftarah's call to water and its ending with Hashem's glory show it.
From the Akeidah the Rav learns that a trial is what brings out yiras Shamayim, so the trials of this generation are its path to fear of G-d.

The Rav links the spread of Haskalah and Reform in Germany to the absence of Chassidus there: the lands the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim did not reach are where the decline, and later the destruction, began.
The Satan's threat to make his own chassidim is, according to the Rav, visible where Chassidus has become rivalry, politics and team loyalty instead of serving Hashem.
The Rav reads the separate gates, nusach and nesi'im of the shevatim, all bound to Yaakov Avinu, as the model for the many rebbes and groups among Jews: different roots, one whole.
Through the parable of grass that grows by the moon, a chassid may admit another rebbe is greater and still know he will grow only by the rebbe of his own root; by the 'sun' he would only burn.
Following the Haflaah, the Rav treats the bond of talmid and rebbe like a shidduch: just as a bas kol announces a match before a child is formed, it announces which rebbe a talmid belongs to.
The Rav says he may teach avodas Hashem beyond his own level because what he says is taken from sefarim and from what he saw by his rebbes, not his own.
Shemini Atzeres, the most spiritual day of the year, is when Klal Yisrael asks for Geshem, because what they truly ask for is the inner side of the rain, a flow of Torah.
The Mabul and Matan Torah are the same forty days of water: the generation that refused the Torah received its outside as a flood, while Klal Yisrael received its inside.

Noach was the neshamah of Moshe, meant to give the Torah; failing because he did not daven for his generation, he was 'replanted' like a sapling as Moshe, who davened with mesirus nefesh and repaired the sin of 'mei Noach'.
'Bashalom' at the end of the psalm hints to the shin, the letter of Torah, so the verse describes the Torah coming down as water; the Rav adds that it drizzled at Matan Torah.
Oil, which makes no noise when spilled, is linked to eight, above the seven days of creation, while wine, numerically seventy, belongs to the seven.
The ayalah that can give birth only when the snake strikes her is Klal Yisrael: the suffering of galus, especially the chevlei Moshiach, is the very agent that will deliver the days of Moshiach.
Inverting the Reishis Chochmah's image, the Rav says it is not Gehinom but this world that lies in the street, while its true Master is hidden, which is exactly why the word olam means concealment.

The heretic who would laugh at anyone saying his house built itself still claims that of the whole world; the Rav explains he must invent a theory of origins only because he refuses to believe the Chumash.

Moshe's blessing to Levi can be checked against reality: of ten roshei yeshiva in Torah Vodaath seven were kohanim or levi'im, and most of the classic commentators around the Shulchan Aruch were too, a sign of Hashem visible in the Torah world.

The Rav distinguishes two lines among the leaders of Klal Yisrael: the moreh hora'ah of Shevet Levi, and the Chassidishe Rebbes, like the Ba'al HaTanya, who descend from David HaMelech and carry malchus.
That the same Chumash and Gemara serve a person for his whole life, with new insights at every stage, is itself a proof that the Torah is from Heaven, since no human textbook behaves this way.
Heresy has nothing to do with science: a baker or a candlestick maker can be just as much a kofer, but no one puts a microphone in front of the baker.
The Rav sees the very fact that bachurim come to a voluntary shiur, with no compulsion, tests or marks, as a present-day mofes fulfilling what tzaddikim said about the generation before Moshiach.
Heaven used the Zionist leader who wanted to save only Zionists, and who had refused the chassidim's money, to save the Satmar Rav, the great fighter against Zionism.

The Rav reads Yosef's words to his brothers, that Hashem sent him ahead for sustenance, as the meaning of the Satmar Rav's rescue: Hashem saved him not simply so he would live, but so he would bring Yiddishkeit to America.

The loss of pre-war American Jewry was not because the grandparents were not ehrliche Jews; it was because the ehrliche rabbanim would not come to America, so there was no kashrus and no concept of chalav Yisrael.
The Rav chooses the Stoliner story not because it was the greatest of the Rebbe's mofsim, but because it happened in public and everyone saw it.
The Rav links the Midrash of the maiden who seized an angel's wings to Elul: the mazal of Elul was itself born of an act of grabbing, so that is the influence flowing down in this month.
The moment of a person's passing is the culmination of his whole life; therefore Binyamin, who came out together with Rachel's soul, is the quintessence of his mother.
Rachel gave away what was hers; Binyamin, her essence, has the merit to grab back what Esav wants to keep for himself.
Esav's share in the months is only an outer hold, since the whole creation belongs to Yisrael; what Yaakov and Binyamin grab is what is truly theirs.
Binyamin grabbed at both ends: the end of Av at Tu B'Av and the start of Teves at Chanukah.
One need not be a Lubavitcher to be on shlichus: every Jew is a shaliach of the Ribono shel Olam, sent into a world full of impurity to stay holy there.
Because Klal Yisrael accepted Pesukei d'Zimra and Maariv on itself, the Rav suggests they may in some way be a bigger obligation than the other tefillos, carrying the force of a vow.

The more kedushah a thing holds, the thicker the tumah around it: bread needs more mitzvos than other food, the Bris is covered by the orlah, Eretz Yisrael was held by the Canaanites, and a tzaddik has a bigger yetzer.
The later chumros in kashrus and the longer davening of later generations stem from one cause: a lower generation needs more refined food and more tefillah to purify itself.
'HaMelech' in the Megillah equals Haman in gematria and also 'Kes Kah', the incomplete throne: while Haman reigns, Hashem's kingship shows only as Yud-Kei without Vav-Kei.
By At-Bash, the Mem and Tzadi of 'mitzvah' stand for Yud and Hei, so the word itself is Yud-Kei hidden and Vav-Kei revealed, making every mitzvah a yichud of the hidden and the revealed.
On Purim we wear masks because Hashem acts in this world in a masquerade; the point of Purim is to rip off that mask and recognize Him.
The Rav reads the opening of the Shulchan Aruch, about rising like a lion, as a statement about going to sleep: only one who lies down like a lion, with kabbalas ol, can rise like one.
The animals and earth sinned in the generation of the Flood because each was part of a sinner's portion of creation; Noach's portion, which included Eretz Yisrael, stayed pure and was not flooded.
When Tehillim calls on angels, sun and moon to praise Hashem, it implies that man's good conduct enables them to praise better and to shine more.
Hashem may cause a tzaddik to stumble so that his teshuvah brings thoughts of teshuvah into other Jews.
A shogeg brings a korban because a careful Jew is helped from Heaven not to forget; the very fact that the excuse arose shows a lack of care.
The alef-beis order of the chapters of praise is itself a statement: David has not finished Hashem's praises, he stops only because the letters are finished.
The exact share of oxygen in the air is a wonder of balance in both directions: less would choke every creature, and more would turn one fire into the burning of the whole world.
The renewal of the body every seven years gives a way to understand a little of gilgul, a soul coming down again in another body.
That the brain cells alone are not renewed is itself the wonder that allows memory: new cells would not hold what was engraved in the old ones, like a calculator that loses its numbers.
The Rav explains that the word tefillah itself means attachment, from the word tafel, so that tefillah is by definition dveikus to Hashem.

According to the Rav, arguing whether Torah or tefillah is greater is like arguing whether the brain or the heart is more important: other mitzvos are like a finger one can live without, but these two are the vital organs.
The Rav says that one who davens with real dveikus davens slowly not by design but because he cannot bring himself to leave a word that means so much to him.

The Rav reads the sudden explosion of inventions in the last two hundred years, after thousands of years without progress, as the Satan's final struggle before Moshiach, like a candle flaring up just before it goes out.
The Rav sees the physical pollution of air, water and food as a reflection of the spiritual contamination of the atmosphere caused by more aveiros.
From the radio, which shows that the atmosphere holds whatever is put into it, the Rav learns that every word of Torah sanctifies the atmosphere and every bad word contaminates it.
The Rav compares this generation to the best soldiers, whom an army sends to the most dangerous front: being born now is a mark of trust and a shlichus no earlier generation had.
A mitzvah can have more than one place: just as milah is tied to both Chevron and Shechem, Rosh Hashanah has its place in the Beis Hamikdash and also at the place of Shmuel Hanavi.
'Haras olam', the world's conception on Rosh Hashanah, is mirrored in Chana conceiving Shmuel, the head of the prophets, on that day.
Eli's objection to Chana's long prayer reflects the way tefillah is belittled: learning and giving tzedakah bring honor, while one who davens long is mocked.
Barrenness is read spiritually: a tefillah that is not accepted and learning without success are 'barren', without fruit.
Chana's new name Tzevakos, linked to netzach and hod from which prophecy draws, fits that her son Shmuel began the era of prophecy.
Although the obligation of aliyah l'regel applies only to the three festivals, Elkanah and Chana came to Shiloh on Rosh Hashanah too, so Chana's prayer there was a Rosh Hashanah prayer.
The Rav reads the Kaddeishim of Shacharis as markers between the worlds: a Kaddish is said each time one passes from one world to another, going up and coming down.

The second half of davening, after Shemoneh Esrei, is the bringing down of the shefa that was asked for; like paying in a store and leaving the goods on the counter, one who neglects it brings nothing home.
Because the words of davening were composed with ruach hakodesh, they effect great tikkunim even when the one davening does not know the kavanos, provided he davens properly.
Waking each morning is like birth: as the yetzer hara reaches a child years before the yetzer tov, it reaches a person first each morning, which is why Modeh Ani must come at once.
Modeh Ani was composed without a Name of Hashem precisely so that it could be said before washing, letting the very first word and thought of the day be thanks to Hashem.

Just as no day repeats another's task, no Jew was created to do what another does; Hashem guides the parents to choose a name that fits the soul's shlichus, and every Jew also has a name from the sitra achra that must be nullified.
A gentile's readiness to die for his country is the product of daily drilling from childhood, while the Jew's readiness to die for his emunah comes from emunah in the heart, inherited from the Avos.

Rashi's question why the Torah did not begin with 'Hachodesh' is tied to the foundation of emunah: Hachodesh was the first mitzvah Moshe taught on the strength of the appointment the people heard at Sinai.
Even mitzvos with a tradition from Avraham, like milah, or from Yaakov, like gid hanasheh, are binding not because of that individual but because Moshe was commanded at Sinai to teach them.
The halachic rule that one wrong letter invalidates a Sefer Torah, together with the mitzvah for every Jew to write one, kept every Sefer Torah an exact copy for thousands of years.

Differences in halachah between tribes reflect middas chesed and middas din, both from Hashem; this is why each tribe needed its own judges, and why Beis Hillel tends to leniency and Beis Shammai to stringency.
The claim of other faiths that Hashem changed His mind comes not from reason but from their inability to accept that the Jews are the chosen people.
Today's hatred of the Jews cannot be explained by religious difference, since the nations themselves no longer keep their faith; its secret is in Vayeshev: jealousy of the beloved son.
Since kavanah in Avos is a return to the root of the soul in the Avos, the Rav ties it to learning Sefer Bereishis: one who does not know the Avos cannot truly have kavanah in Avos.
Yetzias Mitzrayim contains the redemptions of all generations and of every individual, so remembering it is a means by which a Jew can merit his own yeshuah.

The spiritual exile of Mitzrayim was a closed heart that could not daven, the same blockage a person feels in davening today; the Exodus, Pesach as 'the mouth that speaks', opened the gates of tefillah.
Emes V'yatziv is the staircase to Shemoneh Esrei: its fifteen words beginning with vav are the fifteen steps of the Beis HaMikdash and the fifteen Shir HaMaalos.
The four times 'emes' after the mention of the Exodus correspond to the four exiles, since the Exodus already carries the power to redeem from all four.
Of the three kinds of tefillah, of Moshe, of David and of the poor man, the poor man's broken-hearted tefillah 'wraps around' all the others and accomplishes the most.
Rav Yosef Chaim's question to every visitor about the Kosel was a way of protecting the honor of a guest: it showed that people came to Yerushalayim for the Kosel and only stopped by him on the way.
The Rav contrasts the tzaddik with an ordinary person: the tzaddik's thought, even in his own illness, is not to trouble other Jews, while another thinks only of what he himself needs.
In the musaf, na'anuim and eruv stories, a tzaddik sets aside a rule or a mitzvah derabbanan for another person's feelings or honor; the Rav presents each as the way a tzaddik weighs things.
Rav Chaim Ozer's answer distinguishes two obligations: illness exempted him from sukkah, but not from hachnasas orchim, just as Avraham Avinu sat waiting for guests while in pain after his milah.
The Rav treats getting used to Eretz Yisroel as a real spiritual danger that calls for deliberate, ongoing renewal.
Daily davening about Yerushalayim can serve as an indirect tool to refresh one's love for the land.
The same words of prayer for Yerushalayim mean something different to one who lives nearby: he feels close where a Jew abroad feels distant.
The parable of the log and the planted tree: mere presence in the land decays, while being rooted through Torah brings growth.
Morning is called tzafra because the birds (tziporim) sing then, and night ramsha because the crawling creatures sing then; a Jew is not limited to either, but sings to Hashem morning and night.
Pesach is lower than Shavuos and Sukkos in Hallel, yet only Pesach carries kares: kares means being cut off from Hashem, and Pesach, being the bond itself, is where that cutting-off applies.
Just as the first blessing of Shemoneh Esrei ends with Magen Avraham alone and not all three Avos, so among the Regalim Pesach is the 'point' from which everything begins.
The only two positive mitzvos whose neglect carries kares, milah and the korban Pesach, are both bound up with Avraham Avinu, whose Yom Tov is Pesach.
Taking out the Pesach dishes after twelve months is like seeing a friend after twelve months, a kind of techiyas hamesim.

Just as an esrog is a plain citrus fruit all year and becomes a holy object on Sukkos, the Pesach matzah is an envelope for holy Names of emunah and geulah, the same Names that took the Jews out of Egypt.
Lechem equals three times the Name Havayah, while matzah equals three times that Name spelled out in full (45), showing that matzah holds higher holy Names than ordinary bread.
The Satmar Rav proves the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching from halachah: a traveler who fixes his mind on a tree within the techum is treated as being there, though his body is far away.

Bilam and Avraham both claimed to do Hashem's will, but Bilam kept pressing Hashem to agree with him, while Avraham, who could have changed the decree with one word of tefillah, went to the Akeidah in simcha.
Reb Shraga Feivel derived from the Torah's demand for taharah in the Mikdash that Hashem prefers avodah done in purity, so a voided takanah still reveals Hashem's will.
The Rambam distinguished between what he kept himself and what he could write as halachah: a chumrah cannot be turned into a halachah.
If a mikvah can turn a ger into a Yid, it can turn a Yid into a better Yid.
Rabbeinu Tam tefillin are begun after marriage because, following the Gemara's view on learning after the chasunah, that is when a person can be more in taharah.
The Ba'al Shem Tov's new path was not to reveal more secrets but to take the secrets of the Zohar and the Arizal and use them for avodas Hashem, which is why spreading them in his way is a mitzvah.
The Meor Einayim allowed only the teachings he did not remember saying to be printed, since a teaching he could not recall had been said from a far higher state.

Because the Tanya builds its concepts step by step from the beginning, it supplies the foundations that the other chassidic sefarim assume, so one who learns it can understand the Meor Einayim and the Kedushas Levi.
Reb Meir Arik held that one does not truly know hilchos Chanukah, since there is no Shulchan Aruch HaRav on those halachos, only the Shulchan Aruch with its commentaries.
The chassidim explained that the Ba'al HaTanya wanted the boat stopped by the boatmen rather than by his own miracle, because a mitzvah should be done in the natural way.
The Rav reads the parable of the snake and the king's daughter as the struggle with the yetzer hara whose prize is genuine tefillah.
The unprecedented strength of today's tests is itself a sign of how great the reward will be.
The Rav links the new tests of this generation with a new form of Torah, its inner dimension, being revealed.

The Rav explains, recalling the Satmar Rav's drashos, that a leader speaks about the matters his generation particularly needs, while Torah is a general subject; this is why he himself speaks about tefillah.
The davening in the beis medrash was better in its early years because the group was persecuted, which drove them to better tefillos, and because the original members were then the majority.
Tefillah is so great a mitzvah that it is included in kriyas shema itself: within the parsha of accepting the mitzvos, 'to serve Him with all your heart' stands as the example of a mitzvah.
Since pigul shows that a mere thought can disqualify a korban, and tefillah stands in place of the korbanos, the Rav derives that thought is the decisive part of tefillah.
Saying the words without kavanah fulfills only the rabbinic enactment of three tefillos, not the Torah mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart.
Kavanah itself is a gift from Hashem, as the passuk says that He prepares their heart and then listens, so one must daven to be able to daven with kavanah.
Citing the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thoughts are, the Rav explains that one who faces Yerushalayim in prayer is truly there, before the Kodesh HaKodashim, standing before the King.
Like a coin that lands on heads ten thousand times and still has an even chance of tails, the long wait for Moshiach does not lower the chance that he comes today.
Dates when Moshiach was expected turned into catastrophes because the possibility of redemption threatens the Satan, who comes as accuser and brings up Klal Yisroel's sins.
Ravina and Rav Ashi recorded a date for Moshiach that had already passed precisely as a message to later generations that predictions by tzaddikim may fail, and that this must not shake emunah.
The Rambam's account of Ben Koziva is not history but halacha: even an endorsement by Rabbi Akiva cannot settle who Moshiach is.
The explosion of modern inventions is the Satan's arsenal against Hashem and Moshiach, brought out because he is fighting for his life as the end of the yetzer hara approaches.
Unlike Torah, tefillah always contains lishmah: even a request for a bicycle and a dog is lishmah in the very act of turning to Hashem, which is pure emunah.
Just as at the sea emunah came first and then the song, the geulah from this golus will come through emunah.

The Rav suggests that the four letters of 'Tanya' are the four prefixes of the Hebrew future tense, so the very name of the sefer speaks of wanting to become: what was until now is past, and from now on one wants to be good.
Shevuah comes from sheva: since all the forces of creation lie in the seven days, an oath binds a person with the strength of all of creation, and that is why it helps against the yetzer hara.

'Mashbi'in oso' can be read as 'mashpi'in': pei and beis interchange, and in ksav ashuri a pei holds a white beis inside it, so the oath is a flow of holiness sent down from heaven to enable the soul to fulfill it.
Being 'like a rasha' in one's own eyes does not mean thinking oneself a rasha; it means not being sure of oneself.
According to the Raya Mehemna, the 'bad' and 'good' in the Gemara's four types are not what happens to a person but the yetzer within him and who is master over whom.

Unlike most chassidish sefarim, which teach on the parsha without a set progression, the Tanya proceeds systematically from easy matters to higher ones, laying down knowledge before giving guidance in avodah.
The weeks of consolation are a progression through the middos, so each week's consolation has its own character: chessed, then yirah.
Yiras Shamayim itself is presented as a consolation, not a burden.
The word Bereishis holds the letters of 'yarei Shabbos', showing that Shabbos gives yiras Shamayim.
There is a special joy in fear of sin, and this is the avodah of the parsha.
Since a person is where his thought is, one who davens with the Beis Hamikdash in mind is really standing there, and must therefore present himself as one who stands there.
The Gemara's traveler who fixes his Shabbos place by a distant tree may then walk into the city, showing halachically that a person's place follows his thought.
Bilaam also said he would not transgress Hashem's word, but he kept trying to change Hashem's will, while Avraham could have changed it with one word of tefillah and chose not to.
Hashem's insistence on purity in the Beis Hamikdash service reveals His desire, so even after Ezra's takanah lapsed, serving Him in taharah remains what He favors.
Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld reasoned that if a mikvah can turn a goy into a Yid, it can turn a Yid into a better Yid.
Rabbeinu Tam tefillin are begun after marriage for the same reason the Gemara prefers learning after marriage: one can then be in greater purity.

Although the soul is the holy part, the Rav says a person came into the world for the sake of the body: the soul came down only to purify the animal-like body until the body itself can share in dveikus.
The Rav reads tefillah and tefillin as one root meaning to attach; tefillin must be bound tight, and tefillah is the same tight binding of the heart to Hashem.
Even a prayer for one's own needs, which is not for its own sake, is itself a fulfillment of emunah, because one asks only Him whom one believes can give.
Asking Hashem for a small thing is a small request but great emunah, since one recognizes that every great and small thing comes only from Him.
The Rav shows from the Mishnah of one who sets his Shabbos boundary at a distant tree that a person is legally where his thought is, which explains how one davening far away is in the Beis HaMikdash.
In the poritz story, the Rav notes with irony that the poritz would never find his mistake because he does not say Shemoneh Esrei, the time when some Jews do their accounts.

The Rav argues that seeking Hashem with the intellect is a category error, like claiming to listen to a painting or to see a symphony; Hashem is perceived through a different faculty, akin to nevuah and ruach hakodesh, which Klal Yisroel as a whole still has.
The proof from Sinai, as the Rav reads the Yismach Moshe, lies in transmission: a fabricated event would be exposed at once, since children would find that neither they nor their friends had seen it.

The Rambam could engage in inquiry without danger because he felt Hashem so tangibly that denial never occurred to him even while posing the questions; even his yiras shamayim in a state of katnus was too much for the Yismach Moshe.
In Ein Kelokeinu the declaration 'there is none like our G-d' comes before the question 'who is like our G-d', teaching that a Jew begins with the answer of emunah and only then may ask.

The Rav applies the image of Adam haRishon's body twice: within each generation, where the head, heart and hands are the Torah scholars, the masters of tefillah and the givers of tzedakah; and across all history, where the desert generation is the head and ours the heel.
The heel's lack of sensation explains why emunah feels weak today: like a tooth pulled after a numbing injection, the emunah is present but not felt.
Because the people of the last generation are so small, their avodah is more precious to Hashem, just as a king delights more in a parrot's few words than in the wisdom of his ministers.
Having bad thoughts in davening is not evidence of a bad soul: it would be, the Rav says, only if a person had just one soul; since there are two, the struggle itself is expected.
The soul left a carefree heaven where it sang with the angels; it was sent down precisely to fight, so the war is the purpose, not a failure.

The walnut's structure, three inedible shells and a fourth brown skin eaten with the nut around four sections, mirrors the three impure kelipos, nogah, and the four letters of Hashem's Name in the soul.
Nogah is like sunlight filtered through a window shade: there is some light, but not real light, which is why it can go either way.
Salt, melach, has the same letters as bread, lechem, and the Rav connects it to three times Hashem's Name, which is why one dips the bread in salt three times.
The same body that is a barrier to the soul can be elevated: the Jew's yetzer comes from nogah, and how he eats decides whether it turns to holiness or to impurity.

Yaakov Avinu deliberately used his weakest bracha for his own troubles and reserved the stronger three for the troubles before Moshiach, so the present danger is the very time those brachos were kept for.
The seventy words of Lamenatzeach correspond to the seventy sighs of a woman in labor, and since the generation is in the birth pangs of Moshiach, it has reached the last word, kareinu.
Lamenatzeach means both 'to the conductor' of the singers and 'to the One who grants victory': Dovid sings to Hashem as the One who assures victory, and so he thanks Him even before the yeshua.
Only when a person has run out of his own eitzos, as in ad anah ashis eitzos, does Hashem's salvation have to appear.
Hashem is called Elokei Yaakov in a time of trouble because Yaakov's whole life was one chain of troubles borne with bitachon, and he stands for the Jewish people's long journey through galus.
The tzaddikim's pain in their troubles is not for themselves but that Hashem's Name is not complete, so their request is that His Name become whole.
The word va'nisoded comes from 'od', 'still': nations that fall stay fallen, but the Jewish people's fall is only temporary because they are eternal.
Merely speaking about a tzaddik who has passed away arouses his merit to protect the Jews in a time of danger.
The Rav draws the line from the story to the present: just as the Belzer Rav had people speak of an earlier tzaddik, today one should speak of the Belzer Rav himself.
Safety is not a matter of place: danger can reach anywhere, so in every place a person depends on Hashem's help.

The Rav defines serving Hashem with chesed as a love so strong it makes no calculations, like the Rambam's lovesick person who pays no attention to anything else, and he sees this in the Jews following Hashem into a barren desert.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Rav explains that the Torah calls a forbidden union 'chesed' because it is the very middah of chesed, created for loving Hashem, Torah and Jews, turned toward what is forbidden.

Netzach and hod are the two legs: one stands by prevailing and by yielding, as animals in the jungle either fight or give way; in holiness this means defeating false views and conceding to the truth, while winning in learning only to show off is impure.
Customs that once expressed holy love for the Rebbe, such as pushing toward him or grabbing shirayim, become bad middos when people are no longer on that level, and that is why Rebbes abolished them.

The Pirkei Avos of each week matches that week's sefirah: the first chapter, with 'from the mouth of the Gevurah', in the week of gevurah, and the second, opening with tiferes, in the week of tiferes.

A mikveh purifies like a sefer Torah written according to halachah: its waters are bound with holy names, so the higher the names, the higher the mikveh, and on Shavuos morning different names enter it.
The Rav explains that the nations kept customs from Noach whose reasons they forgot: red for stop and green for go reflect blood as gevurah and green as life.
Doctors and bakers wear white, an impractical color, because they bestow chesed; their mazal sees what they themselves do not know.
Water has no taste, color or smell, yet people drink it with relish, because water itself is pleasure and all pleasures come from it.
Anger is a form of pride: a person who has worked on his pride will never get angry, since he does not demand that everything go as he wants.
When a tzaddik speaks simple words, even jests or talk of politics, they can contain great yichudim through gematrios and initials.
Earth is the element that can never be nullified and always sinks downward; from it come sadness and laziness, a life without energy or will.

Although one normally listens to the chazzan's repetition and answers, at Modim each person says Modim d'Rabbanan himself, because thanking Hashem brings such closeness that one does not let another do it for him.
The Rav reads the close of Modim d'Rabbanan as thanks for the very ability and desire to thank, which Hashem places in a person's heart.
The rescue that obligates thanks is a reminder: being delivered from one trouble should make a person thank Hashem for all the troubles he was never put into.
Birkas HaGomel needs two Rabbanan: one chacham to explain Hashem's kindness, and a second to show that after the first seemed to finish, there was still more to say.
The korban todah's short eating time forces its owner to invite more people, so the thanksgiving becomes a greater kiddush shem shamayim.

Knowing that one owes thanks makes a person subordinate to his benefactor; therefore the more he appreciates Hashem's goodness, the more he becomes a tzaddik who cannot bring himself to displease Him.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains that Hashem gave up the fitting punishment at the Nile so that the miracle would happen where Jews could return and make a bracha.
The placement of the twelve princes of Yishmael right before 'these are the generations of Yitzchak' hints that their fall opens the way for Moshiach from Yitzchak.
Political events below reflect what happens above: the earthly ruler falls only after his heavenly prince has fallen.
One need not be a Lubavitcher chassid to be on shlichus: every Jew is a shaliach of the Ribono shel Olam.
The present days are historic: when Moshiach comes, volumes will be written about them.
The Rav reads the Mishnah's 'I made its damage possible' as saying that a person's property is an extension of his nefesh, so the owner of a damaging ox is himself the source of the damage.

He reads the categories of damage as the owner's middos showing through his animal: goring reflects a will to harm, eating another's grain reflects desire, and trampling reflects carelessness about others.
Because a friend is part of one's nefesh, a person who becomes a true baal middos will make his friends into baalei middos too.

The four levels of Torah correspond to the levels of the soul, so the Zohar's stringencies and Rav's ruling for Rabbah bar bar Chana are the halachah for a person on a higher level, not a departure from it.
From the Akeidah, where Hashem Himself commanded the slaughter but an angel sufficed to stop it, Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin learned that a command to harm a Jew is not accepted even from a great angel.
The Rav connects Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin's refusal to harm a Jew with the unbroken chain of great descendants he merited, unusual among the Litvish.

The Rav presents the revelation of the secrets of the Torah as three distinct stages: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai revealed them, the Arizal spread them in preparation for Moshiach, and the Ba'al Shem Tov turned them into a way of serving Hashem.
The Rav says that Rashi at times hints at secrets of the Torah in a comment; one who does not understand simply moves on, but one who understands sees the hint to the Zohar.
Before the Ba'al Shem Tov the Kabbalah of the Arizal was a 'dry' Kabbalah; the Ba'al Shem Tov showed how to use it while davening, learning, and even walking in the street and doing business.

Through the story of Gichon, the Rav shows how close the redemption was in the Arizal's time: reopening what Chizkiyahu had stopped, against the will of the Chachamim, would have brought Moshiach, but the moment of favor passed.

Life itself, the difference between a living person and a body lying beside him, is something no scientist can explain; the Rav identifies it with the soul, a spiritual force in the blood that one begins to grasp through the Torah.

The Rav explains the prohibition of blood: an animal has a lower kind of life, and a Jew, who has a higher soul, should not take the animal's soul into himself; he may eat its flesh, but not its life.

The Rav reads Adam HaRishon's first conversation with Hashem, blaming the wife Hashem gave him, as ingratitude, and sees Bikurim, the first of the gifts, as its direct opposite: a declaration that one is not ungrateful.
The hundred daily brachos parallel Mizmor Lesodah being the hundredth chapter of Tehillim: a hundred thanks each day.
The word Ish, used for a bar mitzvah, stands for ahavah, yirah and simcha, the three things with which a grown Jew serves Hashem.
A korban brought for a sin lacked joy, so the song of the Levi'im supplied the simcha; Mizmor Lesodah teaches a person not to rely on others but to bring joy to his own service.
The devar halacha before davening is meant to be a clear halacha, because nothing gives simcha like understanding a piece of Gemara clearly, and that joy prepares a person for tefillah.
Even the Communist commissar recognized the Rebbe's total self-giving for others, and described it in his own terms as being a true 'communist'.
The Sekulener Rebbe weighed his own danger against the other Jew's life and judged that he must go, with mesirus nefesh.
His joy at the end came from the Jew's release, not from his own safety: he had been thrown down the stairs.
The Rav explains the low state of Tamuz and Av by their height: like a stone dropped from a high roof that sinks deep into soft ground, the loftier a time is, the deeper it falls.
He links the months to the tribes: Tamuz and Av correspond to Reuven and Shimon, and the falls of their nesiim, in Korach and in Pinchas, are read just as each month begins.
A summer vacation is reframed as a shlichus to repair the meraglim, who failed when they left the camp of Klal Yisrael on a journey.

Following the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains that a sender puts part of his own soul into his shliach; Hashem wanted the meraglim to go as His shluchim and succeed, but they went as shluchim of the people, whose intent was not good.
The Torah only hints that Yosef's pit held snakes and scorpions, because one may not speak ill even of a pit in Eretz Yisrael, the very sin of the meraglim.
In the Berditchever Rav's words, rushing exhausted widows for a hiddur in the matzos is putting blood into the matzos; real hiddur mitzvah is good middos.
Contradictory statements of the Midrash and the Zohar about the Avos can both be true, because pshat, drush and sod sometimes judge the same act differently.
Yaakov's bowing to Esav was clever according to the Zohar: it made Esav swell with pride, and that was his downfall.
Avraham's going down to Mitzrayim brought the galus, yet the galus was what purified his children, so he knowingly accepted the harm for the greater benefit.
A prophecy can still change, but a symbolic act of the Avos fixes the outcome; so Avraham took Pharaoh's money to secure that his children would leave Mitzrayim with wealth.
A gift from a rasha carries his character and tumah, which is why Avraham refused Sodom's money, while the wealth of Mitzrayim was purified by Hashem.

Chavakuk's establishing all the mitzvos on one does not mean the others fall away; it means each generation must concentrate its strength on its own avodah, and for the last generations that is emunah.
The term ikvesa d'Meshicha is read literally: the generation before Moshiach is the heel of Adam HaRishon's body, the lowest and darkest limb, which feels nothing and stands only on emunah.
The disappearance of dybbukim is itself a sign of ikvesa d'Meshicha: open glimpses of heaven would make emunah no test, so they were taken away.
The final word of Krias Shema, 'emes', the word the chazzan repeats to complete the 248 limbs, corresponds to the heel, so the last generation's emunah is built into Krias Shema.
Where the Satan invests his greatest effort shows which mitzvah a generation must strengthen: tzitzis in the Divrei Chaim's time, emunah today, attacked through devices brought into the home.
Each bad middah behaves like its element: pride rises like fire against the pull that brings everything else down, while sadness lies down like earth, which falls fastest.
Wild music belongs to the element of air: it has no substance and makes a person ownerless, bound to nothing, like the Gemara's slave who prefers hefker.
Kelipas nogah is like a window shade: a barrier between man and Hashem through which the sun still shines.
Orlah and bris milah share one pattern: three parts that cannot be redeemed and a fourth that is raised to holiness, matching the three impure kelipos and kelipas nogah.
Even a gentile's mercy can be selfish: he gives to the hungry so that he himself can enjoy his ice cream in peace.
A promise from Hashem does not remove the need for tefillah: Eliyahu was told it would rain and still had to daven for it.
The Rav contrasts the other side's wonder at the rocket that did not explode with our own lack of surprise, since we know Hashem is making miracles for us.
Precisely because miracles are visible now, the Rav weighs whether the custom of freely omitting Tachanun for distant yahrtzeits fits such a time.
Hashem's love for Noach lay in saving him even after the plan of a perfected world from the teiva had failed through the sins in the teiva, a love rooted in the future of Avraham and Klal Yisrael.
Noach's drinking reflected his mistaken belief that the world after the flood was already perfected, when it was not.

The shofar parallels the utterance of Bereishis, which has no stated speech because it precedes speech, and parallels the breath Hashem blew into Adam on Rosh Hashanah; so the shofar's wordless sound creates a world above sin and above physicality.
The Klausenberger Rebbe valued the leining of Sarah's demand to expel Yishmael above the shofar, as a way to arouse in Heaven that Yishmael should have no share in Eretz Yisrael.
The second day's reading continues the first: the Akeidah is the culmination of Yitzchak's victory over Yishmael, which is why Yishmael is called an enemy while Eisav is only a hater.
Rejoicing in the King's coronation, even on one's own day of judgment, is itself the merit that transforms the verdict.
The first test, defying Nimrod for a G-d who had never spoken to him, was smaller than the Akeidah because at the Akeidah Hashem, though He spoke, was felt as far away: 'he saw the place from afar'.
At the Akeidah Avraham was brought down from all his levels to the state of the simplest Jew of the time before Moshiach, and his test was to break through from there.
The simple answer to Avraham's question, that Hashem had only said to bring Yitzchak up, was itself withheld from him; not finding the answer was part of the test.
Because Avraham's last test was a test of questions, the last generation before Moshiach will be tested with questions, and the Rav places the questions raised after the Holocaust in this frame.
Giving up one's will for Hashem's is a mesiras nefesh greater than letting oneself be killed, and many small acts of it gather into a great one.

Fish need no shechitah or salting because the souls of tzaddikim who still need a small tikun are placed in fish, while the meat of an animal needs a great tikun; for this reason tzaddikim ate fish on Shabbos, a time to elevate sparks.
The word 'nefashos' in the brachah borei nefashos refers to souls that Hashem placed in foods, which enter Gan Eden when a Jew makes the brachah.
Hashem could have made man need gasoline like a car; that He gave food taste and color is His chein and chesed, and thanking Him for the taste during the meal is itself a brachah.
Even which half of an apple one keeps and which half a friend receives is hashgachah pratis: each part holds souls connected to that person's soul, tribe and family.
In one respect eating non-kosher food is worse than chillul Shabbos: chillul Shabbos does not become part of the person, while forbidden food becomes part of his bones, muscles and brain.

Adam was meant to eat from the Tree of Knowledge, which was a vine: had he waited and made wine for kiddush on Shabbos he would have taken its good, but eating on Friday, before it was permitted, like orlah, he took its bad; a Jew's kelipas nogah is rooted in that tree of good and evil.

Even a non-Jew's pity for a hungry beggar is the natural mercy Hashem placed in people and animals, and he acts on it so as not to spoil his own good mood; a Jew's mercy, even when he is unaware, is deep down for Hashem.
Saying Tikunei Zohar in Elul is not only learning: it is a tikun of souls that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai performs for the Jewish people in these days.
Because all Jews are bound to one another, the few who say Tikunei Zohar help the whole people.
The rectification of these days is described as returning to Bereishis, the word on which the Tikunei Zohar is built, and binding oneself to the Ribono shel Olam.

The Rav reads the Gemara's statement that the Mikdash is 'higher' than all lands not physically but as the top of the globe, the point where Hashem first touched creation and from which the whole world grew.

He connects Har, mountain, with herayon, conception, and hirhur, thought, with 'a mountain on top of a mountain', so that Rosh Hashanah is the conception of the year and Yom Kippur the thought that precedes even that.

He finds the same pattern of a forty-day formation in soul and time: the forty days of an embryo's formation, and the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, which set the destiny of the whole year.

Origins are elusive because they begin in thought; this is why Shmuel did not recognize David, why David and Shmuel first erred about the Mikdash's site, and why the Levi'im erred about Rosh Hashanah.

The Sanhedrin's authority depends on sitting in the place of the Mikdash because that place is the origin of Torah, and Torah is the blueprint of the world; so Yerushalayim, the center of the world, should appear in the middle of the Torah.
The ten pesukim of each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros correspond to the ten utterances of creation, so that saying them with the shofar is an act of recreating the world and oneself.

Because the souls of this generation are small and the temptations huge, a small act of restraint is a wonder in Heaven, like the king who is more delighted by a parrot that talks than by a sage who speaks wisdom.
Saying 'if only' is itself the failure of emunah: the businessman's loss was trivial, but blaming his wife denies that Hashem arranged the delay.
David's refusal to take revenge on Shimi made Purim possible through Mordechai and Esther, and since Amalek equals 'safek', doubt, his emunah is what made him the fourth leg of the Divine throne.
The flood of new inventions that tempt people is the Satan's emergency strength before his end, like a candle that flares up just before it goes out.
The Satan concentrates on whoever carries the fate of Klal Yisroel, as with the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur, and so he concentrates on the last generation.
Esav's kiss is the model for modern exile: when the nations can no longer harm Jews with hatred, they harm them with friendliness and the pull of their culture.
The Rav reads the Ramban's forty lashes together with the Gemara's thirty-nine: of the forty days of formation, the first point, the G-dly soul, never sinned, so it is not punished.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur form the year like the forty days of a child, and Yom Kippur corresponds to the untouched point of G-dliness, which is why one does not eat on it.
The Rav notes that 'rotzeh ani' equals Yom Kippur in gematria: the point that says 'I want to serve Hashem' is the point revealed on that day.

Since Hashem blew the soul into Adam on Rosh Hashanah and renews creation each year, on Rosh Hashanah a Jew blows the shofar with great force from within, giving his soul back with teshuvah, which is why the one blowing turns red.
A person cannot understand Hashem not because he is not smart enough; even a billion times more intelligence or a million senses would not help, just as eyes cannot hear a niggun.

The Rav reads the halacha that wicks unfit for Shabbos may be used for Chanukah as a statement about souls: Jews too distant for the light of Shabbos to touch can still be kindled by the light of Chanukah.

Chanukah is the one exception to the rule that the Shechinah never descends below ten tefachim; its light is placed below ten tefachim, in the public domain and on the left side, because it goes down into the domain of the Sitra Achra to reach the souls there.
Unlike every other Yom Tov, which falls at a full or growing moon, Chanukah falls at the end of the month in the longest nights, so that every Jew, whatever his level, can find his place in it.

Both Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben David came through people whose greatness was hidden and misjudged: Yosef seen as a tyrant, Tamar taken for a zonah, Yehuda rejected by his brothers; this concealment is itself the hidden light of Moshiach.
A spark of Moshiach ben Yosef was hidden in Shechem, the way a person hides a diamond in a garbage can so no one will steal it, and Dina had to draw it out to join it with her own spark.
Spelled out with the full names of its letters, the name Dina has the gematria of Moshiach ben Yosef, showing that her purpose was set from her birth.
