A creature's true place is shown by where it runs when chased; so too a Jew's true belonging is revealed when, in danger, he runs to the Ribono shel Olam.
Honoring a tzaddik's yahrtzeit does not override the need to say Tachanun when the Jewish people need a yeshuah.
Seeing miracles is no reason to stop asking for mercy.

The Rav reads 'Bereishis' as 'bara shis', created the sixth, pointing to the sixth middah of Yosef HaTzaddik, the kedushas habris, at the very start of the Torah, just as milah was the first mitzvah given to a Jew.
Because the bris is the sixth middah, it is Friday, the preparation for Shabbos; so the bachurim who complain that Shabbos is boring lack the kedushas habris that brings a bright Shabbos.
A fine learner may still not merit the true Torah; certainty that one's Torah is true and not distorted comes only through kedushah.
Yesod comes before malchus: the one who guards the bris is called tzaddik like Yosef, and from that he merits kingship, so that people follow what he says, just as Friday leads into Shabbos HaMalkah.
An animal does not harm a person who keeps his tzelem Elokim; it attacks only when it takes him for an animal, and blemishing the bris is what loses the tzelem Elokim.

Following the Pri Tzaddik: the shekalim for the offerings Michael brings above come from the words of Jews saying Parshas Shekalim, as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's words turned into gold; so a Jew's speech must be holy.
The difference between an olah and a shelamim is eating: since only a Jew can make eating itself an act for Heaven, only a Jew can bring an offering that its owner eats.
The Midrash's 'north' and 'south' are the places of slaughter: the nations, who bring olos slaughtered in the north, will be uprooted, and Klal Yisrael, who bring shelamim, will come.

Steam, water and ice show how one essence can be invisible and spiritual at the top and solid and tangible at the bottom while remaining the very same thing; so the differences between souls do not contradict their being one part of G-d.
The temperature of the mashal maps onto avodah: there are places where Nishmas is said cold like a snowball and places where it is a hot glass of coffee that wakes one up.

A soul's root in Adam HaRishon sets its strength but not its direction: a head soul that does not choose Torah becomes a professor or philosopher, and a heart soul that is not a tzaddik writes non-Jewish poetry.
Adam is read as the initials of Adam, David, Moshiach, so the last generation before Moshiach is the heel of that one great soul.
The Rav explains that the Gemara records a date for Moshiach that passed because every date the tzaddikim gave was truly an 'achishenah' time; Moshiach was ready, and only sin held him back.
The Ba'al HaTanya read 'ha'elef' as heh-elef, since heh and ha are interchangeable, and so found 5775 in the pasuk of the vavim.

The silver of the Yidden beyond 600,000 went to the vavim, whose heads protrude outside the Mishkan's curtains; so they are the Yidden outside the camp, and the vav is missing from the alphabetical kapitlach.
The Yidden outside the camp are connected to the last letters of the Torah that came with the forgetting at Moshe's passing, and Moshe's forgetting the vavim belongs to the same idea.
Hashem's anger at Amalek for attacking Bnei Dan, who were outside the camp, still burns thousands of years later, showing He does not give up on such Yidden.
The closing pei, 'Podeh Hashem nefesh avadav', is the redemption of the missing vav: the Yidden of the end of the Torah return with Moshiach.
Unlike other chachamim, whose dates were for their own days, the Ba'al HaTanya gave a sign close to 200 years after him, for our generation at the end of the Torah.
The Rav treats the whole of Parshas Ki Seitzei, not only isolated mitzvos in it, as one parsha of tikkunei neshamos that fits the season of Elul.
A simple lechaim at a tzaddik's hilulah is, in his words, a tikkun for the tzaddik's soul.
Because each Shabbos is drawn from the parsha of its week, the character of the parsha becomes the character of the Shabbos.

The Rav explains the halachah that a gentile may bring only an olah, which is wholly burned, by the root of his animal soul in the three impure klipos, which cannot be used for good, while a Jew's can be raised up and so he may eat holy meat.
Thanking Hashem in one's mind in the middle of eating for the pleasure of the taste is itself a brachah.

The Rav explains chochmah as the two words 'koach mah', a raw potential, the first flash of an idea, and binah from 'binyan', building that flash into a whole structure, like a brick from which one builds a house.
Avraham, who loved and took in guests, embodies chesed, while Yitzchak, who served Hashem with fear and kept to himself, embodies gevurah, and these are the first two brachos of Shemoneh Esrei.
No single color is beautiful by itself; beauty comes from a blend, and so tiferes, a harmony of chesed and gevurah, is the trait of Yaakov, who combines Avraham and Yitzchak.
The teshuvah movement of today is like the drizzle that begins every heavy rain: before Moshiach a little teshuvah comes down, and with Moshiach a downpour.
The Rav sees the spread of chadarim, Bais Yaakov schools and yeshivos across America today as the planting of one man.
Reb Shraga Feivel's insistence on being called 'Mister' is presented as an expression of his truthfulness, not merely his humility.
The Rav sets the Gemara's warning against believing the world's praise against the Gemara's own rule that common opinion reflects reality.
Shemitah is Yerushalayim in time: the constant Shabbos that Yerushalayim holds in place spreads in the seventh year over the whole land.
A person may do melachah in Shemitah because the Shabbos of that year belongs to the ground, not to the person.
The laws that Yerushalayim was not divided among the tribes and may not be rented to pilgrims show that, like Shemitah produce, it belongs to no one.
The twelve weekday requests of Shemoneh Esrei correspond to the twelve working tribes, while on Shabbos, Yaakov's day, one asks only for spiritual needs.
Shemitah turns every Jew into a Kohen, who has no portion of land and whose portion is Hashem.
Because Shemitah is itself a tosefes, an extension of Yerushalayim, the Torah teaches the law of adding to Shemitah, and from it one sees that Shabbos too has a tosefes.
Onkelos's rendering of Yaakov's 'bow' as tefillah shows that the Jewish bow of tefillah is what overcomes Yishmael, the archer, and Kislev's mazal of the bow makes it the time for it.
Just as an animal has a life-force beyond its body, Amalek has an inner force that cools Jews' emunah, and Parshas Zachor is aimed at that force, not at physical Amalekites.
Every person carries a small piece of Amalek within himself, his own yetzer hara, and the reading of Zachor weakens that inner piece.
Purim is a day to reconcile with Hashem in which the lowest Jew is precious to Him, because the Purim decree came on Jews who had sinned and Hashem nevertheless annulled it.
Holy things are normally kept covered, but the Megillah is spread open on Purim, because Purim's kedushah spreads over the whole world.
Hashem's name is absent from the Megillah not because Purim is lower but because its kedushah is higher than the name Havayah, so the name appears only covered, in initial and final letters.
The first commandment names the Exodus rather than creation because no one witnessed creation, while all of Israel saw the ten makkos, which displayed the same ten powers.
The makkos run backwards against the utterances: the plague of the firstborn, the 'reishis' of Egypt, corresponds to Bereishis, and darkness to 'let there be light'.
Bereishis has no 'vayomer' because it is the first beginning, before there was any speech; only after it could the other nine utterances be said.
A middah used without daas harms: a person who loves cookies and keeps taking more ends with a stomachache, because his chesed was not guided by his mind.
Because Avraham's chesed and Yitzchak's gevurah were each pure and unblended, Yishmael and Esav came from them, while Yaakov's blended tiferes produced only holy shevatim.
Netzach and hod are opposite strategies with one goal, to keep standing: hod, from hoda'ah, is yielding, like bowing at Modim or running from a danger one cannot beat.
The Rav reads the world's constant preoccupation with so small a people as itself a sign of the Jews' unique place.
He turns a worsening situation on its head: getting worse and worse means getting better and better.
The pesukim the children told Mordechai in his time of danger are, for the Rav, a present-day source of emunah against the nations' schemes.
Complaining that one's situation is bad shows self-love: such a person wants to step out from under Hashem's hand, which is running his affairs the way Hashem knows is best for him.
The letter opens with 'Lehaskil HaBinah' because the root of the chasadim is in Binah, and gevuros raised to Binah are sweetened at their root.
Pharaoh, after the plague of locusts, sensed something drawn from the fiftieth gate of Binah: he saw blood ahead of Klal Yisroel, but not that it would turn into the blood of milah.
Remorse over aveiros is 'by appointment only'; for a real rasha sadness can strike anytime, since he has no program and no appointments.
The higher a person rises, the more a small stain of sin becomes significant, like a stain on a coat that is unimportant for a delivery boy but intolerable before an audience with a king.
Making up the sukkah meal on Shemini Atzeres means, in the Chassidish explanation, that the sukkah escorts a Jew into the house.
Tefillah is not in competition with Torah: a little closeness to Hashem in davening changes the way one learns the entire day.
The Rav reads the Haggadah's use of the pesukim of the bikkurim declaration as a lesson that redemption comes through crying out, which is the call of the present time.
Being chosen for Eretz Yisrael when many are not is itself a cause of greater obligation, not only of joy.
Habits brought from abroad, like spitting on the ground, take on a new seriousness in Eretz Yisrael, whose earth one should rather kiss.

The ten plagues, counted from the last, mirror the ten utterances of creation from the first: makkas bechoros against 'Bereishis', darkness against 'let there be light', locusts that hid the sky against the utterance of the firmament.
Because the whole of Nisan is yetzias Mitzrayim, the Haggadah's thought of starting the telling from Rosh Chodesh has a grain of truth.
Saying the plagues at the Seder breaks the klipah of heresy, brings downfall on the enemies of Israel, and draws emunah into the Jew.
The three dips of bread in salt allude to the Name Havayah three times, whose total of 78 is the gematria of lechem; with that strength a Jew learns, davens and fights the yetzer hara.
'Ha lachma anya' is literally true: the matzah is only an envelope, and the holy Names inside it are the very ones our forefathers ate in Egypt.
Just as no one would put on tefillin written carelessly, the matzah that serves as a Jew's os on chol hamoed should be baked with kedushah.

The bar mitzvah is a real chuppah: the boy is wed to the ruach he now receives, and the Zohar's story shows that the shidduch Rabbi Yossi offered supplied the neshamah still missing, making the chassanah complete.

The bar mitzvah boy who counts Sefirah unites both halves of the passuk: the bar mitzvah gives him 'ner mitzvah', and his Sefirah prepares him for 'Torah ohr'; 'seudah shel bar mitzvah' equals 'Torah ohr' in gematria.
A bar mitzvah boy is like the 'mincha chadashah' brought at the end of Sefirah: he presents himself to Hashem at thirteen as a new, pure gift, ready to receive the Torah.

Food, like a person, has a guf and a neshamah: matzah is flour and water, but its neshamah is emunah, and each Yom Tov's food carries that Yom Tov's gift into the one who eats it with the mitzvos connected to it.
Because whatever a person eats becomes part of his body, the Torah puts great emphasis on food; eating at the bar mitzvah seudah means ingesting ner mitzvah v'Torah ohr.

The Rav reads the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur as the formation of the year, parallel to the forty days in which the Gemara says one may still pray about a fetus; with the Ba'al HaTurim he reads a 'male' year as one of brachah.
The count of pesukim in each parshah, recorded by the Masorah, is itself part of the Torah and carries meaning that can be darshened.

The parshiyos read in the season of teshuvah are layered like its windows of judgment: forty pesukim in Nitzavim for the beinonim's forty days, thirty more for the tzaddikim, fifty-two through Haazinu, and 122 in all for those who have until Zos Chanukah.
The Torah gives two signs of 122: Ki Savo looks back at last year's unused 122 days as an accusing finger, while Nitzavim through Haazinu open the new 122 days.
Following the Chafetz Chaim, the Rav teaches that a disaster in a far place like the Mississippi, or a storm in New York, is a messenger of Hashem meant to awaken the Jews.
Bringing the Maharal, the Rav says that where there is no Beis HaMikdash, the place where Jews sit and learn halacha is the Beis HaMikdash.

The Jewish custom of buying new clothes and painting the house for Pesach, rather than during Sefirah, is part of the renewal of all creation in Nissan, and a Jew must join that renewal inwardly as well.
A promised blessing that does not arrive is like money put into a pocket with a hole: the blessing comes but falls out, because the soul lacks a whole vessel to hold it.
Matzah works like a vitamin: just as each vitamin gives the body a particular strength, matzah gives the soul emunah, the level of Avraham Avinu.
Even a child's prayer for something trivial, or a prayer that one's team should win, is real emunah, since the one praying turns to Hashem knowing He can grant it.
The Lubliner revealed his notebook not to display his powers, which his talmidim knew anyway, but to teach that each of the first days of Nissan governs a whole month.
Like hand matzos and machine matzos, there are hand-made tefillos and machine tefillos; a quick davening on an assembly line is the latter.
The Rav reads the world's frightening events as the shofar of Elul: in a time of great hester panim Hashem does not blow it openly but in another way, through what happens in the world.
He describes the Torah as having returned to Eretz Yisroel after it left with the churban; it was thought to have settled in America, but there it only made a stop.

According to the Rav one need not search the sefarim for hints about the coming year: the hints of Moshiach's coming can be seen in the newspaper, in what is happening in the world and in Eretz Yisroel.
He explains Rachel's jealousy of her sister as a kosher jealousy: one does not begrudge the other at all, and only wants to be like him too.
The Rav suggests that the custom of giving bar mitzvah gifts comes from Hashem's words to Dovid on his bar mitzvah, 'ask of Me': our giving to the boy awakens Hashem's giving to him.
He reads 'everything is in the hands of Heaven except fear of Heaven' as a guarantee: since yiras shamayim depends on the person, one who asks for it will surely receive it.
Haman thought Adar, the last month, meant the end of the Jewish people, but for Klal Yisrael time is a circle, and the last month leads them by the hand into Nisan, the first.

A bar mitzvah on the last day of Adar expresses this circle: the last day of the year connects the old year with the new and leads into Nisan, and so the boy is called to continue his forefathers' chain.
Even the most ordinary acts, like washing negel vasser or greeting a Jew, become many times holier when done in Eretz Yisrael.
A shared davening is built when each person contributes his own spark to the common flame.
Love for one's own chavurah takes precedence over the general love of every Jew, because those close by come first, as the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim taught.
The worsening situation of the Jews is itself read as a preparation for miracles, so the response is for each to do his part.
The Rav presents being confined in Yerushalayim as something Jews prayed for their whole lives.
If confinement must come, the Rav suggests, at least let it be in Yerushalayim.
He brings the example of a great chassid who was confined in Yerushalayim, showing that such confinement befitted even great people.
The Exodus on the first night was a gift that brought the Jews to the level of the Avos; the forty-nine days are the work of earning that same level by oneself.
Over nearly two thousand years of galus, each generation or era passes through one of the forty-nine desert journeys, until the redemption and the entry into Eretz Yisrael.
Going back to repeat the whole line of Ana B'koach after each week mirrors the seven journeys the Jews went back in the desert, turning forty-two into forty-nine.

The Omer of barley, animal food, is a sotah's offering testing the Jews' purity; reaching Shavuos with the wheat loaves, human food, shows they were found pure, and the milui of Hashem's Name beside the brachah equals adam.
The last day of the count, malchus shebemalchus, matches the last daf of Sotah, which speaks of ikvesa d'meshicha, the lowest level of galus right before the redemption.
Prices rising even when supply is plentiful defy the law of supply and demand, and the Rav reads this as the Baraisa's sign that wine will be dear though the vine gives its fruit.

The Rav explains the dearness of the Chanukah mitzvah through mesirus nefesh: just as milah was dear to Avraham Avinu because of its pain, what Klal Yisrael gave their lives for in the days of the Chashmona'im became dear to them.

Abolishing Rosh Chodesh would have meant the destruction of Klal Yisrael, since the Yamim Tovim depend on it; this is why Eretz Yisrael was never left without Jews, so the calendar could be set there.
The Greeks did not oppose Torah as wisdom; they opposed Torah as Hashem's heavenly Torah, accepted even where it is not understood, and therefore they targeted milah, which is its precondition.
Wisdom exists among the nations too, but having a portion in Hashem's Torah is only possible through milah.
The Rav defines emunah as believing even what one does not understand, and leitzanus as dismissing even what one does understand; this is how Pharaoh could shrug off plague after plague.
Although no joke of Pharaoh's appears in the Chumash, the Rav infers he was a joker from the fact that nothing else could have let him withstand the plagues.

Since Malachi was the last prophet, he spoke not only to his own generation but to all generations until Eliyahu, like someone instructing travelers before a long voyage with no word until they reach the shore of Moshiach.

The Rav reads Malachi's 'then those who fear Hashem spoke to one another' as a description of Jews in ikvesa diMeshicha gathering at a mussar shmuess or a Shabbos table with zemiros to strengthen emunah.
He explains Chorev, where the Torah was given, as dry and desolate land, teaching that even when times are dry one must remember Hashem's Torah.
Unlike a secular holiday that recalls a past event, a Jewish yom tov brings down again the very lights of the original event, so each Jew stands at Sinai every Shavuos.
Even one who does not hear the thunder of Sinai must believe, as the Kotzker taught, that believing is greater than seeing, and that his soul hears it.
Shavuos is a judgment more fearsome than Rosh Hashanah, for on it one's portion in Torah and in heartfelt davening is decided, not only bread and milk.
The all-night learning is like the wedding's music and flowers; the davening and the Ten Commandments are the ring and the chuppah, without which nothing has happened.
Listening to krias haTorah is Torah lishmah precisely because one learns nothing new from it, and on Shavuos it includes all 613 mitzvos within the Ten Commandments.
Doubts in emunah are fed by impurity in what one sees: the Rav links the pritzus of the street and failings in kedushah directly to thoughts of doubt and heresy.
In Mitzrayim the fiftieth gate would have been final, but today the power of Torah lets Jews fall even into the fiftieth gate and still hold on.

The Rav compares doubts in emunah to OCD: a person knows the door is locked or his hands are clean and checks anyway; so too a Jew knows the truth, and the doubt is only a 'bug' that must not be indulged.
The Satan fights so hard now precisely because he knows Moshiach is near and his own end is coming, like a man fighting for his life with his last strength.

The words of waiting in davening and in the Shabbos kedushah were instituted for ehrliche Yidden who wait; saying them without waiting would be lying to Hashem, which even an am ha'aretz does not do on Shabbos.
Only one who hoped for Moshiach will be able to say 'hinei Elokeinu zeh kivinu lo' when he comes; one who did not hope will not be able to say it.

The fact that printers now issue a separate Sefer Nechemia, against the Gemara, is itself hashgachah: for a generation that has lost confidence, Nechemia's 'remember me for good' becomes the right approach.
Balak's opposition to Klal Yisrael was a struggle to keep the spark of Malchus Beis David captive inside himself, so it should never come out.
Balak himself is the orla over the kedushah of Moshiach, and Pinchas, read right after him, is the mohel: killing Zimri was a milah that removed the klipah from Klal Yisrael.
The Three Weeks are not inherently sad days but the holiest days of Moshiach, covered by an orla of mourning that will be removed and turned into blessing.
Since Hashem acts like a person's shadow, a Jew's mitzvah of milah is as if he were telling Hashem to perform the milah of the whole world.

Mesiras nefesh is not reserved for giving up one's life: since life is simply the greatest thing a person wants, every overcoming of one's own will for Hashem's will is the same act on a smaller scale.
Dovid Hamelech, introducing yiras Hashem, defines it by guarding the tongue and pursuing peace; so anything that contradicts those pesukim, however pious it looks, is not yiras Hashem.
The berachah on blossoming trees, made because they were created for people's enjoyment, applies to all of creation: its beauty is a gift for which one must return thanks to Hashem.
The interruption of 'Mah rabu' in the middle of Barchi Nafshi shows Dovid Hamelech so overwhelmed by creation's beauty that he could not wait until the end to praise Hashem.
Reading 'tzafra ve-ramsha' as birds singing by day and insects by night, the Rav notes that a Jew can sing to Hashem both by day and by night.
Looking out at creation can itself be looking into the siddur, since the pesukim one says are describing exactly what one sees.
Hashem could have fueled people with something like gasoline; that He gave foods that are tasty and beautiful is a reason to make each berachah with kavanah.
